BAFL: Brakes Are For Losers:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

I have been a car fanatic for many years. In fact, I follow the Formula 1 calendar every single year. Not in person but via Pay TV. In any case, I heard about a racing arcade game where you hardly ever use the brakes, and I thought to myself, what the BAFL is this about?! And then, the light . . . shining above my head with a big inscription – Brakes Are For Losers!
BAFL is retro arcade racing / local multiplayer game where you take on seven other competitive and crazy racers, with a view to winning the mighty BAFL championship.
As you start the game, you will appear in a roundabout in control of a rather spunky, funky car. From here, you choose which direction you want to take. If you go north, you’ll see the credits of all those who were involved in creating the game. Going south, you’ll see a parking spot where you’ll be able to swap cars. Make you way east, and you’ll find challenge modes where you’ll be able to participate in one of several time races. Here, you’ll have to go around a track for certain number of laps as fast as you can. Hopefully you‘ll become the fastest driver on the leader board.  Choose to go west and you’ll be able to select either the championship, which involves ten races, or a quick race on your favourite track.  Otherwise you can create your own free brakes championship.
The gameplay is a top down eighties/nineties arcade style of game. Depending the mode of play, you have to do a certain number of laps or you have to go around the track until the time runs out. It’s super fun and fast either way! The main feature of the game is the fact that you don’t have brakes and you have to navigate tracks without touching any edges or any other competitors. If you do, your car will be damaged and you’ll stop for a few second in the middle of the track for repairs, which will allow the other cars to overtake you. Don’t worry, it will happen to both you and your opponents several times during the course of the races. One way to help you keep rolling through the laps is to stop at the pit when your car is about eighty percent damaged. Repair it all and keep going around until the end of the race. And yes, pit stops will be frequent and must be a part of your strategy. But that’s not all! You have power-ups popping up left, right and centre to make your race as difficult as possible. Icons such as missiles, an old man with a stick (slow motion), sunglasses (blindness) and others will appear randomly on the circuit. All you have to do (if you can, of course) is to hover over these icons to activate them. Most of them will slow down or stop your opponents for a few seconds. Also, some of the tracks are surrounded by water, which will spill onto the asphalt. A pirate ship might fire cannonballs on the track, or maybe you’ll race on the moon with meteorites hitting your car (which will be rather unfortunate).  And with all of that, you’ll still have no brakes! Rather fun, don’t you think?
Depending on you position at the end of each race in the championship, you will earn coins that give  you the ability to upgrade one of six components of the car: speed, armour, handling, brakes, repairing and adhesion.
The graphics are retro and fun. The soundtrack is ok and the controls are pretty responsive, either using a gamepad or keyboard. I would have loved to have seen a track editor, as ten tracks is not a lot. However, there are three types of difficulty which can give you plenty of re-playability.  It is also really fun racing with friends on a local network.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great retro graphics
-	Fast and fun
-	Quick race, championship and time attack modes
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards as yet
-	Need a race editor in my opinion
Have your eye firmly focused on the top spot. What the BAFL?! Well, Brakes Are For Losers!
7/10

Cook, Serve, Delicious I got off a Humble Bundle a long while back, and it was the best dollar I have ever spent. This game is just one of those games where you never feel pressured to succeed, unless you are trying to pressure yourself to, because their seems to be no real consequences for your actions. Failure just restricts your progress, but at the same time, you don't really benifit much from perfecting every customers order either besides earning an extra $250 and getting additional restaurant buzz, and that makes this the perfect game to just chill out to when playing it.
The thing about Cook, Serve, Delicious! is it has no definitive difficulty spike, the game is only as hard as you make it. Even on Extreme Difficulty, if you just serve Salad and Fish all the time, then you can breeze through it. The difficult is more so based on what foods you choose to cook and upgrades you choose to purchase, and I like that alot. It give the player more freedom through their actions and give them a better overall playing experience.
One thing I will fault Cook, Serve, Delicious! for however is the 20 Days Of Service requirement for getting your next star rating. This really is just here to drag on the game even further than it should be (even though its a simulator game) while also restricting player progress. Cut that number down to 14 days and I'd be more content with it. Besides that however, Cook, Serve, Delicious! doesn't have many flaws besides its lack of variety in menu options, which is something I hope the new game which is coming out soon will admend, but also makes up for it through the upgrading process of menu items.
Overall, Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a rather fun and addicting game in short bursts. Again, there isn't really much to say regarding the gameplay of Cook, Serve, Delicious! since it's rather simple and self-explanation, and by that I mean make food for customer, don't make customer mad, but you quickly realize that alot of the food options in Cook, Serve, Delicious! are kinda similar to one another. I definitely say it's worth the full $10 is costs, due to the mix of cooking challenges, betting options and text messages that you get being rather quirky, fun, challenging and overall enjoyable since it spices up the gameplay a bit and really shows the amount of love and care Vertigo Gaming put into their game. I can't wait for the sequel!

This game needs a lot of work and they're working on the wrong stuff.
1:  There are 2 item slots but even after buying new items in the shop, players can still only select 1 item to take along.  Challenging, sure.  Lame too.  Counter-intuitive.  Players choose between being effective in combat and being effective at repairs.  On the item selection screen it actually shows 2 slots with only 1 slot available for interaction, which implies that this feature simply isn't implemented yet.
2:  There's a massive, huge, horrible game bug where sometimes holes and even enemies appear for Player A (the holes fill the ship with water that can drown all the players and the enemies attack all the players) but no player but Player A can see the hole or the enemies.  This is especially awful when Player A is the helmsman or the gunner, especially if they've chosen to bring along say a firearm instead of a wrench so there's no point getting off their station, and isn't even looking for holes in the ship.
3:  The mechanic where more enemies spawn the faster the ship moves is stupid.  It's stupid.  The whole idea is idiotic.  The enemies should be there to begin with and if you're moving too fast and attract the attention of more of them than you can handle at a time, that's one thing, but making them actually appear out of nowhere just because you're moving fast is stupid.  Having them spawn right on top of the ship, rather than out some distance where the gunner would have time to actually get off a shot at them before they start biting/stabbing/attaching-to the ship, is even stupider.  There isn't actually a manual or even a legitimate, official wiki for this game where the devs explain this - it's just hinted at in one of the silly "newspaper" headlines that appears whenever you die in-game and experimentation seems to prove it out.  The lack of a manual or dev-maintained wiki outlining game mechanics deserves its own mention.
4:  The game devs, as of 04-27-2017, have released a recent update that includes new cosmetic gear (hats/clothes) and addressing none of the above.

If you want to play this game I strongly suggest playing the browser version:
Reviewing this as someone who has played the browser version of the game.
Everything feels very sluggish. Player and zombie movement speeds need to be increased and either a significant increase to mouse sensitivity or a mouse sensitivity slider is sorely needed.
Overlaying the minimap with NPC avatars who are contacting you is a terrible idea. Having them pop up at the top of the screen, like in the browser version, was fine given their brief length.
There should be arrow indicators at the edge of the minimap pointing to items on the ground, like money and strongboxes, just like there is in the browser version.
The graphics feel too bright and clean compared to the browser version.
Grenades only throw forward so throwing them at hordes of zombies in pursuit of you, which is basically the only time you need grenades, is suicide. The grenade should go where your cursor is like in the browser version not only thrown at an arbitrary distance in front of you. Mouse cursor grenade precision is crucial to surviving heavy encounters.
The turret support UI element at the top of the screen is annoying, its blocking very valuable aiming space and I constantly click on it instead of shooting the zombies I'm trying to aim at, and should be moved to the lower right corner as it is in the browser version.
What happened to the alloy+money crafting system? Where are the XP/Alloy bonus rounds?
The only thing I like about this version is the added red dot sight and that is literally it.

I just finished my playthrough of the game, taking about six hours to do so. As other reviews stated, this is a visual novel.  If you want a nice, relaxing experience without quick time events or the need for quick reflexes, you'll enjoy the 'game'.
The voice acting is as good as any AAA title.  Some of the scottish slang confused me, so just try to get the gist of what they say and you'll still be able to follow along, be sure to have subtitles turned on.  The artwork is excellent, and a joy to look at.  With many scenes, I would take the time to admire the detail, which is likely why it took me so long to finish the story.  Sound effects, audio cues, a lot of attention to detail was paid to this adaptation.
I would play the game in the evening, with the lights dimmed in my living room, using my TV as a display to a PC running SteamOS.  Thanks to the developers for porting this to linux / SteamOS for I would not have had as enjoyable experience sitting so close to my main PC in my computer room.
I am looking forward to the next title the developers release.  I honestly, had never heard of the original book until playing this title, and may look into reading it now.  The main character also appears in other books the author had written.

I bought this game on recommendation from a friend, and a vague memory of playing it before. Was it in flash-game format once upon a time? The music is glorious retro, and the loading screen will send you back to the days of the Spectrum ZX. Graphics are inevitably classic retro, the screenshots say it all.
The gameplay, due to controls and level design, is very unpleasant for me. The concept is decent, with an interesting mechanic where you flip your own gravity to overcome obstacles, but the puzzle-platformer I was expecting is nowhere to be seen. It's an arcade-platformer through and through and if that's not what you're after then it's not the game for you. The left/right controls have a little acceleration, so movement where you need precision is sloppy and largely guesswork. If you play long enough you'll probably get it, but that's not the point - the controls should work for you, you shouldn't need to work around the controls.
Level design is at times cruel and unfair, with a forced-speedrun section courtesy of a rising floor, and various traps that are only found through trial and error. For example, want to know what's in the screen to the left? There's a bump, so you need to jump, but you can't do that so you have to invert gravity, and there's no ceiling. Hope there aren't spikes in any of the 3-4 screens you have to fall through. Of course there are spikes. There are spikes in so many places (as there should be!) that it really makes the game mechanics work against you. There are the usual timing sections, but there certainly isn't a lot of leeway. You'll be dying a lot. And there's a slight delay on the respawn. Just long enough to wind you up as you retry a section (particularly the forced speedrun) over and over again.
Lastly, the game mocks you. All the screens are individually named, and the developer has taken the time to use them to mock you. Not the endearing mockery as found in Portal, no, this will feel like genuine malice that in combination with the levels they refer to will give a good idea of the contempt the developer has for the player.
I truly regret paying what little money I did for this game, as it has brought nothing but frustration. Incidentally if you want a game that hates you (and not in a good way, like Darkest Dungeon), this game is for you. No, my money would've been better spent donated to the developers of the (free) SHIFT.

The 39 Steps is an enjoyable adaptation of a work I have no experience with, although apparently it has been a novel, play, and film and well. It's well adapted here as a visual novel, and full of beautiful art. The story is presented one sentence at a time and the game does not burden you with walls of text or too much pointless clicking around scenes. It's extremely linear, and adding in adventure game elements would only weaken the presentation, just take it as a well illustrated novella rather than a game. When certain characters and events have a backstory, the game brings it up as no more than 2-5 bullet points. For a text-based game, it certainly does not bog itself down with text.
The beginning is very slow, perhaps the first 5 chapters. Partially because the protagonist is boring, partially because the story needs to be set up. You really need to get past this to decide if you like it or not. Once I was over the hump, I was hooked until I finished the story.

This interesting game that started out as intriguing and engaging quickly turned into an exercise of frustration and anger. Dexterity challenges and puzzles became mean spirited and unenjoyably difficult. I found myself cursing the game on many occasion &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥this game!" I only finished it because I knew that my friend had and that it is mercifully short. Overall I'm pretty disappointed in the overall experience of this game and wouldn't recommend it.
The Good:
Open world to explore. I really dug this aspect of the game. Even though it is a fairly small world it makes the whole game feel more cohesive.
Some really great mechanics and level design.
Fun challenges
The Bad:
Shoddy controls. Half the time I died was because the character wouldn't stop when I wanted or go as far as I needed it to when commanded.
Lame graphics. The 4 bit art style itself was not offensive to me. I thought it kinda charming. It was the "enemies", obstacles, and "glitchy" elements of the game that just were just plain lame or ugly.
The music, which was pretty catchy at first, overtime became annoying due to how much it repeats as you replay a section over and over again.
The Ugly:
Level design that just feels mean. I seriously felt like the designers were laughing at me as I struggled to overcome some of the ridiculous sections of the game. The frequency of some of the check points are an indicator of just how difficult some parts of the game are.

I've been waiting for this game for more than a year, alas - all for $ 40.00 wasted
Now I've been waiting for this game with great anticipation for more than a year. But all along, in the back of my head, the tiny voice of rationality kept telling me that there really is nothing else to add to the Hearts of Iron II series.
Regardless, I pre-purchased the steam version a week before the release. I left work earlier and even skipped college just to get the first glimpse of this grand strategy - instead I got a stinking pile of $hit.
Loading times, with my Quadcore 3Ghz was insanely long.
Gameplay:
Unplayable. Instead of the fast way to link or separate divisions by the easy use of a "SHIFT" button, we get a whole other display of the selected army on the upper left side of the screen. And for each division, we have a cute button all the way at the end that says "SELECT". Which means that we cant highlight divisions anymore, we have to "SELECT" each one of them. My favorite scenarion of all time was, of course, Gotterdamerung 44, playing as Germany. Now, with the HOI II series, it took me around 20 minutes at most to set up the right leadership, divison production, etc. With this game, it took me an hour, and not because I didn't know how to manage the game, but because of the tedious ways in which the game works. The leader icons are miniscule, you can barely see other icons indiciation either the ESP, or even ORGANISATION level. I mean seeing your organisation level is one of the most important things
Bugs:
Quite often, you aren't able to select leaders for your armies, instead you might end up leading a leaderless army. Second, why in the world would we need a whole separate window for the Army leaders? what was wrong with the easy accessible leader-board on the left side of the screen? and what's with all down-grading generals? We can actually downgrade 5 star generals to 2 star generals? why is that an option? that makes promoting leaders just a silly joke. Promotion should involve long-term investment into the leader if you want him to lead either a 6 or 12 divison army. There might be more bugs in the game, I only played it for around 4 hours
Production and Technology:
The tech tree is $hit, plain and simple. Upgrading your infantry division with a couple dozen tiny upgrades, like better river crossing, better land fortification assaults, better mortar fire, etc over the YEARS is tedius and unmemorable. We all know that feeling when we get "infantry divison 1941 developed" or "Medium tank 1941" developed, instead of a max of 5 techs that we used to develop, we can now develop up to 20 mini techs. Do we really need "mountain equipment", "desert equipment", "jungle equipment" etc? or can we just get a nice 1941 division and add just ONE brigade to characterize the division's mission? And what's with these damn brigades comprising divisons? We all know that a panzer divison doesn't just consist of tanks, but of hundreds of trucks and thousands of personel and infantry. So why, would we need to customize our divisions by adding either extra artillery brigades, motorized brigades, etc? That just gives us more options which are confusing and time consuming.
And I guess the ships are upgradable now. May I ask why? Dont we all remember playing as Japan and bracing for that "Carrier 1941" tech to deveop in order to start catching up with the US while we prepare for Pearl Harbor?
The MAP:
12000 provinces...really? why do we need thousands of provinces in South America? or Africa? or endless Siberia? Is anyone actually going to wage war there? wouldn't it be better if they just added more provinces in all the theaters of WW II? Since that what the game is about? Some people complained about the scrolling speed, I personally cannot complain because my PC can take this game easily. However, I thought the 3d water effects were pretty useless. And why don't we see armies sort of exchanging fire with one another like in HOI II?
The good:
Finally, they have introduced this following feature - casualty list. After each battle, you will get the amount of casualties on both sides. And I gotta admit, its pretty effective, it makes you want to immidiately research tech on reducing attrition, improving medical equipment etc. And so far, that feature is the ONLY one I enjoyed having while playing the game. If they could put that in HOI II, I would play it even more.
There are definitley more things to say about this game. And I would be glad if more people tried enjoying this game. I tried desperate to enjoy it. I didn't want to spoil it for those who already bought it, but for those who are undecided, just think a little more before buying the game.

An early 20th century adventure novel by Scottish author John Buchan. The first of five novels it follows protagonist and narrator
,  an upper class toff, retired officer from her majesty's armed forces and expatriate of South Africa.
Not so much a game but an interactive book with some lovely artwork, you enter the story bored and lonely in London, a man waiting for life to begin again. The basic controls are introduced as you are encouraged to explore each scene. The amount of detail available, through the likes of newspapers and maps, had me entertained for sometime and helps to remind you of the social, economical and political differences between now and what most consider a short time ago,
After the first chapter I began the "game" again with my partner and found the experience even more rewarding. We continued on a few more chapters and went to bed. The funny thing is the next day I found myself thinking about Hannay and his predicament and we couldn't resist returning that evening to see what was next. It is quickly becoming part of our schedule, our bedtime story and a favorite in our hearts.
Recommended for entertainment, not really a game but great for those who enjoy the lost arts of reading and imagination.

Considering that this game was high on my list to begin with I entered this game looking to get scared...boy was I rewarded! The studio behind this game knew EXACTLY what they were doing. The intimidating lighting, sound, and music added to the overall creepy and eerie feelings that I got whilst exploring the Asylum. The detail put into this game clearly makes it a work of art. Brilliantly textured interior scenes with well laid out and vegitated exterior scenes. Outlast makes the player actually FEEL as if they were taking part in the story. The characters were believable in the setting that they were in. The story was well planned out and didn't leave the player wondering 'why is this happening' or 'why did that happen' the game explains it all as you progress through, finding both story pieces for your article your character needs to write, but finding documents from the staff that once lived and worked in the asylum.
Overall Score: 9.95/10

Similar to the film Grave Encounters, the game is set in some kind of mental institution and you are armed with only a digital camera with a nightvision toggle that consumes the batteries. The story is told through notes you make when you have the camera out and through documents you find strewn in the levels.
It borrows from the Amnesia series in that you can't actually defend yourself against any of the unpleasant things you might encounter. Your only course of action is to run and to hide. However, whereas in Amnesia you might have had something chasing you and you knew it would kill you so you ran until you were safe with your heart pounding, in Outlast you are required to backtrack past the same enemy over and over. Far from being scary, it just becomes an annoyance.
There are many sections where you need to find a key (or other item) but when looking for it you will be seen by an enemy, then you'll run, hide in a closet, wait for him to leave, then go and search again, the same thing happens, repeat ad nausem or until he finally kills you. The scariness is gone and it just becomes frustrating. You know what you have to do; you might even know where the key is, but you have to get past something that will chase you and instantly kill you.
There is functionality to look over either shoulder using Q or E. It is not very useful though because it is disorienting. I suppose that was the intention: when running from something you take a quick glance over your shoulder and see it just behind you. The trouble is, in real life we are unaware of the movement of our head because our brain processes it for us. We don't see the world spin when we turn our head. When the game shows you everything spin it's not actually realistic, it's annoying and makes the "look behind" function not very usable.
The need to use the camera with its night vision to see does add some tension, which is helped along by your character breathing heavily etc. There is an outdoor part which is reminiscent of The Blair Witch Project in its atomosphere.
If you like horror games then this is worth a play. It has a great atmosphere and some nice visuals. There are a few jump scares and to start with it's quite immersive until the gameplay gets a bit samey and you know what the threats are. But by that time you'll probably see it through to the end to find out what happens. The game is about the right length in that respect.

Banished is a simple 'settlement-builder' game which, I imagine, will continue to take up many hours of my gaming-time. If you jump straight into the game without tutorials then you won't last long, but if you take the time to learn the basics then you will be set for building your cute little villages.

This is a great simulation game!
At a first glance, this game looks like it'll be tough as nails. It appears to demand perfection and punish you harshly for mistakes - but the very opposite is true!
Your very first items are all very simple to make, and help teach you the base mechanics and buttons of the game. While serving up corndogs and soda might not be the most exciting thing ever, it'll help to automate things like picking up orders and serving them.
The difficulty in this game is always determined by the player. If you miss a ton of orders, there will be less customers the next day, allowing you to learn at a slower pace. Additionally, there are many different recipes that vary in difficulty which you can put on your menu to make things easier on yourself.
The food all looks great, and is enormously satisfying to make. The sound effects of a burger being slapped together is a feeling like no other, and you will feel like a gaming champion when you reach a perfect day with difficult recipes on your menu.
There are a ton of small fun things that the game offers to enhance your gameplay. Some emails and characters will ask for you to carry certain recipes or combinations, gently nudging you to change up your status quo and use recipes that you normally avoid.
Becoming good at cooking in this game is satisfying, and it remains fun throughout the entire experience!
The only Con I can think of is that the checklist for upgrading your restaurant takes too long to complete. Not because the challenges are demanding, but because it always requires 20 days of gameplay before you can advance. Sometimes this means you need to play through 7-12 days just to advance your restaurant and unlock new upgrades.
Also, a few of the recipes can be tricky in their wording, which sometimes leads to frustration and an inability to complete the recipe. ( I'm looking at you, Stacked Enchilada's! )
All in all, this is a great game that I would recommend to anyone. Go for perfect scores on online leaderboards, or just do a few casual rounds trying to perfect that soup recipe you unlocked - it's all fair game!

'Banished' is the purest city-building game on the market. There is no external enemy to vanquish, no quests to fulfill, and no help with resources along the way (a la Tropico). Players must turn a group of banished settlers into a town using the resources at hand and proper balancing of roles.
As far as that goes, the game hits the mark. The first few years of any map are tense as the possibility of failure looms overhead. As your city grows, you are faced with new challenges or setbacks, either because of random events (infestations, tornadoes, etc.) or resource depletion (out of stone, out of available workers). If you're a fan of the genre, you should check this game out.
This isn't to say that there aren't deep-seated flaws with the game. Even on the highest difficulties, the game is quite easy after a certain point. Some forward thought eliminates most challenges. Build a trading post early and you can set aside some food and firewood in the early years of abundance to help out in lean seasons. Keeping up with firewood demands by building stone houses after your first few frees up leather from hunting lodges to be turned into coats, which then can be sold to traders, thus providing a passive source of income. Once you're over the hump of the reasonable learning curve, your town becomes unstoppable. You learn, for example, that building a church, hospital, herbalist, or tavern is pointless. Food variety and a graveyard will keep health and happiness both at 4.5, so save your resources.
Lastly, this is an indie game, built by one (very talented) person. While certainly impressive, it means that you can only expect so much. The endgame is nonexistent. At a certain point you're growing your town for the sake of growing your town. But if it's self-sufficient and pratically runs itself, why bother? If you're not aiming towards something, why upset the balance? Suggestion to the creator: *force* the town to grow (e.g. make happiness plummet if adults don't get their own house and/or don't give the player the choice to refuse nomads).
In sum, you have to expect your mileage with this game to be limited. Don't buy it on the promise of what is to come. It may not be reasonable to expect one person to be able to fix everything. It's not clear that modding can turn this game from good to exceptional--that's usually the opposite of what happens. As it stands, $20 seems a bit steep, but $10 seems perfect.

Get ready to set sail and dive deep into the depths of the ocean, to explore and plunder whatever treasures we may find. But be weary sailor, the ocean is unforgiving and many sea creatures lurk in the dark depths. How deep will you go? Will you survive? Come aboard if you’re with us, the Captain just gave his orders, “We Need, to Go Deeper.”
Thomas from
here with We Need to Go Deeper, an Early Access Title from Deli Interactive that came out February 8th of this year. You can pick it up for $9.99 on Steam from the link in the description.
You are a member of a submarine crew of four, traveling down into the depths of the ocean to explore, plunder, and find whatever you can to aid your journey. The deeper you descend, the more dangerous it becomes, but the rewards are even greater. See how far you and your crew can go before you all die due to the monsters of the ocean.
We Need to Go Deeper is a rogue-like co-op game with two to four players. Really, if you don’t have at least three, you are going to struggle in this game and I’ll get into the details of the gameplay so you can see why.
You start each game at the top of the ocean, diving down into the first generated biome. These biomes are randomly generated each time you start a trip, and contain caves to explore, fish and sea creatures to combat, and sometimes various obstacles and such too you’ll need to avoid.
The sub has four positions on it. A captain that steers and pilots the vessel, an engineer that controls the power distribution to the sub, a magazine area containing torpedoes to load, and the turret position to fire the torpedoes and defend the ship.
Technically, you can play with just two people, one captain and one loading/shooting. But this is not going to bode well for you over time as the time to load, jump back into the turret, and repeat takes quite a while. Plus, as you are attacked by various monsters in the sea, your hull takes damaged and needs to be repaired. Too much damage and your sub will start leaking, causing you to begin drowning. You can repair the holes by beating them with a wrench or other tool that does repairing that you have found along your journey.
For me, the best experience with playing with a full group of 3 other friends so we all took turns on stations and were able to make it REALLY deep into the game.
To wrap up gameplay, this is a rogue-like, so every time you die you keep any coins you collected. You can use these to purchase items from the catalog which include cosmetic character attire and tools, weapons, and items that you have found in previous journeys. Once purchased, you can start with these items instead of the basic wrench you begin with, so it can give you a better start and help you in the future runs. At the bottom of each biome is a boss you have to kill, then you can move into the next area/biome and start again. The deeper you go, the better the rewards, but the more dangerous and difficult the game becomes.
Visually, this game has a really fun art style. The animations are in a puppet-like form, and look hilarious. I personally loved the art style, and even though the game is in early access and has a lot of place holder things that may change, they are off to a fantastic start with a cohesive theme throughout the game.
The audio in this game is pretty good as well. There’s a neat effect when you are in the sub where sounds on the inside of the sub sound a bit different than when you are viewing the outside. The sound effects are fairly basic right now, but they may improve in the future as this is an early access title. Otherwise, there’s not too much to talk about here in a positive or negative light, the menu theme is great and I liked the soundtrack overall.
Replay ability is where this game absolutely shines. Provided you can find a crew of friends to play with regularly, this has all the tropes of a typical rogue-like. You can set off on as many voyages as you like, with loads of unlockable content in the current game to keep you coming back for more, trying to plunge deeper and deeper. I had so much fun playing with some friends on stream, we didn’t realize we were passing hours and staying up later than expected just enjoying the content. The game is in early-access now, and there’s a lot more content coming such as other submarine variants, bosses, items, outfits, and so much more.
Overall, this game is $9.99 and worth every penny, provided you have a crew to play with. If you don’t have friends to play with, I would stay away from this. The player base isn’t big enough yet to be able to play with random people reliably, so you really need to have some friends to hop on with you into a lobby. I can’t wait to see where this game goes though and I know I’ll continue to play it as long as my friends are willing to go deeper with me.

Tomb Raider: The Angel of Darkness is one of the most underrated video games I've ever played. For its time, it was running off of a truly next-gen engine, coupled with gorgeous graphics. It introduced many new additions to the series, such as  a large and expansive world filled with interactive environments, conversing with NPCs, furthering your quest through conversation, sidequests (unlike "secrets" in previous games), a playable second character (with a dark side of his own), and cleaver implementation of stealth, RPG, and horror-elements found in various levels throughout the game. The game's controls had a learning curve, like all Tomb Raider games do, and camera isn't always the best, but these issues seem minor when stacked up against the overall value of this package. Last but certainly not least, the story is at the forefront of the series. What initially begins as a neo-murder mystery (pertaining to the death of Lara's mentor), eventually turns into a massive conspiracy that Lara must unravel. AoD has the best story of the series, easily! And I am including the games of both reboots too. One unfortunate fact is that this game was the first part in a trilogy that was never completed due to many issues between the publisher and developer. It's sad really, especially since it concludes with a rather questionable cliffhanger ending. Buy this game, and give it a chance for yourself. It's so inexpensive, and I'm certain you will feel you got your money's worth from at least a single playthrough.

Everyone I've ever talked to who liked this game either liked every game with Lara Croft in it regardless of its flaws, or had an almost fetishistically creepy attraction to Kurtis, the new "character" in this game. Despite that trend, I tried, against my better judgment, to like this game. Tomb Raider: The Prophecy for the GameBoy Advance was a better use of my time than this. If you absolutely must play another 3D(ish) Tomb Raider game from Core Design, go play that instead. I've heard all about how The Angel of Darkness was rushed, how it had potential to be great, and believe me, I sympathize fully with Core Design, and I don't fault them for what happened. But we're reviewing the game, here, not the team behind it. This is the product we got: it's unfinished, and it's subpar, to put it politely. And no amount of Kurtis can carry this game for the rest of us.
What you have to understand, theoretical prospective buyer, is that this game is not just controversial, it nigh literally tore the franchise's fanbase in half (look no further than the proportion of thumbs up to thumbs down on this very review for evidence of that). While The Angel of Darkness was rushed out the door to coincide with the release of the movie that was coming out, it still spent three years in development, whereas the series had seen new releases yearly up until then. The game divided the fans between those with rational opinions ranging from "it sucks" to "it's the most average Tomb Raider has ever been," and those who developed a Stockholm Syndrome for it, because they invested their money and their time, spending hours finding convoluted ways to master its awful controls using engine quirks like making Lara roll in order to immediately put her into full running speed. Watch any gameplay video from someone who likes the game: they'll screw up, and it's clearly the game's faulty controls or awful physics at play, but they'll say they were just playing badly. These people will defend this game until the end of time, because they can't admit that theirs could have been better spent than playing this. If you've seen fans of Sonic '06 try to defend that game, you've seen what fans of this game are like.
The game is less immersive than its predecessors, and when the series standard was a game environment composed entirely out of blocks, that's saying a lot. Defenders of this game will praise the story and the ability to interact with characters, but the story doesn't go much of anywhere; it ends on a cliffhanger that assumed that The Angel of Darkness would be part one of a trilogy (spoiler alert: parts 2 and 3 never got released due to how poorly this game turned out), and the aforementioned characters only exist in the first quarter of the game, they are uninteresting, and they simply repeat themselves whenever you talk to them without getting a new plot device first. The game world's environment is also unconvincing due to the poor physics and bugs. When Lara falls in lava, she simply ragdolls on the surface like she would if she fell to her death on solid ground; she doesn't even catch fire. This game literally does LESS than the previous games to convince you that you're exploring a world rather than playing a game, and the previous games at least had the excuse of working with an inferior console. Defenders of this game will praise the graphics being better than the previous games, but if they can't produce a cohesive, believable world, I don't see the point; and yes, this game is VERY buggy, and even with the patch that comes with the Steam version, not everything is fixed. Sometimes huge chunks of the world will simply disappear. Lara will sometimes simply disappear. My sanity simply disappeared while playing this game.

This game is really a must have for any WWII enthusiast. Though it has an absolutely massive learning curve (there's some good tutorials on Youtube), once you learn how to play the game, it is incredibly fun. Perhaps its most alluring facet is that, though you are restrained by historical realities, you can take nearly any nation and turn the tide of the war, giving the game an almost "sandbox" feel in that you can do pretty much whatever you want (if you know how), such as taking the US to communism.
However, it must be noted that this is undeniably a complex, hardcore game, so do not be expecting flashy battles and lots of action. You must instead embrace the art of navagating menus and ordering divisions on a map. Again, it is a GRAND STRATEGY game, not an action arcade game so just know what you're getting into as it's absolutely fantastic if you're into this kind of game, but could be an effective torture device if you are not.

Apparently they also have a very authoritarian government that forbids anyone but the assigned wood cutter from making wood small enough it will fit in the fireplace.  There a a million logs on the stock pile, yet people freeze to death in their homes.
If you have had some foresight you have also probably built a few small strips of land and started farming, if you could spare the labour and got it harvested before winter, you will be just in time to start the struggle again except without the starting resources…  and because you cant farm in winter this means you have to fish for survival were upon everyone starves to death!
This game should have been called Famished, not Banished.  9 times out of 10 the poor people with their crazy sense of priorities starve to death because they are preoccupied with an earlier task, say clearing resources (trees, rocks and iron) which really was a back burner project compared to the newly ordered building of shelter, food or fire wood…  Which kills them.
On the odd time the people don't eat their own children before starving to death it was largley due to the close and easy access to a suitable location to build as many fisheries as possible…
The maps are quite restrictive in space, you either choose hills or valleys and so have the obstacle of small rivers or mountains to build bridges over or tunnel through…
Glad I got it in the sale.

Heroes in the Sky,
Is an old(er), arcade flying game with an MMO community geared towards the asian market. That's something that can be felt throughout the enitire game.
Translations might be a bit off, buttons might be placed in at a weird position and the overall feeling is not that of the regular Steam game.
Does that mean Heroes in the Sky is a lame game? No, not at all. The thing is that you should know what you get before you even start playing.
You get an easy to master flying game that presents the user with mission that beome harder and harder to complete throughout your tour of duty. Most of the later missions should only be completed in a group (Co-Op), because they got split objectives scattered all across the map.
The graphics are good enough for a game of this age and everything runs smooth.
A big no go for me is the pay to win style that gets across on the later missions. At some point you're not able to fly anymore because you spent all your energy and the only way to refill that energy is through buying some items or by waiting 24 real hours. And that's just bad.
But, on the other hand, that's what Heroes in the Sky is all about, like with any MMO; trying to get your money.
Until you hit that "we want your money" part; you'll be having lots of fun with the many different planes, weapons and missions. So, if you like a nice arcade flying action game with Co-Op/ PvE and PvP; Heroes in the sky might deliver you some good old skool fun.

VVVVVV is a platformer game revolving around the mechanic of changing your own gravity. The mechanic works great and you need to get through different areas that all use this mechanic in a different way. It is hard at some parts, but it doesn't get extremely irritating because of the frequent checkpoints. The game has collectables called trinkets that provide an extra challenge, both in the puzzle as in the hand-eye coordination part of the game. This includes the pretty much legendary 'Doing Things The Hard Way/Veni Vidi Vici' trinket, and seriously, it really is very challenging. They are optional. The story is nice, but in my opinion it doesn't have a proper ending which is a bit of a shame. I really love the world of this game and when I first played it, it felt like a great adventure. The music is nice as well.
Pros:
Mechanics
Challenging
Trinkets
Exploring of the map
Art style and music
Cons:
A bit short (but it has player levels so it doesn't matter that much)
Story could've been better with a better ending
Character slides a bit, can be frustating
The pros greatly outweigh the cons, especially because it's so cheap. Get it if you're a fan of platformers, if you're into well-crafted indies in general or if you like Terry Cavanagh's other stuff (which all is fantastic btw, and a lot of it is free, so check it out if you haven't!).

The 39 Steps, based on novel of the same name in 1915, is simply a digital adaption of the written form.  This is not a game.  There are several interactive elements (e.g. using mouse to make specific gestures, looking for hotspots within rooms) but those elements are just to provide some layer of interactivity.
The real schtick here is the superb voice acting, hand-drawn backgrounds/props, sound effects, and music.  In the traditional sense, this would be classified as an adventure game.  But there are no personal/story choices to be made as there is only one path, and that path is the novel.
Alfred Hitchcock created a movie, which I have not seen, based on the novel, and other similarly themed movies like North by Northwest, which I have seen and do like.  If you like spy/deception stories like these movies, there is no reason why you wouldn't like this digital novel.
I would love to see more adaptations like this; simple and easy experience to relax without dealing with the craziness of modern gaming.  It takes audio books to entirely new level. Also imagine doing this format with branching storylines.
It's a well made game for what it is, just really didn't grab my attention though.

This is NOT a game, but an experiment to digitally adapt a classical book. It is a new form of entertainment.
I bought it out of curiosity when it was on sale. I haven't read the book myself in real life, but I know someone who has and she has practically told me every explicit detail of the book itself. This digital adaption remains true to the original work, while the movies are notorious for taking liberties in every kind of direction.
Each backdrop is a hand painted background. This makes me wonder how long this actual production took to make? Also when you see the list of people's names in the credits at the end, your jaw will drop with the sheer army of people needed in creating it. This therefore makes me question, especially in this day and age, if this style of entertainment and the amount of money which is needed to create and publish it, will honestly be wasted when trying to sell it to the gaming community at large?
The interaction which is needed to propel the story forward is negligible and while the story has it's moments of suspense here and there, there are still large blocks of moments where nothing much is really happening. The digital adaption will largely play out as an audio book decorated with backdrops, however there are also significant parts which require you, yourself to read or click to skip it entirely. The option to have it all acted out for you is simply not there, which since it most of the time plays out like a movie, I was disappointed that it did not do this all the time.
Most gamers today are conditioned to want constant visual stimuli at high octane speeds, to be entertained every millisecond. This type of production does not do that. Having said that, I still enjoyed it myself as something different. Though they have given birth to a new form of entertainment, this concept while it is still in it's infancy stages it does have a lot of room to grow and mature and it will be interesting to see how this concept flourishes. Might be a worth a look if your into classical literature. Definitely a wait for a sale.
On a sidenote apparently 1914 welsh/cornwall/English was as jibberish as Klingon. Have a google translator on standby...
Simple video narrative with some click and point to keep you somewhat involved. It was a nice story to experience.

This is actually a really rather excellent little experience. It's everything you might hope it would be, from the limited description as an "interactive book". It's an atmospheric, detailed, and ultimately engaging way to enjoy a classic novel. I'm still early on in the story, but I'm already sold. It really is rather excellent.
The developers have done a great job, and you'll really enjoy devling into 1914 London. Quite frankly I hope they do some more books in the future.
It's true that you don't actually "do" all that much, but you honestly don't notice. The way you engage with the game world to reveal the story feels pretty organic. It's a bit like GONE HOME, but more honest and enjoyable.
One tip: You can pretty the left mouse button to progress if the "rotate the mouse" doesn't work for you (as it didn't work for me).

The 39 Steps is an animated, illustrated espionage-novel with sounds, music and linear narration - and without any real choices for the "player" during the whole story. So don't expect a full pc game, but instead anticipate a classic digital novel adaption, which totally knows how to entertain the audience.
You'll find yourself in an authentic England of 1914 and you'll be able to enjoy wonderfully painted illustrations.
All actions one is able to do are: examining various objects, clicking at things, or moving the cursor from time to time into specified directions to simulate actions, like for example running away, shaving, building explosive devices, opening doors, etc. And it works - and raises the level of immersion during the narration.
It looks great, the atmosphere feels great and the narration has a fluent feeling to it. Plus it's easy to get the 100%-achievements just along the way.
Altogether its an exciting, enthralling Spy Fiction Story with a lot of moments of suspense! Couldn't have asked for more.
I recommend it for relaxed autumn evenings, when reading is just the perfect thing to do.

This game is fun and engaging. You press buttons according to what food gets ordered.. all over the keyboard. You'll have buttons for each little ingredient and spice, requiring you to act quick to prepare foods. Each day or 'round' you'll have access to a main interface from which you'll check your emails, change up your daily menu and more. The emails add some humor and interest, making you want to continue. In short, the precise button-mash gameplay is great; it requires planning and strategy along with quick reflexes.
If you've been limited to action or FPS titles, it may be easy to see this one as a "typing game". Your input UI will be lined with letters, but you'll still have to read the recipe and press accordingly, so in no way will it feel scripted. To complicate things, your foods are upgradable, adding in new recipes that customers will love to change things about. The game is fast paced and gets challenging, even offering competitive leaderboards for an "Iron Chef" style experience, complete with new background scenes and an impressive roster of playable chefs.
The sound effects pop and sizzle satisfyingly and are combined with tight controls. The music is enjoyable, and also relevant to how busy your restaurant is. Additionally, the art direction shines and contributes to displaying your progression towards being a 5 star restaurant.
If it's on sale, or even if it's not, you're looking to have some fast fun with this gem. You'll see quickly that a lot of detail went into making this game enjoyable, and that's something you aren't going to see with every title.

8/10 - Fun, addictive game with lots of growth potential.
I gave it a 8/10 instead of a 10/10 because the game isn't easy to learn or it's not user friendly and it needs more cars; there are only a little more than 200 cars available in the game.  That said once you learn how to play, this game is amazing.
'The Crew' reminds me of my beloved racing game Gran Turismo, but much better and with traffic, an open world and random weather.  I played Gran Turismo 1-5, I'm familiar with the game and engine, this game is most definately built off the same platform.  The vehicle modifaction system has been changed and the game has a story with a plot as well as being massively multiplayer.  You're allowed to play all the game's different modes in a "Crew" or a 4 man team of your friends.
When you start out you have a choice of cars available at the Detroit car dealer.  As you unlock the game by beating story missions, there are 5 car dealerships and 1 motorcycle dealership.  I recomend starting with either the 2011 Mustang GT or the Nissan 370Z as they have several different specs the vehicles can be tuned to.  Much like Gran Turismo the vehicles are rated based on what 'The Crew' calls vehicle levels or Gran Turismo players know as performance points.
There are several different spec's a full stock car can be tuned to.  The game comes with 5 specs.  To unlock 'extreme specs' you need to purchase the 'Wild Run' upgrade.
Standard Specs:
1 - Street
2 - Dirt
3 - Performance
4 - Raid
5 - Circuit
Wild Run 'Extreme' specs:
A - Monster Truck
B - Drift
C - Drag
and a new vehicle type: Motorcycles... which kick♥♥♥♥♥by the way.
Each spec a vehicle is tuned to can level up by unlocking parts via challenges, game missions or PVP events thus increasing it's performance point rating.  1299 is the max vehicle level/performance point rating available at this time.
As you complete missions new areas unlock, new vehicle specs and new vehicles are available.
The best way to earn money, rep and league points is to PVP.  It's by far the best way to earn money and rep.  You compete against other players based on how much you play, not how well you finish in races.  You have a choice of 5 PVP factions you can join.  The wolves, the snakes, the gators, the eagles, and some other faction that isn't memorable.  Your rep is compared to the rep of the other players in your faction.  If you have the highest rep in your faction, you're the boss and get a base salary of $150,000 per day.  If you're not the highest paid player, like most people, you fall somewhere in the middle.  Underboss = $100,000 daily, Street Boss = $60,000, Lieutenant = $30,000, Thug = $10,000.  I don't remember what Gangsta pays, but it isn't much, maybe $5,000 daily??  Yes finishing in 1st place pays better, but the difference between 1st and 8th isn't much.  The Devs encourage people to PVP with this system.  Traffic and collisions can be turned off to enhance your gaming experience.  Every player in the PVP lobby gets to choose what map they would like to race on.  Then based on what the players chose (5 players, 5 maps) the computer randomly selects one of the maps all of the players in the lobby chose and then everyone races on that map.  You can PVP solo or with a crew (4 man team).
To start I recomend the 2011 Mustang GT or the Nissan 370Z.  Both of these cars can be tuned to Street, Dirt, Raid, Performance or Circuit which is why I recomend them.  Money is tight early on in the game.
My recomended cars/bikes:
Street: KTM 450, Nissan GTR, 2015 Mustang Fast Back
Dirt: KTM 450, RUF 3400K, Hummer
Raid: KTM 450, RUF 3400K, Buggy, Hummer
Performance: Ford GT, Mclaren F1, Pagani Huayra, Lamborghini Superlegera, BMW 1000RR, Ferrari 458 Special
Circuit: Ford GT, Lamborghini Superlegera, BMW 1000rr, Ferrari 458 Special

While Hearts of Iron III isn't for everyone, people should not be grossed out or write the game off based on its screenshots. Despite most of the game being looking at a map, it offers in depth detail into being the government and military of a country with total countrol. Most players find peacetime the most boring time throughout the game, this can be worse if your playing a country like the United States which doesn't enter WW2 for quite sometime. However, people may find it boring during this peace / build phase but if its not thought out well you'll be quickly regretting and possbily restarting because you found that phase unimportant. If you are like me, and love to add flavor of events and hard decisions during peacetime especially and wartime I would highly recommend the Black ICE mod. This mod adds hundereds of historical events and decisions which have major to minimal impact on the game. These events can both be helpful and hurt you but I feel like it makes the games events harder as its not always a easy decision. For those reasons and the diversity of units and divisions that can be accomplished give you a more fun and tough time, as the AI also build more diverse and recieve events just for them to keep them up to par with you. If anyone ever has any questions or thoughts about getting or already has the game and just wants to discuss anything about it I encourage you to message me. As stated above I strongly recommend this game in its vanilla state or its various mods such as Black ICE, HPP and August Storm.

This game is awesome.
You can play as any country before during and after World War II
It runs from 1936 to 1948, but you can play longer than that with mods.
You can control all aspects of the country, politics, diplomacy, espionage, military, everything.
There are multiple start dates that go from early 1936, to mid 1944.
Each start date has everything set up as it was in the world at that time.
The earlier you start, the more you can change history.
There are also multiple specfic scenarios to chose from, such as the Spanish civil war, the winter war, initial Japanese expansion into south east Asia, the Battle of the Buldge, etc.
There 3 factions in the game; The Allies *Capitalist, democracy* Britain is the leader, and is the only member other than France from the beginning.
The Comintern *Communist* The Soviets are the leader, and the only member from the start.
The Axis *Fascist* The Nazis are the leader, and the only member from the start.
Any country in the game can join any of the factions, as long as certain requirements are met.
One time I got America into the Axis, and it was a serious "Where is your god now?" kind of moment.
Anyways, it's an amazing game, and it has multiplayer, I would love to play it with some people.
I highly recommend it, playing alone or with others.

The 39 Steps is an interactive crime story adapted from a book.
So you might be not challenged clicking through a text adventure, but otherwise everything is well made. The graphics are painted nearby realistic landscapes uncommon to other comic adventures. There are several historical pictures included. The story takes place in 1914, a few weeks before WW1 breaks out. You are searching for a conspirancy that leads to the upcoming events.
There are rarely search screens during the whole story, but sometimes also a nice gesture function is used. Mostly it's very atmospheric. Only the characters are shown as outlined ghosts. I liked the most when somebody was telling yarn. Then an artistical silhouette movie appeared. The language voices of the characters differs from British English, German, Scottish accent to French accent.
In the end it was getting hard to unlock all awards for the last achievement. But with a little help of the community you mustn't be desperated ...

Let's be clear: Going through this will be exactly as if you're leafing through the novel with illustrations of the various setpieces, while voices act out the various dialogues and music plays in the background.
You'll be looking at gorgeous, static illustrations, reading the novel's text phrase by phrase, and listening to the dialogue voiced very competently by various actors.
There are no animations, except for some story-within-the-story segments presented as a puppet theatre, very entertaining, sadly in short bursts.
Some sound effects help to set the scenes, and the soundtrack is very engrossing and does the most to add thrill to the experience.
Even the characters are not shown; you'll only see static silhouettes. I really didn't like that. Maybe it was meant to not impose an image of the character upon the reader. But combined with the rest of the static experience, it just felt lazy.
Besides, you unlock character cards as extra content viewable in the main menu, and the characters are illustrated there, in full detail. So why not expand it to the rest of the adaptation?
-------
(the 1915 novel) was important because it was one of the earliest examples of the man-on-the-run thriller. As such, it is held in high regard, and has been the subject of many adaptations in film, radio and theatre.
But let's face it; for today's reader, it's a pretty dull story.
And seeing how this is a digital adaptation of the novel, it's impossible to view the two separately. It's inevitable that you'll experience some boredom due to the source material. So the question now becomes, what does this adaptation add? Does it present the story in a way that enhances the experience? Is it immersive? Does it expand your view of the story's setting and details?
I'd say yes. I read the novel for the first time, right before playing this. And putting aside the vague boredom I felt both times, my understanding and immersion was definitely higher while playing this.
This being England and Scotland, and the 1914 version of both at that, seeing them illustrated before me certainly helped me be transported there, since I'm so separated from the story's setting by both time and space.
Unfamiliar terms and objects now made sense because I could see them (e.g.
) Certain sequences now played correctly in my mind. Etc.
It could have done more. It could have shown characters in full detail rather than as silhouettes. It doesn't have to become a cartoon, but animations for important actions would have greatly improved the storytelling.
------------
Personally, I would have preferred a completely different way to present this novel. I would love a proper, 3D first person experience of the whole thing, think
or
. Even if it was still entirely linear. But I understand how that would be difficult, even impossible (how do you present a linear story if the player can run around London and the moors of Scotland?)
For what this sets out to do, it does a very good job. Not perfect, but a very good job indeed. I look forward to more adaptations from
and I hope they improve their formula.

The 39 Steps has always been one of my favourite stories.
This PC version of the story is doing it great justice (I have followed the first 7 chapters of 19 so far). The mood captures the novel perfectly and the location graphics are beautiful and very real.
What I particularly have loved so far is all the period settings and the newspapers of the time. We are shown newspapers with parts of the story embedded among authentic pages of the day and I have been on a kind of side quest to look up some of the places in the advertisements, such as shops and hotels. It has been very interesting to read advertisements for places such as the Empire Hotel in Buxton (to name just one of many) and then do a google search to find out more, like when it was built, when it closed and what happened to the buildings in subsequent years before demolition. Amazing stories and pictures. A few of these places still exist today, but not many. Britain was a very very different place 100 years ago and we have lost a lot in the process. Gone is the British Empire and what an Empire we had, with the map in an earlier chapter showing this.
The sounds in the scenes are also spot on.
Anyway, I'd strongly recommend this title, not as a game, but as a great story with a very well produced atmosphere. I am really looking forward to steadily following the next 12 chapters.

So, to be comprehensive, I would like to address the pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
The game is simple enough that just about anyone can pick it up and play.
-Simple flight model makes it very forgiving
-silly power to weight ratios make planes fly very easy
-lack of proper stalls makes it nearly* impossible to crash or spin your plane
-fun races and military campaign
-just flying around is very fun; I like to put on chill music and relax.
-the options for creative designs are quite fun. tiltrotors, for instance are a bit challenging but very fun to create.
-you can build cars, too, if that's your thing. I built an Antonov A-40 style flying tank. that was a fun afternoon.
*I was once able to spin a nearly unstable plane in a speed-based stall. However, it was not recoverable. I think I will test them more.
Now for the Cons.
-Overly simple flight model is very unchallenging, almost boring.
-lack of proper stalls (AoA) is upsetting and unrealistic.
-lack of realistic or in any way really limited engine power makes designs fly funky. you really only need control surfaces, barely wings
For the most part, most players will have a lot of fun with this game. people who like the Challenge of FAR will likely get bored quick, but it is "Simple Planes", not "Totally Accurate Area Ruling and Everything Planes." My gripes are really just personal, and I would refer you to look back through the positives, as they are more important that my negatives.
If you just want to build and fly planes, this is probably the game for you.

I saw this game and figured, well I really like WWII, enjoy flight games, and it's free, I guess I might as well try it. Boy was that a mistake. To say this game is a simulation game is an insult to even the worst flight sims out there. You have two directions of movement. Up and down, Left or Right. Essentially you only have Pitch and Yaw. They attempt to make it look like you have roll by automatically in the direction your turning, but that's it. Also, you pitch stops at the 180 degree mark. You can go straight up or straight down, but you can't do a loop of any kind. So basically you can't preform even the most basic of combat manoeuvers. In other words the controls are very basic, which you would think would be a good thing for a casual game, but it goes against even the most basic principles of slight. As far long term gameplay and progression, I really can't say much as I never intend to play this game again. Seriously, if you are interested in a free WWII flight sim, go for Warthunder. Much better graphics, much better controls, basically much better everything. And you can even drive tanks too! Seriously guys, avoid this one like the plague. World of Warplanes is significantly better than this, and that's saying A LOT!

Best WW 1 FPS I've played or seen so far. If you want a realistic WW 1 experience get this. If you have the attention span of a 2 month old cat with ADHD and a wallet fatter than a fat cat get BF 1.
Likes
+Great visuals
+Great audio
+Good maps
+Immersion
+Solid and responsive, yet "realistic" gunplay.
+Variety of squads, weapons, roles and maps
+Pace is very WW1 trench combat like
+Character progression
+Overall feel of the entire game gives a rough WW1 feel
+The game has 54 weapons and I have seen a lot of reviews that there is no or very little weapon choice. So judge yourself is 54 enough for you or do you need 120 with all DLC, skins and red dot sights
Dislikes
-Hitpoint based health system. Can get killed in a couple of seconds in barbed wire. Would much prefer Red Orchestra 2 style damage system with different body parts
-Too many HUD elements. I would prefer if it would have an optionl Realistic game mode with minimal HUD only showing objectives and time. The HUD could work like in RO 2 realistic where it comes up by pressing a key. Also would be more claustrophobic if you wouldn't see the ammo count and would have to try to count how many rounds you still have left in the rifle while the enemy swarms your trench around you.
-More maps and more variation is always good
-Servers almost always empty after match and you play 3v3 for half of the next match. Ruins the flow since if you wanna play a good populated match you always have to leave and rejoin another match.
-Bugs like arty not dropping are very annoying devs please fix it
-No squad chat except voice, but the sound options don't work and you can never hear the people talking. Their voices are super silent while the in game combat sounds even at minimum drown anyones voice.
There are some issues and they can be very annoying, but at the moment the positives outweigh these negatives. However I hope that the devs will address these issues.
If the voice chat, arty bugs and the constantly empty servers will not be fixed before Tannenberg I will not buy it for sure. If you will have constantly 3v3-8v8 matches in 64 player maps it will be absolutely awful. Maybe the developers could have dedicated servers for the next game or limit the amount of empty public games so that people would be reinstanced to more full games if the servers are almost empty.
Also be sure to check out the YouTube channel called The Great War. It is the best history channel I know and will give you great insight to World War I

Hearts of Iron III is, literally, the most complex strategy game ever developed. Created by Paradox Interactive, the game starts in January 1936 with your selected nation from the Allied or Axis, and win dominations of your choosing. Want to play Germany? Go ahead and research technology before everybody else and invade nations before they can stand a chance. Play as the United States? Declare war against Japan before they can strike against your interests and prevent them from dominating Asia before Japan can even start conquering them. These scenarios are one of the very few that has an endless of possibilities, bringing up the replay value with maximum outcome. What surprises me the most is how complex the game is, like diplomacy, research, production, and a whole lot of other factors that you can think of for a strategy game. Regardless of the game's strong presentation, Hearts of Iron III has its flaws...particuarly of game crashes, little patches that brings little outcome, and a very steep learning curve with a failure of basic tutorials that cannot teach or instruct well. In addition, the game is ONLY recommended to those who are interested in general history, military history, political science, and/or in social sciences. Reason is mainly because many gamers are not interested in these subjects and the game only appeals to small audience (mentioned in the previous sentence). It is not a discouragment, but an understanding of how tolerant that you are willing to play the game since the main gameplay element is seeing "boxes" move around the global map with a strong emphasis on military tactics, like coordinating strategy in a military map. I would not be surprised if anyone would say the game sucks because of ignorance and expect a lot of action (because of the stupidity of the Call of Duty generation). Again, this game is NOT for everyone and those who actually play a good amount of othe strategy games like Total War series, this game is very different from the others. If you are actually interested in the game, I strongly suggest for you to watch Youtube videos on the gameplay to see if it is suitable to your game interest. If not, then it is not for you. Only recommendation is for gamers with strong interests in social sciences and military.

Similar to the film Grave Encounters, the game is set in some kind of mental institution and you are armed with only a digital camera with a nightvision toggle that consumes the batteries. The story is told through notes you make when you have the camera out and through documents you find strewn in the levels.
It borrows from the Amnesia series in that you can't actually defend yourself against any of the unpleasant things you might encounter. Your only course of action is to run and to hide. However, whereas in Amnesia you might have had something chasing you and you knew it would kill you so you ran until you were safe with your heart pounding, in Outlast you are required to backtrack past the same enemy over and over. Far from being scary, it just becomes an annoyance.
There are many sections where you need to find a key (or other item) but when looking for it you will be seen by an enemy, then you'll run, hide in a closet, wait for him to leave, then go and search again, the same thing happens, repeat ad nausem or until he finally kills you. The scariness is gone and it just becomes frustrating. You know what you have to do; you might even know where the key is, but you have to get past something that will chase you and instantly kill you.
There is functionality to look over either shoulder using Q or E. It is not very useful though because it is disorienting. I suppose that was the intention: when running from something you take a quick glance over your shoulder and see it just behind you. The trouble is, in real life we are unaware of the movement of our head because our brain processes it for us. We don't see the world spin when we turn our head. When the game shows you everything spin it's not actually realistic, it's annoying and makes the "look behind" function not very usable.
The need to use the camera with its night vision to see does add some tension, which is helped along by your character breathing heavily etc. There is an outdoor part which is reminiscent of The Blair Witch Project in its atomosphere.
If you like horror games then this is worth a play. It has a great atmosphere and some nice visuals. There are a few jump scares and to start with it's quite immersive until the gameplay gets a bit samey and you know what the threats are. But by that time you'll probably see it through to the end to find out what happens. The game is about the right length in that respect.

As this being a visual novel and not a classic video game it might not be made for everyone, but I was pretty much hooked from the first chapter onwards. This digital adaption of an english literature classic is executed pretty well, with beautiful hand drawn background stills for most of the time and an overall excellent atmosphere. The rare voice acting is good overall, the animated portions are great and the reading of the text isn't painful. There are one or two game mechanics which could have been handled better, but as this being the first of its kind that I am aware of, I must say the developers did a pretty good job and I am sure they are able to improve the really small annoyances in potential next installments.
Highly recommended if you like to read (interactive) books/thrillers on espionage in the dawn of World War I, because this one is worth it and I really hope to see more digital book adaptions in the future.

Ultimate Chicken Horse (UCH) is one of the best (local) multiplayer games out there when played with friends. It is a 2D-platformer with simple graphics, where each player chooses a farm animal of his or her choice to compete against each other. Up to four players can play together in a total of 10 different levels, both local and online. Most of the levels (and some other stuff) is locked in the beginning and is randomly unlocked by playing certain levels at the right time (you'll know how and when to do this).
Basically, UCH is a Super Mario like Jump n'Run, where you have to reach the end of a level. However, there is a pretty cool twist to this old-school mechanic: After each "race" in the current level, players have to chance to place an object to "make the level more difficult". In other words, they will try to f**k you up. Of course, they still want to finish the level as well. Thus, the placement of objects is a dilicate matter. There is a rather sophisticated point system involved to determine the winner of a level. For example, you can get "post mortem" extra points...
The game offers some other game modes as well, but I think that the real fun begins if you play with three friends locally in the described "party mode". While the number of levels is low, the replay value is immensely high due to a random selection of items which can be placed each turn. In a recent patch, the developers also added the possibility to share levels between users, i.e., you are able to prepare a level with a choice of items and then send it your friends to see them fail. It really is a bit like Mario Maker for PC, but with chickens and horses.
One drawback is the rather small selection of items right now. There is definitly room for improvement, but certain mechanics and hillarious traps make up for it. Especially the fact that you can combine different items via "honey" to make terrifying death traps. This also works for the various moving objects.
Overall, I really can recommend this game. It is one of the funniest multiplayer games I have played and has a good controller support. It works nice in local multiplayer and different options allow to customize the game modes further. However, I have not tried the included online mode yet, but this possibility exists as well.
Buy this game, you won't regret it! :)

The graphics are definately kinda bad, but if I had to place a year on them, I would say the game looks like an Xbox 360 game from around 2005-2006, which isnt too horrible, but not great compared to War Thunder.

Dark souls 2 is great, genuinely. Great items, great combat, great story, great bosses, great enemies, great locations, great everything. But I just can't recommend it. It's not actually hard like people claim it is, once you have played for an hour or so, it becomes trivially easy, what makes it hard, is that there is just SO. MUCH. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T. From bugs to dodgy hitboxes, 95% of your deaths will feel like you were cheated, and are unfair. Enemies will hit you through walls, will damage you even if you COMPLETELY dodge an attack, and with enemies that have insta kill attacks (eg mimics and ogres), half the time you'll just teleport into their hands and instadie. As a result, rather than the game being "oh damn I died, better adapt my strategy next time", it just becomes a frustrating mess of trying to get through the crap. Not to mention that in a ton of places they just cheat the difficulty, eg putting a mass of enemies in a tiny room that you cant dodge in, or have a ton of enemies spamming homing missiles so you can't dodge them all. If you can get through all that, then pick it up, it's fun, at least, when your deaths are your own fault, and not the fault of bad mechanics and bugs, which the VAST majority will be.
