This is still arguably the best strategic WW2 sim available, despite its flaws. The one chief complaint by many seems to be the inherent level of micromanagement contained within this game and its predecessors, but if you're someone that dislikes micromanagement, then why are you even looking at this game in the first place?
This is a game for someone that loves history, loves hardcore simulations, and loves to manage things down to the lowest possible level. Sure, you certainly can automate some game functions to a degree. But HOI3 gives you the power to take control directly, and the possibilities are endless because of it. And with the latest 'Their Finest Hour' expansion, your inner field marshal will shake with joy at the addition of battle plan editing, which allows you do do your own operational-level chief of staff work and create battle plans complete with movement arrows and other annotations, just like something out of Manstein's 'Lost Battles,' or Patton's memoirs.
So the bottom line is that if you love love WW2 history, historical simulations, and don't have a short attention span, then this game is most certainly for you!

Lemme start by stating for the record: NO THIS GAME IS NOT PAY TO WIN.
This is a game where you pick up guns and shoot zombies. Simple, yes? Well, that's the very short version of it.
It's basically an RPG like game, where you collect loot, equip it and then kill stuff. Simple, but it gets more complex. Different weapons have different statistics, including but not limited to: reload time, damage type (fire, energy or normal, for example), clip size and so on. And up to three of these statistics can be upgraded, for in game currency of course.
With me so far? Good. The game also features armor, which, like the weapons can also be upgraded: fire defense, poison def, normal def, weight, revival rate, and so on. And different armors also carry different statistics and bonuses, so depending on your play style, you can have different gear for different scenarios.
The meat of the game is definitely in the weapons, but the character you play also has some statistics that you can build upon, using levels which are gained by leveling up. The basic stats are your speed, weapons damage and so on. So if your build is for speed, get the lightest gear, put all your points into speed, and start running. On top of all that, your chosen class can also be upgraded; you want to build a tanking medic (That's paladin, in medieval terms)? go right ahead. I know I did.
The game has several gameplay modes, all of which use your selected character. There are up to seven solo missions (Though the browser version has 9, I believe), which you can use for your grinding. Then there are also the contract missions; short missions of two and a half minutes or so, which give you special bonus rewards of some kind. Multi player games are also available, which include the general mission multiplayer, nightmare games (Much more difficult enemies spawn, with a slim, but not nonexistent chance of getting super rare loot) and special multiplayer missions, where you rank against other online players.
There are in game microtransactions, but they are not and do not make the game unplayable. They just make it easier for those financially able to finish their missions. There are indeed premium guns, but they are only marginally better than the regular guns you can find in loot boxes.
Finally, I want to talk about customer support. The day the game came out, I decided to download it and play it. And what do you know, I moronically deleted my saves both on mobile device and on  the steam local saves. So what do I do? I contacted their support. Today, my save is back to normal, and I'm able to play as though there was no problem whatsoever. A big thank you to their support team, particularly Sam, who was both helpful and understanding. Sam, if I meet you in real life, I'll shake your hands so hard you will temporarily lose feeling in them.
9 out of 10 (1 point deducted for making the game so frikken hard to unlock the black boxes.)

This game is a more-or-less interactive rendition of the homonymous book by John Buchan. I haven't read the book but i tend to see as more respectful to the book and therefore tending more to a storytelling version of it. Therefore the game itself hasn't a great deal of anything interactive added to it.
The real quality added to the story itself is the mode of delivery, because both the visuals (hand painted landscapes) and the overall good voice acting add a value to the game, which otherwise is merely a travel through checkpoints with no chance left to the player. Does this completely make up for the whole game being not truly interactive as one could imagine? No, there are plenty of things (including animations, which are non existent) that could have been done to achieve a better "vision" and overall a better implication of the player. That said tho, it's an interesting experiment, which mostly turns out to be positive because of the plot itself (being exalted by the visuals and voice acting qualities), which isn't never to be taken for granted.
It's fun, a good time killer with addictive gameplay. Short campaign but the missions have high replayability with randomised spawns and new monsters as you level up.

Simply the most frightening game I've ever played.  It presents a shockingly well polished game for a budget title price, and has become my favorite surprise hit of 2013.  Outlast masters both the art of pop out scares and a slow burn tense atmosphere, made much more compelling by music that reacts to the situation and dozens of small touches like seeing your hands as you clutch to the edge of a corridor to peek around the next hallway or the heavy ragged breathing of the player's character exerted from fleeing for his life but desperately trying to keep quiet in his hiding place to escape the horrors chasing him.  Also effective in building the tension is that the player's only way to see in the dark is through the night vision of the camera... which gives the world a very limited distance green/black view and also will quickly drain the batteries.  You force yourself to creep through darkness and use up every bit of electricity from each set of batteries even though your vision is failing just to save those precious batteries for when you can't make it without them.  As the song by Radiohead goes "You do it to yourself, you do, and that's what really hurts (or in this case, scares!)"
It's not a long game, the designers seem to know better than to wear out their welcome and at 8 hours of play time I feel I've more than gotten my money's worth for a lifetime memorable experience.  Thankfully I'm old and moved out because I'd owe my mother's "swear jar" a sock full of nickles for the outbursts I've had while fleeing in this game.  Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys a good scary story.

Going to be straight here. Just Cause 2 is a lot of fun and one of the more over the top games I've played ina long time. You play Agent Rico Rodriguez as he is sent to the mythical island of Panau to stop a mad dictator from taking over the world. This is true open world goodness. You can fly planes, blow stuff up, steal cars, assist rebel factions and cause a whole lot of damage.  The game looks great, the voice acting is good and the story isn't meant to be taken seriously. While this game is a blast to play there are some issues that keep it from home run status. The biggest problem with the game I had is in order to progress with the story missions you have raise your "chaos" rating which means you have to blow stuff up, finish rebel missions, etc. So if you plan on finishing this game in 8 hours or so, well it won't let you. Because it can take a while to accumulate a high enough chaos rating for you to unlock a story mission. The variety of missions you get are nothing you haven't played before. Escort here, blow stuff up there, disarm bombs with limited time, etc. A lot of them are fun but some are an exercise in frustration. I do like that there are a myriad of ways to accomplish missions so if one way doesn't work you can certainly try another one.  Overall I'd definitely recommend Just Cause 2. It's been on sale I don't know how many times but you'll defnitely get your money's worth whatever you paid for it (I think it's been down to $2.99 for the complete package). An easy 8/10 from me and I hope to see a Just Cause 3.

Dark souls 2 is great, genuinely. Great items, great combat, great story, great bosses, great enemies, great locations, great everything. But I just can't recommend it. It's not actually hard like people claim it is, once you have played for an hour or so, it becomes trivially easy, what makes it hard, is that there is just SO. MUCH. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T. From bugs to dodgy hitboxes, 95% of your deaths will feel like you were cheated, and are unfair. Enemies will hit you through walls, will damage you even if you COMPLETELY dodge an attack, and with enemies that have insta kill attacks (eg mimics and ogres), half the time you'll just teleport into their hands and instadie. As a result, rather than the game being "oh damn I died, better adapt my strategy next time", it just becomes a frustrating mess of trying to get through the crap. Not to mention that in a ton of places they just cheat the difficulty, eg putting a mass of enemies in a tiny room that you cant dodge in, or have a ton of enemies spamming homing missiles so you can't dodge them all. If you can get through all that, then pick it up, it's fun, at least, when your deaths are your own fault, and not the fault of bad mechanics and bugs, which the VAST majority will be.

Demonheart is a well thought out VN with a gripping story and solid background. As far as the reviews of it being short because of modular releases, admittedly I had the same notion, but with a variety of choices based on personality the story turned out more impressive with each new run uncovering new subtle hints and teases of information.
Most other VNs I have played are usually one love interest at a time, just an A or B option and no deviance from the main experience. But what I have discovered instead with Demonheart is that it is so fluid in presentation. You can build multiple relationships at once, which can bring some interesting reactions from others. A few times along the way, there are chances to unlock a portion of story, almost like a side quest, that seem to alter the game in a significant way. Conversations more at the pace you want them, with as little or as much interaction as you choose.
This is worth different playthroughs to try and uncover a rich and compelling story full of betrayal and magic. A labor of love that has proven unique and so thoughtful that it is so much more than just reading a romance novel between MC and love interest.

Apart from that, the art is very good in setting up each scene and the voice acting is perfect for conveying each of the characters. Pick this up if you have any vested interest in spy fiction.

A fairly poor low res HOG by these developers (
). Since the games release on Steam it has been reported to have a nasty string of reported bugs and I myself ran into them from chapter three onwards. So saving your game constantly is a must, unless you love restarting the game from the beginning.
Each HOG scene requires you to find an assortment of listed objects from scenes that look like a tonne of grenades have gone off in an op shop. With the low res and high frequency of HOG scenes you will probably develop a headache in no time thanks to the constant mashing of the hint button with your forehead.
Occasionally the game breaks up the monotony of HOG with 5 dress up your dolly scenes and 5 open this vault scene by solving a series of puzzles. The puzzles were so easy I was able to solve them by breaking wind randomly in the direction of the keyboard and letting wind power do its magic.
There are some interesting and novel quirks to the game like the limiting of people in a crowded room to find the subject you’re looking for that fits all the listed requirements, and even the pick lock system which starts to shrink its correct hit box the longer you procrastinate.
The story is that Melissa a cat burglar who is a wizard at breaking into top notch banks using mundane objects like a pair of scissors and some blue tack has had her son Noah kidnapped. Demands of her illegal services are made if she ever wants to see her son alive again. While performing this last job she must uncover the identity of the kidnapper and outsmart them and bring the bad guys to justice. It should come to no surprise that Melissa super power of combining things like garden hose, mirror, fish hook and bread roll saves the day.
The real biggest problem against Melissa finding her son is not the bad guy, but more the nasty sudden crashes and glitched sounds that many experience from chapter 3 onwards. It seems the developers at Gojii are even worse than the bank systems she has to break into. As no objects whatsoever are needed to break this game. For the price it is advertised you would think that the developer and publisher would at least offer a properly working product.

The good.
Interesting take on the HOG genre that doesn't involve the supernatural for a change, (Although you are looking for your kid again ... *sigh*) , where you play a master thief who needs to come out of retirement for one last job.
Original story-line with lots of voice acting.
Lots of HO scenes, that have HO scenes within HO scenes, and inventory items are also used within the HO scenes.
Some object elimination scenes which were different.
The bad.
The graphics are average to below average in some scenes. Object definition on HO scenes can be grainy.
The lock picking mini-games were incredibly easy and were basically QTEs (quick time event.)
There were very few puzzles and again, they were easy. It felt that over 80% of the content was based on HO scenes.
Although I only experienced one small bug that I could cancel and continue, others are reporting glitches and being unable to complete the game as a result.
Part of the game is "dressing up" the character between chapters, which involved more HO scenes, and seems a pointless and tacked on time sink. It adds nothing to the gameplay.
The object elimination scenes were stupid. Original, but stupid. For example, you are looking for a woman in a crowd, why can't you just eliminate all the men and children? You can't. You have to go through pointless clues to eliminate every man, woman, and child, one by one, and some of the clues are ridiculous as well. "He doesn't like lucky charms." Apparently, that meant having to eliminate someone wearing a sports jacket with the number 7 on it, or someone else with an outline of a horseshoe on their jumper! It made little sense.
Overall, the game, while not executed perfectly, with minor annoyances, is a very different from the usual HOGs in the use of it's setting and storyline. I enjoyed my time in the game, and believe the journey was worth the few speed bumps.

As far as games go, this one gets kind of mundane after a little while. I found myself not enjoying the game after a number of deaths and a lot of times where the end of the level was just right in front of me. And when I eventually did beat all the levels the game had to offer, I found that there wasn't much else to do. The challenge mode is redundant and not enough to keep me hooked, and I didn't care enough to find people to play the multiplayer function. There are many other games I'd play if I wanted to play with my friends. Dub Dash is not a game to play with grit teeth or sweaty hands, the fact that it's also a mobile game should drive home the fact that this is just a distraction game. Something to play when you're not doing much else. It's pretty cool, but definitely not something to write home about.
Having said all that, though, I did enjoy the game quite a bit once I settled into the groove of the gameplay. Listening to the music, feeling the flow, and letting it carry me through the level. Like I said before, Dub Dash is not a game to play intensely, but it is something to play after a long day where all you want to do is sit back at your desk and play a little Dub Dash. The game allows you to turn off your brain and relax for a little bit while you go through a level or two before fixing up dinner. In other words, Dub Dash is a quintessential casual game for the casual gamer.
Wrapping it all up, the game is definitely good for what it is: a relatively simple rhythm game which its graphics and gameplay make it a cut above games like The Impossible Game and Geometry Dash. Which is why I'm giving Dub Dash an 8 out of 10. If you like Rhythm games, this one should revitalize the genre for you. You should pick this one up.
PROS
+ Vibrant atmosphere and visual style
+ Clear and engaging audio
+ Tight gameplay mechanics
+ Expands the rhythm game genre
CONS
- Light on level content
- Offers limited replayability

Going to be straight here. Just Cause 2 is a lot of fun and one of the more over the top games I've played ina long time. You play Agent Rico Rodriguez as he is sent to the mythical island of Panau to stop a mad dictator from taking over the world. This is true open world goodness. You can fly planes, blow stuff up, steal cars, assist rebel factions and cause a whole lot of damage.  The game looks great, the voice acting is good and the story isn't meant to be taken seriously. While this game is a blast to play there are some issues that keep it from home run status. The biggest problem with the game I had is in order to progress with the story missions you have raise your "chaos" rating which means you have to blow stuff up, finish rebel missions, etc. So if you plan on finishing this game in 8 hours or so, well it won't let you. Because it can take a while to accumulate a high enough chaos rating for you to unlock a story mission. The variety of missions you get are nothing you haven't played before. Escort here, blow stuff up there, disarm bombs with limited time, etc. A lot of them are fun but some are an exercise in frustration. I do like that there are a myriad of ways to accomplish missions so if one way doesn't work you can certainly try another one.  Overall I'd definitely recommend Just Cause 2. It's been on sale I don't know how many times but you'll defnitely get your money's worth whatever you paid for it (I think it's been down to $2.99 for the complete package). An easy 8/10 from me and I hope to see a Just Cause 3.

This is a graphic adaption of the 1915 book by John Buchan, not an actual game.  You follow this spy yarn by clicking your mouse to progress the story.  There is a lot of reading spiced up with some good voice acting.  Occasionally, you have to perform some very simple searches of a scene in order to get all the exposition provided.
And then there are the silly mouse movements that you have to follow in order to do things like open doors, make telephone calls, or create explosives.  These consist of following the on-screen instructions and matching your mouse movements to the graphic - up, down, left, right, clockwise circle, counter-clockwise circle.
The graphics are 95% static, the only movement being the occasional smokestack spewing smoke, a flag flapping in the wind, or falling rain.  The artwork is lushly handpainted, not your typical computer game graphics.  There isn't much music, but they do a fine job with the voice acting and a few sound effects.
Even if you take your time and read every word carefully, you can reach the end in 5-6 hours.  There are achievements, but they are for completing chapters.  So if you finish the "game", you will get every achievement.
If you don't mind reading a Reader's Digest version of a 100-year old spy novel, then this might possibly be your cup of tea.  I suspect that most of today's gamers would take a pass, but I found it mildly entertaining.

This game was a hidden gem for me! It didn't think it would be that good as there's quite a lot of these on steam but after I started playing I really got sucked into the story!
As there's only three chapters out so far I'd give it like an 7/10 recommend.
The story is interesting and keeps you entertained. The artwork is nice and the characters are too. There are plenty of options when responding to events in the game and it actually feels like most of your choices matter. A lot of these games make it so obvious that you need to select specific answers in order to get very specific outcomes, but with this one I was able to play how I wanted to and have the story end up the way I wanted without having to follow any kind of guide and on my first play through; Maybe I was just lucky though. I like that not all answers affect your character's personality which adds a bit more depth to the story while giving more flexibility in how you choose your answers.
A few wishes for the game though, would be:
*A longer story.
This isn't to say I'm not happy with the length of the chapters because they are quite long and fleshed out but I don't think that five chapters is enough for what you pay compared to other games of this kind, I know some of those games are dirt cheap and the good ones can charge a LOT but they are pretty good quality and I see that kind of potential here. I bought the game with 20% off and feel like it was quite worth it at that price ($15). In saying that I would be happy to pay around $30 for ten chapters each with the same chapter length that is already there, realistically. But that's just my own opinion.
*More characters that impact the story would definitely be a plus.
Having only two characters that it seems like you can romance doesn't seem like quite enough. Maybe another two would make it more interesting but you'd need to be careful not to let this take away from each character's story/personality.
*More CG's in the story.
You really only get one or two good CG's in the three chapters that you can play. I'm not expecting to get much more because there is only supposed to be five chapters coming out and this is really disappointing. The artwork in this game is good and the creators would definatley benefit from putting more CG's into the game.
So far I recommend buying this only with the sale until all the chapters come out at least (:

This game is to BF1 what a chinese OUYE console would be to a Playstation 4. This would be the kind of game a non-game savvy grandmother would buy for her grandkids instead of Battlefield.  I know, a bit unfair given Verdun came out a full year and a half before BF1, with probably hundreds million less in the budget.
But let's face the truth here: this would be the best WW1 infantry game. Bar none. Because there were none other. That until BF1 came out. Darned EA released a very competent game. Light years ahead in every conceivable department. Some might say: "Oh but Verdun is a sim". Well, it's not. Sorry. Arma 3 is the closest you'd get from a military sim without a multimillion dollar tech powering it. Verdun is just an indie-run-of-the-mill game. Nothing is really well done. Nothing stands out. It's a very flat shooter. Heck, even BF1 isn't all that stellar, although much better than the recent years efforts.
Again, it's very unfair to compare it to a 100-million dollar budget game. Very unfair, let me say. So, if you're really tight on the budget, go ahead. The game is very unpolished and ugly, with nothing in particular standing out, but it's WW1. It's either this or BF1. Unless we are talking about planes, which this one have none. In this case, Rise of Flight is the way to go.

The 39 Steps is a virtual novel with very little interaction. It is 100% impossible to get stuck on this game, because you've got to left click through text or objects (with a big diamond-shaped icon right in the middle of every objects), or simply do a series of left, down, up, right, clockwise or counter-clockwise mouse movements for every single puzzles in the game.
The only part of this game I liked, are the voice acting and graphics, especially the graphics, they are truly amazing! Though, the important aspect of a virtual novel is the story and in the case of "The 39 Steps" I didin't understand much of the story, it kinda ruined it for me. Now i've got to say, my first language isn't english, but I really couldn't understand the beginning of the story. I also couldn't understand any british dialogues, because they were all slang. Some parts were also in German, with no translation what-so-ever.
Another complaint about this game, is how the game is saved. The ''chapters'' takes about 15 minutes each, but if you want to alt-tab (probably a bug) or quit the game, you might have or might not have to restart that chapter all over again. This made me replay at least 3 chapters (which, by the way, you cannot skip any text or cutscenes) and effectively made me watch all of the dialogues and cutscenes again.
I am quite disapointed with this "game" so I cannot recommend it. If you were going to purchase this virtual novel, I really hope you understand english very well and don't mind not being able to have any influence in the story nor have any puzzles to solve at all while playing this.

Pros: Excellent infantry combat. Probably the best bolt action rifle gameplay since call of duty 2.
Cons: No dedicated servers or server browser, everything is done by match making. Due to this the game is nearly dead. Even during the free midweek period the game barely breaks 100 players in my local area(NYC/East coast).
The maps vary wildly in quality, while some are excellent the bad ones do spoil the bunch. Nobody wants to play on a bad map and people leave. The premiere gamemode trench warefare is restrictive and not really run. Rifle deathmatch is a blast but it needs to be expanded to include all weapons. TDM is probably the worst mode. Due to the spawn system it feels like you're on a merry-go-round/carousel when looking for enemies. Most people camp because it's the best way to get kills.
The weapon selection screen is a joke. It's too inflexible. Cant have a Pistol, Grenade or Melee weapon at the same time. You are limited to one of the afformentioned weapons and a primary. No way to resupply ammo without dying and believe me you either die within the first minute or live long enough to rely entirely on melee bashing. Cant pickup another mans weapon. The attachment system is lackluster. The most basic necessities like stripper clips and rifle mounted bayonets are unlocks solely to pad out the gameplay.
The damage system is crap. Take 3 shots from a pistol and go hide for a few seconds to regain your health. I've been involved in many fights where I needed just one more bullet to kill an enemy and he lay down for a 3-5 seconds and was fully healed and ready to continue fighting. Grenades are very very weak. The enemy has to be withing a meter or two of the grenade to even get damaged and pretty much right next to it for a kill.
I believe that the biggest problem is the server issue. If this game  just had dedicated servers that would build communities and the game would still be alive. As of 5/31 this game is dead. Would not recommend. You'll have fun for the first hour or so then the glaring flaws will get on your nerves.
Full Disclosure. I played this game during the free midweek period and I know I've seen enough of it to make a judgement call.

I played so much hearthstone and since I discovered this, I haven't touched Hearthstone.
Pros
- More skilled gameplay (Can't just win via aggro and hitting face)
- More cards (250-300 per expansion)
- Incredibly Free to play friendly (At minimum 1 pack +450 gold +2 uncommon cards EVERY DAY)
- More interesting cards than many another CCG (Compared mostly to Hearthstone)
- 8 different game modes (4 singleplayer, 4 multiplayer)
- Every colour has a very distinct and individual theme and feel (Combining 2 or more colours just increases the variety of playstyles)
- More variety in decks (Ranked isn't dominated by 3 or 4 overpowered expensive decks)
Cons
- Art is a little uninspiring
- Playerbase is fairly small atm (I read on reddit that at any point the number of online players is estimated to be ~1300, compared to Hearthstones ~100,000)
- Events are not as fun and don't come as often as Hearthstone's Tavern Brawls
Overall, all of these negative aspects can be fixed by constant work from the dev team and support from the player base. The game is harder and more strategic/complex than hearthstone, which many players can find boring, but for people who want a slightly more mentally challenging experience compared to Hearthstone, I highly recommend Eternal.

This game is... intense. I've been playing more of deathmatch and less of squad. Sound is your best friend. I don't like that sometimes there is more reverb then there should be, in bunkers and in trenches. You'd think all the wood would dampen most of the noise. This is like the WWI version of Red Orchestra 2. I wish there was peek, like RO2. That'd make this game a bit more realistic and frustrating. No cover system, which is a plus, in my opinion. Transitions from running to prone very naturally. It seemed kludgy at first, but you get used to it, and realize it's just as it would be IRL and not a videogame. You can literally dive into trenches and craters. But gunplay seems a bit tooooo FPS-ish, in that half the time instead of taking cover (crouching behind something) and firing, you find yourself strafing just before the guy shooting at you shoots, so he misses; at least in deathmatch. It's still fun, but it takes away a notch of realism. Graphics are pretty, and the gore is done just right.
Half the time you're running around shooting at the first thing you see, just as it should be. Dead bodies pile up over the place, their lifeless ragdolls making you waste bullets while you give away your position.
4/5. Very good game.

Vault Cracker is a very low-resolution, really old-school hidden object game with an astonishingly good storyline.
It’s really hard to write a review on Vault Cracker: The Last Safe, because it’s incredibly good and incredibly bad at the same time.
The story is excellent; a heist thriller that could easily hold on its own in a modern action adventure game, or even in a movie. It is also devoid of all supernatural elements– something that is almost never seen in modern hidden object games.
On the other hand this 2010 product feels like something created at the earliest days of the hidden object genre. The resolution is locked at 800×600. The image quality is horrible with JPEG compression noise everywhere. There is no puzzle variety, just HOPs, which also reminds us of the ancient HO games. And I still don’t quite understand what purpose did the character dress-up sequences serve.
Still, if you don’t mind the outdated mechanics and visuals, and the short length, then play it for the story, it will be worth it.

Very well done game. Graphics are done smoothly, and the better the PC you have, the better the graphics. It does take a bit of power for ultra, although. Gameplay is very fun and done nicely.
PROS:
Every car has potential and can be used for many different things. So if you find a well rounded car you really like, there won't be that "Aww crap, it's outdated now and I need to replace it" issue.
Gameplay and graphics are smooth.
Vehicle handling is done very well. Some games have very choppy driving experiances. This game does NOT!
The fact you can play solo, with a team, and/or with your friends is very nice. All things are pretty much doable in either of these 3 different ways.
Bugs and glitches are very rare in this game.
CONS:
As stated in many reviews, season pass does not include all content/DLC.
Some cars, like the Skyline, are a bit OP when it comes down to it. You can obtain this car very early on for a very cheap price. It has the option to do any spec, and performs like an absolute boss. Why is this a con? I feel like due to the handling and how open the variations are, it should be tuned down a tad. No reason for an early starting car to be able to match an end game car. Plus, you may find yourself stuck on this car and not wanting to use any other car which can take some fun out of the game.
If you do not own Wild Run, Ubisoft tends to force it in your face whenever it can. Constant adds, constant reminders, and the fact that all the WR DLC races are all over your map as listed races and events, but noooo, can't do them till you buy our DLC type crap.
The option to use real currency to buy things. Many different reasons why this is bad.
Once you are max level, have all the races done, the game does slow down a ton. Seems like there isn't a lot to do at that point. Gets very repetative and a tad boring. May discourage players at that point.
OVERALL:
Do I recommend this game? I do. Many hours of fun! Nothing like doing a 2+ hour race with friends on Skype! If a game can give you one hell of a good time, laughs with friends, and make a night into an awesome night, then yeah the game is worth it. The fact that I listed more cons than pros is not a final determination. The pros listed certainly outweigh the cons by a longshot. Plus, everyones opinions are different. Some might find the cons not a problem. This game keeps updated really well. They patch it pretty frequently with fixes and content. I have yet to come across any game breaking glitches or bugs. I have discovered a few glitches, but had a ton of fun with them. For example I have found a few areas that if you carefully drive into the water, you can drive underneath and have a blast! If you do chose to purchase this game, I hope you find your buy worth it and that you have fun as me and my friends have!

I have already written reviews for the other Space Pilgrim episodes, so I won't be super annoying here.
Let's just say that this is a complete series made up by four games and created by Pilgrim Adventures. The games all cost less than 1€, and they're all worthy definitely.
They're made with RPG Maker and althought the window may seem small, everything turns out to be extremely entertaining and well-designed.
This is the second episode of the series, which is connected and takes place in the same extraterrestrial environment; you of course will play different characters, switch between them, make choices and so on (some achievements need two playthroughs since they rely on your choices).
The game itself is a little bit like a RPG, but you don't have to fight or such (apart from some little parts); it's most of a point n' click adventure except for the fact that you have one character to explore everything, collect items, mix them up and so on.
For what concerns the series, yeah, it gets better for every episode (feel free to check the Steam guides if you're stuck, 'cos sometimes they get difficult!).. the first one is the easiest and shortest, and then they go on with length and difficulty.
I'd have loved to be able to review the whole series in a single page but I can't, even though it's different to review single episodes.. I strongly recommend the whole series, even 'cos you need to get through the complete story and its ending. Playing episode 2 alone it's still ok, but way less charming and interesting!
Apart from the plot things, the game runs smooth and characters and environment are always greatly designed - like a RPG - and the sound effects are ok too. If you're into sci-fi adventures with lots of combinations and secrets to solve, this series needs to be played from the start to the end :)
Have fun with Space Pilgrim, you won't be disappointed but.. come here after Episode I - Alpha Centauri, trust me :)

Logistical: British Isles expands the game with a huge amount of towns, offering a lot of content for the price.
Below you can find my review of Logistical!
----
Logistical is a nice and relaxed transport based puzzle game which has undergone some major improvements lately, thanks to the constant updates by the developer.
The main objective of the game is to "complete" the towns spread over the map (the base game offers the whole Australian continent, which comprises about 1200 towns). In order to complete a town, you need to deliver to it a set amount of goods: once this is done, the city will get coloured, to indicate its completion. At the beginning this operation will be simple enough, sometimes trivial even, but by proceeding into the game, you will discover cities that will need careful planning to be completed. The problem is that the citizens will start consuming the goods you deliver to them, so once you begin supplying a city, you'll need to do that efficiently and quickly, up to the fulfillment of all the required goods amounts. If your trucks are not enough in number, and/or not quick/large enough, the goods you delivered will eventually be consumed and you'll have to start over in your "quest" to complete that town.
Any industry present in the city, anyway, will still be operative even after the city is completed. Industries, of course, is where goods are produced. So if for example you need motorbikes, you'll have to first find an industry that produces motorbikes, then supply it with resources (like tyres, steel and engines) and only after doing this you'll be able to transport the motorbikes to the city that needed them. Differently than goods delivered to complete towns, those delivered to industries don't ever get lost: they always get used to produce goods or stored for an infinite amount of time. Industries can get upgraded (by delivering certain goods to them) and after reaching level 3 of a given industry type, you'll be able to build it in a completed town which still has room to accept more industries.
A part of the game which could be labeled as "casual" if not almost "idle-game like", at least on the vast Australian distances, is the repairing of broken roads, that prevent the trucks from reaching certain parts of the map, and blocking access to industries that eventually will be critically important to complete certain towns. To repair a road, you'll need a given amount of Gravel/Rock/Asphalt/Concrete, which, like in the case of industry supplying, you'll be able to do with no pressure whatsoever from the game.
Roads come in various sizes and this affect the trucks that can use them: the smaller roads, for examples, you won't be able to drive a truck larger than a 8tonner. Purchasing new trucks is possible, but the roads limitations do require a careful planning of the fleet (max 15 trucks in Australia): having many 200 t trucks, that can only travel on very few roads, could not be a wise move.
Logistical is not a very hard game, but this is exactly why it risks becoming so addictive: its greatest "pro" lies probably in its sense of scale and in giving the player the freedom in approaching the map as he sees fit. You're never told what you're gonna do: you can tackle the game however you want. The amount of towns to complete will seem really intimidating at first, but if Logistical -clicks- with you, trying to complete them will not feel as a chore. You'll WANT to complete it: the true challenge will be doing it in an acceptable number of hours. ;)
Almost anything in the game will trigger a Steam achievement. So if you're an achievement hunter, this game will be like heaven for you. :)
If you can get past the UI, Logistical has got what it takes to keep you glued to the screen civ-style... "Just one more city..."

What is a roleplaying game, and what makes it so? Levels? Progression? Items and Artifacts to collect?
If you think this is what a roleplaying game consists off, you are wrong - and totally so. A lot of old school Pen & Paper Roleplaying games didn't need levels, or a progression scale - and often Items and Artifacts just were something that were used against the players, not by them. Ever heard of classic games like Traveller, Prime Directive, World of Darkness (Vampire, Werewolf, Mage, Changeling among many others), Call of Cthulhu, Aria, Immortal, Nephilim or Shadowrun? All those games were good old school RPGs some made it to the Computer others like Aria and Immortal were torn beyond recognition, others like Prime Directive became known to a bigger fanbase through Starfleet Command and Starfleet Command II. Others like Shadowrun, Vampire, Call of Cthulhu became their direct ports.
The argument, that already arose when the genre was young in the seventies was the artificial "Plateaus" Leveled games offered and caused. Those pleteaus caused two things, which we still see in a lot of RPGs nowadays... One is the so called Monty Haul campaigning, to push the Characters over this Plateau artificially by supplying them with a lot of assets (Items mostly) and the other was the so called "Min Maxing"-Power creation, every player wanted that his character should survive therefore you often had fighters with scores of 18/00 and Constitution of 18... those things threw the concept of intelligent playing, and overcoming foes and obstacles over board, because every Character was a fricking demigod... which got worse by leveling up in both issues (More magical items, to push that plateau even further, or to raise the stats even to higher levels).
This said, this game is an RPG. Even though it doesn't offer progression or levels. And another thing that is quite unnerving by now, and Steam could change is the User defined tag system - you see a lot of false tags on games that don't offer what the tags are telling. It would be better to offer a developer driven Tag system. How many games are tagged with sexual content, that don't have anything in it with sex... and is it necessary to make a "Jewels" clone with just one spacey background to be tagged with "space"?
Since it is an uncommon RPG I will change the table for this kind of games.
Yes, I recommend this game, since it's a nice game telling a decent Science Fiction story, nothing too fishy and it includes some mysteries and clarifications about the background of the Space Pilgrim Setting.

LOGistICAL is a great, great game. It truly is, and the way it combines pure logical puzzles with fleet management is both unique and brilliant. LOGistICAL: British Isles is a huge stand-alone extension tot he game, giving you the entirety of the UK, plus Eire and the Channel Isles, to deliver to.
The basic set up is this: Every town and borough is represented, and every town's citizens have their own needs. You start out with an old banger of a truck, and you order that truck to drive to town B to deliver what town A wants. When you complete the delivery, you get money, so you can buy bigger, better trucks and go about appeasing the population of the entire country, one town at a time.
Here's the basic game flow as an example:
Town A wants apples.
Town B has an orchard, which means the town produces apples as a resource.
Town C has fertilizer, which the orchard needs to produce apples.
You take the fuel (fertilizer) to the industry (orchard) and wait for it to make the product (apples), at which point you can deliver the apples to town A.
Your truck will automatically go back and forth, until the number of apples the town needs is met, at which point the town becomes 'completed', and it's icon on the map goes from black and white to coloured, to reflect that. From now on, the town will never need another delivery.
So that's the puzzle side of things. The management side of the game comes from how and when you work on the towns. You see, until a town is completed it will consume the resources you provide it, and so you have to make sure you're assigning enough trucks and over not too great a distance to meet the demand, and finish the town.
L: BI features over two-thousand towns to complete, and has dozens of industries like the one I give an example of above, and many require multiple ingredients to complete. To compound the difficulty, there are also roads which will need to be repaired to be able to be used, and quarantine roads which don't allow the transfer of restricted goods via them.
And now the inevitable caveat: for everything the game does brilliantly, it obfuscates and behaves obtusely about something else. Even with the tutorial island included in the game (The Isle of Man), I remained mystified about changing game speed (which comes after completing capital cities) and unlocking industries to build manually (upgrade an existing industry to level three to get to these). The UI is absolutely awful. Even the old, original version of Transport Tycoon was more intuitive and friendly – here, everything is in hovering windows with nonsensical icons, with occasional other markers popping up now and then. Some things are just badly labelled: A truck action, 'skip', actually means set off now, even if it doesn't have a full hold of whatever it is it's going to deliver. Not, as I thought, skip the next destination in the chain. There is a small icon in the bottom right corner of the screen which give you instant tool-tips on everything, but it's still an obscure game to get into. I owned it for a couple of months, and it's only now I've really started to get the fabled 'one more town' feeling LOGistICAL fans crave.
Regardless of the UI, once you've learned it, it sticks. The game also integrates seamlessly with the base game, which features the entirety of Australia and has very full, satisfying DLC to bolster it's longevity, into the hundreds of hours. You can currently deliver goods to the entirety of Australia, New Zealand, California, Germany, The Netherlands, Hawaii, Egypt... The end goal is for the whole Earth to be represented, and skipping from one country module to the next is as easy as clicking on the globe and clicking a different country.
In summary, LOGistICAL is a fantastic puzzle game with a very addictive management mechanic, and if you spend two or three hours reading a guide and the manual and retrying the tutorial island, you'll end up loving the game and wanting to play it every spare second.

Simply the most frightening game I've ever played.  It presents a shockingly well polished game for a budget title price, and has become my favorite surprise hit of 2013.  Outlast masters both the art of pop out scares and a slow burn tense atmosphere, made much more compelling by music that reacts to the situation and dozens of small touches like seeing your hands as you clutch to the edge of a corridor to peek around the next hallway or the heavy ragged breathing of the player's character exerted from fleeing for his life but desperately trying to keep quiet in his hiding place to escape the horrors chasing him.  Also effective in building the tension is that the player's only way to see in the dark is through the night vision of the camera... which gives the world a very limited distance green/black view and also will quickly drain the batteries.  You force yourself to creep through darkness and use up every bit of electricity from each set of batteries even though your vision is failing just to save those precious batteries for when you can't make it without them.  As the song by Radiohead goes "You do it to yourself, you do, and that's what really hurts (or in this case, scares!)"
It's not a long game, the designers seem to know better than to wear out their welcome and at 8 hours of play time I feel I've more than gotten my money's worth for a lifetime memorable experience.  Thankfully I'm old and moved out because I'd owe my mother's "swear jar" a sock full of nickles for the outbursts I've had while fleeing in this game.  Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys a good scary story.

If you're looking to take control of an action spy and punch your way to glory, turn back, but if you want to experience an excellent man-on-the-run thriller in a more compact and interactive manner than it's original form then you've found your game. Lets be clear right from the start, this is a faithful adaption of a book, you can't change the outcome, you don't become the main character, and there are no headshot bonuses. So what do you get?
First off each scene is depicted in a beautiful hand-painted style. Given that you lose most of the scene description when you adapt in this manner it's very important that the artwork properly conveys each scene, and they really hit the nail on the head. You get voice acting on at least half of the text, most of the conversations or internal monologues, as well as atmospheric sound effects to add depth to scenes without voice acting. Generally the voices are unique and well done but the "heavy breathing while a character runs" was a little off-putting, at least for me. The final piece to the adaptation is the interactivity. Mostly you simply control the pace of the story but scattered through out are more interactive moments. Completing actions by drawing simple gestures with the mouse and selecting various objects of interest out of a scene make up the most of the interaction. While simple, these moments are well placed and definitely help with immersion. The later also lead to how most of the backstory is delivered. When you pick the objects out of the scene it brings up context and filler for the story often accompanied by historical photographs or newspaper clippings that add depth to the world.
As someone who has not read the original text I felt like I got the whole story and it was much smaller time-sink. The balance between reading, listening, and interacting is precise and kept me interested and engaged.

One thing that I love about video games is how they can take a story I've already heard several ways, and turn it into an entirely new experience that's just as engaging as if I was hearing it for the first time. The 39 Steps by The Story Mechanics is the first in what they call "digital adaptations", which fall somewhere between a visual novel and a radio show. The idea if simple, but the execution highly stylized and the pacing tightly wound to make what could have been a dry collection of text a surprisingly compelling and intense narrative piece.
I shouldn't have to tell you what The 39 Steps is about (as I imagine most should be familiar with the classic novel and numerous film adaptions and spin-offs), but as a refresher it follows Scottish man Richard Hannay, recently retired and now lost in a series of humdrum days and occurrences. All of this changes when a stranger barges into his life and revels a German plot that if carried out could throw the world into a war the likes of which it had yet seen. Shortly thereafter the man, now revealed to a spy known as Scudder, is found dead in Hannay's apartment, leaving him the only one alive with the knowledge of what is soon to unfold, and the only person who could possibly prevent it.
While the narrative of The 39 Steps is as intriguing and thrilling as ever, it's the way that it's told in this instance that makes it worth revisiting (or checking out for the first time) as opposed to numerous other formats you could choose. The Story Mechanics haven't settled for a simple text format in retelling Josh Buschan's tale, instead using a collection of visual tricks and clever insertion of backstory to create an brilliant interactive story that far exceeds the simplistic adaptations that have been experimented with in the past. Fantastic use of camera angles, deliberate placement of text to draw your eye toward parts of the watercolor backgrounds, and excellent voice acting from all parties make it incredibly easy to get swept away in the plot even during the slower, some may even call mundane, moments.
The only real instances where The 39 Steps falls a tad flat are the awkwardly implemented gestures that sometimes accompany moments like opening doors or reading letters. They were obviously intended to make the game feel more like, well, a game, but they're shoehorned in in such a way that feels tacked on an unnecessary. Thankfully they're infrequent enough that they never amount to more than a bit of a bother nor take but a few seconds to complete.
Though some might scoff at the emphasis on exposition and almost complete lack of traditional gameplay, those that can appreciate The 39 Steps for the bit of interactive fiction it is will be rewarded with an exciting and wonderfully paced tale of spies, murder, and more than a few close shaves. Having no real idea what to expect, I was very pleasantly surprised with the end result of The Story Mechanics's first attempt at a "digital adaptation", and it has gotten my mind spinning thinking of so many other books I'd love to see turned into future games. Hopefully this is only the first to come.

39 steps is an story-driven adventure about murder and espionage, politics and crime. The story is taken from John Buchan's eponymous 1914 book, and so well-adapted into a game - it lets you experience the story by only giving you remarkable lines and phrases and showing you minimalistic, but well-designed background pictures, thus there is some free room for your imagination (which is a plus about books, but a con when talking about films).
As critics might say, "its a text adventure with background graphics", I strongly recommend to view some videos and get some information about the game before buying it.
For there is a thrilling espionage plot to discover which speeds up after an hour. Interesting characters to meet along the journey from whom one does not know which side they are on. A hunt that begins at London, moves on to Scotland, to go back to England and has its dramatical final at the high circles of politics in London.
If you haven't read the book yet and fancy for innovative adventure games, you should (first inform yourself about it! and then) give it a try! Oh, and the OST is available for free!

Oh man, I am so glad I backed this game on IndieGoGo! I'm always a bit hesitant to back games like that, but this was definitely a winner.
Where to start?
Pros!
- I love the fact that there are numerous choices and extremely frequent at that! Most VN games have you make a choice once every 20 min of real time continuous game play, which can get a bit boring after a while when it's all reading and less choosing. I like having more choices, but I find myself rewinding a lot just to see how they all play out!
- Love that you can really truly build your own character with this game. You are not a cookie cutter docile doormat for everyone to tromp about, like in several other VN titles.
- Sexy mansprites, mmm.
- Just gorgeous art all around.
- Music is nice and appropriate for each setting; same with the sound effects.
- Enjoyable cryptographs to solve (I think that's what they are called? Or word jumbles?)
- Characters are memorable and great personality-wise.
- Lots of fun twists in this game, definitely expect the unexpected, and I am sure more to come!
- Devs actually releasing chapters when they say they will and keep their promises unlike other devs... this makes me trust them and want to buy more games from them in the future (keep up the awesome work!)
- If you backed this on IndieGogo, they sent out little padlocks with characters on them depending on the level of support... so now I have a padlock with a sexy demon man on it to bedazzle my...uh... anything that could use a demonman padlock! xDDD
The only "cons" right now...and I say that loosely because some of these aren't really cons, but just either room for improvement or it's such a different flavor that I am not used to it yet... :-x
- Have to wait for each chapter to come out. (Can't wait! AHHH!)
- I had no idea that I was supposed to be solving a puzzle to "translate" the demon language in this game. (Sorry if that is a spoiler... but yea, they did not really explain that at all, or maybe it was explained and I just missed it somehow? But I constantly kept clicking "give up" because I didn't understand what the heck was I supposed to do.)
- Some of the outcomes of choices don't really make any sense... but at the same time, this could be considered a "pro" since oftentimes VNs are too predictable...
- Voice acting can be a bit...uh, rough at times. But hey, I would rather have this than no voice acting so I guess I can't complain too much. The voice acting helps me keep my attention focused (I have really bad ADHD so it can be tricky to stay focused even with an amazing story!)
- Knowing exactly what happens when you pick something in terms of stat alignment is causing me to rewind and skew my choosing a bit... (e.g. "oh crap that made me +1 evil, I wanted +1 tact instead!" *savescums* LOL) One might argue this is good in the sense that you can really tailor your character to your own liking but I wish there was an option to toggle it off just to have a total blind playthrough...
I plan to update this review as they release the remaining chapters. Until then, I will probably go and replay the available sections just to get all the 'chievos. ;-3

Game runs very well on my phone and tablet which I have played the majority of hours on.  Even my 4-inch phone is easily playable due to clever interface design.  The game is also synchronized between your devices and steam account.
Presentation, artwork, and progression/card collection are derivative of Hearthstone.
What this means (if you never heard of Hearthstone) is that the "cards" animate themselves on the game board so it's easy to tell what their doing (attacking creatures smack the enemies, flying creatures hovering, spells shooting across the battlefield).  Not much is left to imagination (as would be the case in physical card games) which helps new players keep track of what's going on.
Card artwork skews toward "cartoony" but not in a childish way.  Admittedly I'm not a fan but that's personal taste.
Players earn cards through gameplay or opening packs but cannot trade with other players.  At the time of this review, the first PvP win of the day rewards a pack of cards.  This is an extremely generous way for players to complete their collection of common and uncommon cards with minimal grind.  Rares and legendaries will still require grinding or $$.
The gameplay itself is derivative of MTG.  So expect 5-color, playing resources, defender choosing who blocks, and instant spells on opponent's turn.  There are many keywords that take advantage of the digital space like warcry and echo.  Eternal features PvE modes but they feel more like a temporary thing to train up until you're ready to PvP.
I'm giving this game a thumbs up because:
- easy pick up and play
- well-polished presentation
- strong support for mobile devices
- room for complexity and growth
Now for the issues...
-Many players complain about the MTG style resource system that causes some games to be unplayble due to not drawing enough or too many resources.  The mulligan system and certain cards try to mitigate this, but it is still there.  Expect power screw, but no worse than MTG.
-75 card minimum deck reduces consistency.  This can cause deck building to lean toward high quality cards that are strong regardless of the deck instead of weaker cards that better synergize with the deck.
-There is also a massive power disparity between legendary cards and uncommon/commons.
^ These two points may be how Direwolf plans to $$ players towards legendaries, and how they can practically give away common/uncommons.
-Eternal requires an internet connection to play, even to PvE or tinker with decks.

If you haven't played Logistical before, I recommend you check out the base game (just called "Logistical") and look at the reviews on that, as they cover the game in much more depth than this review, which is mainly focusing on the content addition of the British Isles.
If you have played it before, you know exactly what you're getting into, and Logistical BI is more of the same. So far it's probably my favourite module in the series, playing similarly to a much larger version of the Netherlands. There's no scenario-specific ruleset (like New Zealand's unavailability of industry-building, or Germany's quarantine), but that just lets the game play to its strengths in my opinion, giving you a solid pack of uninterrupted content that you can do without needing to focus too heavily on any individual step of the process.
Importantly, this standalone module syncs up with the base game + DLC perfectly, letting you play any module you own no matter whether you're running the base game or this standalone British Isles version, and saving your progress between the two. This update also came with a revamped tutorial situated on the Isle of Man, and that proved to be a much more comprehensive guide to the game in an environment that was actually fully completeable, and a tutorial that I enjoyed completing despite having over 370 hours in the series by this point.
All in all, if you're a fan of Logistical, you'll love this content addition. If you're new to the series, I'd recommend starting with the base Logistical game, but if you live in the British Isles (or for some other reason would prefer to start on this module), then you'll find it easy to jump into and learn the mechanics of the game. Either way, I can't recommend it enough.

Let me start out by saying that Banished is awesome. It truly is what a city building/sim game should be. You have a handful of people and you need to make them survive.....The End. Don't expect warring factions, or alien attacks, just sit back, relax, and let Banished be what it is. I love this game so far, it's difficult but simple to play and the tutorials actually do a pretty decent job of actually telling you how to play it.
Now having said all that, I HATE THIS GAME! Banished has a knack for kicking you when you're down. Oh whats that? You had a good summer and are ready for winter? Guess what mofo......ALL YOUR CROPS JUST DIED AND YOU FORGOT TO MAKE WARM CLOTHES FOR THE NEW CITIZENS! MWAHAHAHAHAAHAAA!
This game is cruel, it will definitely test the patience of even the most skilled Sim players, and as you scream at your cat because your cattle has all disappeared and an outbreak of the plague is destroying your populace, you realize....this was all my fault! My god! I could have done things differently! I could have saved them all! I could have built a hospital and added just 1 more person to tend the flock! This is all my fault! Now my citizens are too sad to work effeciantly and winter is fast approaching!
The only complaint I have, and this is something I'm in the minority on, is that it would be nice to be able to advance your technology. Banished sticks with a single era and makes you ride it til you die. Oh and the the trade post can be quite unfair with how much you need to trade for whatever the trader is selling.

Honest Review (Spoilers might included):
This is the first time I play a game made by Ubisoft. I enjoy this game a lot (since I can explore the USA). And I don't care if the game have to launch Uplay, it's their game anyway.
Let's start.
It's true some (or most) of the missions usually have a same kind of objective, I don't deny it and it's kinda boring. But hey, I'm not rating the game only from the missions they provided to us.
The driving style kinda nice, but not too good, it's not way too simulatoristic, but also not too arcadish. For the perfomance part, you might want to farm it a bit since it's kinda hard to get a good parts.
The physics, yesss, I also notice that, the glitches and stuffs, but I found that funny to derp around. And no, the game not way too glitchy, don't worry.
The playground also HUGE, they cut a few parts of USA though, but whatever, it's BIG ! The map have a lot of activities to do, mostly just the same type of skills run, like speeds, precision. Don't worry about going from place to place, they got Fast Travel (After you explore the area first of course).
The AI catchup system might be the annoying part of the game, but that also keep me awake for the entire races, making the races not boring. Depend on how you see it in the end.
The cars, they don't have too much of it, but still have a nice modification, even though we can't freely modify the vinyl and the size of wings, etc etc~, but it's still nice to me. You don't have to go to your garage everytime you want to change your car, just a few buttons tap and voila! You use another car!
Pros:
- A large playground for you to play.
- You learn how to activate product on Ubisoft.
- Buy this game when on Sale!
- A new photo mode when freedrive!
- A Sexy nerdy girl, why not!
- Wild run expansion might be needed for more fun (Monster Truck! but you can't run over civ's car with it, only for stunts like flips and 360).
- You can have up to 4 person (include you) in a crew.
- Canadian border works!
Cons:
- Need to farm to get a good perfomance part and money.
- AI catchup might be annoying if you can't handle it too well.
- Overpriced Cars even though they look cheap.
- Too bad you can't save your race in the middle of it. if you tend to lose connection, I suggest don't buy since this game required a full internet connection.
- Most story missions contain same kind of objective that might make players bored.
I'll add more stuff to this review later.

"I've played through hundreds of games, what is this one amongst the others." I thought to myself, but the moment I put my foot into the first area where I found myself standing before a towering behemoth made of black steel my once strong spirit turned into a husk of its former self, that no amount of embers or effigies could return. So I continued to mentally strain myself attacking every creature in my way farming enough souls so that I can purchase a weapon to take down that beast. And so I did I took the weapon proudly down towards where I later would fall and die in the cold murky depths of the ocean. So thus I bring you my conclusion on this game. The digital interactive novel is still a medium in its infancy, piggybacking on the video game as its nearest cousin in the entertainment industry. The 39 Steps shows that there is great potential for this medium to spread its wings and achieve legitimacy as a distinct form of entertainment.
The presentation of the events in this work is simply stunning; everything from the artwork to the music to the way the text appears on-screen is always true to the tone of the moment.
The story itself is rather good, too. Many of the characters are absolute delights to see interacting, and the voice work for them is really top notch.
As long as you go into this expecting not a game, but a dynamic and mildly interactive retelling of a classic story, I am sure you will be pleased to play/read/watch it. (Incidentally, we really need a new verb for this.)

Outlast is a horror game par excellence. It dark and shadowy asylum is thick with atmosphere, and a regular string of scares builds tension that leaves you feeling genuinely on edge. As the game progresses and the player grows used to this sensation, things are kept fresh by slowly transitioning from being scary to being tense with more emphasis on a string of intense chases. The game is visually stunning on both a macro (level design, effects) and micro (texture work) level. Special mention should be made of the audio, which is excellent and really ads to the suspense. The only real letd own was an ending that broke with the atmosphere of the main game and somewhat confounds the player's expectations; full points for a willingness to experiment, but this ending felt like it belonged on a different game.

Alright, just played through The 39 Steps today. Took about 4 hours all told to complete, although there was probably an hour of idle time mixed in there. Anyway, I thought it was pretty stellar. A digital adaptation of a book. They say it was the inspiration for Ian Fleming style of writing, I think it bore a lot of similarities to Hitchcock's North by Northwest (and it turns out Hitchcock did in fact do a film adaptation of 39 Steps earlier in his career) as well. A very good and interesting story set in the early 1900's. Although there aren't branching paths, I thought the game till did an excellent job of immersing you into the story completely. Sort of non traditional from a point and click perspective due to a little twist in manipulating some object. The artwork was very nice, mostly done in watercolors and more traditional painting styles as well, with some silent film style cutscenes mixed in. Definitely recommend playing this one.

Interesting. A visual novel of the classic World War One era spy novel by John Buchan. You'll follow an English gentleman who has made his fortune in Africa and has grown bored out of his mind, when he stumbles onto an international conspiracy and rapidly gets in over his head.
Beautiful art, funny and innovative storytelling techniques, great music. The interactive segments are integrated with the narration well and feel like they serve the action rather than just pad it out. That said, interactivity is not its main attraction, so if you're not content with story alone this may not be for you.

BugZy's Review: Dub Dash

Rhythm-based games are my jam. Pun intended. I love games where you play to the beat (like Audiosurf and Guitar Hero) and Dub Dash is a great example of them, with its fast-paced levels and the ability to make you feel terrible for failing but constantly wanting to try “just one more time.”

Your ultimate goal in the game is to beat each level, and in each level is to not crash. You are presented with a bunch of tracks containing obstacles that you must avoid to the beat of the music playing by using the left and right arrows which bounce your wheel-like character to the corresponding side, then occasionally using those same keys to bounce up when the level changes to a Flappy Bird-like mode and a few others. This is challenging but very rewarding when you manage to finish the level successfully.

There is currently no way to create your own levels or play your own music which is an opportunity missed out on as lots of games available do have those options. There
a “Challenge Mode” that randomly generates levels for you to earn more lives though, and a practice mode to hone your skills while you get your body ready to play the actual level.

There are definitely some negatives, such as having to press the left or right key slightly earlier than normal because the game beat is ever so slightly out of sync for some of the levels. There is also mostly no beat-like element when the game switches to the flying mode, just trying not to crash into anything.

The game features bright and colourful visuals which resemble something like a 3D Geometry Dash and an awesome soundtrack with music from the great Bossfight and DJs from Geometry Dash (the main element it needs, after all it
a music-based game.)

Overall the game is a great play and I believe it is worth the money paid for it. It is genuinely a very fun experience and I enjoyed almost every moment of it. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys rhythm-based games.

This is the first time I play a game made by Ubisoft. I enjoy this game a lot (since I can explore the USA). And I don't care if the game have to launch Uplay, it's their game anyway.
Let's start.

The driving style kinda nice, but not too good, it's not way too simulatoristic, but also not too arcadish. For the perfomance part, you might want to farm it a bit since it's kinda hard to get a good parts.
The physics, yesss, I also notice that, the glitches and stuffs, but I found that funny to derp around. And no, the game not way too glitchy, don't worry.
The playground also HUGE, they cut a few parts of USA though, but whatever, it's BIG ! The map have a lot of activities to do, mostly just the same type of skills run, like speeds, precision. Don't worry about going from place to place, they got Fast Travel (After you explore the area first of course).
The AI catchup system might be the annoying part of the game, but that also keep me awake for the entire races, making the races not boring. Depend on how you see it in the end.
The cars, they don't have too much of it, but still have a nice modification, even though we can't freely modify the vinyl and the size of wings, etc etc~, but it's still nice to me. You don't have to go to your garage everytime you want to change your car, just a few buttons tap and voila! You use another car!
Pros:
- A large playground for you to play.
- You learn how to activate product on Ubisoft.
- Buy this game when on Sale!
- A new photo mode when freedrive!
- A Sexy nerdy girl, why not!
- Wild run expansion might be needed for more fun (Monster Truck! but you can't run over civ's car with it, only for stunts like flips and 360).

Cons:
- Need to farm to get a good perfomance part and money.

- Too bad you can't save your race in the middle of it. if you tend to lose connection, I suggest don't buy since this game required a full internet connection.

I'll add more stuff to this review later.
I rate it 7.9/10
Cheers!

You are Bright, a young woman living in the slums with her parents in a peaceful little town. Everything changed, however, when the Fire Nati--wait, I mean until a witch named Orchid requests your presence. What could this possibly mean? Dark times of course.
The game’s choices are entirely up to you. The story is an interesting one full of betrayal, death, resurrection, and a whole lot of debauchery. The voice acting is pretty good too. There aren’t spoken lines all the time, but when there is, it accentuates the story’s plot points, giving depth and personality to the characters. The voice work is quite nice and aren’t grating or out of place. The Demon in your head is especially witty.
So, you arrive to talk to Orchid after the summons, but soon find there are others who are meeting with her as well; a boy, a mean wench, and a rather suspicious looking hooded girl by the name of Ari. Orchid holds a contest to see who will work for her. You can select whichever choices you want when the moment comes, but if you’re curious about how the responses will be, you can always save in the pause menu and reload.
You can also see how your responses are shaping your character overall. The character alignment shows various personalities Bright will take on depending on which answer you choose. There is Good/Evil and Tactful/Defiant. I’m on the Tactful/Defiant alignment because I found myself immediately disliking Mark, Bright’s betrothed. So I never responded nicely to him. You get the option later to
. And I so did it, no remorse. :)
You’ll have instances where you decipher Demon Speak which is sort of like Scrabble, unscrambling words. You will also be identifying key objects of interest with your mouse in some scenes that will reveal more about the location you’re in or more about the plot.
The one thing that often pulled me out of the story were the expletives. Some of them were alright and fit with the story and lore. Other times, they felt a little out of place with certain situations and dialogues because it caught me off guard or came out of nowhere.
Controls use a mouse to either click or select things on screen, so there’s not much to it.
The art is gorgeous. The attention to each character and detail brings out their personality. Even more so when you hear their voices. The one thing that also stood out to me was that the world feels alive. The characters breathe and blink, smirk or squint. They feel more 3-dimensional for a VN where most of the time, the characters are images that don’t move at all. Very nice touch.
The music is also fitting for the story and works well to build suspense and add to the drama overall.
I highly recommend Demonheart. It’s a very different VN that does some things others have, but better. I enjoyed the voice work, the depth of the different characters, and the strange and mysterious story unfolding.
Episode 3 is slated to release August 21st, 2017 and I will definitely be all over that. So, if you enjoy VNs with some dark humor, gorgeous artwork, interesting cast of characters, and the ability to fully flesh out your protagonist and align them how you want, Demonheart is definitely one to pick up.

If you’ve heard a lot about the Dark Souls 2 franchise but aren’t sure with how you’d fare with the franchise trade-mark “punishing” gameplay, this is the best jumping off point. Purists will justifiably criticize the game for its easier difficulty through weaker enemies, easier bosses, and frequent checkpoints (known as bonfires), but I feel that these all fall by the wayside when considering the lengths the game went to top its previous game in almost every single aspect. But make no mistake - its combat system will challenge you to think before you go in for an attack.
In the process, there are two glaring issues with this game that have gotten the goat of casuals and die-hards of the series. Of the two, the most unforgiving is how nonsensical aspects of the in game world can be. Yes, this is a tall order when compared to DS1, where the map had to link up well because you only had to travel to some parts of the game half-way through it. But in this game, it’s understandable that the map design can get a little lazy because you can teleport to every bonfire. In light of the wonky topography, I needed it to be pointed it out to me because of how brilliant the overall design of every level is. It’s one of those instances where the individual parts are greater than the whole. The other is soul memory, which was sort of a ranking system based on the overall amount of souls. Because I was playing with a skilled friend, it was a bit of a nuisance to grind.
Aside from that, the game has a diverse amount of enemies and ways to kill them that vary in difficulty and combat style. This game also started the fad of “Fashion Souls”, where people would make hilarious outfits based on how much you could customize your appearance through the amount of strange wearable gear you can find.
There was also just an insane amount of detail to the levels in terms of crafting unique ways to traverse them, placement of loot, and just the sheer prettiness of the map design (via graphics in 2014). You’ll want to keep a guide nearby to fully appreciate both their trolls and elaborate interactions with environments in the interest of leading you to secret areas and top tier loot.
You can gaze the reviews or watch amped up PvP videos of this game all day long. But the 7.49 USD investment of this game when it’s on sale will definitely have a return on your investment as an RPG that will rope you in with dazzling environments, a quirky cast of NPCs and enemies, and a highly customizable combat system that encourages player progression from level to level or just plain farming to further customize your gear. If you had any inkling to dive in to the series, I would start here. The story is hard to figure out, and is not required to enjoy these games.
NOTE: You must buy this version (Scholar Of The First Sin /SotFS), as the additional DLC will add another 10+ hours of content. If possible, do it as you go along for an extra challenge and more powerful loot to make the game that much more interesting.
