Games of the horror genre usually don't hold my attention well, (either because I find them a bit over the top in the scare department, or they are lacking in anything but jump scares).  Outlast however somehow manages to keep me playing, and feeling nervous at the same time.
Before I go into any sort of detail let me place Outlast's concepts in 3 simple steps.
Step 1- Give players an eerie atmosphere with a basic creepy concept, such as I don't know, say an insane asylum? (Wait this does work, trust me)
Step 2- Tap into the human psych and our deep down fear of being chased and hunted and place them in an interactive story 20 inches from our faces.
Step 3- Continue to attack that primal fear relentlessly until we actually have to put down the controller/keyboard/mouse.  Then make us come back so we can experience this thrill as soon as our heart rate settles down again.
This shouldn't be a working formula for a good game, but for some reason, this works fantastic for Outlast.
This basic bit of thought pattern is what I call the "Outlast Effect"(Yes i have been using this term out of the game!) The best way to describe this sensation is when you turn out the last light in the basement and quickly run up the stairs because you can feel or sense something lurking in the dark behind you.
Given the fact that your character is only equipped with a video camera, which can record the horrors you face( and also provides you with semi-good night vision), the action can get quite intense.
Outlast often makes you feel like someone is watching you, and this is usually the case.  You always feel as if around every corner you'll get a nasty surprise or find someone who wants you dead.  Yes, there are a bunch of jump scares, but they are very well placed and they seem to be placed strategically rather than in obvious spots.  The true horror this game provides is during its countless chase scenes. The game mechanics can add to this sensation greatly if you choose to use them well.  You can spin your head to look backwards to see if the enemy chasing you is gaining ground, you can also dive through doors, turning quickly to slam it shut on your pursuers. You can hide under beds, in lockers and sneak through small cracks that you can barely squeeze through.  The ability to hide from the enemy makes it interesting as well, and the AI reacts quite well to finding you.  Early in the game they rarely check for you in the correct hiding spots but as the game progresses the enemies seem to act more randomly and tend to catch you hiding more often. The game mechanics work excellent in this setting as well.  The mental hospital provides small narrow corridors, which are perfect for providing you with a claustrophobic feeling once the bad guys start chasing.
The sound in this game is fantastic, from your character's breathing when you are hiding, to the sounds of the mumbling maniacs pursing you down the narrow corridors.  The different types of enemies come with their own sounds, some of the larger baddies carry chains, and one even has a massive pair of scissors.  You can often hear muffled footsteps in a room close by, or echoes down long corridors.  The music is very well orchestrated to fit the tone of being helpless and it seamlessly fades in and out according the danger.
The visuals are also done well, the graphics are on par with any of the newer releases and the animation is fantastic.  When learning around corners your hand can be seen pressing against the walls or doorframes.  These items may seem like small detail, but that's actually what makes a good game noticeable in my opinion.
Overall this is a fantastic addition to anyone's steam library.  The story is a bit lacking and considering the action is all about hiding and fleeing rather than fighting it may not be for everyone.
Outlast gets a 9/10, and a big thumbs up!

I've played this game before on mobile. As a matter of fact, I've played ALL the SASZA games. SASZA2 was probably the first one that I actually invested time into (did free offer, got some mochi coins, got the MP7, kicked major♥♥♥♥♥. When SASZA3 came out, I came. It was amazing in every single way. It came out on mobile and well....holy crap, it blew the desktop version OUT OF THE WATER. Till this day I STILL play SASZA3 proudly maxed out my rank 3-4 times with every single weapon unlocked. One thing I disliked about SASZA3 is that at the time of writing this, you can't transfer your mobile profile to desktop via cloud syncing, hopefully one day but probably not happening. Aside from that, SASZA3 was EASILY better than SASZA4 (IMO).
Is SASZA4 bad? Nah its alright. Everything ZA3 did was better IMO. However, today I must give ZA4 some credit. ZA4 allows us to connect our mobile account to Steam. Thats still only one point for ZA4 but its an important point as not many mobile games allow that and I've played PLENTY of mobile games and well....not many are ported to PC in the first place so theres that but this game started off as a flash-game found on sites like Freewebarcade, Ninjakiwi, Mochigames, etc. then it moved to the mobile market but when they made the move, the thought of allowing us to transfer our PC accounts over to mobile and vice versa was not implemented at the time. I truly hope ZA3 comes to Steam with the ability to connect/log into mobile profiles, I haven't touched the PC version of SASZA3 ever since Mochigames was shutdown and all our accounts were transferred over to Ninjakiwi (I lost all my account progress for every Mochi/Ninja game like Counter-Snipe and ofc, SASZA2/ZA3).
So lets start with some pros:
- Nice gear catalog. Its not SASZA3 large or cool IMO but theres plenty of guns/armor. As you go up the levels, you get higher rarity CRATES which have a chance of dropping higher rarity/level guns.
- Augmentation of weapons/armor. A litle more in-depth compared to SAS3's super simplistic upgrade system. Some of these abilities/augmentations are amazing. Biosynthesis for example. Every kill regenerates a certain amount of health back. Combine that with health regen character skill, you're not dying anytime soon.
- Character skill upgrades (universal and class specific), once again its a lot more in-depth than SAS3 so you can change up your playstyle and whatnot. Universal skills would be like health regen, or energy regen. Class specific would be like medkits for the medic class. Universal skills are generally passive. Class skills require energy to use but energy regenerates over time.
- Cross Platform. This version is specifically a port of the mobile version, NOT the web browser version. Therefore you can play on your phone by simply connecting your accounts.
Oh boy...the cons:
- While the weapon/armor catalog is nice, you can't just buy weapons/armor like SASZA3. It gives you freedom but at the same time its restricting. Plus you can ONLY get guns/armor through crates. Yes, crates or strongboxes...like getting skins from CSGO...except you get guns which are basic pieces of equipment...not skins...essential pieces of gear that shouldn't be obtained through the damn lottery.
- Crate/Strongbox system. This game relies SOLELY on the crate system. In my eyes, ANY game that relies solely on crates deserves AT LEAST 10 gaming sins. So ding it 10 or more times. Yes that was a CinemaSins reference. Games that have crates on the side like CrossFire, Combat Arms, or CSGO deserve 1-5 sins at most depending on what the crates provide. This game deserves AT LEAST 10 sins for SOLELY RELYING ON CRATES ONLY. I play games like CF because I have the freedom to buy whatever gun I want. I dislike games that a) restrict weapons to classes (unless its Battlefield) and b) Crates. I'm not here to win the lotto, I don't plan to spend $100 just to have a 1% chance of getting a weapon I want. I'd rather be a P2W noob and spend $100 get exactly what I want over winning a weapon after spending $2000. CSGO deserves at least 1 sin only because of what the crate system has done (people buying and selling skins and being cancerous) but at least those are just that...skins. CF and CA have their fair share of standard permanent weapons and special weapons out of crates so 1-5 sins at most. SAS4 however, you can ONLY get guns/armor through crates. You can get daily crates for logging in, you can usually find them around the map, you get them through leveling. Is that really a better system than SAS3 and its "level up, unlock, buy" system? Keep in mind, in SAS3 had premium weapons for a small price, or you can buy a premium weapons package which unlocks ALL present AND future premium weapons. Eventually SAS3 introduced SAS Bucks which is freemium currency. You can either buy premium weapons with real money OR freemium currency which can be earned.
- Inventory limit. Because of the damned crate system, you're bound to get a duplicate gun which could be better or worse. In total you have 20 inventory slots for weapons and armor. 3 weapons you bring to the field, 17 storage. Once you're full and you pick up a crate and you get a new weapon, you either sell that new weapon or sell something you own. 5 slots for equipped armor (head, body, hands, legs, feet) and 15 storage.
- Complicated. So the introduction of Augmentations for weapons and armor, character skills plus classes is cool and all but theres one downside compared to its predecessors. Things get much more complicated. Before in SAS3, you buy a gun, you level up, you buy the next gun and so on. When it came to upgrades, all guns get 5 stats that can be upgrade 5 times. Simple. Armor was the same thing. There were no character skills or specific classes. You just join with your selected loadout and let off some steam. Now you need to manage your weapons and what to bring because of the MANY different types of zombies and their immunities, you need to manage your armor combos, you need to manage your augmentations for both weapons AND armor to make sure you've got the right stuff for what mission, finally you need to make sure you have the right passive and active character skills. Oh and of course, make sure its on the right character/class.
- Character slots. Without premium you get 4 character slots which you unlock via leveling up, you have 3 classes total so thats simple enough, you use 3 slots, one for each class. However, your Exp does not transfer from one to the other and obviously neither does your gear. They are connected to the same account but are completely seperate at the same time. In SAS3 you had one character, maybe one AI buddies gear to manage and that was it. SIMPLE. Now I gotta decide if I want to play with my highest level character or grind through the levels on my other two characters. Plus you CAN'T transfer weapons and armor over to other characters.
- This game is an absolute GRINDFEST. So is SAS3 and its predeccessors but this game....to me is much more grindy compared to SAS3 and the payout just isn't that great compared to SAS3. Even SAS2 was better.
- The lack of maps. In SAS3 you had MANY different maps. They had a world map, you select a region and it'll give you 5 maps from there. You had 3 different modes PLUS "daily" missions of various tasks. Not so much the case for SAS4.
Overall, the game is fine, but compared to SAS3 mobile which unfortunately won't be coming to Steam (confirmed by dev) this game was really a giant letdown. I still play this obviously but compared to SAS3 nowhere near as long. SAS3 was simple. None of the class complications and 11 weapons/armor augmentations and 19 character perks/skills and inventory limit. Instead of joining a game with guns and killing, you're now managing skill points, and your inventory...FUN AMIRITE?! Oh and no Strongboxes or crates bullcrap.
HIGHLY ADDICTING. If only we could get a real release date for the second one...

When they say 'hardcore', that is not an overstating buzzword.
This game is probably the closest any cooking title will ever get to being a Hell's Kitchen simulation. The recipes are simple in execution, but what is not simple is the VOLUME in which you be cooking them. If Cooking Mama was to cooking at home, Cook, Serve, Delicious is to cooking in an environment where your lifestyle is on the line. The game eases you in with some simple difficulty and really easy to make recipes, but as you progress through restaurants in which you're going to be held to a higher standard, so to must you be able to go above and beyond. In case the day to day tedium of completing service days isn't giving you the proper motivation, the game also includes a devious betting system, which dares you complete a chain of perfect orders in a row with specific items on your menu, so no comfort zone here, unless that comfort zone is LITERALLY EVERYTHING.
But this game is by no means boring or unfair. Getting perfect days is still possible, but you'll have to manage your money wisely and deal with the ever unpredicatable orders of customers. It's no wonder this game got a sequel. I would recommend this game, but be forewarned, you're going to take a lot of hits until you eventually succeed.

If you had told me before VVVVVV that a difficult platformer with a simple concept that is based around precision-timing jumps would not only
give me a burning desire to throw the controller at the screen in frustration, but that I would actually have a hard time letting go of said controller for almost the whole duration of the game, you probably would've gotten a face full of sarcastic laughter (which sounds eerily like the Super Meat Boy tune). Or, more likely, I would've ignored your suggestion until I got the game half-free as part of a Humble Bundle (sorry, brother, your suggestions are the best!) and had no excuse not to play this highly-praised game.
I enjoy quality platforming as much as most gamers and don't mind the difficulty that typically comes with such games, especially when they are indie-made. But I need to be in a very specific mindset if I am to endure countless re-attempts at the slightest mistake and I run out of that energy eventually regardless of how far I got in the game. VVVVVV rectifies the image of indie platformers you have in your head with a surprising breath of clarity - even the confusing name makes perfect sense after staring at those same spikes room after room. Instead of jumping, you switch gravity back and forth so that you're either standing on ground or on the ceiling - and that's all there is to it. No upgrades, no weapons, everything you come across is doable from the get-go. The world is open, reminiscent of Metroidvania games, but even with a minimal plot and the ability to choose your own path, playng is straight-forward and you never feel lost.
What could've been only a gimmick or
-gameplay comes together as a tight, addictive package, thanks to the gratituous use of checkpoints. There is typically at least one in each room and as you die you reappear next to it without further hassle, so once you figure out how to gravity-change yourself out of the next pickle or ace the pixel-tight patterns of moving obstacles, you're safe again.  Dying constantly is not only allowed, it's
, with the total number of deaths in your current playthrough proudly displayed in the menu. There are Steam achievements for finishing the game with a small number of deaths, but you don't have to care about that unless you really want to. You can collect trinkets in the game, which unlocks some extras, and there are a few which can test your patience, but thanks to the checkpoints, you don't have to memorize minutes of tough manouvers; it's all finely chopped down.
Of course, the platforming in this game is still challenging - if you didn't enjoy the joys of precision jumping in a game like the original Super Mario Brothers, you probably won't enjoy this. But the game isn't needlessly or falsely difficult. VVVVVV presents itself as exactly as it is, trial-and-error gameplay in the word's most positive sense. You can focus on the platforming puzzles without being punished for dying while trying to get a "feel" of each room's pattern. Each new checkpoint reached feels like a little win and you get through even the more difficult parts with the knowledge that the gameplay is logical and rewards your patient learning, not luck.
Of course, the game also has a great soundtrack and little details like the amusing dialogue and room names. My biggest grief is with the Steam Achievements; they should be more varied. Finishing with less and less deaths makes sense as a challenge, as do the flip mode and no-death mode achievements, but the many Super Gravitron and perfect Time Trial achievements seem pointless and don't motivate to play more.

Outlast starts off really well and the setting of this game is truly terrifying. You have no idea what to expect as you nervously explore the Asylum. Each corner, each room, there could be anything waiting to jump out at you. Armed with only a camcorder you are left helpless against attacks. Its this constant fear that keeps you on your toes and makes this game so great.
Unfortunately, there is a gradual decline in gameplay quality which lets it down. It becomes a repetitive game of cat and mouse as you run around different mazes trying to find an exit. Finding a key for the locked door/elevator over and over becomes tiresome and the fear factor was lost.
Overall this game is worth a try, especially for those who are easily frightened ;)

A full choice story game with romance and violence that doesn't control your every move? You better believe it.
For the first time, I was actually shocked and delighted such a well designed visual novel existed. I really wish I could draw more attention to this game.
With their ambiently animated cast, it really added that tiny bit of realism into them so you didn't feel like you were just talking to a portrait like a low budget otome. You can feel as if you have more to look at than just words.
The characters were all fleshed out and ANY questions that arose were excellent for story progression and (HIDDEN) answers.
Really well thought out in the fact that normally, whatever you feel as your own personal reaction to a situation will be a choice you can make. These heavy choices may be taken lightly, but they can alter your 'alignment' throughout your story; which actually DOES affect how characters react to you, or how things happen to you in the story; especially with your 'Infernal Patron'.
The story holds strong and may seem a bit fast paced if you're really rushing through to devour the story, or if you're a fast reader. Sometimes even I felt that it moved a bit fast, even for no reason. Honestly, I don't suggest blazing through this like some cheaply made Visual Novel or Otome. There is a lot of underlying story you need to pay attention to.
However, it holds a very "colorful"(dangerous) world and somewhat predictable backgrounds. Sometimes, it feels like your choices don't really matter- and there are no threats to speaking your mind (Or simply opting to be a ♥♥♥♥♥) other than a character becoming annoyed with you for 2 seconds. There are times when a character may say or do something that won't make any sense, either- especially if you didn't gather everything storywise along the way. There was one time in which even that wasn't an excuse, and a character may become very... odd.
The backstory for each character (pointing fingers to the patron) gives you the insight to the bigger picture, which is very important to not be blindsided later on; and is in general, worth replaying to test all the choices to find them. It took me personally 3 playthroughs to realize my 'patron' didn't know what a goat was, and he seemed to have a great distaste for things the player could know or have read during the game. Either way, he might not take kindly to every choice you make. This 2nd main character is made up of your choices (Somewhat?? but is mostly an infernal ball of sass). All in all- he's very worth the play to 'meet' in the new chapter.
Voice acting was the only SLIGHT negative as it was picked only for some lines. While sometimes you might expect something important spoken, it likely won't be, even if the comedic effect would worked better that way.
I personally really loved what was available for this game, and truly and honestly recommend it for people who want to really feel inclusive in a story or play as a woman capable of being a badass 'don't need no man' type.
I'll also say to buy it BEFORE it is complete, as the creators might raise the price.

EDIT: I've gotten through just about everything now and have eventually decided to stop playing altogether. I have nothing more positive to say about the game and my opinions remain unchanged.
Let me say first off, the music is awesome, the graphics are great, this game clearly has a lot of time put into it to make it look good. From what they were trying to execute I can understand what they're doing. But that is immediately where the praise stops because this game is a non-enjoyable amount of infuriating.
- The gameplay: Dub Dash is an edgy and trippy rhythm game where you avoid obstacles to the beat of the music, or so it seems. The first thing you will notice is that the controls get very strict, especially in more dense sections of levels, because if you slip up once and start going off beat then there's absolutely no way to recover until the obstacles slow down. Additionally, as someone who has played a multitude of rhythm games, Dub Dash has fairly mediocre syncing to the beat of the music they use. In almost every single level I've played I've had to hit my buttons ever so slightly earlier than oncoming measures in order for my racer to remain on beat. I'm also really not cool with how some of the sections play out. There's a flying section that I feel is completely absent of any rhythm mechanics and turns into a mediocre space flyer game with very slippery controls. There's also the maze segment, which is a lot less enjoyable than it appears to be because instead of using the directional keys to move in that direction you're just limited to the left and right controls (like all of the other segments), which makes things really awkward when you're going in the opposite direction, and of course I shouldn't even have to go into detail on what might as well be called the "Flappy Bird" segment, which features gameplay I can only describe as "exquisite." If this is supposed to be marketed as a rhythm game then all of the non-rhythm segments (the flying and flappy bird segments, for example) need to be scrapped from here permanently. There are so many different play styles here it all just feels exceptionally inconsistent and choppy. If you're going to make a rhythm game you need to keep it a rhythm game. Of course you can mix things up as long as it retains a consistent theme all throughout, but this is not the way to do it. The way I see it this is just a poor combination of different ideas that didn't have a leg to stand on on their own, and it shows extremely well in the presentation.
- Practice Mode: If you're having trouble beating a certain level then you can enable practice mode, where you can crash as many times as you want and still restart from the last checkpoint. That sounds really helpful, right? Unfortunately there's one huge problem with it. The actual game music doesn't play when you practice. So if, for example, you wanted to practice the song Milky Ways then it's not going to play that song and instead play the generic menu music throughout the level, and because the songs have differing BPM values that throws the entire level off sync. For a game that's all about rhythm and staying on beat this is 100% counter-intuitive and often makes the practice mode harder than the actual level.
- The life system: If you crash you can resume right at the last checkpoint you reached, which again sounds really helpful doesn't it? Unfortunately there's a limited amount of times you can do this, as denoted by the amounts of hearts you have. What happens if you run out of hearts? You have to start all the way from the beginning of the song, sort of like running out of lives in Super Mario and having to start from the beginning, which doesn't sound so bad until you realize your hearts don't refill if you run out and have to start over, and if you're playing a level for the first time without any prior knowledge of what the rest of the map looks like then you'll be expending these hearts exceptionally fast. The only way to refill your hearts is to complete monotonous challenges outside of the main game mode. These "challenges" involve completing a repetitive map that is just as long as the normal levels, and you have to beat these challenges without crashing once, which proves to be just one big chore when it comes to doing something as simple as getting extra lives. You may also notice that as you unlock more main levels the challenge stages get more needlessly difficult, adding more tedium to, once again, something as simple as getting more lives. I should also mention that the life limit caps at 15, thus preventing you from farming up to a much more acceptable amount. In all honesty I think the game as a whole would be so much better if the whole lives concept was scrapped altogether and just allowed you to always respawn at the last checkpoint. Repetition does NOT count towards challenging gameplay. It would be a lot more fun if it worked more like Rhythm Heaven, where you can make as many mistakes as you want and play all the way up to the end of the song, and then you get a rating based on how well you performed.
Overall from what I've played Dub Dash has proven to be very disappointing to me, which I in turn also find to be disappointing because the game has so much going for it. Unfortunately the way it controls and plays has left me quite bitter. It is not a good game, it's all flashy with nothing of substance to show, and it has utterly failed as a rhythm game.

Now I myself am a "tabletop player" but there is a problem with all these tabletop simulators. It plays like a real tabletop game, and not a PC game. When you play a game of Mario Party, you don't freely move around the pieces, everything is automatic, you roll the dice and your character moves so the following spaces themselves. All of these games don't do that, it gives you all the pieces, a rulebook, and no tutorial on how to play the game. People who are not tabletop players have no clue what their doing, its like giving a random person a blueprint for your house and all the pieces to the house, and then telling them to build it with no explanation on how to do it, just the blueprint. If this was marketing for PC gamers (which it clearly was) it failed miserably. Just look at other negative reviews on this game, its 99% of people saying they have no idea what their doing.

When someone mentions movie tie in games do you get a little knot in your stomach, the sheer amount of garbage we've gotten over the years is rather astounding.  Well rest assured Cars: Radiator Springs doesn't come close to even trying to resemble a good or even a half way decent game.  This was a time when THQ was trying to find a way to stop the bleeding of money, so they went head long into licensing any and every movie tie in they could get.... err well they could get before activision swooped them up..
I went into the game looking at it as a young child would, after all this is Cars, one of the ever popular Pixar movies.   My expectations were low but I trudged onward.  Upon starting up the game I noticed it didn't fit in my resolution which is 1920 x 1080.  I said ok, and went searching for the option menu..  awesome no way to change the resolution.  Not a problem I just sucked it up and continued on.
The game presents you with 3 options as far as the main menu goes. Activites (which are just mini games), Legends race and Lighting McQueen's Racing Headquarters (awesome name for the options menu, but that sums up this game in a nutshell) which is pretty much just the options and a few little benefits, like unlocked movies (don't get excited it's just cut scenes from the game) car customization (which isn't really anything more than some color swaps) and some photos you can unlock..
Starting with.. Mini games, it's a real hodgepodge of stuff, I can admire the attempt at trying to teach kids memorization and puzzle solving skills.  Even a little eye hand coordination thrown into the mix.  I had no real issues with the mini games except a few very glaring glitches and poor explanation on a few of them.   A few of them were set up like that old Simon game (the circle with 4 buttons that light up in a pattern)  much like the Simon game the concept seems fun for about 10 minutes, then you're left saying, man this is kind of boring..
Another mini game see's you guiding a nut through  McQueen's tailpipe... (Woah there Pilgrim this is a Disney game, it's an actual nut.. get your mind out of the gutter), Yet another finds you catching tires, while another has you rearranging cars so McQueen can leave the drive in movies..
Enough with the activities, onto the meat of the game..   It's Drag Racing !!!!  Wait what? This is a game for children (i'll assume young children) and it's about drag racing?  With that moral dilemma aside lets talk about Legends racing... or Drag racing a cheating AI as I like to call it..  The AI cheats, even on the easist race, winning in a lesson in futility, in fact the racing is little more than holding the drive button, while at the same time watching a meter (not the awesome tow truck) fill then pressing the mouse button at the right time to switch gears.  It's boring, even for my 9 year old, he played the game for little more than 2 minutes before he was rushing off to do something else.

Hearts of Iron III is the long awaited sequel to probably the best Grand Strategy game available today and it's a fairly big change.
The most noticeable change is the change to the Clausewitz Engine which means everything is prettier and better presented although this was never an area that really needed much improvement it is nice to be see graphics not being completely forgotten by Paradox.
The most meaty of the new changes is the new AI. Every level of command can now be assigned an AI to simply the sometimes unmanageable big armies and while this seems like a nice feature I can't help but feel much like I did the first time played Master of Orion 3. Out of control.
Paradox has also, like with EU3, taken as much determinism out of the game as possible and while this opens up the gameplay quite a bit it also increases the chance of games that never get going when some of the big players never enter the fray.
A great game but I still like Hearts of Iron II better.

Outlast is a horror game par excellence. It dark and shadowy asylum is thick with atmosphere, and a regular string of scares builds tension that leaves you feeling genuinely on edge. As the game progresses and the player grows used to this sensation, things are kept fresh by slowly transitioning from being scary to being tense with more emphasis on a string of intense chases. The game is visually stunning on both a macro (level design, effects) and micro (texture work) level. Special mention should be made of the audio, which is excellent and really ads to the suspense. The only real letd own was an ending that broke with the atmosphere of the main game and somewhat confounds the player's expectations; full points for a willingness to experiment, but this ending felt like it belonged on a different game.

Games of the horror genre usually don't hold my attention well, (either because I find them a bit over the top in the scare department, or they are lacking in anything but jump scares).  Outlast however somehow manages to keep me playing, and feeling nervous at the same time.
Before I go into any sort of detail let me place Outlast's concepts in 3 simple steps.
Step 1- Give players an eerie atmosphere with a basic creepy concept, such as I don't know, say an insane asylum? (Wait this does work, trust me)
Step 2- Tap into the human psych and our deep down fear of being chased and hunted and place them in an interactive story 20 inches from our faces.
Step 3- Continue to attack that primal fear relentlessly until we actually have to put down the controller/keyboard/mouse.  Then make us come back so we can experience this thrill as soon as our heart rate settles down again.
This shouldn't be a working formula for a good game, but for some reason, this works fantastic for Outlast.
This basic bit of thought pattern is what I call the "Outlast Effect"(Yes i have been using this term out of the game!) The best way to describe this sensation is when you turn out the last light in the basement and quickly run up the stairs because you can feel or sense something lurking in the dark behind you.
Given the fact that your character is only equipped with a video camera, which can record the horrors you face( and also provides you with semi-good night vision), the action can get quite intense.
Outlast often makes you feel like someone is watching you, and this is usually the case.  You always feel as if around every corner you'll get a nasty surprise or find someone who wants you dead.  Yes, there are a bunch of jump scares, but they are very well placed and they seem to be placed strategically rather than in obvious spots.  The true horror this game provides is during its countless chase scenes. The game mechanics can add to this sensation greatly if you choose to use them well.  You can spin your head to look backwards to see if the enemy chasing you is gaining ground, you can also dive through doors, turning quickly to slam it shut on your pursuers. You can hide under beds, in lockers and sneak through small cracks that you can barely squeeze through.  The ability to hide from the enemy makes it interesting as well, and the AI reacts quite well to finding you.  Early in the game they rarely check for you in the correct hiding spots but as the game progresses the enemies seem to act more randomly and tend to catch you hiding more often. The game mechanics work excellent in this setting as well.  The mental hospital provides small narrow corridors, which are perfect for providing you with a claustrophobic feeling once the bad guys start chasing.
The sound in this game is fantastic, from your character's breathing when you are hiding, to the sounds of the mumbling maniacs pursing you down the narrow corridors.  The different types of enemies come with their own sounds, some of the larger baddies carry chains, and one even has a massive pair of scissors.  You can often hear muffled footsteps in a room close by, or echoes down long corridors.  The music is very well orchestrated to fit the tone of being helpless and it seamlessly fades in and out according the danger.
The visuals are also done well, the graphics are on par with any of the newer releases and the animation is fantastic.  When learning around corners your hand can be seen pressing against the walls or doorframes.  These items may seem like small detail, but that's actually what makes a good game noticeable in my opinion.
Overall this is a fantastic addition to anyone's steam library.  The story is a bit lacking and considering the action is all about hiding and fleeing rather than fighting it may not be for everyone.
Outlast gets a 9/10, and a big thumbs up!

The Thirthy-Nine Steps is one of the earliest and arguably most influential novel in the history of espionage thriller. The book by John Buchan, published in 1915, is now public domain which means the devs could get away with anything in this digital adaption. But what surprised me is they were extremely loyal to the plot. This digital adaption is even told in 1st person like the original work. They did not offer any changes, which can be termed as lazy. But a novel that doesn't need change shouldn't be changed anyway. Voice acting is good. Story-telling is done right. The only thing that bugged me is the lack of character "appearance" in the artwork. But that's not a big deal. Anyway, this is a good digital adaption of the novel and I highly recommend it.
Warning - Do not buy if you're looking for a game. This is NOT a game, not even a point and click game. This is basically a audio novel with some relevant artwork.

My review for Fallout 3! (And my Pros/Cons)
PROS:
Hundreds of hours of epic gameplay in the Capital Wasteland!
With DLC's about 50+ hours at least (plus new perks, weapons, enemies, quests, and other stuff)
Varied terrain, enemies, weapons, quests, armor, perks, and other items
Crafting/repair system
Game that is open-world
Graphics are phenomenal for its time
Karma System
CONS:
After completing largely everything in the game its hard to play again (can get sick of playing too much)
Graphics need reworking (in my opinion)
Some weapons largely have no effect on enemies
Pistols in game need to be completely re-worked (e.g. sights, recoil, damage, animations sometimes)
Some quests are variations of each other
If you dont like large games you wont like this
Game might erase your save
There are certain enemy and graphics glitches that are known to happen
OVERALL: This game is revolutionary! I highly recommend this title to every gamer! Even though my CONS outweigh my PROS I still believe this game is still very good but with limited replay. 9/10

The game was very promising when it first released in early access. However it seems like nothing changed since then. I still see people in the forums having the same issues that they had before. I personally don't think I had any major issues however the game has always seemed somewhat lacking in content. I don't think it's a terrible game, in fact it's very fun cracking the code, as you do in these types of games. However, the problem is that it is probably one of the least satisfying games once you've cracked it. I can think of at least a half dozen games that are similar and much more enjoyable, as well as cheaper. If you are a big fan of the genre I would say it is worth a try but don't expect the world. In fact I would say if you have relatively low expectations you will be pleasantly surprised. But if you go in expecting it to be really great and really dig into it you'll probably exhaust the fun long before other games such as Dwarf Fortress, Tropico series, Startopia. It really is a pity though, because if it had even approached the variety and depth of Dwarf Fortress it could have gone down as one of the best city building genre games of all time. It is an effort of only one person however, and for that it is commendable. It just falls short of the mark I'm afraid when compared to the alternatives. Still better than Space Base DF 9, hopefully they pull their act together.

After 3 years of on and off attempting to learn Hearts of Iron 3 I finally gave it a real shot. Its not that complicated if you just put a little time into it and by a little I mean around 30 hours (and thats because Im stupid). They can be painful those 30 hours, as the game has such a crappy interface. Now with that out of the way, this is the best BEST ABSOLUTE BEST WW2 strategy game money can buy. Paradox thought of so much here, the scope, detail is just amazing and rich. The gameplay absolutely can absorb you and before you know it an entire evening can be spent playing HOI3 without hardly scratching the surface. Anyone out there that slams or ridicules this game usually does it because they cant grasp it. Detailed land, units, brigades, generals, officers, technology, spy rings, diplomacy, government all from the 1936-48 are within your control. The decisions you make literally shape the globe, whether you decide to push for that 1000 year Reich or your trying to overthrow the horror of the Nazi's or u want nothing to do with any of that and want to Dominate Asia and make it completely communist. I have made Canada join the Axis, attacked the USA, destroyed Greece as Italy and turned all of Europe into ash. No other game offers this amount of flexibility or option to let you run a nation with such ultimate control.
Battles are exciting, although thats a matter of opinion, they are stats, with sprites and numbers showing casualties, morale and so on. Its not the battles themselves which are exciting, its your plotting, positioning and planning for those battles and how they unfold which is. Hearts of Iron is very much about planning then execution, then developing more to defeat your enemies. Dont overlook this title, its brilliant and Paradox should be commended on this.

anyways this is a top down zombie survival/objective game. there is single player and multiplayer PVE (up to 4 players including yourself). Objectives include: retrieving, defending, and scavenging (find an item and bring back to a location, usually the spawn point). You can also create private matches and invite friends.
You use your left click to fire and you can deploy items such as grenades and turrets. Weapons include : pistol, SMG, AR, shotgun, sniper, rocket launcher, LMG, and even cooler♥♥♥♥♥♥down the road. Armor choices are  helmet, vest, gloves, pants, boots. Each weapon type uses their own ammo supply, with an additional ammo type being High damage ammo, which can be bought mid mission or awarded for special missions (known as Contracts. essentially SP or MP missions with special rewards such as HD ammo aka high damage ammo, extra experience per zomibie kill, bonus cash rewards, and more)
Some weapons/armors can be "augmented" or essentially adding an extra passive boost to your gun/armor, which buffs you in many ways, such as:  increase base damage, crit chance, rate of fire, clip size, damage penetration, faster reloads, and more (weapons). For armors, your augment choices include: increase protection against the various elements (will explain more about these elements), increase "energy" (will explain more about this soon), max hp, hp regen rate, faster multiplayer revive times, and cause melee attacks to reflect some damage to the attacker, to name a few. You can use "energy" to use class-specific abilities, such as the medic's Biocleanse Bomb, which slows and lowers zombies' resistance for a certain amount of time.
Elements include basic physical zombie attacks, heat resistance, and toxic resistance.
There are lootboxes or as theyre called here, "strongboxes." They are earned after a level up and sometimes you can find them within a mission. Of course, one can also buy them should you wish.
There are 3 classes at the moment: medic, assault, and heavy. So far i have only played as medic and its been havin a blast so far. These classes not only have unique skills exclusive to your class, (such as AOE armor buff,)  but you have access to general skills such as increasing money rewards after a mission, increased armor/health, crit chance, movespeed, fast reload, and many more. In addition to this, once you get a certain amount of kills for a weapon/grenade/turret, you gain that weapons "mastery." a mastery level up includes more movespeed while holding a specific weapon type (example +5% movespeed when holding a pistol), more range (on a shotgun), +25% crit damage on a sniper and more.
you gain access to 2 class slots right off the bat (meaning you can swap between a lvl 8 medic and a lvl 14 assault) and new slots unlocked at lvl 20 and 60. additionally you can buy 2 slots with real money.
the hud includes your weapons and their hotkeys for swapping, abilities, purchasable ammo/grenades, HP/ energy meter, and your teammates portraits which can be interacted with to perform short messages such as saying hi, asking for help, regroup command, and an exclusive "good game" near the end of a mission.
TL;DR game is at least worth a try, easy to run and a good game if you just want to turn your brain off and shoot some zombies/monsters/robots

Interactive fiction is something I've longed for for many years.  With the dawn of gaming PCs and e-books, I fully expected an explosion of the sub-genre, but very few surfaced after the era of "choose your own adventure" paperbacks and the Zork text adventure games.  Japanese manga took sole ownership of the visual novels, which left linear interactive novels without a landlord or tenant.
As an ardent Hitchcock fan, I was thrilled to see another modern adaptation of Buchan's "The 39 Steps."  Up to this point I'd never heard of its developer, The Story Mechanics, but Steam's frequent sales made for a relatively risk-free purchase.  I expected a loose narrative voiceover with a focus on visuals in the spirit of Myst and Dear Esther, but I got a fairly straightforward rendition of Buchan's work, with occasional interactivity which can mostly be ignored if the reader/player wishes to maintain the flow of the narrative.  In all, given the the modern interactive novel of this type is mostly newly broken ground, I highly recommend this simply to experience something a little different: a compelling narrative set to beautiful hand-painted visuals, with some very capable voice acting.  I hope this title finds a degree of success because I would love to see more follow in its footsteps.

Like many, I'm familiar with Demonheart from its original platform as an NWN module, but let me just say -- whether you've already been introduced to Demonheart or if you're a brand-new player coming into this visual novel, you're going to love it. The visuals are absolutely gorgeous and have been lovingly rendered, the game-play is smooth and I personally experienced nothing in the way of bugs, and the story-telling is absolutely superb -- wonderfully immersive, totally engaging. I was a little leery about the prospect of voice-acting in this visual novel, but was happily surprised -- the characters are so well-voiced that I ended up disappointed that there wasn't MORE voice-acting.
Trust me, if you DO happen to be a newcomer to Demonheart, the creator of this story will definitely hook you with her storytelling. The plot is fantastically unique, the characters will suck you in, whether you end up loving or hating them. And Bright, the protagonist you play, feels like such a fleshed-out character, given how many options you're allowed in how you play her and how she reacts to the world around her. It also promises plenty of replay potential.
Honestly, the only complaint I have is that I want more! I can't wait for the future chapters! A big "thank you" to its creator(s) -- the platform might have changed but this game remains a masterpiece.
All in all, Demonheart is delightful and definitely worth the cost. Highly recommended!

Dub Dash. It looks like a Geometry Dash clone, and you're half right. Dub Dash takes Geometry Dash's core mechanics and spices them up to make essentially a 3D and more colorful version. It has the normal jumps, but it makes them more interesting where instead of a jump you weave around spikes. it has the ship, that feels way more tight than it should be, yet feels perfect for the game. Dub Dash also adds it's own vehicles to the genre also, such as the maze, where it almost feels exactly like a maze, then there's a 3D infinite runner style vehicles, that plays like your stereotypical Agent Dash. Every vehicle changes your perspective too. With the jump one, it looks like you are orbiting a planet, where as the ship looks like your normal 2D platformer ( in it's own 3D way ).
Gameplay feels perfect. Controls are simply left and right arrow key, allowing for the 3D aspect of the game to actually work. The game seems like you could get about 10 hours in, which is good for 5 dollars!
Graphics are fun to look at, but can hurt your eyes especially if you have epilepsy.
Overall: 8/10 can't wait to see updates!

Today we are happy to feature the Steam debut of German developer Incodra and yet another game published by Headup Games who we very recently ran a gameathon for. Dub Dash is a rhythm racer where the entire point of the game is to successfully complete each of the seven levels contained within the game. Experts at this type of game may be disappointed at the relatively low number of levels but for those like me you’ll have to work incredibly hard to see them all.
I really enjoy the feeling of utter rage and contempt that I get for this game while playing it. For whatever reason I find completing maps so much easier in the multiplayer version of the game (I’ve not failed to complete a level in multiplayer whereas I haven’t completed one in single player). I can’t complete one for the life of me in single player. I always manage to screw it up somewhere along the line. It’s a frustrating experience when you die over and over again. However, the musical beat in this game is so addictive that I overlook the tiny little fact that I royally suck at this game at the single player – and arguably the most important aspect of the game (you can’t unlock the next level until you complete it in that mode).
Aside from the rocking beat of at the very least the first level of the game I like the graphics. They’re really cool and vibrant. The gameplay mechanics feel really tight. If you press the left or right key the wheel will move into the according lane momentarily before returning to the center lane. This makes the rhythmic nature of the music and graphics really play well together. So much so that the game becomes quite addictive – even when you find yourself unable to progress. It definitely provides a ‘the next time will do it’ kind of feeling.
Multiplayer is the absolute bomb on this thing. While I admit its the only thing I’m actually good at in the game (probably because the lanes are smaller to fit in your opponents) those who I’ve played the game with have really enjoyed it as well. It’s just a blast. Games are over in about a minute and you can always play again very quickly.
Although this is not an original idea by any means the best way for the developers to improve their game would be to allow players to import their own music. It would expand replayability to almost an infinite degree. Dare I suggest that it would also increase sales dramatically. The addition of Steam trading cards would also help boost sales perhaps to a level where adding this previous feature is possible if it isn’t already.
One negative is that the game is allegedly free on Android devices. Those who are considering purchasing the game on Steam but who have access to an Android device may want to test the game out there as a demo before committing to their purchase on Steam. If the game has been directly ported from mobile to PC then it is of a high enough quality that I can appreciate.
Even though I’m not very good at this game I can appreciate its absolute quality. If you enjoy difficult and challenging rhythm based games then you’re sure to fall in love with Dub Dash.

THE PERFECT CHEESECAKE
1/4 cup butter 1 cup graham cracker crumbs 2 tablespoons white sugar 1/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon 2 cups cottage cheese 1/2 cup milk 2 eggs 3 tablespoons all-purpose flour 2 tablespoons lemon juice 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 2/3 cup white sugar 1/4 teaspoon salt.
Preheat oven to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C). Melt butter in an 8 inch square pan. Stir in graham cracker crumbs, 2 tablespoons sugar and 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon. Pat over bottom and onto sides of dish. Set aside.
In a blender, combine cottage cheese, milk, eggs, flour, lemon juice, vanilla, 2/3 cup sugar and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Blend until smooth. Pour into prepared crust.
Bake in the preheated oven for 60 minutes, or until filling is firm. Allow to cool completely.

Wait why is their health going down? Why is everyone dying!! This happened until my city was a ghost town, (game doesn't tell you game over). This is what I learned. You need to set up a trader, so that you can get seeds, so that your farmers can grow more then one thing. People don't do well when they eat the same thing everyday. Also learned you need a herbelist, they will help you improve health as well. Lastly, make sure to build houses, if you want more population you need more houses... Once you learn the rules of the game it becomes a time sink that makes you want to bash your head on the table, but still over all enjoyable.

This is an open world sandbox game in which you have to cause destruction to overthrow the dictatorship oppressing the nation. Join factions and gain their trust so that they can aid you in your effort.
Firstly I want to express the good points of this game:
.HUGE and I mean HUGE, varied open world sandbox containing various islands all with unique and interesting vistas.
.More destruction than you could ever imagine
.Eye candy eyerywhere, despite it's age the game looks amazing, bright vibrant colours galore.
.Wide variety of transport such as boats, planes, cars, bikes, jets, helicopters, maybe even the odd missile.
You may be thinking "this sounds great, what's with your negativety at the start?" Well now we get to the bad points:
.The physics are really bad, you never know what certain actions will do because the game acts so drastically different under identical circumstances.
.Hope you don't like driving across expansive maps because the cars control awfully (mainly due to the poor physics) they slide and roll even when driving at a moderate speed and trying to take the slightest of deviations.
.Because you can cause all the destruction you want, there is nothing left to possibly impress you as the game throws all the explosions and action it can at you constantly, it can't ever top it and after not too long the action becomes too repetitive and dull.
.Worst of all is the missions, these are some of the worst story missions in any game I've ever played, boring characters, bad voice acting, inconsistant damage intake, huge difficulty spikes and overall bad gameplay due to lacklustre gunplay. AVOID these missions at all costs if you want to like this game.
Overall I'm giving this game a 7/10 (If heavily playing missions) or an 8/10 (if only embracing it's sandbox nature)

Gameplay - The 39 Steps is like an interactive combination of a book andmovie with very limited gaemeplay.  Essentially, there are parts where you have to click and drag the mouse up, down, right, or left and in a clockwise and counterclockwise manner.  In addition there is pointing and clicking similar to point and click adventure games but without any puzzles.  This undoubtedly sparks a debate as to is it a game or not?  In my opinion it is, because you do have some interactions and you can miss achievements if you don't try to experience all of the options in the game.  If this lack of gameplay does not sound good to you, I would recommend avoidng this game.
Story - The focus of 39 Steps is the story which is set right before World War I in England and Scotland.  It is a spy thriller, but feels close to Sherlock Holmes in my opinion.  Much like in Dickens, there is a lot of happenstance or good fortune that you don't see in modern stories, but I think that is part of the charm of a story like this.  I love many things set in World War I and appreciate British literature so for me this was a very enjoyable combination.  The story starts a little slow, but once it picks up, it is really good and I had trouble not wanting to play through the whole story as fast as I could to find out what would happen.  There are some thick Scottish accents and a few British words that Americans don't know or use, but overall, if this story sounds at all appealing to you, then you will enjoy the story.
Presentation (Graphics and Sound) - There are a few simple cut scenes, but most of 39 Steps is painted background images with text over top.  Fortunately, these are all very attractive and help you "see" the story.  There are also authentic looking maps and pictures from this era of history which was also appreciated.  The sound is really solid and the voice acting is well-done.  Hearing the protagonist pant after running or yawn after waking up makes the story come to life.  For an Indie game, I thought the presentation of the game was very good and it enhances the story.
Overall - The 39 Steps may have limited appeal because of its lack of gameplay and historical setting, but I loved the four hours I played and thought it was totally worth buying on sale.  If you're looking for perfect games, the achievements are very easy to get and only require that you play through the game and look at/inspect every item or option as you go through the story.  It doesn't get any easier or quicker than this.  If you think this game sounds fun or interesting, then I highly recommend buying it because I really enjoyed it.

This game is easily one of my favorite games of all time, just everything about it I love. Bethesda really nails the whole post-apocalyptic feeling, because everything just feels empty and deserted. These days the game looks pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and even back in 2008 when I first played this game, I didn't think it looked that impressive (Dem Mods though). I admit that I'm a little spoiled by New Vegas, so the mechanics in FO3 don't feel quite as good as they do in New Vegas, but using VATS and the gameplay itself is excellent. I enjoyed all the songs in the game, but I really wish they would have added more, especially with all the DLC this game has. The karma system is something I feel all RPG's should have and while some of the decisions you make don't really affect things as a whole, it's still nice to have multiple choices to the quests you do. Audio as a whole is excellent (as stated with the music) but it just feels limited with the amount of the voice actors and the songs on the radio, the quality is definitely there though. I honestly could keep going on why I love this game so much and there is a lot of stuff I haven't even seen yet (DLC and Mods) but there is one big issue that makes me question this version in particular. On Windows 7, this game would crash at least every hour for me and sometimes it would be even worse. You would think with a game as popular as FO3, that Bethesda would at least fix something as big as this is, but they haven't. I have played this on Xbox 360 before and it maybe crashed 1 or 2 times (it's pretty sad when the console version of your game, performs better than the far superior PC). If you can deal with the technical issues, then you're in for one of the best RPG's of all time, up there with games like Mass Effect 2, Dragon Age: Origins, Skyrim, and KOTOR. Regardless of any of the negative things I said about FO3, I think one of the most important aspects of any game is fun and if I can sit and enjoy a game for extended play sessions for weeks and keep coming back to it after I already beat it before, well I think that's what every game should strive for.

The 39 Steps is a digital adaption of a John Buchan's espionage thriller.
And since I don't want to spoil the story for anyone still waiting to enjoy it, I won't reveal any story details.
But I will say this, the story is brilliant and has a lot of twists and turns and will keep you hooked till the end. At least that's how I've felt.
The art in the game is absolutely gorgeous and the sound design is spot on as well. This is like reading a book, but you interact ingame with a mouse at certain situations and click objects on screen such as newspapers or items of interest. There are also times where you have to imitate real movements with a mouse ( sort of like in Fahrenheit / Indigo Prophecy if you have played that game).

Dub Dash is a rhythm-based game that translates the "wobbly" beats of dubstep music into a giant, revolving disco ball and has the player dodging and weaving around obstacles by tapping left or right to "jump" or holding the key down to "bounce". Levels range from simple-but-tricky to complex, mind-bending challenges.
The level comes to life as you time your keystrokes successfully, with equalizer-like structures popping up around you and rather euphoric-looking smiley faces silently cheering you on, all of which are changing color like a chameleon suffering with multiple personality disorder.
As you progress, the game likes to throw you curve balls mid-song. Level make-up will transition from revolving globe to side-scrolling and top-down modes, each requiring a new type of finesse to beat. I found the side-scrolling sections very tricky to master and it's worth noting that they are not based on rhythm.
One mistake and you're back to the start of that track, unless you beat a randomized level in
, which will net you 5 lives that allow you to restart from checkpoints upon failure. These random interpretations of the songs also add some replay value to the game, which is most welcome because there is no option to import your own music library or create your own levels. You could also try
, which enables checkpoints so you can more effectively train yourself to beat the segment you're stuck on.
Unlike other games in the genre, there are no bonus points awarded for perfect timing, the only goal is to survive until the music stops. Also omitted are any sort of obtrusive noises or chimes for successfully interpreting the musical cues.
Up to 3 other players can tag along for some competetive
fun that's sure to go down well among like-minded friends up for a challenge.
Dub Dash is an addictive rhythm action game with refreshing mechanics and pretty visuals. The controls are simple but timing is crucial and the challenge is high. Skill with music/rhythm games and fine motor control is required to beat most levels, so unless you have supreme mastery over both, Dub Dash is going to provide you with many hours of entertainment. I believe the developers are also planning to add more songs, so keep an ear out for those too.

Dub Dash is a beautiful looking music rhythm game.
The game plays quite similarly to The Impossible Game.
Your wheel/character rolls in the middle lane until you press left or right. The wheel will then jump momentarily to another lane, and return back to the middle. If you hold the left or right button, then the wheel will keep bouncing from middle to the side, as opposed to just staying on the side lane. This makes for some pretty cool looking and satisfying rhythm based movement.
The visuals in this game are incredibly bright and colourful. It's like you're at an alien disco. The effects never get in the way, and are there to just immerse you in the cool looking world.
Levels keep the game fresh with new visuals and music, but the coolest part is they add a new mechanic into the game. At certain checkpoints, the gameplay for example might change into a side-scrolling flying game. Where holding a directional button will lift your plane upwards, while letting go floats down. It's a good change in pace to keep it interesting and go with the music.
Everytime you die in a level, you have to restart right from the beginning. It isn't too frustrating because the levels aren't incredibly long, and the music is quite good. You can however, similarly to the impossible game, turn on a practice mode that changes the music to a slightly more relaxed one, and respawns you at the last checkpoint as opposed to the beginning, which allows you to learn the layout of the level and master it in the normal mode. You can only unlock the next level if you beat the previous one in normal mode.
If you want to make the game a bit easier, there is a challenge mode that allows you to complete a random track for 5 extra lives. These lives basically bring practice mode into normal mode. So you can still unlock the next level, but have atleast 5 checkpoint retries within the level.
There's a multiplayer mode that allows you to play with up to 4 players on the same track. You each have your own lanes, and gain points as you are alive. If you die, you have to wait until the other players reach a checkpoint for your respawn. However in that time, they were gaining points, and might have even gotten some bonus dangerous collectibles to boost their score.
I would love if the devs added a way to import your own music into the game, because the gameplay is fun, and the visuals are great, but eventually you'll run out of songs to play, as there aren't that many. It's a decent replay value for the price, but it could be even better if you could import your own stuff. Great game overall though!

I've tried a variety of digital card games over the years, and none have impressed me nearly as much as Eternal.
Eternal is the first legitimately free to play DCG I've found. While others have had varying degrees of generosity for free to play players, it was always still a grind, trying to get the cards needed in time. Playing those games free was "possible," but not especially enjoyable. In Eternal, you are rewarded for playing the game in whatever way you want, whether it be constructed, draft, or even single player against AI games. Whereas with other DCGs I always felt pressured to spend money just to keep up, with Eternal I spend money because I want to. The game is excellent and something I CHOOSE to invest in.
Eternal also allows for a greater degree of complexity in cards and in gameplay. Defender's choose whether or not they wnat to block, and with what, which helps prevent games from boiling down to "player goes first and curves out for the win." Since units can't just ignore the defending player's units and go face, units are more than just a pile of stats.
Eternal also features fast spells, which can be played at times during the opponent's turn. This makes the game engaging and fun, as apposed to a game where you "play your stuff, pass the turn, and alt-tab until it's your turn again." Between defender's having the choice of how to block and also the possibility of fast spells to play as combat tricks, there are very clear decisions that affect whether you win or lose.
There are countless viable and fun deck types, and cards are very well balanced. Any balance issues that do arise are addressed in a timely manner.
In conclusion: rewarding, elegant, and engaging. 9/10

Quick and dirty: it's the old Sim City from the 80s, except that you will die horribly in the wilderness and explorers will one day find your crumbling huts and bleached skeletons and wonder what went wrong.
That's not entirely accurate, but I wanted to open with a memorable hook for the TL;DR crowd. I say it's like the old Sim City because there's only a handful of structures you can build. However, it differs in that each sim (villager) has a name, a gender, an occupation, and they are individually represented on the screen. Each villager walks around, works, runs errands, and sometimes goes to the cemetary to ponder the meaning of life. I found myself growing quite fond and protective of the little villagers.
And it is important to be protective of them, because horrible lingering death is never too far away. It is not hard to get behind the curve on some essential supply and for things to snowball horribly out of control. Lack of food, obviously, is the easiest way to lose a village, but there are other less obvious paths to destruction. I almost lost a village for lack of tools, because I had not made enough blacksmith's shops to keep up with demand. Villagers started trying to do their jobs without tools, and they are less efficient when they are lacking. Suddenly the farmers were producing less food, fishers less fish, miners less iron, loggers fewer logs, and so on. It was like being squeezed to death by an anaconda.
This game has wrecked my sleep schedule. The same way that Civilization keeps people up all night playing "just one more turn," Banished keeps me up all night to see what will happen with the harvest, who will move into the next house that I build, and so on.
I heartily recommend Banished.

An interesting, unique, engaging video game that constantly breaks immersion and often tries to make you dislike it.
The gameplay is fun and rewarding but underdeveloped and sometimes lacking. The game has bad animations and outsourced mocap-work, and paired with some mediocre hitboxing it often makes you very sad with visions of how good the game COULD have been, were FROM to have a more allowing budget and more time to polish the game.
DS2 is strangely a lot easier than DS1, and has more 'cheap' elements such as boss attacks and enemies that kill you and surprise you with yet
move you didn't know they had. The game too often breaks it's own rules.
The game is VERY pretentious and does not let up on it's draconian Japanese design philosophy, but if you absorb that there are a few very evocative pieces of art in the game, told to you through both gameplay and exposition that will make you appreciate the game. And a word of wisdom: Avoid the fanbase, as it is split between elitist snobs and untolerable dregs that make dry jokes and poor erotica.
The co-operative aspects of the multiplayer are sometimes great fun however, even if they are extremely dictatorial in the same vein as the entire game is... it is decidedly stemming from the Japanese developers mindset.
In terms of gameplay, i'd reccomend a purer, more polished experience such as Castlevania 1 or the Metal Slug series. In terms of story there are few immersive stygian experiences such as Dark Souls but the alternatives ususally convey their message better, such as perhaps BioShock/System Shock or the Metro series.
Dark Souls 2 is not the game for someone looking to immerse themselves in more acclaimed video games for the first time. It is for someone who already has played many video games and has patience and understanding for the medium. Buy the game only if you're ready for the unapologetic experience that is Dark Souls.

For experienced city builder, I'd say this game might worth about 15 dollar so wait for a discount of at least 25% before getting it. For anyone else still sitting on the fence, I'll go into the details a bit.
For starters, the graphics in Banished isn't top notch, but acceptable. Soundtrack fills the silence but is in no way memorable. I suppose for a one person development team it's fairly impressive enough but I wouldn't expect any award committee to knock on the Dev's door anytime soon.
Gameplay wise, I would say it's functional but not exceptional; as an average gamer who enjoy as much about city building/simulation as the next gamer. I immediately notice a few developing tools that I've seen in other similar games which I would consider a great asset in creating a fluid experience are absent in Banished. For example, the buildings in Banished doesn't snap onto pre-existing framework such as roads. The boundry between buildable land and unbuildable land isn't marked out so building placement could be like family vacation when you have a big family and have to stuff every thing into the car, the experience is especially unpleasant if your random seeds gives you a very uneven terrain. The dirt road/stone road only provide what appears to be negligible speed boost to traffic; even though it occupy one unit of land, I'm still having trouble placing it on what I perceived as fairly flat area in my very first game. Lastly, Banished can't place bridges/tunnels automatically so the player will have to do that separately. While none of these issue is technically game breaking. It does make the game more frustrating than it has to be. Partly because of the random seeds generation, while I haven't personally look at the coding myself, I suspect that the game have the tendancy to create a very weathered/uneven terrain to create a visually complex map but is in no way beginner friendly.
Next up, replayablility. Preliminary experience would suggest that Banished doesn't have a lot of replayability, mostly because even with random seeds map generator, the map lacks interesting variation to keep people coming back for more. The most you can get is a slightly different hilltops or a slightly twitchier river. But overall you'll be building the same village that you did last time. In Anno 2070 every island have a different resources and you'll have to construct your little settlement accordingly, in Caesar 3 (if memory serves) every map have different resources which effects how you design your town's industry. In Banished, you're always building a town, the very same town in which you'll have to scrambble to satisfy the towns unchanging needs.
Lastly, though it wasn't strictly speaking part of the gameplay, I think it's worth mentioning that for a city building games, the community base is surprisingly unfriendly and not in any way helpful. And this is part of the reason why I wouldn't recommend this game to any gamer that's new to the city building genre; with a primitive tutorial and an unfriendly user base, a new player doesn't have a very good chance of succeeding in this game.
To sum in up. Banished is a game with some great ideas that failed to execute properly. If city building is your thing, consider gettign this while it's on sale. If you're new to city simulation games, stay away from this game, this game will eat you alive and spit you out.

I'm really not quite sure what the developers were aiming for when they designed this simulator. What is claimed to be a 'Search and Rescue' simulator is more like a 'chase the red dot, and find the tiny objects hidden in the grass' simulator. You'll spend mission after mission traversing the countryside, searching for asthma inhalers, inflatable crocodiles, baseball caps, boots, and if you're really lucky, an immobile human being. Although the people looked more like broken animatronics slowly thrashing in the grass than any kind of real, injured person.
You have two modes of transport: your feet and your trusty bicycle. Although your bicycle seems to tear across terrain at the speed of an F16 Falcon fighter jet. Furthermore, your character seems to suffer from chronic fatigue syndrome, and has trouble traversing the landscape for more than a few minutes at a time. Whether you're on foot or on bike, you'll likely become exhausted before you can complete your arbitrary mission. Once you get exhausted, your boss blessedly will end your outing... "You're in no condition to continue, Ranger."
You'll encounter all sorts of wildlife that meander around aimlessly, oftentimes with their hooves slicing through the air and failing to come into contact with the ground. They do not mind your presence, until you come within spitting distance, and then they'll leg it like a bank robber on methamphetamines. I approached an alligator, largely because I was bored out of my skull. I expected it to lurch forward and tear me limb from limb, a fine diversion from the monotony of collecting lost miscellania. But it did not even turn its head to look at me; it scrambled away like a frightened rabbit, and disappeared into the opaque water of a nearby river. There was nary a pixel shader or transparent surface to prove that there was ever an alligator there.
Graphics wise, the game is not particularly acceptable. Don't expect graphics along the lines of theHunter 2013 or Crysis. I turned the graphics quality up, and my hefty gaming rig experienced repeated stuttering and pausing. The grass became so dense I could barely find anything, and it even began poking up through the solid floor of my ranger station and through solid rock. I turned the graphics quality down, and it felt like I was playing on my old Nintendo 64. And in the default graphics quality midpoint, the object and grass pop-in was so obvious and awkward that I began to feel like a mystical druid from a discarded fantasy novel, causing plants to spring up and grow in seconds, whereever I tread. I also noticed z-battling issues on some of the textures (flickering between two textures for two objects occupying the same physical space), particularly on the battlements of the fort.
The boss of the ranger station, who only appears in text messages and never actually seems to appear in game, makes the attempt to be a lighthearted sidekick and ally, and the primary source of the weak 'stories' that might exist. He makes 'quips' when you find the wrong objects during your missions, and makes lousy excuses as to why he is not taking the missions himself: "I'd do it, but I've... uhh... I've got a migraine." One particularly strange mission requests you to find a little girl's diary, and a couple of emphatic comments are made about never, ever looking inside. Presumably she keeps her plans for world domination within.
The game might be fun for people looking for a very simple hunt and click game, and who are willing to overlook the aforementioned shortcomings, but I could not tolerate it for long. Perhaps worth the price for a few dollars, but not full price.

I'll start this review off by saying I enjoyed Solenars Edge Rebirth way more then this game, but it's still a unique and crisp game nontheless.
Restoration is about a boy Oliver who is a Dream-Catcher and he keeps the evil spirits *monsters* known as Nightmares away from the world. I think it goes
if the heart gives way to negative emotion then the person in doubt turns into a nightmare aka a monster. I guess that is why depending on if you fail or
succeed in the challenges depends if they turn into a nightmare or be restored. I guess that is why the angry boy turned giant tree became a nightmare because he gave into negative emotions. It kinda reminds me a bit of kingdom hearts and the heartless stuff.
Details:
1. The flying mushroom in the beginning played the battle music from Solenars Edge Rebirth and was obviously a cameo appearence of a shroom face if you ever played the game.
2. The teacher in the school was Maria, one of the main characters of Solenars Edge Rebirth who played boss battle music from the game. That whole area played some of the BGM from Solenars Edge Rebirth and was meant to be a secret boss and extra out of the way level for fans of Rebirth to enjoy I think. It just makes sense.

4. To my understanding, Oliver has the cure ability and Penello restores herself after each battle. Certain spells do massive damage and you get ultimate abilities around level 20 kinda like Solenars Edge Rebirth. Also enemies have weakneses that are pretty easy to figure out. But some enemies I can imagine aren't actually meant to be defeated but are mean't to be run from instead. It's a risky game mechanic, but it oddly works.

I mean you could use the other fishing rod, but lets be honest. It sucks. You'll need the money for better gear and to finish some challenges anyways.
