I've been playing The Crew base game for a while since November and I only came upon it after the late-2015 patch which upgraded the graphics and physics of some cars.
I love the game, yes.
The Crew is simply the best driving-in-an-open-world game available on the PC, and the highlight of it is the virtual continental America with a great variety of enviroments for driving enjoyment.
The cities in this game does not have a living-breathing feel, yet they act as huge playgrounds for driving the somewhat limited line-up of cars available in the game. I think Manhattan in The Crew is no smaller than GTA IV's Liberty City. The mountains and seasides in The Crew, however, are truly great places to get yourself lost in. The great open Americana-esque environment with ever-changing weather and time of day indeed provide a immersive experience which is hard to be found in any other driving games.
This is a game made for virtual world explorers who happen to sit in a car seat and don't really care about too much about serious racing. The Crew's missions and racing can have result varying from exciting(compete in the snowy mountain road around Salt Lake City) to very boring(it totally miss the opportunity to make NYC as racing tracks interestingly). But the overall 'road trip' feel in this game is awesome.
Then there's this always-online problem. I love the idea of 'Never Driving Alone' but the real experience is having the very common 'lost connection to server' headache... An offline 'Enjoy Driving Alone' will be appreciated, really.

This is the second installment of the Space Pilgrim adventure.
It occurs a year after the first chapter.
Some changes have obviously taken place seeing how quite a bit of time has passed.
Some of the characters' past interactions have lead to the blooming of a friendship, and this is depicted in this second chapter of the SP saga.
One of the passengers from back then grew closer to protagonist Gail Pilgrim (the pilot of starship 'Quicksilver' - where most of the scenarios take place in the former chapter).
This friendship blossomed to such an extent that the former passenger now co-manages the starship with Gail. The character in question is also intermittently playable (which allows for a bit of variation & excitement). Meaning, the player is handed control over Gail first & then her friend when the story calls for it.
In this chapter there is yet another handful of passengers on board (and some of these turn out to be allies, and others turn out to be antagonists), as was the case in SP1.
The starship serves as both a passenger & cargo ship (meaning it transports people but also goods). And there's more of an emphasis on the latter in chapter II.
And just like chapter I, the game is divided into 3 main acts, which each focus on a specific issue.
The story now contains elements of one (playable) flashback (which is totally awesome and revolves around a trained individual who was meant to serve as a soldier, but somehow ended up as a fugitive).
How this happened is explained & depicted as you play.
It's interesting to note that the starship still looks the same as before and this chapter feels like a plausible sequel to the former (meaning the story makes sense and does unfold logically).
The dialogue system has been expanded as well (i.e. more questions to ask).
And I appreciate that very much :).
NB: this game contains some brash language & risqué jokes at times (you've been warned!)
Trivia:
In the former chapter, there was mention of a particular organization (the J.A.C.) which was only named by it's abbreviated form.
In the second chapter the role of said organization is clarified (i.e. full name is revealed) and further expounded, to such an extent where the subject becomes of great interest to the crew (and story in general).

So, I've played Magic: the Gathering for 15 years or so. And the recent wave of digital CCGs have been nice, but overall lacking. They're super simplified to the point where a lot of the strategy and meaningful interaction seems to disappear. Additionally, they can be stingy with giving you access to the very cards you need to play the game.
None of those apply to Eternal, from my time playing it.
I've played for a few months, and have access to every common and uncommon in the two sets released as of the time of this writing, as well as most of the rares. Legendaries are still a crapshoot, but I have plenty of shiftstone to craft whatever Legendaries I need. I mean, packs just give you 100 shiftstone each, and you get a free pack for your first win of the day. The rewards are so plentiful, and you'll sometimes have a reward chest just randomly upgrade. (Those rare times you see a lowly copper chest upgrade all the way to platinum are just glorious.)
Eternal feels like what Magic would look like if it was made now. All the strategy is there, and so much of my Magic knowledge easily ports over. Some things are streamlined, but not in a way that removes strategic depth. (No clunky phases, for example. Everything smoothly moves from start to combat to end and everything in between.) And all the interaction on your opponent's turn that other games shy away from? Not this game. (Similarly, it's not afraid to give you tools against cards sitting in your opponent's hand.) And there's plenty of mechanics that take advantage of the game being digital without overly relying on randomness.
This is one of the rare F2P games where I'm happy to spend money to help the devs. And quite frankly, the devs are names I trust coming from my Magic background. (Seriously, most of these guys are big name Magic pros.) And with a mobile version that let's me carry my entire collection over, I can show it off to my friends wherever I am. I don't know why it's still carrying the Early Access tag, but I do hope for great things from this game's future.

If you think Dark Souls is one of the greatest games ever made and that Dark Souls 2 will be every bit as glorious as its predecessor, so you might as well get it--I mean, it's a no-brainer--well, then, you're a fool just like I was. Dark Souls 2 is a disgrace to the original. It didn't take me long before I had a suspicion that something was wrong. There was a cheap look to the characters, no facial animations (and, yes, there are some facial animations in the original), and the textures looked worse. Everywhere the ground and sky look like they were ripped right out of the late 90s--hell, I am certain games on the Playstation, Saturn, and N64 had better textures than this game does. And the enemy animations: for example, the green flesh-eater with the corpse weapon and hanging blob belly, looked choppy and unfinished. Everything the original did so brilliantly: epic bosses--remember how you felt the first time you encountered the Asylum Demon or Ornstein and Smough or Quelaag; a tightly woven world of deviously designed levels; a rewarding yet challenging weapon-crafting system--these three elements, just off the top of my head, were utterly discarded in Dark Souls 2.
You won't care a lick about any of these bosses. There's no buildup and then a boss is before you and chances are it looks like trash (compare that desert scorpion queen to Quelaag) or that Rat Authority boss you fight for seemingly no reason as a way to get into a guild or the bunch of rats boss that you fight again to get into that guild... And level design? Take a trip up a tall windmill and then find yourself in the airy heights of a wavy blob lava world! Lava in the sky! Weapon crafting? Don't worry, you'll find titanite slabs about 2 hours in. I didn't even finish this game and had 4 of them and a fully upgraded zweihander that I just spammed regular titanite at--some shards, some chunks, and a slab for +10 Zwei no problem. Or how instead of getting a boss soul and combining it with a well-upgraded weapon for transmutation into a boss soul weapon, as is the case in Dark Souls, you just trade a boss soul to some guy who gives you a special weapon with said boss soul in it? So you pay some regular souls and get the boss soul back inside a weapon. This character isn't a blacksmith either. You just "trade" these things. So some souls and a boss soul and he trades you a boss-imbued weapon... no thought went into this at all.
If Dark Souls didn't exist, Dark Souls 2 would be an average game. Because Dark Souls is a masterpiece, this game is exposed for what it is: virtual diarrhea. There's no order, no thought, just the name Dark Souls 2 stamped onto it with a bunch of the great things of the original included but done so much worse at almost every turn. Only the multiplayer and co-op work better. If you have a willing friend, and incredibly low standards, and the stomach to grind through this mess, pick it up only at the steepest of discounts. I played it 60 hours or so before I accepted that I was only trying to beat this game because I loved the original so much. Then I stopped because good Schopenhauer once taught me that "Life is too short for bad books." This applies no less to games. Don't waste your precious time. It will be over before you know it.

First Impressions:
Recovery Search & Rescue Simulation is a simulator for wannabe park rangers, by the team over at Excalibur Publishing. It's supposed to teach you how to be a park ranger and I, not being a park ranger, have no idea if they've accomplished this. If the game really depicts how a park ranger's life is, then it must be pretty dull.
Recovery Search & Rescue Simulation basically has you run around looking for different items every mission. It's okay if you fail a mission, because the next one is unlocked just for trying. I abused this mechanic, as I could not complete the first several missions, due to the sheer difficulty of each task. There's two problems with most of these missions, one being that my character's stamina would rapidly drain, even with energy bars equipped. Some missions I could not even get to where the objective was simply because I ran through three stamina bars trying to bike there. I may be doing something wrong, but I wasn't really instructed with how that works.
The second problem with the game's missions was the fact that each was the same. The majority of the missions were all "fetch quests", were I was tasked with finding an item (or animal footprints) in a general area marked on my map. I failed to even accomplish something as simple as that because there was little indication of where these items could be other than a red circle around the general area of the item on the map. You've got to be a hardcore ranger in order to complete some of these tasks.

This game is outright horrible. Apart from the epic title music, there's no other music in the game. The sound effects are minimal. The interface is unhelpful and the mission progress is baffling. The game is nearly unplayable.
The most frustrating element is that the tasks are incredibly vague and difficult to locate. This game is mostly about finding small things like watches or footprints, but the graphics are so poor that these are nearly impossible to locate and the game does not make it any easier to identify. To make things worse, the game doesn't even tell you what to look for. Mission 5 involves searching for a red hat, but when you get to the area you waste time looking for a hat, but you're actually meant to find footprints that lead to the next clue area.
The stamina system is unworkable. You get tired from running or riding the bike - which is fair - but there are only two ways to regain stamina: either wait, or buy energy bars. Waiting is unfeasible because you only have a few minutes to complete each mission. Energy bars cost points, which are earned by completing missions. However, EVERYTHING you buy and use is persistent. If you use an energy bar and then abort the mission, the game saves that, which means you lose both your points and your item even though you left the mission. You could literally make the campaign unbeatable and you have to start another one from scratch.
The game is also buggy. On mission failures (very common when you're not told what to look for), the game may not take you back to the menu and you cannot quit the game, forcing you to force-quit the game.
Presentation is mystifyingly poor. There is NO ambient noise. No birds, no animals, no wind, no water. The visuals are downright lazy. There are perhaps five tree models and the same tree has clearly copy/pasted into an area to save time. The items are often plain models without any skins rendered. Then there are invisible walls everywhere. Don't touch water by the way: water is death!
The worst thing is that the title is an outright lie. Except perhaps "Recovery", since you spend most of your time finding lost hats and mp3 players. This is certainly no simulation. You go to this vague waypoint, look for something undefined, click on it, and done. There's no rescue or first-aid or any interactivity AT ALL.
The game basically allows you to cheat in order to get through the levels. You can call in a helicopter to take you ANYWHERE on the map at the cost of points, which is desirable and less expensive than having to ride there and consume energy bars. And if that doesn't excite you, by aborting the mission, you unlock the next mission anyway.
There are 40 something missions and they are literally all the same.
I'm a sucker for these cheesy little buys, but this isn't even worth the low cost. You are buying a headache. Playing this will necessitate a search & rescue for your sanity.

A brilliant city-builder that takes time to understand, in the sense that there are many ways to start out and how to achieve basic stability with your population. The difficult part is that it is unforgiving. Don't do something fast enough or early enough and your people can and will die. Things take time to build and they need the resources, which are mostly finite. You can control which things to build first and pause others when you need the resources elsewhere. You can set professions so that some citizens build while others farm or fish.
The attention to detail is amazing for a game created by one person. The shadows follow the path of the sun and the water looks beautiful. The people and their families can be seen working in their different jobs and buildings are built with multiple levels of completion (foundations, frame and finished).
The only bad point is the lack of a terrain editor, or terraforming tool, to remove pesky hills that appear, but this just adds to the already difficult challenge of the game in a good way.
All things said, this game is amazing for the price and the music is very soothing and fitting. This is how a city builder should be.

The 39 Steps leads you on a journey through lush hand-painted backgrounds, moody music, and excellent voice-acting. You are Richard Hannay, a well-to-do British gent living a boring life in London in 1914.
Calling 39 Steps a game seems to be doing it a disservice, as it is more of a interactive story that just has you along for the ride.  There are points in the story where you 'control' the protoganists action, but you have no real power to affect the momentum of the narrative. The story is gripping, though, and these attempts to insert a more direct hand in the game are infrequent.
I have never read the source material, so cannot say how well it holds up to the original. The 39 Steps stands well enough on its own, though.
Achievement hunters interested in 100% games will find this one easy to complete, as achievements are awarded through story progression and are impossible to miss. I'd recommend not reading the achievement list before you start the story, though, as they could spoil some future events.
So, if spy thrillers are your thing, grab up your pipe and your brandy and dive into this one.

VVVVVV is a simply mind-bending platformer where the ability to jump has been replaced with gravity inversion. This leads to a lot of possibilities, but also a lot of problems.
- - - - - - - - - - - Commence argumentation - - - - - - - - - - -
-interesting, addicting gameplay (once I started, I finished it in a single run because I could not stop)
-simple C64-style graphics (seriously, these graphics make you think you're playing on a C64)
-nostalgic NES-style sound (simplistic, stereotypical video game sound and fast-paced music)
-fluid gameplay, even on weak computers (works perfectly on many old computers)
-very challenging (it is hard, but you know what you did wrong every time you die)
-very, VERY hard (I mean it, I died about 700 times during the course of the story)
-quite short, even for such a cheap game (it literally took me just about 100 minutes to complete the story)
-very frustrating to get all trinkets (some are nearly impossible to get)
-quite confusing variety within the different areas (especially with the whole gravity bouncing)
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -Print results - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
9/10 (seriously very hard, but still possible)
7/10 (quite nice, but slightly confusing and rarely unresponsive controls)
8/10 (graphics and sound fit very well together, but it still is not quite perfect)

It's worth the price, but do not hunt for every achievement. It will drive you insane to get 100%.

I found this to be a wonderful experience, but it certainly won't be everyone's cup of tea. You interact with the plot, but only to drive it almost constantly forward and there is no branching of any kind. However, despite that rigid structure, the presentation of the world and characters is beautiful. The graphics are generally quite static, but commonly overlaid with subtle animation, lighting effects and focus shifts so that it never feels like you're really looking at just a still image. The voice acting, music and sound editing are also exceptional and I must confess that I liked that they didn't dumb down the period vocabulary or authentic accents. It is a slow affair, however. I really wouldn't be able to argue with someone who finds the story plodding. Still, as a fan of classic Hitchcock, games like The Last Express and Dear Esther, and the works of Agatha Christie, I quickly connected with this interactive novel and consider it a very worthy addition to my virtual library.

The game offers some nice additions compared to the previous instalment in the series. I suppose you are reading this review after playing Roads of Rome 1. If not, you can start by the first game, as every one of them has completely different sets of levels.
Stairs and ropes are used to better exploit the relief of the map. Just look at the screenshots to get an idea: levels generally gives the feel that they are more complex, with far away areas harder to reach (so more rewarding in a sense).
Some animations have been improved. By example, the roads are now built in several steps, so it's nicer to watch.
Yes, in terms of assets, the game is very close to the first one, but the efforts put in the level design (especially the will to put more relief) show that the devs work on the game to make it look better.
The first game was asking you to put a ton of resources in rocks on the road. On the contrary, this game asks you to sink your resources into a single "obstacle", one (or several) barbarians standing somewhere on the map.
It helps to lighten the obstacles use, by using them only when necessary. Besides, the barbarian requirements vary a lot and are designed to fit each level, so resources needed per level are better controlled.
This second game is close to the first one, with welcomed improvements.
If you liked Roads of Rome 1, you should definitively buy Roads of Rome 2.

Here's everything I wish people would've told me about this game while I debated buying it, summarized from most to least important:
-From a complete simulator geek obsessed with race sims, on hardcore mode with a Logitech G27, the physics lean much more towards simcade than arcade. In fact, the physics remind me a lot of Gran Turismo 4, with much better low speed differential physics (aka you can actually do a proper donut)
-The vehicle upgrades can be used to vastly impact vehicle handling, and if the car feels unrealistic, swapping around differential parts and tires makes a huge difference, and can make an upgraded car that feels arcade-y, to VERY sim feeling.
-If you own a Logitech G27 and you don't own this game, WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH YOUR LIFE?
-It's the TRUE spiritual successor to Test Drive Unlimited, and you should forget TDU2 ever existed.
-While the graphics resembles TDU2 (same lead environment artist, who is now employed by Rockstar) NOTHING ELSE DOES, SO FEAR NOT, that POS game can be forgotten and/or nuked into eternity.
-The developers who created this game LOVED it, and it shows.
Tips:
-If you have a low end processor, turn geometry settings down. The visual impact is minimal (a little more pop in) and it will vastly boost your FPS
-If you have a low end GPU, turn Ambient Occlusion to SSAO or off.
-If you love race sims, have a wheel, you NEED to buy this game. PERIOD.

I've been playing Eternal for a few months now, and I've really been enjoying it. If you like collectible card games like Magic: The Gathering or Hearthstone, you'll probably enjoy Eternal. I've been a Magic player for a long time, and I really enjoy how Eternal uses the digital medium to do things that would be impossible in a paper game. The campaign is a pretty good way to get started, and after you've completed that Guantlet mode and Forge mode really help you start building up your card collection and other resources. Once you have enough of a collection to build a fun and/or competitive deck, the casual and ranked PvP is a great way to get in a few games. If you want to buy gems with real money, please do, as it supports Dire Wolf Digital, but it isn't necessary at all as long as you are patient enough to let your gold build up to do the occasional draft. If you get good enough in the draft queues, you can even earn enough gold to just keep drafting. Overall, I'm having a lot of fun playing Eternal every day, and I'm looking forward to continued updates in the future. Definite fun for anybody into the genre!

I have played Might and Magic: Duel of Champions, Hearthstone, Elder Scrolls Legends, Shadowverse, Magic: The Gathering, among other card games. This is the only one I have played that is close to as good as Magic, and the only reason I wouldn't rate this game higher is solely due to Magic having been around for 20+ years and having so many sets. I have hope that Eternal makes it that long, because the game is a lot of fun.
I started playing a little less than a month ago, and it's the only online card game that has kept me going back every day to do the daily quests without feeling like it's a chore. I am entirely f2p, and I already have pretty much any cards I need to make somewhat competitive decks and have well over 50% of each set completed so far.
There are enough cards and enough variability in deck building that you can create several decks of the same colors which leads to tons of variety in gameplay.
There are single player modes that reward you with chests that drop cards and gold and have a chance of upgrading into chests that just drop packs. There is also a mode that is essentially "arena vs AI" where you get to keep the cards you pick, and you get chest rewards that can reward up to 4 packs. This mode "forge" is the same as the cost of 2.5 packs. The single-player mode where you use your own decks to play against AI that can also reward you with chests is entirely free.
Then there's casual and ranked, and then there's "draft" which is similar to drafting Magic packs. You get a pack to pick a card then pass the pack. This costs the same as 5 packs, and gives chest rewards along with being able to keep the cards you select.
The only downside, as with any CCG that has cards for mana, is mana flood/screw. It happens, and it's annoying when it happens, but it's only about 25% of my games if not fewer.
The game is the most "new user" friendly CCG online as well as the most free-to-play friendly. There's also a Discord where you can easily contact the developers with any concerns you might have as well as a strong presence on Reddit.
There are also events where you basically pay for packs that are guaranteed and are also able to win more stuff by beating other players.
Overall: 9/10
For the community, design, development team, built-in story that's actually fairly interesting and engaging, and card art. It'll probably become 10/10 after a few more sets are released.

I wrote one review a long time ago of Skyrim, but the words were, "It's awesome, duh" so this will be my first real review of a game on this platform.
tl;dr: Eternal is one of the best card games I've ever played, and I have a lot of time in many different games. The game is worth your time, it respects your time, and it's very much worth your money.
Now, for my longer review. I first started playing Eternal back in April of last year, I was one of the first closed beta invites (I believe I was in the second or third wave, some others had a week or two on me) and I was instantly hooked. The game was like playing a really great mix of Magic: The Gathering's depth and Hearthstones visual style. Both games that I have extensive experience with and love. I have hit legend on Hearthstone multiple times, and I love tournament Magic: The Gathering as well as casual magic like EDH.
What Eternal does right:
Now, I will go into what Eternal does that I do not like, but hey it's early access, almost anything can change right?
As you can probably tell, I have a lot of time on the game, and I've waited this long to review it because honestly, I figured it would be out by now. The game is very polished. However, every time I think the game is ready for release they add some new element to it, or some new level of polish and just really keep improving the game. Is it ready for prime time? I think so, and so do many others, but hey if they want to keep it early access that's fine.
If you like digital CCG's like Hearthstone, I say give Eternal a shot, if you like TCG's like Magic: The Gathering, but do not like how Magic Online is handled, and you cannot wait for Arena, then I say give Eternal a shot. You'll probably be surprised at how disappointed that you aren't.

I love Eternal.
I played MTG since I was little (I am 30 now), played HS, played Gwent, played Duelyst.
For a couple of months now, Eternal's been my go-to CCG. I really, really like this game.
Yes, there's the mana flood/screw issues some people write in their reviews. Truth is, it does not appear nearly as often as those people make it seem like. Some games are frustrating. Some games you are cursing because you cannot believe the luck the opponent had, or the bad luck you had, not drawing one of your 123 possible answers to win it. It's part of the game. It makes you appreciate those hard fought, fair victories all that much.
Eternal is the best possible in-between in complexity from MTG to HS. And there're no fury-inducing RNG cards (like the attrocities you'd find in Duelyst or HS). The complexity of the game is in its deckbuilding, and I just love that.
F2P wise, it's super generous. A couple of free packs a day are easily obtainable (one with the first win each day), and whenever you draft, you keep all you drafted (although draft prices are a little bit higher than in other tcgs for this reason).
Bottom line is, yes, I do recommend this game. Very, very much.
Set 3 is about to be released, so this is as good a time as ever to come play Eternal.  Come, play Eternal.

Wow! I have to say that I'm so pleasantly surprised at how well-thought out this game is. Aside from the details about the game, the developer clearly put a lot of love into this idea enough to create an engine for it. He took into consideration others' imagination to make sure modding is easy (for modders, a circle of people to which I do not belong). I have only been digging into this game 15 hrs more or less at the time of writing this and by no means am I proficient. I've killed off all my populations thus far, but I've played enough to motivate me to share my thoughts.
As someone who is drawn to the outdoors, I've always been disappointed with the way the living world is depicted in games. Granted, you are still harvesting resources in this building game, but there room for success through many different means. Yes, you could build a large bustling town that depends on farming, animal husbandry, and orcharding and all fueled by industries of coal and iron mining. But you could also supply your population with staples of venison, forest tubers, mushrooms, and other wild edibles by maintaining deep forested areas. This flexibility is a first in my experience, and one I have been long awaiting.
Controls are rather straightforward and the tutorial is succinct.
Cycles of seasons alter priorities for a town, as do losses of skilled members of the community, and Banished places the gamer in an enjoyable predicament of balancing interests. Population booms may well lead to busts in several decades time, and slow-and-steady seems the safest strategy for the beginners.
The graphical quality is appealing without being a load on older systems when zooming in and out of the map. Thanks to developers for keeping some great games accessible!
The music is innocuous (a step up for the genre in my opinion) though not noticed for its greatness. This is expected for a nearly one-person project as sound isn't integral to the
No tech trees to unlock, which affords all the more opportunities for alternative roads of development.
Some games I happily buy full price, this is one of those few. If you are interested in town-city builders or like me and looking for a break from fast-paced games, this is the best I've come across by far.

Outlast is the best horror game since 2010's Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
A bold statement, but after fully playing through the game I believe it is warranted.
Outlast sports visuals that could easily top most Triple A studio releases, yet it is technically an indie game, released only on Steam by the developer (and later PS4).
Visuals are actually somewhat important in a horror game, as they can help propel good atmosphere into total full blown atmosfear.  There is an area later on in the game, a open courtyard for the asylum that has rain pouring down and is completely pitch black, save for intermittent flashes of lightning.  It looks absolutely spectacular and I haven't seen such good lightning in a video game since STALKER.
Most horror games will have high quality sound design and Outlast has some of the best sound design in any horror game I've come across.  The music is haunting, subtle and memorable, and when you're cowering in the shadows you wish it would go away just like the crazed denizens of the asylum.  Sound effects are executed perfectly, everything from footsteps to slamming doors and ambient noises will leave you questioning whether that noise you heard was just ambient noise or something sinister in the darkness.
Arguably, the story is the only thing that could be really criticized as being underwhelming.  The story of a reporter who investigates an asylum due to an anonymous tip and the horror and events that unfold is definitely not an original idea.  Then again, if you're looking for original stories in horror you'll probably be disappointed most of the time, as most ideas have already been done.  The final area of the game and the ending could potentially not sit well with some people, but I enjoyed it.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed Outlast and I don't think a horror game will come out that will top it till Frictional's next project, SOMA.

Made to resemble an old C64 game both on sound and graphics department, VVVVVV (that's 6 V's, and there's a pretty good reason for that) is a charming short game about limited controls, pixelated graphics, pulsating soundtrack, and Nintendo-hard difficulty.
You are Viridian, the captain of a spaceship whose traveling has gone wrong, and must rescue all the remaining five crew members. Your only control options are moving left and right, and inverting gravity - but only when you are on a floor or ceiling, not floating around. This simple control scheme allows for MANY puzzles, frustrating moments, and crazy stunts to be performed all around the game!
It's a bit short, and the second playtrough can be made in about an hour or two, but definitely worth the trip.

I know that many people complain about it being a "waste of money" because it can't run on Windows 8. Guess what? I AM RUNNING IT ON A WINDOWS 8 COMPUTER. It's simple, all you have to do is download the update for "Games for Windows Live".

What lies beyond that update is a world of Super Mutants, Zombies, assault rifles, hookers, mini-catapults that shoot mini-nukes, severely enlargened animals and bugs (most of which try to kill you), missing fathers, guys who try to make you blow up settlements, blown up settlements, and much more! Oh, and a huge city where you blow sh!t up, and test all of the above. Almost forgot the totally ironic 50's culture... Overall, I'd give this game a 9/10. People say it's like "Skyrim with guns". However, it's much more than "Skyrim with guns". Imagine the world of Skyrim with guns. Now imagine that world with a huge city in the middle, then the whole thing was blown up with radiation seeping through about everything, and people heavily affeted by said radiation, and a 19-year-old kid (you) who either goes around killing these creatures and being the savior of the citizens of the wasteland, or goes around killing everyone, taking their wealth and working with the "president" (a super-computer with evil AI) to create some sort of "utopia", where you 2 and the "enclave" are the only inhabitants. ALL OF THE ABOVE DESCRIBE THIS GAME. Have you ever tried out a texture pack for Minecraft called "last days"? THIS IS THAT. It has a very strong post-apocalyptic survival feel to it. Then you get mods.
The modding community isn't as present with this game as it is for "Fallout: New Vegas", but still pretty nice. You can add thousands of new weapons, new creatures, and new places to explore. You can turn the wasteland into a true unforgiving hell of a place, or you can make it a beautiful tropical paradise with mutated horrors awaiting you, like I did (Dead Island?). You can add in so many perks, it's like your character's a god when it's all said and done, or make the overall theme of survival EXTREMELY present, having to actually eat 3 meals a day, with drinks included. You can add in amazing vehicles, or make travelling a chore.
In conclusion, I would HIGHLY reccomend this game. Enough said. The only reason it says I played so few hours on this is because I use FOSE (look it up), which doesn't rcord playtime. But I would imagine my playtime would be in the high hundreds right about now.

Fantastic digital card game and by far the best on the market currently. While it does not have MTGs rich history and gigantic card pool, it has vey similar mechanics with some original twists of its own. The game world is rich with flavor both in the lore, and in game. A great variety of different strategies and deck archetypes are viable, some unique to this game, and many well-known from other card games (traditional aggro, control, midrange, and combo all make an appearance).
As a free-to-play game the game is extremely giving, and unlike Hearthstone, it is very easy to get a solid collection just by playing the game. The story campaign is rewarding in enjoyment and card gains, and the repeatable play-versus-ai gamemodes offer the chance to test new strategies or relax away from the competitive player-versus-player. (although, admittedly, I mostly focus on pvp). The Puzzles provide interesting challenges for even the most experienced players and also reward a decent amount of cards.
The laddering system is very much alike other competitive games, and provides considerably more rewards just for playing the game than othe similar card games. Additionally, the daily quests make an appearance as well, being a direct clone from Hearthstone.
All in all the game is a great digital interpretation of the classic TCG/CCG, and is far easier to play competitively without spending real money.

Wow! I have to say that I'm so pleasantly surprised at how well-thought out this game is. Aside from the details about the game, the developer clearly put a lot of love into this idea enough to create an engine for it. He took into consideration others' imagination to make sure modding is easy (for modders, a circle of people to which I do not belong). I have only been digging into this game 15 hrs more or less at the time of writing this and by no means am I proficient. I've killed off all my populations thus far, but I've played enough to motivate me to share my thoughts.
As someone who is drawn to the outdoors, I've always been disappointed with the way the living world is depicted in games. Granted, you are still harvesting resources in this building game, but there room for success through many different means. Yes, you could build a large bustling town that depends on farming, animal husbandry, and orcharding and all fueled by industries of coal and iron mining. But you could also supply your population with staples of venison, forest tubers, mushrooms, and other wild edibles by maintaining deep forested areas. This flexibility is a first in my experience, and one I have been long awaiting.
Controls are rather straightforward and the tutorial is succinct.
Cycles of seasons alter priorities for a town, as do losses of skilled members of the community, and Banished places the gamer in an enjoyable predicament of balancing interests. Population booms may well lead to busts in several decades time, and slow-and-steady seems the safest strategy for the beginners.
The graphical quality is appealing without being a load on older systems when zooming in and out of the map. Thanks to developers for keeping some great games accessible!
The music is innocuous (a step up for the genre in my opinion) though not noticed for its greatness. This is expected for a nearly one-person project as sound isn't integral to the
No tech trees to unlock, which affords all the more opportunities for alternative roads of development.
Some games I happily buy full price, this is one of those few. If you are interested in town-city builders or like me and looking for a break from fast-paced games, this is the best I've come across by far.

Having played hearthstone extensively and liked it a lot my interest has slowly waned over time, being mostly interested in limited formats which is pretty poorly represented in Hearthstone with arena compared to draft in Magic: The Gathering (MTG), a mode i enjoy much more there.
I stumbled over this game on the android gaming reddit, before which I was not at all aware it existed, something i am very happy I did.
Very polished and fun gameplay. Much more similar to MTG than Hearthstone but takes full advantage of being a digital game. A lot of mechanics will feel right at home for the MTG player but takes some getting used to if you're primarily a Hearthstone player for instance. The game uses the blocking system from MTG making combat a bit deeper than Hearthstone I feel. You can also cast some spells during the opponents turn (Fast Spells and Ambush units) making the game more interactive. The deckbuilding is in my opinion much more interesting than hearthstone, and the meta is quite varied.
A respectablwe mobile client (atleast on android) that performs perfectly in matches but a bit long loading times outside of matches.
The game has plenty of game modes that all reward you with in-game currency to spend on packs/drafts/misc things.
is a vs AI mode where you can play with a deck of  your choice until you lose. More wins net better rewards making this a really nice game mode when you just feel like chilling, being much more rewarding than just playing against the computer. This gamemode has it's own "league" netting you extra rewards if you manage 6 wins without a loss.
that are well designed and also nets you gold rewards. Serve as a deeper tutorial to the game's more complex mechanics.
which is basically hearthstones arena mode but vs AI opponents. You keep the cards you pick for constructed. Also has leagues that grants nice rewards if you manage to rank up. Costs gold to play.
represented by casual/ranked. Build a fun deck and play to your hearts content. Ranked gives quite substantial rewards. End of season rank gives rewards depending on the league you reach.
Extremely well thought out representation of a limited mode that is very similar to MTG. You keep the cards you pick. Very good value for building your collection. Play until 3 losses or 7 wins with generous rewards depending on how far you get. Also has leagues that give end of season rewards depending on how far you reached.
that is similar to Hearthstone in that it gives you a full smaller set when you complete it. Also has interesting mechanics.
that occur every now and then with special rules where you try to create a deck that does well under those rules. Thus far these have given very good rewards too.
with basically all modes giving you some manner of rewards, even if you just feel like trying out your new deck in gauntlet mode and see how far it takes you. You also have faction based levels that give you rewards when you level up. I do not know of a more F2P friendly digital CCG.
The presentation is rather uninspired in my opinion with lower quality art than MTG and Hearthstone. The over all presentation is also a bit dull.
The tutorial that you can't skip if I'm remembering correctly that is pretty long. Stick with it...
The pack opening experience: not as exciting as Hearthstone mainly because you get a certain number of uncommons/commons and then a rare or legendary.
Coming from hearthstone it can be hard to get used to the manaflood/screw problem, its not fun to play a game where you had no chance at all because of no mana to play. Unlike hearthstone the mana you get are actual cards you draw.
Over all a very strong recommend for this game if you have any interest in deckbuilding/MTG/hearthstone style games. Can't remember when I last spent this much time on a game.

It's a pretty decent game, overall.  There's a constant sense of dread and anxiety that blankets most of the experience, mixed in with a few early jump scares.  The atmosphere and the sound are really well done and help drive the whole experience home.  However, the whole "hiding from any enemy you see" starts to get a little tedious and stops being so terrifying after a while.  I understand the devs not providing you with a way to combat them, but it's fairly easy for you to get trapped in a corner and you can't do anything about it.  A simple shove mechanic would of helped alleviate this.
It's worth your time if you're looking for something creepy to play through in the same vein of Amnesia, but don't expect anything extremely terrifying (in my opinion anyway).  The ending also leaves a bit to be desired.

After about 23 hours as of this review I'd say I have enough time under my belt to write a review so here it goes (If there are any spelling errors or gramatical errors, forgive me I type pretty fast and make mistakes). And yes UPLAY is needed for the CREW (some say this is bad some don't care. I'm one of those that don't care)
The crew I had many speculation's about because people had said that it wasn't an MMO or very open world, and that you had to drive up on hills to find these stations that reveal the map like in assassins creed. People also said the story is very short and not interesting at all. So firstly let me make my claim over these.
Is the crew an MMO?
A. No it is not, you are locked into a session of 8 people and you will never see more than that. Someone may leave the game and a new one will join in your session but that's about it. For the most part you see people here and there and maybe you drive by them or pull up and rev your engine to race, but that's it. Other than the PVP events and races you're pretty much flying solo on this one.
Is the crew open world?
A. YES and in a very big way. Ever since Need for Speed hot pursuit I wanted another racing game with a very open world aspect and the CREW (for me) delivers in a big way. You start out in detroit but you can drive on down to Miami and then drive to the Grand Canyon, up to Niagra Falls and down to L.A. To me, that's pretty damn awesome. Now, is The CREW a realist representation of the USA? Yes and No, Yes they have included many major cities and landmarks as well as some famous and surrounding towns but for the most part it's highways and open roads. But they have done well to add in many other key things in between such as marshes down in Miami, many farmlands in the Midwest. And a lot of the forestry seen is pretty on par with what would be in the surrounding terrain. So is it a 100% accurate rendition of the US? No, because otherwise you'd spend days to just drive down to Miami. But is it a big open world that is like the US and offers a lot of Free Driving fun? Yes, in a BIG way.
Do you reveal the map with Viewpoints like in AC?
A. Kind of, you have data stations which detail monuments and skill mini games found on the roads, that's pretty much it. Where the revealing of the map comes into play is when you drive on a road or in an area it starts to reveal the map where you drove. The only other kind of "Drive and find this" is the hidden car parts for hot rod's and that's about it.
Is the story bad?
A. In my opinion it's OK, it feels like Ubisoft was going for a Fast and the Furious kind of story in a sense. But the bulk of the story is cutscenes and using races to solve issues which makes the story kind of boring here and there. But I do keep guessing as to how the story will play out so it's kept my attention at least.
Now I'll detail Pro's and Con's of the crew
Pro's
-Open world
-A fair selection of cars to choose from
-Lots of customization for your cars
-Driving and racing is fun
-Driving controls are good (I use an xbox360 controller)
-Many different car customization options for off road, racing, street racing, circuit racing, etc.
-For a racing game it doesn't look bad, you generally focus on the roads and your car (cars look like they are a high texture though) so texture quality isn't a huge biggy, up close you can see the lower textures but like I said, you're driving and racing in 3rd person so it's not an issue.
Con's
-Not an MMO, an 8 player session is not an MMO, I'd prefer if anything a 32 player session or maybe 50. I think an MMO style with hundreds of people racing could become hectic.
-Framrate dips in big cities with lots to load. I'm running a GTX 980 Ti and see frame rates of 20-30 FPS in larger cities, all other times I usually got around 40-50's even in forests.
-Even more customization options would be good
-Microtransactions to buy more money and "CREW credits." You don't have to do this and can easily earn your money by just playing but this micro transaction method in gaming really needs to stop. You can also pay $3(I think) for some other vehicles that can only be bought with your real money but they aren't anything special luckily.
-No custom music options in-game, this is something I really wish they put it. No idea why they can't. It's not a huge issue because I can just run it in borderless windowed and run a playlist of my own stuff on the side but it's still a minor inconvenience.
Overal I'd give the crew maybe a 7.5/10. It's fun and a really awesome open world driving game, I just wish more people could be in a session and framerate dips in larger cities weren't a thing.

This game is a grindfest. The amount of time it takes to create a competitive deck is enormous. The community is very small and tends to attack anyone who has any complaints about the random number generator, drops, the meta, etc. I will attempt to write a relevant and fact based response on why I don't think people should play this game.
1) It's a Magic: The Gathering clone (not necessarily a bad one, but it's certainly not as good as MTG) and if you wait until December 2017 you can play the new version of that game.
2) It requires a tremendous amount of grinding and Direwolf has followed their status quoue by making it even harder to grind by reducing rewards in the game, after developing a large enough player base. What was tolerable before is exruciating now.
3) It's meta top heavy. The vast majority of meta decks require the same cards, which you only receive from the campaigns, which cost $10 or 20,000 coins. To give you an idea of how long that takes to earn, in a week of playing 3 hours a day, I barely scratched 20,000 coins. Yes you can get them for free, but only after playing the equivalent of a part time job.
4) I stand by my argument that the random number generator is bogus.
5) The MMR in Ranked also tends to go against you if you're not playing a meta deck (which is very expensive to create).
6) The Developers are in cahoots with the forums, so people who complain about the game tend to get banned.
In closing, this is not a game I'd recommend, the unethical actions of the developers, releasing player account information, regardless of the reason, something Blizzard has never done, and their consistent movement towards making it harder to play this game for free, means that you'll spend a lot of time playing with minimal rewards, as time goes on. They've done it in Elder Scrolls Legends, and they'll do it in this game too. Save yourself some time and just go find something else.

With Dark Souls 1 being a modern masterpiece, a sequel would have a lot to live up to. How can you change enough of the game to make it fresh but keep it familiar enough to not put fans of the series off? It’s a tough job for even the best developers. Whilst I don't think that DS2 managed to be as great as it could be, I still think it is a good game.
The whole time playing this all I could do is compare it to the first. I think everyone will do that. I know that that's what FromSoftware were thinking when making this. The amount of recycled enemies and bosses in this game prove that. The Gargoyles, The Dragon Slayer (Ornstein), Giant Demons that are obviously recreations/reskins of enemies from the first etc. The status that the Souls Series has for being difficult really got to the director here. Instead of making fights interesting or challenging, they just become unfair and repetitive. Why have one actually interesting and challenging fight when you can just throw loads of opponents at you and make the bosses stronger once you get their health half way down? Why make a boss look unique and interesting when you can just make them a large knight with a fire/magic/lightning sword? It just feels lazy and unexciting after the third one you fight.
It's not all bad though. I still have a lot of fun playing it. Some of the areas are beautiful and are amazing to explore. I love trying to find all the little secrets that the game has to offer. The characters are still pretty interesting and can even make for some weirdly sad moments (Looking at you Lucatiel). The amount of Weapons is pretty insane and I have had a lot of fun trying to customize my character to provide a different play style (Customizing my character to look and fight like Guts from Berserk). I'll finish by saying that the Surface level game isn't all that exciting. The bosses and locations that made the first one memorable just aren't there in this one, but if you want a fresh set of locations and bosses to play a Dark Souls game in then give this a go. You might be slightly disappointed but you will most likely still be happy to play a Dark Souls Game.
7/10.

Not a book, and not quite a movie, The 39 Steps is hard to describe.
If you've played any, this game is probably most like playing Visual Novels, except the story is on a set course and there are no choices to be made. Instead interactivity comes from other places: You preform certain actions that have no real impact on the story, and get to choose exactly how deep you get into details and backstories.
If that sounds a bit boring, it's really is a lot more like reading a book than playing a video game based on one, and I suggest you approach it as such.
Visually, it's very impressive. The text is accompanied by beautiful backgrounds mixed with old photographs and very fun animations, directed in such a way that really makes the text dance.
Fair warning though, this game is quite obviously really aimed for touch devices, the mechanics would work a lot better there than on PC, and it lacks real customization options, so if you have the option go play it on one of those, if you don't it won't bother you too much though.
All in all, I'm definitely looking forward to their next work. This is a very unique and new way to experience books, so if you like reading I'd definitely check this one out. If you don't, keep in mind that this is not a video game in the traditional sense, and this might not be for you.

When I first saw this game, I was excited because I was expecting a modern twist on Anmesia: the dark decent, but as I was playing through it, it gradually became more and more disappointing. Most of the time when your in danger, the game seems to warn you with music or your character starts freaking out a bit, even when your not fully aware something is hunting you down.
Even when you are aware of something chasing you, half the time the game leaves you with no idea how to save yourself without dying several times, forcing you to learn the lay of the land and finding the escape routes or effective hiding places. Oh did I mention the hiding places? At first I thought I got lucky when the monsters are looking for me, but I realized when your hiding, they ALWAYS check the wrong place, unless they see you hide, your always safe. Even when monsters don't know where you are, their Ai forces them into places near you, so even when you have taken the effort to lure them away, 80% of the time, they will find you again, especially when you least and/or most expect it.
The biggest horrors the game puts in are often basic and unimagiative, as other critics have mentioned, often relying on jump scares (though I will admit, you don't expect 70% of them) and gruesome scenes. As stated before, the atomosphereic horror, although scary, is merely a thin illusion that can easily be broken by anyone.
The ending was also a disappointment, but to be honest, its probably because the build up too it was rather epic, but when you finish it, it feels like the dev's slapped you across the face... but again, its probably a bit more realistic then what I wanted.
All in all, although the horror isn't anything new, the adventure itself.. I did find some entertainment in, collecting files and making out of the videos I've taken, I found it rather interesting, so even if your a hardend veteran to horror games, theres still some enjoyment to be had. Just don't expect to find yourself truamatized.

Seinfeld is an American sitcom that originally ran for nine seasons on NBC, from 1989 to 1998. It was created by Larry David and Jerry Seinfeld, the latter starring as a fictionalized version of himself. Set predominantly in an apartment building in Manhattan's Upper West Side in New York City (although taped entirely in Los Angeles), the show features a handful of Jerry's friends and acquaintances, particularly best friend George Costanza (Jason Alexander), former girlfriend Elaine Benes (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), and neighbor across the hall Cosmo Kramer (Michael Richards). It doesn't have the gripping cinematics of a movie. Its interactivity fails to draw in the player like a more fleshed-out game. I love the idea, and the story is a classic, but it really falls short on all fronts.
Beyond the presentation being not quite to my taste, the game has some glaring issues. There are a few misspellings/typos throughout the game's text. There are a couple quick milliseconds of distortion in moments where the VO recording volume peaks. I would like a final product that has more attention to detail.
If you're a big audio book/storytelling fan, I'd say it's worth a shot if you get a discount. Otherwise, if you're just an avid reader and gamer, and you're just a bit curious, you're probably better off getting the original novel or watching Hitchcock's adaptation.

Im writing this initial review a day after I downloaded it. I watched the tutorial "how to use tabletopia" videos, and then jumped in and browsed the menus, and played 1 small game just to try out the controls. I am on a decent gaming laptop, so my experiences may be different in running/operating this game.
1. Loading Times - The devs obviously fixed the loading times before I downloaded it, because I see all these negative reviews about loading times but I have not had any issues whatsoever. The software itself took about 8 seconds to load to the menu's. The board game I chose (roll player) loaded in about 20-25 seconds. This really isnt that bad. About the same as TTS.
2. The controls - I like the controls in this alot better than TTS. In TTS, you HAVE to learn all the hotkeys, shortcuts, ect. In this, almost every command can be accessed by right clicking. This is a great implementation.
3. The games - Tabeltopia has a really good selection of games. I own about 15 board games in real life, and I look at alot of reviews, and playthroughs of games on YouTube. I recognize ALOT of these games. There are alot of games I have not heard of, but I think those are probably user submitted games. Your average family gamer "monopoly, life, batttleship, ect" player may not recognize most of the games on here, but anyone who plays more complex games will recognize alot more of the games on the list. MOST of the fun ones are FREE. The people saying that the free games are all crap unknown games are mostly wrong. If they added 4 or 5 more really good games like Pandemic, King of Tokyo/Newyork, Splendor, Machi Koro, ect. I would DEF pay the $10 / month subscription.
4. The monthly subscription - Like I said in the previous statement. If they had 4 or 5 more games like I said above, I would definitely pay $10 / month. I dont think that is a rip off or anything. You get some really good games for free already. Terra Mystica is one of the highest rated games in the world right now, and its FREE on Tabletopia. That game is $80 if you were to buy it! I would like to see maybe a "silver subscription" level. $5 a month, and you get more games, and a "Gold Subcription" for the $10, unlocks everything. I would be more inclined to spend $5 a month. Or maybe do a "rotating games list" for $5 a month, where you get to play those "premium only" games on a rotating basis. (EX - 1 week you get access to these 5 premium games, 2nd week you can play these 5, ect ect.)
Overall, this really is a decent program with alot of potential. Right now I rate it a 6.5/10 just because of the game choices. It has 350 games, but only about 20 of them are real printed board games. With that said, 20 board games that are actually published games is ALOT.

I don't recall when I got this game, in all honesty. I think it was in a bundle of some kind. But I got reminded of its existence through a weird set of events and wanted to give it another go.
The tutorial is alright - it tells you how things work, which is quite essential for something like this, and the playing field on which you experience things lets you mess around with things for the sake of practice. I came away from the tutorial with a vague sense of how to play - run into basic enemies, shoot flowers and bullets. The gameplay is rather interesting, with a neat premise that can prove rewarding if you can put the time into it.
The main issue I have is that the entire game's aesthetic is a god damn mess. Visuals are psychedelic, which might be some folks' cup of tea, but I found myself dying more often than not due to one of the things I was meant to shoot getting lost in the overwhelming visuals. And this is coming from someone who can play Beat Hazard on Suicidal. The audio makes me think I'm shooting up some bizarre children's toy that communicates in barnyard animal calls, random phone noises, and the occasional phrase repeated to the point of annoyance. Not to mention the weird kid at the start screen reading out numbers in Welsh. The text of the game is just as "wacky" and "random", with references to older games dotted around, intentional misspellings, and the word "goat" being shoved into other words for seemingly no reason.
There's certainly a good game to be had from this, but the nonsensical art direction and reliance on random humour can easily grate if you aren't into that sort of thing. After ten levels (which I understand is less than a tenth of the actual game) I had to turn the game off for fear of giving myself a migraine. It's got a niche appeal, and unfortunately it's not for me.

I personally purchased this game. I reviewed it for my 99 Cent Gaming series.
(Just to note real quick, the original video was recorded on release day so I made a quick update video to reflect the fixes made by the developer. Thank you for caring about your game!}
What I love about doing my reviews of 99 cent games are the many different genres that can come out of the category. While there aren't many gems that come out of the low-budget spectrum, there are games that do a pretty decent job of giving people who love a certain style of games to have more to sink their teeth into. That sums of Alpacapaca Dash for me.
This is the first endless runner I've played since I on Steam (that I can remember) but I've played COUNTLESS of them on mobile devices, and while most of them were F2P they had a certain "one more run" aura about them that made you want to keep playing for better upgrades, great unlocks, and ultimately bragging rights on being the longest distance runner of them all. Alpacapaca Dash isn't F2P but manages to touch on a few of those points for me, but what about those still looking for an entry point to the genre?
Alpacapaca Dash is an endless runner that sports both platforming challenges and enemies to avoid and destroy. Platforming is self explainitory, but you get LASERS to fend off bats, blobs, and snakes. Along the way you can rack up coins to unlock costumes while working your way up through the leaderboards. Let me break it down.
First, here's what I've enjoyed about the game. It definitely hits on those "one more run" addictive traits due to the game keeping track of your furthest distance and putting them on a global leader board for bragging rights. A lot of low-budget games that require quick thinking don't have that option which cuts down replayability, so I'm happy to see it here. Another addition that helps with the desire to keep playing is getting coins that unlock different characters to play as during your runs. Now I haven't unlocked everything in the game, but from what I've seen they are purely cosmetic...and very very cute.
Secondly. here is where I'd like to see improvements. As a personal preference I would have loved to see controller support due to the control scheme being very confusing for me...at first. The developer has since updated the game to allow key rebinding which is a godsend, but controller support would still be pretty neat. Another thing I would like to see is allowing the coins you get to be used on upgrading your powerups. Let me use the Jumper save more than once if I upgrade it. Let the laser be homing for a short period of time if I upgrade the Power Up. Finally, I'd love to see a mode where you don't have to kill enemies at all, instead just allowing the player to enjoy some relaxing platforming.
I have no doubt the developer cares about this game due to fixes that were made post release, and my hopes are that they continue to work on this and fine tune it so when players decide to get their endless runner fix, Alpacapaca Dash is on top of that list.
I have more to say in the videos below, but is Alpacapaca Dash worth the .99 I paid for it: YES. When I first saw this game, I was excited because I was expecting a modern twist on Anmesia: the dark decent, but as I was playing through it, it gradually became more and more disappointing. Most of the time when your in danger, the game seems to warn you with music or your character starts freaking out a bit, even when your not fully aware something is hunting you down.
Even when you are aware of something chasing you, half the time the game leaves you with no idea how to save yourself without dying several times, forcing you to learn the lay of the land and finding the escape routes or effective hiding places. Oh did I mention the hiding places? At first I thought I got lucky when the monsters are looking for me, but I realized when your hiding, they ALWAYS check the wrong place, unless they see you hide, your always safe. Even when monsters don't know where you are, their Ai forces them into places near you, so even when you have taken the effort to lure them away, 80% of the time, they will find you again, especially when you least and/or most expect it.
The biggest horrors the game puts in are often basic and unimagiative, as other critics have mentioned, often relying on jump scares (though I will admit, you don't expect 70% of them) and gruesome scenes. As stated before, the atomosphereic horror, although scary, is merely a thin illusion that can easily be broken by anyone.
The ending was also a disappointment, but to be honest, its probably because the build up too it was rather epic, but when you finish it, it feels like the dev's slapped you across the face... but again, its probably a bit more realistic then what I wanted.
All in all, although the horror isn't anything new, the adventure itself.. I did find some entertainment in, collecting files and making out of the videos I've taken, I found it rather interesting, so even if your a hardend veteran to horror games, theres still some enjoyment to be had. Just don't expect to find yourself truamatized.

With Dark Souls 1 being a modern masterpiece, a sequel would have a lot to live up to. How can you change enough of the game to make it fresh but keep it familiar enough to not put fans of the series off? It’s a tough job for even the best developers. Whilst I don't think that DS2 managed to be as great as it could be, I still think it is a good game.
The whole time playing this all I could do is compare it to the first. I think everyone will do that. I know that that's what FromSoftware were thinking when making this. The amount of recycled enemies and bosses in this game prove that. The Gargoyles, The Dragon Slayer (Ornstein), Giant Demons that are obviously recreations/reskins of enemies from the first etc. The status that the Souls Series has for being difficult really got to the director here. Instead of making fights interesting or challenging, they just become unfair and repetitive. Why have one actually interesting and challenging fight when you can just throw loads of opponents at you and make the bosses stronger once you get their health half way down? Why make a boss look unique and interesting when you can just make them a large knight with a fire/magic/lightning sword? It just feels lazy and unexciting after the third one you fight.
It's not all bad though. I still have a lot of fun playing it. Some of the areas are beautiful and are amazing to explore. I love trying to find all the little secrets that the game has to offer. The characters are still pretty interesting and can even make for some weirdly sad moments (Looking at you Lucatiel). The amount of Weapons is pretty insane and I have had a lot of fun trying to customize my character to provide a different play style (Customizing my character to look and fight like Guts from Berserk). I'll finish by saying that the Surface level game isn't all that exciting. The bosses and locations that made the first one memorable just aren't there in this one, but if you want a fresh set of locations and bosses to play a Dark Souls game in then give this a go. You might be slightly disappointed but you will most likely still be happy to play a Dark Souls Game.

I suppose one way of dealing with the challenges of interactive storytelling is to remove any trace of interactivity. Ultimately, this game is only slightly less interactive than To The Moon, but The 39 Steps lacks To The Moon's brilliant original story and competent pacing.
I had a tough time deciding whether or not I should recommend this game. I think maybe if it were under $5 and you are a patient person with 4 hours to spare, it might be worth the ride. The game does have some truly compelling moments of storytelling, but the slightly confusing and underwhelming climax undermine the otherwise fine story.
The biggest problem with The 39 Steps is that it has no idea what it wants to be. It's marketed as a game, but that is one of the few things it is not; it's part graphic novel, part film and part radio play, with a ton of clicking thrown in for good measure. Some elements work, others fail miserably. I found myself consistently thinking I'd rather be reading the book on which this semi-interactive experience is based. Since that book is available for free, and can be experienced at my leisure without the uneven pacing presented here, I can't bring myself to recommend this version of The 39 Steps, despite all its ambition.

39 Steps is a kinetic novel. Click to progress, click to look close at a newspaper relevant to the plot, do a series of ridiculous mouse movements to open a door. There's no choice, next-to-no gameplay, just text, voice acting, images, music. And in and of itself, that's all right. I'm also working through the When They Cry series, which are also kinetic novels. The problem with the 39 Steps as a kinetic novel is that it's decidedly the wrong format. You have a story about running, disguises, lying, code books, and you don't let the player do anything with any of those? Come on now. When They Cry works because it's essentially observational and relationally complex (and even then, I'd hesitate to recommend them idly). 39 Steps is an espoinage thriller, flat out. Our protagonist is driving the action, and the action is fairly active. This is not a thoughtful story, this is not an explorational story about human nature, it's a man-on-the-run tale. As such, I can't really recommend it in this format. If you want the book, read the book, if you want an adaptation, there's the Hitchcock film. This particular game format adds very little to the experience.

I'll get straight to the point and say that We Need to Go Deeper has a ton of potential to be a game that could easily become a cult hit. The art style is charming and the basic gameplay elements are solid. I'll go ahead and list of what works thus far:
Pros
+Great and endearing art style.
+Fun and sometimes chaotic/intense co-op
+A sense of teamwork and everyone serving an important purpose.
+Reasonable price
Cons
-Networking issues
-Shoddy interface, pop-window warning about IP wouldn't go away until I clicked something in background.
-Confusing and too simplistic combat
-Lack of voice chat
I understand the game is early access and so far it seems the developers have tried to remedy the issues with connections, but seeing as how the game is co-op only, the issues stand out way more. SimplePlanes is a game about designing and flying planes, and I love it for that.
Now, I say it is about designing planes, this is a total lie. The game has a ton of non-planes too (tanks, cars, boats, cities, butterflies, iphones and I think I saw a dragon at one point)
Though the first statement was a lie, the flying bit of this game is spot on (though the physics could be thought out; yes, I'm looking at you invincible cockpits...) But beyond that, it is alot like KSP's spaceplanes (move the C.O.L back, plane becomes stable but sluggish). BUT this game goes into ALOT more depth than KSP, for example, the control surfaces in KSP are seperate parts, but in SimplePlanes they are integrated into the wing and can be configurated. Secondly, THE FUSELAGE BLOCK, my favourite block in the entire game (minus the miniguns, of course).
Now, about negatives... Here is a list of what I believe, are this game's shortcomings:
No symmetry mode (there is a symmetry option, but it's manual right now)
Game seems empty (they are working on this, at this moment)
Limited Part Palette (Steam Community is being added for mods)
In total, this game is probably the most in-depth game based on what you can build with the selection of parts avalable. And even though it has some problems, it will always be the first game I turn to when I wanna have some fun with planes.

The game does it's best to emulate WWI as best it can with it's maps, firearms and atmosphere feeling as close to authentic as your imagination can drum up.  Deaths are properly brutal with gas attacks causing you to slowly fade into death, and gunshots often causing your corpse to writhe and gurgle.  The Frontlines gamemode, featuring attack and counterattack style gameplay could not be done better, in my opinion.  Just be warned, the game has a pretty steep learning curve, and many of the members of this small community have been playing for quite some time.  It's a small but dedicated playerbase, and they are VERY good at the game.  Do not let that discourage you.  You'll get the hang of it.  For those of you that hate reading, I'll go into a Pros and Cons list
Pros
Authentic atmosphere, units and firearms as well as terrains
Frontlines gamemode is fantastic (Also definitely try out Squad Defense! It's great with some friends)
Gunplay feels satisfying, and successfully getting a long range kills feel great, as do trench assaults.  It's fantastic
Cons
Trenches could be a little bit wider, currently there's hardly enough room for 2 men to stand side by side
Steep learning curve could be a pro or a con, depending on who you are.  I put it here based on my own tastes (though the game is satisfying once it starts to click, even if I still suck)
Desync can be a somewhat common issue, though that could just be something that I was personally experiencing due to internet issues.  Your mileage my vary.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game, especially if you have an interest in WWI history.

This game happens around one year after the first episode. Unlike the title name, this episode has a standalone story from the first one, although there are some references. This is the greatest game that Jeff Minter ever made. And hardly anyone realises this because they don't know how to play it, because they try to play it like some other game.
Let me tell you how to play Space Giraffe, and let that explain why this game is so good.
You need to relax, and pay attention to the game. Give it your full focus. What you do in this game is you don't shoot the basic enemies much, just enough to keep the power zone going, and then ram into the side of them as they reach the rim of the grid. That's the basic idea.
When you ram into enemies like this, it's called "bulling". Try to ram through as many as you can at once. It builds up your score, the multiplier, gives you extra lives... it's the main thing you want to try to do.
The power bar is the horizontal line that keeps coming towards you. You want to keep it away from you, otherwise you can't ram into enemies side-on and they kill you instead. The space between the power bar and you is called the power zone. You can also briefly make the power zone get big by collecting a "pod" power-up and jumping.
You can use the right stick of your joypad to aim your bullets through the power zone - just wiggle it a little and you'll probably hit a few enemies, enough to keep the power bar going. In later levels, you'll be specifically trying to aim for flowers, or spheres, or the other annoying enemies.
Now, this game throws a lot at you. So much that you can hardly see. But the thing is - that is what makes this game so amazing and different. This is a shooter that you don't play by shooting, and this is a game with visuals so intense that you need to play it by ear. Turn the volume up if you need to! Wear headphones if it helps!
Each enemy, each bullet, each power up, each collision has a different and distinct audio sound. Pay attention, listen to the game. Record the sound of each one in your brain.
Turn down the music and turn up the SFX if the music's getting in the way. You can't play this game without sound effects.
For levels where there's too much distortion on screen, you're going to feel your way through the level by sound. Listen for the announcement of each enemy, each bullet. You are endlessly auto-shooting, so you can hear when you've hit a flower, how far away it is, and when it "pings" off its stalk to come towards you.
The overall effect of playing this game with heightened sonic awareness, semi-blinded by the lights, racking up high scores, is that you end up with a feeling that is the nearest thing to "using the Force" you have ever, and possibly will ever feel. At least, that's how it is for me.
This is why this game is so good, so important. It is completely different, but it totally works. You just need to be receptive to the game and let it teach you how to play it, how to improve.
And good luck when you get to level 64. It's going to really mess your brain up and you're going to love it for that. :)
