First of all let me just say, I really like this game. The pixel graphics are very good and the art style is very distinctive and this gives the game a 'character', which you often see in good indie games. Here are the positives:
-It's very cheap
-The game runs smoothy
-The game is suitable for both younger and older players, and the controls are very simple, in fact you have a choice of both mouse control and key control, however I preferred the mouse because it was easier to aim and click all with the mouse.
-At the start you can choose a name for yourself, I like that you can change this as often you enter a name and then it becomes permanent.
-There is a reset game button and this means you don't have to re-install the game if you want to re-play and eart the alpacas again.
-The cards are extremely cute, and the game has cards full stop. Usually small games don't have cards like turbopug, but I like that this one does as it just makes it more fun. It also has more cards than a normal game, so the game takes longer to complete, which I like. You know you want to get that alpaca badge!
-There are a range of achievements in the difficulty factor, so beginners and more experienced players have achievements to work towards. Plus, when you've just started playing a game, it's almost heavenly when you get your first achievement, so I guess it kind of encourages you if there are easier ones to get too.
-The soundtrack is very funky and lively, and there were several which it switched between so one song doesn't give you a headache xD
-The menu is very clear and background is pretty
-There is a high score system, so even if you've completed everything else you still have the re-playability factor to beat other people's high scores
-The alpaca buying system is clear, and I like how you don't know what you're going to get as you can't see them until you buy them.
-When you first start to play there are clear instructions as to what everything is and how to control the alpaca
-The colour changes halfway through, which is a really nice effect, and although I was a little confused at first if the person hunched over was an enemy or not, I finally got it, and it just adds some humour.
-The enemies look very cool
-There are tips on the bottom of the home menu that appear, these are useful
-The gray background makes everything look mstical
-When you're playing on the bottom left it has the charge of the lazer, I like that it runs out or the game would be too easy
-It has power downs, which makes you quicker on your feet and more careful
-Sometimes the sky goes magical with many stars and I think this is when you beat your own high score (however I got the magical sky and died right after, and I still needed 1 point to mach my high score)
-It's easy to get the hang of.
Here are the negatives:
-More types of enemies as you progress?
-Maybe more achievements could be added within the difficulty range that's already there
-Is a little slow to load up, and the first time I loaded it up it stopped responding
-Although there are multiple music tracks it could get a little annoying, especially if playing for a longer period of time
-There is no option to change the key controls if you wanted to
-There is no option to change graphic settings bu this isn't really that important as this will run on anything pretty much, so no turning down graphics to increase fps is needed xD
-Sometimes it takes a while to exit out of the game, or exit to the main menu
-The lazer is too slow and the enemies appear very quickly, this could possibly be slowed down a little
-When I've landed on the edge of a platform I can't immediately jump back up and so I die, but this may be purpouseful
-Maybe instead of when you die the second button should say back and not exit, as exit implies exiting the game
-Some alpacas could do different things? I haven't unlocked all of them yet so if this already exists in the game I apologise.
-Most baddies are grey and I understand that's because they're  from the grey world. However once they pass the halfway line their colour could change, for example the worm/snake could turn red.
-Sometimes I don't actually think it's possible to go on without dying, as there are too many things at once in the same place. A downgrade, a baddie, coins, it comes down purely based on luck. Or maybe I'm just a really bad gamer.
-There could be a bigger colour difference between the normal and pink alpaca, I can hardly tell the difference. Colour a little brighter?
-The game is based on reaction time and luck. If the enemy is moving slow enough then I can turn on the lazer in time, like the blob. However if it is a bat, often if I don't have my lazer already turned on it's too slow to kill it.
-The lazer level gague could be bigger, quite a lot of the time I run out of lazer and I die because there were too many enemies to avoid
-You could make an option that makes it possible to turn off the instructions when you play the game, it could get a bit annoying if you play thre game a lot
-It would be cool to be able to kill perticular enemies like bats by jumping on them.
-Also, sometimes when I am playing a gap appears, so therefore I have to jump, and then I land on an enemy I can't avoid, because I can't move around in mid air or double jump or anything, so I just die. If I try and jump before I fall in the gap, and if I try and jump after I fall in the gap.
-Maybe add so that when you die you can press enter and it starts again for people who are using the keybord control options.

Alpacapaca Dash is an endless runner with shooting elements.
The levels are randomly generated, so you will most likely never face the same level combination twice. With the coins you can collect in the Levels, you’re able to unlock a variety of different outfits for your Alpaca. One of my personal favorites is the “Sailermoon-Alpaca”
What I really like about the art style of the game is that the world is all black and white, and you bring it to life with your Alpaca while running. Has a really nice feeling to it, to see the world change colors while playing.
In my whole playtime the game ran smooth at any given moment, I never had a stutter or anything like that. The only technical problem I encountered was a crash once when I exited back to the main menu after a run. But since it never happened while I was running I wouldn’t count that as a minus.
Overall, I really enjoyed my time with the game. The gameplay is fun and always motivating. Alpacapaca Dash has this typical “just one more try” feeling to it.
The game also contains a high score list, so you can compete with others.
What I would personally like as an addition is a high score list which only shows the stats of your friends.
If you like endless runner type games or want to try one, I can recommend Alpacapaca Dash to you! The game only costs 1€ so you can’t make much wrong with the purchase.

I have had used Steam for about 12 years and this is my first ever steam review. This game is fantastic.
It's easy to pick up but there is lots of tactical and strategic room for growth. Some say it is like Hearthstone but much better, and I would agree with that. It has a healthier economy (ie it is more rewarding and gives you more cards without having to spend money). But if you want to spend money to speed up your collection, that is always an option.
I would compare it more to the card game Magic the Gathering. It takes the best of Magic and Hearthstone and leaves the worst out.
The single player campaigns are pretty fun and give you a good start for your collection, then there are several game modes to play after that:
The card quality is great, and the game is surprisingly well balanced. The developers have done a great job to maintain balance in the card pool. There is diversity in the "meta," which is to say that there hasn't been one single deck that has dominated over everything else, because every strategy can be countered.
The game is still pretty new, and there is only the base set and one expansion set out so far, but there are already a TON of cards and there is no shortage of cards or ideas for decks.
The game was just made in a way that makes sense, and the devs have really put alot of thought into it. Have a cool deck you want to share with your friend? Easy, there is an export button in-game. Find a cool deck online that you want to try out? Easy--you can copy the deck and import it with one button. Super user-friendly.
If you are interested in theorycrafting, there is a great community here, on reddit, and other forums as well. People post deck lists all the time and there are plenty of startegy articles to get you started. Here are a couple sites that are pretty popular to check out:
All in all, cannot recommend this game enough to anyone who is interested in this type of game. Good luck, and I hope you try it out!

There is nothing really special about this game, it doesn't add any new twists to the horror genre, or go to a type of setting you have never seen before.  But just because there is no gimmick in this game, doesn't mean it is bad.  On the contrary, this is one of the best horror games I have ever played.  The atmosphere is erie in the asylum where everything seems a little off (that may be from all the corpses and blood) and where the patients are as crazy, and deformed as it gets, and you never know how they will react.  Sometimes they just curl up in a ball and scream, and other times, they are chasing you through the sewers.  The camera that you hold to record what is happening also adds a creepy layer when you use the night vision.  The game is excellent at making tension.  There are times where you don't get attacked for twenty minutes, but you are always on alert because of the excelent sound (from the heavy breathing and heart pounding from the main character, to the sound of chains and foot steps in the distance) and the closed corridors with many doors that you don't know whats behind them.  There are also a couple good jump scares that got me, but not enough to get tire-sum or take away too much control from the organic scares that happen.  Some of the scariest parts of the game are unique to the player and not cutscenes.  For example, I was in the sewers when this big mutant who stalks you throughout the game appears.  I try to sneak past him, but he sees me and I start running.  I see a little drain hole and a quickly crawl into it.  Once Im in this cramped space, I look back to see his feet right there.  He pauses for a while before walking off.  Calmed down now, I start making my way through to the other side, when to my surprise, he had gone around and was waiting for me.  I tried to go back, but it was too late.  He dragged me out and beat me up.  It was one of the biggest jump scares for me, and it wasn't a cutscene.  They also add different scare elements and different locations (hospital, normal asylum area, office, sewers, etc) so it stays fresh, and keeps you on your toes.  The story is nothing new in the horror genre, but it isn't terrible.  The little notes that your character writes about diferent things that happen thoroughout the story, adds a bit of personality to the silent protagonist.  There were a few things that took me out of the experience though.  One was the ridiculous amount of pain the protagonist could tolerate.  He had things done to him that would normally make someone pass out, but he just grabs his camera and moves on.  Another thing that made it less scary, was when you realise how easy it is to lose someone chasing you in some cases so you don't feel the need to sneak, because there are practacally no penalties to being spotted, but this is only about halfway through.  They do a few things later in the game to freshen it up again.  To sum it up, this is a geat horror game that I would recommend to anyone who wants some thrills and solid gameplay this year.

The 39 Steps has been designed with such attention to detail that it positively oozes the stuff, which makes it more intuitive than many other interactive visual novels I've had the pleasure of reading. As per the title, there are a total of 39 chapters, each of which is a self-contained slice of the overall story, with beautifully drawn scenes and objects. Gameplay is fairly simplistic, and is no great stretch to the player - or should I say reader or watcher? - as in some other titles such as Puzzle Agent. Flowing seamlessly from one element to the next is no easy feat, and yet this game manages to accomplish it.
Maybe it's ironic that an interactive novel creates an experience that is hard to describe using words alone. Definitely a hidden gem, if any title on Steam is underrated it is this.

Overall, for an Early Access game, We Need to Go Deeper is awesome. It is not yet very complex, but as I state below, the devs are absolutely amazing and I have no doubt they will add many more features in the future. Please don't decide to not buy the game simply based off the reviews that talk about ridiculous server trouble, as they were outdated pretty much as soon as they were written. This game has a lot of potential and a great dev team, so I think we can expect an awesome game upon full release!
First off, I don't think that I have ever seen so many updates pushed out in so little time, so I would like to mention that not enough people appreciate the devs for all the hard work they have done to get the servers into the shape that they are in. For example, around 4:45 (I don't remember the exact time) on February 12th, they sent out a message saying that they were attempting to fix a relay server problem, and in about 1.5 hours they had completely erased the issue. Great job, devs!
Just a few days ago, it was very hard to join a server without the game crashing, and to be honest the game was just about unplayable. Now, they are much more stable; I don't think my friends and I have had any troubles joining games even though a few of them have the IPv6 problem. Also, the most recent update adding private servers was a much needed fix; people joining games was really annoying without lobby chat (another awesome addition).
To me, the gameplay is great. It doesn't get boring quickly at all. I think it would benefit from more random map generation and more extensive caves, as long as health is better balanced so that the crew doesn't have to run in, defeat three or four crabs, and run back to the sub to heal. Also, once more subs are released, I think the game will be much more fun.
The only other complaint I have about the game is that it can only be played multiplayer co-op, but the purchase is for one copy. I think that a $15.00 - $17.50 two copy edition would be a great addition. Other than that, I would definitely recommend this game to just about anyone!

The 39 Steps is (as most have previously stated) an interactive novel, and NOT a game. There are some elements of interactivity in the form of mouse clicks and even "drawing" patterns with the mouse from time to time, but that's about it.  That said, if you know going in you're going to read and occasionally watch/listen to a story, you shouldn't be disappointed.
For the most part, I thoroughly enjoyed my time in the story. I would sit down and play one of the 20 or so "chapters" at a time. Having them broken down into 10-15 minute chunks like this helped and allowed me to play at my own pace.  The art is very well done, though there is really no actual animation. The voice acting is well done and the ambient sounds and music are a plus.
Being that the story is set prior to WWI (and that I'm American and this is set in the U.K.), some of the dialects and terminology were a bit tricky to follow, but not so much that it detracted form the story itself. Other than that, my only real complaint is that the ending seems somewhat . . . abrupt. I certainly won't spoil anything, but I felt that another couple minutes of gametime could have wrapped it up a little better.
All-in-all, the playthrough was an enjoyable experience and I'm looking forward to The Story Mechanic's next project.
My personal rating for what it is: 7.5/10

Space Pilgrim II kept me hooked from beginning to end. It was a late night shuffling through Steam games before deciding that it was time to take a look into the next Space Pilgrim episode. 2 hours later & before I knew it I was finishing the game. There is a creative story in this episode involving religious fanatics, mad scientist like doctors, and crooked cops. It has two of the main characters from the previous episode, especially Gail Pilgrim the main character. It gives you more of the interesting story telling, simple but fun problem solving, and interesting plot twists that you would come to expect from playing the first in the series. I appreciated the little astronomy lesson in the titles of the games as well. The style is obviously retro/RPGmaker, but the dialogue has some winks and nods to modern situations and delivers with the humor and suspense. These aren't the epic time consuming games that you will spend huge portions of your time to dig into and finish, but for a short narrative driven experience Space Pilgrim has delivered twice for me and I look forward to seeing the rest of the series.

Fallout 3 has to be one of the best Open World RPGs I've ever played and has to be one of my favorite games. Now I know what you're thinking and before you say anything about how long I've played, but I owned the game on xbox before rebuying it because it's just that great of a game. This game has one of the best post apocolyptic setting and style I've ever seen.The game play is obviously like any RPG made by Bethesda. You can really get a feel for your character and have relativly nice control over who they are, even if it's all put on a morality system that sometimes can be a little off. The situations you're put into have multiple outcomes and ways of going about them and the game gives you a sizeable amount of freedom without giving you everything. The combat and weapon variety is awesome, even if some weapons are better than others. If you are really committed to having your character be a certain way, you have all the freedom to do it and the tools available. It really is a game where you can get a feel for how you want to do something. And the large modding community this game had gives this game even more replay value because mods can add so much more to this game.
Now there will always be obvious problems in these games. While the game is mostly great, you will experience your occasional bug but that is pretty standard with Bethesda RPGs. And the fact that when you try and zoom in with a weapon, it just ZOOMS in was a pretty bad choice(which I'm glad can be fixed with mods and that Bethesda later chose to change for Fallout: NV). Also that third person was also a little weird. While I'm sure some people may have enjoyed it, I usually stayed with first person. I think this could've been fixed if you had more control over where your character was located(I.E. To the right, left or centered). The game is also EXTREMELY easy if you're a thief. You actually have to force yourself into not being successful because it's too easy to be successful in this game.
But all and all, I recommend this game to EVERYONE who even has a slight interest in trying it because it's an experience that isn't worth missing out on.

Space Giraffe by Jeff Minter is a game where the player controls Elfie - the first giraffe to ever be sent into space. The game begins by quickly going through the two decade’s worth of intensive education which Elfie must first undergo before he can become the first space giraffe. Completing many assignments and even making a few friends along the way. At the end of the first level, Elfie is awarded a space giraffe diploma, and there is a beautiful shot where the player can see Elfie’s parents in the audience at the ceremony. Since the game is made with the same graphics engine that powered Sony’s Afrika on the Playstation 3, the level of emotion that Elfie’s parents are able to display was quite impressive at the time. Elfie finally boards a rocket in level 2 and is shot into the vast vacuum of space, wherein for the first time in his life, Elfie comes to the realization that he will have to spend the rest of his life alone. Over the course of a year, the player gets to witness Elfie’s descent into madness, and as he loses his mind, the universe around him starts to change in colour.
The rest of the game just rips off the end of 2001: A Space Odyssey, but instead of a space baby, we get to see the ghost of J. Allard.

Space Giraffe is a game I've spent six years both loving and hating the hell out of.
On one hand, its iterative take on Tempest 2000/3000 is super engaging and satisfying. While it may invoke those older games on the surface, the bulling and Power Zone mechanics really make Space Giraffe feel like more of it's own game than the rehash it's often accused of being. The shooting and dodging are tight and satisfying and the risk vs reward elements make for some crazy intense shooty action. When all that comes together with the visuals and audio in the way that it's supposed to, Space Giraffe is simply astoudning to play and you can almost feel like you're in a trance when you're on a roll.
When it doesn't work however, the game just feels plain unfair and frustrating. Far too often, the emphasis on eye-searing visuals over gameplay can and will cause many unnecessary deaths due to how obscured the playfield can get. A large chunk of stages also to alter the game's rules subtly without telling the player, which just seems like a cheap and sloppy way to prohibit progress.
There will inevitably be frustration with this game, but I highly suggest at least trying the demo. It's something I've stuck with since its release and if you can manage to get over its initial quirks and don't mind some frustration later, Space Giraffe feels about as satisfying as Portal can be once you finally "get it."

"The 39 Steps" is, down to its core, a slightly-interactive-novel. That being said - it's not "bad" by any means. For what it is, it's incredibly well done, and a means in which I would love to continue consume various forms of classical fiction.
Based on the original espionage thriller "The 39 Steps" by John Buchan, you can definitely see where modern day spy stories came from - predating popular fictional characters like James Bond by at least 30 years. This story takes place on the verge of WWI and introduces a character named Richard Hanny, a man on the run after a young American spy divulges sensitive information to him. The game is presented mostly in beautifully painted backdrops, fuzzy silhouettes and the occasional shadow puppet show (of which are quite entertaining). These backgrounds take you from inner-city London, to the moors of Scotland and back again. There isn't much gameplay to be had (to my slight disappointment), but what is present is likened to that of a game like "TRAUMA" - drawing shapes and clicking on things to carry through the cutscene-like chapters.
Simply put - the game is awesome for what it is - but it really needs a bit more interactivity. There is one part that involves the character decoding a notebook. I got really excited, thinking that I'd at least have a mini-game or a puzzle to figure out the code, but alas - the game just carries on like the book. They allow you to zoom in and out on objects you see in the environments - here I am, thinking that I'll have to do some Sherlock Holmes work and pick out clues from the zoomed-in objects, but alas - there isn't much to discover but a few timeline-appropriate advertisements and newspaper articles.
I would love to digest all sorts of fiction this way. From Sherlock Holmes to H.P. Lovecraft to Franz Kafka - I would love to have this sort of artwork and voice acting and sound effects, mood, pacing, attention to detail, and the ease of taking it in via separate chapters (just incase I need to leave and come back to it) - albeit, more interactivity would be preferred.

cough, so yeah it's an adaption of something constantly adapted. there ain't much here to dissect besides the story and literary analysis ain't really my thing unless I'm impressed. so let's just go with a classic: the game is fun. awww yea boy you know what that means. it's a regular good game that's what. what we got, what we got, we got some painted scenery. gog DANG have you seen the artwork. it's bleeding brilliant, it spills all over the screen. the attention to detail is always impeccable. and that doesn't just sit with the art! the writing is mindful of the time while adeptly conveying background without awkwardly hamfisting the narration. the segways and different menus that pop in and out while you're playing to convey different information is delightful. also those newspapers, the freaking perfectly accurate newspapers. man I could write paragraphs on those newspapers

Toy Story Mania is one of the many Disney released games on Steam over the years; this game is based on the idea of the extremely popular attraction in the Disney World Theme park, Hollywood Studios, in Orlando Florida. The queue times for the ride it self are sometimes over five hours! With the physical attraction being so popular, it is hard not to imagine Disney wouldn't try and squeeze a little bit more out of it in a video game.
It is essentially a shooting gallery style game, based around the Toy Story franchise. It was actually initially released on the iOS first, before later being released on PC and then consoles. The game had it's biggest hit on the Wii since this also came packed with a peripheral device in the European markets to use to play.
The gameplay it self is very simple and family friendly, just aim with the mouse and click to fire. You can be throwing pies, darts, rings, balls and all sorts in the six different galleries.  Different targets grant more points, there are also a number of different tasks to complete on each stage such as knocking over a certain amount of one target or finding a secret entrance etc. These add a little variety to the stage rather than a simple shoot and aim mechanic.
Unfortunately the graphics in Toy Story Mania really let it down. You cannot play in 1080P which nowadays is an absolute must, and there are minimal graphical options which can sometimes look like you are playing a extremely outdated game. It doesn't look like any work was done at all on the PC port of the game as it is so poor graphically.
Whilst each stage offers a spinet of a story, there is no overlaying plot, I would look at this game as a casual pick up and play sort of game. Don't expect any new story from the Toy Story gang.
All of the original voice acts play their respective roles in Toy Story Mania, some of which I believe are just ripped straight out of the films, but I believe there are some original lines to be found. This is a huge bonus when you compare to Toy Story 3 on Steam, which don't have the full cast.
Each of the gallerias are well designed and offer a lot of variety on each stage, I really liked how the whole screen can be full of targets to hit, but I still had trouble hitting them! There is so much to look at and you only have a small amount of time to do it in, you really feel a sense of urgency on each level.
Another negative point would be the game's length, I actually finished the whole game's single player mode in just over half an hour. Toy Story Mania really encourages you to replay levels to get better scores and to earn more tickets to unlock new characters and bonus stages, so if you really want to squeeze every little bit of content out, you can probably get about five hours to action here.
This game is no by no means difficult. It is clearly heavily aimed towards a younger audience, which is a shame since the majority of the Toy Story fans will have grown up with it and be in their mid twenties now. You can get to the harder stages by really aiming to get the very high scores on each stage though.
Apart from the horrible graphical options and no higher resolution support, I didn't have any other technical problems such as crashing or bugs. It's just a badly ported PC game.
To conclude, it's actually a bit of a difficult one for me - I really enjoyed playing Toy Story Mania, mainly because the ride at the theme park is my absolute favorite and I love the idea that I can boot this game up and feel like I am back at Disney World about to go onto the ride instead of waiting for five hours in the blistering sun.
People who don't have that nostalgic feeling will probably find this game dull, and boring. So I am still going to give this a thumbs up review, but with a recommendation to only pick it up when on sale for about £5 if you want to try it out. Fans of the ride will really want to jump on here and bask in nostalgia

I've been in a search of different "games", and so, this one intrigued me, specially since it didn't even advertise itself as a game, despite being release on Steam. So... if not a game, what is it? A "Digital Adaptation" is what it calls itself. It's essencially an adaptation of a book into a more visual format, with a little more interactivity.
I've got to say, I'd rather read a book most of the time, than "playing" one, unless there's something to take from it that I wouldn't from a book. Well, in regards to that, this is a much shorter form of a book, focusing on the essential only, and at the same time, giving some additional insight into the story's time and world through journals and such, for those interested... and, again, not a game.
I usually play games for more interactivity than this has given me, at specially choice and consequence, which is something that I can't really get from a book, and which this still doesn't provide.
So, all things considered, I don't think it surpasses a book for those who tolerate/like reading.
BUT, it was still really well done (for what it was), and I'd say it was a totally positive experience, with lots of potential for the future. The story was really interesting (although the pacing was too slow, at times), and the whole art design helped a great deal, it was highly stylised, in a good way.
For the developing team: I'd love to see this done with a "Choose your adventure" type of book, I think that would be the format where it would shine! Maybe do some research into old Text VideoGames and try to adapt them as well. Who knows? But experimenting is the way to go, and, for the first "Digital Adaptation", I think it was pretty good. I'll follow you closely and see what else you can provide.
Oh, and also, a little bit more exploration, maybe with Diary Pages or Audio Logs spread throughout the places one can explore to provide more information about the story and the era it's set in.
Bottom-line: Not a game, still not quite as content-full as a book, but a nice experience overall, with fitting Music and Art Style. I'm interested to see where it goes! If you think you'll take some enjoyment out of something like this, go ahead and buy it, it's pretty good!

There are many great games in Tabletopia and the interface is wonderful. However, unless you are playing with others who understand that this is a tabletop simulater you will not be playing anything. It tries to simulate you actually playing at a table with the real game sitting in front of you. By that I mean EVERYTHING has to be done by you and other players. If you want to play chess for example, nothing is automated at all. You both can pick up and move any piece on the board, and you will need to. If you want to take their pawn with your pawn you have to pick up theirs, move it off the board, then move your pawn to where theirs used to be. I have tried to play a half dozen games on there now and they all end up the same. No one knows what to do because they don't understand that everything is manual. It quickly devolves into everyone just flipping cards over and over again or moving pieces randomly just to see what they can and can't do. I'm really frustrated so far trying to play with people. My suggestion to the developers is to have a popup at the start of each game telling players that everything is manual and what to do to get the game started.

While it's far from a perfect browser-to-standalone program adaptation, it's not all bad. Load times could be improved slightly (or drastically, depending on your internet connection or system settings), but, so far, I see no real reason for this program to be recieving so much crap. It's essentially a free 'version' of Tabletop Simulator, not a fully-fledged, fully outfitted game-playing program, without the price tag.
The program allows players to design games as well (via browser, I believe), which means, if a game you want hasn't appeared yet, you could always make your own game. These player-made games can be browsed and downloaded for your entertainment.
There are, of course a few gripes.
1. Load times. This has already been mentioned, but the load times can be a little tedious sometimes. This applies primarily to the loading of various tabs. However, when exploring the program myself, I noticed that tabs opened faster once you have visited them at least once. The address bar on the top center of the window makes me wonder if this more of an internet connectivity issue, rather than something else. The only thing I can say is to give it a little time, and maybe the devs will work on it.
2. Premium. Some games are locked behind a Premium condition, one that asks that you either pay $2 to play Premium games for 3 days (Weekend With Friends is the option name), or pay for a full month. You don't need Premium to enjoy the vast majority of games, but it seems just a tad iffy to ask players to pay to play certain games. Of course, developers need to earn money somehow. Here's hoping that doesn't go off the rails.
3. Translations. Some games, obviously, are not written in other languages, which can be a downer for those who want to try the game out and perhaps add it to their favorites. Perhaps adding options or opportunities for some of these games to be translated can come along at some point.
Not many issues (for me), but I do hope the developers work on improving the game. Many players, apparently, also have issues with starting this game up entirely, which I think may be more of a systems issues, rather than a programming issue. I have a VERY basic gaming rig, one from 2014, with no new upgrades, and it runs this game just fine.
In summary:
Not perfect, but certainly not terrible. Has a few issues, but those can be worked out over time, or worked around with relative ease (and patience). Has plenty of F2P games available, with the option to create new ones, or download player-created ones via internet browser. It has promise.

Defunct has a story. You're a robot with a broken motor trying to reach the repair shop to get your engine fixed.  You'll have to jump through hoops (literally) to get there, all the while trying to keep up momentum so you don't have to sputter along.
I enjoyed playing this game, but it's a lot harder than I expected.  Controls are very responsive, but the amount of precision required to avoid accidentally braking uphill or perfectly land a jump on a small platform is far more difficult than I was ready for.  The game is clearly designed to encourage speed runs (and there is even a Time Trial mode for each level), but I wasn't able to make a fast finish on any of the levels.  I often crashed into a wall or piece of debris, causing me to lose nearly all of my speed, and the levels are usually difficult to finish if you don't maintain your momentum.
There's a lot to like here, but it may not be for everyone.

How do you make a sequel to a memetic masterpiece? Let alone Dark Souls?
After many playthroughs of the first game, I can see why From didn't just go "ok heres more of Dark Souls 1 but with polish" like they did with Artorias. That would have been to familiar, too comfortable, and that goes against the point of the franchise.
2 is inferior to 1, but in a way that creates a haunting, surreal, and uncomfortable experience, which is powerful in it's own way. It's like Dark Souls was recollected in a fever dream, which is almost aggressive in how little sense it makes (windmill elevator, you'll know what I mean). The engine has been improved in small ways, but the combat (at least early on) is deliberately sluggish and many of the tactics that were so strong in the first game have been stripped away.
If this appeals, play the Scholar version of 2. If you care more about gameplay, or just want more of the first Dark Souls, skip to 3.

Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is an enhanced version of Dark Souls 2, including all DLC, (barely) enhanced graghics, DX11, a 64x executable, and some remixed enemy locations.
This Western-style Japanese RPG mixes fighting game mechanics with role-playing, complete with invincibility frames, dodges, punishes, and careful timings. The moveset of your fighter is determined by the weapons you choose, the armour you wear and the speadsheet you add numbers to. Weapons are varied between polearms, blunt objects, blades varying from daggers to longswords to Final Fantasy, talismans and magic staffs for miracles and spells respectively which range from fire to lighting to Final Fantasy, bows and crossbows ranging from shortbows to Final Fantasy, and gloves ranging from Mike Tyson to Ryu from Street Fighter, complete with a literal Hadoken. Armour ranges from light to heavy to Tetsuya Nomura, and shields range from bucklers to heaters to a mural of two messengers from the hereafter. Items of varying effects and abilities round off your equipment, and since you can mix and match armour pieces, up to six weapons and/or shields (two in each hand at any one time, plus two extra per hand to swap to), there's almost no end to what you can potentially create.
As such, Player versus Player, should they occur, interactions flow like a 3D fighter, with players dancing around the field with their unique fighters. And unique they are. Be they recreations of historical warriors, cosplay of their favorite heroes, scantily-clad waifu bait, buster-sword weilding over-compensaters, or nudists showing off, the playerbase has no end to the kinds of things you might witness. These people, called Invaders, are tasked with finding and killing the world's host player, to gain their souls and various other items related to the game's covenants. If you don't feel like fighting others, never fear, some may drop in to help you, be it getting through a tough patch, killing a boss, or repelling an Invader, reaping similar rewards. Covenants give players who engage in these activities, be they a help or a hinderance, incentive by offering rewards for their loyalty to the cause.
Regular enemies are not quite so graceful, but do manage to catch newcomers to their lands off-guard, surprising them around every corner. Not every enemy waits around corners, however. Some are invisible in fog. Some snipe you from miles away. Some hit you without actually touching you. It's not entirely uncommon to be unfairly hit, as per the games' apparent desire to live up to the Dark Souls promise of ensuring your death appears to superseed it's attempts at fair gameplay. Luckily, the game gives you limitless lives to try and try again, and these unfair moments are few and far between. Most of the time, death is you're own doing, reverting you to your last bonfire, which serve as checkpoints you'll respawn.
Death may be limitless, but it's not without it's detriments. Souls are collected from fallen foes, which serves as your currency, experience, and upgrade juice. Should you fall, a glowing green bloodstain is left near the spot you died, containing all the souls you'd collected, giving you a second chance to recover them. Die before you recover them, however, and they'll be lost forever. You'll be pushed back to your last rested bonfire, forcing you to fight all the enemies, which respawn upon your demise. Additionally, your health is reduced each time you die. Die enough, and you'll be left you only half a health bar to work with. As if that wasn't enough, when you die, you look like a zombie, meaning all those hours creating the perfect waifu will be wasted. There is an item to recover your lost power, but the item is finite. This feeds back to invations and helping others, as defeating a host as an invader or defending one as a helper grants you more of these items.
Not that death becomes a huge issue later in the game. Lifegems, a healing item, of varying quality drops from enemies occationally. Your Estus Flasks, a health potion, replenishes upon death or rest at bonfies. Between these two items, your potential health pool may was well be infinite, with only enemies capable of ending you in a single swipe or in a combo, or a drop from a high place possibly ending your life. This is a strange gameplay choice considering the intended difficulty and the story's intended impact. To have an item that directly contradicts the game design and story is odd to say the least, and it's not hard to acimmulate a surplus of these items either, making their inclusion all the more baffling.
Speaking of baffling design, far too many enemies boil down to a dude in armour, and too many bosses boil down to a taller dude in armour. Considering some of the very creative enemy and boss designs, such as a large frog with a skullface in it's mouth, a large bipedal humanoid with two upper bodies, and a voilent jack-in-a-chest, it's odd how many times I see the same boring knight. That's not to say some fights against these dudes aren't great, or that there aren't wyverns, trolls, walking mushrooms and scantily-clad waifus, but a little more variety could have helped tremendously, especially since most of them churn out roughly the same movesets. Learn to dodge one, learn to dodge them all. Some of these enemies pose some unique challenges, but these amount to gimmicks, such as remixing them with sniping mages, or by making them straight up invisible in a foggy forested area. The few enemies that divert from the tradition tend not to pose a huge threat, though some challenging mob fights keep you on your toes.
The locations you fight them in is sufficiently diverse to distract you. From a castle sinking into a volvano, to a forrest shrouded by fog, to a dark gutter, to a sinking kingdom of giants, to a rising castle of wyverns, you'll get your fill of vistas and scenery. A ruined castle surrounded by water while you bath in the sun in all it's glorious incandescence can be a true sight to behold. It's a shame that what follows is yet another baffling design choice; the level design. Falls you have no choice but to break your shins on, ladders that you can't climb from the midpoint, would design that doesn't make sense at the best of times. Not to mention how much the game relies on ambushing you. I don't mind the odd ambush, but it starts feeling a little bit cheap sometimes. Luckily, the game grants you access to a fast travel ability from the start that makes the level design an easier pill to swallow, but some individual areas aside, the level design is nothing special.
Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is a great game at best and a good game at worst. While it may shift between these two more often than I'd like, good and great aren't bad choices to make. It's a game that'll keep you playing, but once it's done, returning may not be your first choice.

A challenging precision platformer, with a joyful retro ambience, in which flipping gravity is how you get about.
The setting is that of a somewhat surreal, silly scifi, and largely is there to provide a framework for you to bounce around space equipped with an amazing soundtrack, and interesting platforming mechanics. The game is nonlinear, with the player exploring a large "hub world" to find the levels, the order in which they are found not mattering. The various levels provide new mechanics atop the core gameplay of switching gravity, keeping the platforming novel.
Despite the challenging nature of the game, frequent checkpoints, fast resets, smooth controls and a jovial atmosphere goes someway to offset player frustration. Additionally, the hardest challenges are presented as optional collectibles, and can be sidestepped for those who aren't in it for crazy challenge. The core game respects the players' time, and explores the game mechanics and aesthetics without overstaying it's welcome, at about 3 hours. However, for those who would want more, collectibles extend that by a couple of hours, and the speed trials and surival mode provide further replayability to this retro-styled gem.

This is a fun game with clear roots to sonic. This game is best when you go fast. I tend to try to go for collectibles when I see them, but that made the game a bit tedious. The game is well designed. There's several path ways to go, meaning a lot of replayability. The story is short (I went for collectibles in the beginning before just switching to play for speed.) The one big difference from sonic is you use your mouse to gain speed while going down hill, and it causes you to slow down or break going up hill. It can be a bit frustrating, versus Sonic where you just hit things and keep going. It does as a skill mechanic though. The story is short (speed running it you can probably get through it in under an hour. But with collectibles, different paths, and the ability to just treat a zone like a Tony Hawk game and go for air there is a lot to come back to. There are some parts of the map where the camera glitches out, or a part of a plane or terrain sticks out and if you clip it you kinda get sucked in. But this didn't happen frequently. The story was simple and cute. The Mascot is very likeable, he's a older model robot (or Defunct) in a seemingly post apocalyptic world. Robots seem to be the only ones left, using the universe as thier racetrack/playground. I'd buy dlc for this game or a sequel. What I'd like to see in a sequel is more narrative or world building (I really like what they have so far, it seems like it could be a interesting universe). Maybe a multiplayer racing mode besides time trial. Also if they could encorporate tricks through button combos (currently e in the air does a random trick from my understanding). You can also unlock skins/ colors for Defunct/ The character robot. This game was apart of a bundle, and I've really enjoyed it.  10$ might be a bit steep for content, but if you want to support a promising developer then do it. Otherwise grab it on sale its worth a few playthroughs, or a pick up when you want to play a 3D sonic-esque game, but want some variety.

An amazing party game. It actually has a pretty large population (online play) for being a random indie title (As of this post Nov 17th, 2016).
The premise of this game is to select the cartoon animal that appeals most to you and join a level with 3 other players. The basic setup of each level is you start at point A, there is an end goal at point B and there is some sort of gap between the two of you that drops off into a bottomless pit. At the start of each round, each player gets to choose a tool to place on the map. These tools come in multiple varietys such as floors, doors, traps like saws, spinning blades, punching arms, spikes etc. You can wall jump and double jump but after each setup you run the course. If it is too easy and you all make it, no points are scored. Otherwise, points are scored for the first person to make it and additional points for each person thereafter - seperate points to people whos traps killed other players during that round. You continue playing and building an even crazier level until someone eventually becomes the winner based on the hosts set limit.
This game is amazing. Just go buy it. Support awesome indie devs and populate their servers even further. Even though, honestly as of now, this game is doing just fine on its own.

There are ten levels you can play on, and each level has it's own quirks and even seperate soundtracks. You can play as several different animals, like a robotic bunny, a white squirrel, a chameleon, and yes, a chicken and a horse. They don't play differently, but they each have different sounds, dances, look up and down differently, and you can even dress them up in different cosmetics! (although very limited; two per animal, with different colors)
The devs made the animals look different and they made their colors diverse, which is totally important since you can pretty easily lose track of your animal when you're rushing through the level. Speaking of the devs, they're very vocal and consider ideas from the community. Any bugs that're discovered usually get patched, and they're even kind and patient with angry players and don't get mad or throw hissy fits.The game they made is definetely entertaining, and although the selection of objects to build a level is pretty limited, they're still adding new features, animals, and levels.
The game's online is still pretty buggy, and disconnects happen regularly when you join a lobby, but it's usually smooth sailing from then on. You'll play Ultimate Chicken Horse and you'll find plenty of AFK players or hosts, but there's a kick function, and this game is definitely kid friendly, so expect to play with children once in a while. Players can be annoying at times, and I've had two players (probably an older sibling and a kid) play a match where they just began to block the whole starting area so they could keep the lead for a few more turns before the game automatically ended, and some players have very poor judgement when it comes to placing objects, usually making it impossible to get to the end, destroying objects that made the level difficult so it becomes a total cakewalk, or adding useless objects. Thankfully, explosives can destroy objects in the game and trolls are not a frequent sight (I haven't come across one yet). Playing with your friends is the better choice if it's possible, but it's not mandatory. Watching other players is very glitchy, as you will often see animals get nailed in the face with arrows, fireballs, and hockey pucks, but they will not have actually gotten hit and die. You see yourself perfectly fine, though.
I totally recommend Ultimate Chicken Horse, because now it's a joy filled ride, and it's probably going to get even better when bugs are crushed and more features get added into the game. It's totally worth buying, even without a sale, and I encourage doing so if you have the money just to support the devs.
=================================

=================================
PROS:
+++Good devs
++Good amount of features already, more planned
++Diverse characters
+Some character customizations
+Various traps
+You can create your own levels in a seperate mode and then run through it once it's completely finished, and even share with your friends/post it online
++Character animations are fun to do and to watch
++Balanced gameplay
+++If it happens that one of your friends is better than all of you, they can handicap themselves to make it fair
++Online play and local play
+Levels have their own way of playing and each have different soundtracks
CONS:
--Some levels are not as fun as others
--Buggy, not very game breaking but it's definitely noticeable and annoying
---If you're hosting a game and you have to leave, you need to end mid-game
-Community may not be very enjoyable; AFKs are common although kickable, some players have questionable judgement, and you may or may not play with children
I also just want to add a little note, the controls are not unpredictable and are very simple, regardless of what some may say.

A year after the Alpha Centauri Incident, Gail Pilgrim is still in the passengers business, though she has Sabina White, the clever scentist that became her co-pilot. Unfortunately, now in Epsilon Indi, she's under the investigation of the J.A.C., the corrupt space police. Between the rebel scientist, the priestess of a strange cult and the young man that want to be a Jackal, Gail and Sabina have to survive the encounter. And what surprise is in stock for them?
This game is the sequel of Space Pilgrim Episode I: Alpha Centauri. So, you bet that you're familiar with the ship. The story is still well-written, with the same humor as before: Gail still in dangerous situation, not really trusting herself, Sabina still logical and in her world and now, on top of that, a young man overconfident with himself, a scientist that is too absorbed in his work and a priestess that makes sense but not really. You still have Galactic Hospital as the sitcom on TV and the cat Zubar, though he's not useful in this opus.
The game is an adventure game made in RPG Maker - so don't expect any leveling or xp or any skill to upgrade. However, the gameplay is still take items, use them, combine them, examine them and discuss with people around (so that you can get more information about everyone). Again, you'll play two characters: Gail in the first two acts and someone else in the last one.
The graphics are correct, though we lost Gail's goggles. Anyway, if you liked the first episode, you'll like this one and like the fact that you will have some other landscapes to walk in. The soundtrack is as usual good and the trick with intercom is still working: activate the music and you'll hear something else than the ambient sounds.
Epsilon Indi is a little longer than the first game, given the fact that you have more to do around.
Anyway, again, the price isn't a factor to prevent yourself to buy it. Go for it!

Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm is surprisingly approachable "hardcore" strategy. By hardcore I mean it aims for realism, it's still no War in the East in amount of detail and that's just fine. Flashpoint Campaigns that kind of games in sheer playability hands down.
Pros:
+ Relatively easy to play. I might not be the best guy to judge the UI since I have played quite a lot of strategy games which usually have quite bad UI's and thus have build up a tolerance, but I guess Flashpoint Campaigns UI is ok in that department.
+ No unneccessary micromanagement. You give orders to troops and then they (try to) fill those orders by themselves. You don't have to move them every turn, they move by themselves. More hex based games should do this.
+ Because of the former point, scenarios move at a nice pace, and playing isn't taxing.
+ Innovative electronic warfare system. Give too much orders in too short a time and enemy pinpoints your HQ by radio locating (works both ways). This discourages micromanagement.
+ Campaigns are not just bunch of scenarious in a row. You keep your core units between scenarious and get varying amount of temporary support. I don't think there's any kind of variance or branching in campaigns though (haven't played any campaign twice yet)
+ Wego-system with a twist. That means both sides give order simultaneously at the beginning of the scenario, but alternate after that with varying lenghts of time between turns (shorter is better). Generally Soviet side get's less turns with longer time in between, but this can vary even within a scenario. Number of orders per turn is limited too (iirc optional). Kill enemy HQs and they get less orders and longer turn delays.
+ Editors. I'm not personally really into making my own scenarios and campaigns, but you can if you want to.
Cons:
- Only one time period and setting. Because visuals are simple, and thus new units don't demand a lot of graphics, I would have hoped that there would be more variance. I believe there are mods that expand the setting, but base game itself is just cold war gone hot in Germany in the 80's.
- No skirmish mode/random battle
- For such simple looks, game doesn't run that well. For me at least, playing bigger scenarios for a long time makes game behave kinda sluggish in turn resolution. It has no real effect on playing but doesn't look nice.
- Unit information is not very informative. For example armor and firepower is represented as numbers but there is no information on what those numbers mean. Not a big deal if you're somewhat familiar with the equipment of the era.
- Not enough information on combat resolution. If my unit shoots the enemy but doesn't kill anything, why is that? Did it not hit or did the hit have no effect?
- Occasionally it's somewhat difficult to know why something happens the way it happens. For example why aren't my guys returning fire when fired upon. Usually reason can be found out (for example different sensor quality) but it's not always obvious.
- Supply is abstract and not very realistic. There are no real supply lines or supply carrying units. Combat units just resupply and depending on whether they are in contact with HQ and not in direct combat (or something like that), they get supplies at some rate. Could be seen as a pro (and for me it kinda is), but if supply management is your thing, look elsewhere.
- A bit awkward scale. This is probably a matter of taste, but for me 500m per hex doesn't work perfectly. I don't know if it's the graphics or what but I constantly underestimate distances and have to remind myself of the 500m per hex scale. For example a tank platoon shooting an enemy 4 hexes away looks like it's shooting an enemy right next to it, but it's actually 2km away.
- Scenarios can be wildly unbalanced. Usually the reds can have as many as five times the number of tanks than NATO has (not to mention other troops). It's realistic and not a problem on single player but I can see it could be a problem in multiplayer.
- Let me choose scenario first, side later. This is no big deal but still mildly annoying when several scenarios have a recommanded side.
It seems my cons list is longer than my pros list but don't let that fool you. Flashpoint Campaigns is an absolutely excellent game. While it may look complex on pictures, it is actually not much more complex than for example Combat Mission series (maybe even less, haven't played that series since Barbarossa to Berlin). I think this could also be recommended as a stepping stone from casual to serious wargaming, even price is kinda reasonable compared to many other serious wargames (and there's always Steam-sales). Interest and some knowledge in Cold War era warfare is recommended though.

This is an excellent game that combines playability with a design philosophy that rewards authentic gameplay. You give your subordinates broad directives and waypoints, which they will carry out to the best of their abilities. The game abstracts the busywork and assumes that your subordinates are handling their own responsibilities. Fire support can be automated in case plotting artillery targets becomes tedious. Battle command becomes the player’s main concern over micromanagement. It’s very easy to plot out a battalion or brigade-size action and coordinate timings between the component units.
The command system is well done. The game runs in a WEGO system with “command cycles”—a representation of the time a commander and his staff take to react and issue orders. One player might be able to issue orders every 13 minutes, but the other might only do so every 20 minutes. There's also an orders delay representing the time that a subordinate takes to receive and implement the order. The cycles and delays encourage you to think about time, space, and speed. Developing a pre-game battle plan is important, as is predicting the situation in the next 10-30 minutes. Engagements can become tense as you’re hoping that your plans and contingencies will work out on the chaos of the battlefield! The 1980s Cold War backdrop with its focus on mechanized warfare is more appealing than the 2010s “high-tech war” setting seen in many other military games.
However, I would like to see the Soviet forces use more flexible tactics. While the current depiction might be fine for “average/below average” tank and motorized rifle units carrying out “ordinary” missions, it is less satisfactory for depicting better-trained units. For example, 1980s Soviet journals had articles on using BMPs (without infantry) in enveloping/outflanking detachments, and discussed in length on non-linear tactics and combined arms battalions—drawn from their Afghan and field exercise experience. At the very least, leaders down to the junior officer level would have been familiar with the concepts, and those assigned to certain “elite” formations would have certainly have employed them in battle. I see that the Origins scenarios use a Soviet data file with slightly higher quality values. I haven’t played those yet, but that data could be a basis for future scenarios featuring “crack” units. Hopefully Southern Storm or future entries might see more Soviet mechanized action outside of the ordinary tank and motorized rifle formations.
Aside from this quibble, I recommend Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm to anyone interested in gaming out 1980s mechanized warfare. It successfully mixes good gameplay with authenticity—a rare quality in the computer wargaming world. I’ll be looking forward to
and the other Cold War titles coming in the future.

This is a genuinely good F2P card game that's worth your attention (or at least trying!), and I've been hooked since I've found it. It's a lot more fair on pricing and handing out cards than similar games (looking at you, Hearthstone), and there's some genuinely cool mechanics that make use of the fact that this is a PC game without just making them all "lol random effects" (such as Warcry).
There's quite a bit of content here, including several campaigns and roughly 100 puzzles to help you learn and mess with the mechanics in the game. Plus you can do drafts, free gauntlets against the computer with interesting "boss" mechanics, and others.

This simply is the best and most gripping simulation of the Cold War gone hot that I can imagine. Reading Harold Coyle's Team Yankee, I just had to play this game again.
Now, I am biased - the first scenario I played took place in July 1989 - exactly the time I was in the Bundeswehr, quite close by and I had actually been at one of the unit's barracks described in the mission briefing. So for me there is a whole lot of reminiscing in the game.
But apart from that you a great "what if". There seems to be a never-ending horde of Russian tanks and other vehicles, coming through somewhere, and you have to stop them. Every one of your own losses hurts - and the NATO concept in Germany does not allow you to yield any ground. It's do or die.
If you are interested in war games and this period of time, this is a must buy.
The one major con I have encountered so far is the victory condition calculations - they seem quite arbitrary to me. Going up against a major force I nearly stopped them cold. Turned out to be a 54% score -  a Contested Battle. Well - judge your achievements for yourself, I guess!
Talking about achievements - that's another point. Too bad it doesn't have any, neither can you post screen shots. In today's world you call that a major social media marketing mishap.
Still: Go buy it, support fringe publisher!

This game is hilarious. You go around with three other people building upon a level template to be able to get to the end, while also trying to put down traps to kill everyone else, which can and usually will lead to funny shenanigans. You can play with three friends together on one machine, or you can play with three people/friends using a slightly buggy online system. There are ten levels you can play on, and each level has it's own quirks and even seperate soundtracks. You can play as several different animals, like a robotic bunny, a white squirrel, a chameleon, and yes, a chicken and a horse. They don't play differently, but they each have different sounds, dances, look up and down differently, and you can even dress them up in different cosmetics! (although very limited; two per animal, with different colors)
The devs made the animals look different and they made their colors diverse, which is totally important since you can pretty easily lose track of your animal when you're rushing through the level. Speaking of the devs, they're very vocal and consider ideas from the community. Any bugs that're discovered usually get patched, and they're even kind and patient with angry players and don't get mad or throw hissy fits.The game they made is definetely entertaining, and although the selection of objects to build a level is pretty limited, they're still adding new features, animals, and levels.
The game's online is still pretty buggy, and disconnects happen regularly when you join a lobby, but it's usually smooth sailing from then on. You'll play Ultimate Chicken Horse and you'll find plenty of AFK players or hosts, but there's a kick function, and this game is definitely kid friendly, so expect to play with children once in a while. Players can be annoying at times, and I've had two players (probably an older sibling and a kid) play a match where they just began to block the whole starting area so they could keep the lead for a few more turns before the game automatically ended, and some players have very poor judgement when it comes to placing objects, usually making it impossible to get to the end, destroying objects that made the level difficult so it becomes a total cakewalk, or adding useless objects. Thankfully, explosives can destroy objects in the game and trolls are not a frequent sight (I haven't come across one yet). Playing with your friends is the better choice if it's possible, but it's not mandatory. Watching other players is very glitchy, as you will often see animals get nailed in the face with arrows, fireballs, and hockey pucks, but they will not have actually gotten hit and die. You see yourself perfectly fine, though.
I totally recommend Ultimate Chicken Horse, because now it's a joy filled ride, and it's probably going to get even better when bugs are crushed and more features get added into the game. It's totally worth buying, even without a sale, and I encourage doing so if you have the money just to support the devs.

So, here's the thing about Tabletopia: for a while their Steam client ran like garbage and the best way to use it was to actually use Firefox with the Unity plugin. I think the majority of bad reviews came from this fact.The latest update seems to fix this, so hopefully more of the reviews will focus on the actual content of the platform, rather than the technical challenges.
For me, it's an excellent platform and the subscription model is only required if you want to host games and a good chunk of the money you pay each month goes to the publishers of the games you play. I think that's a great way to get good games that are well put together onto the platform instead of the janky, pirated messes that you often find on TTS. That's not to say TTS is bad, but I do feel guilty firing up games that are breaking all kinds of copyrights.
Pros:
-Good UI, better than TTS in a lot of ways, not as good in others
-Good model, you can play for free, host some games for free and only pay for premium features.
-Almost all the games are tightly and professionally made.
Middling:
-Selection is not as good as TTS, but the quality is so much better and games like Terra Mystica and Scythe are amazing.
Cons:
-Bad Lobby System. It's not super hard to get connected to a game but sometimes people can't join after a game is started, you have to load in and out of the game and they made some UI "improvements" to it that were just as confusing as before.
Overall, I have no reservations about recommending it. It still needs a little maturing but the rough edges are not deal breakers at all. For the record, most of my play time has been in Firefox, so my play time on Steam clocks in at about 10% of what it should be.

A hectic mix of combat, steering, and submarine management.
You use WASD to move, E to interact, and the mouse to use whatever item is in your hand. Steering your submarine is inverted, so holding W will cause you to descend and S to ascend. It also controls like a brick, but what were you expecting of something that size?
As you explore the open sea, your one destination is down. You’ll encounter various aquatic life, obstacles, and explorable caves that contain loot. The majority of the game is played aboard your submarine, so you will need to maintain the structural integrity of your hull, which is indicated at the top right of the screen.
On your sub, there are four main areas:  a bed to heal, a helm to steer, the engine bay that controls where power is routed, and a place to
!
The majority of combat is done aboard your sub. The engine room allows you to allocate a total of 4 points to:
--light (for dark zones)
--shields (to protect against enemies)
--engine (to increase speed and maneuverability)
--torpedos (up to three slots for subsequent shots)
Allocating more than one point will make your shields stronger, allow you to maneuver faster, and allow you to load more torpedoes simultaneously respectively. Depending on how many people are in your crew, you’ll need to alternate between steering, mending the hull, fending off creatures that board you, and firing torpedos. Teamwork is the name of the game.
Enemies attack in one of three ways: 1) by ramming into the sub, which create holes and cause leaking, 2) by boarding your sub and attacking your crew directly 3) by latching on to your craft. These must have all of their invading appendages cut off before they can be dealt with. Be careful to patch holes in your hull or else the sub will fill with water and you'll drown.
The game is very good about auditory feedback; you’ll hear water filling some part of the ship, enemies that board, and the battle cries of specific oncoming enemies. Each sea creature takes a different number of torpedoes to kill. Larger enemies take 2 or 3 while smaller one take a single shot.
Boss battles occur at the end of each biome zone and will be specific to each region. There are currently 2 regions that we know of. Ship problems and character sickness are biome specific. For example: in the ice biome, the doors will freeze and you can catch hypothermia by standing in icy water.
As you descend, you will discover undersea caves which can be explored on foot. These are filled with monsters, gold, lootable corpses, and a submarine upgrade (1 per cave). If you die, you can be revived by a friend at the cost of having your HP permanently reduced for the remainder of the run. This means you can revived 5 times in total before truly dying. If the submarine's structural integrity reaches 0 health or your entire party dies simultaneously, it’s game over.
After you've been given the game over screen, you are returned to the main menu where you can spend your gold to purchase outfits and items that you discover during your playthrough. These items are used as part of your loadout as when you start the game, you are able to choose one starting item. You can carry up to two at a time and swap between them at any time by right-clicking.
Communication is key here, because if everybody starts with a weapon, you will have no one to repair your submarine.
This is a hectic cooperative experience and one that most anyone can enjoy with a bit of practice. In its current state, the game is 100% playable, enjoyable, and recommendable--and it will only get better from here.

Defunct is a very short game, as is evident from my 'hours played' counter, but while it does last it is an enjoyable experience. The game involves controlling a tiny little robot as you traverse various biomes by manipulating gravitational pulls to enable you to move at incredebly fast speeds. It's kind of like Valley meets Wall-E. The sections where you race down a hill and break-neck speeds are exhilarating but the game also consists of sections where you must slow down and explore a given location to solve certain environmental puzzles. These breaks serve as a nice change of pace between sections of whiplashing speeds down sloping terrains. The only problem I had with the game is that the puzzles lack creativity, I feel like they could have done much more with the existing mechanics. Features like being able to magnetize to surfaces allowing you to ride sideways and upside down are barely utilized. Sure, the game gives you many places to use it but rarely any incentive to use it. The other complaint being that it's just so incredebly short that I can't really recommend the game at full price, however if you happen to pick it up on sale, like I did, then I'd say it's worth it. It's the best 3D Sonic game that was never made.

The idea for Crash Bandicoot came about when the creators-to-be were discussing how a platformer in 3D would work. They concluded that you'd spend a lot of time looking at Sonic's butt. Crash ended up being very much its own thing, but I think that if they stuck to that description, they might've made something like Defunct.
It's like Sonic decided to take a vacation skiing through the Wilderzone. Dive down a hill, run through boost orbs, slide on a ramp, use your magnetism to ride the wall, jump off to another platform, and slide down another hill.  If you do it right, you might snag a collectable trinket along the way.
The game is also very speedrunner-friendly, with its online leaderboards and level selection. Heck, there's even a GDQ skin for your character.
All in all, Defunct is some good fun for both the casual and speedrunning crowds. I say pick it up.

This game is a simulator. But, compared to other wargames, it's not the nitty gritty details of mechanics or equipment that it focuses on simulating (yet it does both well), it's the communications and chaos of combat. This, combined with the WEGO turn system, provides some pretty spectacular and unique gameplay.
Nothing is more nervewracking that pressing the "start" button after issuing what orders you can, always far too few, and hoping for the next sixteen minutes (or far, far longer) that nothing drastic happens. Nothing is more of a relief when your troops somehow work through you plan in ways you didn't expect and save the day. Nothing is more depressing that looking at a clock that states the next orders phase is over forty minutes away as T-80 tanks form up to punch through your forces.
The turn-based system is based on the real military philosphy of the OODA loop. It models the chaos of military operations perfectly. This, combined with a smart AI (that tries to model how actual troops would behave, think dwarf fortress-esque) and a well crafted modelling of units, logistics and terrain, means for extremely solid gameplay, albeit with a high learning curve.
I really wish more games used this system, it just feels right.
Also, the game has play-by-email, something so small to write about, but really appreciated.

Video Version of this review:
You play as a little robot, and you are supposed to take photos for an investigation of some strange activity at some cabin. You take orders from your boss, Barry. Funny, he actually looks like Barry from Resident Evil.
“I’m usually the master of unlocking.” Yeah, that's actually what he says.
So, in order for some things to happen, you have to take pictures of certain things, and some images you have to send to Barry. Because otherwise, he’ll be all like, “What am I looking at here?”
You have to photograph notes in order to read them. It turns out that the last owner of this house has been experiencing some spooky scary stuff. You have to send Barry photos of supernatural stuff, but he keeps dismissing them as some sort of bug in the camera, and keeps making new updates to the camera.
The doors and lights must be controlled remotely, since Barry is opening some doors for me, and yet, he doesn’t seem to be physically here with me. I don’t really see the point of making the first-person view use up battery. Seems unnecessary to me. You don’t often need to use the first person view, but if you are stuck in an area, it’s a good idea to look around from the robot’s point of view.
This game is rather short, but I think it’s pretty good. It has some good scares, and moments where you need to remember the layout of the house in order to find stuff. So I recommend people give this game a try, it’s only $2 if you live in Canada. Don’t know how much that is anywhere else, but still, check this game out.

The ability to make maps, and restructure units, formations and organizations is good.

The Campaigns and Scenarios are about what you would expect. The representation of British, West Germany, and the US is nice.
The lack of Warsaw Pack members is a little disappointing, then again in truth they are the same as Russian just older. In truth the east German troops had better training, and the Equipment was better maintained. This is more or the the case with the rest of the eastern forces with some better and some worse.
What should be clear is that the US Weapons Had been dramatically underrated in just about all categories, as well as the post draft troops, and the Russian weapons Highly over rated in every way, added to the fact that Training was little more then how to point the pointy end, wear the uniform, and even those very few with maps could not read them.
These things should have been corrected , and inputted into updates along with new maps, today's issues locations, forces, and potential real system of tomorrow (not the fake Soviet T-12/14 that is total BS).

This is one of the most fun, funny, cute and clever multiplayer party games out there. Highly recommended. Everything about this game works together really well, and offers full customization to game rules as well as three well-rounded game modes (Creative, Free Play, and Party).
Party is really the main mode of the game IMO, where you have limited choices to work with and this keeps the rounds quick and contentious. Creative is probably more satisfying to expert players, or novice players who need to learn the game mechanics. Free Play is primarily for level designers, and there is a level sharing feature to the game, and these custom maps are more or less the basis of the single-player game, where you can challenge and hone your skills on the craziest Mario Hell type levels you desire.
The game is fairly easy to pick up, but there is some learning curve for new players, as some of the building elements kinda need to be seen in action to fully understand. Also there are some synergies that can be unexpectedly satisfying, such as firing projectiles through teleporters, and devious use of sticky glue and slippery ice.
Wonderfully realized and animated, although I have experienced a couple crashes. My kids have a blast just playing hide-and-seek in the main menu, which says something about how fun and cute the playable characters are to control.
