Absolutely amazing party game, especially for those who enjoy seeing chaotic gameplay.
It is also a great tool for teaching how gameplay in level design works in a low pressure, hilarious way. It demonstrates very well that even the slightest addition can have deep consequences.
Here's how it works. Depending on the game mode, you and your friends are required to choose one of a limited selection, or an infinite selection, at the start of a turn. In the limited selection, it is a 'party box' that you all must scramble to choose the one piece each one of you would love to use against the others or cause the most hilarious outcome - while in the other infinite selection, you are given the complete catalog to choose from but can only add, move, or remove one object.
What results is a wild, astounding mess. The editor feature is done very intuitively, you simply select what you want to add and put it down wherever you want. This can result in very relaxed and silly gameplay, or highly competitive gameplay where one is trying to screw over the others while trying to maximize his own chances of success.
The unlockable content is a wonderous bonus, from levels, characters, and cosmetic options.
Done over voice communications with friends or family, I cannot see you regretting picking this up.

Supposedly the game was suppose to feature an editor that let you make and play your own senarios, what was given was a confusing and unhelpful web page with a ZIP file. I picked up CSD during a summer sale for $0.99 and I consider that to be an absolute steal. Although at $2.49 I still think it's worth picking up; it's clear the developers have a lot of love and effort put into this game, and I'm extremely excited for CSD2.
When you boil this game down to its base components, CSD 95% time management and hitting specific keys rapidly and accurately (eg, putting the correct ingredients down in the correct order), and 5% strategy/simulation (eg, picking which of your foods are going to go on the menu). However, this simple gameplay still has a significant learning curve and level of complexity.
One thing that shines CSD is the sense of accomplishment as you progress. As your restaurant grows, you'll unlock nicer decor and fancier dishes, and you really do feel achievement going from your one-star shop selling french fries to eventually a five-star boutique serving complex arrangements of sushi, soups, and pastas. In that journey from a mom & pop shack to Michelin's finest, you'll eventually master all these complex dishes and figuratively be able to make music in the cacophony of your kitchen. Every key you press is punctuated with immensely fulfilling sound effects: the crinkle of 'L'ettuce as you drop it in a salad or the plop of a scoop of 'M'int ice cream as you prepare a sundae. When you're able to string together a group of complex ingredients and cooking steps, it comes together in this wonderful, satisfying feeling that you've
.
I recommend this game to anybody who wants a fast-paced, bite-sized, hectic, and fulfilling game, similar to One Finger Death Punch. Bonus points if you really enjoyed the theme of Ratatouille and the idea of running your own restaurant and cooking in your kitchen.

I'm on the fence about whether or not I "recommend" this game -- I'm putting it as yes, because I did enjoy my time with it. However, I don't think it's a game for mass audiences.
The key aspect of LoA is that it is a STRATEGY game in the truest sense. Not strategy a la real-time-strategy games that in reality emphasize tactics over strategy, this game is about coming up with a grand overarching plan, sticking to it when it's working, modifying it when it's not, and coming up with new ones when your old plan gets blown out of the water.
Combat is very simple: Two armies meet, time passes, and people die. The victor is determined purely through strategic-level elements: How many troops are on each side of the field, how rested those troops are, how good those troops are, and what magic influences the field. I appreciate the change of pace.
One reason people might want to not buy LoA is that there's only one real campaign right now (plus a tiny tutorial campaign which doesn't count) and it doesn't seem like there's much replay value after you beat that campaign, and once you understand everything the campaign's not that difficult. I beat it on my second or third "real" try (not counting early plays where I didn't know what was going on, some experimental plays where I was intentionally doing "stupid" things in order to learn new tricks, etc) on the medium difficulty.

While Verdun has it's obvious flaws, there are many great things about this game. In order to organize this review I'm going to just leave two different categories with my thoughts about the game.
-The playerbase is pretty chill with the game, and they have fun just as much as they want to win. You won't really see anyone roleplay, which can be annoying in other games. I've only encountered cheaters twice to date, but I know others say they've encountered alot more, so I don't have a concise answer
-The developers are great and are really interactive with the community. The listen alot of the time and they actually try to make the game better for it's players.
-The maps of the game are well-made, and they tried to make them feel as life-like as possible, meaning as wore down and tore up as the actual war. There's a great variety of settings, to the French forest, the mud of Flanders, a fort that's decayed from bombardment, and even a nighttime map. All in all I don't really have any complaints
-The weapons and first-person animations are expertly made. They really do look nice, but they're not AAA tier, which is alright. The gore system is very well-made, and different parts of the body respond with different wounds. My one complaint is that the hands can look kind of blocky and weird with some certain weapons and reloading animations
but besides that I appreciate the effort that went into the weapons
-I think a good place to start is the sounds. This has been brought up many times before, but I really think they could do with some updating. As for right now they sound like something out of Call of Duty 3
-I know they're working on optimizing it better but sometimes Verdun is really frustrating to play when you can see your bullet go through someone's head and then they shoot you back. I've also experienced sudden frame drops, and while it's not as bad as the past it still takes me out of the game.
-My final complaints are with some of the apsects of the game itself. There are times when I've been standing at least 15 feet away from a grenade running away and I was insta-killed from the explosion. I'm not sure if this is the normal damage system or just a bug, but it's happened more than once. As for the barbed wire I really like it's inclusion in the game, but having death by barbed wire count as suicide seems dumb because you can't even tell when the barbed wire is going to kill you.
Verdun is a game with lots of effort thrown in, with a mostly-positive result. The playerbase and devs are generally nice, and the game itself is packed with content. My complaints mainly consist of the game not being optimized enough, and weak sounds accompanied by some clunky animations in-game. Most of this can be fixed however, and I'm sure this isn't the end for Verdun.

This is one of the best wargames around. It may not look flashy at first glance, but once the action starts it is surprisingly gripping. I think the reason for it is that at first glance it looks like a hexgrid counter-based wargame, but unlike most other similar games (thinking of unity of command here), action plays out minute-by-minute and losses are tracked down to individual vehicles and teams of men. The result is that things like the charge of a soviet tank regiment or that desperately needed artillery strike coming down on enemy positions on the far ridge feels - while perhaps visceral is too strong a word - fresh and alive, even through the hexes.
If you just jump in it can take a little while to get a grip on what each of the commands you can give a unit do, the tutorial helps a lot though. I skipped it at first but later came back and played through it, was worth the time though.
If you are interested in serious wargaming at all, I highly recommend this one.

Saw this in a discussion of Tabletop Sim vs Tabletopia and the legality of it all. This sounded pretty nice so I gave it a go.
-
Seemingly fixed in the latest patch?
-It's clunky as hell. Some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the game's discussions has constantly posted about how this game is much more responsive than TTS but he is full of crap. Everything from drawing a card to stacking them back again to moving things around the board is way worse. The right click context sensitive menu is nice but the interface as a whole is just slow and the game is missing obvious things like cards automatically stacking on others or even the vaguest hint of snapping to the board depending on what you are playing. Even the zoom feature is bad, doesn't zoom in as close as you can go and makes no effort to present models from up close as it does in TTS, just certain tokens. At any other time it zooms in on the board like you were trying to headbutt the thing.
You can't even draw a box to select multiple things because clicking and dragging pans the camera, I mean really?
-It just feels cheap. So cheap. Everything from the animation used to flip cards (aka barely any) to the sound design to the way figurines and meeples wobble on the spot when you drop them? It looks and feels terrible. It's so bad it frankly makes me question if all the people saying this looks way better than Tabletop Sim are not shills.
-No joke: if I so much have the temerity to press the ALT key, games immediately hard lock. Why? How? I have to kill the process just so that the app dumps me back to Tabletopia's main menu/browser. This is so dumb I'm willing to say that it's something wrong with my setup because otherwise I couldn't fathom how this is possibly a thing.
-The whole "200+ games!" is right only in the vaguest definition. The game's library consists of about 30 easily recognizable games, 30 more obscure but well recieved games and then a mountain of indies and generic things like "Chess!" and "Dominoes!" so don't get your expectations too high. The free status of games can be deceptive too, like in the case of Terra Mystica, which APPEARS to be free (menu icon has no premium tag) yet only offers an introductory game with no choice of race or anything like that. The true base game requires a premium sub.
-Finally: NO players. During the time it took me to write this review I've seen a grand total of four games being hosted and like three of them were Scythe (which incidentally is also available as a completely legal DLC for TTS). Right now as I'm writing this there are no games to join and no one talking in the ingame chat. It's a bad look no matter how you slice it.
In conclusion? We have a problem here. For the longest time people have shied away from Tabletop Sim because it's kind of a legal mess but when the alternative is something like this, it's just... horrid. Tabletopia is such an inferior product that even if the consumer has the best intentions they are still getting shafted and shafted hard. This is really no alternative, much less a competitor and quite frankly I pity any boardgame designer that wasted their time getting their work on Tabletopia instead of just making DLC for TTS.
It's just that bad. It's worrying too when Tabletopia is angling itself to be some sort of premium service and apparently has so many designers on board.
Honestly if you are looking for a boardgame fix I'd just buy Tabletop Simulator. IF you want a boardgame fix and care about boardgame designers getting their due money, I'd honestly still buy Tabletop Simulator and maybe buy a subscription to Tabletopia but never ever play it. Maybe that's the one benefit that Tabletopia can provide.

However!
This is the most realistic hex-based tactical game out there and I think the only one that deals with a Cold War Gone Hot scenario. It's also very engaging and addictive, you just want to see what happens the next turn. It's also the only strategy game I played, that makes you analyze the tactical situation and try to predict the enemy's moves. Were are the going to come from, what forces? Do they have attack choppers? Where is the main tank force going to attach? How do I position my troops for optimum efficiency against the enemy? Did I cover my flanks?
All those are questions that you as yourself each mission. And it's great. It makes you think, plan, consider multiple options and try to make do with what you have. Because another aspect that makes the game shine, is that it shows that nothing works perfectly in war. Comms will get broken, unit will panic or will be unable to fullfil orders and the whole situation will go south after several minutes. And that is how combat is. There is no hand holding here, no tactical tips in the briefing, you have what you have and try to make the best out of it. But even when the whole situation get completely out of control, your forces get decimated and you begin to doubt your judgment, sometimes, it still works out, you hold your positions, bruised and battered, but the enemy starts retreating. And this is the ultimate satisfaction in strategy games and in Flashpoin Campaigns, it's more rewarding than in anything else.
If you like turn-bases, hes-based games, you need to get this. If you like realistic depiction of modern combat, you need to get this. If you like the late Cold War era strategy games, you need to get this.
A solid 9/10. The best hex-based strategy ever created. Not flawless, but best one so far.

Absolutely amazing party game, especially for those who enjoy seeing chaotic gameplay.
It is also a great tool for teaching how gameplay in level design works in a low pressure, hilarious way. It demonstrates very well that even the slightest addition can have deep consequences.
Here's how it works. Depending on the game mode, you and your friends are required to choose one of a limited selection, or an infinite selection, at the start of a turn. In the limited selection, it is a 'party box' that you all must scramble to choose the one piece each one of you would love to use against the others or cause the most hilarious outcome - while in the other infinite selection, you are given the complete catalog to choose from but can only add, move, or remove one object.
What results is a wild, astounding mess. The editor feature is done very intuitively, you simply select what you want to add and put it down wherever you want. This can result in very relaxed and silly gameplay, or highly competitive gameplay where one is trying to screw over the others while trying to maximize his own chances of success.
The unlockable content is a wonderous bonus, from levels, characters, and cosmetic options.
Done over voice communications with friends or family, I cannot see you regretting picking this up.

What in the actual heck even is this game?
A racial stereotype, mocking the simple ways of us kinder British folk?
No.
No, that's not right. Not right at all, dear chap. Let's get out a cuppa and talk about this game.
This is a game, apparently. It's... Certainly something. Ampu-Tea is a frustratingly fun puzzle game wherein you attempt to assemble the Great British Beverage according to an order on the mystical blackboard, by manipulating a poorly-mapped prosthetic limb.
The controls on this game, while somewhat obnoxious to grasp, offer solid means for grabbing, prodding, turning and even impromptu profanity. They could certainly do with improving if you want to make the game more accessible and enjoyable, but I genuinely believe the difficult control mechanisms are what make this game so frustratingly fun.
As a party game, it's fantastic. Gather your friends and have a giggle as you struggle to undertake even the most simple tasks with your new, blue, robotic prosthetic.
Picture the scene; it's a family Christmas. Eight of you are gathered around the fire, with little Timmy being the bored brat he is. "Hey, twinblade, can we have something to do?".
Shut up Timmy.
Nobody likes you.
But ugh, fine. Your father knows how to make a good cup of tea, and I'm a lazy twonk. Uncle Rodney always made a killer brew.
"Fine." I mutter, turning on the computer to boot up this masterpiece of software engineering.
At first, people are confused. Scared even. They don't know what to make of it. But soon, soon they'll understand the wonders of Ampu-Tea.
Aunt Greta goes first. She Falcon Punches the mug straight through and ends up flipping the table. I hope there's no cats in this game, because they wouldn't be Schrodinger's cat. I can personally confirm with the ammount of stuff that went flying, it would certainly be dead.
Great Grandpa Booboo wasn't much better. Despite his real-world experience with a prosthetic limb, he flailed around in this game like a hamster on LSD. Weak.
The annoying little stain that is Timothy screeches for his turn. Ugh, I wish I was home.
Wait.
I am home. I wish these other people were at home. Not my home, though. This is my fortress of solitude.
Timmy tries to play the game, but he's like six so doesn't understand what on earth he's meant to be doing. It's okay though, because everyone is laughing.
Grandpa laughs.
Auntie laughs.
The clock laughs.
I shoot the clock.
Timothy starts crying again. He's always crying. Just ignore him.
Overall, I would certainly reccommend this game to anyone who needs a time-filler for a group of friends.
I personally found it saddeningly frustrating when played alone, though some of you might prefer games which deepen the void of eternal depression and that's okay.
One final thing:
If any of you put the milk in first, I'm disowning you.

So if you're like me, your first impressions of this game were probably "Oh look, another casual restaurant game." Well, that's not actually that accurate. This game can get very fast paced and hectic. It's not so much a management game as it is an arcade type game where you are the one serving the food.
Each food has buttons that correspond to a different ingredient (like C for Cheese) or action (like the down arrow to fill beer into a mug). Guests will come in during the day and order something and you need to fill their order quickly and accurately. Most foods have different stages - for example, you prepare a steak the way the customer wants it, then start cooking it. After a certain amount of time, you need to serve it to the customer within a certain window - too soon and it's not cooked enough, too late and it's burned. By the late stages of the game you can have 6 foods on the menu each day and up to 8 customers with orders being filled at the same time. There are natural rush hours about 1/3 and 2/3 of the way through each day, providing a pretty good ebb and flow to the day.
The difficulty also scales well. Most foods can be upgraded multiple times, often getting new ingredients or new recipes that guests can order. This adds greater complexity at the benefit of higher profits. It's a good way to mix things up when you become comfortable with a given food.
There are some small things that add to the appeal, like humorous e-mails you receive at the end of each day, as well as various challenges you can get to encourage you to try new foods.
Just don't serve soup. Ever. Soup is the worst.

Tl;dr: Great story-driven game, but buy it on sale.
Just got this game today and decided to play it since I've been on a gaming binge. Gotta say, I really enjoyed it.
This game is a walking simulator, where you walk around your family's house and explore various rooms and interact with objects. What makes this game so enjoyable is the story. You play as Katie, who returns home after a year abroad to her family's empty house. As you go from room to room, you discover notes left by your younger sister Sam, explaining her disappearance from the house. Additionally, you discover clues left by your parents that hint at their own internal struggles and journeys over the past year.
I am a person who loves story-driven games, so I didn't mind the game's very simple gameplay style that comes with most walking simulators. Sometimes, I find it relaxing to just explore an environment instead of fleeing from monsters or fighting boss battles. The graphics are pretty basic, but, again, I was hooked by the story.
I did get this game on sale for $2.99, and I think that was a good price. While I greatly enjoyed the story, I don't think it would be worth full price ($14.99 at the time of this review), since the story is very short and may not have a great replayability factor.
If you enjoy walking simulators or gradually unlocking interesting stories, this is a good game to add to your library.

As a kid from the 90's this game resonated so well with me. (Spoiler, well not really) the game thanks you for playing it right at the end, but I want to thank the devs for making this for us to enjoy. Let's start of and say, this is an exploration, atmospheric and story driven game, not a horror. Probably more aimed at a teen age female audience, or 90's kid like myself. It's not for everybody, but it has a magnificent story to tell that needs to be heard.
This braught back so many awesome 90's memories for me, "Street fighter", arcades, vcr, "Tank Girl", Nirvana, "X-files", grunge, 90210, "Charmed", "Ouija" and Alanis Morisette anger, it's all in here :) The game is a short love story, about coming home, going away, while coming of age, in a time when some of these things where a lot harder to explain and do then what they are now. I can't tell you more without spoilers, so I will stop there. But surfice to say, this really is more like a time capsule and art, than a game. Probably not a lot of replaybility, but what a journey. I loved it, you will too.
Gameplay evolves reading letters, memos, listhening to tapes, finding keys, opening safes and locked doors and exploring an old house that is hiding secrets about your family, while a thunderstorm rages outside. At times it get's quite scary, but it really is just your imagination playing tricks on you.
Pros - A 90's capsule, great story and great voice acting, atmospheric
Cons - Very little replayability, and does have a few moments in beginning when it's not immediatly clear what you need to do.
Strongly recommended. 8.5/10

This is okay if you like micromanagement.
Or maybe even stellar if you like micromanagement.
Think "control every switch on a railroad" and you pretty much understand how this game works.  The engineers on the trains might as well be trained monkeys.  So you have to micromanage whether to stop a train to let another train go by.
Also you can lay track and figure out what gives the most flexibility for running as many trains as possible in parallel without pausing them for too long, since the longer they are on the track the less valuable the cargo becomes (i.e. the more maintenance or running costs you incur).
So this is nothing like Railroads! or Railroad Tycoon - this is a micromanagement game, and there is some satisfaction from running the game mechanic (but personally not my taste).  This is a good looking kiddie game.

The 39 Steps isn't necessarily a great book, but the way the novel has been made interactive is a step in the right direction. Personally, for me, the story contained too much politics, which I hate with a passion. I can't help it. I just have no interest in it.  But the way this 'game' has been executed is done in a terrific way.
I was actually talking with my girlfriend about how I'd love to read books like this, with beautiful high res pictures and dynamic text in it, and the voices recorded like you're listening to an audio book, with each person doing his/her part instead of just one and the same person.
So, basically, this is an interactive novel. Reading this novel should take you anywhere between 3 or 4 hours. Short enough to keep you interested and long enough to tell you its story.
One thing I didn't care for was the fact that there are a few Scottish conversations in it, sometimes being spoken with a certain accent. It was hard to follow at times, so it would've been nice if there were extra subtitles for those parts. I really had to concentrate to understand it. It's the only flaw I can think of, so if you're an avid reader you might want to give this a read.

I have to say I am disappointed by this game.  The art style suggests it could fit right into Ratchet and Clank and there was a great deal of potential with the concept.   "Not used" is an accurate description to most of this game.  The graphics are clean and pretty to look at, the levels are wide, open and leave any places to explore...if only there was something to find. The huge and detailed zones are barren of anything gameplay related, making any exploration almost pointless, and I have to wonder why.
It very much seems that there was a lot more planned, a much deeper game set up then the one we got,  and all we are left with is a very very basic speed and puzzle game.  There is junk scattered all over this world that suggests a much more expansive story, and strangely the other robots first instinct when finding the junk seems to be to set up shops.  You can't interact with any of it yet there is enough of it scattered around and some in town like groups that really says something else was suppose to be going on.
The controls are not bad, but unoptimized.  I recommend changing the setup if possible.  There is no mouse look, which I find odd.  There are sections that can bring Sonic like speed only to be abruptly stopped by very basic puzzles only made difficult by the controls.  Oddly, how you get through most levels does not seem to matter, as there are half a dozen routes in each, which only made me feel lost as I barreled forward, unsure of where I was going or even if it was the right way.
In the end I beat the game on the first go, all of an hour and 10 minutes, and I have no desire to play again, or explore the content that unlocked on completion.
Support the developer for the graphic content, maybe they will make a better game, but skip this one for the game play.

To clarify, I backed this project on Kickstarter. But this means I paid to get access, my opinion here is unsolicited.
Tabletopia is amazing. There have been other virtual Board Games available on steam, but none of them come close to having the scope of features TT does. I have played hours of games on here by myself and with friends.
Pros:
*Huge selection of popular and new games. They aren't just games owned by one developer, or only from new start-up projects. Some of Boardgame geeks favourite games like Terra Mystica and Vitticulture are here, along side new Kickstarter games you can't even get yet like Vikings gone Wild.
*Play with friends anywhere. All you need is an internet connection. Friends who don't have an account can join in using a web browser from a link you provide.
*almost No set up for games, the pieces are populated in place. Mostly all you need to do is select which 'faction' each player is going to be and put any spares away.
*No packing away!
*No need for large table space.
*Rules are available from a click in the game window.
*Everything looks great, and feels 3 dimensional and tactile.
*It's so easy to take a screenshot and share or record your game with others.
*Great support from the TT guys. I've had a few bugs (it's a beta after all) and after speaking with the developers they've been fixed super quickly.
*Growing Library. They constantly add new games.
*Demonstrations. I've not watched any of these yet, but TT have been organising live hands-on demonstrations of some of the popular games - which is a nice way to learn how to play.
Cons
*Some small bugs and connection issues. It is still in development so this is to be expected, but the bugs are becoming smaller and less frequent as time goes by.
*I find the steam platform the easiest to use - but only people with a paid account can play it on that platform. I know at least one friend who would be excited if he could join my games via steam (rather than firefox) without buying in.
All I can say is if u love Board games, and ever have trouble getting together in one place with them to  play games - then you need Table Topia.

After the initial frustration of fixing the game so that you can actually start playing it, Fallout 3 is satisfying enough. If you played New Vegas first, you may be dissapointed (mostly with the lack of endings and content).
I'll start with this games downfalls. If you had trouble fixing the game, the crashing will always be a frustrating and ever present. Save often. As for problems with the game itself, exploring can be tedious and also... boring. Especially in DC. The Enclave and Super Mutant mobs will be spread about, so expect to spend a bit of time just fighting and dying if you don't have the resources or damage output to power through these mobs. Also, I found quite a few spots to get stuck in. This probably won't be a problem for most, though. Finally, there is not enough side content to this game that I think many would expect. Locations are spread far too thin for my liking, making exploration of the Capital Wasteland a bit dull at times, and it sticks true to it's name. The packs of raiders and various other hostile robots/animals/humanoids do little to make it more interesting.
Good news last. Fallout 3, I believe, has a more enjoyable main storyline than New Vegas. I became attached to the characters I interacted with, and had a bitter resentment for the Enclave. Also, to make the most out of this game, take as many quests as you can, and talk to most of the NPCs you see. They're all very interesting. Save and try out something you wouldn't usually do. Go bonkers. The atmosphere is entracing, get involved and you'll have a good time with this game.
Overally, I'd give this game an 8/10. If you're not that interested, pick it up during a sale. If you are, it's worth the $10 if you really want to spend time just doing side content, which is just as fun/if not more fun than the main quests.

I honestly wasn't sure I'd like it, since I hadn't played a hex-based game in ages. The thing to remember about this game is that just like in real life, the commander doesn't have a Gods-eye view of everything. You get contact reports as they come  in, and acting on them on any larger level takes time. A platoon of Abrams will react to Soviet armor on its own, yes, but if you want to counterattack, depending on the situation, expect it to take a bit of time to get the basic plan worked out and orders passed down to the units involved. The game invisibly abstracts all of the fog and confusion that comes with modern  warfare, frankly, I think they did a pretty darn good job. This game seems to fill a void between a division-level game like Hearts of Iron 3, and a company-level game like the Combat Mission series (not on steam, but highly reccomended.).
Basically, if you want a challenging game that gives you map-on-a-table awareness on a realistic delay that can brutally punish mistakes and reward skillful planning and execution, I'd definately look into it. If you're not sure about the hex based system, get it on sale. It's one of the few that covers this time period that even tries to be realistic.

What a wonderful little game! Exactly as everyone says, it's a fun mixture of oldschool mechanics from the golden age of survival horror but updated with a clever conceit of being based around a home surveilance company, with the fixed camera angles being security cameras and your character, replete with the traditional tank-style controls, being a small remote controlled camera drone that obviously would control something like a tank. It's only about an hour long and the story, overall gameplay, and presentation are all good but nothing teribly special, but that actually adds to its charm. It's not trying to be earth shattering, it's just trying to be a nifty little ghost game with a few fresh ideas and a hefty dose of nostalgia. It made me jump a few times, it kept me interested throughout, it was paced perfectly, and it ended before it wore out its welcome. By the end I was all smiles, exactly how you should be after finishing a goofy little haunted house story. This is the game equivalent of settling down at night after getting off of work, turning off the lights, and trying your luck at picking a random no-name, low budget, diret-to-DVD horror movie on Netflix, and being pleasantly surprised at how fun it actually is, and it ends up being a great way to finish off your night.
My only quibble: The notes that you find throughout the game that fill out the game's story were incredibly blurry on my screen, I had to sit back far in my seat and squint my eyes to read them. And the "Officer's Report" note from the main menu was too small and too blurry to read at all. I'm not sure what the problem was, I had it set to max resolution, and everything else looked fine. Just those notes I had trouble with. But Windows 10 has also been feuding with my display drivers ever since I updated, so it could very well be a problem on my end. In any case, it wasn't enough of a problem to really take away from the experience.

Shutter is an indie horror title in which the player controls a remote controlled robot that takes photographs of evidence of crimes in a creepy mansion. The atmosphere of the game is chilling. Shutter is inspired by the old school Biohazard games, This can be seen in the use of fix camera angles and clunky controls. There is no combat system; in order to progress in the game the player must photograph certain objects and read e-mails that indicate the current objective.
Indie horror titles are often immensely disappointing. Whilst Shutter is not among those types of games, Shutter is unfortunately unworthy of a recommendation. The game suffers from annoying bugs and glitches. After multiple playthroughs, the game consistly crashes. Before the game crashes there is a bug with the photographs that cause the image to distort. The distortion is most likely not a game mechanic. If the player pauses the game, there is a note from the developer in red that suggests to restart the chapter is this happens. Not only that, but at times the exit menu glitches and a blank menu opens.  All four achievements are glitched as well. Players may find themselves beating the game multiple times and noticing that the achievements do not unlock correctly.
Whilst Shutter is a decent indie horror title, it cannot be recommended to anyone. Perhaps the sequel might be better and free of annoying bugs.

Games are reviewed in context. MMOs are about the gameplay, not the story, so we can forgive them if the latter is lacking. Singleplayer games that sell themselves as story- AND gameplay-rich are examined on both. But no matter what, gameplay is always assessed because that's the defining feature that turns a movie into a game.
Gone Home is an example of what happens when you try to make a game without gameplay. Sure, if the gameplay sucks you could still scrape a 6/10 or 7/10 with an excellent story, but Gone Home falls short in both departments.
Spoilers, I guess:
It's another love story, young lovers separated by external and internal forces, much like Romeo and Juliet (except if Romeo was also a girl). The small twist makes Gone Home's story mildly interesting, but overall the story can be described as being on the better side of "okay". Not a poor story but nothing amazing either.
The other aspect that Gone Home sells itself on is immersion, specifically, allowing the player to piece together electricity bills and handwritten letters to discover the relationships between the characters, and the "psycho house". Like the story, this can also be described as just "okay". People seem to forget that you do this all the time in games in a more subtle way, like Deus Ex: Human Revolution and Bioshock Infinite.
There's a strong smell of 90's nostalgia around Gone Home, but this seems to just be subtle selling point as it doesn't develop the characters or story, only the setting, which itself adds little to the story.
Okay, so what about everything else?
The gameplay is boring. You walk around reading pieces of paper and/or listening to a voiceover. About as interesting as it gets is when a few secret passages are revealed on your map after finding them scrawled on a note. The navigation is somewhat lacking, you can only see what room you're in but not where you are in the room or what direction you're facing, which can be a little disorienting.
Also, this game is very poorly optimised. Reminding you that this is a game from 2013, my GTX 1060 struggled at times to keep even 60fps on max settings.
I finished the game in 35 minutes, or ~0.5 hours (okay, perhaps I could stretch it out to 1 hour if I tried) and ostensibly this game costs USD$15 when not on sale. That puts it right in the territory of Deus Ex: HR (~30 hours) and Bioshock Infinite (~20 hours), two games who balance both story AND gameplay effectively.
So from me, Gone Home gets a B- in story and immersion and a D everywhere else. Those D's wouldn't have mattered if I could see an A+ or at least a few A's in there, but if your game falls short on its main selling point then the flaws stick out like very sore thumbs.
This game is not a 10/10 or even a 9/10. To put it on the same level as (or above) games like Bioshock Infinite or Deus Ex: HR is an utter joke. It gets a 5.5/10 from me.

PROS
- 2-4 Players. Although some would say that the lack of a solo mods is bad, I wouldn't see it that way. You are forced to cooperate with someone. If you don't have a friend at hand, that means randoms, and can lead to interesting situations! It's a lot of fun to start talking on discord, and learn to cooperate as a team with a few random players. We got very far with just two people!
- Procedurely generated. Whilst almost mandatory for a game like this, I think it's well done the way it is. The map can even hide valuable caves for you, and can force you to explore other ends of the map, instead of just going deeper.
- Diversified threats. You rarely die in the same way, and the devs keep on adding. Of course you learn all about these different biomes, but for now it's quite refreshing.
- A goofy, yet scary artstyle. You're like hey, these fishes don't look so scary, that one even looks cute! But when you go deeper, that is where the scary creatures come along o.o, I hadn't expected fish could even look scary with an artstyle like this, good job devs!
- A dedicated dev team. Lots of response to the forums, and generally they work hard on improvements. I remember that after an update a few areas became a lot more challanging!
- Customization is always fun.
Cons
- Some networking issues, a priority of the devs, will get fixed soon!
- Potentially repetetive. Although this depends on the kind of gamer you are, you may find it repetive, especially if your crew never mixes up roles. This often happens in a crew of 3-4, try playing with just 2 for more challenge, diversity! It's a lot more intense!
- Kit system. Rather underwhelming in its current state, you only ever want a wrench or a sword for starters, if you take almost anything else, you'll lack the ability to repair properly, or fight properly, which causes many issues.
- There is no cuttlefish in the game.
- Some bugs, but nothing major.
REMEMBER: This game is early acces, a lot of the stuff will get updated, but for it's current state I would say it is very strong already!

After the initial frustration of fixing the game so that you can actually start playing it, Fallout 3 is satisfying enough. If you played New Vegas first, you may be dissapointed (mostly with the lack of endings and content).
I'll start with this games downfalls. If you had trouble fixing the game, the crashing will always be a frustrating and ever present. Save often. As for problems with the game itself, exploring can be tedious and also... boring. Especially in DC. The Enclave and Super Mutant mobs will be spread about, so expect to spend a bit of time just fighting and dying if you don't have the resources or damage output to power through these mobs. Also, I found quite a few spots to get stuck in. This probably won't be a problem for most, though. Finally, there is not enough side content to this game that I think many would expect. Locations are spread far too thin for my liking, making exploration of the Capital Wasteland a bit dull at times, and it sticks true to it's name. The packs of raiders and various other hostile robots/animals/humanoids do little to make it more interesting.
Good news last. Fallout 3, I believe, has a more enjoyable main storyline than New Vegas. I became attached to the characters I interacted with, and had a bitter resentment for the Enclave. Also, to make the most out of this game, take as many quests as you can, and talk to most of the NPCs you see. They're all very interesting. Save and try out something you wouldn't usually do. Go bonkers. The atmosphere is entracing, get involved and you'll have a good time with this game.
Overally, I'd give this game an 8/10. If you're not that interested, pick it up during a sale. If you are, it's worth the $10 if you really want to spend time just doing side content, which is just as fun/if not more fun than the main quests.

I have a premium subscription to Tabletopia.  Based on several games over the past few weeks, I can say that this product is a great sandbox for playing Tabletop games.  That said, I'll point out some caveats.
The community is generally positive though a bit too small to have games running 24/7/365.  It's hard to find a game or players.  That said, they do have organized events for teaching and playing games and are expanding the roster of teachers/organizers.  Also, after the game reaches final release; more players will be able to be available.  Game discussions are generally positive and feedback is welcomed.
As a premium member, I can easily create rooms and invite others into the game with a link through a Unity 3d Web Plugin.  As for now, that allows Microsoft and Mozilla browsers to work with the product.  Support for deployment through iOS and Android is coming.
The quality and polish of the virtual pieces is high.  With professional assets, the game is better than live with really sharp looking pieces.  The physics engine work to stick the game to the table there are quite a bit of custom tricks to ensure that the game plays with as many shortcuts as possible.  The camera can map to 9 different locations and angles.
That said, there is a learning curve to the interface that takes a while to overcome.  There are keyboard commands that need to be learned, there are mouse button commands, ....  It took me a few mistakes and a few lookups in the help sections to smooth out my skills but, after some time; the interface doesn't fight me as much.
In short, I recommend this product.

Having played Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm for 22+ hours, I think I can't recommend this game to war game / TBS fans because the game suffers from some serious gameplay issues. My complaints about this game are all related to the gameplay mechanics and the AI. Although the graphics, the UI, and the sound effects are just mediocre, they're still acceptable to me. As a strategy fanboy, I care about gameplay and AI the most.
1) The Achilles Heel of FC:RS is that it's actually a turn-based *tower defense* game, *not* a war game. It's a tower defense game because of 2 reasons.
First and foremost, you *cannot* order a combat unit to attack a specific enemy target in the game. In any tower defense game, you can only position turrets at particular locations. It's up to the turrets' AI to determine which enemies to attack. In FC:RS, the gameplay mechanics are the same. You can put combat units at strategic locations and issue different defensive orders to them (e.g., Hold, Screen, and Resupply). However, that's all you can do. It's up to the friendly AIs to determine which enemy units they want to attack. If you want your AT (Anti-Tank) unit to attack a T-80 unit, sorry, you can't. Your AT unit may decide to attack the T-80 unit. But it may also decide to attack another LAV (Light-Armored Vehicle) unit instead. You have *NO* control over which enemies your units choose to attack. It's just like a tower defense game in which combats between turrets and their enemies are 100% decided by the AIs. The only thing you can control is the positioning of your combat units. Sounds boring then, doesn't it? Yes, after 22 hours of playtime, I'm already very bored of such over-simplistic gameplay.
There's a unit command called "Assault", but it's just basically a *movement* order giving a combat unit better accuracy while it's on the move. It does *NOT* allow you to order the unit to target a specific enemy. Once the aforementioned unit reaches the final destination, it's up to the AI to determine which enemy to attack.
I really wish there was an "Attack / Target" command for each combat unit in the game. Any enemy targeted by this command would be the top attack priority of my combat unit. If, for any reason (e.g., enemy having moved out of my unit's line-of-sight, or my unit's weapons unsuitable for attacking the enemy), the chosen enemy isn't a legitimate target anymore, the friendly AI will then decide which enemy should be the appropriate target. ALL of the RTS and TBS titles (from the classic Harpoon series to the recent Wargame series by Eugen Systems) have allowed the players to choose enemy targets and to formulate their own offensive strategies. Unfortunately, you can't devise your own offensive strategy in this game. Every attack move is decided by the AI. It's just 100% tower defense in nature.
I don't understand...I'm supposed to play the commander's role in this game. Why ain't I allowed to order my combat units to attack specific enemy targets? This is just totally unrealistic at all.
How would you feel if Xcom didn't give you any ability to order  your troopers to target any specific alien enemy? A game with zero tactical depth and variety.
The second reason why FC:RS is a tower defense game is because the enemy AI is really stupid. They just charge at your units in a straight line without considering terrain effects and potential threats. If your unit is next to a forest and a plain tile, don't worry, the enemy AI would usually choose to move to the plain tile and attack you from there. Instead of using tanks, the AI opponent would sometimes use infantries, AAs (Anti-Air), ATs and even utility vehicles as the frontline units. This is just the same as the enemy AI in any tower defense game: advancing towards the player's turrets in a straight line without any strategy involved.
2) Another shortcoming of FC:RS is the poor documentation of damage calculation. There're several types of damage in this game: AP, HEAT, Area and AD. However, neither the game manual nor the tutorial explains how damage is calculated when a unit successfully attacks / hits an enemy target. E.g., what's the formula for calculating the damage when a Challenger successfully hits a T-80? Is it [(AP+HEAT) / 2] - Armour Value? And what's the formula for calculating damage inflicted upon an infantry unit? Also, how about air units? Sorry, damage calculation is always a mystery in this game.
3) My last complaint about FC:RS is that weapons' accuracy values are *NOT* displayed in-game. Yes, every weapon used by each combat unit has an accuracy value. However, when you open the unit information panels, you can never find the accuracy values. Based on the official forum's posts, you need to read a mod's guide called "The Poor Mans Mod Guide" to learn how to crack some game files in order to view the accuracy values. Seriously, why doesn't the developer just do all players a favour and have the accuracy values shown *in-game*? Without knowing the accuracy potential of my combat units, how can I formulate my assault strategy?
Conclusion:
Game score: 6 / 10
To me, the severest issue of FC:RS is the lack of an "Attack / Target" command for the combat units. This basically turns this war game into a turn-based tower defense title. Players have to *blindly* follow the AI's attack decisions and this significantly undermines the tactical depth of the game. I've never written such a lengthy game review, but the gameplay mechanics of FC:RS are just very disappointing. A TBS game based on the cold war / modern warfare setting has always been my dream game. I think that's why I have so much to complain.

They actually discussed the issues mentioned in this review and they planned to implement significant changes to the next game engine (e.g., several new assault mechanics will be introduced to give players more control over their units' attack decisions). I really appreciate their responsiveness and consideration for the players. Also, they're bold enough to take constructive criticisms and think of new ideas to improve the game series further. The implementation of the OODA loop through an asymmetric and dynamic orders cycle makes this an interesting game.   Submitting orders and watching things play out is great, and the tension that builds from waiting for your next order cycle is palpable. Reading the manual, the level of detail in what is modeled and taken into account seems to be quite high, which is a good thing, though I at times I wish more information was relayed to the player (has the unit received the order? Is it still planning it's movement or is it stuck for some reason? etc).
The use of hexes and unit-level control requirements is an obvious departure from Panther's Command Ops series, which remains one of my favorites on account of its superb AI, but these differences are what makes FCRS a worthy title to enjoy alongside Command Ops because it's not trying to directly compete in the same space.
I haven't tried PBEM or PBEM++ yet, but anticipate that the turn based nature of the game may make it easier to maintain an ongoing game with someone than CommOps, whose realtime pausable system means both players need to be in the hotseat at the same time.
All in all, I'm very impressed from what I've seen so far!

I feel that the OTS crew is on to something good, and that FC:RS has a lot of potential. However, I also feel that there are a few areas of this game that feel extremely 'indie' and poorly completed, that make the game fall completely short.
UI
Does Matrix Games have a rule for its developers that UI's need to be as bland, unhelpful, clunky, and lifeless as possible? It is the feeling I get from many of the past Matrix Games that I've played (I'm looking at you, Advanced Tactics!), and FCRS is no exception. Things just dont run smoothly within the UI, and 90% of the data that players recieve fall into two poorly sized boxes along the bottom and side of the screen. The map is also cheaply done - there is no natrual zoom for the map. More zoom does not equal more fidelity, just more pixelation. It is the same problem when players zoom out.
Gameplay
The game engine seems very primitive. Instead of seeing units seamlessly move across the screen according to march speed and formation, they simply just jump from one hex to the next. It lacks the smoothness of Panzer Corps or Order of Battle, and it looks extremely odd when you see an entire Brigade/Reigment formation on the move - each unit moving 1 hex at a time.
I dont enjoy the unit management - Players are forced to direct platoon-sized units. This wouldnt be bad, but most of the pre-made scenarios/campaigns are Battalion,Brigade,Regiment and even Division sized engagements. This requires a ton of micromanagement, and when the AI has a mind of its own (units will randomly move or make decisions on their own) it can be very frustrating managing a large battle.
AI
I dont enjoy the pre-made scenarios; they're too large for my taste, and managing EVERY platoon throughout a Regiment/Brigade is time consuming and micromanaging. Most of the scenarios are meeting engagements or defensive missions. I created some small custom scenarios in the editor and realized why....the AI is really terrible at defense. On offense, the AI will not look for any advantgous terrain, and will not use any doctrine or military-technique for moving.
Hopefully the OTS team will develop momentum from this release, and future addons for FCRS and eventually be able to upgrade the game.

Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm is one of those unique games which I keep in my favorites and would play it anytime along with Combat Mission series, The Operational Art of War III, Command: Modern Air/Naval Operations and AGEod games.
FC:RS is a mix of TOAW III and Combat Mission series set in 80'th Cold War era where it became(in-game) not so cold.
Game features lot of interesting staff: Along with military units and formations, game features hybrid asynchronous WEGO system(OODA Loop), which is based on your side capability to give orders - it results in situation where player one for example can give orders each 10 minutes, but second one can do this every 30 minutes and using this timing player one can get inside opponents loop and react almost in time on any change on battlefield. This is not random and its based on lot of factors - Electronic Warfare in the area, available HQ units, C3 lines between subordinate units and their commanders and etc.
Scenarios scale varies from company to brigade scale operations on map sized 20x20 kilometrs divided by ~500 meters hexes.
FC:RS modeled lot of cold war advanced weapon systems including US M1 Abrams, Bradley IFVs, UK Chieftan, Warrior IFV along with Soviet T-80s and Hinds.
Game also features artillery weapons like mortars and SP Guns with diffirent munition like HE, Smoke, minlets and ICBM, chemical and even nuclear arms.
Really worth to say that developers are working hard on game, for example Players Edition which is currently available on Steam is a result of great work between Developer team and community. Even today game continue to become better and better.
Hope this short list will help you to decide if this game worth your moneys.
Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm это одна из тех уникальных игр, в которые я играю почти всегда, рядом с  играми серии Combat Mission, The Operational Art of War III, Command: Modern Air/Naval Operations и играми AGEod.
FC:RS это микс между TOAW III и Combat Mission в сеттинге холодной войны, как раз в тот момент, когда она переста(в игре) быть такой уж холодной.
Игра имеет много интересных реализаций, например наряду с огромным кол-вом военной техники игра предлагает интерсный гибридный режим WEGO(OODA Loop) тайминг ходов в котором основан на возможности стороны отдавать приказы - в результате этого бывают ситуации, когда одна сторона может отдавать приказы каждые 10 минут, а вторая каждые 20, тем самым время реакции первой стороны на ситуацию заметно меньше второй, что в свою очередь ведет, при правильном применении, к своевременной реакции на изменения на поле боя и к победе. Циклы командования не рандомны, а основаны на многих факторах, включая РЭБ, доступность штабов, существование линии командования между подчиненными и штабами и т.д.
Размеры сценариев варьируются от ротного уровня до уровня бригады на картах размером 20 на 20 км, разделенных 500 метровыми гексами.
Игра моделирует много современных боевых систем, включая М1 Абрамс, БМП Бредли, Чифтаны, Варриоры на стороне НАТО и Т-80, Ми-24 на стороне Советов.
Так же в игре представлены различные артиллерийские системы начиная от минометов и заканчивая самоходными гаубицами имеющие немалый арсенал боеприпасов - ОФ, дымовые, мины, кластерные, химические и даже ядерные заряды.
Стоит упомянуть и то, что разработчики совсем не забыли про игру, например Player's Edition, который уже сразу доступен в стиме это результат огромной работы разработчиком вместе с комьюнити.
Игра продолжает развиваться и совершенствоваться.
Надеюсь это маленькое ревью поможет вам с выбором - стоит ли эта игра ваших денег.

TL;DR
Buy it if you prefer the individual levels to the overal world or the bosses. If you prefer the gameworld, buy Dark Souls 1. If you prefer boss fights, buy Dark Souls 3.
Compared to Dark Souls 1, this game is much more consistent in its quality, with lower highs but higher lows. There's nothing in DS2 that's awful on the level of Lost Izalith, but there's also nothing nearly as good as the Painted World outside of the DLC. However, with the DLC included for free in the SotFS edition, the game is elevated to much greater heights. Sinh, Fume Knight, and Ivory King are among the best bosses in all of Dark Souls, better than almost every fight from DS1 and a good chunk of the DS3 boss pool as well. They also contextualize the story of the game in a way that makes the game far more personal -- it's much easier to be invested in the world of DS2 compared to DS1 and 3 where the stories feel like a backdrop rather than motivation.
COMBAT
Combat is Dark Souls combat, I don't feel I need to explain much more than that. It lends itself more to larger groups of enemies, and magic is greatly improved, but it's still Dark Souls, and it's just as good as any other Dark Souls game -- faster than DS1 as your attack options are better, but slower than DS3 because multiple enemy encounters require patience and picking a good time to attack -- the Dual Pursuers in NG+ play more like Ornstein and Smough than as a generic combat encounter. PvP is also great, but my experience is too limited to comment on it in depth here.
PRESENTATION
The game is, unfortunately, ugly -- much less creative enemy designs than DS1 and 3, with most of the new enemies being fairly standard humanoid enemies or bland looking 'fantasy monster' -- Ogres, those weird mushroom things, and the long-armed green enemies in No Man's Wharf are all forgettable enemy designs, a far cry from the unique appearance of the basilisks, the unnatural bodies of the mimics, and the horrifying bug/human hybrids in the depths of Blighttown. Boss design suffers from a similar lack of quality -- there are no fights as visually striking as Sif, Gaping Dragon, or Gravelord Nito. The most creative boss design is the Executioner's Chariot, an optional boss that culminates in a fight against a pretty generic horse enemy with dodgy hitboxes.
LEVELS & BOSSES
Speaking of bosses, outside of the DLC the boss design in this game is downright bad. I can honestly say that there wasn't a single fight that impressed me in the entire base game. In stark contrast, the levels between these boss fights are fantastic, and with a couple exceptions they were all well designed. I didn't like Heide's Tower or Earthern Peak, and I still can't tell if Shrine of Amana is a great zone or an awful one, but every other zone felt satisfying to fight through and explore, with plenty of secrets to discover and interesting enemy set ups that forced me to adapt to a very steady difficulty curve throughout each 'path' -- the first zones, like Forest of Fallen Giants or Shaded Ruins, were generally pretty simple and straight forward, with some kind of mechanic the zone wanted to teach you, be it curse pots, poison build up, combat against large enemies, combat against many smaller enemies, etc., but each level path would iterate on these ideas, often culminating in a final stretch to the boss that is a grueling test in all of the lessons you've learned -- the cave before Freja, the flooded hallway before Sinner -- or in an optional but very difficult boss with an even more challenging run-up -- Smelter Demon, Belfry Gargoyles if you're online -- that makes the rest of the zone easier to tackle in some fashion.
WORLD
The most conflicting part of this game is whether or not I hate the gameworld or adore it. Dark Souls 1 had an amazingly interconnected world throughout the first half of the game, but threw this concept out the door in the second half besides a few cool moments, like seeing Izalith through a hole in the wall in Tomb of Giants. Dark Souls 3 didn't have many interconnected paths between zones, but instead focused on feeling more like a journey than a quest, moving through the world in a linear fashion with a tightly controlled difficulty curve. Dark Souls 2 has multiple paths that you can tackle in almost any order, allowing you to tackle the game the way you choose to -- and not in the "well, technically" fashion of Dark Souls 1, but by having a more consistently challenging game that retains its difficulty regardless of what path you go down. However, these paths do the infuriating and yet somewhat fascinating thing of refusing to make any logical sense. You walk through tunnels that teleport you from daylight in a forest to rainy nighttime on a mountain, you climb elevators that lead from the top of a tower upwards to the base of a volcano that doesn't even exist, and your tutorial zone is called Things Betwixt, as though its lodged between worlds in some way, and the only exit is through a crack in the barrier between the world of Drangleic and the world of Things Betwixt. If it wasn't a concept that was explored further in Dark Souls 3, culminating in the complete devolution of time and space in The Ringed City, it would be easy to call this lazy design, but its clear in retrospect that this game is very intentionally building an atmosphere of unreality that is utterly fascinating to look closely at once you start to pay attention to it and look at how many ways the game's story and world ties into this idea.
DLCS
Sunken King plays like a Zelda level, with a bow and arrow being necessary to explore the level. Most of the bonfires are hidden and well spaced, and I could see somebody getting through the whole DLC only ever finding two of them. Enemies are challenging to fight, and the ghostly suits of armour are a very interesting challenge that I won't spoil, even if I struggle to imagine being able to defeat them all on just one life. Sinh is the best endurance fight in the series, and possibly the best dragon fight in the series -- I'm still torn on whether or not Midir is the ultimate challenge or just obnoxious -- with his movements making him difficult to follow across the room and his damage being difficult to avoid. Taking him down feels like a triumph simply because the odds are so stacked against you, with the durability damaging armour plating, the toxic building flame he spits at you, and the massive hitboxes of many of his attacks.
Old Iron King has the best level design in any Dark Souls game ever, with an absolutely perfect understanding of how to pace the DLC. The DLC only has one mandatory boss fight, and he is an incredible challenge, and certainly the best humanoid boss pre-Dark Souls 3, where the humanoid boss bar was raised so high that nothing could ever reach it. When you activate the elevators that span the tower, what was previously an incredibly difficult to navigate maze becomes much more accessible, and dozens of secrets are opened to you. Incredibly satisfying level design elevates this DLC to the top of the pack.
Ivory King is the worst of the DLC, but has the perfect fight to end your DLC experience with, as Ivory King is the most gorgeously presented boss in the entire series. However, exploring the level twice after melting the ice feels tedious, and the Frigid Wastes are a war crime. Although great, I spent more time being lost than making progress in this DLC.
FINAL THOUGHTS
Overall, this game is a solid 8/10 for the base game, weighed down by poor boss encounters and bland presentation but carried by a top-notch combat and progression system, but a 9/10 once DLC is included, with the drought of good bosses being augmented with several fights ranging from great (Aava, Elana) to fantastic (Fume Knight, Sinh, Ivory King), the story being heavily improved, and the already great level designed being honed to perfection.

It is always nice to see when the appropriate games get greenlit by the community - Shutter is another great example for that. This is a neat little game where we control a small RC car equipped with a camera - this surveillance unit is to be used to discover the strange occurrences surrounding a house.
We are constantly in contact with a software engineer, a guy who asks us where to go and what to take a photo of. The photos we then upload and await his further instructions. Occasionally he upgrades our software which basically means a camera with different modes for shooting (night vision, spectral vision). We take photos of objects, apparitions while experiencing some good-old survival horror scary stuff: suddenly closing doors, flickering lights, sudden blackouts and ghostly sounds / voices.
Regularly, we find notes telling us the story of the place and while it is not much it still contributes to the great atmosphere the game has. Graphics-wise the game is a bit rough around the edges - in-game menus are particularly ugly, still, Shutter has a good entertainment value for a couple of hours especially in case you are interested in something different than the AAA games out there.
I look forward to playing its sequel - I have to admit I have my expectations, though.

This is a game that I keep wanting to LOVE.
The story is interesting (despite what some people say about it not fitting the rest of the series), and I find the characters intriguing enough that I can stay in character.
As a sorcoress, I feel like I have UNGODLY AMOUNTS OF POWER... and that even that much power is just not quite enough.
It has it's faults, though; and they are some real whoppers.
* If you have never played a Souls game, prepare to buy replacement controllers every time you get into an area that requires jumping. The jump mechanics of ALL these games are crap.
* In this game, the healing flask is abysmally slow. Better off using purchasable healing gems all the time.
* The one really huge downside is the layout. The world map in Dark Souls 2 was designed by a pack of tindalos' hounds. Say you are running along the edge of the ocean with the water on your left... you pass through a tunnel that curves left, and come out into dense forest that curves slightly left... by the time you reach the end of the forest ruins, a part of you, deep down inside, is convinced that you should be a mile out at sea. And lets not get into the part where you take an elevator up near the top of a huge tower, and come out from underground at ground level, into a volcanic crater...
It IS a good game. It should have been a lot better.
Personally, noted issues aside, I do highly recommend it.

Ampu-Tea: A basic bootleg of Surgeon Simulator with none of the fun.
Every big meme-game is boundless to have a few knock offs that float down the Greenlight River. A few joke simulator games when Goat Simulator was big, a few click-a-thon jumpscare games when FNAF was big, and Ampu-Tea is a bare bones clone of Surgeon Simulator. An un-fun, little variety experience that isn't worth the trading cards.
Basic logic is that you're trying to make tea with a prosthetic arm, sounds basic and normal. You have to deal with two things, the tediously slow motors in your fake hand, and the game's♥♥♥♥♥♥controls. With Surgeon Sim, you were fighting the fact you were learning how to use your hand. In Amptu-Tea, you're fighting your hand, the game engine, the physics engine and the tiny motors that make your fingers function.
So no, don't buy this game. It's a janky game that aims to do one thing and fails at it. It wants to be Surgeon Simulator but doesn't have the time neccesary to refine the experience and make it an actual competitor to the throne that Surgeon Sim sits at. The potential to make this game some kind of decent game exists but there's no desire to make it better, so pass it on, cause the cards aren't worth it.

By my playtime it's obvious that I like this game and I like it a lot, although it seems that Dark Souls II is somewhat frowned upon by people who liked the first or maybe the third one better. I admit that it's a game that you have to get used to, because some very important core mechanics were changed. One of the biggest things is the roll mechanic, in Dark Souls 1 you had different weight catagories with <25%, <50%, and <75% that determined how much use you get out of your invicibility frames while you have to actively increase your agility to increase the numbers. You start pretty low with 80 and by leveling up adaptability and/or attunement you can increase it to I think a maximum of 120, although 110 is considered the softcap and should be a pretty comfortable number.
Another thing that I noticed it that it seems like you need a little longer to raise your shield which isn't such a big deal in most situations, but it can become very important when you're not sure if you can squeeze in another attack, especially with a slow strength weapon, so keep that in mind.
Compared to the regular Dark Souls 2 it seems like Scholar of the first Sin replaced a few enemies here and there and overall increased the number, it's not a rare occasion that you have to face around 3-5 enemies at the same time, but if you play in a defensive way with a shield equipped you should be fine for most occasions. There are instances where the game punishes you this way and you'll pretty much die for sure, but you'll learn from your mistake and do better next time. Personally I don't think it's the best way to make things more challenging by just placing more enemies in certain spots, but it's not the worst thing either.
Keep your weapons as good as possible, carry a few different types like a thrust and a slash weapon, maybe some elemental weapons like lightning and fire and you should be good to go.
Two hints for everyone who's new to the game or wants to achieve 100%: Don't join the Covenant of Champions right away just because you can, it make things even more challenging and can be frustrating for a few people who are not used to the game and its mechanics. Also join the Sunbros asap and farm medals while you're still in a good range for co-op, it's absolutely no fun to farm enemies for these medals.

Outlast is a short horror experience developed by a small team of ex-Ubisoftians.
In this game you take control of Miles Upshur, a reporter who is assigned to investigate Mount Massive Asyl...whoa what?
Now, even though the plot feels a bit pretentious at first, it still holds its interest due to great characters who inhabit the asylum. The graphics feel really great for an indie title, and the sound design is impeccable, from excellent acting to Samuel Leflamme's intense strings playing.
How about the scares? The world has a surprisingly creepy and disturbing atmosphere, but it relies too much on jumpscares and gore, even though it has genuinely frightening moments. Outlast is filled with intense chases instead, with sometimes several madmen hunting you from almost every possible direction. This fills the game with great pacing, which sparingly lets you breathe for a moment as you run away from disgusting monstrosities. And it's still scarier than Machine for Pigs.
Outlast stumbles mainly on the repetitiviness and level design of the middle act, which confused me far more than it should have. As I stated earlier, this game is short, with my playthrough lasting approx. 5 hours. Devs have promised additional content though. Enemy encounters can also be easily predicted and their AI is as predictable. And they have big, wobbling ♥♥♥♥♥.
My final verdict is 8/10. (Special thanks to Kiiro for gifting me this game.)

When it comes to storytelling, narration is a difficult one to handle. In many movies and tv shows, stories are told through a quick glance, or a one-liner. But narration is rarely used, it seen as drab, expositional, lacking in action. And often times, it is. However, I think Fullbright’s beautiful
creates an atmosphere that utilizes the medium effectively.
The game itself is simple. A “walking-simulator.” However, I give the creators a lot of respect on how they let the story be discovered. To have a full house, and manage to make the right tape come on at the right time is, in my opinion, impressive to say the least.
As for the story,
is a witty, tear-jerking story about a unique LGBTQ couple, Sam and Lonnie, while accurately displaying the emotional toll not being accepted as who you are. As a member of the LGBTQ community, I cannot appreciate enough how much the representation that this game provides means to me. June 7, 1995. That’s when this game takes place, in a normal U.S.A. Support of the LGBTQ community wasn’t very public, let alone common. While slightly unrealistic at times, there are so many details that make this game that make this story not unbelievable. It is definitely unrealistic in the fact that you explore every crevice of a brand new house to discover what’s happened, but the narrative that Sam’s tape describes is one that so many can relate to. A feeling of wanting to scream at the night sky and plead for some peaceful acceptance. I cried, and I hope that whoever plays this game will cry with me.

(NOTE; THIS REVIEW COMES FROM SOMEONE WHO HASN'T YET BEATEN THE GAME)
TL;DR: Yes, I'd recommend this.
This game is one of those "8-bit level hardcore with 8-bit design" games that have arose quite a lot in the indie genre. However, while it's not completely trying to go off of 8-bit nostalgia (In fact, it seems it really isnt at all, not really taking much from games of that era other than difficulty) Its definently taken inspiration from this type. So, while that may be a selling point: I, personally, didn't live during this time, although I do like playing games from these times for the challenge/experience. So, it doesn't ride on nostalgia expecting it to carry it to victory, as I have no nostalgia there, and I still love it. No, the main point for VVVVVV (Which, I'd like to note, is a very difficult thing to name in verbal speech. I always resort to saying 6Vs if they dont understand from saying VVVVVV) is its simplicity and puzzles. The game's controls consist solely of running and "jumping" Well, not jumping in a traditional sense, more in a, say screw gravity and go on the ceiling sense. Thats it on controls, and it works just fine. Each puzzle is displayed on a single screen, often involving anything and everything killing you. From spikes to shapes to busses to stop signs to ghosts to almost anything that has a face, everything wants your head on a silver platter. And this is one of those games in which you die in one hit no matter what, so often times whatever wants you dead gets its previously mentioned wish of your head on a fancy tray. Unfortunately, they are completely dissatisfied with this, and come back for your head again with just as much vigor as before. So, moving away from the overly complex analogies, the game has those two features and asks you to find these people from your ship and escort them back to said ship. Which, leads me to the story, Which is simply, you and your brightly colored crew are on a ship travelling the galaxy, when some sorta glitch of sorts happens and you all get separated. Leaving you, being the captain, to find the rest of your crew back to your ship. It has little trinkets that you can collect for an additional challenge, usually at the end of some difficult obstacle course that can create a rage quit like attitude in you (Doing things the hard way, I'm looking at you.) Back on track, the obstacle course statement is a decent summary for the whole game; an obstacle course. Some on 1 screen, some that go over multiple screens, some involving tons of trampolines, but all in all, they're obstacle courses set to fun little techno 8-bit tunes.
VERDICT: Overall, this is one of those "You WILL die your first time through probably" Games, that can be a lot of fun if you enjoy puzzle games such as these. Each scenario can seem simple, but almost all has more to it than originally suspected. If you enjoy puzzle games, you'll like this. If you like platformers, you'll like this. If you like 8-bit hard games, you'll like this. If you think you'll like this if you have knowledge of what the game is, you'll like this. All in all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who fall under that category. I'll close this review with one final statement; Vermillion can go screw himself. I hate him and his ignorance.

Short version: Some connection issues, but if it works it's a LOT of fun! 30 second summary of the game:
Long version:
Got this on day 1 of Early Access, and completely without testing or preparation fired it up with a couple of guys from around the planet.
The online lobby system is a bit problematic, sometimes the game takes a full minute to be able to connect, complaining about online components initializing or similar. Only one of the 3 of us was able to successfully host a game so the other 2 were able to join it - I tried to host and someone outside of our group was able to join, but neither of the other 2 players I was playing with could join. I could not join any server unless I had a VPN on, with the VPN on the component initialization issue wasn't there, but I couldn't join anything. Quite odd, would love to get more information on how to make this work better, by doing port forwarding or similar. The latency and other issues that the VPN likely caused apparently made the game lose sync of the status of things, and broke our ability to navigate the ship completely a few times. You cannot simply invite the friends you want to the game, and you cannot kick off players from the lobby, or set a password.
However, once you get the game running it's a LOT of fun. We had a party of 3 guys on Discord voice chat, and it was a constant stream of "oh no a shark!", "cut the engines", "leak in navigation", "WHAT IS THAT?!". Lots of very fun hectic moments with everyone running around the sub trying to fight off the monsters attacking the sub and fixing leaks, while trying to balance power distribution and keep torpedo tubes loaded.
While it's rogue-like, there is some permanent progress in the game. You collect gold in caves, and you can use that to unlock certain kinds of apparel and tools.
The game feels great for an Early Access -title on first day, the only problems we really had was with the lobby system and connections in general, and I can see this game being absolutely amazing fun in the future as they make the online connectivity better.
Our longest run lasted a little under 30 minutes and the time simply flew by. Everyone had a great time, and was constantly busy, and we had a feeling that we were progressing even when we encountered issues like when we couldn't navigate the sub due to some bug.
So, while the game has some network issues the game is still a lot of fun to play. Another thing worth noting is that it looks like the game will be very hard to play with only 2 people, with 3 people it was really hard and only with 4 did it seem like we had enough time to manage status quo, but when things got hairy we still had a hard time keeping up with things.
