Convinced another friend to buy it + gifted it to a 4th person and tried out some 4 player games. It's even more fun with 4 people although even with 4 it gets really difficult by the 3rd level (I've only gotten about 4900 fathoms deep). Now that I've played it some more there are some bugs/glitches I've noticed so I'm going to put it below so the devs can see it:
1. My 2nd time playing it (3 people) when we entered the 2nd level/stage the game crashed for 2 people but the host stayed in the game and could play by himself.
2. Both with 3 people and 4 people occasionally when someone picks up a item from the ground when they already have 2 equipped and then place it back down the others can't see it. So for example: you have sword and wrench, you grab cleaver from ground and put wrench down. Now you reequip the wrench and put the cleaver back down but the others can't see the cleaver or equp it, only you can. This only sometimes happened and other times it didn't.
3. I'm not sure if this is a feature or a glitch but if you're in a cave and you shoot into the wall with a gun and there's a snail or something else down on the floor it takes a damage. This also happens at different angles where you can't be attacked but you can shoot with gun into wall.

However these are all minor glitches and the game is still a ton of fun, I'll update this as I play more.

*Early-access review!* We Need To Go Deeper is being actively developed and bug-fixed! Although you may still encounter some problems and bugs, be sure to keep the devs informed! They've been doing good work with hotfixing the product.
UPDATE: Reformed the review to fit the circumstances.
--
Short version: We Need To Go Deeper is a co-operative game about exploration and survival. Thanks to its' simple interface and fluid mechanics it should be an interesting addition to the legion of co-op games out there. 4/5.
--
Long version: We Need To Go Deeper is a co-operative game about exploration and survival. Albeit the game can be played solo, it is highly recommendable to either play with friends or join random lobbies available in the game's menus. The gameplay is about controlling a submarine mutually with a crew consisting of up to 4 people, whereas 2 seems to be recommended minimum. The co-operative gameplay supports *both* Internet- and LAN-connections, which is a huge bonus to this game's value! Hosting and joining lobbies is very easy and fluid, and the text-chat within the game allows players to co-ordinate their actions if microphones and external communication software are not readily available.
The control mechanics themselves feature minimal keyboard usage and a mouse, no support for a controller as much as I could see -- cardinal directions, use-button, overview of the submarine's surroundings, use of equipped item and switching the equipment. The crew need to control basic things such as engine power, steering, weapons and hull-integrity while inside the submarine. Optimally one person should be always in charge of steering while the other handles engine and gunnery control. Obviously the more people, the easier the control will be.
All in all, the biggest strength of the game is its' easy-to-approach style and intention to keep the gameplay fun. We Need To Go Deeper seems like a nice co-op game with a lot of potential, possibly keeping you entertained from several to even a couple of dozen hours. 4/5.

In terms of sheer enjoyment for a racing video game, The Crew has to make the Top 5! (...when it's working...)
- The Crew has a
open world map! The map is probably about a 20:1 scale map of the United States; the map is by no means cartographically accurate, but the major landmarks and cities are there. Everything is down in scale (similar to Midnight Club: LA or the GTA games), but that doesn't mean that the world doesn't feel humongous! It is a daunting task to think about driving from Miami to Seattle, or LA to Niagara Falls, but as one who has done it, there are few things more exciting! There are many little easter eggs on the map to find in addition to the hidden objects and challenges that make simply driving around in the open world interesting and fun.
- The Crew has a fairly large list of cars that are available in the game and all of the cars available look great in the game. You can customize your car with different body sets, colors and stickers to make your vehicle one of a kind. The cars also handle pretty well all things considered; The Crew is definitely not a simulator when it comes to driving but for an arcade style racer the car handling is more realistic than it could have been. It should be said that by the time you beat the game and level up your first car to Level 50 parts and a 1200+ rating, however, you
have a favorite car or two and for the most part only drive those cars.
- The Crew has pretty decent graphics too. I have found myself taking screenshots of the scenery, much like I do with Skyrim, because the world really does look great! Of course, the world looks better at 60-80mph than it does at 180-200mph, even with the best GPUs, but that's to be expected.
- This game is buggy. There is no simpler way to say it. And there is no denying it. My friend and I have constantly been thwarted by programming issues within the game. During open world travels we will inevitably come across at least a major bug or two every 30-60 mins. Some of the worst, especially since the new expansion has come out, include (1) infinite loading screens, (2) game freezing during fast travel, and my personal nemesis - (3) the road/world disappearing in front of you [this bug has an relatively easy fix - just open up the map and quickly exit out again, but it is annoying nonetheless. It is also potentially game breaking when you are in a mission or co-op event when the open world map is not accessible.] There is no way to enjoy The Crew without experiencing bugs. Maybe if there were more people online the makers of The Crew would be inclined to fix them, but since there are not, you just have to deal with them. This creates a Love/Hate relationship with this game.
- The AI in this game is... wonky, to say the least. For missions/co-op events or in police chases, the AI seems counter-productive (as opposed to challenging) and even vengeful at times. Rubberbanding
occurs in these types of events and should be expected (heck, sometimes I think they designed it that way just so that you
a crew playing with you). In the open world, expect AI driven cars to suddenly swerve in front of you, especially if you are going 200+mph. If there were any corners cut in the programming of this game, I would think that they were cut in this AI department.
- If you do end up convincing a friend to buy this game with you so that you can play it together, then you should also know that forming a crew in the game can be difficult at times too. It is normal for my friend and I to spend 15-30 mins trying to get into a crew together and forcing the game to put us on the same server. Game restarts should be expected, and it should also be noted that The Crew doesn't always play nice with Steam's voice chat (probably because it's a Ubisoft game and uses UPlay. **As a side note though, I have not had as many issues with Uplay as I have had with other games they put out**).
- Many others have said it on forums and discussion boards, but this game
a multiple waypoint system. The gigantic map is just begging for one! It is very frustrating to try and create driving routes and races with your crew/friend with only one waypoint to lay down. Honestly, I am very surprised by this huge oversight!
-  Along with that, this game would be vastly improved if there was a community based Player Created Races/Challenges feature. Since open world driving is the best (and most advertised) feature in the game, having a community of racers all creating their own races/routes/challenges would add content and excitement to the game.
- I have put over 80 hours into this game and about 70 of those hours have been genuinely enjoyable! Open world driving is by far my favorite activity and with the help of my friend I have come up with several fantastic driving routes that are always a blast to drive! There is no other game quite like The Crew and my heart wants everyone to buy and enjoy this game.
- The remaining 10 hours I have spent in this game, however, make it so that I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this game for the $30/$40 listing price. Even on sale, if you
have a friend to play this game with, I would
recommend that you stay far, far away! But if you do have a friend to play with, I would want you to seriously consider the issues presented in this review and weigh them against your desire for this game:
(1) If there is any hesitation, then spend your money elsewhere.
(2) If there is still excitement and a "devil-may-care" attitude, then all I can say is, "Good luck!"

A good game on the whole but there are still things that are questionable.
Been playing a few scenarios and a couple of campaign games and find the game quite challenging.
As NATO player you usually face hordes of russians and success is based on getting everything just right. The T-80s you face are usually easy to knock out but at times you get surprised when a company of T-80s, on the move, fire a bunch of ATGMs from four kilometers and knock out two M1A1s dug in, in 90% cover. The same applies to artillery and the AI russian artillery is really the hammer of God. It responds in seconds and eats dug in tanks and infantery as a snack. The russian helicopters are condensed evil which is nearly impossible to knock out of the sky with you SAMs. I´m also a bit surprised at how much better the M1A1 is compared to the T80 in all other aspects than the ATGM.
As Russian you somehow seem to lose the chopper and artillery God mode and it isn´t unusual that your hinds get knocked down from stray shots from infantery. It´s more difficult to get your artillery to knock out the NATO tanks.
Problems to both sides is the unclear priority of fire from your units. It isn´t on rare occasions you sit and scratch your head  and wonder why your tank platoon decides to fire on the two recon vehicles two and a half kilometers away instead of the two charging tank companies five hundred meters away who are in the open and clearly charging your dug in position. The same applies to your artillery if you use the staff controll.
The most annoying glitch is when you have your units in screen mode. Your recon don´t move and your land units can screen right out in an open field, towards known enemies instead of moving in cover, away from the enemy. I´m not sure if soldiers in the eighties really were that suicidal or if it´s a programming thing.
I would also like to be able to tell my recon units to stay hidden. In my army days recon units observed. In this game recon units, maybe two light APCs love to open fire on a company of T-80s rolling by. The result is obvious.
Despite these issues I like the game. I can recommend it to everyone liking a tactical simulator in a military setting. I would also love to see expansions with other nationalities and geografical regions as in WarGame - Air Land battle.

It's a haunted house story; the main gimmick is that instead of exploring the house in first-person with a flashlight, you instead pilot some kind of remote-controlled rover through it, with which you occasionally take pictures of suspicious-looking phenomena (hence the title of the game). The whole thing takes about 90 minutes to complete. There's diary entries to be found, and ghosts roaming the halls, etc. You know the drill.
There's nothing offensively bad about
There's also nothing particularly remarkable about it. I'll give the developers credit for an original approach to a shopworn genre, and for eschewing the use of cheap jump scares. I didn't find it scary, mainly because piloting a remote-controlled robot removes any sense of personal threat from the experience. I also don't remember any blood, so squeamish types should be all right with it.
I could just as easily have given this game a thumbs-up, because it's competently made and well-priced. I'm only voting it down because I just can't picture myself actively recommending it to anyone; it's too, well, not-scary for that. I wish the developers the best though, and the screenshots of the sequel (which apparently takes place in an abandoned prison, and are included as an "extra" with the game) look interesting.

I sat on the fence for a long time with this game. 100% because of pricing. i waited for a sale, and picked it up right away. i must say, this is a GREAT hex based wargame. its got a great amount of depth, everything under the hood is working smoothly, and i have yet to encounter any bugs. however, it takes A LONG TIME, to get get at this game. ive got like 75 hours as of this writing, and i still suck. it does a great job of realisitcally recreating units, tactics, docterine, and other aspects of the warsaw pact/nato forces. this means, that the nato side will almost always be outnumbered and have to rely on tactics, traning, and terrain for their advantages. at times it might feel unfair, but its not the game that is unfair, its the fact that in real life, if ww3 went down in germany, as this game has set up for us, nato would, in fact, be outnumbered on the ground...big time. the developers didnt beef up nato unnecessarily or unrealistically just because they are outnumbered. they do, however, tend to have better equipment, and thus, use it to their advantage. docterine is also simulated. the soviets tend to use stick together in large groups, forgetting any idea of individuality found in nato forces, and listen to their commanding officers, without question. take out their HQ and they may end up being far less effective than if a similar event happened to a similar nato unit. the game trys hard to simulate the muddiness and fog of war, including that on your own side. commanders are often limited to giving only a certain number of orders, to simulate the fact that during battle, its not always possible to get in contact with all your units to give them any order at any time. electronic warfare can also have a negitive effect on communications. each turn is played out in a we-go style, where both teams make their moves, and simultaniously play them out. during that time, orders can not be given, and you are often forced to watch your units destroyed or decimated because of a  bad decision you made. the time in between orders is effected by things like electronic warfare, communications jamming, unit organization, staffing, etc, etc, etc, and can be anywhere between 10-45 minutes or so. after it plays out, you can give new orders, but again, you may be limited to giving only a few orders at a time, especially if your forced to use runners due to radios being made useless. still i probably wouldnt pay full price, just because, for a digital download, is a bit much, but if you can get it on sale, pick it up right away.

Eternal is great. Instead of saying why its great, I'll address some opinions ther are here on why its not.
1. Its a Hearthstone reskin.
This is baffaling. Its has a mana system akin to Hex and MTG. It has a combat system in which defenders block, and units do not attack directly. Calling this a Hearthstone skin is the same as calling Clue a Monapoly skin.
2. Its an MTG reskin.
While the game is obvisouly inspired by MTG, its not a skin. The best way to explain why is because it is a digital game, it can use digital design space that MTG can't. Abilities such as Warcry and Warp could not be made in MTG.
3.  Recent changes to the PvE made the game unplayable for new players.
People don't like things taken away from them. In the past, PvE was the best way to grind gold by a very far margin. This is a bad thing for a game that is focused on PvP gameplay. The recent nerf, and then slight buff, made it less certain what is the best way to grind gold, with PvE being probably still the best way. Calling it a impssible for new players to progress is just false, as it takes very little time to get a top tier deck. The math shows that Eternal is the most free to play friendly on Steam.

For starters, this game isn't one you can manipulate like most of its ilk. You will assign people to jobs, such as building, hunting, blacksmithing, cleric-ing (?), forresting, planting, tailoring... and some will go straight to the nearest river and stare at it. You are not an all-powerful god who can crush people.
The beauty lies in its simplicity. While it lacks "tech trees" everything is able to be built from the beginning, provided you have the supplies.
And the supplies.
Oh yes, you will have to balance them. Whether its mining in a quarry, cutting down a swath of trees near town to finish some housing, or deciding to have your people labor in the dangerous iron or coal mines, everything is a balancing act. Even storing the items requires some kind of trade off: working to store items will take away work from making those items.
The music is simple and soft, yet seems to go with the environment quite well.
If I had a complaint about the game it would only be these two things: lack of diversity in the building types, as well as the inability to speed up the game more than 10x.

I asked for a refund. It's bug riddled as hell, in addition to some very legitimate complaints about the game itself. Reading some of the descriptions, and some of the more positive reviews, I figured I'd like this game. I'm a 90's kid, like most of you, so I grew up playing the clunky tank-control horror titles with cheesy dialogue, like Silent Hill or Resident Evil (both of which I'm a huge fan of). Other than controls (to an extent) do not expect anything like those titles out of this game. It's not the worst $1.50 (on sale) you'll spend, but it's still not worth the purchase.
Gameplay:
A huge, huge reason I give the gameplay such a low score is that taking pictures is a huge part of the game, and half the time the camera bugs out, so you can't see what you took a picture of, requiring a restart of the level. There's even a warning about this bug in-game! Spoilers, but a lot of the gameplay consists of roving around looking for shining objects to take pictures of, to recieve jumpscares. The handling on the little robot is pretty good, and the general concept is something I'd love to have seen from a competent or more experienced developer. However, the jump scares lose their draw after the first one. You'll spend a big chunk of the game wondering what the hell to take a picture of next, and it's usually a shiny dissapearing shovel (not kidding). I literally expected a skeleton to pop out and go "boo" most times. If you're not doing that, you're wondering why doors keep locking you in areas for over-used, and plain boring, set-pieces.  I (obviously) didn't finish the game.
Graphics:
Looks like something made with community assets in the Unity engine or something. The rover and the house you explore aren't that bad, but the "ghosts", props, UI, and other things are just plain bad. Nothing blends together, nothing is believable, nothing is scary. Try again.
Sound:
I couldn't tell if the sound bugged out a lot, or if the developer thought it was a good idea to have loud repeating annoying noises at random times in the game. Jumpscare? Expect the same sound to repeat 5-6 times as loud as possible. Ambience? Expect the same sound to repeat 5-6 times as loud as possible. Something changes somewhere else? (Rinse, repeat).
Story:
What story? You're apparantly investigating the security concerns of a clearly abandoned house that kids have been spraying with graffiti (nevermind the fact that the roof/windows are busted). Someone had time to install security cameras all over the place, along with a recharging/calibration station for your UGV, yet they couldn't just simply send in a dude with a camera, cell phone, and note pad to check security issues on a ran-down abandoned house? The scares, notes you find, and things your email partner says have nothing to do with eachother, and it's all very juvinille level writing all around.
In conclusion:
Do not buy this game, it's ♥♥♥♥ing terrible. The concept is nice (piloting a UGV to hunt for ghosts and such), but this team cannot produce, as is apparant. I wish I could say better for this game, but I cannot and will not reccomend anyone purchase it.

Dark Souls 2, the only Dark Souls not directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, but rather From Software´s B Team.
Right from the start, we see some small details that hints us the big difference between this and the previous Dark Souls. Comparing both, this one is way easier, not having any boss that made me almost rip my hair off like Ornstein and Smough did, except maybe Sir Alonne when I tried getting his unique death animation for the first time. And overall, it´s barely above average in terms of difficulty from your standard everyday RPG.
Another bad thing it has is a mechanic called Soul Memory, which determines your multiplayer matchmaking depending on how many souls you have acquired throught your journey. In theory, this sounds decent, but it is basically a must for any player that wants to do something multiplayer related to create another character so he isnt matched with people 100 levels above him, because a new player will die multiple times and wont exactly know what to invest in at all times.
But, besides a relatively mediocre singleplayer and a bad matchmaking mechanic which can be solved by wearing the Agape Ring (which is a must have for anyone who wants to actively PvP or co-op), this game is the most enjoyable out of the three, having a way more balanced and less glitchy PvP, more stable servers than the first game, an overall better PC port, etc.
Anyone who wants to start with Dark Souls, I would highly recommend this one if they want and easier time with the other 2 (and Bloddborne and Demon´s Souls if they own consoles).
NOTE: Another problem, which is more of a problem that I have is that reporting hackers here in Steam is very very hard, so watch out for that.

understand, even for someone like myself that hasn’t had the opportunity to play these kinds of games much.
The causal games against other players is also rewarding.  You start seeing some ingenuity and coming up with your own as well. Makes things interesting.
Once you start ranked games I did pretty poorly. Some of it was luck of the draw and of course bad discussions due to lack of experience no doubt. The complexity of the cards and people playing multiple races/color decks makes the things more difficult to understand.
An example of this if you an enemy unit card 2-2 and yours is 2-3 you know your unit will win so you would choose to attack or defend with it. After you executed that action cards come in to play to buff their unit or hurt your unit and you lose your card without you knowing going in.  Course the same could be said for the other team, just know going in your going to need to practice and gain experience.
I played for quite a while, had a good time.  I have like 5k of gold but there seems no where to spend it. To advance from here and get better cards and build decks it appears it’s pay to win on the ranked side of things.
If your looking for something casual and free the causal games this is a good pick.

If they implemented a system to be able to grind the cards and deck, such as being able to use the gold you get from winning then I could see my self playing a great deal more.  I’d do a one-time payment to “buy the game” to gain access to everything everyone else has. If you’re not in to microtransaction and play to win the scope of how far you can go is pretty limited. But you can obtain casual entertainment out of it, for free.  My motto is, if its free, it’s for me!

Basic concept of the game is that you are exploring an abandoned cabin with a RC robot car thing. As the game description says, as you progress you upgrade your robot dude giving you a better camera to keep getting pictures of paranormal things like floating objects, shadows, and orbs. The more pictures of paranormal activities/shadows, the more you progress.
Controls are a little janky, but felt fairly appropriate considering you arent controlling a person. You can use your battery power to get into a first person view, but when the battery runs out, you need to let it recharge. Letting you switch between the RC camera and a 3rd person view was a very nice touch.
In my opinion, they absolutely nailed the atmosphere. I might spook pretty easily, but I know I sat there jumping, flinching, and squeaking like a little girl the entire time I played (and especially at the end).
Graphics are a little dated (as a nod to PS1 era I guess), but the audio is very well done. Would have loved for an audio setting though. Im also very happy the dev didnt 100% rely on cheap jump scares. Also absolutely loved the story. Make sure you actually read the papers you find, as well as the police report in the menu (after you finish the game of course).
Outside of the bug mentioned in the description, I didnt find any major bugs. My mouse didnt lock in the window on windowed mode, but Im not sure if it was intended to be locked in or not. It wasnt game breaking for me though.
The only downside to the game is the length. The game is pretty short. Theres actually an achievement to finish in under 10 minutes I believe. So, expect to spend 30 minutes up to an hour on your first (blind) playthrough. I do wish the dev's had added some more meat to the story and expanded the house. It would have been cool to have more rooms to explore for more story pages.
All of that said, I very highly recommend the game. The story was creepy and the RC robot thing was a pretty cool/interesting concept. I definitely look forward to their next release.

Defunct tries to harness the swooping mechanics of Tiny Wings for an adventure like Journey or Flower, but, although at times it gets up to speed, it doesn't quite stick the landing.
There's a kind of weightlessness to your character—as if the game is set to be a little too fast—that makes it frustrating to navigate any given path.  You might spy an opportunity to race along a wall and jump off onto a bounce pad to reach some high platform likely hiding a collectible, but even if your approach is perfect you will probably miss the pad or hit it and then slam against a rock wall; the angles involved are just too fiddly and unpredictable.
Because moving efficiently so that your speed stays high is enjoyable (and kind of the whole point of the game), it's frustrating when you're failing to do so.  Even though there are no consequences, it's annoying to constantly be trying to do cool things but not have enough control to pull them off.  This doesn't feel like a game that can really be mastered with any amount of practice.
It's also quite a short game and not altogether satisying, lacking as it is in any real danger.  I mentioned the collectibles; these are there both to provide replay value and to create an incentive to explore various criss-crossing paths built through each area, but trying to find them not only keeps you engaged with that fiddly frustration but also outright kills the momentum as you stop racing forward and turn back to search them out.  Secrets just don't seem to be a good fit for this kind of game.  It's more fun to keep a straight course to the end.
Despite its flaws, I do like Defunct, and I resent Steam's binary review system for forcing me to give it a "not recommended" because it's a sweet little game that I think you
pick it up and give a play—but only at a steep discount.  I just wish it were better.  It has a lot of unmet potential, a promising machine badly in need of some tuning.

Is this game the perfect clone of AW that we have all been waiting for no? No.
Is it close enough to tide me over a while whilst Intelligent systems decide to make a new AW? Most defintely.
TINY METAL is trying to take up the mantle of the spiritual successor to AW and it succeeds to a certain degree. Somehow despite me not objectively liking the game, it keeps tugging the heart strings and old nostalgia of the old AW series. TINY METAL is not an exact clone of AW, think of it more as a nicotine patch to my AW addiction.
That being said it does bring a few elements into the mix such as focus fire and flanking, as well as assault and the complete and utter absence of ammunition and fuel. Now whilst focus fire is interesting, all it does is force you to use it ad infinitum - there is no reason not focus fire with two or more units (the only disadvantage is if you forget to activate the focus fire command after you have locked on with your units). The assault command pushes a unit off a tile, at the cost of the unit taking damage first - there is however nearly absolutely no reason to use unless it is an armored unit against a soft target (any bonus that you could deny the enemy like being on a hill is completely negated by the damage received).
The story was the typical anime drivel - war is bad blah blah ...twist... fightey fight bad enemy. Yet I find myself being drawn back in. It feels like meeting an old friend from your childhood.
And that's why I like TINY METAL despite its myriad of flaws and imperfections. It gives me a little of childhood back at a price! The Devs have promised to improve the game and only time will tell if they can live up to those promises.

Defunct:
~~~~~~~

Being a robot can have its problems . . .  well, look at yourself - you look like a unicycle centaur	 with a broken motor! The only good thing about you is this special apparatus which can separate gravity around you. Use it downhill and you will reach extraordinary speed.
Defunct is a racing / adventure game where you control a unicycle robot who was accidently flushed out from a cargo ship. Your goal is to get back to your vessel before it is too late. You will crash land onto a planet inhabited by robots; after all this game takes place post human race. In the story mode, you will move from one level to another. Pick up all the collectible items within the level (they vary from one level to another) and make sure you gather as much speed as you can. It is really all about using your gravitation engine when you are going downhill, but you will be able to use the blue roundish orbit to give you an extra boost. If you are losing momentum (especially uphill) do not worry, you still can use your broken motor to move forward! One thing I really like in the story mode is that in some levels, you will have to power up a pylon to open a door/crate to the next level.
Time trial mode is very hard, to be honest, but fun! You have to reach your destination under a time limit to score a platinum medal. You will be able to freeze the clock each time you pass over the one second icon. In my case it will take some time due to the fact I have a tendency to use the gravitation engine uphill and keep missing the one-second icon. However, I do have an excuse . . .  I only have three fingers on each hand!
I really enjoy the gameplay, the levels are well designed; they are fun and the game runs very well. Graphically, this game looks great. You can unlock skins for your robots, which is a nice. The controls are well balanced which makes this game really enjoyable to play.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Fun gameplay
-	Story and time trial modes
-	Good replay-abilities
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Some levels are too long (vast) for the time trial mode
Defunct is a very good game and it deserves to be on in your game library!

I'm going to give this game a thumbs up, because it's basically the only new game out there that scratches the Advance Wars itch. It does a pretty good job at, too, though it's definitely not perfect and I consider it a rather serious mistake to release the game with no multiplayer (not even a local hot-seat variety) or map editor.
That said: the gameplay is pretty solid, if you ask me. Some people lament the lack of naval, transport units and a bunch of other AW staples. However, I think none of these hamper the game in any way and TM has enough additions and changes in other departments to make up for it. For example, the lack of APCs is not felt as hard as you'd think since most units are significantly slower than their AW counterparts, meaning that infantry is comparatively mobile in this game. The variety of infantry has also increased and infantry is the only type of unit that can heal on cities. Altogether this means that infantry play has become quite interesting and rewarding even without transports.
Without going into many of the other details, I found that the same holds for other gameplay features that the game removed (compared to AW): TINY METAL didn't dispose of these elements without thinking, but with a clear goal in mind. Overall, I think the developers succeeded in creating a compelling strategy game that can exist on its own merrits rather than just being an AW clone.
Now if only they can finish it off with a decent multiplayer (both local and online) and a map editor; that would be fantastic.

Okay, let's get one thing out of the way right now. If you're a completionist, VVVVVV is difficult. It lies pleasantly between hand-holding inanity and the masochistic slog of insanity like Super Meat Boy, but it nevertheless will require many, many deaths in order to get all the collectables.
With that being said, this game *oozes* charm, mostly by pretending to be a Commodore 64 game. You get it all here: The loading screen, the simplistic pixel graphics and gameplay, the baffling choice of obstacles... the only thing missing are rockin' SID chiptunes. The soundtrack is more Mega Man than Dizzy.
Besides that, I've always been a sucker for gravity flip mechanics. You'll have to spend a significant amount of time on some screens in order to pass them, but the checkpoint system is forgiving, and respawn time is near negligible. If you have a little patience, and you're willing to fail, you'll go a long way without getting frustrated. (Be warned, though: Some of the collectables are rough.)
Bottom line: As long as you have a little experience with 8-bit platformers, VVVVVV isn't nearly as bad as modern day hyperdifficult platforms. It's actually *enjoyable*. By the time you're done, you'll come to love these goofy blockheaded astronauts, let alone the game itself.

If you're familiar with the 'Advance Wars' series of games (or the 'Fire Emblem' series, to a lesser extent) then you're likely already comfortable with the concepts presented in TINY METAL. If not, then to put it most simply TINY METAL is a turn based tactics game. Each turn, you will move your units, attack foes, capture buildings or build new units. Your entire turn is taken, and then opponents are given a chance to go.
Units have a Rock/Paper/Scissors like feel to them. Anti-vehicular units do better against armored vehicular foes, while those foes themselves do well against infantry (who in turn, are best against anti-vehicular units). Of course, there are a number of units and so it more resembles a ten way game of rock-paper-scissors but the basic idea is there.
Capturing buildings helps your economy, building new units lets you spend money to replace your broken toys with new ones. The entire battlefield is divided into a grid, with spaces like hills and forests. These terrain features grant defensive bonuses as well as utilitarian benefits such as being able to scout further, often coming with a hinderance such as requiring more movement to occupy those spaces.
The combat is well done, with a few abilities available. First, your units can outright attack foes they are adjacent to. Secondly, they can combine fire with other units to try and overcome very defensive units. Both of these options see your units attack first, deal damage, and then take return fire from their targets. Another common combat option is "Assault", which has you take an attack from your foe first and if any units survive they deal damage and then push their target away. This is useful for stopping foes from capturing buildings or putting them into less defensive terrain.
Quirks indeed, the game seems to be trying to ruin your time if you're using a mouse and keyboard. The game was designed for a controller, and if you don't use one you'll have issues. One thing I disliked, scrolling the screen around to get an overview of the battlefield was cumbersome, as though I was fighting the UI for dominance. It doesn't prevent you from playing but it does feel less than good.
Also, the soundtrack is very servicable but not memorable. Voice acting is... funny. Not in how it's written but how it is delivered. And there is a LOT of talking, which wouldn't normally be an issue for me because no matter how hard I tried, I couldn't care about their story. Neither the narrative nor the characters are particularly interesting, although this does not detract from the game itself.
Also, the lack of typical PC options when fiddling with graphics, sound or controls feels lacking. This is pretty par for the course from Japanese developers, but it's still disappointing.
While I enjoy and recommend the game, it's not a replacement for Advance Wars. If you're looking for something to scratch that itch, it might not make the itch go away but it'll feel good while you get scratched. It has flaws, and as long as you're ok with those flaws then you'll probably end up having a good time.
Oh also, something weird that isn't really here or there: look at the publisher. It's "Sony Music Entertainment". Not "Sony"... it's odd to me that they would use their music label to publish this game while they already have a publisher label to publish under. It might mean Sony didn't want this product to be associated with their name. So weird.

12/30/2017 Looking at this review from the perspective of someone who opens my walltet to gaben willingly and with pleasure on a regular basis but hasn't played games on other platforms in years. Played a lot of Advace Wars when I was a kid, and EVERY SINGLE ARTICLE about Tiny Metal (that I've seen) makes some comparison to the Advance Wars series, including two of the three "buzz" quotes on the steam store page while I'm writing this review. I'm probably going to keep playing this game and will recommend it in the future, but right now it probably isn't worth it at the price for a lot of folks.
Pros
+Is p much Advance Wars clone in visual style and many mechanics (again, only bringing this up because clearly they want that hype - for better or worse).
+Uses Unreal Engine, doesn't kill my gpu
+Relatively intuitive mechanics where it deviates from AW, other reviews called it "rock-paper-scissors strategy".
Cons
+Goofy plot, purple prose, cut scenes are difficult to get through sometimes. They tried, though. They really, really tried.
+Lack of diversity in units and missing some AW mechanics that would make a lot of sense (like fuel, ammo counts), From the few other reviews I've read, it seems other people have also noticed this and the developers may be working on it. So far it seems like there are only 3 air units and then about 10 ground units, several of which feel redundant after a certain point on every campaign level.
+Some other goody mechanics like weak AI, frustrating camera controls, a "coming soon" sign over the multiplayer section, and no hotkeys (that I've found) make it feel like an early release (which, to be fair, it is, sort of).
Again, they seem to be working on a lot of things with this game, and I hope to recommend it in the future.
It just probably isn't worth the price yet for people who aren't particularly interested in this type of game or AW-style games in particular.

I've played several games already, and I must say I'm really impressed.
First of all, what's most appealing to me, is the opportunity to try new games that I would never be able to try in "real" life. And what's more cool, is that many of those games are not yet avaialble in print! And I can try games I'm not sure I want in my real collection to see if I like them first! In a nutshell, I can discover so much more games with Tabletopia, and that's what I like best. And they're all licensed, so I'm not pirating or stealing in any way!
Also, I love that I don't have to wait for a game night to play with my friends. We live rather far away and can only arrange game nights once every two weeks. But with Tabletopia, I can create a room, send a link to my friend and jump right into action! No need to arrange anything, drive anywhere, and so on. I can have a game night literally anytime I feel like it.
Also I like it that I can save the table in case I need to dash and just come back to it later and start from the same place.
What else is great, is that the experience is much more lifelike than one might have thought. With 3D and excellent graphics, you almost feel like playing a real game. Much more so than on BGA, for example.
Sure, the controls need time getting used to. And that's my main complaint. At first it is rather hard and takes a lot of time. My advice will be to learn the hot keys, it gets considerably easier with them. Sure, it's still no replacement for moving the pieces with your own hands, but, let's be frank, with games like Scythe or Anachrony, I might never get the chance to put my hands on those games, in the first place.
All in all, I do recommend to give Tabletopia a try!

Unfocused, unbalanced, but enjoyable nonetheless. Part 2!
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 improves on some issues while ignoring others. You play the role of a security guard again and everything else is pretty much the same. The main difference is that there is a story now, more or less, focused around child abduction/murder. I would praise this choice of storytelling for being bold and daring except the narrative is a bit...muddled. Try to play the game blind and you'll see what I mean. The visuals get an upgrade with the biggest noticable, appreciated change is the way the camera smoothly pans from side to side. The choppy way it clunked along in the first game was annoying and ugly. Another change, that is more than welcome, are the light switch buttons; you no longer have to double-click to turn them on and off. You merely have to click it once and it turns off automatically when you move the cursor away. The annoying power save nonsense from the first game is removed in favor of a flashlight that can run out of power, causing a game over as the flashlight is used to keep the mascots at bay. Although it is the same, in theory, I found the power management feature of the flashlight to be more manageable and less stressful. Don't think that the game is easier, though, because you couldn't be further from the truth. The mascot count jumps up to fourteen, there are three areas that you must check for your would-be killers, and you must click to wind a music box in order to keep one of them from insta-killing you. There is alot to absorb and do in this game and time management is more important than ever if you expect to 100% this game. Upon beating night six you get a series of challenges for night seven that grants small prizes upon completing each individual challenge. While the prizes are nice for bragging rights; unlocking a legitimate cohesive explaination would've been better.
Everything is random, again, and just like in the first game you may find yourself being startled again by the jumpscares because you think you're playing correctly only for the game to decide otherwise. One of the worst features added to the game is the mask. The mask is used to scare off the mascots if they are staring at you from the vents. The most painful part of the game is trying to close the camera and then trying to quickly put on the mask which can be very unresponsive. In order for me to finish the game I had to condition myself to make very wide circles with my mouse so that I could flip the camera and put on the mask. It's annoying and it killed my wrists making for a very unenjoyable experience. Since the game uses the control button for the flashlight I'm a little perplexed as to why another button could not have been mapped for the mask for a much smoother experience. Upon completion I, again, didn't feel as though skill brought about victory but a very lucky level set up. At least this was part of the extra content and not the main game. Another thing that needs to be mentioned is the fact that this shouldn't be classified as new but more like...more. Perhaps things are a little different in the indy scene but in mainstream gaming this feels more like DLC than an actual sequel. I suppose my expectations are a little different.
I recommend the game but only if its $4. Improvements to gameplay, adding a flaccid story, and a small handful of extra content barely qualifies as a sequel, in my personal opinion. However, if you're a fan of the content, then buy all means make Five Nights at Freddy's: The Lost Levels a part of your collection.

Nirvana Pilot Yume is a combination of a visual novel and a classic DOS game, Skyroads (Which I've never played or heard of). This game was one of the interesting games that I've ever reviewed and it was a pretty good experience overall. Though, I've experienced some times that I've become frustrated to this somewhat addicting game that I had to stop playing. This is a rare gem in the Steam library as a game that can be seen in many perspectives for different players.
There's two main gameplay mechanics that the game is mainly focusing on, the visual novel and the 'skyroads' sections. You play as Aldaine, a former G.U.R.U (Great Ultrathought Race of the Universe; woah that's a mouthfull!) racer who retired after losing his partner, Celeste. You are approached by a young woman named Yume who wants to compete in the G.U.R.U. You are requested by her to help train and compete for the G.U.R.U. There are multiple sections in the story that you'll need to make choices on that'll affect your relationship, reputation and Nirvana sync, which gives you the amount of chances to complete a race.
The characters are all attractive (Except for one and maybe others since I only got the bad ending) and they have their own uniqueness to them that would make you love, hate or not so sure about. The girls in this visual novel, are very attractive and likeable. Overall, they're pretty damn awesome and even sexy as!
The 'Skyroads' sections are the most interesting part. There will be sections that make you frustrate out loud in situations in where your jump was too short or restarting from all over again. There's an arcade mode where you can simply race without the story and give you a chance to practice the 'skyroads', before or after you do story mode. And for that, it kind of gives me a few different arguments against myself as somebody reviewing a game for someone who might be hesitant about giving this game a shot. For fans of Skyroads, this might be a very good tribute to the original DOS games but to other newer generation gamers like myself, will most likely be frustrated for the first few minutes or even hours where it discourages us from playing. The races, can impact the story of the visual novel. Depending on how you do, you could either get a decent or not so decent ending. And for me, I've experienced the (probably the most baddest; not bad in terms of story) bad ending (I think) three times now. I'm not saying that the developers should make a difficulty setting, in fact if they did implement it (which right now, there isn't) or adjust the game to be more approchable, it would probably ruin about the nostalgia for Skyroads players. Overall, the skyroads section might be a frustrating experience to you especially to some of the other stages.
Also, I'm not too sure if it was just my laptop specs but I've experienced some freezes which sometimes impacted my gaming experience(also experienced this with other games as well). I also occasionally experienced a screen of white flickering (from the retry screen; without the text) while I was playing which really turned me off. I also couldn't get the game to pause by pressing P. (My P key works btw)
Instead, I was forced to click the exit button on the top right of the screen. I reinstalled Windows 10, and the freeze issue got somewhat better, but the other issues still remained. So yeah, don't let my isssues discourage you. Everyone has different specs for their PCs.
The game runs on the unity engine, a pretty well known free game engine for developers. The graphics look very good especially for the skyroad sections. The colours look vibrant and look very appealing for an indie game. Though there is a disclaimer that I definetely need to talk about for players:
As for the visuals for the visual novel, they look pretty good. Though, I sometimes I didn't feel like the visuals looked like an 80's Sci-fi anime (e.g Ghost in the Shell; no I haven't seen it, sry :{ ), it felt more western to me. And that's not a bad thing, it's just my own personal opinion that I first thought to myself. Overall the visuals look pretty awesome and faithful to classic anime but the skyroad sections can make the game unplayable for epileptic players.
The music sounds pretty awesome and very fitting for the game. I haven't heard who Retröxx is, but I'm sure that they've done pretty good tracks before. Other than that, there isn't much I can say for the visual novel music. I'm not too sure if it's just me but I just ignore the music as I'm reading this. This usually doesn't happen with other visual novels but this one... eh... the music is definetely not horrible to say the least. There are moments where there is a dramatic sound effect when something dramatic happens which is a really nice touch. Overall, really awesome music.
Nirvana Pilot Yume is a really interesting game. There'll be moments where you'll say, "Oh, the visuals and music look great as well as everything else," to things like, "C'MON! WHY!!" It's a rollercoaster of emotions when you play the game, but for me as I've experienced the game, I've found it to be (As I said before) one of the most interesting games that I've ever played as a reviewer. Is this up your alley? Well, it depends on your decision really. Don't like being frustrated in games or in visual novels to be exact? Well, I wouldn't reccommend it, but this isn't a bad game. Just a frustrating one. A frustrating one that makes up for its fun and replayability.

Flashpoint Campaigns: Red Storm is a somewhat unconventional but very welcome gem of a hex&counter wargame.
The twist it has going for it over so many wargames of this type is a very tight focus on what you command, limited capability to command (organization and electronic warfare interference), and most interestingly the variable turn length, which alters as the game progresses due to the influence of various factors, lose a few commander units and watch it rocket right up. Commands are issued at the start of each turns, and then the results play out themselves. Units also do not instantly react to your inputs either, and take time to begin doing what you order them to, and may be delayed not by just enemy action lowering their readiness levels but by roads getting clogged with traffic if you try and push too many units at once down a certain path or their commander's being too distant and the units worn down from extended battling.
The focus on regiment level command is something that could not really be replicated on tabletop in the same way, as it’s a very hands-off approach. Units, once set on their path, will use their own abilities to locate and attack enemies. What helps this is that much of the numbers are hidden (though they are viewable if you wish to check things) and so you’re not getting a face-full of dice rolls thrown up every time something happens, but rather audio cues, arrows indicating exchanges of fire, and explosions for artillery and counting off casualties, which all lends greatly to the atmosphere and sense that you are attempting to control the chaos of a battle in your favour.
Speaking of which, the atmosphere for the game is a kind of intense tension. With fog of war in place as intended (there’s an option to remove it as well as the limited orders per turn) contact with enemies is often fleeting unless a real slugging match is taking place or you've managed to secure good positioning for recon elements; an essential part of not getting surprised by a full companies of tanks and infantry barreling down a road towards you. The tension is a constant as you sit and watch a turn play out, making mental notes of enemy positions to direct artillery to and hoping your plan was good enough, or that you can adapt it in time to exploit an opening or counter a move.
When it comes to the armies themselves you do get the best results by playing them to their general doctrine. Brits cannot (most of the time) be used in fast armoured counter attacks like the West Germans, who in turn cannot normally successfully emulate the Soviets and send massive stabbing attacks of armour and mechanized infantry, shrugging casualties to envelop and breach their target objective’s defences. Whilst many scenarios as they come feature relatively high quality Guards units of Soviets with a myriad of BMP-2s and T-80BVs in their arsenals, a huge mass of equipment sporadically appears and can be used in creating your own scenarios.
Overall the game sticks well to it's intended style without getting confused or overwhelming you with mechanics, and produces some great battles and challenging campaigns.

Long story short, this game is fantastic. Elaborating a bit further, this is as described, a plane building game. You have a range of parts to choose from in order to construct an aircraft. These parts range from undercarriages, to jet engines, to props, to guns, to bombs, to fuselage types, to different wing types. The list is pretty much endless. And the game supports XML modding too, so the list is even more endless.
Probably worth pointing out that there's a right and wrong way to build planes in this game. As a rule of thumb, keep the centre of mass in front of the centre of lift. That will help you make something that is partly flyable.
Obviously, there's a dedicated website for all the uploads, which also has a forum section, which is useful for mod requests, logging your progress, starting discussions and complaining about how you're going to quit because nobody upvotes your planes... I imagine a lot of the negative reviews here stem from the butt hurt from that last point.
Although, if you're hell bent on getting upvotes, you have to be an active member of the community and make unique concepts or good replicas... of just your own thing. I've noticed a few people making some really nice looking battleships ... yeah, you read that right, this is a pretty versatile game. People can make anything from cars, to tanks, to ships, to flying houses. Obviously, the primary aspect of this game is the planes though.
The Dev team is pretty damn dedicated too, and seem to work their backsides off in order to provide new content, keep the website running, and probably a lot of other stuff that has flown over my head. A relatively new feature from the Dev's being the tournaments, in which users compete to make the best plane for its class. Currently there are three classes: blade, unlimited and mod class. Each has there own set of rules. Also, if your wanting to hoard points, I suggest entering these too. Oh, and the live twitch stream of the tournament gets put on youtube.
Given the clear amount of shear effort put into this game, one has to wonder why people would not recommend it.

My only complaint so far is the amount of awkward rule bending it takes with the larger card text allowance, similar to MTG. There are a lot of keywords and psuedo keywords going on, with some cards feeling overloaded for the sake of being complex, when they end up, so far, complicated and goofy. The designers seem to want to add strategic depth with an extreme amount of possible interactivity and deckbuilding options (with a lot of success, I must say), but it can be overwhelming. Not a game breaker but feels like something the card design team could improve on. I'm not certain so many cards need 4 or 5 different keywords and a paragraph of special text. But definitely not a deal breaker. The legendary cards also seem to have quite a bit of power creep but it doesn't hinder too much on the solo play, which allows you to grow your collection anyways.

I love the concept for this game - visual novel + SkyRoads (which was an amazing DOS game where you piloted a little space car hopping along interstellar highways) is such a good, fresh idea. Nirvana Pilot Yume also throws in a great synthwave soundtrack as well as an artistic style that reminds me of 80s anime and vaporwave music videos. The visual novel aspect of the game is really well written, and the dialogue is enjoyable and the sex scenes natural and non-cringy.
The racing sections are a little rough at the moment - I think my biggest problem is that the tracks are REALLY hard, or at least the difficult bumps up dramatically after the first track, which is dirt easy. It's quite hard to see what exactly is coming your way, because the vantage point is directly at the horizon whereas in SkyRoads, you had somewhat more of an overhead view, and thus more time to react and move your ship around obstacles. In Nirvana Pilot Yume, I feel like there's almost no time to react at all because stuff is coming at you so fast, and the collision detection is VERY sensitive. The brake option also doesn't seem to do much at the moment but pull the camera in closer, and currently when I try slowing down in all tracks after the first one, the speed meter at the top doesn't change. (Not sure if this is a bug or not.)
The difficulty of the tracks might turn some people off, since I believe it is mandatory to pass a certain number of them to progress to the true ending... I myself have gotten the "bad" ending twice because some of these races I just haven't been able to beat. =( You have to restart from the beginning when that happens, which isn't terrible since the game's not too long, but if some kind of Save File option could be patched in at a future date, that would be excellent.
Overall, if you like old anime and don't mind hard games then this is worth checking out simply for the ＡＥＳＴＨＥＴＩＣ, as the kids put it these days. I'll keep practicing in Arcade Mode and hopefully get a better ending for Yume in due time...

This is a serious wargame. None of that fake crap that people like to call wargames but are really wussy arcade RTS chump simulators. Flashpoint Campaigns has hexes and counters and orders and turns. All of the classic components of something designed by and for true grognards.
It is my first PC "hardcore" wargame, and after nearly a dozen hours, it's a pretty neat game. Most wargames and PC strategy games still focus around manouvre and ordering each of your units with razor-like accuracy, with each tank and squad and platoon responded to and executing your will without delay and without question. Flashpoint Campaigns isn't like that. It focuses on the hair-pulling, hypertension-inducing hell that is being helpless while you watch your men, each devoted to his nation and its cause (even if its cause is stupid) really trying their best to carry out your moronic plans only to be cut down at once by enemy fire. Confusion and lack of cohesian are the killers on this battlefield. Each turn you give orders and then click the button to play the turn out, where your guys, in accelerated time, spend the next 15 minutes to an hour on their own, trying their best to get things done. Only when the turn is up and the alotted time has passed are you allowed to give new orders and react to the situation. And the more chaotic things get and the more torn up and splintered your force gets, the longer the turn takes to playout before you can react with orders, meaning that you can end up giving orders every 40 minutes whil your opponent is able to give orders ever 15, which leads to very interesting, very asymmetrical and very unique gameplay. And if you play with the optional rule limiting the number of orders you can give per turn--something I recommend for increased realism and increased stress--things can only get more jacked up if you don't have a solid plan and the flexibility to ammend that plan when needed.
There is a lot of Cold War tech to play with, and battles move extremely fast and are extremely bloody once contact is made. The graphics are clear and attractive and have a pretty striped-down, utilitarian feel to them, which works but if someone needs to actually _see_ a tank model to have a good time playing war, you might want to look elsewhere.
The AI seems smart as hell, and you can go toe-to-toe with it across numerous individual scenarios and four separate campaigns where you keep your forces between battles. I haven't actually tried the campaigns yet, but I am excited at the prospect. I just want to hold off until I can go through a battle without getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me first.

This game models my experiences serving in Germany in the 80’s better than any other war game I have played. It captures the flavour of the cold war gone hot and just as important the command issues.  For example as in real life, after giving  your orders,  your subordinate units do not always do or go where you want them to depending on many factors for example communications or lack of, morale and readiness to name a few.  There is a lot under the hood.
The AI will punish mistakes’ in the most brutal fashion, and many times it will do the unexpected. You can play the same scenario over again and the AI will often play it different from your last play through. Most importantly is the support that On Target Simulations has given the game. They have listened to what the community has asked for and have continually improved what was already a great game.
The game is not for micromanagement. You do not tell units let alone individual tanks what targets to engage. You have to plan, out think your opponent and position your units where they can be successful. You have to use different tactics depending if you are playing the NATO or Soviet side. That being said you can fight small battles with just a few troops on the map to large battles with up to Brigades or a Division in size.
The community forums are very good and provide great support for new players learning the game.

This game neatly fills a gap in the war gaming genre with combat set in the cold war era 1979-1989, featuring 3 main NATO countries vs Western Group Soviet forces (other forces due for release in the next expansion). The game itself is a grand tactical/operational level war game where you take control of up to NATO brigade or Soviet Division featuring fixed wing air-support, helicopters, artillery with several forms of fire missions including counter battery fire missions, electronic warfare, tactical nukes and chemical weapons, in either H2H play (via PBEM or via the matrix H2H server) or solo play.
In solo play mode you will find the AI to be highly aggressive seeking out your weak spots and punishing any errors by exploiting gaps in your planning, if the AI detects a highly defended position it will attempt to find another route to attack down resulting in a near endless replay ability.
Game play is set around a unique WEGO type of system where each side issues orders during a command phase, at which point the system will play out the action until the next command phase of either player. The command phase timings are different for each side based on several factors such as EW or suppression/destruction of C3i elements, allowing your opponent to get inside your command cycles can be deadly, likewise getting inside your enemies command cycle allows you to take the initiative often resulting in a deadly encounter.
The game engine/equipment tables take into account numerous factors with armor/penetration data for each nation, explosive reactive armor (ERA), fire control systems native to each tank, cluster munitions for both aircraft and artillery, all allowing for a viable demonstration of each sides tactics resulting in an interesting exploration of ‘the war that never happened’.
Modding:
The game devs have taken an open approach to player’s modding, allowing OOB/TOE to be modded for each nation and the floor is open to modding nations not yet represented ingame. Maps are fairly easy to produce as are images for different types of equipment fielded during the games time period. The game devs have also produced 3 guides (with a 4th due soon) explaining in clear how to mod the various aspects of the game.
Dev Support:
I’ve been playing this game for nearly a year and throughout that time the game dev’s have shown  unending patience and willingness to listen to the player base for not just bug reporting (thankfully game breaking bugs are few and far between) but suggestions for new features as well as tweaking existing features. They have showed no sign of slowing down their level of outstanding support.

I have become completely addicted to this game.
What I like about it is that it's your typical city simulator but with mechanics that were totally designed by a city sim player. The ability to plan basically your entire town and queue it until you have the resources available is incredibly helpful, especially when you hit that critical growth stage.
The UI is clean and easy to navigate and the learning curve is next to none. Even a player new to city simming will be able to pick it up within 1 or 2 towns after the tutorials. The strategy to make a successful town, however, comes with a few more hours of play.
I also like how it isn't too difficult on the medium level, but it offers enough challenge that I can play a good game without being too stressed out that I can't make it work. It's a great introduction to start with.
The soundtrack is also amazing. Some songs are cheerful and relaxing, while others put you into a more serious mood. However, more variety might be nice, such as music that only appears in certain seasons, or for a rare occasion after a certain event (a la AoE).
One of my peeves, however, is the iffy AI. The citizens need to be really kept on task or else they will start floundering despite having everything they need. I also find that it is nearly impossible to keep up with stone and iron production, but that may just be my own shortcoming as I continue to figure out strategies.
UPDATE: This is definitely just poor balancing. I have played with every combination and the only way to keep a moderate production going with mines and quarries is either to have too many citizens working in them early on (10+ usually helps, but then your food production slumps), or use mods, which precludes your chances to earn achievements.
And, finally, I would love some more map types. Valleys and Mountains are nice, but more variations like swamp, islands, plains etc. would certainly help make each game more different than just having one more river, or one less lake or hill where you spawn.
Definitely try this game! I look forward to more updates (hopefully with balance fixes)!

By my playtime it's obvious that I like this game and I like it a lot, although it seems that Dark Souls II is somewhat frowned upon by people who liked the first or maybe the third one better. I admit that it's a game that you have to get used to, because some very important core mechanics were changed. One of the biggest things is the roll mechanic, in Dark Souls 1 you had different weight catagories with <25%, <50%, and <75% that determined how much use you get out of your invicibility frames while you have to actively increase your agility to increase the numbers. You start pretty low with 80 and by leveling up adaptability and/or attunement you can increase it to I think a maximum of 120, although 110 is considered the softcap and should be a pretty comfortable number.
Another thing that I noticed it that it seems like you need a little longer to raise your shield which isn't such a big deal in most situations, but it can become very important when you're not sure if you can squeeze in another attack, especially with a slow strength weapon, so keep that in mind.
Compared to the regular Dark Souls 2 it seems like Scholar of the first Sin replaced a few enemies here and there and overall increased the number, it's not a rare occasion that you have to face around 3-5 enemies at the same time, but if you play in a defensive way with a shield equipped you should be fine for most occasions. There are instances where the game punishes you this way and you'll pretty much die for sure, but you'll learn from your mistake and do better next time. Personally I don't think it's the best way to make things more challenging by just placing more enemies in certain spots, but it's not the worst thing either.
Keep your weapons as good as possible, carry a few different types like a thrust and a slash weapon, maybe some elemental weapons like lightning and fire and you should be good to go.
Two hints for everyone who's new to the game or wants to achieve 100%: Don't join the Covenant of Champions right away just because you can, it make things even more challenging and can be frustrating for a few people who are not used to the game and its mechanics. Also join the Sunbros asap and farm medals while you're still in a good range for co-op, it's absolutely no fun to farm enemies for these medals.

If you are buying this expecting that Tiny Metal is a complete clone off Advance Wars, then don't get your hopes up too much. Some Pros and Cons of the following game:
Pros:
- Graphic wise, it's definitely more updated than Advance Wars.
- Full Voice characters and storyline. Including changing of Languages.
- Still as addictive as Advance Wars.
- Skirmish Mode
- New lock on mode to allow multiple units to target a unit together.
- You can level up units as they destroy more enemies
- There's multipler mode but is not available yet. Hopefully it will turn out great.
- Mobile Radars allow players to see targets in the fog of war.
Cons:
- Compared with Advance Wars, the number of units are far too little. In the end you would just keep building Heavy Metals and Strykers to attack the enemy.
- The Stryker (Mobile Missile Launcher) is far too Overpowered. Able to strike land units at a distance as well as Air units. Double as artillery and Air defence. A couple of these with some tanks would make an area heavily defended.
- The fortress is useless against a group of Strykers. Not to mention the cost of these.
- There are no naval units or naval battles.
- There's no such thing as refuel or stocking up on ammo. Basically you can keep fighting without getting more supplies.
- No infantry transport. Makes it really slow in capturing buildings as you have to walk a long distance.
- There's no such thing as a powering up of Field Commander's special abilities to use in battle.
- No such thing as combining of units if there are low on health.
I liked it. It's got a story to tell, and it tells it well. Gameplay's mostly nonexistent, but that's not really an issue in this case. Good solid purchase.

Dark Souls 2, the only Dark Souls not directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, but rather From Software´s B Team.
Right from the start, we see some small details that hints us the big difference between this and the previous Dark Souls. Comparing both, this one is way easier, not having any boss that made me almost rip my hair off like Ornstein and Smough did, except maybe Sir Alonne when I tried getting his unique death animation for the first time. And overall, it´s barely above average in terms of difficulty from your standard everyday RPG.
Another bad thing it has is a mechanic called Soul Memory, which determines your multiplayer matchmaking depending on how many souls you have acquired throught your journey. In theory, this sounds decent, but it is basically a must for any player that wants to do something multiplayer related to create another character so he isnt matched with people 100 levels above him, because a new player will die multiple times and wont exactly know what to invest in at all times.
But, besides a relatively mediocre singleplayer and a bad matchmaking mechanic which can be solved by wearing the Agape Ring (which is a must have for anyone who wants to actively PvP or co-op), this game is the most enjoyable out of the three, having a way more balanced and less glitchy PvP, more stable servers than the first game, an overall better PC port, etc.
Anyone who wants to start with Dark Souls, I would highly recommend this one if they want and easier time with the other 2 (and Bloddborne and Demon´s Souls if they own consoles).
NOTE: Another problem, which is more of a problem that I have is that reporting hackers here in Steam is very very hard, so watch out for that.

TINY METAL is a fun but rushed little game that should have released in Early Access first. If you are looking for something to scratch your Advanced Wars itch, you won't quite find it here, but there's nothing else that's better and it could be much worse. I rated it positively because while it is flawed, it is still a quality game and I wish to support our best bet at getting an enjoyable successor to Advanced Wars.
+ Graphics, artwork, and animations are quality.
+ Good voice acting in English and Japanese.
+ Simple but cute story and cast.
+ Decent amount of unit and terrain types.
+ Focus Fire (ordering multiple units to attack simultaneously).
+ Assault (push enemy units out of a tile at the expense of letting them attack first).
+ Flanking and rear attack bonuses.
+ Hero Units.
+ EX missions.
+ Lots of skirmishes, some introducing 3-4 player matches with AI.
+ I'm still going through it, but New Game+ is very appreciated and improves the experience.
+ Getting frequent updates so far, and should get more down the road.
- The AI can be bad. It doesn't prioritize capturing buildings, hunts after weaker units obsessively (and will even travel the whole map to get to them sometimes), "kamikazes" units even when there is no chance of doing any significant damage (e.g. infantry against a max hp metal, why?), prioritizes defending factories over headquarters, and doesn't utilize Focus Fire or Hero Units.
- Can't combine injured units for healing.
- No multiplayer yet (but there's a menu option for it, at least).
- No naval or transport units.
- No biome variety, even across different islands.
- No additional strategic elements like ammunition or commanders with abilities.
// I would have liked Hero Units to be a more advanced feature and to have more unique models.
// I would have liked the experience / ranking system to be more advanced, for example, surviving units with their ranks carried over in later missions.
// I expected to see the White Fang Army as AI-controlled blue units on at least some of the campaign maps and was disappointed to never see them.
// AI-controlled civilian or militia units, or campaign missions with a third army in general, would have been nice.
// Multiple AI armies don't work together in skirmishes when there is an army obviously in the lead. While the AI doesn't have to tag team others all the time, it doesn't make much sense for two AI on their last limb to continue killing one another while I steamroll over them both the next turn.
// I think that Snipers shouldn't be able fire over hills. Also, in the campaign, I never found them to be cost effective (they are useful in the skirmishes though).
// Ground units cannot pass under air units, meaning you can use air units to block ground units. While you seem to benefit from that in NG+ it would make more sense if you could at least pass ground units over the Fighters.

I decided that I would do an In depth review of Verdun.
POSITIVE:
It looks fantastic. One of the cheapest games that can test a GPU. It's also very well optimized. Now I should note my PC specs.
Graphics: MSI GeForce GTX 1050 2gb
RAM: G.SKULL Ripjaws 8gb 1600
CPU: AMD FX-4130 Quad Core
Now that I have my PC specs out of the way, lets continue with the review.
The sound design is wonderful. It sounds great, even on cheap speakers. I am the person that pays attention to sound quality in video games. This game sounds terrific.
The historical accuracy is pretty well done. It still had to manipulate some things. However, they manipulate things so it is a more enjoyable experience. Even then, it doesn't stray too far away from what it was like.
Finally, the levels are well designed. I love it when developers actually take their time and go to the real exhibits to see what the real areas looked like.
NEGATIVE:
The borders can get a little irritating. I feel the trenches are a little too small. I think they should be more vast, and have more areas to shoot enemies. When I go up, the enemy trench is either too low, or too far away for me to aim at anything.
I said the graphics look great, but unless you like that Borderlands style of cell-shaded art, then play the game on medium.
The auto-assigned key combinations are wierd for me. Now note that this is my review, so you are only hearing my opinion, and I honestly love the Garry's Mod control layout. Thank goodness in this game you can change each key. You would be suprised to see how many games I have played that don't include that.
CONCLUSION:
I love this game, and cannot recommend this game enough. It isn't perfect, but it is really close to it. Not to mention it's cheaper than Battlefield 1.
