Alrighty then, everyone who reads this bare with me because this is my first review. I have beaten the game and completed all secret missions. Thus I feel as though it is my duty to paint a fair picture of the game and the state it is currently in.
This game is coming from a SMALLER company, hence the reason there is NO MULTIPLAYER, various bugs, and other features not in game YET. This is the reason some if not many players complain about as reasons to NOT RECOMMEND.

However after speaking with the devs, there is a lot still coming to the game. People are buying a game expecting more now, when more is coming later.
IF you are the player who wants more now such as character spefic traits/units, multiplayer, and other features. I suggest be PATIENT good things take time, you can BUY it LATER.
IF you are the player who has researched the game, do not mind waiting for extended features, and LIKE turn-based STRATEGY games. I suggest you BUY IT NOW you will not regret it.
Now back to GAMEPLAY the FIRST run through is relatively EASY and the secret missions are easy. However to unlock some HEROs you have to do some SECRET missons.
Overall the game is Fantastic I believe the devs make the first play through relativaly easy just incase beginners are playing the game, they do not want to overwhelm them.
If you want a challegne you have to beat the game first and then it unlocks the NEW GAME + mode for those who WANT more of a challenge.
Futhermore if you are still reading this review it is worth pointing out many players compare Tiny Metal (TM) the "spirtual successor" to Advanced Wars or (AW). Without realizing that TM has bigger things planned than (AW).
AW did not have Focus Fire which is when 2 or units can lock onto a target to do increased damage with increase crit chance, and did not provide a directional combat system.
All of that being said IF you know what kind of player you are and want to support the "spirtual successor" of Advanced Wars (AW).
By the small company who only wish to improve upon the genre and make this game the best that it can be. Then by all means BUY THIS GAME because it appears that alot of DLCs will COME INCLUDED with the copy you purchased.

This game is advertised as local co-op. The term "local co-op" means two things:
- The game can be played locally by more than one person (meaning on the same machine)
- The game is co-op, which means "cooperative"
It's competitive. A throwaway creative mode is not a co-op experience.
I will withdraw my negative review if
1) The game ever gains local co-op as a feature, or
2) The game page stops (incorrectly) advertising the game as local co-op.
I'm not interested in other factors, as the only reason I'd buy this game is for a couch co-op feature. In fact, I found the game by searching for the local co-op tag, which is included by the decision of the developers.
Comments on my review seem to have vanished (maybe they'll come back?) but they mainly object by the following (my rebuttals are included)
1. The video or text says the game is competitive
Rebuttal: Competitive modes aren't exclusive with co-op modes in *many* games. The fact that the video didn't include co-op seemed to be an advertising decision.
2. The game "is" co-op because multiple people can play.
Rebuttal: Clearly there's some problem understanding the word "co-op" which is short for "cooperative". Maybe cooperative play is a foreign idea to many of you, but I assure you it is NOT equivalent to the tag "local multiplayer" which was available to the developers and should have been used instead of co-op.
3. The game is co-op because there's a level builder and "free play."
Rebuttal: While the free play mode does exist, and could be said to be cooperative, it's just disingenuous to call the game "local co-op" based on this feature. The "real" game is not free play, and creating levels isn't playing at all. This is like calling Mario Maker cooperative because you can collaborate on level design.
Cooperative *play* is what's important here. Not "some cooperative element, however small."
What I can't figure out is why you're so adamant. The game isn't "a cooperative game". Anyone can see that. I'm frankly confused with the amount of argument I'm receiving for something so plainly true.
But go ahead and keep downvoting my review just because it's negative and points out that the game advertises inaccurate information.

Back when the trailer was announced for The Crew, I was actually highly anticipated. The huge map, the car spec system, and being set in an alive world with players playing around (basically MMO racing) is like a dream come true for me. I never got into playing the beta, so I have to wait until the game is released. But at that point, I haven't bought the game yet. When the reviews first rolled out, it turns out it wasn't that great, so I decided to hold out until the price drop.
Apparently they released a demo, and I downloaded the demo and played it for 2 hours (the whole duration of the demo) to get the feel of the game. Needless to say, the resolution was to
.
I find the driving to be extremely relaxing. Driving to an undiscovered area isn't a complete chore - in fact, in some places, even fun. The spec system is genius, allowing you to have that same car without buying another one (because the prices for it are ludicrous). And, of course, you have the WHOLE US to drive in WITH ALMOST NO RESTRICTION. The collectables are also fun to collect. The game also provides a lot of content (besides the map).
Providing a demo is also commendable - not a lot of AAA pubs provide a demo nowadays.
But, of course, the game isn't perfect. In fact, it's more flawed than I thought it would be. The physics are probably the main weakness of the game. Cars drive fine at the intended purpose, but when you don't use it as intended, it starts to bounce around literally everywhere. The collision physics is also bad, because as you bump a car, instead of colliding as usual, the car sometimes slides off it and you lose control. Not to mention, you can just drift into a wide corner, ignoring the fact that you'll smash a few fences and go through nasty bumps without losing a single speed. Story is pretty clichéd  and predictable. Game can be a bit grindy. AI racers are inconsistent (most of my encounters are easy though).
Not to mention, it's Ubisoft, so expect MICROTRANSACTIONS.
About Wild Run, I think I made a bad decision for buying it. It's not a bad add-on, but it's not worth buying. It allows you to buy a few bikes, an access to the monthly Summit event, and Extreme specs. The Extreme specs are, needless to say, lazily done as they only use customizations from Perf and Dirt specs. Drag spec physics is also too random, which pisses me off as it won't allow me to get the best time at Drag events. Monster physics are also messed up, and is easily exploitable. Drift is actually pretty fine. Bikes are pretty weird to control - it's not as agile as described.
I am, myself, a racing fan since I got my first PS1 back when I was 7 years old, so if you're like me you'll probably find The Crew to be favorable. However, if you only moderately like racing games and would expect a game like the earlier NFS or something like Project CARS, you won't get it here. After the price drop, it is worth it, but I recommend you try out the demo provided by the developers.

I've never been able to put my heart into a TCG, before. The appeal of the genre was kind of lost on me. Eternal, with its slick UI, interesting use of the digital medium, and relative generosity towards players without a lot of money to spend (like myself) have all turned me around and made me a fan.
First, let's talk about the UI. Everything is incredibly smooth and fast, and matches can go by pleasantly fast even at lower levels like mine where we're prone to not immediately recognizing the right moves, or needing to read the effects of a card that was just played. In fact, we're probably the level most helped by this UI; the card's full text shows up quickly when moused over, and easily understandable explanations of all the keywords on any given card pop up alongside it. Now granted, there can be confusion about how keywords interact with each other; for example, it'd be easy to not realize that Deadly and Quickdraw makes a unit auto-destroy any blockers, or that Deadly and Overwhelm means the blocking player will take nearly the full damage of the card even with a blocker. But this feels like part of the learning curve rather than an issue with the UI. In short, the UI is fast, informative, and visually satisfying, with simple visual effects that add a sense of drama to the decisions playing out on the board.
Next, I want to talk about the use of the digital medium. Paper TCGs are limited in what they can do by a lot of factors: mainly that anything that would cause a card to not be or do exactly what it says on the card itself requires it to be and remain visible to both players, and that the more malleable you make that card, the harder it is for players to keep track of. Eternal's digital format, rather than trying to replicate those limitations, uses the benefits of its medium to full effect. Cards can have their stats and effects altered in your hand or even in your deck. Cards can be pulled from the deck without any need to reshuffle the deck, since no one saw the card order in the process. There's a really cool mechanic called Revenge that makes a destroyed card return to the top ten cards of your deck, and auto-play for free when it's drawn again. Games like Hearthstone use the digital medium to have absurd levels of variance, creating cards like Unstable Portal. Eternal has some variance with cards like Siraf, but its main focus in its utilization of the medium is a permanence of card effects that could never be achieved in real life, and it's extremely fun.
Lastly, this is one of the two most generous card games I've ever played in my life, the other being Shadowverse. It's hard to say which is more generous, but both games find ways to shower the players in cards and packs at no monetary cost. It's worth keeping an eye on if they maintain that level of generosity (I think they'll need more cosmetics like card sleeves to sustain this, but I have no way of knowing their financials), but at the moment it's extremely generous, and thus easy to get into even if you can't afford to drop money on the game. I would suggest dropping
a tiny bit of money, though; at the moment, doing so will earn you three free booster packs of the current set, along with three free booster packs of every major set going forward, which is an extremely good deal for as low as $5 on a free to play game. (Granted, they have been
to release new major sets; there are only two in the game, currently.)
As a final note, I'd also like to give mention to just how many modes there are. There's a story Campaign, which is frankly boring to play through, and slow to get interesting with its lore - but has some paid expansions that offer interesting gimmick fights, ala Hearthstone's campaign expansions. There's a Puzzle mode, which tests your understanding of how keywords interact. There's a Gauntlet of AI opponents, ending in a gimmick boss fight. There's Forge, which works like Hearthstone's Arena mode except against bots, and with the notable exception that you keep all the cards you pick. On that note, there's also a Draft mode, which works exactly like Draft would work in real life (except that the people you're playing are not the people you're drafting with), and also lets you keep all the cards you select. Neither mode is priced unfairly, and you get more value out of them than simply buying packs almost every time. Plus Draft gets a ranking board, making it feel like just as legitimate a game mode as constructed Ranked. On that note, there's both Casual and Ranked matchmaking, both offering comparable enough rewards for winning. And finally, there's occasionally Events, which functions like a combination of Hearthstone's Tavern Brawls, and the "play until 7 wins or 3 losses" format used in Draft and Forge, with its own leaderboard separate from Ranked and Draft. All in all, the variety of modes, and the fact that Draft allows you to keep the cards you draft
has its own set of rankings - making it feel like a full and legitimate mode to get good at - really give you a lot to do outside of just playing constructed against other players.

Shutter is a cool little indie game available for a few dollars on Steam and it pays a lot of homage to classic horror games, calling itself a "Retro Puzzle Horror" experience, and pretty well lives up to that name, with a few slight shortcomings. It even has a few sneaky little references to classic RE games thrown in for fans.
You play the role of a little RC drone and you drive it around through a fixed-camera environment similar to the old Resident Evil games with similar tank controls. It's an interesting game mechanic having a game of this style where you can't actually directly interact with the environment, all you can really do is observe, take pictures, and communicate with your off-site HQ, and you have to solve the mystery through these methods.
The graphics are pretty primitive for a newer game, though still competent enough, and doesn't quite give the sense of immersion as better visuals would, but it works well enough. It's also very short, as are a good majority of games of this type. The biggest issue I had was getting used to the controls. The game starts you off in a very confusing place and doesn't do terribly well at communicating what you're supposed to do from the start, so it takes a little orientation to get into it because of this. Definitely worth a few dollars to check out if you like classic 90s horror games.

Don't trust the trailer. Well, sort of trust it. It shows a game that's all about going fast, which is great. Sometimes that's what the game is like, but sometimes it's not.
Defunct is at its best when it looks like the trailer - when you're racing over open terrain, chaining together boosts, making smart use of the whatchamadoozie to speed up down hills, figuring out ways to preserve your momentum uphill... all of that is great. What's less great is when the game decides that you need to unlock a door before you can continue. This requires you either finding keys or blowing up little red... things... to power up... some other thing... to let you move on. In these sections you're given wide open areas to play around in.
Here's the thing: opening these doors? It's not hard. It's not even that time consuming. So on the whole it doesn't detract *that* much. But it's a little disheartening to be on a tear, blasting through terrain almost as fast as the game can load it, only to then be ground to a halt so you can go do some mild platforming bits. The same is true of a few other sections, where it's not a door that blocks you, but a jump that's unmakeable the first time, so you fall into a pit and go through a convoluted new path to get back to the jump from another angle. And a few little interstitial moments between chapters where you putter along with your Broken Engine, watching other lil' robots zoom ahead of you.
None of these sections are bad enough to sink the game, but they stand out for the wrong reasons. It's a little bit like the 2D Sonic the Hedgehog games. You'll get one or two stages built for "Gotta go fast!", and then you'll get that Pyramid Stage from Sonic and Knuckles, or Casino Night Zone from Sonic 2. Sure, they're fun(ish), but the game gives you mechanics centered on speed, then drops you in a level not made for speed. Defunct occasionally feels the same way. "Let's make a game all about movement, but force them to slow down every now and again." If it was intentional, I think it was a bad call.
Fortunately, while those spots do stick out like a sore thumb, they are relatively few. Most of the time, Defunct is all about cruising at high speeds and navigating tricky terrain, and it does both very well. If you gun it through the campaign (for lack of a better term), it should only take you 30-40 minutes, but it's the kind of thing you may want to play again, this time trying a different path, or next time trying to collect all the doodads, or even putting on some music and just enjoying the ride.
tl;dr: It's short, mostly sweet, and replayable. Solid purchase.

Extremely satisfying gameplay, short story mode, high replayability.
I played through the story in about 1 hour, but there are still tons of things to find in the levels.  It's a lot of fun just zooming around looking for secrets and alternate paths through the semi-open-world levels (it isn't truly open world, but you do have a lot of freedom).  The game does a good job of creating a sense of speed and rewarding skill: it has a high skill ceiling and is difficult to play well, which makes it that much more satisfying when you hit a line just right and blast through a level quickly.
It feels like there is a lot of replay value if you're an achievement chaser and you enjoy the core gameplay.  It's going to take a lot of time to find all of the secrets and unlockables, and then an even longer time to beat all the time trials.  I'd guess it's going to take me 20+ hours to 100% the game.
If you think the gameplay looks like fun, and you can see yourself playing through multiple times to finish all the achievements, unlocks and time trials, I think you won't be disappointed.  If you're the type who plays through the story mode and then uninstalls, you will find it to be too short.

And out comes Defunct! Defunct is a fast-paced exploration-adventure game with some racing here and there. You’re a small robot that drives around on one wheel and you’re living on some kind of cargo ship travelling across a post-human Earth. Unfortunately for you, your motor doesn’t work properly and so you can only travel at a fraction of the speed of other robots. Thankfully you’re a smart little bot and you’re equipped with a device that you can use to harness gravity and increase your speed, and that’s good because you just fell off the cargo ship. It’s been one of those days…
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the publisher.
Please note: While I don’t have a huge amount of game-time I have in fact completed the main game mode (it took me just shy of two hours) but I’ll talk more about the length of the game later on.
The first thing you’ll notice when you load up Defunct is that it’s a good looking game. The graphics are by no means cutting edge and a few of the textures are a bit bland but most of the game’s levels take place in bright and colourful biomes which do indeed look great, particularly the desert biome levels. The actual models for the player’s robot and for other robots and vehicles you come across are all great. On the subject of your robot’s appearance, there are paint jobs which can be unlocked in the game though I’m not certain what the unlock requirements actually are.
Once you’ve stopped gawping at the game’s appearance it’s time to actually start playing it. You have two ways of increasing your robot’s speed. First off, you’ve got the broken motor which will get you moving, even up steep inclines, but it sure as hell is going to take its time about doing it. Your little motor is really just there in case you run out of momentum in the middle of a level or there’s a hill you want to get up. Now the other way of getting around is a lot faster and a lot more fun. It’s called the gravitation engine. The name gives an idea of what the engine actually does, it uses gravity. It’s mainly useful when you’re going down a hill of any length as a way to increase your speed. Going down the hill will give you a speed boost anyway, that’s how forces work, but when you use the gravitation engine you’re effectively ‘pulled down’ and as you can imagine that makes you pretty zippy heading down a hill.
Now accelerating is all well and good but it’s pretty pointless if you can’t keep that speed. Defunct’s fast-paced sections are all about getting to a high speed and then staying there. For the most part this means you have to pick out a route through the level that’s going to keep you downhill or at least flat-ish for most of the level. You’ll also find two kinds of speed boost pick-ups, one which gives you an immediate and rather short boost of speed and one which is stored in a tank and gives you slightly more bang for your buck, especially if you get an entire tank of the stuff.
I eluded to the fact in that last paragraph that Defunct isn’t the same all the way through the game. Depending on how you look at it, this is either a good thing or a bad thing. While most levels do require you to keep your speed up to some extent, possibly to reach a battery that’s high up and needs to be activated, there are some parts of the game which are quite slow, usually the up-hill sections. Personally I wasn’t too keen on the slower parts where you’re metaphorically plodding along looking for stuff but they do offer a good opportunity to take in the world around you.
Speaking of the world, now would be a good time to talk about the fact the game has eleven ‘main game’ levels and a further five levels which are made for the time trial mode only. As I said earlier the main game took me just shy of two hours to beat and since the levels are roughly the same length that works out to about ten minutes per level. The length of the game doesn’t necessarily make it a bad game and with the time trials and collectibles there are reasons to return to levels you’ve previously played but when you consider the price of admission I’m not convinced that it’s worth it.
The time trials are where the Trials mention in my title come from. Depending on the level you’ll have a certain objective to complete, such as pass through a certain number of points as fast as you can. While the time trials are pretty fun they are pretty much just bolted on to the game as the same levels with a different objective. There are medals for certain times so if you’re a completionist you may be able to squeeze a few more hours out of the game. While most of the levels are reasonably well suited to the time trial mode a couple of the longer levels felt like they didn't really fit in a should have either been shortened when playing time trial mode, i.e. remove the battery objectives, or skipped over completely.
Just a few more things to mention. There are a couple more gameplay mechanics, tricks and a magnetize engine, but they don’t play a huge part in the gameplay as a whole and the game does a good job of explaining them. The game runs very well, I’m below the recommended spec for my GPU but I was still able to run it at 30FPS on max settings though, as others have mentioned, the game does suffer from occasional FPS drops. There have been a couple of complaints about controller support not working correctly but I didn’t have any trouble using my Wireless 360 Controller. Lastly, while there is a story there to give you purpose for moving through the levels, it’s pretty too basic to be at all interesting which is a shame because the robot is a pretty cool character.
Defunct is a fun little adventure game with good graphics and gameplay but it’s let down by its length and price. If you’re a big fan of time trials or you enjoy completing games to one hundred percent you’ll probably get your money’s worth but if not then I’d recommend picking it up when it gets a sale.

Tiny Metal is a passion project developed by an almost exclusively Japanese team.  In short, they love Japanese War Games in the Advance Wars vein and, since nobody else has been making such games, they wanted to make one of their own and add their unique spin.
In my opinion, they succeeded wildly.  This is a great game with loads of personality and a solid balance underpinning.  It looks good (with tweakable settings on PC to make it hyper-crisp), sounds good, and aside from a UI that could use some tweaks (that the lead programmer has already said he wants to address), it plays well.
As of right now you get 19 campaign missions, a New Game + mode (with enhanced difficulty) and about 52 skirmish maps, some of which are labeled "Fun" difficulty, and some which are Expert level.
There is a multiplayer option -- it's just greyed out, but the devs have promised that it's coming soon and they have Sony's budgetary backing to make it happen.
Does the game have all the features and nuances of the later Advance Wars games -- a series, mind you, that started in the late 80's as Famicom Wars?  No... those games had several iterations to cram in as many features as possible.
This is Area 35's FIRST game.  They focused on getting the core gameplay down.  Additions will come in the form of patches and DLC, but it's unrealistic to expect a tiny studio to deliver, in their first outing, what a Nintendo-owned developer achieved over several franchise entries in a 10+ year time frame.  So the endless comparisons to the later Advance Wars games are off point.
The bottom line is that if you enjoy fun, tactical, turn-based war games and you were a fan of the AW games, you WILL enjoy this game if you keep in mind that the current feature set is barebones, with more planned to come.
I must give Area 35 massive props for breaking the decade long dry spell that Days of Ruin left in its wake.
This is a solid 8.0/10 for me right now, and with multiplayer and additional features, I could easily see that score jumping higher.

Overall, this game is well designed and enjoyable to play.
The cartoonish style and unique mechanics make the game itself fun to play. Unit movement speed and quick combat limits the annoyance of lengthy turn-for-turn fighting you see in most TBS games. The lengthy campaign and amazing number of Skirmish maps give the gamer a lot to play with. Especially in reqard to the skirmishes/missions with no unit prodcution, forcing you to play the game a little differently to try and outlast your opponent.
The User Interface could use some improvement here and there, and there does need some unit balancing, but every game release has rom for improvment. With the game still in under development, I have high hopes (especially for Multiplayer.)
Now with the Main Review out of the way, I can list a few specific things that I think need to be rebalanced/redone.
-Camera follows cursor. It's an interesting design, but it becomes more of a annoyance over a long playtime. I would have at least made it an option to disable.
-Land units can't pass under air units. This means you can use most airborne units (who can only be attacked by "Strikers") to take up tiles and interfere with ground combat.
-A.I. direct-attack units don't play by the same FOW rules, moving and attacking a unit they couldn't have seen until after their action was complete (WITHOUT the assistance of Radar.) This is actually a HUGE advantage in lot of situations and makes the campaign far more challanging than I think was intended...
-Snipers are too devistating against infantry when attacked. I get that they're suppose to be hard to hit for artillery and gunships, but a battalion of infantry should be able to overwelm a squad of Snipers in a single attack WITHOUT getting eveserated.
-Spec Ops are too expensive for thier low combat effectiveness. While they are tranky and hard to kill, you might as well just but 2 units of infantry and 2 units of Lancers for the damage output, and they are pratically useless at taking out Strikers and Radars, which is kinda the point of IRL Spec-Ops.
-Strikers effectiveness is purely situation. In some situtaions they can turn the tide of a fight with a little edge, but most the time they're actually pretty pathetic... They move slow without roads, have a rather limitted range, and their minimum range also applies to air-units (which it absolutely shouldn't... if only to make them effective against attacking gunships.)

TINY METAL (caps needed) is Advance Wars without the supply/ammo system and CO powers. It instead adds interesting tactical abilities in the form of FOCUS FIRE and ASSAULT and special units that can be called in through the use of radio towers found on the map. FOCUS FIRE allows you to have multiple units lock-on to one unit before the other unit has a chance to fire. This allows for the tried and true tactic of "meat walls" to be a bit nulified and allows you to push without losing attack power. ASSAULT allows the unit you are attacking to attack first, but you push them away from the tile they are on. Great if they are on one of your factories, airports, or even HQ. You also can have units face a direction after they move, and flank other units that are not facing the direction you are attacking. The special units are just supped up normal units, such as a mech unit (lancer in the game) that has extra movement. There are a lot of small subtle changes from Advance Wars that makes it a unique experience, while also satisfying the urge to play an Advance Wars-type game.
The story is extra cheesy and the dialogue is hammy, but there is just something charming about the game. I would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a varied Advance Wars experience.  It can never replace the originals, but it adds something nice to the genre.  They are also going to be updating this game with multiplayer and other gameplay elements, so keep an eye on that.

*As an avid fan of the Fire Emblem and Advance war series', i feel as though i have some merit when writing a review for this game. That being said, i will try my best not to compare it directly, as that would not be a fair and objective review.
Having only currently played under 2 hours (At the time of writing this review), one might think that the game could not be properly fleshed out whilst it boasts a whopping 20 hours of campaign.
However with the limited amount of units, characters and gameplay elements to be introduced it is easy to get a proper grips and feel in a short time.
I really want to like this game, i really really do...
But in its current state it leaves something to be desired
- Visually appealing artwork and cartoony animation
- Excellent gameplay mechanics
- Well balanced map design and units
- Fully voiced characters and units
- Multiple Languages supported
- Controller Support
- Well optimized for low end PC's
- Arcade style Gaming
- Unstable UI elements
- Small roster of units
- Poor voice acting
- Poorly optimized for mouse and keyboard
- Strange and unorthodox menu systems (Fast forwarding text rather than skipping entirely, Limited settings)
- Lacklustre battle scenes
- Forced Tutorials
- Visual clarification issues (same coloured units, visually similar units and buildings)
- No multiplayer
- No difficulty settings
- No custom playability (apart from skirmish)
- Mediocre storyline
Tiny Metal has hit the nail on the head in a lot of areas and for some this game is thoroughly enjoyable with only minor surface issues. The inclusion of Lock on targetting allowing multiple units to attack without consequence is a great feature and adds a new layer of strategy. Flanking is also another thing that when put into practice makes perfect sense and i would consider an excellent addition as well.
I am going to grade this part on a Better/On Par/Worse basis, similar to that of my Pros and Cons.
- Tag team assaults
- Varied unit effectiveness
- Directional combat system
- Tiered infantry units
- Character Design
- Fog of war
- Unit strengths/weaknesses
- Defensive tiles
- Mobility
- Map Design
- Small roster (No naval units)
- No Custom maps
- No unlockables
- Less replayability
- No Difficulty Settings
- Less unit co-operation
Tiny Metal is not a spiritual successor to the advance wars series. It takes great inspiration from it and it has the looks and feels of an advance wars game, but it doesn't quite make it all the way.
The game in itself, is entirely playable and enjoyable with a lot of minor flaws and a small amount of major flaws that have been overlooked.
I was very eager to buy this game upon release as i felt it would fill that advance wars shaped hole in me, but it didn't quite fit.
I will continue playing and enjoying this game as much as a i possibly can and i can safely say without a doubt that my money was not wasted, as i have high hopes for the future of this game.
That being said however, i do not recommend that people purchase this game in its current state, as much as it pains me to say. Wait a while and give this game time to properly bloom and i am certain that it will meet all my expectations if not more.
There is still hope for you yet Tiny Metal.

On a more serious note, Verdun is a very fun (look at my hours) team-based game with a high skill ceiling. While the game is very authentic to WWI and the damage model is mostly realistic, Verdun has a more arcade flair to it compared to, say, Red Orchestra. The movement is very fluid with the exception of going prone from standing, you can shoot perfectly accurate while jumping (if you're aiming down sights; you have less than a second to take an accurate airborne shot), your characters rechamber carbines and short rifles insanely quickly, there's health regeneration, and there's no bleeding mechanics to speak of. Having said that though, if you like old-school WWII bolt-action gameplay, I think this is the best iteration of it thus far. It's in a bit of a niche though, with very a very realistic setting and slow, tactical gameplay mixed in with rather arcadey weapon handling mechanics and regeneration.
And if you didn't like Battlefield 1 because of its low skill ceiling or inaccuracies to the time period, I think Verdun is what you're looking for.

The digital board games catagory has been expanding from the websites, to engines such as Octgn and Vassal, to these 3d tabletop enviorments.
This is just one of the clients to access Tabletopia. Something you can install and open easily. There is also a web version and future mobile versions.
There are bugs. That is pretty much expected as this is the initial version that is in early access.
There are also a few improvements with room to grow. The steam client added room listings, voice chat, friend status and there are more service features planned.
Tabletopia is a subscription based model which sets them apart for better or for worse. There will be free access to games but will require subscribing for expanded access such as expansions or extended setups.
You do however get access to the entire library of games that are available so you can try any out and explore all the different games out there.
While you do not have every game you want to play, the catalog is legit and offically approved by the game makes or uploaded themselves. The money also goes back to the devs on a pretty good split (70%).
Cross platorm between standalone clients, web based access, and future mobile clients is nice so you can open it however is easist to you.
You want to play as a group, give them your room (url) and all they need is to put in a name.

Review:
Works just fine for what it wants to do. The more popular games are well implemented. Designers can feed their own games into tabletopia. Not all of them are perferct. Also, if you look for the perfect physics simulation of game component behaviour, well, play a physical game.
But if you have a big screen and want a jolly old time with your friends, the tabletopia app has what you need. I expect it only to improve when the game catalogue growths and an own steam community develops.

What I liked:
- Game setups are ready-to-play based on the number of players in a room, you just have to know the rules.
- Wonderful Steam integration, shows who plays what inside the game, and who can be invited.
- Awesome interface, very 'social'-ish, makes finding a game and communicating quite pleasant experience.
- Great game catalog, helpful filters and previews, bookmarks.
- Room system, lobbies, ability to watch others play.
- Cross-'platform' play with the browser players.
- Overall polished, 'adult' look and feel, and optimization.
- Little things like:
-- Turn timers and notifications.
-- The playing hand is always on the bottom side of the screen.
-- Little icons of the actions on the hand cursors. Really helpful when you see what others are doing right now.
-- The camera locks at 0-90-180-270 degrees while turning around, just feels really nice.
-- Camera states (0-9 different positions to switch freely and an overlook).
What I didn't like:
- Horrible synchronization. I had to leave the table and return several times because I wasn't getting any messages and no updates on the screen (stuff others did), while all my messages and actions were actually transmitted to the others properly. I had no idea when I was desync'd, no errors, nothing.
- Clunky camera controls. While not exactly bad, the degree of a camera's turn on Z-axis is really narrow, and the transition while zooming in and out is weirding me out.
- The physics. It's kind of there, but I don't feel it while interacting with objects, and it's also weirding me out.
- Dice rolls. These are just horribly animated and not actually randomized by a physical roll, which is one of the points emulating a table with physics.
- Context menus of the objects are weird and very unintuitive. When you right-click an object, it presents you an action wheel, and the actions available are dictated by an object type, so some objects have, for example, 6 actions and others have 3, so the action wheel is divided by 6 and 3 parts accordingly. The weird thing is, if these two 6-action and 3-action objects share an action, which you want to use, the first one might have it somewhere top-left, while the second might have it at the bottom. The action icons are not helpful at all, because they look really bulky and therefore similar. Because of that, you can't just quickly click through what you want to do, and actually have to look over all of the icons, find the one you need and only then click it. I guess it's easier to show an example:
and
look at the 'Rotate' button. It's really unintuitive when the same element moves and forth between different objects. It's even more weird when the same objects have different actions, like
and
. I'd rather see the unused actions greyed out instead of having to search where to click.
- Some textures like the game boards, for example, are really low-res, but that's the problem of the people who ported it, I guess, and not the Tabletopia developers.
- Room system. Although I said I liked it, I have to say it needs some rework. Some people create rooms and are clueless that they have to shut them down after they play by clicking 'Abandon', because they leave them open and close the game, leaving a lot of 'ghost' rooms in a room browser. People join these rooms, hang around for a bit hoping to play, but the host is not even online, so they just leave. What I mean to say, they need to make the rooms temporary, for example, if the host is offline for half an hour, the rooms is shut down automatically, or make an option of temporary/permanent room which defaults to temporary, so they're left open only when a host is consciously making it permanent.
- Game options. Where are they really? I'd really like to change some keybinds, camera smoothness, graphics (High-Medium-Low option in an in-session menu doesn't cut it). Not a lot of control over the game.
- 'Back' button, but I guess it's just me being an idiot. After a session at the table, going back to lobby and pressing 'Back', hoping to return to main menu, sends me back to the table. This happened every single time I went from a table to a lobby.
Neutral:
- Couldn't figure out how to add anyone to the friends list.
- When I was testing Scythe, I noticed that the small objects like the resources and the workers have textures stretched across their surfaces, despite being simply single colored, which created some color/texture artifacts near the edges (because of the texture compression):

Seems to be an issue with Scythe, haven't noticed this in other games. I guess, only standard pieces are colored in-code, and the custom models have to be textured even if they're single colored.
What I don't want to discuss:
- Monetization system. I just don't care.
- Legal vs illegal rant. My review is only about the game mechanics.
- Comparison to Tabletop Simulator.
In conclusion:
Although the 'meta' part of the game feels complete and looks really great, I can't really recommend it because the main part - the 'playing board games' part - is clunky, mainly camera controls, the physics, the context menus, mouse controls, the dice rolls, the lack of control over the game options. Sure, the assets, the objects, the game setup look nice and all, but the main process of using them feels broken to me right now.

A security company puts cameras in an old vandalised house recently acquired by their client. You're moving around in the house at night, with a little robot, equiped with another camera, trying  to catch the culprit red handed. So basically, the game goes for a "found" footage idea, which could be really nice, with a proper budget, art direction and game design skills.
The game looks bad. Not in a charming "Baby-Sitter Bloodbath" or "Power Drill Massacre" / PlayStation 1 era kind of way. Just in a poor Unity kind of way. Low texture, not even stylised, decent lighting projection but terrible use of it, generic environment...nothing that can stick to your brain. The sound-design is the same. Though the game tries to use it correctly (I'd say it's "ok" for the mood it's trying to create) it's just annoying when it tries to actually scare you with some random loud noise of a guy mumbling.
But that is actually not the real problem. The problem is, the narration and the pacing suck. First of all, why should I be scared for a robot? I don't really know who is driving this thing, where is that character supposed to be, and why is he/she not with the rest of the crew (that seem to be coding software in only few minutes to update the damn thing). Secondly, the notes don't need to be there. If you actually create an environment, and put so much effort into putting the player in a position where he can take pictures, move around, just use the environment. Do not use notes. Notes are good for human beings actually opening drawers, desks etc. The notes come out of nowhere and the story flows mainly if not only through these...I won't even talk about the actual story, which is average or below average. i've seen worst in the amateur creepy pasta realm, and I've seen better too.
Overall, I'm sorry to say, but it feels far to amateurish to be sold. It's a nice idea, sure. I like the concept of making fixed camera angles diegetic. But it's use with such a mediocre ghost story, bad graphics, poor level design and overall lack of skills, that it feels like I've been robbed.
Had the game been free, "of course" just try it. But even for a this small amount of money, don't bother.
PS: I'm arsh, but there's something to make out of this. The developer should try again, and again, and again. But don't make us pay until you REALLY have something.

Defunct is an odd little game that I really wanted to love, but in the end, there was too much holding it back. It’s a 3D platformer all about speed, and using momentum to quickly traverse the levels. It’s got a Wall-E quality to it in terms of the theme, with what looks like an abandoned human planet now occupied by little quick robots.
The developer clearly understands style and colour. There are a lot of sections of the game, most notably sections like Oasis, which really pop out of the screen. The environments were really varied, with desert highways and meadow-like hills neighbouring unrealistically, but welcomely, near each other. It’s a shame that, I feel like, there was some pretty gross framerate drops and it always seemed to happen in the pretty areas. The thing is, Defunct looks good from afar, but bad up close. The textures are really low res, even with the setting at very high, which makes the cutscenes look pretty damn ugly. Luckily for the majority of the game you won’t be looking at the textures too up close, and you’re supposed to be going fast, so it should be that the environments are a hypnotising blur of colour as you traverse the landscape.
Unfortunately though, that was the real issue with the game. The game is definitely at it’s best when you are travelling at high speed, jumping from platform to platform smoothly. The issue is that it’s too difficult to keep up momentum most of the time. 90% of the time I was able to identify the path I needed to take in order to do awesome jumps and travel quickly, but the handling of the character is so finicky and slow I could almost never do what I MEANT to do. I do think there should be challenge in games like this, but it should be based on your reaction times and making snap decisions to travel in certain directions, not based on whether or not the volatile physics of the engine want to agree with you. Far too many times I’d be travelling at high speed, feeling great, and then smack into a wall because I was travelling TOO FAST and missed the platform I was supposed to land on. And if the pacing of the game wasn’t being undermined enough, there are these weird puzzle-like sections where you slow down and collect batteries to power up the door that lets you progress. The gameplay is fun when it works the way I want it to, the issue is, it almost never works the way I want it to, and it becomes frustrating. Maybe the game would be more fun for someone who spends a lot of time with it and gets familiar with the controls, but my bet is that is not going to be the majority of people.
The story isn’t anything crazy. You’re a little robot who fell off his ship, and now you have to return to it. Even so, there was some surprisingly satisfying story beats, and that’s backed up by an interesting world that tells you a bit about itself just from looking around the environment. For example you see old rusted cars and highways around the place, so you can gather that humans used to live here, and the music is often your que that the story is progressing. It’s little details like that that make this world one that you want to be in. There’s also some really interesting sections of the game where your character is supposed to be feeling a certain way, and it’s reflected really well by the mechanics. For example, during a moment where there seems to be little or no hope, you’ll find yourself having to push yourself up hills, and failing jumps that you could easily have made with a bit more speed. The mechanics of the game allowed some of the story to be told, which I think is really cool.
In the end, I finished this game in 90 minutes. That’s short, but for the right price that can be reasonable. The price the developers gave me was 11 euros (I am writing this review pre-release). Converting that, is 12 dollars, so the final price of the game could be anywhere between 10 and 15 dollars in the US, probably 12 or 13 dollars. 13 dollars is way too much. 10 is better, but still not really a good price. This should be a $5-7 game in reality. So the price isn’t great, maybe pick the game up on sale for around the price i recommended, but even then it’s gonna depend. If you appreciate an interesting and sometimes quite pretty world and a fairly satisfying story; oh and also can look past frustrating mechanics? Sure. Buy it on sale. Otherwise, I’m going to have to say avoid.
Presentation: 6
Mechanics: 4

Defunct is getting a score of 5.2 out of 10. So, you know, maybe a tiny bit better than meh? The story was the driving force of what got me through the game, and the presentation was pretty good all around leaving aside the textures; that said, the mechanics were flawed; 12 dollars is far too expensive for this, kind of, meh experience, and I just found myself frustrated most of the time.

So I'm about eight missions into the campaign and played five skirmishes. From what I can tell, here's how it differs from Advance Wars on first impression:
- No naval units. Probably the worst difference.
- Apparently can only heal foot soldiers and not other units at cities.
- No unique COs :( There are, however individual "hero" units (not particularly unique or interesting)
- Music's kind of annoying. Not catchy. This coming from someone that loved every single GBA and DS game. Recommend turning it off and playing some cutesy whatever in another window instead.
- Fog of war is on every map at all times? Would like some variety.
- Can't combine damaged units into a single unit.
- A map editor would be nice?
+ It's on PC and it's new, shiny, and affordable to make up for the lack of depth. It's an Unreal Engine game with cutesy chibi graphics and looks like it. It's polished. No idea how well it scales on weaker machines. Cranking up AA+motion blur seems pretty overkill for this art style. I think I just might turn it down to give my video card a break.
+ The combined focus fire is a REALLY good addition. Love it! Just might make up for the inability to combine units.
+ The orientation of your unit apparently matters, though not by much.
+ LOTS of skirmish maps to choose from!! Wow.
+ New radar units are great. The sniper and spec op units are great. And they're all cute as heck
? No multiplayer (yet). Eagerly awaiting and looking forward to.
? The indirect fire units (artillery, rockets and missiles) are combined into the STRIKERs. This could be a positive or a negative depending on how you look at it, but it's definitely a simplification I don't much care for.
? Don't have to worry about refueling or ammunition.
I paid $25 and I don't feel ripped off. It's currently (as of December 2017) probably the best option you have if you want to scratch this particular itch, besides going back and playing actual Advance Wars games from 10+ years ago if you haven't already. Look into Ogre (rough around the edges), Dai Senryaku ($$$, almost simmy, unfortunately not on steam), the upcoming Into the Breach or WarGroove (both look promising) if you're looking for other similar alternatives to evaluate.

Well honestly I had no idea that there was such an outstanding CCG out there. I play this kind of games since literally two decades (just saw a video of the old "Pokemon TCG play it!" and I feel really old now) and this really hooked me up.
The last that did so was Hearthstone (HS from now on) and I really must compare Eternal to it.
The thing is Blizzard makes really good games, but has a huge flaw, it's greedy, like most game companies.
I'm not saying Eternal is different in this, the microtransactions are there as everywhere, BUT this game actually gives you something as a reward when you play it. HS's gold system (after the unique quests), just gave you the daily quest and 100 gold max from pvp (30 win exactly). With that you could buy just a pack (or 2 in best case scenario).
Rewards in Eternal are without a doubt superior, in just a couple weeks I almost completed both Omens of the past and The eternal throne sets, never ever got close to this in HS (and I played for months since the end of the beta). You can play pvp ranked or not, just as in any other ccg,  BUT you can also play the Gauntlet (against AI) for FREE and farm it really fast (got to master and even completed it without a sweat), play Forge wich is a Draft against the AI, and the pvp-Draft both of which let you keep the cards that you choose from opening packs. You get reward even from using man colors, even if you end-up losing.
Another feature of this game is that there is really a lot more MTG (if you don't know what that is stop reading please) in it. Mana! Multicolor decks! Instant spells! and more!
The icing on the cake is that it's not shabby at all, and you can see a lot of polishing in the game art and animations, that is the only thing that I think HS has a little better.
Anyway long-story-short:
it's really good and free, try it if you like  CCGs,  9/10

Tiny Metal is a great spirtual successor to advance wars; while in many ways its not a carbon copy of advance wars, that is a good thing in my opinion since I do believe the series had some issues this game tackled very well (and I'd highly recommend anyone bashing the game because its not a carbon copy of advance, such as @unsubstantiation review )
For one, Fog of War isn't boiled down to hiding in forest since they no long provide near perfect camo just by hiding in them. Another thing I like about this game is the new radar unit, they give extended "radar" vision which goes over anything; what it does is spot targets, but you don't know what they are, so if you have strikers in tangent with that, it makes for a solid duo. Its also helpful for direct units since they won't be going in blind with a radar to spot, they too can attack the unknown enemy knowing that they are in the spotted cordniate.
Another set of cool mechanics is the focus fire; in addition, if you're familiar with advance wars, this review goes over a lot of the differences
For a newcomer, this game is a lot more friendly compared to its cousin, i heard there is a new game + but i haven't gotten there yet myself but its suppose to make the game more challenging for those who are interested
The story is pretty basic, not amazing, not god awful, just enough to give the world substance, which isn't bad, but don't expect a Fire emblem like story with a fleshed out set of charcters. Instead its a bit more serious and straight forward, i'd put it between the cartoony-ness of advance and the seriousness of fire emblem.
Gameplay wise that 20+ hour marker for the story is no lie, the story maps work well in introducing units and mechanics to the player without overwhelming them; as the story progresses, there is more units to work with and the maps get bigger and more intense. I'm over 10 hours in as of writing this and I'm having a good time with the story mode overall.
Finally the game has an extensive 56 single maps via skirmish mode which tell you there size and diffuculty, but no preview of the map itself, but i wouldn't call that a deal breaker personally, but for some a title may not be enough.
In conclusion, if you want a straight forward fun turn based strategy similiar to the works of intellegent systems; I'd highly recommend giving this game a go; its also going to have more features and multiplayer implemented in the future so look out for that

I received this as a Christmas gift from a good friend. The atmosphere was amazing. I felt really creeped out at first, and the game did a really good job of creating that "what's going to happen?" vibe. I felt very much immersed in the story, just as if I actually was the character coming home after being away for a long time. I was very emotionally moved as I explored the house and found out what became of the family. It was a very touching story, and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys well-crafted, emotional stories. I say this as just another soul, and as a person with a degree in Creative Writing.
I've played several visual novels and only thoroughly enjoyed a few of them, and I think I prefer this type of storytelling game to the visual novel format. I felt much more immediately immersed in this than most visual novels. There are exceptions in the visual novel genre of course, ones that really moved me on a very personal level, but I'd recommend this game if you like games with good stories but don't like the visual novel format.
I think the length of the game was appropriate as well. If it was much longer I think it would have felt overdone, but it was perfectly paced and of reasonable length.
Anyway, I thoroughly enjoyed this and definitely recommend it. I would recommend it even if I hadn't gotten it for free, as a gift. It's worth the money if you enjoy a good story.

On a more serious note, Verdun is a very fun (look at my hours) team-based game with a high skill ceiling. While the game is very authentic to WWI and the damage model is mostly realistic, Verdun has a more arcade flair to it compared to, say, Red Orchestra. The movement is very fluid with the exception of going prone from standing, you can shoot perfectly accurate while jumping (if you're aiming down sights; you have less than a second to take an accurate airborne shot), your characters rechamber carbines and short rifles insanely quickly, there's health regeneration, and there's no bleeding mechanics to speak of. Having said that though, if you like old-school WWII bolt-action gameplay, I think this is the best iteration of it thus far. It's in a bit of a niche though, with very a very realistic setting and slow, tactical gameplay mixed in with rather arcadey weapon handling mechanics and regeneration.
And if you didn't like Battlefield 1 because of its low skill ceiling or inaccuracies to the time period, I think Verdun is what you're looking for.

I actually bought this game twice.  I Greenlit it on Steam and then found a copy online.  Knowing that not all games I vote for ever get approved, I purchased it direct from the publisher.  As I always buy games I vote for, I bought it when it came available on Steam.  It takes some getting used to, and it is sometimes hard to find the info you need.  I'd like to see a mini-map so I don't have to swap between the map and the screen.  I'd also reccomend that you deploy your troops left to right (or visa versa) so that as you cycle through your units, you're not jumping all over the map.  Battles can take awhile and depending on how many airships you have, a "turn" could take quite awhile.
Also reccomend you save after every successful battle in case you accidently quit without saving (only did it twice, was in a big hurry so it was my own fault).  Additionally, keep a decent cash reserve,  Tempting as it is to upgrade tech every turn, you need money when the AI does its turns.  Say 1000 to 1500 per AI you border.  More, I imagine later in the game when they have more airships.  Remember that fielding troops and arming them take cash.  Offensive troop numbers are determined by the size of the attacking airship (5-10-15), defending numbers are determined by the type of terrain.
AND how much money you have to spend!
Combat is sequential, but the non-moving side can do opportunuty fire if it has reserved action points from it's
previous turn.  APs are used for moving, attacks and reloading.  Units have weight restrictions on how much they can carry.  Reloading has to be done manually, so while you may fire at a target of opportunity if you have enough APs remaining, you cannot do a "reload of opportunity", so to speak.  A word of caution:  attacks of opportunity with
explosive weapons can be hazardous to your health.  If you are too close to a wall, rock, tree, or even a slight rise,
your weapon could impact that, killing yourself.
Visibility ranges from 50 to 300 .  The attacking trooper has to be able to see the target himself in order to fire
at it.  And has to be within his weapon's range.  There's a helpful counter that tells you how many enemies your
active trooper can see.  Click on it and a range will appear to the right.  Click on the range and you will turn to
face that target.  You need to keep an eye on that counter while you are moving.  You also get reports during
the AI's movement phase if something enters your viewing range, so don't use the AI's turn as an opportunity to refresh your beverage or make room for more, you might miss something important.
That's the mechanics.  I have only played the P. campaign where you chose one nation (for ease of recognition, they resemble UK, USA, France, Zulu, Far East and Germanic) and fight the rest.  Each side has distinctive uniforms.  All sides have the same initial equipment (rifle, pistol, grenade, first aid kit).  Every turn, cash allowing, you may research an item for specific class troopers.  There are 4 ot 5 developments per class.  Classes are Sapper, Reccon, Gunny, Grenadier, Marksman and Fusiler.  All sides have access to the same developments.  It gets progressively more expensive as you progress up the tech tree.  For example, at Medium difficulty the first tier weapon research costs 1000, the second
tier in the same class cost 3000.  The AI does its own research.  In my current game, the Chinese AI developed grenade launchers before I did (Grenadier tier 1).  It was NOT a pleasant surprise.

There is a huge amount to enjoy and admire about this game. Anyone who favours gameplay over graphics, has a fondness for turn-based play and enjoys X-Com style games will likely get many hours of fun. The steampunk style gives a refreshing feel to the combat genre while the combat itself is gritty, nail-biting and hugely rewarding when you get your tactics right. The weapons, meanwhile, give a very satisfying thump or crack on firing and the resulting impacts are great to watch. The ability to recruit and upgrade your squad and develop new weapons adds a rewarding element to the gameplay. To think that this was produced by one dedicated developer is pretty amazing and helps account for the few shortcomings with the game. First, setting up your squad for each battle can be tedious as I could not find any way to remember "loadouts". Second, the opening turns can also be tedious as units can only be moved individually and watched all the way to their location. Finally, the campaign itself may feel a little underdeveloped at times. That said, a great wargame and a developer whose future efforts will be eagerly anticipated by this grizzled gamer.

Tabletopia is a fantastic product that is worth the subscription.
Unlike TTS, Tabletopia is supported by the publishers and the designers. This means that most games are created by the publishers with the help of people at Tabletopia, which is fantastic because it means every game features the original art assets. Since TTS is community-created, every game features scanned art. This is why the components in Tabletopia look so crisp and infinitely better than TTS.
Thankfully, Tabletopia does not feature the wonky physics engine of TTS, so you don’t have to worry about a tiny error ruining the game. The interface is slick and easy to navigate. Shuffling and bag drawing is simple. Rolling, while not as fun without the physics, is still incredibly easy. Each game has pre-defined starting setups to make things simple. The interface is bright and beautiful. Every game looks like its original counterpart. All of this combines to make you feel as though you’re playing the real game at a table surrounded by friends.
I’ve played many Tabletopia games with the designers of the game! This is just an amazing experience. Many people upload their prototypes to the system so you can experience the game WAY before it hits stores.
The problem most people will have is the payment structure. I understand there are a lot of poor students that play games and they can’t afford 10 dollars a month. If you can afford it, however, it really is the best option. TTS does not provide ANY money to publishers or designers. Tabletopia, on the other hand, contacts each publisher and makes sure it has permission to produce a game. They get original art assets and provide the publisher/designer with a cut of the monthly profits based on the popularity of the game. This is fantastic, since designers are not rich people. I’m a big fan of knowing that some of my money is actually going to the people who are making the games I love and enjoy.

The Elements saga continues with Elements II: Hearts of Light.  From what was presented so far, it looks like this game is shaping up to be an awesome game like its predecesor.
Story: 10/10
The story presented so far is very intriguing and well written.  The characters are unique and interact each other very well.  The story so far is flowing well and is not dragging which Elements I tend to do at times.  In addition, the game is doing a great job in keeping the mystery of why our current foes are after Vril.  I am looking for the remainder of the story as it seems like it will be as good or better than Elements I story.
Music: 10/10
I am enjoying the music.  I especially love the overworld theme and the boss battle theme.  The music flows very well with the scenes and battles.  The mostly guitar style of the Elements saga has grown on me and I hope in the future there will be a DLC for the soundtrack.
Gameplay: 10/10
Elements II did a complete face lift on the gameplay.  The most notable difference is that your actions in the game affect how your character grows.  Want to run away from an ememy? Be careful because this will cause your negative attributes (cowardice to be exact) to raise and your positive attributes to fall.  Like looting for treasure in private homes.  Once again be careful because these actions will effect positive and negative attributes.  This system makes the game more emersive and provides the game a lot of replay value as you can do different runs (e.g., pacifist run).  While the battle system is mostly the same as Elements I, Elements II do provide new features such as combos attack amongst characters.  Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay from Elements II so far and I am looking forward to any other surprises as the game progresses forward
In conclusion, I would highly recommend this game especially if you enjoyed the first Elements game.  I look forward to the next installment in this saga.

- popular commercial games, that were uploaded someone with a scanner and a free afternoon. Now don't get me wrong here,
, but let's be completely honest here - it would lose a huge part of content, if every workshop game, that was uploaded without permission of its rightful author/publisher, got taken down.
has a different approach to this issue. It has subscription based business model, think of it like Spotify with board games - you can play for free with some restrictions or get some more options for a monthly fee (please note, that although prices stated below are directly from devs website, they may change in the future or after release). The 3 types of membership are:
- Free, access to free library of games. Ideal for casual board game player.
- 5€/month, premium library access. For passionate gamers.
- 10€/month, premium library access and GAMING ROOM - play premiun titles with guests you invite. It's the GM package basicly.
Also every game in their library is added with permission and support of the original author/publisher. This means, that on top of better quality assets and stuff, part of your money goes to the people tha actually made the game. This unfortunately means, that there are not that much games available right now, because not everyone can just upload things. But the library is slowly and surely growing and new titles are added each week or two.
tl;dr
Those 10€ are for early access. You will be able to play this for free. Or you can subscribe for a monthly fee. Think of it like Spotify with board games.
Tabletopia has better approach to rightful content owners (authors/publishers) and fair business model for players.

Note: This review has been edited to make mention of the retail release subscription model.
For two years now Tabletop Simulator has held the crown of being the king of Steam board games as it allowed you to play various games in a virtual environment. This was a boon for tabletop fanatics who for various reasons never possessed the opportunity to get one of their favorite games going. Whether it be because they've graduated from college or high school and have lost their social group or they're a professional who is constantly on the road or whatever reason. Now there is a challenger to the Berserk Games crown as Tabletopia Inc. launch their greatly anticipated Tabletopia. And let me tell you this much if sheer weight of numbers has anything to do with who will come up trumps it may just claim a famous victory.
From day one of early access players can expect to have access to more than a hundred games from some of the most well known tabletop gaming publishers around the world as seen in the graphic in the Steam Description. When I logged onto the game there was already a list of 202 different board games in totality to play and the developer-publisher expects to add almost countless more to their library.
Something that I thought was a fantastic touch was how the games are categorized. You can sort games by age requirements with games ranging from as young as three years of age and up, the number of players required to play a game, the time requirements with some games being as short as five minutes ranging all of the way through to many hours and finally but by no means less important is that you can find games that are language independent (meaning that you're not limited to a certain language) or for games that are language dependent you can narrow the list down to English, French, German, Italian, Russian and Spanish. I hope that for our Asian and speakers of other languages that more languages are added soon.
Another good feature is 'Find & Play.' This feature allows you to see which games other people are waiting to play and how many more people are required before you can play the game. This should theoretically make games quickly accessible if you're not too set on playing a specific game especially for those of you who are solo players and haven't got friends with the program.
Before you play a new game the game must download the required files for that specific game. For example, Scythe required an extra 30MB download. I have to say that I am a fan of this system. Rather than downloading every single game - including those that you have no intention of ever playing - and increasing the initial download size tenfold you only have the base features of the game downloaded when you first start. This may be annoying to those of you who live on slow Internet speeds but if all of the games are in the roughly the same sized download then these extra downloads wont be given a second thought. The downloads for the games that I have played were relatively quick and simple affairs.
(A late addition to the post): Arguably the most controversial issue regarding the retail release of the game to date is the game's subscription model. I personally do not take any issue with the game running a $10- per month subscription for the premium model. However, I can understand and accept that some people will take issue with this. The main software will be free to play with the retail release and this model will give you access to all of the games without the ability to play with the game's expansion sets. The premium model comes with the ability to play with all expansion sets. Buying into the Early Access version will award you with one month of gold premium subscription when the game is released to retail. Though I have yet to find where the developers state that only premium subscribers will be able to create games this is something that needs to be considered.
The one thing that needs to be determined is the quality of the player base that the software gets. Although there are games available that can be played by a single player the success of software such as this is more often than not determined by those who play it - the number, their friendliness, the personality of the game. I hope that this software brings out a wide audience towards it full of newbies and helpful experienced players, those who are incredibly skillful and those who are mature enough to play a game responsibly and enjoy it for what it is without tarnishing the experience of other players. For many this will be their first time learning and playing tabletop games so I hope that people understand and appreciate that not only will players be learning individual games but also that they'll be learning the software simultaneously. I urge people not to scare the newbies away.
Tabletopia has an opportunity to take over a significant market share of the online tabletop gaming experience. Their development and press staff are  truly dedicated in making their software the very best that it can be and with the type of professional clientele behind them have given themselves every chance to succeed.

I recall a forum debate which raged a ways back, regarding the game Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs and its rather controversial decision to eliminate the "lantern oil" mechanics of its predecessor, The Dark Descent.  At the time I defended The Chinese Room in this decision, and while I still agree with the general reduction in The Dark Descent's many unnecessary mechanics (including superfluous sanity systems and borderline-inconsequential "healing" items), the extraordinary suspense created by Outlast and its battery-conserving antics made me rethink my stance in regard to such issues.  Having said that, Shutter takes such matters to new extremes of extraneousness, by arming the miniature "droid" you control with a battery which not only controls your ability to switch to first-person mode, but requires constant recharging whilst adding precisely ♥♥♥♥-ALL suspense to the matters at hand.  Indeed, I am wondering if the only reason for this mechanic to exist are:  a. To shut up the kinds of people who complain incessantly about lack of "gameplay mechanics" in recent horror games, and b. To pad out the length of an already very SHORT game.
Here's another theory.  After coming up with an admittedly VERY clever and VERY original concept for their little-horror-game-which-could - one in which the player commanders a Mars mission-style robot in its explorations of a haunted house, and the unravelling of the mysteries therein - the developers of Shutter then faced the difficult decision of whether to make it a first-person or third-person game.  The smart money would probably have been on first-person, but their love for early Resident Evil-style camera angles apparently won out to the degree where the player can now readily switch between first and third-person.  In its own right, not a bad idea at all, but then that dreaded need for "mechanics" reared its ugly head.  After all, what fledgling development company wants to become the new Chinese Room, and be "hated" by all and sundry (except ME, of course?  Hell, I even liked Gone Home).
(On a side-note, I'd also like to thank all the ♥♥♥♥ers who whined about A Machine For Pigs for the current plethora of horror games in which the protagonist can't run for more than seven seconds without stopping to catch his breath.  All of these unnecessarily overdone "mechanics" are thanks to YOU, ya whining pack o'♥♥♥♥♥♥♥)

Anyway, back to Shutter.  Oh, and if you need further evidence of the aforementioned Resident Evil obsession, you need look no further than the fact that your "boss" looks like Barry Burton and makes a joke about being a "master of unlocking".  'Nuff said.  So what of the game's GOOD qualities?  It's certainly not lacking in atmosphere or spookiness, but the genuinely "scary" factor is a little hampered by the fact that, at least until the final chapter, you're just a little electronic thing on wheels which can't really get hurt or be emotionally traumatised.  It's an inspired idea just the same, and the "story" you uncover is interesting enough (if told in the slightly ludicrous manner of finding pieces of a "diary" plastered on walls here, there and everywhere), but its a little difficult to recommend to all bar the horror-faithful at the price of five bucks for barely over an hour's worth of gameplay.  By all means, pick it up in a sale, and I'll certainly be eager to see what the devs get up to next, as this shows an awful lot of promise.  But less of the gratuitous mechanics next time, eh, Cosmic Logic?  You guys were brave enough to try something genuinely different for your first foray into game design, and if there's one thing horror games are in dire need of right now, it's a bit more risk-taking.  Let's all stop quaking in the shadow of The Chinese Room's "epic fail" (minor masterpiece, if you want MY ♥♥♥♥ing opinion), and keep things moving forward, whad'ya say?   Definitely a very solid, if flawed, first effort.
