I wanted so badly to love this game, but even from the first cutscene I was already beginning to dislike everything about it.  DS 1 spends the first couple of minutes setting up the theme of bleakness and inevitability, introducing the major players who shaped the world into what it is, and explaining your place in the world.  DS 2 has some omniscient old ladies nearly breaking the fourth wall to laugh at you about the game's difficulty, in between explaining the exact mechanics of the undead curse without any mention of why the curse is significant.
I came close to putting the game down when I unlocked the This is Dark Souls achievement, which you get when you die for the first time (I'd missed a jump in the tutorial area), and again on finding the death counter in Majula.  Dark Souls 1's difficulty makes sense in-universe--you're a single person trying to take on gods and heroes and legions of enemies, of course it's not going to be an easy journey--but Dark Souls 2 completely misses the point and goes for difficulty for difficulty's sake.
Then I met Majula's NPCs.  The Emerald Herald's first words to me were to ask me if I was the next monarch, never mind that I don't know who she is, she doesn't know who I am, I don't know why I'm in Drangelic or Majula or what I'm trying to accomplish or why she's talking about monarchs.  Then she gives me leveling and tells me to go kill some random people.  Again, I don't know who this lady is.  She's a character the player's meant to like, but Frampt, whose morality is much more ambiguous, is at least polite enough to introduce himself first and explain what he's asking of you.  I listened to her dialogue, got annoyed when she kept referencing things the game knows I don't know about yet, and didn't feel the slightest bit bad about killing her.
(Another thing: NPCs don't try to defend themselves until after you've shaved off about three quarters of their health, which makes it easy to kill people who should logically be able to off an early-game player character without particularly trying.  The Emerald Herald doesn't defend herself period, which does fit her role, but seemed strange considering she'd met me barely a minute ago.)
The other NPCs go the opposite route: they introduce themselves, give their entire backstories, and start talking about topics unprompted, when one of the things that made me love DS 1's NPCs is that they don't go on unexplained tangents or give out their entire backstories and motives within twenty seconds of meeting this stranger who they may well never see again.  There were other small things about the NPC interactions that rubbed me the wrong way: I could go into their houses and steal from their chests without them reacting, the blacksmith can't get into a house that has one wall and most of the roof missing, a few bits of dialogue were unintentional reminders that I didn't know what my character's goal or motivation are supposed to be.
I stopped playing partway through the first area, Forest of Giants.  There were a lot of reasons, but the two major ones were the enemies and the level design.  The hollow soldiers in the Forest of Giants meander about aimlessly, which is something the hollows in DS 1 explicitly don't do.  Even the unclothed pink ones in Lordran, the weakest ones with the fewest remants of humanity, generally have a sense of purpose to their movements--when they a swing a knife, they're doing it because they're trying to kill you, that kind of thing.  It's probably something to do with the way they're actually looking at the person they're fighting, whereas Drangleic's hollows' heads lol around like their necks only exist for decoration.  It sounds like a small issue, and maybe it is, but it's not very engaging to fight an opponent that doesn't care about fighting you.
Aside from the enemies, for every area in DS 1, it's possible to tell what that area must have been like in its prime, but I couldn't tell at all what the Forest of Giants was meant to be.  Some kind of fort, maybe, but nothing more than that, nothing about who must have built it or why they would have felt the need.  At that point, there was no reason to continue.  My character didn't apparently have any motivations worth speaking of, the NPCs weren't people, and there was nothing else about the world interesting enough that I felt compelled to explore it.

Dark Souls 2 is quite different from Dark Souls 1. It's exactly what its reputation says it is, to start with. If you played as much Armored Core 5 as you could stomach, gave up on From games for years, and decided to give the Dark Souls series a fair chance (like I did) you'd feel an immense sense of relief upon playing the first several hours of Dark Souls 2. It's far better-designed than its predecessor (other than, arguably, the weapon durability changes and the glut of enemies in ordinary suits of armor), better looking, and far better balanced. If something jumped out at you and killed you in one hit in Dark Souls 1, there was a regrettably good chance that it was the game's problems at fault and not yours. In the sequel this has been almost entirely resolved. Enemies are still quite tough, can kill in seconds, and are very thoughtfully designed, but you can overcome them with sufficient skill. The likelyhood of getting caught in an enemy's attack animation in a way that doesn't make any sense is also drastically lower in 2 than 1. If you've blocked Dark Souls 2 with your firewall(s) explicitly, it won't cut right through and start chatting with the servers anyway like the first one (somehow) did. If you're looking for a legitimately great game that's very difficult, yet very fair, it's hard to go wrong with Dark Souls 2. It's absolutely deserving of its reputation as a masterfully crafted classic. You literally couldn't pay me to play Dark Souls 1 again, and my memories of it have ruined Dark Souls for me entirely, but that's not Dark Souls 2's fault. Far from it. Someday I might very well go back to this one, on purpose and for free, even. I highly recommend it.

I say to hell with that it's not pretty and if you're that hard up for cash, wait for a sale. But it's a nice way to waste a quick hour if you like a quick horror game. If you liked Paranormal, you'll probably get some enjoyment out of Shutter. This storyline is a little bit more believable but the scares are dialed down. Play both games for a fun night of video camera footage horror.
There's no huge learning curve. The camera takes a moment to fire up and I'd prefer rapid fire shots, but that would make it too simple to take a ghost's picture, now wouldn't it? As you move along in the game, you get "upgrades" to your equipment to take better pictures of "camera issues" and such that may hinder your investigation. Personally, I enjoyed that. You can also go into first person mode. This is complete rubbish when you're first using it but you'll be counting on this later on to help you flee. Yes. You will be chased. Your drone will need you so it doesn't get boogled by ghosties. A love story between man and drone. Except man uses drone to capture footage of ghosts so I have to ask what sort of relationship this is.
The one thing I would have enjoyed was a little warning that there was flashing lights used (not like you're obligated to, but this is why I make myself the health guinea pig!). Yes I should have guessed when I noticed there was thunder and lightning in the videos, but I subject myself to this so that other gamers don't have to go "HOW BRIGHT ARE THE FLASHES, REALLY?" Enough to put you into a migraine or a seizure easily. There are lots of bright lights. Tread with caution if you are a gamer with a handicap that may be set off by flashing lights. Take breaks between chapters. I know the final chapters are about ten minutes long, but TAKE A WALK. Give your eyeballs a rest.
If you don't care for horror and want a little taste of something unusual, I say give Shutter a shot. If you're a diehard horror fan and you only like extreme experiences, skip it. This is a bit tame for your tastes. If you like collecting horror games because they're pretty fun to compare differences, then you needed to get this game YESTERDAY. Why didn't you get it yet?
I personally enjoyed it. I wish it could have been longer and a little bit more polished, but I can comfortably say it's not something you'll regret in the morning. Like that ghost lady. I'm pretty sure she doesn't regret anything, either. She was pretty happy to suck the battery life from my drone.

This game is basically a cheap knockoff of Magic: the Gathering.  While it has some interesting new mechanics, it's in essence just straight-up intellectual property theft.  It was enjoyable for a while, until I realized that it has learned none of the balance lessons that were learned by MtG over the years: they use rarity as a balancing factor, something MtG figured out was fun-kiling very early on, and they have lots of cards and mechanics that reward luck over good play.
What finally drove me away from the game was the atrocious mulligan system.  You get a single mulligan, and the new hand is guaranteed to have 2-4 lands.  There's no guarantee that they'll be the proper color lands in a multicolor deck, and the game has clear problems with its RNG as it'll land starve/flood players far more regularly than is statistically likely.  These factos combine to render a large number of games unplayable by one side or the other.  When these games happen in the play-at-will constructed multiplayer it's annoying but not a huge deal.  When they happen in the limited formats that require either arduous grinding or the expenditure of real money, it's enraging.

I'm a few hours in now, and so far the game is pretty good. It pretty much functions almost exactly like advance wars, which I think is what most people are looking for. There are quite a few issues though that should be pointed out that I hope they will fix:
Keyboard and mouse control is not good - things like not being able to use escape to close menus and issues navigating the map with the mouse. Makes the whole interface feel clunky.
The level score system is totally broken. It does not track scores correctly.
Fog of war system - I have no problem with the fog of war coming back when you leave an area, but what I do have a problem with is when I move a unit and the fog of war doesnt go away until after you end your turn. I understand why it was done this way, but it's really frustrating to place your unit somewhere, have no option except ending your turn, and having an enemy in the tile next to you that you could have attacked except for the fog. an option to let that unit attack if something is revealed would be nice.
Map scrolling - You are locked to scrolling only the areas you have revealed. Since the zoom out feature doesn't really zoom out much, it makes it really hard to see which directions you need to head, or gauge how large the map is. This is frustrating. Even more frustrating about it though, is that during the enemy turn your camera will follow enemy movements in these unrevealed areas. Just let us scroll the whole map man, like literally any other tactical top-down game.
Story - Jesus there is a lot of useless dialogue going on. Don't get me wrong I find the story interesting for the most part but it takes so damn long to get through the dialogue sometimes.
These are my main issues. Aside from these things, which are definitely bearable but annoying nonetheless, it really is a lot of fun. If you enjoy these types of games and can look past the issues, i definitely recommend it.

Patch 1.26's changes to gauntlet lead me to strongly believe that this change negatively affects players of all modes except Ranked. Especially new players.
Gauntlet is negatively affected for the obvious reason - less rewarding.
Draft is negatively affected because it takes more time to get gold (which would still be through grinding gauntlet albeit slower) to play the mode that is a big selling point of this game.
Casual is negatively affected because by equalizing the rewards of Casual and Ranked (post-3 silver chests), you're incentivized to play casual instead of ranked because it should, in theory, equate to more wins and thus more gold.
My biggest concern is the demographic that this affects the most - new players. If casual is now filled with people who are trying to score free wins (more so than it currently is), there's no safe haven for new players with poor game knowledge or unoptimized decks. Reducing the gauntlet rewards also increases the amount of time it takes for these new players to fill out their collection via draft and opening packs (and as a result, increases the amount of time it takes for them to be competitive in Ranked).
I only began playing this game a month ago because I heard it was very easy to play F2P and catch up with players who have been around  a while (which is a very important selling point in the current card game climate with so many viable competitors). If I were considering joining now and saw discord and reddit filled with people discussing how these changes do nothing but hurt most players I'd be strongly discouraged from joining and as a result would not spread the word to any potential new players that they should try this game (which I have been doing up until today).
I believe that this race to the bottom hurts everybody and only helps ranked in a short-sighted manner. By highly incentivizing a mode that is not friendly to new players, it hampers the ability of the game to grow. If the goal of this change was the equalize the incentives, it would have been better to increase the ranked rewards (I've heard that they were higher before). I understand that as a business, you need to make money but instead of making it harder for the current playerbase to achieve their goals, I believe it would be more financially prudent to keep this game in the conversation of best F2P card game which would grow the playerbase and thusly grow the amount of players willing to spend money.
In summary, this change to gauntlet rewards has hurt the game in all 3 of its best selling points (the low barrier to entry, the draft mode that allows you to keep the cards you draft, and the ability to become competitive in a short amount of time). I strongly hope that you will listen to the community and its negative reaction to these changes and undo them or offer an alternative solution. This game has provided me with plenty of enjoyment and I worry that my positive experience is no longer able to be had for players who would start today and decreases the rate at which it could grow as by hurting the unique features, it stands out less compared to competitors than it did this morning.
If you are a new player, you may enjoy this game but just know that your experience will be worse than anyone else's who started prior to this patch.

Tiny Metal captures the feel of Advance Wars nicely without being an exact copy. Apparently there's a new game plus once you've finished the campaign which will hopefully be a bit more challenging.  Plus there's lots of one off maps which I haven't even looked at yet.
A more detailed comparison of the game:
1.  There's no fuel or ammo limits.
2.  Tanks and helicopters are slower.
3.  I'm half way through the scenarios and there's no boats yet.
4.  Multiple units can gang up on a single enemy unit.  Only the last attacking unit assigned takes return fire (if the enemy is still alive).
5.  Vehicles can only be healed on factories, so for most games this means you don't heal vehicles.
6.  It doesn't cost money to heal units.
7.  Healing a unit is an action, it doesn't happen automatically at the start of your turn.
8.  Each unit gains experience when fighting, similar to later Advance Wars games.
In short if you liked Advance Wars, you'll like this game.

Tiny Metal by developer Area 35 and Publisher Sony Music Entertainment is a Japanese turn-based strategy game where you control various military units to complete the assigned mission goals. As you progress through the campaign, you unlock new units and learn new tactics to better control your army and complete your mission.
When you start the campaign, Tiny Metal presents a short tutorial on basic unit movement and combat. It covers the essentials but leaves some of the more advanced options to be discovered and learned by the player. One by one it introduces some of the advanced controls during later levels when they are needed, which feels a lot better than being introduced to all the concepts all at once.
Tiny Metal noticeably focused the most on making the main gameplay feel good. The gameplay is extremely addicting once you get past the tutorial stage and have more control over how you want to complete the missions. The player has suitable control over all their units and can decide various unit actions depending on the situation. These two features dictate the rest of the gameplay, whether that is beating all the enemy units, strategically capturing buildings, maintaining map visibility, or just keeping all your units alive.
The strategic side of Tiny Metal is also influenced by many tiny details within the gameplay. Units can attain different benefits depending on what type of tiles they are currently occupying. This can give you a needed boost during very close battles. An interesting feature that also has strategic merit is the focus fire option. With this feature, you can lock multiple units onto a target and attack with more damage, which helps immensely during some of the tougher battles.
Tiny Metal is also very visually appealing and sounds great. Unlike a huge majority of turn-based strategy games that have pixel-art, Tiny Metal has a very colorful and pleasant environment and game art that makes it easy to see what is going on and identify different units. The music is also different from many games which have 8-bit music, and instead has enjoyable music which lets you concentrate more on your strategy and tactics. The voice acting also sounds genuine and full of emotion.
One of the downsides I noticed in Tiny Metal right away was the long introduction to the campaign. Although most games need to explain the premise to the player at the start, Tiny Metal had a long introduction with a ton of information. Even though there is a fast-forward option, this takes away from the story. I became more immersed in the story during the short bits of dialogue before each mission, although the short interruptions during the mission were always a tad annoying.
Another downside I noticed was the level select map. Initially, I wasn’t sure what button to press to begin the next mission. I was also a bit off-put by the lack of mouse selection allowed during the level select, since it was a bit confusing on how to go back to the main menu without a mouse. After loading up the game again, the mouse came back for the level select screen, but occasionally it wouldn’t appear.
In short, Tiny Metal is a strategic turn-based game where you command your army and complete a variety of missions. If you’re a fan of most strategy games, then you’ll enjoy the amount of control you have and tactics you can use in Tiny Metal. The vibrant colors, art style, music, and story also make it a pleasant experience for any player, making it worthwhile for anyone to give it a chance.
Rating: 8.5/10

A steampunk-themed tactics game with an overworld. Unit models and graphics are okay (~N64 era quality). There is no tutorial, only instructions pages to read through.
There are a few hotkeys, but it's largely a mouse-driven game. I would've liked to be able to do orders (like move) through hotkeys instead of having to click the button every time.
As far as I can tell, there is no free camera, so you can't keep a traditional overhead view. The camera always resets to behind the unit when you move, which is annoying because I prefer an overhead camera that looks over all the action (and lets you see the big picture). It also means it's easy to get confused when switching between units if you have them moving through different areas at once. I gave up trying to move tactially with small groups (because I had to reorient myself every unit switch) and ended up doing a big groups of death for expediency's sake. It's easier if you group units by unit order (so the camera switch won't be as bad). Even so, I still made it a habit to check the map for every unit to make sure I sent it the right way.
Your move orders are cancelled if you switch units, which means you're forced to watch your unit move all the way to its destination. That feels like an unnecessary slow down of gameplay and a waste of time when you have to command up to 15 units each turn.
As a side note, pathfinding is non-existant (you click to move and it takes the straight line towards that point) and you can't queue up moves for future turns. However, it's nice that you can reserve AP for passive fire. There is a map for tactical battles but it's very barebones and you can't see structures/obstacles. If your unit seemingly randomly stops movement, it's probably because a new enemy target was spotted. The target info shows distance to target (so lower is better), not % chance to hit.
There are a lot of little things going on that it would have been nice to have a complete tooltip system. It would have also been nice to be able to create equipment presets that you could use on units (instead of setting equipment manually) and deployment presets.
If you're really into tactics games and steampunk, this might be worth a look. However, I personally can't overlook its flaws. I think someone could get into this game and learn its intricacies, but I don't enjoy fighting the camera/UI.

Airship Dragoon is an uber-hardcore, turn-based strategy game. Players take control of one of six factions and fight for control of Pangea.
I really didn’t think I would like this game. Most of the reviews, and even the description, say it’s for hard-core wargamers only. And there are lots of comments about bad UI. Not being a wargamer, much less a hard-core one, I wasn’t enthusiastic about this game until I played it. AD is really fun, though the UI is troublesome. The UI isn’t confusing per se, there’s just a lot of options. Before going into battle, you have to recruit soldiers then equip their gear. When on the battlefield, you need to press the move button to move units and the shoot button to fire at enemies. This takes some getting used to.
Each battle is basically a capture the flag scenario. You can place up to ten units on the field and maneuver them through the various structures. The goal is to capture the enemies flag while protecting your own, but I’ve yet to win without eliminating the opposition. This can be difficult because the weapon accuracy is ridiculously low.
One of the interesting mechanics is morale. Each unit has morale and as units die or are fired upon their morale drops. If their morale drops too low, then they can freeze up, run away, or even go nuts. When units go nuts they fire wildly at the enemy. Sometimes this results in enemy deaths. Either way, the announcement that someone has ‘lost it and gone nuts’ was always hilarious.
I’ll admit I’m still not sure what I’m doing most of the time, and I don’t take the game too seriously. But I’ve enjoyed every minute of this game, even when I’m losing. That’s unusual. This is definitely a niche game, though, and isn’t for everyone. While this isn’t typically my kind of game, I will be playing more of it.
Verdict: Get it on sale. It’s worth trying, but it has a limited audience and a high price.

The tag line doesn't lie - this is a pretty hardcore turn-based tactical squad game. Troops utilize action points to perform all of their actions and have varying attributes which are reminiscent of old X-COM - strength, reaction, courage, accuracy, etc. The only difference is health which is uniformly 100 regardless of class. You don't distribute points upon soldier promotion - instead they are boosted automatically based on class. Each class does get specific class upgrade equipment such as specialty explosives, weapons, and so on. These must be researched in the strategic layer, one upgrade per turn. Each one costs a set amount of money. I haven't found too much to do in the strategic layer other than purchase more dirigibles and research upgrades.
Essentially you assault a hex with enemies utilizing a dirigible transporting your squad. You'll need to outfit them prior which costs you cash. Equipment includes frag grenades, rifles, pistols, first aid kits plus specialty equipment previously mentioned. If you perform well you'll recoup your investment and then some after combat is finished. The tactical combat is slow and methodical. You select a stance for your soldier prior to movement - cautious is a crouch move which requires more AP per unit distance moved. Standard is regular movement and charge! is a sprint. You can specify whether to save AP for reaction fire as well. The stance selection is a bit annoying as once you've moved a soldier you can't change their stance. So once you move a soldier in standard stance, for example you can't have him crouch once he reaches a decent cover position. This doesn't make much sense tactically, though I can accept it for gameplay balance purposes. Crouching of course increases accuracy and decreases enemy hit chance. I assume charging carries an accuracy penalty. Typically your soldiers can take 1 hit, though if they get caught in the leg they might survive one more. Enemy 'hidden movement' can take an excrutiatingly long time and will likely test your patience, especially when the enemy squad is composed of only 9 soldiers. The tactical layer only provides bare bones information, for example if you spot an enemy you'll see the distance and whether you can fire. It doesn't provide hit chances at all. You can change soldier facing through the use of a button on the UI which allows you to click to change your facing. Trying to position your soldiers properly behind cover is an exercise in frustration though, as you click about trying to get them positioned properly. Enemy soldiers have always had reaction shots on my movement while my soldiers appear to stand about watching lazily, even when the have enough AP to fire and the enemy is in plain view. Frustrating.
With the realism mod enabled the terrain graphics are sufficiently attractive in the tactical layer though hardly amazing. The images on the store page are exactly what you should expect. Animations are stiff and unattractive but passable.
I recommend this game but only to hardcore fans of turn-based squad tactics. It requires an extreme amount of patience and fortitude to enjoy considering the wonky movement system, tactical stance limitations and 'what the heck' moments.
Edit: Please disregard Steam hours. I had originally purchased through Gamersgate and played fairly extensively before activating here.

Tacky jump scares galore, copious cheesy ghost laughter, and abysmally animated apparitions.
Shutter is a fixed camera (except when it's not) horror game that clocks in at roughly one hour of gameplay. There are no side quests, no extra content, and no collectibles. It is one hour of slow, linear gameplay. One of my favorite games, Thirty Flights of Loving, finishes around 13 minutes. The difference is, a games like Thirty Flights of Loving offers a unique and engaging experience, whereas Shutter only offers boredom, confusion, and the occasional mocking laughter when something goes awry.
Shutter’s story is played out both in real time and through several ~100 year old diary entries you discover around the property of a client's old house you’ve been assigned to investigate for vandalism. You control a small robot using fixed security cameras installed around the house, as well as a camera mounted on the robot itself, in order to investigate reports of graffiti. You’re a part of a team that does this professionally, and you have a dispatcher named Barry who checks in with you via R.A.V.E.N. Shield (Remote Access View of Environment and Navigation). Barry guides you through the game and provides software (and somehow hardware) upgrades to your robot. The house ends up being haunted by ghosts of the past, including the author of the diary pages. In a strange way, this aspect reminds me a bit of Luigi's Mansion. But the story creates more questions than answers...

Who is IGT?  IGT has been the leading company specializing in design, development, manufacturing, distribution, and sales of computerized gaming equipment, software, and network systems worldwide.  You can read more about the company
.
IGT Slots Paradise Garden is named for the Paradise Garden slot machine present in the package.  The package consists of a total of 15 IGT slot machines.
Functionally, the machines deliver a game of slots one would expect, especially those that have played these actual IGT slot machines.  For most of the machines I did a youtube comparison and the machines look to be very accurate.
IGT Slots Paradise Garden has two modes from which you can choose.   These modes are Career and Free Play.  For each mode you create 4 profiles.   For each profile you get a club card.  The career club card is broken down into Career Points, Bank Roll and Time Played.  The Free Play club card is broken down into Reward Points and Bank Roll.
The starting Bank Roll for Career is $1,000.00 and at first you are limited to penny denominations at each of the machines.  Only when the game determines that your career bank roll has grown sufficiently will the denomination be increased.  Denomination enumerations are 1 cent, 5 cents, 10 cents, 25 cents, 50 cents, $1, $5 and $10.  Playing career, it might be a while before you can bet and win big bucks, but then again, for that quick fix there is Free Play until you can elevate your career bank roll high enough to be able to activate the higher denominations.  The starting bank roll for Free Play is $10,000 and you can quickly increase your bank roll playing denominations of $10.
The denomination is essentially the value of one credit.  Credits you bet and win are displayed when you spin the reels.  When you first sit down at the machine you will be awarded a maximum of 10,000 credits for that session if your bank roll is large enough.  If you have a bank roll of $5000.00 and select a denomination of $10 the machine will display 500 credits.  A selected denomination of a $1 will result in 5000 credits available for the session and so on.  Credits are reset as you scroll through denominations.
Each machine as in real life has a Game Menu button and though I cannot vouch for it's authenticity the Game Menu button has a "Rules and Pays" option that will illustrate how to play the machine.  Oddly, each machine has a functionally duplicate button, sometimes renamed to Game Options that serves the exact same purpose.
From a functional view the IGT Slots Paradise Garden package delivers but like all video games there is the concept of immersion.  In other words does IGT Slots Paradise Garden  immerse you enough that you can believe that you are at the casino.  Unfortunately this is where the package falls short.
There are two casino themes that are available but each looks to be rendered as low resolution FMV and this detracts from the immersiveness.  The reels and icons on the reels are crisp enough to support the maximum 1080P resolution selectable from the game's options menu but the rest of the machine including many of the buttons are rendered in low resolution which also detracts from the immersion.
Immersive game-play is not just defined by video and by graphics but also by sound and music and while the reels are spinning the sounds and music are near authentic, based on my viewing of the machines on youtube.  However, once the reels stop spinning and the payout animations finish the game goes silent.  No casino ambience, no idle ambience, no visual or auditory feedback from the machines.  Further the package does not convey the illusion of video slots.  The reels do not look like they are spinning on a monitor.
Functionally IGT Slots Paradise Garden delivers authentic games of slots and on this alone the package can be recommended but I wish the developer had gone that "extra mile" and delivered a more immersive package.

I have to admit when I started playing this game I had very low expectations of it. But suprisingly I really enjoyed it.
I would describe this game as a puzzle horror game. You control a robot that is equipped with a camera. The robot has access to a computer that you use to receive orders from the person that sent you in there. The orders generally relate to power problems in the house that you are exploring and you are told to investigate these. However as you progress through the game you realize that there is a ghostly presence in the house haunting it.
This is when what I like to call the puzzle mechanic comes into play. The ghost will leave small clues around a room such as a floating plate. You need to take pictures of these items to trigger the puzzle. After taking the picture a new "clue(?)" will be revealed which you need to discover by taking pictures. It is kinda detective style investigations. This is what I really enjoyed throughout the game. Sometimes it can take a while to find these clues but that just adds to the investigative fun.
The game does also feature a story. This is told by notes found around the area. It tells the story of the women who used to live in the house. In my opinion this is the weakest aspect of the game. The story is very cliched and is frankly not told very well. I noticed a fair amount of grammar mistakes in the story as well. Although I believe you can just leave the story and the rest of the game will be enjoyable. The story of your robot and investigation is also told via the person giving orders on the computer. This is also not very well told in my opinion but can't be skipped because the gameplay revolves around it.
Shutter features a very unique control system. It is meant to represent old school horror games. You see the robot through fixed camera angles. This means the robot is very hard to control initially. You use classic WASD and mouse to control it but due to the fixed camera angles it can get very confusing with what direction you are travelling in. This takes a long time to get used to but I believe that after you get used to it the unique control is what is another main strength of the game. If you don't like this control scheme you also have the option to view in first person mode. However this is on a timer and needs to be recharged frequently so can't be used constantly.
Now the horror aspect of the game is done fairly well. There were many points in the game where it made be jump through typical game jump scares. They were very well done and the majority of the time I wasn't expecting it. The voice acting on the ghost and atmospheric music is also very effective.
Theres also a few other smaller points that I feel I should mention-
Overall I really enjoyed playing this game and I would definitely recommend it to people that enjoy horror and puzzle games.
Disclaimer: I was provided a review key of this game by the developer ahead of the games official release.

Shutter takes place in a seemingly abandoned property, where break inns are very common place.
For this reason the owner of the house has need for the players services, which are remote CCTV's and a little mobile Mars rover.
The mars rover is the games biggest part and controlling it and it's primary tasks, surveillance and picture taking is mostly okay and fun.
But then the so called horror element shows it's head.
The abandoned property is of course haunted by the spirits of the dead and for some reason they decide to try and scare the poor little mars rover.
Who of course is made out of circuits and metal.
And that is my biggest gripe with the game. Usually in horror games we control someone or even something that we can relate to and empathize with.
A person or an animal even, has the possibility of feeling fear and dread.
I myself can't find the emotional connection to the mars rover, that is needed for me to feel the fear it might be experiencing.
The player's character isn't in any danger. You just happily control the rover probably a hundred or more miles away from it. If you "die" its the rover that dies. It's replaceable and so it's possible battery drainage or death hasn't the same impact as a death in other horror games.
I do love the idea though with the camera surveillance and the rover itself but it would have needed some more refinement.
I can guess that it draws some inspiration from Fatal frame and Five nights at Freddy's, but in both of those series the player is in some sort of danger.
Now imagine this. You have the opportunity to go to Mars. First person to land there.
Amazing right?
Or you can send another rover there and take more pictures and soil samples which is important work of course.
I don't want to diss the rovers.
But I can guess which sounds more appealing to a lot of people.
Its an okay game, but for the horror I can't recommend it.
Maybe you'll manage to get a connection to the rover and proof me a heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

The developers absolutely aced the sound design, enforcing the tone at every turn, and though not necessarily a huge deal, the main character doesn't wear steel-toed boots like some other protagonists of similar games which, in those games, varies from distractingly loud to sometimes actually masking important noises.

I definitely recommend the game, but I personally got it from a Humble Bundle along with a bunch of other decent titles. if you can't get it in a similar form, wait for it to go on a super steep sale, as it only provides, at most, a few hours of exploring to open every little thing and consume all that there is.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a hardcore restaurant management simulator. You do all the cooking and serving (and the delicious *wink* *wink*) in your humble restaurant and, with the money you earn, you unlock new recipes and a variety of features to make your restaurant manager life easier.
Warning: I'm not kidding when I say "hardcore". This is not a relaxing strategy/management game. It is more a "get into flow mode" kind of game. More like Tetris level 15 than Cooking Mama. ;)
Cook, Serve, Delicious! is an amazing game that, in a way, redefines management games. Instead of a casual linear experience with a series of short levels, you're given a lot of freedom over how to manage your venture. It does require coordination, reflexes, strategic thinking and some trial-and-error guesswork.
If you love cooking games, try it.
If you're sick of casual management games and are ready for the next level, try it.
If you like a challenge, try it.
If you like games that push you all the way to a "flow", try it.
If you hate playing with strict timing or frantic situations, stay away.
If you like your games easy to master, stay away.
Overall, I think most people could love this game if they gave it a good try (knowingly getting into it)... and I cannot wait for the sequel.

Tiny Metal is a turn based strategy game heavily inspired by the Advance Wars series.
For people who are still waiting for Intelligent Systems to make a new Advance Wars, Tiny Metal is a pretty good alternative.
The gameplay revolves around producing units and controlling them on a square grid map with variable terrain and buildings, the goal varies but usually routing the enemy's units or capturing their HQ base. This can become addictive as you get rewarded for good plays throughout the game.
As a strategy game, it has an added element of luck with the introduction of critical hits which I'm kind of hesitant about, but it's not entirely game changing, the percentage to crit is really small but only goes higher with strategic positioning.
The Battle animations are pretty slow as they transition into the scene of the battle, something like a fast foward button will fix this but turning off battle animations amends this right now and heavily improves the pacing of the game.
The artstyle is appealing and fits the game imo, the units you produce are chibi styled as they are generic and you will have 0 attachment to them in comparison to Fire Emblem or Disgaea, since those games allow you to build your characters. Tiny Metal focuses more on the strategic aspect in gameplay.
The Dramatis Personae (gonna call them COs for now) are pretty distinctive in terms of character design, they represent their regions pretty well and are supported with voice acting which is pretty good. I wish the COs had their own abilities and powers but perhaps that will be added in as the development of the game progresses.
The music is pretty good as it generally has an upbeat rhythm, fast tempo and military arrangement which fits the setting of the game. The sound design could be better though given the cartoonish artstyle of the whole game, the sounds used work pretty well but it can be more distinctive.
The multiplayer has yet to be added yet at this time of writing the review but PLEASE add a 4 player free for all, it goes against the design of a fast game pacing but it works really well with friends.
The gameplay is addictive with unit producing and battling, the artstyle is cute and fits the mood of the game. the ost is great as it correlates with the setting.
Tiny Metal is my recommendation for an Advance Wars alternative or another Strategy game.

This review is a bit long, so get ready for some reading.
After about 6 hours of nonstop play from the moment I could buy it, I can definitly say that I recommend this game to anyone that's into Turn Based Strategy games. If you've ever played Fire Emblem or, most obviously, Advance Wars, you'll get the hang of things fairly quickly.
I have a rig that's overkill for a game like this, with an i7-7700k processor and an Invidia GTX 1080 GPU, this game ran perfectly for me, but I imagine that much weaker systems would have an easy time running it as well since it's not particularly graphicaly intensive.
While the graphics may not be to die for, the presentation is...alright. I know that this was made by a small indie team with a budget, so it is, to me, forgivable. The main menu is somewhat basic with many of the units from the game hanging out, looping through thier animations and making a little noise to accompany the music as you scroll through an easy to navigate menu, nice and simple. It's with the campaign that you can see where the budget was even more lacking, with a handful of background portraits set for most scenes and still images of characters with only thier mouths moving as they speak and or thier expressions changing as they or someone else speaks. It's all very basic.
From what I've heard so far, the music is just fine. A mix of orchestral and electronic, if I heard it outside of this game before playing, I wouldn't be sure if it belonged in an arcade beatem-up or an old WW2 shooter. The English voice over only affects what units say in a match with thier usual chatter as you move and use them, and I've found them quite charming, personally, but I can see how some may get annoyed by them. The rest of the game, however is spoken entirely in Japanese.
The gameplay has been very satisfying so far, my only complaint being that there are no naval or transport units. Since the game was made without those in mind, adding naval units without making new maps to accomadate them would be meaningless, but I'd love to see a naval update for it in the future.
Speaking of transport, though, it is a bit of a pain that you can't spend the extra cash in game to create a transport copter or APC to fly or drive your foot soldiers to a key point to capture or an enemy lab to explore, like in Advance Wars, since most of the units in the game are vehicles, your foot soldiers are outrun at times, but for the most part, foot soldiers have a much easier time taking shortcuts through hills and forests that are impassable or impractical for vehicle units to go through so that they may catch up.
As far as Enemy Labs are concerned, unlike in Advance Wars, where Enemy Labs were far and few between, there are several in every map, some giving you lore to read in the main menu, hidden extra missions to play in the campaign, or unlockable Hero Units for use farther along in the campaign. Without transport units and with the game's Fog of War, it can be a REAL pain to find and explore these labs for thier benefits since most of the important ones are hidden deep behind enemy lines and MUST be explored with any of the foot soldiers, generally, the weakest units in the game, meaning you must be sneaky with them or you have to pave the way to the lab, possibly accidentaly forcing the end of the map by destroying all enemy units on the way to it.
One of the most important features that Tiny Metal has over Advance Wars is the Focus Fire mechanic. You can have any unit that can directly attack any one other unit choose to Lock On instead of attack, which means that you can have up to four units attack the same unit all in one go. The last unit that you choose to fire has to pick the command Focus Fire to initiate and if the enemy unit is still alive after Focus Fire, they will counter attack that unit and no other. After playing for some time, I accidentaly found that you can Lock On with the same units over the course of multiple turns, with the same units attacking more than once in one Focus Fire sequence! Make sure to make liberal us of Focus Fire, since the combined firepower of several units makes for greater damage than each of them attacking individually with the added bonus of only one unit being counterattacked if the victim of Focus Fire even survives.
The next important feature that may be a deal breaker to some is that there is a constant Fog of War, it never goes away. It is explained in the opening of the campaign as to why that is. You will see on every map, blocks that signify the end of your line of sight, you cannot move your cursor farther than this until you explore near it. If you have any unit get near these blocks, they dissapear for the rest of that match amd you can see as far as that unit allows. Move away from that space, however, and you can still see that part of the map, but not what the enemy may be doing in it until you have a unit close enough to it again. Some may not like this feature, but with the use of the games Radar units, you can attack units in space that you have explored, but can't see into, making Fog of War something more tactical and less annoying, allowing you to play more offensively rather than defensively.
Taking a page from Advance Wars and tweaking it, Tiny Metal has Hero Units. Similar to CO Units from Advance Wars Days of Ruin, Hero Units are special units that have all around greater abilites than a standard unit, and can be summoned once into a match if a foot soldier interacts with a Relay Base. These Relay Bases can only be interacted with once, if you want more Hero Units on the field, make sure you reach these bases first. These Hero Units can then be placed any where within your units line of sight, but will be unable to do anything until the next turn, so put them behind some cover, but near the action so that they can tear into the enemy as quickly as possible.
As for the story, it's fairly simple, like something you'd expect from Advance Wars, but it takes itself somewhat more seriously, it's not terrible, but it's not impressive either. I feel that if the devs had more time, money and manpower, the story here could have been something pretty good, but for the most part it's just something that explains why you're moving from one part of the map to the next in the campaign. You don't see very much of most characters except for Nathan and Wolfram for the majority of the game and there isn't a whole lot of character development from really anyone. Overall, don't get your hopes up for a super compelling story.
There are plans from the devs to add multiplayer and mod support, both of which would extend this games lifespan exponentially, so those are things to look forward to in the future.
Aside form the main campaign, there are also Skirmish Maps that can be played one at a time, like Advance Wars, if you're looking for some fun with all of the narrative cut out. The AI seems to be hit or miss with me though, but I geuss milage could vary. There are times were I steamroll through a map with nary a hiccup, and other times where I'm given a run for my money, but can still see myself winning. For those looking for a challenge, you can play the skirmish maps marked for experts, or you can beat campaign mode, since I have heard, there's a challenging surprise for anyone that can get past it.
Overall, a very fun experience that I definitely recommend to anyone that is into turn based tactical games. The game is a complete product right now, as far as I'm concerned, contradictory to some other players out there, but hopefully, with some more support this game will become more filled out over time. Hopefuly, more people can get inot this game to show the devs that this is something to keep supporting, so if you like it, tell your buddies about Tiny Metal.

Unlike AW, I feel that the rocket units (Strikers in this game) are far too weak. Aiming at a regular tank (a Metal) deals a measly 30% damage, where an rpg troop (Lancer) can do up to 60%. It just feels weird to me. But that's a personal opinion.
As far as I can tell, you can't join units together to heal them like in AW, but that's excusable. Would be nice to have though.
Voice acting is excellent, but some of the subtitles are misspelled. Very minor.
A few semi-major gripes I have/bugs I've found:
1. When using a controller it's hard to tell what you're highlighting for selection because the color of the highlight is so dark.
2. If you use a mouse and keyboard on the mission selection screen the mouse cursor disappears. It's easy enough to navigate without it though. (bug?)
3. There are no transport units. No transport copters, no APCs, nothing. That's kind of a big deal to me, but they said they would continue updating it so perhaps they will add those later.
4. If you fast forward a battle sequence (A button on an XBone Controller) shooting animations become glitched. Rockets no longer leave the barrel of the Lancer's guns, cannons recoil but no explosion to launch the projectile is there, etc. (bug) Although it is worth noting that this issue seems to resolve itself after a few engagements.
5. Fast forwarding a battle sequence also seems to force future dialogue sequences to be force fast forwarded as well, as though it defaults to the "Fast Forward" option rather than the "Next" option. (bug)
6. Game is really, really easy. I breezed through a good chunk of the campaign in about 2 hours without really ever running into a situation where I felt like I was in trouble if I didn't play flawlessly.  It's really easy to run Shock & Awe strategies because the AI really doesn't do much aside from capturing buildings and sending their units to certain doom (riflemen against a tank, yeah, that'll work for the fifth time this turn). This allows you to build up a massive army and overrun them very quickly. The tactical layer leaves a lot to be desired.
However,
So far, I'm really enjoying it, but I do feel a slight twinge of buyer's remorse.
If you liked Advance Wars or enjoy turn based strategy in any way, I would reccommend this game to you maybe on sale, just don't expect too much of a challenge.

Airship Dragoon is an old school squad tactics game.  This game is not for everyone.  It is really only for hard core wargamers.  I love this game, but I have been playing games like this for a long time.  The graphical interface is a bit clunky and difficult to use, but it gets easier after you are used to it.  There is a map, but you have to switch screens to access it (maybe this adds to the realism since it feels more like reading a map).
This game is frustrating at first when your squad consists of militia.  Tactical gameplay elements like morale and accuracy mean that the conscripts will have trouble hitting anything and will run away when shot at.  But once you separate the men from the boys, you can build an effective squad.  The game has well thought out promotion, class, and technology systems, so your squad will improve in capability over time.  Eventually your men will be able to hit distant targets and will keep fighting even after being wounded.  This also means that it can be a major blow if one of your veterans is killed in action.  Fortunately, critically wounded soldiers can be evacuated if one of their comrades can reach them in time.
Like many tactical games, the strategy aspect is mainly a mechanism to make the battles significant and give them some context.  But the strategy game is also well thought out in terms of game elements and play balance.  There are some imporant strategy elements like dirigibles, garrisons, and terrain types.  They each play a role in strategic operations and game economics.

Game : Outlast
Score : 8/10
Summary :
Without spoiling the plot and or storyline i can tell you this game is amazing, do i dare to say it? yes, yes i will in my oppinion it surpasses the first Amnesia.
Outlast is a very nice designed game where you as an journalist have to infiltrate an abbandoned mansion, or is it abbandoned? there is not a single moment in the game where you feel safe.... well maybe if you hide in a locker, but thats the only moment really! ;)
The only "weapon" you have is a camera that has 2 modes, dark mode and a bit less dark mode... called nightvision among the people that know what they talk about.
I highly suggest you buy this game if you are a fan of Horror/Tense/Suspension and jumpscares, trust me, if you play this game with your lights out, you will be afraid.
I finished the game in rougly 7+ hours with friends at my side... yes i was to afraid to play it on my own
Good things about Outlast
- The graphics are nice and it perfectly fits the entire atmosphere of the game
- Its good that you can not carry a weapon around cause that will take away ALLOT of fun from this game
- There are ALLOT of jumpscares in this game
- The ending has a very nice plot-twist and it will screw with your brain a little.
Bad
- There are scripted events in the game, unfortunately you know when they happen taking away some of the fear.
- The camera still works eventho its batteries are dead ( it works less tho )
- The AI of the enemies are a bit meh, you can kite them in circles for minutes!
All in all Outlast is an amazing addition to the Horror genre in the gaming industrie, it deserves a place next to Amnesia and the first couple Resident Evil

The Crew is an okay game, it offers such a wide variety of feats. Skill challenges, Races in PvE and PvP and now including The Summit with stunts and freedrive challenges in it's latest expansion. In return however, the game has so many pet peeves that can bother a player to stop playing forever. Like a finish line delay that could lose you some seconds while playing with people outside your region, the ability to exploit some obstacles to gain seconds and a slightly messed up balance between vehicles.
People hope for the best experience in every little aspect of the game, but The Crew is so massive that it can not offer this. As a result, The Crew does just about average in everything. You're not supposed to like The Crew because of sounds, amount of cars, customization, graphics or handling specifically. It expects you to like the wide selection of literally everything it has. Would it do better for players liking specific feats if the game chooses to minimize it's offers? Yes. You'll leave other people disappointed however. It's up to the developers to offer the best experience out of everything it has. You can see they 'slowly' improve on some stuff, but with each pro comes it's cons.
I like The Crew because of it's variety and I try to look through the well-known pet peeves to enjoy an actual fun game. So far I think I'm doing a good job at it. I'm coming back to the game from time to time to see if anything new happened.
Should you buy The Crew, the Season Pass, the Wild Run expansion or anything named together for the full price? No. Wait for a 50% discount. This will cause you less annoyance, but still have a jolly good time in a fun open-world racing game.

This is a pretty good game, for the most part.  However, it has some rather glaring annoyances that prevent it from being a great game.
First, the pathfinding of airplanes on the deck can be a little unpredictable at times, and if you accidentally send two planes down the same path, the AI does *not* handle traffic jams.  The two planes will just sit there and glare at each other until you resolve it yourself (and by the time you do that, they're probably *both* too late to do any good).
Also, there's no way to change the type of plane assigned to a mission after it's queued up.  If you rush an F-18 onto the catapults to deal with the battleship that's about to blast your carrier into flotsam, but you selected an A-3 when you queued the mission, then it will just refuse to launch.  Your F-18 is fueled, ready to take off, and loaded with the correct weapons, but it's not the exact *type* of airplane you wrote in your schedule, so apparently it must be meant for some *other* mission.  Can't go sinking battleships without following the proper *procedures* now, can we?
When this game works, it works *really* well.  Sort of a controlled chaos as all sorts of threats fly at you, but you're on top of things - your search planes are in the air, your fighters go out to destroy targets, other planes come home, and nobody explodes in a giant fireball because you forgot to clear the landing strip.  And when you screw up, it's just as delightful trying to salvage the situation - rescue the crashed pilot, abort the next landing so you have time to put out the fires, scramble a chopper in the nick of time to sink that submarine, and now you can start to claw your way back.  But because of the fast pace and the way that one mistake can snowball into total disaster, these small annoyances can quickly turn into keyboard-smashing frustration.
I'm still giving this a recommendation, but be mindful of these annoyances so you don't get screwed over.

This game is a bit challenging. Not in the least because the mistakes of now only come to sight for you later, when it can be too late. With the wrong starting map seed, it is very hard to do things right on your first (or second, or third, or fourth) village. This can easily make you give up hope of ever succeeding. That almost happened a couple of times here. But don't give up. Look it up on Google or a source like that, find a recommended map seed, then try again. You might stumble a few times and have half the village starve to death (like when you accidentally run out of tools or clothes), but that means that you have a chance to recover from the error because the demand for that particular resource is less for a while.
If you lose half your workers in say, farming, shut down half the farms during the next winter and slowly build up a new workforce. You can do it. And if it becomes very hard, don't hestitate to play on easier difficulty. There is no shame in that. Not in a game like this one. For this game is fun because it doesn't hold your hand the entire way like some games do. When you make a mistake, you have to figure out for yourself where the mistake was and how to best fix it. As such, the game is highly recommended, simply because it requires more effort to learn and to do right. Easy in this game can easily qualify as hard or even brutal in another game. But that is simply because life as a settler like this is brutal.

Having just finished this game after about 35 hours, it's left me with mixed feelings. Dark Souls 2 is a solid game, it was fun to play, and I was entertained enough to play it all the way through. Having that said, the game is by no means without flaws, it has many flaws in fact, some that are excusable, others that really take away from the overall enjoyment of the game.
Let's start with what this game does right: it's still dark souls. All the combat still feels like the original dark souls, there's still multiple ways to play the game, and this time there's even character customization. Leveling up still feels good, putting souls into making your character better still feels like it's worth it. Same with weapon upgrades. Most of what the first Dark Souls game did well, this game does well. One thing I like that Dark Souls 2 did that the first didn't, is the NPC invasions, I like this idea, even if I'm not fully human I'm still presented with the invasion challenge. I just wish they made it a bit more random than they did.
Now getting to what I didn't like so much, I'm going to start with the most blatant issue to me: the progression. The progression in this game is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. From the hub area of the game, off the bat, there are so many areas you could go to, and there's no way of really knowing which is the right one without looking it up. If you don't go to the correct area it feels like the game is being cheaply unfair. This shows even later in the game, it's never like the first game where things are blocked off until you get to it through the first area. Everything is more like a spiderweb than a cleverly constructed chain with ties into itself. Another huge problem with progression is, in my opinion how estus flasks were handled, until I looked it up I didn't know estus flasks existed, and I was just using the crappy one time use healing items. It would've been helpful if the game made it a bit more apparent that these items were in the game.
Speaking of the areas feeling like a spiderweb, let's get to the level design. The level design in this game is overall solid. Nowhere near as good as in the original Dark Souls, but it stands it's own. It has a different feel from the first game, if they threw an area from the original Dark Souls I would be able to tell, which is an aspect I like about Dark Souls 2. I just wish the progression between these areas was better. There is one exception to this, there is one area in the game that felt poorly designed, and the only reason it was a challenge was all the poison projectiles everywhere, but apart from that the level design was solid, but nothing too special.
Another problem I had with the game didn't show until the end of the game. Towards the end of the game, I feel like Dark Souls 2 realized it wasn't difficult enough, and decided to just buff everything. At a certain point, there's a massive difficulty curve, which felt more annoying than it should've. Normal Dark Souls difficulty shouldn't work that way. The rest of the game doesn't have any horrible difficulty curves, but the final areas of the game really didn't need to be as artificially tough as they were.
Speaking of difficulty curves, I should mention hollowing. Hollowing in this game lowers your max health, a lot of Dark Souls fans have a problem with this mechanic, I actually really enjoy this new twist. It gives hollowing a real reason to reverse and makes it feel like dying is ever more of a game mechanic instead of a necessity. Also, it makes player invasions more likely than in the first Dark Souls. In the first game, you can completely avoid player invasions, in this game, it's more of a mechanic than an annoyance.
As mentioned in the beginning, the combat was as good as it was in the first game, except for one element. Parrying, in this game parry timing, is not at all what the first game was, and I never got used to it, for me parrying was a waste of time and health. Giving a delay between when the button is pressed and the actual parry makes it really annoying.
The final complaint I have about this game is a minor complaint, but for me, it took me out of the experience. The NPCs in this game didn't serve any real purpose. There were a few NPCs that you could do a lot of work for, and maybe get something cool. But for the most part, it was more worth killing those NPCs. In the first game, the NPCs clearly had a use, and although you could get a cool item by killing them, you'd lose something in return. In this game, most of the NPCs are better off dead.
Overall it's a solid game, but it won't have any special place like the original Dark Souls did. Once I got to new game plus I didn't see a reason to go again like I did in the original. It's a solid game, but to me it's not worth another playthrough. I'd say this game is worth it at a sale price, or buy the version without DLC, this is not a 40 dollar game. If I didn't play the original game and have it as a comparison, I'd give it a 7/10. But having played the original game, and loved it, I can't help but feel this game just disappoints a fan like myself, if you loved the first game like I did, it's more of a 6/10. If you're looking to getting into Dark Souls I'd say start here, it's a good place to start, it's in my opinion the easiest Dark Souls game. Or if you'd like you can skip it all together and start at the first game, it's really up to you.

multiplayer, something interactive where you can react to, be it coop (send planes to your friend) or versus.

This is not the first review I wrote for this game. My first attempt was fueled by annoyance, thus it wasn't exactly objective. I will try harder this time :)
The game is a 'Souls game. That is solid. The game is solid. Graphics are better though less spectacular compared to DS1.
Controls are better, Keyboard+Mouse support is better (it does forget I disabled doubleclick every time I exit the game), no need to use mod for that anymore. And yea, don't let anybody fool you, it is fine to play with KBM. I personally blame controllers for the lock-on targeting, which I hate greatly - though the feeling is mutual for sure.
The game is hard but... okay, not fair (souls games being fair is a lie, always was) but still enjoyable. If I could end the review here I would give it a thumbs up. I didn't because I can't end it yet.
Cheap traps and ambushes are frequent, hitboxes are ridiculous. You get grabbed and eaten or just plain stabbed by enemies who missed you 2-3 meters.
And yea, pvp.
The game sports a weird multiplayer system.
You play alone in your world but other people enter it. Either you summon them or they force themselves into it.
There are different signs for those who want to engage in "jolly cooperation" and those who want to fight you in pvp but those are all summoned by you by activating their signs.
You get penalty from dying, your max health is lowered (commulative, max. 50%) and you cannot use signs until you remove the penalty.
The problem comes from invasions. Certain items and covenants allow the player to forcefully enter (invade) other players' worlds.
- Invader is not attacked by monsters.
- Invader cannot heal with normal healing items.
- Invader can heal with healing spells.
- Invader can use item to leave the world.
- Defending player can be hollow.
- Defending player can heal properly.
- Defending player is still attacked by area monsters.
- Neither player can leave the area (save for defender going inside the boss's door, thus initiating the boss fight).
- Defending player cannot forcefully evict the invader save for killing them.
- Defending player cannot exit the game or they suffer a penalty for a while.
- Neither player can use the waypoints (they are bonfires here).
So, at first glance it seems pretty balanced right? But let's go into it a bit deeper!
- Drinking main healing potion has slow animation and you are standing still. Yes, you are only alive if the other party is nice enough to not kill you 3 times during this time.
- Other healing items may not force you to stand still but will still slow you and only heal over time, slowly. You will have enough damage to heal from at the end of the animation for sure.
- All of the above assumes you have any of those left. Even spells have limited uses, that are replenished at the waypoints, akin to the main healing potion.
- Neither player can replenish anything at waypoints since they are locked after invasion starts.
- Defending player is geared towards PvE and PvE items and spells are usually not that good for PvP. They need time to change their equipped items and as for magic, you can't use any spell, only those you could equip (have limited slots)... at the waypoint... which is now locked.
- Defending player has been fighting monsters all this time so their healing items dwindled, used up their spells, damaged their equipment and are most likely not on max health.
- In DS1, having death penalty you couldn't play multiplayer at all until removed it. In DS2, you cannot use signs to summon help but can be invaded. Remember, death penalty involves lowered HP.
- The invading player is in top form, they expect to fight a player, have every item repaired and are geared towards PvP not to mention all their consumables, spells, etc. are on max.
- Also, the monsters are still there, with all their love for your a*se.
Supposedly, once you fought against an invader, lost or won, you cannot be invaded for 30 minutes. This would be nice - except it's not true. There are certain areas in the game which are "protected" by certain covenants - players who belong in these covenants can automatically invade you anyway given you enter these areas and many of these areas do not allow coop play. Lovely.
The following people might invade you:
1. NPC
Predictable but cheats obviously.
2. Those that don't know what's happenin.
"Entered some covenant, got some ring. Why is there a loading screen? That ba*tard is attacking me!" - you can win. They are more confused than you are.
3. Those that want to try pvp.
They are prepared, got their best items in. Not favorable but you might best them.
4. Those that play pvp and want your ar*e.
Knows what's effective and uses them. Knows glitches and uses them.
5. Respectable PvP player.
They don't invade. Stabbing some already half-dead guy is boring, not worth the loading time.
At the same time it's pretty good if you are offline (eg. steam offline mode) though. NPC invaders are still there but they are not that much of an issue. If you can put up with that, then the game is worth playing, quite a bit. I got it on a sale, was worth it but do yourself a favor and buy DS3 or DS1 instead.

The main con for myself is the small community.  For example only 65 players were online for US servers on a monday at 4pm.  All the squad slots were full so you can either create new game or wait for a new one to come up.  We joined a game and it was full in around to 15 minutes so that was cool but just minor inconvience.  You can run this game fine on older hardware but I feel like anti-aliasing is a must because there will be jagged edges everywhere in the distance if you have it off.  This can make spotting enemies hard if you dont have the power or if you are not willing to sacrifice other graphics for AA.
Mechanics and gameplay feels good and is pretty fun.  There are a couple different game modes but you will only find yourself playing the main one called frontlines.  This gamemode introducing the trench warfare is pretty unique as others have stated.  A quick glance is it is basically attack and defend but if the attacking team does not take over the trench within time, the attackers immediately has to get back to their trench as they are now the defenders.  Failing to fall back will result in death after a small timer.  There are several times at which your game will end in a draw because sometimes it is hard for either team to capture trenches.
It only takes a bullet or two to drop someone to their death so this means you will probably die a lot, especially in the beginning.  Rushing across no-mans-land is intense and takes teamwork, dedication, skill and some luck to get across.  The heavy machine gunner will need to have the bipod down in order to shoot. Each kill feels satisfying, especially if you manage to fight off multiple enemies in front of you.  The rag-doll physicis are pretty funny, especially when watching a dead guy twitching in the barbwire.
This game is intense, fast, and fun.  Even with the small community I rarely have trouble getting into a full server and always have fun.  With that being said I recommend this game.

Pros:
+ The few back and forth matches that happen from time to time are actually incredibly complex and fun
+ Constant stream of packs, generous rewards
+ Mana system allows for wide variety of decks
+ Similar to Magic the Gathering
Cons:
- Most games go into top deck mode
- Mana screw/flood is absolutely infuriating
- Legendaries are very expensive
- Stubborn playerbase (will elaborate)
Here's the official developer's stance on getting mana screwed:
I think this is very misguided. CCGs are fun not because everyone is a serial gambler who wants to coin flip everything away. Variance is fun when it allows every match to be different, with different decisions to be made. Take League of Legends for example, variance and depth both come from champions picks, which you can counter by changing your playstyle. As far as I am concerned, every match where I'm mana screwed is the same. I have no decision to make except watching a slideshow of the opponent interacting with my face.
Since the playerbase is comprised of mostly Magic players, anybody who is not satisfied with the mana system is usually discredited and directed to play chess instead, which is very insulting. Also, while the deck-building element is fun and a strong argument for the system, it simply becomes available too late to new players since a diverse collection takes a very long time to build.
Another praise I often heard for the game is its complexity and decision-making, which is why I became interested in the first place. Again, this holds true for deck building but during a match, you go into top deck mode pretty often and the game is often decided when one person gets mana flooded.
Verdict:
Overall, Eternal is a near exact copy of Magic. To me this is a good thing, since the base gameplay is already very fun and unique. However, I cannot recommend this game, since it will also result in some of the most infuriating gaming experiences you will ever face, and the developer's stance on the issue means the situation will never be resolved, and the game will never significantly differentiate itself from Magic.

In short, CSD is probably the most satisfying "mash buttons in a sequence" game ever made.
The gameplay loop is simple:
1. Pick a prep station;
2. Read the order;
3. Perform the order specific sequence of actions;
4. Optionally wait some time and push the station's button again.
Learning the sequences required for different dishes and performing them lightining fast is extremely satysfing thanks to a multitude of great game design choices. Many simpler meals can be cooked in a single motion, thanks to how well thought out the 'recipes' are, and the more complex one can be easily memorised (on keyboard), due to logical key bindings, such as all meat toppings in a pizza having their first letter of their name as their hotkey, and all veg/fruit toppings the second letter.
Additionally, the visual and audio design in the cooking proces is top notch. Placing an ingredient will often shower the screen with crumbs, the slap with which, for example, the dressing and toppings hit the salad bowl is both visibly and audibly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic and the music matches the mood perfectly, with slower tunes during off hours, and more dynamic, tension building tracks during rush hours and various challenges.
Outside of cooking for 12 hours of every day a weak, the game tasks you with trawling through a spam ridden mailbox, taking on catering challenges and participating a cooking show, upgrading your foods and choosing your menu for the day. While the UI can be sometimes suboptimal in those parts, it never stops you from enjying the meat of the game, while adding some spice to it.
No matter how you slice it, CSD is an extremely solid, if somewhat limited in scope, game. If you enjoy games that make seemingly dull and repetitive tasks fun, such as Papers Please, you will enjoy this little delicious treat.
Do note that the sequel to this game should be coming out soon at the time of writing, and it seems to be bigger, better and with a richer pallete in every way, so you might want to hold back from buying this one at the full price.

Verdun is a WWI game about combat in trench warfare.  There are many squads to choose from, each with their own perks and challenges.  I, for one, love this game.
For the point of view of gameplay, it is a bit slow, and I die a lot (maybe that's because I'm bad at the game), but it is definitely fun and exciting.  It is a fun game to play with friends, too, as it's nice to shoot some guys together or shoot each other.
From the point of accuracy to history, this is phenomenal.  I studied WWI for a bit, and it is just very interesting.  I played the game and saw a good amount of accuracy involved.  The gas masks are different from class to class,  The guns are specific to each squad, and so much more is so good with this game.
I highly recommend this game for history nerds, but not exactly the WWII thrill-seekers.
