-Brief Review-
Looking for a Metriodvania with style? That is Sundered in a nutshell. Gorgeously illustrated (you'll know what I mean if you look at the previews on the Store Page), Sundered creates a unique atmosphere and feel with its alien Lovecraftian aesthetic coupled with some fairly frenetic gameplay at times. I recommend this game if you're looking for something in the genre that does things well while tweaking the formula just a bit. For a more in-depth discussion of Sundered, please continue reading below (does not contain story spoilers).
-Long Review-
From Jotun developers Thunder Lotus, Sundered is a true-to-form Metroidvania experience. The player character Eshe roams different regions, collects power-ups and upgrades, and pits herself again some truly alien foes and environments in the process. On the surface, it is exactly what one might expect from a Metroidvania kind of experience. But Thunder Lotus alters the experience in a few ways to make things a little fresher. While not innovative, these changes affect the pace and challenge of the game.
As a Metroidvania experience, Sundered excels when it comes to the bread-and-butter experience of the genre. The environments invite (and require) non-linear exploration and offer a feast for the eyes and the mind all the while. The color schemes and feel of each region are very distinct from one another: tech-based armories, soaring alien cathedrals, claustraphobic caverns, and some visually memorable vistas for puncuation and flavor serve as backdrops to the exploration and combat.
And speaking of combat, let's talk about hordes. Rather than statically placed enemies, Sundered uses a dynamic horde system that sounds excellent on paper: you've just nailed a serious set of jumps without taking damage, landing in a chamber you've safely trod before, but then the bizarre gong and chimes sound and dozens of enemies begin to crawl and fly and lurch into view! On the one hand, it's great because it definitely keeps you on your toes and feeling a little anxious even when retreading a region. You never know when the hammer's gonna fall and you'll be knee-deep in mobs. On the other hand, when you're legging it back to a platforming section half a region away that you just can't nail yet, it can get tiresome.
Sundered does a reasonable job with enemy variety in my opinion. Each region has native enemy types, and like a real rogues gallery, the player will get very familiar with the strengths and weakness of each one as they spawn in horde after horde. Combat in Sundered gets very hectic very quickly once the screen gets chock full of projectile spewing fliers, lurching melee, and sorcerers that wall you off and spawn AoE attacks on your head.
Fortunately, Sundered has extremely tight controls, responsive air control, and a fairly excellent dodge rolling system like many action oriented side scrollers have nowadays. Eshe feels nimble and, after enough upgrades, is a real force to be reckoned with, capable of mulching and blasting through hordes of mobs. Eshe's power is in fact dependent on killing enemies and being killed herself, as she both earns upgrade currency from fallen enemies and containers found during exploration as well getting thrown into the level-up screen on death back in the Sanctuary, the game's hub and "bonfire" if you like your Souls terminology.
Eshe's statistical advancement does allow some choice in her upgrades with a number of branching points in the upgrade tree. These, however, are largely closed advancement loops, and with enough grinding you can max it all, though it would be largely unnecessary depending upong difficulty and skill level. Customizing Eshe's playstyle is accomplished through perks. Perks are earned through boss kills and by getting through endless horde spawning challenge areas. The changes perks can wreak can be rather transformative when it comes to how Eshe plays. Like being a crit monkey? Or would you rather be tankier? Maybe you just want to blow the hell out of things with you cannon? Perks accomodate the player in a way that's more typical in a straight action oriented game; so that's nice to see in a Metroidvania title.
Eshe's powers and world-found upgrades are what you might expect: double jump, air dashing, etc. However, I'd like to make special note that Thunder Lotus didn't waste or cheat with the upgrades by only making them "key" powers: i.e. they just get you to another place or open a door. While they do that yes, they also affect how Eshe plays and contribute to the power curve she climbs. For example, you acquire a power that lets you charge up a melee strike in a given direction: this both hits like a train and is useful in combat but it also allows you to shatter certain barriers, making Eshe more effective at both combat and exploration. Kudos, Thunder Lotus. None of the powers felt like duds to me.
Sundered uses both static and procedurally generated environments. While the regions themselves have a rough lay-out, the connective tissue, like rooms and corridors and such change between deaths. It's never so great a hurdle that it feels like a pain but it does make each run from the Sanctuary a little different. And I mean just a little. Thanks to the assets used in each region's palette, you hardly notice the shuffling once you get used to it. So mixed points there: I doubt Thunder Lotus really achieved their design goal of it being an ever shifting environment as it didn't particularly feel drastically different between deaths, but it also didn't detract from the experience in my playthrough.
Each region was a joy to explore thanks to the art and the occasional exposition-dumping chamber that doled out some interesting voice-over and lore. Environmental and platforming hazards are present and vary in concentration between each region; being able to bypass these quickly and gracefully as Eshe becomes more mobile is particularly satisfying.
At the heart of each region is a boss. While the regions contain mini-bosses, each a souped-up version of a region-appropriate enemy, each main boss is very visually unique but sort of similar in terms of mechanics and tactics. Your mileage may vary, but I found them distinct enough in gameplay for it not to be a gripe. And, it should go without saying, that their art assets are just breathtaking.
Without going into spoilers, I will just say the story delivers on themes of exotic mystery, alien motivation, and cultural strife, and I found it quite enjoyable.
Finally, let's wrap things up with replayability. Sundered does a good job of encouraging the player to run through it a couple of times, try out different perks, and even affect the story a bit through multiple endings. Having just finished through my first run, I'm looking forward to playing through again. Which is not something I can say often about Metroidvanias save for the best examples of the genre, so high marks there.
For the time-oriented crowd, my first playthrough took about ten hours, and as I feel I'll get at least another playthrough out of it, I'm very satisfied with the purchase. Thanks for reading, and have a good one!

When it comes to open-world racing games, this is one you'll at least want to try. The story is pretty boring and as generic as it gets, and the selection of cars seems somewhat random, but let me tell you where this game shines the brightest; the open world.
Ubisoft has managed to take the entire country of The United Sattes, and shrink it down and put it into a racing game. The car customization is pretty good if you are looking to make your car the way you want. The performance tuning isn't wonderful, mainly just a "this piece is a higher level than this one so it's better for your car" but that being said, at least it has actual car parts to upgrade (tires, suspension, gearbox, etc.) instead of just upgrade speed or handling. But like I said early, where this game shines is in the open-world exploration. It has dynamic and chaning environments with rain and day/night cycles, a vast variety of landscapes raning from the tropical florida keys, to the big NYC, the snowy mountains of the northern rockies, the dry deserts of the southwest, and the beautiful coast line of California. And taking a large road trip in your favorite custom car and exploring the world is one of the best things I've done in a video game before.
There are plenty of side activities and challenges to do, and plenty of fantastic roads to explore and drive on. If you are looking for an open-world exploration game with car customization and racing, this is the game for you.

I was absolutely surprised from the get-go how stunningly this game performed. I've dabbled with Flight Sims previously, but Flight Sim World has really allowed a smooth transition into a more serious manner of Flight Simulation. The introduction missions, easy-to-learn and setup controls paired with ongoing compatibility additions with equipment really make for a welcoming experience. My Thrustmaster T16000 set was easily configured and I was flying in no time.
Loading into my first flight was quick and easy. I chose my plane (beloved Seneca), selected my destination in the Flight Planner and even adjusted my fuel and payload to add to the experience. I set the weather to an average fair conditions day. The cold-and-dark checklist is fantastic for newbies to each aircraft. They really allowed me to get a grasp of starting and eventually shutting down the aircraft. Controls are responsive and realistic. All operable facets of the aircraft models worked exactly as expected. The fantastic, tedious design of each aircraft really shows. Each plane has a very high fidelity model like you've never seen before - each and every one look amazing. My one suggestion - an issue every flight sim runs into - is to improve upon ATC and surrounding AI. While surrounding AI are smarter than any stock AI I've experienced, I've love to see an emphasis put on them along with ATC.
With the implementation of TrueSKY weather, no flight is the same. Having to fly around (or through if you're brave enough) thunder storms, blizzards, heavy shears makes for a truly immersive flight. TrueSKY will only continue to improve and add to this wonderful immersive flight facet. Weather affects aircraft performance as it would in the real world - colder outside air temps will naturally improve performance, for example, while a hot day would burden it. Weather is an important factor to get right in a Flight Sim and FSW have nailed it. As it stands, there is no similar weather experience - and I can see it only getting better as improvements are made.
The graphics in FSW are outright glorious to gawk at. The graphical teams really did a number. Reflections, weather, shine, cockpit fidelity all look gorgeous. The sounds of each aircraft also sound accurate and realistic - an issue many Flight Sims have to start with (and continue to do so). Performance has been spectacular on my 1060 6gb. To my knowledge there's optimization tweaks in the pipeline - I'm already experiencing fantastic performance and I can only imagine what the future holds. I would definitely like to see a V-Sync feature as well as more in-depth graphical options however.

The new DLC "The Crew Wild Run" seems pretty cool, I don't actually own it. But from what I've read all the new "Extreme" specs for vehicles are pretty well useless outside of the actual DLC content.
Cars aren't very accurate in this game either, and the customization isn't all that amazing. The exterior of cars you can do a bit of stuff to but the rest of the car not so much.

More on the tuning system real quick though. I bought a Koenigsegg Agera R which only has perf spec, but I thought "you know, this is a game all about cars right? so even though this car can only do a perf spec it should still be incredibly fast since its actual specs are amazing right?" Well in real life the car stock can do 273mph which is roughly 439kph right, but in this game with perf spec, AND fully upgraded with NOS and all that fun stuff, this car struggles to even get close to 400kph. I don't actually know what the stock car can do in this game, but im assuming it'll be close to like 200kph. Moral of the story, if you wanted a game all about cars, and thought "wow I can take a stock Lamborghini and put NOS and do all this stuff to it, this is gonna be ammazing, it'll be so fast omg" it won't happen. My fully upgraded circuit lambo can do like 430kph while using NOS going down a really steep hill, even though the car should be able to do over 400 stock.
Probably sounds like a rant, but for real, I bought the game to tune my badass cars to my liking, not have every vehicle cap out at the same speed based on what "Spec" it is.

Thanks for my friend's encouraging me to get all three soul games on Steam after I've completed them on Xbox last year. Also his willingness to do all those achievements for me is appreciated.
First of all, I do have to say, the graphics on PC is much better than Xbox. It's not obvious for DS1 since the graphics is real, but I was stunned the moment I walked out of the cave connecting Majula in DS2 (I even dropped a tear). Praise the sun ! I've always believed that the world of Dark Souls is perfect but this wonder makes it beyond perfect.
DS2SotFS is my favorite soul game. The story is rich and the game has the best DLCs (with my favorite Ivory king boss fight and Fume knight of course). Oh and Lucatiel, my love. I'm always following your steps. May your sorrowful-but-charming voice lead the way.
And warn me once more : Do NOT release Navlaan, the Royal Sorcerer.
Unlike DS1 or DS3, DS2 begins as a traveler, not a prisoner or a nobody crawled out of a coffin, and a traveler is to persue a truth. Wondering around in this world, I know that there's a king for my to find and a castle for me to explore. Where are they ? Why are they gone ? The desire for truth drives me throughout my journy. From the extra title of GoTY edition, the second soul game is about a "scholar of the first sin."  What could "the first sin" possibly be ? I believe that it means to link the fire. "The great king's gone, to link the fire." Hence the world falls into darkness. People blame the king for his absence.  As a scholar, you found the truth and save the world. Is the story really this simple ? If King Vendrick was wrong, could Gwyn be wrong ? We thought we saved the world. could we be wrong ?
"Be gone."
NPCs keep telling me this. First by the Head of Vengarl and last by the Queen in Ivory DLC. Dark Souls II's world needs to be left alone. Covered by fire or ice or darknss, the world we encountered is quiet and still, and dead. I love this deadness in Dark Souls II. It shows eternity and respect, not like some mosquitos in DS that will die if I don't feed them or squirming worms in DS3 (stop squirming, please).
No words can describe my love for this series.
In your darkest time, someone will always be there to guide you.
Have faith.

This is an awesome idea, and the gameplay is... ususally fun, and tense at times, with great graphics! But unfortunately, the UI issues and AI pathing issues plague this game nearly to the point of monitor-breaking frustration. The UI often simply doesn't respond to your hectic clicking, or will select the wrong option or aircraft. In other cases, the hitbox to select a certain aircraft or selection is ridiculously small. And the AI pathing is mind bogglingly bad, with two aircraft heading to places near each other simply not able to find a way around each other. Also, there is no queue system for your movement orders, so you cannot queue aircraft to do action x after completing y, or to move to spot a once the aircraft in that spot moves. Which leads me to one of my biggest frustrations: if an aircraft is rearming, and you give it a move order, it will CANCEL the rearming to move the aircraft immediately, meaning you have to start from scratch!
Finally, go-around probability is waaaaaaaaay too high. I understand that if it was the same as real life, it might not happen in 50 or 60 hours of game time, but this is still kinda ridiculous! Aircraft go around practically every other landing, resulting in frustrating crashes with aircraft that would have been safe had the landing aircraft not gone around. I understand it's a gameplay mechanic, but it needs to be toned down a good bit.
EDIT 8/17: Aircraft come back damaged waaaaay too often, which screws you over 9 times out of 10 because your only available heli to kill a sub came back damaged after one mission, and crashes on takeoff. Or even worse, your 4+1 Battleship missions get screwed over because You can't mix and match aircraft? Need 4 blue aircraft, and have two blue harriers and two f18s? Nope, sorry, absolutely impossible.
Tl;dr: I want to love this game, I had quite a few fun moments with it, but awful UI and AI issues make the game unreasonably hard due to it's own rather iffy design.

Having given myself time to chill out after my decision to play this game a tad too long after being on tilt due to the RNG screwing me over, and over, and over, and over again, I'm going to try making this review simpler and speak/type with a clear mind. If you only want to read this opening bit, I still recommend this game if you like Hex or Magic already, but don't make the mistake I did and take a break from time to time. To anyone else, read on.
I've said this game is surprisingly good, which is true. I'm a Hex player, but I find myself coming to Eternal when I'm bored or just want a quick card game run. This isn't my main card game and may not be any time soon, but it's nice to have as an option.
I've said the AI seem to cheat and the RNG may favor them over the player. I still feel this way, though I have started to see the AI get screwed with their resources, but not nearly as often (2 or 3 games thus far) or for as long as I have as a player (2 turns max, while I can either screw or flood for anywhere from 4 to 6 turns minimum). It feels somewhat unpleasant going to a Forge run at this point, knowing my cards are completely random and may lack synergy from time to time (though I also do still feel the drafting system in this game will help you build your strategy IF you can start it early enough) while my AI opponents have preconstructed decks built around a single tactic with no variance. At this point, it feels better losing to a player than losing to an AI. With a player, I know I was outplayed, or their deck was simply better than mine. Against an AI, I only feel they drew exactly what they needed right when they needed it, such as a flying blocker one turn from death against my flight deck, or an instant kill ability the minute I play something (anything) large to break a stalemate or defend myself with.
Despite my frustrations at this point, I'm still glad there is an option to play PvE to either advance a player's collection, or simply as an option against only playing PvP. I've been working on a Fire aggro deck, most of the pieces coming from Forge or Gauntlet runs, so while what I have now isn't very powerful, I know I can keep working to make it better by earning packs for 100 stones a pop, saving up for the cards I need for the decks I want. Did some Casual play as well, and I was able to at least hold my own with what I have. Do I expect to win often with my current collection? No, but as it stands, I know I at least have a chance.
I still love that you keep what you draft. It's a simple thing, I know, but still. I can advance my collection 25 cards at a time (if I specifically pick cards I don't have/will need later like I'm currently doing for Stranger cards, instead of building something that could possibly win) in Forge runs, and I intend to do an actual draft to see if the amount of cards I can get is different or not.
However, I still feel my biggest complaints are the AI due to how much it feels like they cheat and the incresed wind-up as your units get bigger. While it may be petty, the increased wind-up time is time I could be using to advance my current duel and move to the next, instead of sitting at my PC doing nothing.
Again, if you already play Hex or Magic, give this game a try. For Hex fans (specifically PvE ones), it's a nice, though obviously less feature intensive, alternative/addition while we wait for things like Raids, Guilds, Keeps, and AZ3. For Magic fans, it can be a good replacement for Duels. At least you'll know WotC won't randomly decide to screw you over by killing it, like they seem to often do with anything that isn't Standard for their paper product.

Gone Home is a great experience and I can't believe I didn't play it sooner. From seeing short gameplay clips without context and the setup of you coming home to discover your family is missing, I assumed it to be a generic horror game, and how wrong I was. The greatest selling point for me is the incredible detail of the house, modeling everything from light switches to invoices lying around, which adds a great deal of flavor to the experience. The developers really put a lot of thought and effort into making the house feel like a real, lived-in place.
Even without supernatural happenings or scary imagery, the game manages to evoke a mix of dread and curiosity, sucking the player into the surprisingly grounded narrative. While the whole setup and style of delivery could be considered gamey, it serves the purpose of guiding the player through the game without them missing important storybeats. While heavily based upon how you play and explore, I found the pacing to be really focused and enjoyable.
Although the story plays around the time of my birth and internet or even computers are absent from the house, I felt right at home in the world of Gone Home. If you struggled with themes like mental health, sexuality and identity during your teenage years (and who hasn't), I'd wager this game will heavily resonate with you.
This all sounds great, but the truth is that you probably already know if you like this kind of experience or not. There is really limited gameplay and only light puzzle solving and if you don't want to spend your precious gaming time with lots of reading, listening to diary entries and no action at all, you'll probably be disappointed (and I guess you won't even read this far).
In short:
+ great story
+ great atmosphere
+ great pacing
+ topics that don't get explored often in games before recently
+ punk soundtrack!!!
- lots of reading
- little gameplay
If you read this far, buy it.

I'd say AuroraRL is basicly the spiritual sucessor to the Starflight and Star Control games for MS DOS, which by itself is amazing since there hasn't been anything quite like those for decades. For fans of the MS DOS game this is a nice game and you'll most likely enjoy it, despite it's shortcomings here and there. Almost everything's in here, your ship building, and traveling and exploring space, researching sciences, contacting with alien races, scanning planets and landing where you want and adventuring with your landing party, however, unlike the original, you can't create your crew from scratch. You can contact with your ship's crew, although to be honest I can't stand Gordon and Sarah, I get that you are a smart and merited scientist Gordon, but don't tell me you want to run complex psychological tests on an alien you know nothing about, I know damn well that your Ph.D doesn't cover that! I'll let your morphine addiction pass but I won't tolerate clinical malpractice on my ship.
As for Sarah, I just don't like that she lets my ship fall apart and lets everything break and I'm afraid of going to her quarters because I dislike the music she has playing there.
Other than that I enjoyed the characters so far, and the music is excellent throughout the game even that one at Sarah's I guess, I just personally dislike it. The visual side is very good, although the textures on planets could be more varied. Something I really miss in this game is that there aren't energy shields (or at least I haven't found them yet) I think they would add a lot to the space battles because so far they are pretty straight forward. Lastly there's also the english translation that could use some proofreading. Personally I don't mind it, but I imagine some people may be put off by this. Overall i'm very happy with AuroraRL even considering that it's still in early access I had a lot of fun with it. I think that any person that enjoyed the Starflight  and Star Control games will enjoy this to some degree, and in case you haven't played the these games, perhaps you'll enjoy this as well because it uses a very unique formula that isn't used at all anywhere else (that I know of).

This game is the PC answer to Mario Maker but with the added feature of 4 player simultaneous multiplayer both local, online and any mixture of the two.
UCH is a sandbox and a platformer with a dollop of strategy merged in to a competitive multiplayer experience.
Gameplay Summary:
Overall objective: Get the highest score before the match ends to win.
Gameplay Details:
Get from the start to the goal on a round by round basis until a score threshold is reached or the round/time limit for the match is up.
The beginning of every round is a build phase, either creative or a random assortment, there is also a twitch integrated mode where chat can vote for the objects to be used by the players.
After all participants place their objects the round begins and everyone controls their character in an attempt to reach the finish while avoiding being caught in traps and navigating the placed objects.
If all players of the match reach the end or fail- no one gets any points.
Making the object of the game to make the level difficult enough for the other participants to lose while you still succeed.
The controls are tight and responsive. Directions, Jump and Run is all you need.
Plays well on both gamepads and mouse/keyboard setups.
Sound design is above average until you get to the music which is absolutely excellent and clearly has a lot of love put in to it.
There is voice acting but it's fair gibberish at best though it does add quite a bit of personality to the controllable characters.
I highly recommend this game for the fun factor.

This game has recieved a lot of criticism due to the combat being "messy", "chaotic", and "unfair". Personally, I love how fast paced and unpredictable it is. It's really refreshing for a metroidvania, and it makes other metroidvanias seem slow and predictable by comparison. The random element means that sometimes a horde of enemies will spawn when you're in an inconvenient location, like on a narrow platform or surrounded by environmental obstacles, but that doesn't mean you have to stay there. In most cases, you're free to move anywhere you want. A large part of the strategy is using the environment to your advantage, finding temporary safe spots and choke points so you don't have to deal with too many enemies at once. Sometimes this means frantically running for your life until you find a suitable arena. I find it quite exhilarating.
The combat never feels unfair to me, mostly thanks to a very forgiving damage system featuring an energy shield that regenerates over time. You don't take damage until the shield runs out, meaning that, with a little practice, it's entirely possible to get through most normal encounters without taking any damage at all. Seriously, it's not that hard (at least on Normal, I can't vouch for the other modes).
I'm choosing to focus on the combat, since it's such a divisive topic, but the whole game is great. The controls are very responsive, and it has just the right amount of open-endedness without being overwhelming (see Hollow Knight). And, of course, the animation is outstanding, but that goes without saying. I just got to my first real boss fight, about 3 hours in, and I already feel like I got my money's worth. This game deserves more attention.
UPDATE:
Just finished my first playthrough, still love it. I've always had mixed feelings about metroidvanias, and this is the first one I've ever actually completed (I usually get hopelessly lost about half-way through). The map system gets extra points for always giving you the information you need to progress without holding your hand, and I'm a big fan of the half procedurally-generated design that constantly keeps you on your toes, and prevents you from relying on memory.
The hordes do get pretty overwhelming at times, and there are certain areas where they spawn infinitely, far faster than you can kill them. In those situations, your only hope is to just get through that area as quickly as possible while minimizing damage, almost like an auto-scroller. It's pretty intense, so I guess not for everyone. I think it's comparable to Cuphead, in terms of both the overall difficulty and the quality of the animation. Like in Cuphead, most of the individual enemy attacks are simple and easy to avoid, but you're always dealing with a bunch of them at once. It's tough but fair (the Cuphead of metroidvanias?).
I realize that my update slightly contradicts my original review. The difficulty ramps up significantly after the first boss, and the final boss took me at least 2 hours. So yeah, it's harder than I thought, but that doesn't change my recommendation. The boss fights are epic, btw.

Sundered is a fun game- frustrating at times, but overall really enjoyable.
The graphics are easily the best part of the game. Animations feel impactful and fluid, which is important considering how difficult it can be to keep track of your character in the middle of a horde.
Speaking of hordes, it's a gameplay decision that feels kind of inconsistent. Enemies attack in groups, which come in different sizes of groups, but overall it just leads to a jarring sense of back-and-forth between downtimes and active combat. The quiet sections are nice for traversing the map, and eventually you catch on to tricks that help you maximize the downtime (for example, interacting with an ability shrine or "lore" room will instantly kill all active enemies).
My personal favorite part of the game is the procedurally generated rooms. It's an odd design choice but feels really well executed, as portions of random corridors separate key locations such as perk locations and boss rooms. The biggest complaint is that there isn't enough variety- all of the rooms become very familiar once you get to the point where you've explored most of an area.
Second favorite part are the "first" two boss fights. While it's true that The Cathedral's boss can be fought before the other two, I went in the same order both playthroughs. It was almost disappointing for the final bosses that I feel like the first boss you find naturally had more effort spent on him than the four final bosses combined. That said, the art style is a redeeming quality, especially for the final boss of the Embrace path.
Overall? A very solid game. Very enjoyable and well worth the price tag. It feels like it would have been so much better if it simply had a bit more development time, but it's still a fun and conceptually interesting metroidvania.

This is a nice atmospheric version of the old Warhammer Quest board games.
Rather than taking just the spirit of the old board games and making a modern, turn-based video game, this plays and feels very much like the actual board games played out.  This means that the strategy of the game comes more from character choice, equipment, and tactics rather than making different character builds by leveling up stats and abilities.  The old board games had static level-ups for each character that could not be altered, the choice was who you took and leveled up, not how you leveled them.
That is reflected in how this game plays out and, with the deluxe version, you have a fair cast of characters to select from.  Plus there is the ability to delete characters from your roster and have new ones take their place, but you have to level the character up at least one level to do so which can be a pain (because you are probably just deleting the character because he was too hard to level up in the first place).  Characters gain exp based off of how many kills they had in a dungeon run (with no exp gained if they died), so if a character has a low hit rate and can't kill enemies, they are prevented from leveling and improving their hit rate.
But, these old board games were designed to make it hard for a party to finish the adventure.  These were co-op games (maybe playing against a GM), and what fun is a board game if you are going to win every time?  That difficulty is reflected in the game with frequent misses and large hordes of monsters that can quickly overwhelm your party.  This isn't poor video game design, but a mechanic imposed by the board game so that each adventure wasn't just a walk in the park.  As this game is recreating that board game experience, so too does it recreate the high chance of failure.
Still, I wish they would have added a die roll for attacks and such (just a little die shaped icon with a number popping up would have sufficed) so that I know what my chances are for hitting enemies with each character.  Maybe they are underpowered for that enemy type, or maybe they just had bad luck.  Without some indication of the math that is going on, it makes it harder to choose targets and attack types with the different characters in my party.
As far as the in-game purchases go (I'm always against those), I say only buy the deluxe version.  The content is priced way too high and should have been included with the base game.  And you should probably wait for a good sale on the deluxe version at that.
All in all, the production of this game is quite nice with animations for the towns, beautiful artwork and music, and fluid dungeon battles.  Even the quests are presented with short story texts just as they had been in the board game versions.  If you are looking for an immersive game that has that old adventure board game feel, this is a nice ambiant recreation of that experience.  If, however, you are looking for a more straight forward, turn-based, strategy video game this may be a little too oldschool for your tastes.

I'm writing this review of Flight Sim World as a flight simulation enthusiast since 1979.
After obversing Flight Sim Worlds development over the last few months it's clear that this will be an extremely expensive ride for those that wish to take advantage of what the extra memory available for addons that will be provided by the move to this 64bit update to Microsoft's FSX.  I am prepared to spend considerable money, and have done so over many years with FSX and X-Plane to get the most authentic, interesting and fun experience I can in flight simulation.
I'm not sure how many engineers, modellers and artists Dovetail have working on this sim but I don't think it's very many and it's clear every little feature that will advance the product to the quality we've all come to expect will be provided by 3rd parties at 20-40 dollars a pop.  Buying addons like this is fine (and necessary) on an old stable engine but on a new release? What are they bringing to the table? Currently, apart from a few minor enhancements and a huge amount of lost content it seems it's just a DLC store on steam.
For those of you who don't play Train Simulator, Dovetail have clearly demonstrated their lack of interest in product quality and passion for their craft by their treatment of the train simulation community over the years. They have produced copious amounts of generic, often low quality content at extreme prices on a very unstable engine that constantly breaks existing purchases that often never get fixed.  Train Simulator only becomes fun for me when buying buying 3rd party products mostly from a small number of vendors who really care about train simulation and have the ability to develop addons that reflect that care. In addition the workshop (which I'm sure they will advertise for FSW  as a major feature as well) is an absolute nightmare to use and finding content that will work with my existing trainsim purchases is a way too much work to bother with.  Nearly every scenario to download from the workshop for trains and routes I own requires about $100 or more worth of DLC purchases to work.
I for one have no faith in this company to execute on developing a platform that I want to invest in. If they win out I think we're in for an incedibly mediocre and frustrating flight simming life over the next decade.  I would wait to see what's in the base product at release day before making a purchase of Flight Sim World and its DLC.
The fundumental problem with Dovetails strategy on Train Simulator is to force yearly upgrades to the latest versions. By a competent company this might work but with Dovetail this provides an unstable and moving target that is always buggy and always breaking existing purchases. It's a stupid strategy that has already proven horrible for customers and I'm expecting they will implement the same release strategy for FSW.
I received this product for free when Dovetails Flight School was cancelled. I certainly would not pay for it and after a quick look at what was on offer I have no interest in playing it at this time. Let's all be smart about this and wait until they actually have a final product we can evaulate before making DLC purchases.   FSX came with considerable content on it's release day as part of the base product which has now been removed, will Flight Sim World come with considerabe content as part of the base product? Please, let's make them work for our money by forcing them to make a high quality product that actually advances our experience as flight simulation enthusiasts.
I'm extremely worried we'll see a repeat of Train Simulator for flight simming, believe me, we do not want that.

For a long time, I had the 'not interested' checkmark on this game.  I had it on my iPad - and its a reasonable game there.  Not great, but nice graphics and there for a dungeon crawl if you want it.  But $15 for the game on PC and another WTF price for the item pack to get the other characters?  Nope. Not interested.
And today, the package is on sale for about what I'd expect to pay for a good game on the iPad.  And while it didn't show up for me in various screens, the Warhammer sale thats on now I cought a glimpse of it and said to myself "well, $6 is an 'I can be interested price'".  So, now its in my library.
Now, first and foremost - this is a tablet (its a pain to play on the phone) game ported to desktop.  There's no getting around that.  Some of the interface options had to be changed around (there's the "how do I get the inventory? On the tablet I rotate it...").  If you are turned off by good phone games that have a direct port to desktop (but with an acceptable interface), its not the game for you.  If you do buy it, you're going to go "ug, touch interface, don't recommend, give me a refund".
Getting past that, its a good dungeon crawl game.  With the extra content (buy it a steep discount sale), its a good game that you won't be looking at the "$2.99 for a new character?!" screen and delete it out of spite.  It brings me back to the days of Wizardy on the Apple ][+ - select a few characters, go into the dungeon, kill things, go back out.  Repeat.  Except with much, much better graphics and some light tactical gameplay.
There's no question if this will show up on my laptop for play when I'm bored in a meeting or other presentation.
Accept it for what it is - a port of a well done mobile dungeon crawl and you'll enjoy it.  Obsess over it being a port of a mobile game and it isn't the game for you.
I'll certainly get my $2.99 or $5.99 out of it.

Thanks for my friend's encouraging me to get all three soul games on Steam after I've completed them on Xbox last year. Also his willingness to do all those achievements for me is appreciated.
First of all, I do have to say, the graphics on PC is much better than Xbox. It's not obvious for DS1 since the graphics is real, but I was stunned the moment I walked out of the cave connecting Majula in DS2 (I even dropped a tear). Praise the sun ! I've always believed that the world of Dark Souls is perfect but this wonder makes it beyond perfect.
DS2SotFS is my favorite soul game. The story is rich and the game has the best DLCs (with my favorite Ivory king boss fight and Fume knight of course). Oh and Lucatiel, my love. I'm always following your steps. May your sorrowful-but-charming voice lead the way.
And warn me once more : Do NOT release Navlaan, the Royal Sorcerer.
Unlike DS1 or DS3, DS2 begins as a traveler, not a prisoner or a nobody crawled out of a coffin, and a traveler is to persue a truth. Wondering around in this world, I know that there's a king for my to find and a castle for me to explore. Where are they ? Why are they gone ? The desire for truth drives me throughout my journy. From the extra title of GoTY edition, the second soul game is about a "scholar of the first sin."  What could "the first sin" possibly be ? I believe that it means to link the fire. "The great king's gone, to link the fire." Hence the world falls into darkness. People blame the king for his absence.  As a scholar, you found the truth and save the world. Is the story really this simple ? If King Vendrick was wrong, could Gwyn be wrong ? We thought we saved the world. could we be wrong ?
"Be gone."
NPCs keep telling me this. First by the Head of Vengarl and last by the Queen in Ivory DLC. Dark Souls II's world needs to be left alone. Covered by fire or ice or darknss, the world we encountered is quiet and still, and dead. I love this deadness in Dark Souls II. It shows eternity and respect, not like some mosquitos in DS that will die if I don't feed them or squirming worms in DS3 (stop squirming, please).
No words can describe my love for this series.
In your darkest time, someone will always be there to guide you.
Have faith.

AuroraRL is a rather rough, yet very compelling space adventure. Tasked to explore space, establish alien relationships and discover the whereabouts of a missing craft, a considerable amount of time will be required to see everything this game has to offer.
Ordered to locate the disconnected Aurora 1, the Aurora 2 is deployed, taking heed that a successful journey through the Star Systems require resources, relationships, and information. A large galaxy map outfitted with a coordinate system contains many Star Systems, creating the world in which the Aurora 2 will navigate and explore.
Upon completing the extremely lacking “tutorial”, intel lead the crew of the Aurora 2 to the Klisk’s home world. As a race known for working as space merchants, with a very strict code of honor, the first step towards finding the missing craft is achieved with an exchange of favors. A quick escort quest rewards locational information of the major races’ home worlds. With no restriction on exploration, the player is then free to lead the Aurora 2.
When traversing the galaxy map, Star Systems provide locations of major interest. Inside are fully instanced, “galaxy maps” of a smaller scale. Star Systems are comprised of: gas giants, planets, moons, ships, etc. Each object of interest may be scanned or interacted with. Ships (if friendly) can sell goods or information. Planets, moons and other non-gas giant objects can be scouted using a Landing Party.
If a planetary object allows for landing, a quick scan will allow the player to choose the location of landing. A small map will aid in determining whether landing is beneficial by marking resources (needed to repair the ship, etc.), life (for research purposes) or key points of interest. Upon landing, a terrain will be generated and the Landing Party will begin their exploration.
The Landing Party is comprised of variable crew members (Scientists, Engineers, and Military Personnel). Their weapons and inventory may be personalized before deployment. Unless the planet is oxygenated, a decaying oxygen meter will dictate how much oxygen is remaining before a return to the spacecraft is necessary for replenishment. The Landing Party is controlled as a singular unit. A numerical health indicator represents the life of a crew member. Once that number fully depletes, a crew member will die and the number will reset until all crew members are dead.
Each planetary object will have a different terrain/biome. Some will be inhabitable, eliminating the need to utilize an oxygen reserve. Others will have environmental hazards or creatures that will attack upon sight. A flat, rectangular map is provided to mark the relative locations of interest, including the shuttle. Although flat, the boundaries of the map do overlap to create a continuous seam. Regarding planetary exploration, a few minor grievances experienced are listed below.
:
If a hostile creature/ship is discovered, it can be defeated utilizing the crews’/ship’s weapons. The battle system is a hybrid between real-time and turn based systems. Upon encounter, pressing the “Fire” button will project a grid of the applicable range. If in range, enemy targets may be individually attacked. Running away (by physically moving the Landing Party/ship) may result in some free hits from the enemy.
If the ship happens to be destroyed, the game will end. To alleviate this burden, AuroraRL maintains an autosave feature, along with 4 dedicated save slots that can be used at any time. If a save is utilized during a dialogue option, the re-load will start the dialogue from the beginning.
The ship hull starts with 10 pips of health by default. If damaged by an enemy ship, repair is performed by assigning Engineers to repair the hull, along with utilizing resources (bought or discovered from planetary landings). Research, which rewards the player with new weapons, maps, etc. are progressed by assigning Scientists to a particular task. There are only a finite number of Scientists/Engineers, and if deployed on a task, they may not be used in a Landing Party.
The graphics are somewhat lacking in regards to the planetary terrain and outer space. The screenshots in the Store description will help provide some insight. During important discussions/plot-related events, or dialogue, higher quality retro style images will be used. Although the graphics leave a lot to desire, it is a far cry from being bad, just sufficient for immersion and plot progression.
The HUD needs to be reworked to improve the quality of gameplay. During space exploration, it is a bit tedious to continually hunt down the information needed from a quest log, or to assign crew members to a task. During planetary exploration, the HUD will sometimes block the view of a creature in line of sight, creating an opportunity for ranged damage if the player continues moving the party. An auto-hide feature would remedy this particular problem.
Every screen in AuroraRL, with the exception of the space background, is presented through a window (similar to a computer screen window). It would be more immersive if the dialogue and menus would be more incorporated into the background/game. Also, not allowing “Esc” to exit a window also adds tedium to the gameplay.
For those that are not aware of the Early Access concept, it is perfectly acceptable for bugs to be present (only minor ones observed) and game mechanics to be missing. AuroraRL is still relatively new, and a developer update was released last month.
With everything taken into consideration, AuroraRL is definitely recommended to those that are fans of space adventures. Although there are minor bugs and a lacking UI, the compelling storyline and exploration easily makes up for it.

Reviewer Background: I started playing Magic: the Gathering in 1997, when Visions was the new set, gathered cards from much older sets, and finally stopped playing at the time of Future Sight. I'dpoked at Hearthstone but never found it overly compelling beyond the novelty of a digital CCG.
Eternal finaly managed to sell me on the notion and get me to invest in not only my first CCG, but my first new CCG since my M:tG days. The game feels comfortably familiar to old-school M:tG, but with fresher elements at the edges and some of the better ideas I witessed from Hearthstone - and the sort of mechanics only a digital game could provide. The five "Influences" map to the Colors of M:tG roughly - Shadow/Black, Fire/Red, Time/Blue, Justice/White, Primal/Green - but have unique wrinkles to differntiate them (Primal, for example, has a large focus on card-drawing Fliers that Green traditionally lacks, and Time has sturdy weenies and ramp that traitionally would be foundin White and Green, respectively).
The deck-building utility is elegant and efficient, and there are many very playable archetypes with plrenty of room for experimentation.
But most of all, the game is incredibly generous, providing a geat number of free decks and providing daily rewards to gather Packs and cards with minimal effort.
10/10 - if you're looking for an excellent, old-school style CCG, love weird west settings, or jsut want a free-to-play game that is genuinely free? You should be playing Eternal.

Platforming, puzzles and Oh my Golfballs does this game get annoying!
There is nothing actually broken or incorrect wrong with it, per say, but the mental loops and back-tracking you have to do in this game is problematic to say the least.
You are a light plug (I assume) whose job is to find all the blocks in a room.
You start a room with no blocks lit, and anytime you bump into an area where a block is hidden, that block is revealed and blocks you.
Using a jump and bump method, you have to move around a room without falling through the room into another room, until you find all the "lit" blocks.
That is easier than it sounds.
The catch is that if you don't find all the lit blocks in a room before leaving it, the room resets and none of the blocks are visable again.
At anytime you could jump and no block will be there to stop you and you could jump or fall out of that room into another unlit room.
OR, you could land on an automated conveyor belt which whisks you out of the room against your control.
OR, you could have to teleport (a power you get later) and find you don't have enough teleport power to ever leave the room.
OR you could do what I finally did after getting one achievement:
This game would only be "fun" to a sadist who likes to torture themselves and glees maniacally at the prospect of lighting up another pointless room so you can hear the same looping "finish" music that never stops haunting your dreams.
Despite the high reviews on this product, I urge you... if you have a love for life and can find something to smile about at least once a day, stay as far away from this horror as humanly possible.

I'm not really big on writing reviews, but i figured that such a GREAT game deserves one, so here I go about it.
Gone Home is an atmospheric game, as an atmospheric game could ever be. Usually people, when they start a review, tend to give a plot outline on the game but I won't do that. All you need to know is that you character has gone home after a long time away.
Having said that, this game is ALL about it's narrative. There aren't any puzzles, nor enemies, nor obstacles, nor nothing. Only the narrative, and the discovery of what's going on around your home. Figuring stuff out is not hard, but you get sentimental as you enter deeper into the story.
About the story, it is touching, heartwarming and emotional. It's like that movie you see that makes you think about it for weeks to come. Also, it's really short -- took me less than 4 hours to finish it -- but think about it as a movie that you control the steps of the protagonist.
All in all, I get the feeling that I wrote a lot of words that don't really concatenate. If you're in doubt whether you should buy it or not and you read my review thus far, you're probably not getting any conclusions out of it. So let me be blunt: if you like beautiful straightfoward stories, and are not looking for horror, confrontation and enigmas, YES, you should buy it.

This is perhaps my favorite game of the year. Just the right blend of maddening dungeon crawler, challenging horde fighter, insane over-sized bosses, and subtle storytelling. That combined with Thunder Lotus' staggeringly-beautiful hand-drawn art makes this both a beauty to play and story worth experiencing.
Mechanics: This is a fairly straightforward 2D dungeon combat system. It features health and ammo pickups, ability shrines, and an ability tree. The fun part is in the dungeon itself. The map shows the large blocks that you traverse to make your way from place to place, but each of those blocks is made up of numerous, interconnected rooms. While the blocks are constant, the rooms change every time you die, making travel between points unpredictable, not unlike the randomly spawning hordes.
Story: The story is a pretty simple variant on Dark Souls, you are granted immortality on the condition that you clean up after a war that was far above your pay grade. In this case the war was between Techno-Vikings and a Cult of the Elder Gods. You get to wade through the aftermath of a battle between machines and dark magics for the souls of men.

In every metroidvania you get to walk the same map areas a few (or several) times. Well, in Sundered, the map and every room is designed by humans so it's not a random mess, BUT each room is composed by smaller rooms, which are procedurally generated every time you die. This way you never get to perfectly remember each corner, but you get a general idea of where do you want to go. Also, the enemies come in kind of random hordes (something like Left4Dead), so you never know where the enemies are: if you hear the alarm (or bells), you better find a good place to resist or run fast until they get tired of chasing you.
Also, it's a pretty replayable title since you can embrace or resist the darkness (read: buff your skills and be stronger, or not).

I'm mostly so happy with this game I'm not entirely sure how to review it. Seeing as the screenshots basically show you what the game is and there's so many YouTubers who have covered it I don't think covering the basics is even worth it.
It's the most fun "casual" multiplayer game I've played in a long time. And the reason for those inverted commas on the "casual" is if you're playing with friends, you're gonna be real competitive, and bad luck can lead to serious saltiness :P
The game is amazing if you can set it up in the same room as friends as a shared screen coop game, and still very good if you play online with your friends, especially if you use a service like Discord for voice chat. One feature I like is the fact that you can mix & match between online players and split-screen players, for example, I can play online against a friend and his brother using only two computers.
Another great thing about it is while the game requires a certain level of "skill" especially as levels get harder, newer players can still gain great enjoyment out of the game by making the level impossible for everyone, taking advantage of the underdog system, and then the whole point scale handicap system which weights different players victories at different levels against each other.
I would wholeheartedly recommend this game right now, even if there were a couple of things I wish the devs would add to push it high into my favorite games of all time list.
1. A level editor and steam workshop support.
I've played a similar game called Trapper's Delight, and unfortunately it missed out on most of the high profile YouTubers and Streamer coverage, so it's player-base is much smaller by orders of magnitude. However the one main advantage that game has is, like I said, the ability to make custom levels and share them via the steam workshop. I don't know how easy this would be to implement, but I think the possibility of this could explode the popularity of this game even more.
2. More content updates.
This one is kind of unfair, because it was only this month that a new level and block was added to the game. But before that it was several months of literally zero updates that had almost lead me to believe that there wasn't going to be any more content. I do understand that the devs had the monumental task of rewriting the whole system of how the online multiplayer works ( as far as I know it's done now?) so maybe that was part of it, but I'd love to see new blocks added every month, and levels less often. it's fun to even revisit the most basic level (the rooftops) with new blocks to invent new ways of absolutely ruining your friend's sanity.
Only con of the game for me is the fact that I'm not too happy with playing randoms online, because in several of the few occasions I tried this I was kicked from the game seconds before winning.
Finally I think the game is honestly worth at the very least the full price right now, especially if you've friends to play with. If it's on sale sell your soul if necessary to make sure you end up with such a gem of a game.

Warhammer Quest is a tactical dungeon crawler RPG set in Warhammer world. Your party proceeds from one dungeon to next killing tons of trash enemies, finding loot and finishing some short quests. The description stating it is an addictive mix of role-playing and strategy is however fairly overexaggerated, look below why.
Sadly, there is no story in this game. There are two types of quest: "story" quests that are marked red and some random adventures marked as grey quests. Even though, the game tries to sell you red as "story", there is nothing really behind it. Red have simply few more sentences text attached to them, but do not have any impact on the game itself. Rarely, they have follow up quests, so after you finish one you get another red somewhat connected to the red you just finished. Still, they are just single quests, not connected to other red questlines, the world or anything else in that matter. You finish them - you move on, just the same as doing grey quests. The red quests are sold first as "one time only", but you can even reset them in the town, so basically you can farm them endlessly aswell.
Between choosing which quest you want to finish, you spend 90% of the game in dungeons that look the same, feel the same and mostly have same enemies.
The combat in this game is not satisfying at all since it is heavy luck based. After getting my warriors to level 5, some level 1 critters were still taking me a lot of time to kill, simply because my party missed most of their hits. There is no RPG in matter of leveling up or gearing your warriors, since the stats are distributed automatically on a level up and the gear is always determined by rarity and stats, not much choice there. Most of the time you send your two melee warriors into a hallway they can hold while two other ranged warriors pew-pew from behind. Every single dungeon felt the say and only thing changing was who of the enemies you kill first. Sadly, there are also tons of random encounters in dungeon, that do not offer any challenge but just eat up your time progressing.
I liked both the graphic and the interface. The dungeons, even though looking a lot similar, had some nice details to it while the interface or the journal, town, inventory and other activities had some nice engravings that fit the style of the game. Sadly, the enemies were looking all the same, so it did not make any fun to further progress in the game to see something else, since both the dungeons and enemies stayed the same.
The progress in Warhammer Quest consisted of finishing the red quest in the town, moving to next and farming grey dungeons until you were strong enough to take on the next red. Simply put, it was grinding some cheap mass of dungeons, just to be able to finish another cheap dungeon that looked the same, felt the same but was supposed to be different since its a "story quest". There were no mini-games or other activities besides visiting the town to sell the loot and bashing enemies in dungeons, pretty dull.
The music was the most positive point about the game, I actually even let it ran in the background few times. The audio did fit the impact on enemies and the music was fitting different situations encountered (town, battling in dungeon, mystical random encounters).
I cannot recommend Warhammer Quest unless you are a huge fan of Warhammer universe and want to have played every single game on steam with its tag. Otherwise, if you enjoy farming and grinding up a party in repetative combat, you might enjoy the game. The rest of the players will most likely get bored after few hours and probably deinstall the game for its dull grinding sceme.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

How in the world these guys got and have hung onto the official license from both MotoGP and Valentino Rossi I have no idea, I guess agents and product managers dont have time to play the games that the names of their brands are going on to.
Pro`s
Very stable game, Not a crash or a lock up
Ok graphics, For 2016 on a very new gfx card they look functional nothing more.
Sounds are on the whole done well, Music is terrible  but thats to be expected.
Good selection of tracks, But with a slight downside
Cons
Gfx away from the bike models, Very yesterdays jam.. Stick crowds frozen in time.
Non open gameplay, Want to race any bike at any track well you cant.
Handling, This is one of the most major flaws. Turn in turn out is all wrong, Brake zones arn`t in keeping with the simulated speed and rider weight distribution is all wrong.
Wet handling is very suspect, It seems the game forgets about the weather setting and the AI certainly does.
Very poor multiplayer, Don`t expect to race people more like watch they rubber band forward and backwards.
Which leads me onto the most horrible part of the whole game, AI or lack of it. Setting it high for a challenge just adds unrealistic entry/exit and straight speed. Too low and it matches you ... Push it down to very easy and it still out accelerates you thru corners... Pro settings and it openly cheats cutting corners with no penalties let alone riding into each other with also no downsides.
I can`t say the addition of the speedway track added much, To me it seemed like the handling model from Fim Speedway 2016 had just been copied and dropped in. The rally cars however arn`t bad, Sure there is very little realism but they are fun to belt round the Monza special stages.
Milestone need competition from another developement team, They`ve had too long being the only motorcycle sim makers and it shows, Same tire model, Track designs and handling for the past few years have really lead to their products being very substandard.
Could I recommend this game, If you like Rossi and want just an arcade racer then yes but for anything more serious  stay away from this low effort, No love for the genre toy of a game.

An awesome mix of multiplayer platforming and level building, where between 2 and 4 players tries to get through one of many levels by building the platforms as you go, trying to create a path that lets you get there alive while obstructing your enemies.
By far the best game mode is Party Mode, where in between each gameplay round all players get to pick one object from a box and place it in the level before you start, making for a gradual increase in difficulty and requiering both skill and strategy to win. Outside of normal platforms there is also level elements such as moving platforms, saw blades, glue, ice, teleporters, trapdoors and tons of other items available to build with, meaning no two games will play out the same.
The gameplay also feels really nice, having a classic Mario feel to it with a designated run button and a good weight to your character, making it feel like you are in total control of your movements and avoiding cheap deaths due to game engine. There is also a wall jumping mechanic that opens up for tons of creative level designs.
There is two issues with the game worth knowing about though before going in. First off is that there is no real single player mode to this as of now, the second is that the online mode is an open beta that can be somewhat glitchy at times and might require restarting your game on some occasions.
If you can deal with those negatives though this is a fun, original and well made game, all wrapped up in a nice package of a gorgeous art style, great funky music and a development team that keeps supporting the game with patches and new content. Highly recommended for anybody who likes multiplayer platforming

A very condtional endorsement based on where I hope this sim is going. My greatest fear is that the development will be underfunded. Like most things aviation, everything takes three times as long as projected and comes in ridiculously over budget. Serious flight sim pilots have been clamoring for a 64-bit build seemingly since FSX debuted over a decade ago. I initially had no intention of purchasing this title until it was at least a year into early access. But I wanted to contribute to this cause by ponying up my $25.00 towards something  that I hope to see happen in my lifetime: A flight sim that delivers what is promised.  Most encouraging aspect for me is that the scenery loads smoothly and seamlessly on the highest settings even with my low end NVidia 1050ti in low and slow operations which is the type of flying I do. I have my instrument rating (IRL) and look forward to using this platform  to stay sharp on procedures and panel flying. That said, I also enjoy VFR flight but only if I can identify landmarks and checkpoints that I would be able to in an actual flight. This is why I've always prioritized photorealistic satellite scenery over lots of autogen. Yes, it looks ugly on approach, but I'm usually too busy in the cockpit preparing for the landing to really care.  There are plenty of reviews out there if you want to know what's not going well, some spot on in my opinion and others not as much. So for now, I've basically anted up for future. I haven't really flown FSW much since my early assessemnt flights. As they ramp up the weather, aircraft systems and ATC implementation, things will start getting interesting for me.  I remain optimistic.

I may have bought this game for a different reason to most other users. You see, I was planning a vacation course for some of my elementary students based on aviation and flight and had two weeks of activities all laid out. Still, I was looking for a nice way to polish off the course and this came my way.
I know they are into video games and the "Minecraft" way of doing things, so on the penultimate day I got them to design their own planes, which I brought home, built through thsi game and then recorded the test flights and design modifications to play back the following day.
Needless to say, it was a hit (especially when the planes went wrong), so for my review, let's catalogue my journey to classroom success.
Game purchased and downloaded and this was followed by the basic tutorials. Yep, straightforward enough, let's go.
Ambitious start; let's build a twin-engine plane ina fighter configuration. Test fly it... Nope, that didn't work. Make a few tweaks and discover another way of creating a fireball. Forget that! Bin the design and start again.
I decide to base the next design on real-world plane and go for a SAAB Viggen lookalike. Visually it all makes sense. i feel I know enough to judge that, in principle, it should fly. Wow!
More explosions.
Decide to go back to the drawing board, but before I do i download a couple of pre-designed planes. Yep, they work, so I start thinking about where I'm going wrong and slowly, slowly, better working aircraft begin to emerge from my internal design house.
13 Aircraft in, plus 4 variants, I was ready for the kids designs.
All in all, the game has a solid learning curve and presents some nice challenges. The construction screen sometimes moves pieces in weird ways, but practice and patience gets you past this easily enough. Exploring the options and displays helps you figure out what works and what doesn't and (if you're of a problem-solving mentality), will have you sitting there pondering just how to get that centre of balance just right.
It isn;t the most visually appealing sim, I'm not convinced that the physics are always spot on and the game has no real objective beyond that "Yes, I did it!" moment, but frankly, that has been enough for me. It is surprisingly good fun and even though the course has passed, I'm back on the game trying to refine and improve upon myown designs (and will perhaps see if I can improve a little on some of my students' designs before next semester).
As a fun way of experimenting with your understanding of planes, it is great and I highly recommend it.

I will separate this into two categories: Single Player and Multiplayer. Seeing as both have different stories to tell, I feel it would be appropriate to split them up. Warning, there may be spoilers, but nothing that will ruin the whole story. Enjoy.
The single player has a great story, as do most games made by Ubisoft. You start the story as Alex Taylor, a man and brother who gets put into prison and framed for his brothers' death, which was caused by the main antagonist, Shiv. Throughout the story, you compete and earn your rank through a sort of street gang lead by various characters by their status, (V2, V4, V6) ultimately trying to get to the top, V8, where Shiv stands.
Each city you unlock, which I might add are major cities throughout the United States, (LA, New York, Miami, etc.) you gain new members to your crew, or basically guidance and emotional support to your driving and discovery of locations, races and more. Your crew becomes a valuable asset to you, both becoming good friends and especially people you can count on.
Now, for the actual review part:
The single player had some good moments, great scenes, and overall a great racing experience. The handling of vehicles is the best I've seen throughout all my years of racing games, and takes the cake for that. The only thing I
wish they would have done was spend more time on the ending. It seemed very rushed and very anti-climactic. This though does not change my overall feel of the game, I still love it.
Multiplayer can be a separate story on its own simply in the fact you can basically go anywhere, with anyone. Traveling far distances with friends or strangers can be quite a great experience, especially if you can tolerate driving for literally hours at a time in real time. To put into perspective, you can probably make it across the whole map (let's say LA to Maine) in about an hour, or close to. This is driving at full speed, at least at 330km/h (at least I was).
There's plenty of places to visit, plenty of great atmospheric areas to go to. It can be very biased, but if you're not into driving for hours at a time, I wouldn't bother playing multiplayer, I'd just stick to the story.
All in all, it's a great game for what it's worth, can include hundreds of hours of multiplayer time if you're into it, or if not, you can free roam around at your will (and even go offroading in a dirt spec or raid vehicle!).

This game is an action 2D action platformer, falling squarely into the Metroidvainia genre. The controls are tight and the combat is fast. The enemies are numerous and the bosses are huge. The art style is beautiful and the Music is on another level.
The story is vague, the game gives only subtle hints as to the overall story, telling just enough to get an idea as to what's going on but leaving many things up to interpretation. This does not take away from the gameplay and what is told is told mostly through visual means with frequent narrations from a character you meet at the start of the game. This character is your only source of information as well as your only companion, he adds an air of mystery to the world, seemingly only telling half truths and being purposefully vague with what he says.
The game has plenty of upgrades to collect as well as an expansive skill tree that will boost your power as you progress through the story. There are also plenty of secrets to find and unlock, many of them changing the way you play the game on a fundamental level.
Overall, this game is worth a buy, as well as its amazing soundtrack. From cutting down hordes of enemies to searching every nook and cranny for that last upgrade you need, Sundered is a solid game especially if you can pick it up on sale!

So I have been enjoying this game,
It seems to have great promise, the aircraft are currently quite limited but each is very nicely crafted. I'd like to see a little more indication that im looking through a window when its not raining though, its a minor point.
The game is built on FSX as most people are aware and the development team seem to be going through and upgrading it bit by bit. Most recently the sky, clouds and lighting have been upgraded with the true sky update and its really looking pretty nice as a result. I'm hoping we see similar upgrades to ground textures, plant life, buildings and the terrain mesh going forward. at the moment the ground is fairly ugly, and lets be honest, flying is largely about looking out the window so thiese things should take priority in my view, and not be left for 3rd party devs to sort out later.
As I said the base game is FSX so you have the globe, and all the airports and recognisable landmarks etc, that you are familiar with from the microsoft titles, but currently at no greater quality than you will have had with FSX. The flight planner and UI is nice, and in general the game in its currents state hints at what you might expect from the final product without really hitting the mark just yet.
Yes they have released paid dlc already, and recieved a lot of negative reviews as a result. I think these are generally 3rd party add-ons and i'm going to admit that I have no interest in buying them at this point. Maybe later when the quality has been stepped up a notch with the base game, i might be tempted into buying some navigation aids for example, but we arent at a point where im willing to fork out a lump of money to add things I could of picked up as freeware for FSX.
Having said all that, I do think if they carry on down the road of improving the base game, and bringing it up to a level that sits well with modern 'next gen' visuals, as they have done with the planes and started to do with the weather and clouds, then I think this game could fill the microsft flight simulator XI gap, and become the flight sim to have... how long this takes of course is another question.
Personally I'm enjoying the odd flight at the moment and happy that I own it, as I can see its future could well be bright. (and significantly more expensive)

I like this game for its realism and have thoroughly enjoyed it despite the rage factor associated with being crossmapped (balanced out by dealing out some of your own godly crossmap judgement).
My only issue with this game at the moment is I'm really disappointed by the lack of Australian soldiers since they had such a huge impact on the war and were, and still are, regarded as some of, if not the greatest soldiers of WWI. IF you doubt this do a bit of research into our fine ANZAC's (I'm Australian) as there are some incredible stories about them. I will share some quotes with you all that I really love.
"A Yankee who could speak German asked a German prisoner did he think they were winning the war, he replied: 'Yes, God is with us.' The Yankee replied 'That's nothing, the Australians are with us.' " - diary of Sydney B. Young of Campsie, after 1000 American soldiers joined 7000 Australian soldiers to capture Hamel in 93 minutes on 4 July 1918.
"Past wars should be studied as flesh and blood affairs, not as a matter of diagrams, formulae and concepts... but of men. Hence perhaps an element of over-emphasis on personalities in this book and in particular on the personal ascendancy of the Australian soldier on the battlefield which made him the best infantryman of the war and perhaps of all time." -British General Hubert Essame who fought with the Australians at Villers-Bretonneux
If you've gotten this far thankyou, as the stories of what my predecessors did in WWI and WWII have made me truly proud to be Australian. If you have any futher interest such as my 18 y/o self, look at reading books such as 'Victory at VIllers-Bretonneux' by Peter Fitzsimons, which I have just started to read and is the source of the above quotes, and 'The Great War' by Les Carlyon, which I recently finished. They aren't easy reads but upon finishing the latter of the two I feel truly humbled, proud and reverent for the actions of the ANZAC's on the Western Front.
