Hey, how would everyone like to have an archer class that misses her mark fifteen times in a row? How about playing as a Warrior Priest whose prayers never get answered? OH, I know, let's try a big ol' brutish Ogre who has one attack and may actually hit its target zero times while in a dungeon.Or perhaps a marauder who misses more than he hits, unless you gave him a magic nut, at which point the ratio becomes an astounding 50/50, making him the best class just because he could hit almost half the time! Let's throw in a rabbit head item that may or may not do anything for your character and then have the developer be a total♥♥♥♥♥♥when asked about what it does!  That's a formula for success.
Ughh. I loathe this game. This is the perfect case study of frustration, anger, and poor game design bundled into a tablet game gone Steam.  I don't even know if I have anything nice to say about this game and some family member of mine would say, "If you have nothing nice to say, then don't say anything at all..." Now, anyone who sees my steam profile will notice the 126 hours spent in the game, so if I hated it so much, why did I spend more time playing this than anything else in recent memory? Well, that's the thing, I thoroughly despise the game mechanics, but there was some underlying natural force that compelled me. Perhaps it was the Warhammer name, or the steady and slow drip of achievements it fed me, but even after complaining time and again how broken the game is, I kept pushing forward.
My other major hobby is board games and I own the old Heroes Quest, Advanced Heroes Quest, Warhammer Quest card game, and the new reprint of Warhammer Quest, the Silver Tower....I live such an exciting life....I know the underlying mechanics the tablet version was trying to emulate, but the developers did a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job trying to capture that feel. I have never whiffed my attacks so much playing the board game version, and I wouldn't even bring it up if either archer just had one string of bad rolls, but this was nearly every dungeon. And that stupid ogre is worthless no matter what gear you give him. I never played the original version of the board game, but had I missed so consistently back then in my youth, I would have grown up a sports junkie and sworn off from my nerdy ways, that's how bad the Steam version is. I only persisted because I have a unnaturally high tolerance level for mundanity and repetitive mediocrity that I have been able to cultivate and hone over thirty years.
If you have a masochistic streak as large as mine and you happen to make it to max level with your stable of worthless humans, you do eventually get gear that mitigates some of the missing your character will do, but once you get to that point in the game you have orcs to deal with that are covered with psychic Waagh! tattoos, causing you to miss almost as much! There are no winners here, only people who play the game long enough to resign to dismal fate.
Yet, despite all I've said here, I am STILL disappointed that the developer never released the Wissenland expansion area. It's on the map, but you never go there. Dear God, what is wrong with me?!
Oh, I can say one nice thing about that game! The Dwarf Trollslayer is amazing once you have whirlwind...just feed his strength and it almost makes everything bad, feel alright.
Fantasy Flight makes better board games anyway.

I am a real private pilot, part owner of a Cherokee 180, and sometimes fly with a buddy in his RV-7A, so this sim had me written all over it. I loved the idea of an updated FSX engine and graphics, and very detailed GA aircraft, especially the Cherokee. This sim fails hard on execution.
The Cherokee appears to have a detailed panel with the ability to click everything, but it is mostly just an illusion. The audio panel doesn't do anything. COM2 doesn't do anything. The breakers don't do anything. The radio volume controls don't do anything. You can turn the radios off, but if you do, they continue to function.
The altimieters in this sim are either broken, or ATIS/AWOS recordings lie to you, or actually probably both. If you listen to the altimiter setting in the weather reports, and set your altimiter accordingly, the altimiter will read hundreds of feet off of actual field elevations. Also, tower will directly contradict ATIS telling you to take off on runway 3 when ATIS says Runway 21 is in use for example.
At least is one case, the flight model is completely broken. The solo cross country flight has you fly to Sedona. On approach to Sedona, I tried to tune local AWOS, but it was totally inoperative, probably for the better since it gives you totally incorrect information anyway. Without getting the local weather, I got in the pattern with a "Cessna" and a "Mooney" that were labeled as Cherokees. I had a nice approach to runway 3, full flaps, 65 knots. About the time I crossed the threshold, I started climbing for some reason, so I cut the power to idle. With full flaps, power at idle, and 65 knots, I flew right past the runway. In fact, I continued to fly for several minutes in this configuration after the runway, with airspeed below where it would normally stall. I did eventually land at Sedona, but had to force the plane onto the runway nose wheel first, opposite of an actual landing. This doesn't happen in Free Flight, at least not at the airports I've flown to and from, so maybe it is just a huge issue with that one mission.
I had just come back to this game after several months. All of the above issues were issues then, and are still issues now. The devs state they are fixing bugs, and in a recent blog post, they state they are going to fix the "Aircraft rolling to the left" bug. Interesting... are they not aware that single engine piston planes have left turning tendencies? Doubtful, since they also appear to be clueless about altimiter settings, ATIS, and how avionics function. I am thinking the devs just have no clue about anything in aviation.
But at least they can update the FSX engine with awesome graphics, right? The graphics for the planes are okay, but the terrain is awful. The terrain is probably a bit better than FSX at least, but unacceptable for 2017.
I realize I am complaining about bugs in an early access game. However, the major issues I highlighted above haven't been addressed since I bought this game close to early access release. Maybe they will fix them eventually, but at this point, I doubt it. The development of the game now appears to be focused on DLCs. The updates for the core game have been very minor lately, but they have released major DLCs, and for things that should be part of the core game (a moving map and additional view controls, seriously!?). This tells me a lot about the development priorities, and is a huge slap in the face to their early adopters. I for sure won't be buying any DLCs when the core game is this broken.
Verdict: Skip FSW and buy Xplane 11 instead.

===TLDR===
Following the milestone franchise there is a lot to be desired. If this is your first Milestone game you will be mildly happy to start with, but next year you will be disappointed that the game has hardly evolved from when you last played it on the old title. Ironic for a developer that goes by the name of milestone. I suggest they rename to "Little Bits"
===/TLDR===
I played Motogp14/15, Ride and now this. Not because I love these games, but because all the good racers play the latest thing.... Search for gallimar13 on the time sheets and world leader boards and youll see my name up top 20 most of the time.  Now you know about me and my level of play, lets talk about the game. I play multiplyer because I can clear the "Artifical Intelligence" by 10 seconds in 3 laps on the hardest settings. TT and multiplayer is the ONLY source of enjoyment after 20 hours.
Firstly, wow, in 2016 they finally managed to fix the Time Recordings. Until 2016, recording a lap time and saving it on a leader board was a struggle for the developer in all the previous games
A bug which has existed for many years in all previous games has been copied and pasted into this one. When you go to the Pits before you complete the first lap in Qualifying; the game still fails to allow you to register lap times for the rest of the session
The bikes are better, they handle better, very much the same as 2015, but just a little less jumpy and jerky
The bleachers/curbs arent as slippery as Ice, you can actually use them now
Grass is still to much like the asphalt in a straight line and can be used as part of the track
You might be thinking the Physics are amazing but the brakes are rubbish at the start of the game, this is because your rider is lvl1. Get to lvl100 and it all starts to feel like 2015 again with slight improvements here and there. Still Arcade like but some parts of the handeling feel a little more real like late braking
In multiplayer, if you are a lvl1 rider vs a lvl100 rider you will have no chance, you brake later and corner slower and have less control and struggle more.
Single player: As you progress through the game and your custom rider gets higher in lvl and gets good it doesnt get harder and harder. It gets easier and easier and thus more boring and less of a challenge as you get better as a player.
You can not be official riders in multiplayer, you have to be custom riders. So you cant be Rossi, in the Rossi game.
the choice of numbers and font styles for custom riders is terrible. Theres more rossi helmets to choose from than there is numbers and font style. Some combinations look terrible on the bike.
The game feels like to much of a copy and paste of old games, with slight tweaks the developer should of patched in previous games. Your basically buying a patch
Flat track is very fun, i didnt like the car modes.
The old bikes and 2 strokes are fun, if you can find the right players to race them with you
The old tracks from ages ago have been added with the new tracks. This is very nice. Example: Assen is in twice, with the old layout and the new. The Donington track is there. And more
The amount of custom gear to choose from is basically all the same from 2015, except you have to buy it. Theres obviously additional Rossi attire, from the likes of AGV and Dainese
The graphics are heavier on the system than in 2015, and dont look a massive deal better than 2015, but they are better, but just a touch.
Sounds are the same on most bikes and have been that way for years by the same developer, this developer is the laziest I have ever known.
Finally after every race it displays lap times, race times and fastest lap
I can only recommend this game if your seeking to play the best multiplayers or love the pants of Rossi, as all online players have all flocked over to the new game because its only marginally slightly better and it is able to record a lap time properly in the leader boards. If your in for the single player, buy 2015 for cheap. Ride is terrible but good for a change of tracks. You could buy both for cheap and not bother buying Rossi.
Multiplayer lobbies are still cranky, and behave strangely when someone with a bad connection joins. The code is not smart enough to be able to take a player with a bad connection and remove him, without crashing the game back to desktop first; taking everyone in the lobby out in the same way.
Theres still no function to chat in a online lobby, its like this game was made in the stone age. You have to shut down the lobby and kick all those that joined to change the settings like the voting system, the game type or the tyre options. Thats terrible by any of the standards in 2016
The menus are over done and overly confusing, and over animated
Theres not enough smart ways to save your custom bike settings
Also when you win a race, the celebration has been removed and the PITS have been removed, the game has less immersion. There is no video cut scene when you win a world championship. There is no commentary like you get in football games. Its justa excel spreadsheet of the result then then option to start a new season. YAWN. 2015 had these things.
Milestone as a developer does not support its games. Ive seen better support and more updates in Angry Birds and other mobile games/apps. Usually after release, if you have any issues, you live with them,
If money or love is not an issue, I recommend this game over previous titles, but its not a great deal better either
If Milestone is the Developer, dont buy a season pass or any additional extras other than the base game. These guys dont add anything to the base games value afterward.

with fighter jets, but despite the great idea behind it
doesn't deliver on the mechanics anywhere near as cleanly as
did.
You're the air boss of an aircraft carrier with the responsibility of fueling and arming planes and helicopters and sending them off to counter a variety of helpfully colour-coded threats. The threats can appear on any of four threat layers -- Air, Surface, Submarine and Ground -- and require a recon craft to be sent up to detect them first, and then the appropriate number and type of aircraft must be vectored to intercept.  F-18 jets are used to take out air and surface threats; Sea King helicopters are sent to torpedo incoming submarines; and ground threats must often be countered by an Osprey-borne unit of special forces or marines. Using the right tool for the job is key -- while an F-18 can provide radar coverage if it has to, you're far better off using the dedicated E2C Hawkeye radar plane which has far more sensor range and endurance -- and more complex enemies require multiple aircraft or even multiple missions to counter.
The actual gameplay mostly involves shuffling aircraft around the flight deck of the carrier to make all of this happen. You order them to a loading bay, arm them with the appropriate loadout for the mission you want them to do, and then send them onto a runway so that they can take off for a mission. Once launched a mission will
be successful, keeping the focus firmly on the carrier deck where it belongs; the onus is on you to make sure you have enough aircraft of the right loadout type to be able to launch the missions in the first place. If you don't counter an incoming threat before it drops off the left-hand side of the threat display it'll launch an attack that causes damage to the carrier, and the goal of
is to get through a game with as little damage to the carrier as possible.
With three or four simultaneous incoming threats to deal with it can become pleasingly taxing to juggle fighters in the right order to counter them. However, while the theme might fit the gameplay concept like a glove, the actual implementation of basic game mechanics leaves something to be desired. Pathfinding around the carrier is extremely weak, with pilots retreating to their parking bays to sulk if they run into anything at all on the way to the runway. Feedback on what you're doing wrong is practically non-existent; it took me several games before I realised I had to launch missions in the order I had them queued, and while the developers have since added a hint for this (it was a common complaint) it comes in the form of a bloody great pop-up box that completely blocks your view of what's going on. Finally, aircraft that are coming in to land will occasionally abort their landing and careen straight down the middle of the carrier deck, which can cause some rather entertaining fireballs if you're unfortunate enough to have anything taxiing around there at the time. . To be fair to
, it's not really intended to support that anyway since it has a much simpler campaign metagame, but I think that it
have if it had undergone a couple more design/polish passes to eliminate these flaws and I'm disappointed that it's fallen some way short of its full potential.
In summary: do buy
if you like the idea of a naval aviation-themed
-style time management game, but be aware that its frustrations will eventually outweigh the enjoyment derived from pretending you're the angry cigar-chomping carrier captain from

Wow so I finally beat this game and at 100% no less so I figured I'd take the time to share how I felt about it.
I think the game can be a little frustrating, but I liked it a lot to recommend it. The most challenging parts start at the beginning, because you slowly have to find power-ups to help you complete rooms you may have come across originally, or at least make them easier to solve. It wasn't until I reached the 40% completion rate that I think I got a good handle on the game and the puzzle solving came naturally. I honestly got stuck a lot before I could reach that point and I ended up putting the game down a lot as I just played it as a casual passtime game.
If you try to reach for 100% completion, good luck. The map in-game is very blurry and hard to tell which rooms you might be missing. But with the help of some digging in the Steam community, some people have posted detailed maps and help if you get stuck.
There's also a boss battle you need to once you get all the power-ups, and hoo boy. I'll say that I ended up having to fight twice because you need to fight him after you 100% complete the rooms in order to get the official achievement, and the 2nd time was much easier than the first. The boss fight was the most frustrating part of the game at first, because it is definitely a 'learn quickly or else start all over' kind of fight. There are times where these one-hit-'kills' will completely bombard you once you're closer to the end, and its just a mess of trial and error until you finally get it right. But as I've said, the 2nd fight after knowing how to do it came much much easier.
Overall good game. Very cute, very casual in my opinion. Though the music does not hold up, there technically isn't any music? I ended up muting the game as the 'music' is just repetitive notes in completed rooms and it can get a little obnoxious. It's also very simple but it's very similar to VVVVVV so if you like that game you'll love this game.

I like this game for its realism and have thoroughly enjoyed it despite the rage factor associated with being crossmapped (balanced out by dealing out some of your own godly crossmap judgement).
My only issue with this game at the moment is I'm really disappointed by the lack of Australian soldiers since they had such a huge impact on the war and were, and still are, regarded as some of, if not the greatest soldiers of WWI. IF you doubt this do a bit of research into our fine ANZAC's (I'm Australian) as there are some incredible stories about them. I will share some quotes with you all that I really love.
"A Yankee who could speak German asked a German prisoner did he think they were winning the war, he replied: 'Yes, God is with us.' The Yankee replied 'That's nothing, the Australians are with us.' " - diary of Sydney B. Young of Campsie, after 1000 American soldiers joined 7000 Australian soldiers to capture Hamel in 93 minutes on 4 July 1918.
"Past wars should be studied as flesh and blood affairs, not as a matter of diagrams, formulae and concepts... but of men. Hence perhaps an element of over-emphasis on personalities in this book and in particular on the personal ascendancy of the Australian soldier on the battlefield which made him the best infantryman of the war and perhaps of all time." -British General Hubert Essame who fought with the Australians at Villers-Bretonneux
If you've gotten this far thankyou, as the stories of what my predecessors did in WWI and WWII have made me truly proud to be Australian. If you have any futher interest such as my 18 y/o self, look at reading books such as 'Victory at VIllers-Bretonneux' by Peter Fitzsimons, which I have just started to read and is the source of the above quotes, and 'The Great War' by Les Carlyon, which I recently finished. They aren't easy reads but upon finishing the latter of the two I feel truly humbled, proud and reverent for the actions of the ANZAC's on the Western Front.

Gone Home is a beautiful, emotional journey into the hard but liberating process of self-discovery. I will not go into more detail so as not to spoil the experience in any way, but I recommend it utterly. The medium of the videogame can be used for many things, but I believe it is at its highest when it is used to express ideas, experiences, outlooks on life, when it makes us see our lives through the eyes of interesting characters. This is such a case. It is a short game (about 3-4 hours long; I don't understand how Steam counted only two), and definitely not one for those who like skill challenges, action and adrenaline. This is definitely not a quest-based game. It has no fights or loot. What it does have is a great, immersive athmosphere, superb voice-acting, and a narrative and physical setting that involve you emotionally more and more until the very end.
Like all good games, it has its little flaws. Although the environment is very well designed, with lots of unique and significant objects for the player to interact with (letters, notes, invoices, books, cassette tapes, etc.), I felt that the different spaces within the house were  sometimes repetitive, with the same assets appearing several times (e.g. accumulations of papers and supermarket coupons, pens and markers). Although the environment does its job very well, it does not feel (at least to me) completely like a house that is actually lived-in. This, however, does not lessen the immersive experience that is to explore the large house and understand the events that led to the present state of affairs.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

Fallout 3 is a horrifyingly glitchy game that you probably can't play (or at least not without dozens of mods).
If you *can* manage to play the game, it seems almost juvenile, and certainly quite small, in comparison to its successor. It lacks the polish and attention-to-detail that Obsidian would later put into Fallout: New Vegas. By all accounts, the Capital Wasteland feels like a place devoid of life and direction, bar its largest settlements, perhaps as a wasteland, in any case, should, but its somewhat mindless and sparse design, whether intentional or not, forces the player either to wander aimlessly in search of something to do or scour the Fallout wiki for direction.
When you *do* find a quest or a vault or a museum to slog through, you can't autosave (unless the mods necessary to play the game have lied to me). You can imagine the complications that ensue there.
Nonetheless, I love Fallout 3. The rich backstory - the only video game lore I've enjoyed to date - synonymous with the Fallout series appears in full force. So too does the series' distinctive brand of humour.
I'm also quite fond of the game's setting - far moreso than the Mojave - probably because of the wide variety of interesting things found in the Washington, D.C. area (the capital buildling, the Bethesda ruins, the national history museum, the RobCo facility, and the Republic of Dave, just to name a few).
Really, though, good luck getting this ♥♥♥♥er to run.

I came to Sundered from Hollow Knight, and while both are grimdark metroidvanias, they're really very different experiences. Hollow Knight is very deliberate, very soulslike; Sundered instead throws literal hordes of enemies at you and invites you to go nuts. The shift took me a little bit to get used to, so my first few hours felt a little uncomfortable, but after that I was quite happy with the game.
The difficulty felt a little weird to me - it felt way too hard at the beginning, and almost too easy by the end. (First run was full "resist" on Normal difficulty.) Some of the upgrades and perks in mid-game heavily boost survivability, and I was just coming off of the slower-paced, more deliberate Hollow Knight when I started, so between the two that might explain why the early game felt overtuned.
Metroidvanias are all about exploration, and Sundered puts an interesting spin on that with the roguelite randomization of rooms - I love the idea and execution. There are plenty of secrets to be found, and challenge areas hide some of the better perks. The choice to "resist or embrace" not only provides a satisfying customization of powers, but a compelling reason to replay.
Edited to add: After finishing a second playthrough (full "embrace"), I can comfortably say the power choices definitely lend a very different feel to the game, and it's worth playing through at least twice.

Initial impressions:
This game is fantastic so far.
Thunder Lotus Games (makers of the gorgeous, but apparently mechanically-flawed, "Jotun") have created a metroidvania-style, bullet-hell-ish game, also using traditional animation. The animation is brilliant and reminds me of the Frank Frazetta era of films like "Fire and Ice" or "Heavy Metal". The art design of the world is brilliant so far, with various biomes to travel to, including one that makes strong nods to the elder gods of Lovecraftian influence. The combat is pleasant and fluid, reminding me strongly of "Dead Cells". In fact, this game feels like taking "Dead Cells" to the next level, downplaying the rogue-lite concept of having to build yourself back up once you die, but preserving a degree of the randomized/procedurally-generated maps, which it does so only partially (the core layout of the map is preserved, but each sub-section gets changed).
The music is haunting, but the sound effects are what really give the goosebumps. The first time you swing your sword, you'll understand what I'm talking about.Enemies come in waves of various sizes, but a real horde is signaled by an alarm sound (different for each biome), and whether you're looking forward to a horde or trying to avoid one, it's absolutely exciting to hear that terrifying klaxon.
Powerups and upgrades are also enticing, giving the game an addictive quality. I'm about halfway through the game, and I find that there's some thrilling choices to be made in terms of progression, including one big choice to make. As the game tells you numerous times, "The choice to embrace or resist is permanent". While I should be tempted to cheat and look into what various choices yield, I'm finding that I don't want to spoil surprises for myself.
As it stands, I have nothing but good things to say about this game. However, one should be aware of the nature of the game. It exists in a middleground between different genre styles of metroidvania, rogue-lites, and I guess bullet hells. So there is a risk that if one of those genres repells you enough, it might put you off the game. You have to learn to play it the way it's meant to be played. Making the journey back to the boss that just killed you, seems to be a long and tedious one for some. It didn't feel that way for me. Traversing the map goes rather quickly if you play it to be traversed quickly. It's a metroidvania game, dammit. Yes, you die a fair bit. It's rogue-lite and Dark Souls-inspired, dammit. But the more unique thing is the enemy combat style. They DO come in hordes, and that's different to many people's expectations of almost any genre other than bullet-hell. What came to mind for me was actually Doom 2016. I wasn't expecting or wanting horde combat when I started playing the game (I didn't know that was an element of it), but I quickly adapted and learned to be fine with it, and even begin to like it. It's sort of like accidental grinding. You get into the thick of it, and you're just trying to stay alive. Then when it's over, you have a whole bunch of upgrade points. Much better than games where you have to wander to some spot to farm and grind in. Here, you can just focus on exploration and deal with the hordes as they randomly appear. When you get enough ability upgrades, they're really quite satisfying.
Note: I say I'm about halfway through the game (it reports percentage completed), and I've been playing for 13 hours. So it's no "Hollow Knight" in terms of game size.

I am developing a love/hate relationship with this game, but in a good way.
It immerses you in a medieval time, with medieval strategies, and medieval issues.  The game itself is brilliantly built while at the same time not being a burden to your computer.  It cycles through seasons and random weather patterns that can make or break you, and no matter how good you think you're doing, it's nothing but a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for a tornado to come through ripping your town apart, killing half the residents, and causing everyone to die from lack of resources; or a random fire breaking out in a house, and no matter how many buckets of water your citizens dump on the house, it never fails to spread like wildfire and take everything wooden as its victim.
The gameplay in itself is smooth and seamless, especially the transitions between seasons and weather patterns.  There are only a few glitches that I have found so far, like animals moving from your trade post to their pasture, walking on water and through buildings/fences, or citz walking through fences and whatnot to take a shortcut rather than use the path you so graciously built for their convenience.  Nothing important, probably not even noticable unless you stay zoomed in to creep on your people, like me.  #noshameinmygame
If something can cause or be a problem itself, it will be, and I don't care how many resources you have backstocked, DO NOT GET COCKY with your gameplay skills.  My village had so many resources, was doing so well off--no population issues, plenty of food for the new born kiddos, everyone had a job, and all it took was one little tornado to mess it up, UGH.
The part I like best is how much control you have over everything, from how many people work a certain profession and at which place of business, to which part of town gets the nice coats this coming winter with the lovely 14(f) degree weather. This is just like life, only virtual, and you won't go to prison for deciding last minute that a massive genocide is the only route to go to save your pathetic little excuse for a village.

REVISED REVIEW:
Great concept, good execution with a few MUST KNOW ABOUT catches.  For those who may have noticed, my original opinion was NOT RECOMMENDED.  As you can see, I've changed that.  Carrier Deck has a noticable learning curve, but nothing that you can't adapt to.  There are no hot keys.  What that means is if you don't point and click properly, aircraft don't do what you need them to do...that can be annoying.
1.  You as the player are the ONLY intelligent person running EVERYTHING.  The game is stacked so that you're jumping out of your♥♥♥♥♥to make things work.  This has a decent chance of eliminating the fruits of your gaming labor.  There are times where I don't have aircraft to address a threat so the carrier takes a beating.
2.  Several game modes are available.  All are worth your time.  I particularly enjoy survival mode.  Pay close attention to the radar/sonar ranges.  Personally, I think the ranges are way short if you don't have warning aircraft flying...but you can overlook that.  This game is about resource management, (NOT A CARRIER SIM).  I wanna make that clear because a fellow gamer insinuated that.  I never said that, nor have I ever thought it was a carrier sim...I assure you.
3.  The MEATBALL STILL DOES NOT WORK.  So planes keep crashing into one another if the deck isn't clear.  On top of that (no pun intended), helos will land on top of each other if there's no place to land.  I make fun of Navy and Marine pilots all day long, but I also assure you they do have common sense.  They'll swear up and down for you to clear the deck before they run out of fuel.  And if you tell the pilot to ABORT LANDING...that automatically sends them into the drink.  Again, I think that's a foul, because we would have aircraft available to refuel them in the air for just such an occasion.
4.  Game manual is more of a "civilian intro to carrier operations" rather than a "how to play this game" manual.  It could use an actual keyboard/legend layout.
5.  CIWS?  You better believe that thing should be spitting out lead as a last ditch effort to protect the carrier...but for now it's not working...at least not yet (looking at you EverySingleSoldier).
6.  The PATH WITH MOVING AIRCRAFT ON DECK STILL NEEDS WORK!  I lost count as to how many rounds I lost because the deck crews couldn't figure out how to move aircraft on the deck so they just sit there and/or they return to the spot I moved them from.
7.  BE VERY AWARE:  You could do everything right in this game and still lose.  Why is that a problem?  This is supposed to be a game, not real life.  Personally, I play games to unwind.  If I'm reminded of how real life can be and don't have a chance at winning, then what's the point?  Why would I waste my time?
I like the variety of aircraft available for different missions.  If you get a chance, turn the video settings to fantastic and use the free camera mode when launching or landing...you won't be disappointed.
I think the developer can take some artistic liberty here by making a super carrier in future iterations with more aircraft (maybe drones and F-35s in the future?) and even incorporating amphibious operations from the Iwo Jima class like the big hovercrafts.  The jet aircraft look cool taking off and landing.  The developers took time to get things accurate and the hard work behind something like this should be acknowledged.
One cosmetic thing if you get around to it.  Please don't have ground crews standing around  where aircraft roll through.  It looks cool and more accurate when they're running from aircraft to aircraft.  And if you can...add a "shooter", or a catapult launch officer.  I personally was looking for that detail.
Thanks!

If you like Magic: The Gathering, you will like this game.  Period.
It has revamped the "mana" system from MtG to be a little less dependant on what type of mana you have, rather than how much.  Instead they went with an "influence" type system where your mana (power) played gives you a certain influence along with the mana (power).  Playable cards have a power cost and a prerequisite amount of influence to be able to cast.  It's a fairly good system that cuts down on being certain color mana starved/heavy on multicolor decks.
That being said, power starve/flood can still happen as it is still a system based on playing power "cards".  So just like MtG, that can be frustrating when you need a creature and draw power four turns in a row or you need one mana to cast every card in your hand, but you keep drawing more expensive cards.  That's the ONE thing that Hearthstone has an edge on.
As for playing the game itself, the balance between the colors is pretty well done.  There's a lot of interesting synergy with abilities/effects so that deck building is fun.  You start out with a few premade decks and various cards, but building a collection isn't very hard.  Also, while there are some aspects of RNG built into some cards (not including power and the fact that it's a card game based on draw), it's kept to a relative minimum, unlike Hearthstone, who seems to just keep pushing the whole RNG aspect down our throats.  Personally, I like strategy to decide my game, rather than if this cards ends up targeting the right units or if I play X spell randomly, etc.  It's okay if it's a here and there thing, not the entire premise of the game itself.
One of the BEST THINGS about this game is the fact that it's
.  I hope they never change this fact.  Rewards are fantastic and you aren't even required to play versus other players to get rewards, which is how all of these CCG games should work.  The ability to buy in-game currency to support the developers is also an option, but it's not required to progress your collection.  Also, quests aren't too demanding and are also quite rewarding.  There's also an achievement system that gives you various rewards.  It's the best thing about this game and one of the reasons why I think it's the best virtual CCG.
I guess the one complaint I could make is the music, but really, who's going to base a review of a CCG on ... music?  Everything else is phenominal.
Kudos to Dire Wolf Digital.  Please, please keep up support of this game.  It's the best virtual CCG out there.  As soon as I come up with some extra funds (thanks to having a child recently), I plan on giving you some support fundage for your efforts.  They are well deserved.

Eternal is a strikingly familiar game. It borrows extensively from Magic, so a familiarity with that game more or less sets you up to learn how to play Eternal without much translation needed. Power replaces mana, the colours are different, the lore entirely unique.
But the execution is so good, the presentation so well-honed to maximise ease of use while allowing clever strategic play, the progression so rewarding, that it puts any digital version of M:tG to shame.
You can play entirely for free, and it doesn't feel like you're being constantly urged to start spending to keep up. You can play against the AI for free to grind currency and quite quickly start opening real constructed-playable cards to use in competitive play. Sure, one can actually spend money, but at no point have I felt that I need to.
Add to this the seamless spectator mode to let friends hop in to watch, which has made learning decks much easier as they can help teach me while watching me play and seeing my hand in realtime, and you have a thoroughly enjoyable CCG which I can happily recommend. I fully expect the game to keep going and getting deeper, and look forward to ploughing many more hours into it.

In spite of the fact that the smooth, elegant, simplistic monochrome beauty of 1000 Amps is evident from the beginning, if first-minute impressions were more important then they are for me, I wouldn't have liked it as much as I did and might have given up, as you are thrown into its little tile lighting puzzle platformer world with little to no explanation as to what on Earth you should be doing, and the game isn't afraid to throw you around from map to map and inflict a feeling of helplessness, to confuse you right at the stirt. But that, in the end, turned out to be a plus, as it created a genuine feeling of accomplishment as Plug, your little avatar in the game, grew in power, with a genuine feeling of power once he was "fully powered up". While the difficulty in the game is pretty uneven, that's more than likely intentional, as you I've appreciated those little breaks in the current, which didn't detract from the game flow itself. Most importantly, if something isn't solvable immediately, the game will hint at that and you can always return to that place. Precision (more), timing (somewhat less), logic and, most importantly, perserverance are rewarded here. And yes, everything IS solvable - 100% finishes with every seed found and none spent are doable even on a mouseless laptop like mine (it got quite tricky at times, mind). All in all, it's a fun little challenge that I'll remember fondly, a recommended game by all means!

So... Sundered is probably one of the best games I've ever played. Everything about it just feels so well done.
The gameplay itself is really good, there is a Dark Souls type of learning to every boss and enemy, and death just like in Dark Souls is part of this process. After a while you can master dodging, positioning and using your abilities, if you are patient enough. There are a lot of small mechanics that I won't spoil now. You are capable of building your character the way you want using perks and Dead Space like upgrading system, so there are multiple ways of fighting the enemy. Also these are stronger in some situations or weaker. For example: My build makes me invincible when I am fighting against more then 10 enemies at once, melee, but when it comes to fighting bosses it's really skill realiant, but that's not that big of a problem after all. Platforming is also there and it makes the game fell constantly fun.
The bosses are well done I think there is a decent variety in them. The main bosses are all amazing, some of the minibosses are just a stroger version of the normal enemies in the Dungeon. Some of them are a little bit too easy, but it's fine.
Important: This game will be a bit too hard for some people (concidering what I heard from others playing this game) I was playing it on Hard, and ut was perfect for me, but be prepared if you'll ever try to play this game.
The music and the Hand Drawn Garphics of the game are totally amazing. The atmosphere is really outstanding, with an awesome Lovecraftian vibe to it. It magnages to be really dark, crastfallen yet beautiful at the same time. And yeah, I love the music. Feels simple, yet incredible.
The story of the game isn't completely clear for me just yet, but what I know is really interesting. I don't know which ending should I go for. The more I know the more cofused it makes me. MAYBE SPOILER, I DUNNO: Feels like there is no good side and I really like these types of stories....
Bugs: I didn't find a lot and none of them were anoying.
I really reccomend this game for anyone who likes games with Dark/Crestfallen/Lovecraftian atmosphere that are challenging and gorgeous at the same time.

If you like platformers or puzzle games without the attached stress or a fat price tag, go ahead and pick this up when you can.  Though it doesn't do anything particularly

I've done a review awhile ago and well, I've decided to a do a real style of way for the game Verdun, mostly because of what I see in the game itself with players chatting and doing tads of research generally I wish for people to see what this game offers.
Verdun is a World War One death simulator, you rush in and die die die die. But here's the thing, that's what people
it is.
Instead of Verdun being a death simulator, its an unpolished, lack of features, lack of fixxing bugs, and the developers making poor decisions on making Verdun a great game.
Verdun by definition is a problem waiting to be solved, and truly the answer is because of the developers unmotivated actions that effect the community itself and consumers.
Enough with repition, now with the facts.
Gameplay:
Verdun itself looks gorgeous with max settings of graphics, but that doesn't shield the game itself. With an arrangement of squads, you'll find yourself in a spot where you need to learn yourself what squads do and what their roles are. This is the first problem, as it takes time and turns to actually understand what guns are better, what makes it feel like you're specialized in which should be taught already other than showing what squads have that are good or bad. The second bad thing is the god awful hit detection and aiming, you could shoot at a man so close to you and you won't hit them, but run in a Trench and absouletly kill everyone with hipfiring shots.
This is what leads to my third complaint, the ties to new players. How many games of you running around doing your thing and see so many people die infront of you including yourself by one player just wielding a 5 round rifle? It happens over and over and then that's just it, you call him a hacker. People laugh and others agree then there's this stalemate of just argueing in chat justifying your claim but the "hacker" has nothing to say because of just the ability to jump run crouch and still be able to shoot accurate; So you end your day on that then just quit Verdun for good.
Bam, consumer gone and he's probably telling his friends (if he had any) to not buy Verdun because of the amount of hackers and stuff.
Let me get this straight as well, I
care for players who are good nor bad, but if you just get mad because of trench warfare, because this is how it was, then this game is not for you. Because I've done the same and I've fought my way to learn more of this game and it was hard, like hard learning like
hard but with guns.
Community:
The example above would be included into this catagory, but it felt self-explanatory anyway. The community is split with shoot perfect players, new players, then the decent players.
Decent players are off the hook because so much toxicity between the newcomers and veterans of firing guns in Verdun, if you're gonna make a game about WW1 then you need to have the extensive training situations for the game.
You remember drill sergeants? They should be an area for the game because that's how they taught soldiers back then, let alone have commands for NCOs to be tough broad and straight, because that's how it WAS. I think you get the point, this game fails to take screams and yelling and put them into soldiers.
Mechanics:
So you're with a squad with randoms or friends, you hit level 100 and are happy, say you have artillery as your squad NCO command and well god behold you won almost every game because that stuff is really really overpowered.
But that's high-tier stuff, let alone actually able to get into a 4v4 squad match. The commands vary on the squad type; assualt, recon, defensive, and... well that's it really unless you count assualt into two subpars as smoke and barrages. That is so bland, and pasted that I wish you could have more abilities as an NCO. Having just a command to spam that does nothing or one ability that does almost nothing game changing an option is useless, and should have a "move up" or "rally here." That's also another problem! The schematics of the game is
and most of the time your squadmates are running away from your NCOs generally area! You gotta be in a squad formation when defending and attacking period.
Optimizations:
If you have a low-end computer, don't bother trying to have medium graphic settings because these graphics are killer. You gotta face with a stable 60FPS at best if you have computers that can easily run games with outstanding graphics.
Conclusion:
In forever how long this game stands, the game is not worth any purchase if you hate playing this for mainstream.

I give it a thumbs up because I realize that four years ago, it must have been something special, and probably we wouldn't have Games like Firewatch, Life is Strange or What Remains of Edith Finch without it -- the similarities are striking.
Also, it's hated too much already, and for all the wrong reasons.
Having said that, the experience was a little underwhelming; like listening to that one band all your favorite bands cite as their influence and then it somehow doesn't live up to its successors.
In my review of Edith Finch I complained you can't interact enough with the world; here it's the other way around. The house is cluttered with too many generic, identical objects (soda cans, 3 ring binders, toilet paper); you can examine all of these, but none of them are important. In between however, you find letters, notes and other pieces of written information -- and you have to do a lot of reading to piece it all together. So that's the game: opening every cupboard, every drawer, until you've finally found the important stuff between all those binders, coasters and receipts, then putting everything into chronological order. It's not exactly exciting, and a bit muddled at times.
The story itself -- the character conflicts you learn about -- IS great, but it's so tedious to unravel (especially if you don't find everything at once and have to go back and search rooms again) it killed lots of the atmosphere for me.
The single worst decision IMO was to give Katie no voice of her own. Having a silent protagonist at the heart of such an emotional story just doesn't work for me. I spent two and a half hours wondering what the hell she actually THINKS about all these revelations about her own family.
So there is a lot to love here -- the forbidden relationship, the guilt, the nostalgia, the eerie atmosphere -- but all of the games I mentioned above do it better IMO. Probably I should have played Gone Home before them to really appreciate it. So it's more like a 3 out of 5 stars for me.

There are times where you can interact with objects that have no purpose (such as a pencil or a blank sticky note) and there aren't very many secrets hidden in the house. I would say the game is not so much bad as it is uneventful. If you do want to give this game a try, I would say wait until it goes on sale. Other than that, I cannot recommend buying it at full price

I have many hrs experience on MotoGP15.
So far on 'VR the game' I have only played a MotoGP full race weekend in Assen as Valentino Rossi on the hardest setting
First impressions and improvements over Moto GP 15:
- cornering feels more realistic, you need to have all your speed removed before the turn and accelerating out of the corner feels better.
- less rear wheel sliding around from side to side. As your rear tyre wears (presuming you enable tyre wear setting) it spins more and is harder to find traction but doesnt slide around from side to sidelike in motogp 15
- turning into corners feels way better than in motogp15. its sharper and feels more realistic.
- Audio has improved and changing down thru the gears sounds better
- Graphics are better. The rider moves around the bike more realistically. Crowds are better and cheer at certain parts of the circuit.
Dislikes so far:
- Braking feels weak and soft and I cant brake late to overpass someone in the corner. Braking late just means running off the track. Have done all overtakes in high speed sections of the track (have tried the 2 different brake pad choices)
- Background music during races was the first thing I disabled.
Will play more and update the review.

Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin was released after the original Dark Souls 2 version, but it is still basicly the same game, just with minor tweaks and improvements.
The original Dark Souls 2 also received a "Scholar of the First Sin" patch, which contained the new added npc for example, but not the updated enemy placements or graphics.
Also Scholar of the First Sin already contains all 3 DLCs.
Scholar of the First Sin is now the "real" version of Dark Souls 2 and newcommers should start with this.
However the small improvements and changed enemy placements are not even worth the 20 bucks at reduced price though, if you already own the original version, since that price is worth an entirely new game, while this here is still the same game at it's core.
Now some comments on the content of Dark Souls 2 (Scholar of the First Sin) as a whole:
It offers fun challanges and mostly fair in it's challanges.
There are a lot of different weapons to chose from and many different character builds to utalize the different weapons, especially when considering the elemental infusions.
Character builds can also be changed retrospectively (using a limited rescource).
The game has a lot of replay value.
Not only does it increase in difficulty with each playthrough of a character, some of the bosses and areas receive additional enemies.
It is also fun to create new characters and test different ways to play through the game.
Many of the areas look very good.
For example one is a large open lake with ruins and blue glowing flowers. The buildings are lit up with torches and it simply looks very impressive overal. The better lighting in Scholar of the First Sin also adds to this.
This game has the best PvP of all 3 Dark Souls games and invading other player's worlds is always a fun thing to do. It also doesn't take long at all to find a world to invade.
The matchmaking system for the arena is based on the character level and it doesn't take long to find a match.
Coop is also very fun and it is also much easier to play with friends than in Dark Souls 1, since there is a ring with password system for coop play in Dark Souls 2.
The DLC areas that are included in Scholar of the First Sin are very good and probably the highlights of this game.
These dlc areas each have a specific motive and execute it very well.
Also 2 of the 3 bosses in each dlc are very good.
When it comes to the difficulty, this sequel focuses a lot more on fights against multiple enemies at once and requires players to fight without lock-on very often.
This isn't necessarily bad, but several of the areas can become very tedious due to this.
The game also has a lot of traps and some of these can't be seen ahead of time, leading to unavoidable damage during the first time walking though.
This is not very frequent though and is a common trick in the other Souls games as well.
Also the effectiveness of rolling and the healing speed are linked to the Agility stat, which isn't clear for a new player and leads to unreliable rolling, if not increased by leveling up - and rolling is a key mechanic for the combat.
Dark Souls 2 has a "Soul Memory" system, which counts the Souls (currency) that you receive.
This is part of the matchmaking system for coop and pvp outside of the arena.
Sadly, the feature limits the amount of equipment upgrades and rescource purchases that you can make, if you want to play with or against players on the same level.
Even the password ring doesn't nullify this, which gets in the way of coop relatively frequently. Dark Souls 3 handled this much better.
1 boss from each DLC is a boss meant to be played in coop. It is rather clear, that the least amount of effort regarding the DLCs went into the level and boss design for these parts.
The PvP of all Souls games suffers heavily from lag. It is very common to get hit by the opponent while being out of range on your screen. This is because of the latency issues between players, that live are far away from another.
Overall I definitely recommend this game though.

The game features a campaign mode with scripted encounters (you’ll see the same events at the same time in each mission), a survival mode against increasingly more difficult threats, and randomized quick games. The interface allows you to control inbound and outbound aircraft, make missions to search and engage the enemy, and move aircraft around the carrier. There are some minor limitations: time-consuming and imprecise long-pressing is used to arm aircraft  (instead of right-clicking), and incoming threats could be easier to see on the display. Depending on the type of aircraft, planes and helicopters can be instructed to scan and destroy air, surface, submarine, and ground threats. Gameplay involves moving the aircraft around, rearming them for the next mission, performing repairs, and generally keeping things from running into each other. Missions must be completed in the order they are created, which makes a fast-moving incoming hostile problematic when three other missions are already in the queue. Aircraft can be armed in advance, which does reduce panic when multiple threats arrive simultaneously. Carrier Deck takes the click management game into a unique, stressful setting.

This is a game where you make tea. You control a robo-arm and must pick up a teabag, put it in a cup, add hot water, then include any other stuff as instructed by a piece of paper, like sugar or milk. It sounded fun to me because I thought controlling the robo-arm would be amusing and challenging to some degree; unfortunately the controls, mouse feedback, and just about everything else actually, are way too broken for this game to be playable or taken seriously.
Everything is as light as a feather. So when you even
them, they start to topple. This includes the hot water dispenser which is a huge bulky object. The "lightness" makes it virtually impossible to do anything.
Moving even 1mm
with your mouse results in a HUGE movement by the robo-arm, so much so that it's nigh impossible to move properly. You practically have to "tiptoe" with your mouse movement - like maybe 0.1mm or less per move. The same thing happens if you move too fast - the arm will zoom rapidly, knocking down everything in its path.
Forget trying to actually pick up the teacup or anything else for that matter - the hand and its fingers are practically useless - too "weak", and most of the time not angled correctly (wrist rotation only works sideways and not vertically). You'll have better luck with one of those claw machines in the arcade.
I managed to get a teabag into the teacup by pure luck. It was precariously balancing near the cup's edge, so I nudged it a little to make it enter the cup properly. Said teabag then "floated" in the centre of the cup - I made a screenshot of it (check my screenshots). And on another occasion, the British flag on the table got "impaled" by my fingers, so I ended up having to drag it around with me.
Which is what I did, in total and utter frustration. The game ends if your robo-arm gets destroyed. Thank goodness.

An online game that freely rewards you just for playing against IA ALWAYS deserves a positive review! I've played like 10-12 hours on Steam and maybe another 20-25 on my phone. Not much but I'm giving my point of view.
I'm a person who always expects a lot from a game. If it doesn't fit my tastes, then I quickly drop it after an intensive period of trial, so first the negative points:
CONS:
- The collection is really extensive, and the possibility to have in your deck 4 copies of a same card, including legendaries, makes me think this is not purely F2P.
- The crafting system is unbalanced aswel. You can't disenchant a Premium card for half the cost of making that same Non-premium card. Just for those of us who enjoy a "complete collection without glowing things". Please take that as an advice. PLEASE DEVELOPERS. ^_^
- TURN ONE. Guys, you forgot to make up for the player who starts second. Resource differences here are maybe not essential, and the blocking system seems fair... but still, the 1st player can have 2 or even 3 units on board in the second turn while the second player has nothing.
-----> This isn't a CON: The resource system can sometimes make you lose a game, yes, but hey, that's why there are "draw emblem" cards. To cycle and thin your deck.
And that's why the game itself forces you to include a 33% of power cards in a deck. The "old general rule" in any classic card game.
What happens in Hearthstone when you have an awful start while your opponent has a very good one?
PROS:
- Pretty much anything else. Animations and graphics, card design, controls, rules, atmosphere...
- A cheap and challenging way to try your skills and decks out against IA, and getting cards. You can earn gold in Gauntlet then spend it in Forge. Free, without having to play against experienced or P2W players.
- A HUGE BUNCH of mechanics. Making a crazy deck is really fun although 90% times it can be garbage :D
- LOTS of game modes. That got me.
So, if you want some kind of complexity and a huge collection to complete, mixed with intuitive mechanics and amazing tutorials... Try the game. At least. It's free.
An easy 8/10. Maybe more.

I quite enjoy this game, since I wanted to scratch my MTG-itch. It does a lot of stuff right: the game speed is nice, GUI is enhancing the experience and there's a sense of progression as you grind your way up.
What I don't like is unfortunately a core mechanic of the standard game: dead draws! How can they still be in a new card game?!
It feels so punishing drawing resource cards when you want some kind of answer for the board. On top of that the deck size is 75 cards with a maximum of 4 copies per card AND you're forced to make 1/3 of the deck resource cards!
This game wants you to use a more watered down deck than MTG, increase the RNG and restrict your deck building even more. I really feel this is a core problem with the game, so much so that I wouldn't recommend it.
From what I've seen this is also the nail in the coffin for other players.
In my mind the fix for this problem would be: allow Hero/Avatar powers. The 5 campaign Heroes each already have their own 2 Mana spell, which has a little effect (gain 2 armor, ...) and draws you a resource card. Why not make it a permanent ability?
Also remove the 1/3 of deck forced resource, so people have more freedom to build.
I think I'll spend a little more time with this game, but once I'm bored I won't revisit it again unless there's a core change that tackles the dead draw problem. I only wish this promising game would stop sticking with frustrating mechanics of the past or else it will die rather quickly.

The only truly frustrating bit of control now is the final unlockable power, the grappling hook, which will occasionally fail to work with no clear reason why.
So, that's the main thing I wanted to bring across. Other things: The visual style is, of course, amazing. It's a competent metroidvania. The loading times are surprisingly long, but makes sense when you consider the art assets being loaded. Good day once again close friends and strangers of the vast and dangerous internets, I have returned for another review. This time, of Fallout 3. Shall we get started?
To start, I have to say I don't think I've ever experienced a more enjoyable character customisation than the one found in this game. It was full of humour and interesting choices (and said interesting choices often lead to more humour) and this theme continues throughout the duration of the game. Some notable choices include the chace to explode one of the only decent cities in the game, and the opportunity to commit genocide (that's going to remain without context; I don't want to spoil it for you). I honestly can't wait to jump back in and get back to making choices. CHOICES!!!!!!
There's plenty of content in this game. In most of my reviews I mention that there's a need for extra content, or so much of the same type of content that it got stale but, much like the story of goldilocks, this bed was just right (How can a bed be too soft?!) I liked how the game was riddled with locked doors that could only be opened if you had a certain science or lock picking skill
The storyline was admirable, but not incredible. It basically consisted of "You're dad's gone missing, go find 'im" and then turns into "Genocide, yes or no?" However, I really did like the way the environment and various notes and computers could tell their own story and add depth to the game. Not enough games do this. The last of which that I've played was Mass Effect and before that, Skyrim (Both of these score a 10/10, btw)(Although, Mass Effect loses points for not publishing the third one on Steam) Often enough, reading journal entries could reveal more about what was actually going on in the environment. For example, in one particular moment, test chambers had dead mutated humans and, upon walking into these rooms, you could discover that they still contain radiation. This in itself mightn’t reveal much, but reading some journal entries shows who was responsible for these deaths (I shall say no more.)
Now to mechanics. This game was built by Bethesda, so I thought I should mention that I noticed some similar mechanics in both of the games. However, obviously because this game is set in a post apocalyptic Washington D.C and not Viking Tamriel (And I'm not just saying that because of the helmets) There were some different and welcome variations between the two. For staters, the skill trees were far different. I actually liked the one in Fallout slightly (SLIIIIIIIGHTLY) better, although I can't really figure out why. However, I didn't really like how the currency in the game (Bottle caps) Were difficult to come by without performing getting bad karma (And I really wanted the good ending.) I honestly can't remember if I bought anything at all in this game. I just horded my caps until the end (Although, at times I wished I'd repaired my combat shotgun or purchased some health kits) For most weapons (All the weapons? I don't know, I didn't try them all out) There weren't any scopes, which made aiming excessively difficult. There was a cool system that allowed you to target a specific part of the body of your enemy and gave you a percentage chance of you hitting it. This was a great idea, but it was performed badly. A still, unaware target, regardless of the distance, should have a high percentage of hit. This wasn't always the case. Even a target standing 12 cm from your face only had a 95% chance of hit (SERIOUSLY, CHARACTER. DO YOU HAVE TOUURETTES?!) I would've disregarded this mechanic entirely except for the bonus critical chance it offers.
The art style was good. I liked the way everything, even the towns, looked so make-shift and finding American monuments completely exploded was somewhat satisfying (I'm getting arrested for saying that, huh?) The graphics were decent, especially considering when this game was created.
All right, let us summarise.
Character customisation: Good
Content: Excellent
Mechanics: Satisfactory
Art style: Good
I'm just about done. Final verdict- 8.3131932524020387829/10
Thanks for reading.

Sundered from the makers of Jotun is the best true metroidvania experience I have seen so far.
A couple Pros and Cons from what I have played so far.
Pros and Cons Mixed:
The art is beautiful and reminds me of Ralph Bakshi's Wizards if you have ever seen this cult late 70's film.
Though gameplay starts off challenging, the system for upgrading your character creates a harmony between skill and statistics that will promote growth, and assure the player even tough enemies will be brough down with patience.
Though some complain about the horde sytem, I believe it to be a great chance to build on skill, and promotes more of a fight or flight gameplay mechanic.  If a player obsesses with killing every enemy, breaking every pot they are quickly going to be overwhelmed.  It promotes knowing your limits and adaptibility.
You are going to die is this game, it is going to make you mad if you expect otherwise.  The good thing, you dont really have a percieved penalty for this besides going back to the hub, and some random layouts are more challenging than others.  Some area are set even if what is around them is not.  For example: First area has a spot with a thorn bush you have to double jump over, then you turn around double jump to a couple wall jumps and are to the top. Hard at first, but you do it 20 odd times it becomes second nature.
Enemys have set patterns to attacks. If you expect to button mash your way to victory, chances are you will be able to with enough character upgrades, but you are going to die, a lot.
Difficultly wise of the metroidvania style, I use the Castlevania SOTN to Ori and the Blind Forest scale.  Sundered feels like it is right in the middle.  SOTN being super easy, kill mermaids for the first hour and the rest of the game is cake.  Then with Ori there is escaping the tree filling with water...  Died probably 50 times.  If you beat it the first time, good for you.  There is no doubt a reason for it that, be it drugs, trust fund baby, kid, spawn of the devil, watched a video, no social life, or just a lot of experience with other similar platformers.  Good for you.  My point though, this is not as hard as Ori, and much harder than SOTN.
So far I am at the beginning of the second zone and do not have much informations on how your choices impact the game.  More to come once I have done a couple play throughs.
Overall, well worth the 20 dollar price tag.  Would buy it again, would buy it for a friend.

I thought i should rewrite my review, since my old one is.. well old, and horrible, so here we go! This game is probably the most unique game i've ever played, its a open world RPG much like The Elder Scrolls games, but Fallout has much more, such as radiation poisining, cripable limbs, better atmosphere and more realisim.
The story begins with your birth, and in a quick pace progresses to the most important moments of your childhood, such as the time you get your Pipboy 3000. You live in Vault 101, a place made to keep its citizens alive during the nuclear war that happened on the surface. But, Vault 101's doors never opened after the nuclear war. Everybody was to repopulate and die in Vault 101, nobody was to leave and nobody was to enter. But of course you got out because.. who would want to live in a scary vault filled with people for the rest of your life?
After your childhood "dream" ends you are awakened by alarms, you are very confused. Your best friend tells you that your father left Vault 101. You decide to leave Vault 101, as it is no longer safe, creatures from the outside have poured in because of your father opening the Vault door. When going outside of the vault, you can already feel the atmosphere, how amazing it is. In the distance you see cities, and of course, The wastelands. Now you should be ready to feel the awesomeness of the game, the quests.
In Fallout 3, there are many ways to finish quests. Lets say you need to get past a door, but you need a key to open the door. You could always pick pocket the person who owns the key, but depending on your skill level, he will notice, and start to kill you. You could also blow his brains out, easiest way to do it. But whatever you do, it will impact the future of your game. If you were bad throughout the game, and killed lots of innocent people, your Karma will go down. But if you do good things, your Karma will stay at a neutral level, or gain. Everytime you level up, you can choose a perk you would like to advance in, and you will get a certain amount of skill points to upgrade your stats. Also, theres a neat aiming system called VATs, its really hard to explain what it actually does, but you could always YouTube it.

They say you never forget your first love.  Warhammer Quest was my introduction to the wonderful world of tabletop RPGs, and, despite its flaws, I still look back fondly to those long afternoons spent hanging out with my buddies, eating pizza and murdering wave after wave of monsters.  So, when I saw that there was a PC version of it after all these years, I had to try it out.
The game is not without its downsides.  They kept the worst mechanics from the original game, which was that the warriors had to "buy" their level-ups with GP, and whichever warrior landed the killing blow on a monster got all of its GP.  My group quickly house-ruled those away.  This version keeps the purchase of levels, but at least it has a collective purse for the party.  It still has the "you kill it, you keep it" mechanic though, now in the form of XP.  So you still have to carefully manage the battles to ensure that your wizards get some kills, to ensure that they can progress alongside your fighters.
Some other thoughts:
- This game is very obviously a mobile port, with little or no attention given to updating the UI for a PC.  Everything in the game is controlled by the left mouse button: click some things, double-click some other things, click-and-hold yet other things.  Would it be so hard to add, say ability hotkeys, or replace the click-and-hold with right-clicks?  At least they did add in scroll-wheel zooming.
- The plot is paper-thin, and mainly just an excuse for the dungeon crawls.  But, that's not so different from the original game, if you played it straight from the source books and just rolled up the dungeons randomly.
- Some people have complained about the game being grindy.  I didn't find it to be that much of a problem; by the time I reached the last quest, about 2/3 of my party had hit the level cap of 8, and the rest were level 7 with max XP and just needed the gold to level.  So yeah, I might have needed a little grinding to max out everyone, but not all that much.
- In the mid- to late-game, the battles tend to be rather easy with the right strategy.  Just park your fighters in a doorway to create a bottleneck, with an archer and wizard behind for support.  Then laugh as your foes feed themselves to the grinder.  True to the original, though, get a few bad rolls and you can quickly find yourself swamped by two or three stacked random encounters.
Overall, if you're feeling nostalgic and can catch it on a sale, I'd say go ahead and pick this up.  This game won't ever be remembered among the RPG legends like, say, Baldur's Gate or Diablo, but it's a good one to pull off the shelf from time to time when you're in the mood to just mow down a ton of monsters without putting in a lot of thought.

When I go to a museum I take my time reading every single thing and walking around making sure I have missed nothing before I move onto the next exhibit. That is how this game should be played. It's a game for someone who takes in every bit of detail. Because, if you don't, I can imagine it being very bland.
The story is portrayed through audio clips, notes, and the environment. But the game is pretty much entirely static. But it nonetheless feels alive. Although you can still tell it's an indie production, the attention to detail is astounding. Even down to believable blurbs on bottles of ketchup! Multiple stories are weaved around one another, with one taking primacy eventually and which had me on the edge of tears.
And, oh boy, is there a lot to look at! You can interact with most things, and its impressive how seldom objects are repeated. [spolier]Though why does one family need so many phonebooks?![/spoiler] Imagine a game like Amnesia, which also gets its story across with notes and audio clips. Amnesia is a good game in other ways, but this game is to that what a Rembrandt is to something by your friend who's pretty good at drawing.
Every artefact has been individually crafted and even the form it takes can convey a lot to do with the story. And it's because of details like this that I even for a moment forgot I was playing a video game, where you assume things about the environment all the time because you have an idea of how video games work. For example, you might not think that some miscellaneous item in a room means anything because you know that the devs are just filling the space to make it look believable. But in Gone Home it felt like everything was there on purpose.
There's basically no puzzles or gameplay in a traditional sense, but I don't think it needs it. I know I'm way behind the curve only playing this now, but, damn, this is an example of something different which games can be. This was a story as much as a movie, but it was delivered in such a different way that it allowed for some very different things to be done. This is an exciting example of what games can be.
tl;dr: A great game if you like getting lost in the detail of a story, rather than waiting for the story between a bunch of arbitrary puzzles (of which there are basically none). Also a good game if you like 1990s garage bands.

Shaping up to be a great take on a city builder game. It plays more like Children of the Nile or another Tilted Mill/Innovations city builder than the Anno series's capitalism, and you have to work hard to keep people alive. Its still in early access but as long as you save at least once an hour you won't get any major bugs or problems.
The game is more about anticipating needs and surviving than entertaining or making money. It can feel like a drag at the start but the pace becomes increasingly frantic as your citizenry grows with exponential needs.
Moving away from something like Godus, for me the author/studio is refreshingly down to earth as well, and it is seeing regular feature updates with lots of communication. The game is substantially complete and rewarding (if occasionally gruelling); the interface works well; the MIDI style music isn't annoying; and the citizens are reasonably intelligent and free-willed.
If you enjoy planning/city sims and want to do it on a smaller scale, I don't think you'll regret getting this.

Carrier Deck is a simple management game where you control the deck of a carrier, select mission loadouts and manage who flies and where. Don't be fooled by the suggestion of a simulation game. It is definitely not one of those.
While it isn't the most detailed by far, and certainly not hard, it is capable of occasionally providing decent challenges and keeping the action up at a decent flow in the campaign. There are however several issues with it that make it difficult to really get into it.
(Campaign) Missions feel too small, and don't seem to really present a challenge except for the last few. But they are decent enough and enjoyable to play. On the contrary, 'quick' missions and endless mode are not really enjoyable as there is a large amount of waiting and when things do happen they seem to be randomly throwing things at you regardless of whether it's possible to succeed. This makes the endless mode more about luck than actually managing your carrier.
The other flaws include the hitbox for clicking on things being just too small on many things, leading to clicking off something and wasting time, and the airplane/heli pathing being terrible. They only move in pre-determined paths, and when they run into one another they wait for only a second or two before deciding to turn around and go back to where they were before you ordered them. This in turn makes managing any more than two or three things at the same time a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ as you need to babysit almost everything or risk them deciding they don't really want to do what you told them to.
Yet with all that, it's still decent. It's certainly not amazing, but it does what it tells you it will do, and it does so well enough to entertain. But it doesn't go past that, or try anything special, but it isn't bad at least. It's worth the price it asks for, but I wouldn't recommend it if you werent into any kind of management game. For those that are, Carrier Deck is worthwhile enough to try out.

Banished is an ambitious city builder that falls a bit short in nearly every aspect.  The characters are dull and lifeless compared to something like Tropico or Gnomoria, the buildings are an uninspired assortment of what seem like basic structures, and while the sound is pleasant the music is totally forgettable.
A few years ago this would have been an interesting experiment considering its only rival would have been the nearly impenetrable dwarf fortress, but in today's market with Gnomoria, and the offerings from double fine it seems barren and devoid of character.
It does have some positives though, for instance the citizen manager is what ever genre should strive to duplicate, the workers are fairly intelligent when it comes to path finding, and its easily the best looking game of its type.
In short, if you're a fan of this type of game you won't regret buying it when it's on sale, but I feel I should warn people off from buying it at full price.
Up Date:  I have changed my mind.  After the nonsense with Double Fine I realize how hard it is to make a compelling game of this type.  The good out weighs the bad in Banished and it's one of the few games to be as full featured as avertised.
