It turns out the prehistoric “quest for fire” is a little more complicated than you might think. In the opening scene of
, the main character falls asleep when he’s supposed to be guarding a fire in the center of his village. He awakes to find it extinguished and is subsequently banished by the village leader. After eating an apple with presumably magical (or at least mind-altering) powers he is given a quest by a talking tree to rescue a number of small insect-like faerie creatures and, most importantly, get the village’s fire back. Said quest involves, among other things, learning to control the rain, feeding bananas to space-faring monkeys, turning into a bear, and adjusting the rhythms of beat-boxing shrubbery.
Each of the ten levels in the game consists of objects, creatures, and scenery which can be interacted with to produce various effects. The goal of each level, as per the tree’s instructions, is to rescue the aforementioned magical bugs, who then warp you to the next level. Actually accomplishing this involves messing around in each level until you randomly free the bug. This is not a particularly logical adventure game, as the puzzles are quite nonsensical. What are you supposed to do with this bone? Obviously, throw it at an apple.
Despite frequent non sequiturs, the levels are internally consistent and make a fair amount of sense after enough clicking. As expected with an adventure game, once you build up the “vocabulary” of each level and discern what you can interact with and what happens when you do various things it’s simply a matter of combining each effect in the correct order. Most levels have only a handful of objects (and you can only hold one at a time) and everything that you’re able to click on can be highlighted with the press of a key, so overall complexity is pretty low. There are some stumper moments, but they’re more to do with not being on the same wavelength as the designer when it comes to random object combinations (like sticking a bug in a dead dinosaur’s nose).
To some extent this experimentation creates the feeling of discovering the way the world works for the first time, as one might romantically imagine a caveman doing. There’s even a little payoff for it in the last level, which requires you to combine solutions of several previous puzzles. But at the end of the day the puzzles all so wacky that you’re still just mashing things together until something happens. Having played a lot of other adventure games helps move things along, and I completed the game in a little over two hours with some fumbling here and there.
Atmosphere is the game’s strong suit. Though I was not overly enamored with the character design, the levels themselves and all of the objects in them are quite intricate and interesting to look at. The style is a sort of psychedelic oil painting crossed with vector graphics and hand drawn flourishes. It works well and it helps the game maintain its whimsical humor. Aside from a few random screens involving matching spinning shapes and playing a rudimentary version of Space Invaders, the game is fairly enjoyable while it lasts.
Your mileage may vary on the game’s humor (there are more than a few fart jokes and there’s a particularly strange level that involves bringing a tied-up woman to a fellow caveman who then carries her off), but for the most part it strikes a good balance between clever and silly. The main character, for his part, is affably clueless about what you’re making him do and bursts out laughing at a few points.
Serious adventure game fans will probably be disappointed with the shallow puzzle design and the game’s short length, but someone looking for a light-hearted romp through a wacky prehistory will find something to like in
.

Imagine your world suddenly plunging into darkness; all the illumination stolen in a flash. This was the case for the tiny hero Plug, who found himself lost among the branches the Amp Tree and began the journey to restore the stolen light of his world. By gaining a sense of direction from the hologram consciousness of the Amp-Tree-System, a fusion of natural flora with a computerized light power grid, Plug must repower the Amp Tree and defeat the Intruder virus before the world stays dark forever.
1000 Amps is an exciting and intuitive platformer. It challenges the player to use Plug's many special abilities, as well as discovering and adapting to new ones, to solve a number of different puzzles across a vast array of connected rooms. Each room is a piece of an incredibly powerful and awesome system with powered-down blocks hidden in every nook and corner. Every room permanently restored brings the player one step closer to stopping the Intruder Virus and saving the Amp Tree. It's a story of an impossibly small, filament-brained hero set in a world of platforms, gaps, and traps. 1000 Amps is sure to light up your day.

An excellent exploration-based platformer with puzzle elements, a series of upgrades, and a fully connected open world. The final boss was also very annoying and the ending was a little anticlimactic. If you aren't worried about perfect completion, then the game is pitched very well and feels very nice to work through.

This is one of the best card games you'll find out there. I play Magic the Gathering at a relatively high, competive level (GP top 64) and I can honestly say that this game is nearly as deep and engaging as Magic is.
Eternal does things that are simply not possible in a paper game, like Warcry (gives +1/+1 to the next creature/weapon in your deck), Echo (produces an exact copy of the drawn card and puts it into your hand) and permanent stat changes to cards that go to your void (graveyard). Eternal does this without needing to add too many random, game breaking and unpredicatble mechanics like Hearthstone does.
The power (mana) system works well, and you will rarely play a game in which you will be mana screwed. Being flooded seems to be a bit more likely, but that is a matter of deckbuilding choices more often than not.
I have been able to reach rank 8 in this game without having spent a single penny on it. This is not to brag, but just to illustrate that this game is truly free to play if you want it to be. However, I plan to spend money on this game to support the developers (some of which are Luis Scott Vargas and Patrick Chapin,MtG hall of famers). You will sometimes even run into them in game and be able to play against them.
All in all I think this game has tons of potential and will give MtG a run for their money in the long term.

The game is good.
Don't be cheap; buy the packs.  I was cheap, I grinded 130 hours over 12 days for my collection. But in my defence, I am a nut and I really liked the game.  However, before you sink any money in, try the game out thoroughly.
I recommened doing the free campaign modes to completion, skip the Jekk Bounty campaign until u decide you really want to play the game a lot (the Jekk Bounty campaign is behind a 20k gold/1000 gem paywall, you can totally grind the gold for it though and fair warning: it might be hard to complete with a limited card collection).
Then, finish the ALL the puzzles.  There is 80 puzzle scenarios and honestly this is what got me hooked.  Its a tutorial without being a tutorial.
Then do the Gauntlet, its always free and you get stuff from it provided you do well enough. This is the F2P way of grinding for cards, gold and sometimes packs in the beginning.  Its also where you test your crazy deck ideas without embarassing yourself against real people....before you use the deck against real people.
Then try Forge, its much like Hearthstone draft where you decided among 3 card choices.  You play against the AI which is way way way easier than playing against humans.  Your first Forge is free, after that its 2500 gold each time. You keep what you pick. After you pick a second color, the options given to you will always be in that color pair.
Then there is Draft.  Its ruthless, unfair, confusing and totally NOT for the uninitiated. If you don't know what you are doing, you will get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you on a plate.  The first draft is practically free (the new player quest rewards plus what you win from playing cover it) though so you can try it out without too much pain, otherwise its 5k gold to play.  Watch streamers/youtubers go through the drafting process before you do it.
Then there is casual and ranked play modes.  This is against real people. Do not expect to win games with your starter decks though you can totally do so. Variance can work as much against your opponent as it does work in your favor.
There is a competitive scene and tournaments events are happening weekly, google Eternal Tournament Series for more information on that.
Try the game out.  Good luck and have fun.

Normally I'm not one for horror games.
I've played my fair share of games with scary elements and have even delved into the terror-fest that is 'Amnesia', but horror is not a genre that has ever really scratched my gaming itch (ew?).
The reason for this is two-fold; usually I prefer the certainty of being able to set about attackers with a trusty piece of 2x4, and also because I don't tend to consider wetting myself a form of entertainment.
Outlast, however, is a very different breed of horror game to the usual "jump-scare" brigade and even outshines the great Amnesia, popularly considered king of horror, in certain unique ways.
Admittedly Outlast includes jump scares, and like Amnesia is also an incredibly atmostpheric horror experience - but one thing it does well, better than any game or film I've seen, is tension.
Creeping down dark, unlit corridors is a terrifying enough experience in and of itself, but when playing Outlast it feels like the most terrifying thing you have ever done in your entire life; the great graphics, score and sound effects all contribute to providing a really atmospheric experience, and the behaviour of the baddies is unique enough to be terrifying.
The lack of maps or any indicator of where opponents, objectives or escape routes are mean you are literally bumbling around in the dark, which is an incredibly well-crafted experience that made me feel as alone and vulnerable as my character (seriously, play it in the dark with headphones on, it's great).
As odd a sentence as this may sound, I don't wish to spoil too much about the gameplay, for Outlast is one of those games where the gameplay truly drives the story; with dialogue and scripted story events proving both short and sparse, every move you make from running down a corridor to hiding beneath a bed feels like a step forward in the narrative rather than a means to convey you from one plot-point to the next. This is enhanced by the genuinely well-implemented A.I., as watching them react to the player trying to escape or trying to hide is a genuinely scary experience - they pursue and hunt you not like some mindless A.I. bot but act and react exactly as a real-life opponent would; inspecting hiding spaces around where you disappeared and using the environment to their own advantage against you.
The one down-side is that with a little experience, a few cracks do tend to show here and there in the A.I. - it becomes increasingly easy to outsmart certain opponents with a bit of experience, and in earlier levels they tend not to check hiding places as stringently as they do in later ones (e.g. if the player escapes and hides in a locker, they will rarely check the locker he is actually hiding in unless they saw him enter it).
The removal of combat is another bonus. At first I was somewhat skeptical, but after a while I realised that the inability to pick up a nearby standing lamp and whale on the approaching troglodytes made the whole thing much more terrifying.
What do you do when you're literally forbidden to fight back? Run.
And what do they do when you run? They chase you. And by god they will not give up unless you literally vanish.
The addition of a button to make the character look over their shoulder during chase sequences pulls double-duty as both a useful tool to check your progress and as an added mechanic to make you wet yourself when you realise that Stabby McStabberson is actually a LOT closer than you thought he was.
The story is both well-crafted and delightfully simplistic for the most part; you play as Miles Uphshur, an investigative journalist come to Mount Massive Asylum on a tip from an insider about some sinister goings-on within. Throughout the course of the game, you collect data files, compile notes and observe significant characters involved in the outbreak at the asylum, all the while avoiding the crazed inmates (referred to as "variants") - subjects of what appears to be genetic experimentation, making them stronger, faster and more deadly than either Miles or the player would like.
There's more than meets the eye behind the horror at Mt. Massive, however, with a sinister backstory to uncover, a strange priest who seems to think Miles is some sort of apostle, and a huge, muscle-bound inmate called Walker who stalks the halls of Mt. Massive, killing apparently at random, and who relentlessly pursues Miles every step of the way on his journey through a living hell on Earth...
Outlast is an incredibly well-made horror game with jump-scare, atmospheric and tension-building elements out the butt, as well as some truly brilliant moments of game design and some jarringly hard to watch sections (not for the faint hearted!).
Do yourself a favour and get it.

Game could be great, but is very flawed at the moment.
1) Reload animations could be smoother and faster. for example, reloading bolt actions looks extremely awkward and robotic and slow. this goes for most other guns too, but its most obvious with bolt actions.
2) Lighting really needs to be improved, like an HDR type thing that balances out the darkness of the night/trench levels. Literal tunnels in the bunker are brighter than most trenches on day maps. I understand the "realsim", but in real life, eyes ADJUST to darkness.
3) Names or at least a class symbol to notify teammates need to be shown, when NOT looking directly at them. Spotting would be a plus, but teammate tagging NEEDS to be a thing, since you can barely tell outfits apart when the lighting is so messed up.
4) Faster Spawn times in frontline. I understand penalty spawn time add-on, but default spawn times taking over 10 seconds is a pain in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
5) Fix aiming. it feels very unrealistic and not its fluid. Turning while aiming should make the FRONT sights move, not the rear sights, like in real life, when you aim somewhere, your rear sights would focus first, cause its closer to you.  I'd recommend looking at DOI or Insurgency for a more realistic aiming style. movement and aiming both feel very clumky and unrealistic in Verdun.
6) Improved weapon sounds. alot of them sound either very fake or very movie-like. which leads to #7
7) show what direction youre being shot from, especially when you die. its extremely frustrating when youre being suppressed but cant even tell where its coming from. like I know it tells you when you get hit, but most hits are 1-hit-kils, so its useless if you die and it STILL doesnt tell you
8) Add the ability to pick up enemy weapons. its really ABSURD that a squad leader with only a pistol cannot pick up an enemy rifle at all. I've seen people say its unbalanced, but thats just stupid. Plenty other games do it and it works just fine. How is running out of ammo and being stuck with melee only "balanced". I'm NOT asking to take their entire ammo bag or anything, just the rifle and any ammo in it.
9) allow spending of career points in the menu. its a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to go into a game just to spend points, especially for game modes that have empty servers, or for squads that nobody wants to vote to switch to.
10) allow us to check our lvl progress at the pause menu in Frontline mode.
11) extend the desertion boundries on battle lines. especially in Co-Op its stupid how standing on the edge of a trench can get you killed for desertion
12) make climbing out of Wire easier. I'd understand taking damage and slowing you down, but slower-than-crawling movement and making it kill you within 3 seconds is very stupid.
13) Make Gas/Artillery warnings much more obvious. Gas/Arty notifications and The Attack/Defence phase notifications look almost identical, and on top of that, if your C/O is in your area, the red warning is hardly visible, if at all, on the mini map
14) fix transitions between stances. Theres awkward pauses between moving between standing/crouching/crawling. Also, running from a crouch/crawling stance should make you RESUME that stance when you finish running. I mean, at least make it an OPTION in the settings. No other game I know makes you resume a crouch/crawl when running.
Basically, I want to love this game, but it definitely needs a BIG overhaul to fix this stuff. For a game using REALISM as a selling point, alot of issues ruin the immersion, and I know alot of the userbase agrees. I enjoy this game a lot, it does have some flaws but overall it been pretty fun
one of the things that makes the game stand out a little better is the horde mechanic, this mechnic is something you'll either enjoy or it'll make you hate the game. As you play you fight groups of enemies and after a while you'll hear a chime that sends a massive group of enemies after you that you must either fight or run from. the longer you last the harder the horde seems to get
I enjoy this mechanic because its part of a series of game design choices that actually all work together well
The other parts that go with Horde are that
1. there are shortcuts you open up everywhere which make it very easy to get almost anywhere in the game.
2. you upgrade your character and choose perks in the main hub area, you can go there by selecting so from the pause screen or by dying, usually by dying

I've described this game to people as "Cthulhu Guacameleee", but that's not quite right, and I think that disconnect is what turned a lot of people off.  In a game like Metroid or Castlevania, you control the pace of the game by the rate at which you go forwards.  You know that you're generally safe once you've cleared a room until you leave it for another.  Sundered takes away that control, creating ambient enemies at a randomized density, in randomized levels, and spawning hordes on a randomized timer.  The result feels a little like a survival horror game, where the urge to explore and take ones time has to be tempered against the need to push forwards before the next rush.  This is a button-mashy, crowd-controlling game, where the challenge lies in attacking and moving efficiently and recognizing threats in a horde of enemies.
My favorite part of Sundered was the extremely satisfying sense of progression.  The Eshe I ended the game as was orders of magnitude more powerful than the Eshe I started as.  From movement, to combat, to just filling out the map, my ascent left me wanting more in a good way.
A frequent complaint is frustration in the early areas.  I found the key was coming to understand that every death brought progress, even if it wasn't obvious.  Uncovering a new area of the map is progress, even if you die in the doorway.  Learning something about managing dodges, or juggling different types of monsters at once, puts you in a position to do better in the next run.  As the game goes on, you will have more control and understanding, until a new area or enemy type throws a wrench in the works.
The comparison to Dark Souls is informative.  Every death takes you back to the starting point, which makes new shortcuts often the most precious kind of resource.  This also means that some difficult areas or encounters may have you trekking back to it eight or ten times before you beat it, which really walked the line between a cooling-off period, a punishment, and a waste of time.  Progression is not linear, and you will usually have several unexplored branches to work on at any given time.
The art is really striking, and I liked the sound effects.  (The final boss has visible pixel artifacts from compression, which was an odd blemish.)  This game needed more/better lore:  the 'story' rooms give a few simplistic sentences each, and the boring quotes on the upgrade tree are a missed opportunity to do some ambient storytelling.  The names we hear more than once are never humanized or characterized in any meaningful way.  The story twist, if it could be called that, is predictable from the first minutes of the game.
The randomized map works well, especially when later parts of the game show that it's more variable than it looks at first.  The map screen is very clear and informative.  The game never ran out of surprises for me until I was doing postgame achievement grinding.

This game is by far one of my favorite games in existence.
Everything about this game is a masterpiece. The majority of people will instantly point to the aesthetics, which I don't deny include jaw-dropping artwork and animations that make your skin crawl (bosses and corrupted abilities are so epic). But in particular I think the best technical aspect of the game is the balance, which ironically is what all the bad reviews seem to be complaining about.
Having played many of these types of games, the learning curve is perfect. You progress, then you die and use what you gained to level up. You fight a boss and feel your heart sink because of how badly you fail. Or to put it differently, the second boss is absolutely hilarious; anyone who avoids dying in the first 5 seconds the first time around is missing out on a great laugh. And then you move on for an hour fighting in the next area, level up a bit, spend a few minutes thinking carefully about your perks, and suddenly you beat the boss without taking damage. It feels amazing.
I didn't realize exactly how well things were balanced until I beat Normal mode on Embrace and decided to do my Resist run on Insane mode. It was a brilliant challenge. I thought I had mastered the mechanics and was quickly proved wrong. The exact same feelings from before emerged; everything seemed hopelessly impossible, but after a few short hours I was able to bring down the first boss. You feel absolutely amazed at yourself, all the way to the end.
The other thing which really awed me was the map design. The flow of unlocking shortcuts so you can get back to where you were, the way that the terrain evolved to suit the enemies, and all the ways in which rooms challenged you to keep using ALL your abilities really made this the metroidvania I'd been waiting for. There are so many metroidvania games where some abilities get really eclipsed by others, but this is not one. In fact, the only exception to this was the cannon in Resist mode (when you corrupt it, you'll want to use it all the time)... and to avoid spoilers, I'll just say that towards the end I was surprised when the devs made an excellent (and thematic) choice in requiring its use.
I really don't understand the bad reviews at all. The overall game balance is exceptional, the combat is smooth and satisfying (dare I say elegant?), the diversity of gameplay is there, the atmosphere and story are really engaging, the visuals are one-of-a-kind. Randomly generated map sectors in a metroidvania is also wickedly creative, and this game executes the concept well (other games have done it, but I haven't played Dead Cells yet :P). I don't think I even encountered a single bug in about 40 hours of gameplay so far. The majority of bad reviews come from whiners that want all games to be easy, the people that didn't struggle as kid for hours days and weeks when the original Megaman/Sonic/Mario/Zelda/etc games were released.
Buy this game. It's also got ridiculous replayability. I can't wait to completely forget how to play in 2 years and start all over.

TFSW is obviously based on FSX with some addons for weather etc. Main improvement is the updated menus and flight preparation, that is huge improvement over FSX. Somehow it reminds me Microsoft Flight - which is a good thing. Another major improvement over FSX is loading time - shaders and scenery are cached during the first launch and than every other launch is almost instant (at least on my rig).
In the current state of game you will get only few planes, all are general aviation, mostly single engine. Which is not a good choice, because you don't get anything new regarding the landscape, so no eye candy for your VFR flights. Flight models seems to me the same as were used in FSX. Planes that I have tested so far looks and handles well, and the big plus is addition of automated checklist, which again strongly reminds me Microsoft Flight (which is a good thing again). I have to admit that I liked Microsoft Flight a lot and it was a huge letdown for me when they tried to turn it from bush plane sim to casual airplane game - which was doomed to fail from the beginning, because instead of game for VFR enthusiasts it turned into a game for nobody. But the developing team did a great job in terms of graphic and optimization and introduced a lot of fresh ideas, that will be hopfelly re-used also in FSW)
But now for something completely different - the cons
First of all - no real weather - why?
Second - do you remember that ugly text to speech voices from older versions of X-plane? That's what you get in FSW. My guess is that thay wanted to improve ATC communication, but that would mean to re-record everything, so they choose to use speech synthesis. If you are used to FSX ATC communication, or radio chatter in current version of X-plane you will be freaked by this (and probably turn ATC volume to zero).
Third - there sems to be no improvements regarding landscape. So all the FSX problems like ugly linear coastlines etc. remains also here. X-plane is now miles ahead in terms of autogen scenery. This is one of the main reasons I am giving it negative review - next gen sim have to offer much more than unnaturally lit procedurally generated landscape
So at the current state of the game I cannot recommend it. If you want to throw your money into some new sim you can also consider
- either current version of X-plane, which has it's own issues but still is the best alternative to FSX. And I have to admit that current version (11) is huge step forward
- if you dont mind another early acces game try Aerofly FS 2 - it is currently in a similar stage like this game but offers a beautifull scenery for VFR (but I am afraid that it might turn into a cash grab)
So far I don't know if FSX will be able to deliver what I expect from a modern sim. And I have  two more big isues with it.
First - they are releasing paid DLCs for early access game. Dovetail games are notorious for milking it's customers via expensive DLCs, but in early access stage it is (at least from my point of view) simply wrong
Second - rewriting a decade old game core while also keeping backwards compatibility with what have been created for FSX is a nice idea, but it seems like a really difficult task. But if they manage to do this I will happily update this review to positive - untill that I am remaining skeptical...
But I really wish they succeed and give us a fresh and modern sim with lots of additional content. With the progress I will be also updating this review, but for now as a VFR enthusiast I will stick with FSX + Orbx

An extremely enjoyable game, very nice to play when you want something calm and idyllic. My advice is to be stingy on house building; there's no need to feel bad about the kids never moving out of their parents' house. ALWAYS make sure you have more than enough food to support your population. DON'T trade away stone or iron/iron tools or your steel tools. Those are finite resources on your maps, and you always want to trade FOR them. Same goes for coal - it's not worth mining (you have to choose coal or iron, choose the latter!), because steel tools aren't as valuable as you think they are (except for if you desperately need to trade for seeds maybe) and the villagers often take the coal to heat their homes, which is a complete waste. And last but not least (this will save you a headache later) build your cemetery as big as you can, preferably as far away as you can. These are just some basic advice, there are many more tips/tutorials you can find online.
The only drawback on this game is maybe not enough micro-managing, which is something I prefer in my games. Unless you build a huge metropolis, you will find you often run out of things to do other than just stalk a villager or watch the animals roam around.

TLDR Rating: 8/10
-=A Little Background=-
I can explain the Fallout series in one sentence: Post-Nuclear-War version of Skyrim with gun. If you've never played a Bethesda game before, I will point this out now: 99.9% of the time they will not fix bugs or glitches. This has been the case for almost all the Bethesda games, such as Skyrim, Morrowind, Fallout: New Vegas, and Fallout 3. So if you find a gun that can wipe the face of the Earth for a second time, don't expect it to be taken away by and update or patch.
-=The Review=-
Fallout 3 puts you in the hands of a Vault Dweller; A person that has been living in a giant hole in the ground that has been sealed for many years. You don't remember how you got there, but everyone says that 'You are born in the Vault, and you die in the Vault', however this is not the case for you. Your Dad escapes the Vault for reasons you don't know, and you feel destined to find him. However, you haven't seen the world outside the Vault, and tales tell of mutants, raiders, and monsters. Despite knowing this, you venture outside the Vault to find a destroyed world. How you proceed from there is up to you. The game is completely open world, allowing you to do no quests and still have a great time. Beware, however, as the tales that you where told where true! If you want to get your Dad back, you'll have to ventrue through the Wasteland (Mojave Desert) and fight for survival. Will you be the greatest hero the Wasteland has ever seen, or the most feared killer in the world? That's up to you.
-=Misc. Ratings=-
Sound: 7/10
As mentioned above, you have been in this Vault for years. Radios won't be playing 'Summertime Sadness'; Instead, enjoy oldies such as 'I Don't Want To Set The World On Fire' by The Ink Spots and other music from the 1900s.
Graphics: 8/10
For an older game, it's graphics still look pretty nice. You can even see the guns in the raiders pockets that they'll use!
Gameplay: 9/10
I really think that this beats some games produced even today! You can even drag bodies around, just like Skyrim! You can use VATS (Vault Auto Targeting System) to aim if your not that great with a gun!
-=Final Notes=-
Despite this game saying that it may not work on Windows 7 and above, I use Windows 7 with a dedicated graphics card and have had no problems. I have not tested it on Windows 8.

Clearly inspired by 2013's
(which the developer at least have the decency to acknowledge), this game has the quirkiness and tongue-in-cheek playfulness of that title, but with none of the personality, finese or fun. Robotic limbs are pretty damn bad*ss (one day I really hope we'll see some robotic *sses, too! Maybe I'll even get one myself if I'm real lucky), and I guess tea is pretty decent as well, but here, they really don't blend very well at all.
Controlling the robotic arm of a recovering amputee (because they're classy with their set-up like that), you must fulfill the order required to make a satisfactory cup of tea and try your best not to completely wreck the gaff in the process. The arm itself is somewhat unwieldy and very unintuitive to direct, with the motions of the fingers being a particular bugbear. In Surgeon Simulator the controls were laid out in a way that made sense and soon felt pretty natural to use, and the solid, slightly stubby fingers meant picking up items was mostly quick and straightforward. Here, however, an awkward control scheme mixed with long, gangly, slow-moving digits that don't even close properly makes for the majority of the challenge as you struggle massively with picking up anything and wrestling with pretty much every single object you try to interact with.
There isn't really much more to the game other than grabbing a cup, putting some items into it, moving the cup around, adding some liquids then placing the cup on a platter. And after you've done that once, you've essentially seen all the game has to offer. You can always smash everything up or flip the table (possibly breaking the arm as you do), but other than that, nada. Depending on how quickly the controls click with you or how lucky you get, you could probably finish this in anything from 10 to 40 minutes (I think I completed every achievement bar one in half an hour), and after that you've no real reason to revisit it since there's nothing else on offer except to retry the task with slightly different orders or quantities of ingredients.
More frustrating and annoying than bad, given how little content there is here, and how not particularly fun it is, there's no way I could recommend it at full price, and, if anything, fives euros seems like a bit of a p*ss take if you ask me. If controlling the thing wasn't so unneccesarily cumbersome, or there was more content beyond a single "quest" to complete, I'd likely endorse it, but as it stands, it's probably worth something closer to 50c. Though there could be an argument made for it being free. If it's on sale and you just
to see what the fuss is about, maybe it's worth briefly investigating. But in any other circumstances, there's really so many other, better things you could be wasting your time and money on than this.

This game is overrated. The fact that VVVVVV perfectly recreates the arcades of 1980s or challenges the timing skills of players in the fashion similar to “Super Meat Boy” does not oblige anyone to burst into nostalgic tears and rate the game as an indisputable masterpiece. It is not for the lack of atmosphere that I do not recommend the game — old arcades often had an “excuse plot” and that was perfectly fine. It is not the difficulty — these games have nurtured generations of hardcore players that achieved robotic precision mastering the levels (compare “Mega Man”). The overall scale seems too small, the world is not detailed and diverse enough: even within that abstract and geometric style one could have created stupendous mazes with specific traits and unique atmosphere. Could have, but has not. Some suspicion that this game was hyped just because “indie developers must be supported” still lurks in my mind.
Creating a game “à la eighties” to honour the timeless 8-bit æsthetics is such a responsible task, and one cannot just take the mechanics and the look of a different epoch and reproduce them using modern approach. Compare Jamestown — a perfect old-school shoot-'em-up game that is really indistinguishable from the 1990s shooters. It is so easy to trick anyone into thinking that it had been created 20 years ago because the look and feel are very convincing. On the contrary, you can’t plausibly think of “VVVVVV” as an 1980s game. With an aching heart I do post this review, without any hope to gain recognition or ingratiate myself with fans’ favour.

Ampu-Tea is a Surgeon Simulator inspired game where you are an amputee fitted with a robotic arm and are tasked with making a cup of tea. In the style of SS, you control your robo-hand to attempt assembling different kinds of teas with the mouse and keyboard. The silly control style provides a challenge to this otherwise simple task and it will test your patience and eventually lead to some chaos.
Honestly, this game was a disappointment, and I wasn't even expecting anything from it. My experience playing this game was mostly frustration, thanks to the awful controls and mechanics.
There is no grip to pick up anything, so I had to rely on pushing things across the table with the hand and trying to balance cup handles around the fingers. Speaking of the fingers, grabbing with them is incredibly slow and insensitive, along with the hand rotation. It took me
of messing around just to make one cup of tea because of how fragile the mugs are, how easy it is to knock the shelf off the table, the painful journey of moving the cup from each station, and how easy it is to break the arm itself.
There is little variety in what types of drinks you can make, and no story or real motivation to make them except for a sticky note. The game description mentions being the son of an Earl, but I found no connection to that in the game. The achievements are (despite the shocking controls) fairly easy to get, minus the one for opening the game
which I did not have the patience for. There are trading cards, but I uninstalled the game before I had enough game time to collect them.
The only highlight I managed to draw from this game was being able to flip the table in rage. That's about it. I wish I had more to say.
In short, Ampu-Tea relies on the 'joke game' factor and being a silly game for YouTubers to play. There are no outstanding features in this game besides being pointlessly difficult and having more 'Keep Calm's and 'EPIC FAIL's than is socially acceptable. It is not worth the $4.99 price tag, but if you
want to play it, wait for it to hit 90% off  on a sale at $0.49.
I personally did

Game could be great, but is very flawed at the moment.
1) Reload animations could be smoother and faster. for example, reloading bolt actions looks extremely awkward and robotic and slow. this goes for most other guns too, but its most obvious with bolt actions.
2) Lighting really needs to be improved, like an HDR type thing that balances out the darkness of the night/trench levels. Literal tunnels in the bunker are brighter than most trenches on day maps. I understand the "realsim", but in real life, eyes ADJUST to darkness.
3) Names or at least a class symbol to notify teammates need to be shown, when NOT looking directly at them. Spotting would be a plus, but teammate tagging NEEDS to be a thing, since you can barely tell outfits apart when the lighting is so messed up.
4) Faster Spawn times in frontline. I understand penalty spawn time add-on, but default spawn times taking over 10 seconds is a pain in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
5) Fix aiming. it feels very unrealistic and not its fluid. Turning while aiming should make the FRONT sights move, not the rear sights, like in real life, when you aim somewhere, your rear sights would focus first, cause its closer to you.  I'd recommend looking at DOI or Insurgency for a more realistic aiming style. movement and aiming both feel very clumky and unrealistic in Verdun.
6) Improved weapon sounds. alot of them sound either very fake or very movie-like. which leads to #7
7) show what direction youre being shot from, especially when you die. its extremely frustrating when youre being suppressed but cant even tell where its coming from. like I know it tells you when you get hit, but most hits are 1-hit-kils, so its useless if you die and it STILL doesnt tell you
8) Add the ability to pick up enemy weapons. its really ABSURD that a squad leader with only a pistol cannot pick up an enemy rifle at all. I've seen people say its unbalanced, but thats just stupid. Plenty other games do it and it works just fine. How is running out of ammo and being stuck with melee only "balanced". I'm NOT asking to take their entire ammo bag or anything, just the rifle and any ammo in it.
9) allow spending of career points in the menu. its a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to go into a game just to spend points, especially for game modes that have empty servers, or for squads that nobody wants to vote to switch to.
10) allow us to check our lvl progress at the pause menu in Frontline mode.
11) extend the desertion boundries on battle lines. especially in Co-Op its stupid how standing on the edge of a trench can get you killed for desertion
12) make climbing out of Wire easier. I'd understand taking damage and slowing you down, but slower-than-crawling movement and making it kill you within 3 seconds is very stupid.
13) Make Gas/Artillery warnings much more obvious. Gas/Arty notifications and The Attack/Defence phase notifications look almost identical, and on top of that, if your C/O is in your area, the red warning is hardly visible, if at all, on the mini map
14) fix transitions between stances. Theres awkward pauses between moving between standing/crouching/crawling. Also, running from a crouch/crawling stance should make you RESUME that stance when you finish running. I mean, at least make it an OPTION in the settings. No other game I know makes you resume a crouch/crawl when running.
Basically, I want to love this game, but it definitely needs a BIG overhaul to fix this stuff. For a game using REALISM as a selling point, alot of issues ruin the immersion, and I know alot of the userbase agrees. And if you really want to pull a REALISM card on anything, it should be the fact that theres NO FRIENDLY FIRE. again, DOI has Friendly fire (with reduced damge) and it works out really well.

At its core, 1000 Amps is somewhat similar to VVVVVV - you've got a whole bunch of interconnected rooms to explore, and will spend most of your time figuring out how to get to them all. That said, there are a couple of things going on here to help separate this one from its "metroidvania" peers:
- Right off the bat, there's the graphical style, which is built almost entirely on sharp, grayscale squares; it might come off as dull at a glance, but for a world built with such limited materials it actually looks pretty nice. The simple black, white, and shades in between are pleasant and clean, not to mention spiced up by the lighting, which I'll get further into in a moment.
- While most platformers of this ilk immediately reveal the full layout of each room you enter, in 1000 amps the power has been cut across the entire map, so you have to feel your way around in total darkness and touch various blocks as you go to render them visible. The most important of these are "light-up" blocks, since if you find all of them in a single room the power will be permanently switched back on and that room will be "solved"; moreover, each one you find charges your battery, which enables higher jumps and the use of special abilities, so you'll often need to plan your route to complete the circuit. At this point I'll also note that there's no music to speak of until you solve a room, which prompts some manner of synthesized bell tune to pipe in; I can't say I was humming along to most of the music, but the overall effect suited me fine.
- If you're looking for combat you'd best look elsewhere, since there really aren't any "enemies" wandering around in the traditional sense; actually, there aren't any dangerous obstacles here either, or any way to "die" at all. About the worst that can happen to you is that you unintentionally pass through a non-solid floor or wall into a different room and lose your progress in the one you were working on; this can be frustrating, as there's no way to tell what's where when you first enter a new area (at least until you get the Sonar, one of a few upgrades you'll need to progress past certain points), but it usually doesn't take too terribly long to get back where you were, especially if you've already solved some of the surrounding rooms and can pass through them quickly.
So there you have the game's most distinguishing features; now, how do they all fit together? For the most part, pretty well: control-wise all you need are the WASD/arrow keys to move and jump around, plus the mouse cursor to guide the crucial "teleport" ability, unlocked early on. There are a handful of technical "tricks" to discover as you get more comfortable, which are essential to giving yourself that little extra boost you need to sneak over a wall or graze past a remote light-up block; the game doesn't present too many overt hints to this end, but I'd wager that players familiar with platformers in general should be able to figure them out without too much trouble. On the whole, that's pretty much all there is to know about 1000 Amps, which is fine: you explore, you experiment, you light stuff up and fill in the map a bit at a time.
Puzzle-platformer fans should enjoy themselves on the whole, but there are a handful of caveats. First and foremost, the creator's total devotion to the black-and-white art style can sometimes hamstring it: in certain situations you have to look closely to spot a less-than-obvious doorway or other element, and you'll be squinting particularly frequently at the (also grayscale) in-game map as you attempt to visually determine whether or not you missed a particular tiny passageway from way back when...and there's no way to mark or annotate it either. I can understand and appreciate sticking to one's guns artistically, but in this case I'd call it more of a hindrance than it's worth - I managed to get the completion percentage to 99% before finally giving up on figuring out which slightly-darker-than-the-rest speck on the map I'd overlooked.
Also be aware that there's no genuine transporter hub or other means of "fast travel" here: granted, the map isn't super-huge and can be traversed fairly quickly once you're breezing through solved rooms, but there are more than a few lengthy routes which can only be completed in one direction, so if you need to retrace your steps you've got no choice but to slog your way to the starting point (which can, again, be tougher to determine than it needs to be thanks to the map's deficiencies) and begin from square one. This is compounded by a couple of rooms that are particularly easy to fall out of by accident until you've turned all the lights on, and a few others which require some fairly precise tapping and clicking to clear; most of the time things feel fair and forgiving without being condescending, but there is some grumbling to be had here and there.
Hopefully at this point you've got a decent idea of what 1000 Amps has to offer, and what it doesn't: it's only a couple of bucks to acquire, should only take you a few hours total to finish your first time through (though I'd imagine it's ripe for speed-running once you know where you're going), and for the most part delivers on its simple, pleasant concept of a visually-sound, non-violent exploratory puzzle-platformer. If that summary appeals to you, by all means save this one a place in your Library.

Ultimate Chicken Horse is probably the #1 party game currently available on Steam. If you're looking for high energy, hilarious, and challenging couch or online multiplayer, it should be first on your list, before even Lethal League, Castle Crashers, or Speedrunners.

The game itself has seven or so currently flyable aircraft, all of which are general aviation aircraft (Piper Cherokees, Cubs, etcetera.) meaning we have nothing but light propellor aircraft. This is understandable
as the game is still in the early-access, in development phase. Apparently we'll eventually get some larger, turbojet aircraft, so that sorts that issue out, as long as they don't have each and every single future aircraft released as a paid DLC.
DLC. That's my issue with Flight Sim: World.
Yes, some of the DLC are aircraft models made by third parties which is a thing I am fine with, however Dovetail is releasing additional content for the game prior to it being completed - something of which I strongly dissagree with. Surely, one would think, you would complete and fix the game and the issues within, as I have encountered
in my fairly short time on FSW before even considering the release of additional content. For example, lights do not illuminate the ground when taxiing in the dark, and the ATC sounds even worse than that of FSX, shadows often flicker in and out as well as clouds playing havoc with textures on the ground.
That's what I mean. Complete/fix the game prior to releasing extra content we don't (for the most part) need yet.
If you're going to get FSW, wait until it's got a bit more going for it (that's included in the base game - not the ever-increasing amount of DLCs)!

I was initially going to give the game a thumbs up, but as I wrote the review, I realized I didn't really feel like playing it anymore, which constitutes in my mind a thumbs down.
Having said that, it's not an emphatic thumbs down, it's a "sad I couldn't give it a thumbs up" thumbs down. Sundered has lots of stuff going for it.
Without a doubt, it is one of the most gorgeous games I've seen. Ever. Great character designs coupled with splendid animating really make the game a feast for the eyes. We often see great main characters with millions of frames of animations, and then enemies that look like they're from bad flash games. Not so here. Enemies move almost as fluidly as the main character.
I find the skill tree to be well done. I'm always excited to see how many upgrades I can get whenever I get back to the sanctuary. I find the cost/enhancement ratio pretty reasonable, as I've never found myself really frustrated by lack of funds, and I didn't blow through the whole tree too really early in the game.
The skills you can get are okay. I mean there's nothing exceptional about them, but it's always satisfying to get them, and they're well spaced apart, so you don't get too bored waiting for new stuff.
Where the game hits a wall for me is the gameplay and procedurally generated portions of the map.
Most of the difficulty in the game is created by having swarms of enemies siddle up and harrass your character to death. Individually, none of the enemies are particularly difficult, but having dozens - and I do mean dozens quite literally - of annoying critters hack away at your character is a bit frustrating. I've always prefered the Ninja Gaiden (on Normal) philosophy for difficulty : make basic enemies tough (well, tougher) to begin with, which will help develop playing skill, so adding more enemies makes for exciting battles later in the game. Here the battles are mundane and repetitive, with difficulty that isn't rewarding.
The level design using procedurally generated portions is something I don't personnally enjoy. In the end, these portions end up being anonymous and repetitive, and having random enemies shot into these areas also doesn't make for interesting action. In great metroidvania games, all rooms are memorable, and by crafting each room individually they can each present different challenges. Procedural generation prevents this altogether.
It also makes for longish loadtimes. And here I though Nier had long load screens.
All of this to say that I'm sad to give this game a bad review. It just doesn't play to my tastes, even though the presentation and style do. I'm sure some people are going to enjoy this game, but I don't think I can find a way to recommend this game to someone. I'm pretty sure no one answers "Yes" to "Do you like repetitive and unsatisfying battles?", so I give it a thumbs down.

An extremely enjoyable game, very nice to play when you want something calm and idyllic. My advice is to be stingy on house building; there's no need to feel bad about the kids never moving out of their parents' house. ALWAYS make sure you have more than enough food to support your population. DON'T trade away stone or iron/iron tools or your steel tools. Those are finite resources on your maps, and you always want to trade FOR them. Same goes for coal - it's not worth mining (you have to choose coal or iron, choose the latter!), because steel tools aren't as valuable as you think they are (except for if you desperately need to trade for seeds maybe) and the villagers often take the coal to heat their homes, which is a complete waste. And last but not least (this will save you a headache later) build your cemetery as big as you can, preferably as far away as you can. These are just some basic advice, there are many more tips/tutorials you can find online.
The only drawback on this game is maybe not enough micro-managing, which is something I prefer in my games. Unless you build a huge metropolis, you will find you often run out of things to do other than just stalk a villager or watch the animals roam around.

A very light simulation composed of a bunch of randomly-ordered QTE-based meal preparation tasks using fun little widgets. You select what food you'll sell today, start the day and then fill the orders as they come in. At the end of the day, you read your 'emails', which give you hints on what may happen the following day. There's a bit of management sim in here, but it's mostly about the QTEs.
(Note that the food order QTEs are not particularly complex. There are fewer steps to cooking an item here than in, say, Cooking Mama. Although the complexity does increase the further you get in the game.)
The game also boasts some competitive and cooperative modes, an online leaderboard with weekly challenges, etc. I haven't spent much time in those modes yet.
Anyways, if that sounds like your sort of thing, I recommend picking it up.

1000 Amps is a deceptively challenging platformer; you control Plug who can move and jump with the goal of each room being to touch all the lights. Spread out at the far edges of the "Light Tree" are rooms that give you special abilities that make it easier for you to jump, move or turn on lights. Hell technically you don't even have to light every single room up to advance if you can find the exit.
There's not much else to really add. Personally I found it really fun: it was the game I would load up when I had less than half an hour to kill and while there are a few rooms that require you to basically smack your head against the wall until you get the perfect jump or teleport it's not particularly frustrating. The biggest negative I can think against it is that backtracking can be extremely tedious and the map was of little use since it just shows you what rooms are lit up and no actual details.
Overall the game was extremely well designed and the simplistic aesthetics are a neat touch. It's not a must have game, but if you enjoy open puzzle/platforming games you will get a kick out of it.

Hmm, conflicted on this one. On one hand it has mechanics down beautifully and generally good design for each room. On the other hand it revels in the tedium of making the player replay large sections if they make a single mistake, as falling off the bottom of the screen can send you to a room you can't go back up out of. This is especially awful in the map-wide loop to unlock the final (optional) power-up, but generally an issue. The "resetting once you leave a room" bit is also mildly infuriating; maybe it factors in to the puzzles at some points, but it really feels more annoying than clever. Some rooms also really, truly rely on random luck, and I never figured out what makes conveyor belts load properly. Small nitpick but the map is kind of too small to be much help, as well, a zoomed-in option would've really been appreciated. The sound design is also cute at first but quickly becomes grating, as you will hear the poor-sounding piano pretty much everywhere.
So there's a lot of bad things to say about this game, definitely, but it's generally fun, all things considered. The power-ups are all useful and tend to make navigating earlier parts of the map easier. The map isn't overwhelmingly huge and the game doesn't drag on, but there's still plenty to explore. The puzzles are generally clever though there were a few instances of "jump and immediately teleport so you don't go off the top of the screen" that I reeeally did not care for. It's certainly a neat little game and I don't regret playing it, but don't expect to be blown away by it either.

I was torn on whether to recommend this game, so I sat back and asked myself, "How did this game leave me feeling at the end? What was I feeling most of the time I was playing it?" And the answer to both of those questions is "frustrated and stressed"
This game is a puzzle platformer metroidvania, with both puzzle and platform elements very much intertwined. Your goal is to light up all the rooms in the game by touching all the light blocks in the rooms in one go. Near the beginning in addition to standard 2d WASD controls you also get the ability to teleport to your mouse pointer while conserving momentum, at the cost of darkening nearby blocks, so already the platforming has a pretty novel puzzle element.
The game's graphics are minimalist, but that's not a bad thing. What is bad is the minimap. For some stupid reason, it's blurry as drowned newsprint, and that makes it very difficult to hunt down all the areas you need to find and light. So that's an overarching source of irritation. Sometimes the screen will flash due to something that happened in the game, and it won't go away quick enough, and you'll miss something important and have to restart the room. The screen size is tiny and you cannot enlarge it, leading to puzzles that you could solve RIGHT NOW if the camera would just go up HALF A BLOCK, IS THAT TOO MUCH TO ASK
Ahem.
The platforming takes a little time to get used to, because your jump height depends on the percentage of blocks in a given room you have succesfully lit. But you get a feel for it soon enough, and it's not a problem. What is a problem is how often you just plain fall out of a room, or get swept out of it via 'conveyor' tiles, and have to start all over again. Frustration mounts quickly, and by the time you solve a room it may feel like a hollow victory, with little payoff for the effort you invested.
This game is poison if you're a completionist in terms of game content or Achievements. Remember how I said the minimap was blurry? Well, there are two giant secret rooms you couldn't possibly miss... if they were ON the map! Instead, you have to poke at every seemingly solid wall to find them, with no clues to narrow it down. Worse yet, one of them is behind conveyor tiles, and the only way to get to it is to wait for the game to RANDOMLY BUG OUT and FAIL TO LOAD A TILE. That's right, it's a BUG that you can 100% this game. And if you do manage to find those secrets? If you found "The Tower" too EARLY in the game, YOU WON'T GET THE ACHIEVEMENT. How do you fix that? By playing the ENTIRE GAME OVER AGAIN.
*sigh* In conclusion, there are some neat ideas in this game, and it has potential, but you shouldn't get it unless some things about it really change. The time you spend will leave you feeling drained, not entertained.

I started playing Magic the Gathering back in middle school and continued through highschool.  Unfortunately once I graduated and my group of friends moved on, I gave up the game.  Our group was never competative (I'm sure most of us never realized that Magic tournaments existed), we just played the game to have fun.
I learned that Magic Online was a thing that existed shortly after it released, but learning of the pricing scheme there was no way I was going to get involved with it (and this is coming from someone that was willing to pay a monthly subscription to MMO's).  It just seemed rediculous to me to pay for digital cards...when they weren't actually collectables in my mind.  PC gaming was always my main hobby even during my Magic years, and quite frankly there are TONS of PC games better than what Magic offers.
Fast forward to today and Eternal.
The game has everything that Magic should offer to a player.  It has an excellent Deck building system that lets you quickly and easily sort your collection even as new cards are added.  It has a variety of game modes, including both Competative and non-competative options which is very important for me as I need to be in the right mood to want to play vs. another player.  It has great characters and an interesting setting that stands out from other games.  But the most important thing Eternal has is fun.
The game is FUN.
I really appreciate how the developer (DWD) has taken the time to realize that they aren't creating just a card game.  They are making a Computer game.  They have taken the solid foundation that Magic has built and turned that into a game that is actually modernized for play in the Internet Era.
Each game takes ~5-7minutes usually and with how they have structured their game modes and rewards, you still feel like you are making progress towards earning new cards even if that one game is all you have time for.  If you are playing one of the modes versus an AI opponent, you can even leave mid-game and come back later if required.
The most recent (Aug 2017) feature added was an excellent puzzle mode, which to me harkens back to Scrye or Inquest "what's the play" puzzles.  Even though I have been playing the game for about a year I was surprised how many "tips for new players" they were able to add into the puzzle mode to give you a little bit of a strategic level up after coming out of the tutorial.
I am so happy I found this game and honestly very excited for its future.  An account long-term progression mode is coming soon and I am interested to see what that offers.

If you read the negative reviews you'll see people complaining about the slow-paced combat and "campers" (and probably artillery as well). Well, I'll tell you this: it ain't a game for normies. I guess that those who enjoy playing for example M&B NW will enjoy Verdun a lot. This game is way more realistic than BF or CoD, it's combat is actually closer to Arma (you get one-hitted with any rifle). In this game there's no such thing as camping. It's called "tactical combat". Players usually don't run around like imbecyles shooting everything they see, but play rather safe (waiting for the opponent to show his head for instance). The graphics aren't even close to Frostbite, but they are pretty good nonetheless. The biggest downside about this game is its tutorial: there is none. You'll have to figure things out for yourself, this might take a few hours. Ah, and the gore, of course. You have to turn it on in options, and when you do, it's like candy. You'll stumble upon ripped-off limbs in every corner of the trench, and some of these death animations will give you chills. There are (of course) glitches in the game, but I don't think I have ever seen anything gamebreaking.
To sum it all up: it's a game for history lovers (like me) who don't get scared by a few glitches or challenging gameplay. Overall I think it's a good game, worth its price. The thrilling gameplay is addictive, but that's only positive :).

This game is a simple but fun platforming game featuring animals, your goal? Build (or destroy) structures to screw over your opponents and reach the goal
The gameplay is rather simple yet fun, I found myself immediately being able to sit down and play without any real use of a tutorial, not only that but every single structure has a single effect, seeing it happen once will be plenty to know what happens, so experimentation is key here, let's not forget the relatively simple controls that you yourself can customize and you have very good gameplay.
The music I haven't payed too much attention to but is quite nice on the ears, it fits the scenario but I can't help feeling like there's only a single track in the game due to how similar they sound... That is if there's more then 2-3 tracks in the game.
Graphics are simple but work better in my personal opinion, often times game with realism are tougher on the system and this game's simple graphics gives off a nice sense of cartoonish fun, despite the... relatively harsh deaths that can be accomplished, never the less each animals are distinct from one another and it's pretty clear which one's which, add in accesories that you can unlock and extra maps (which I have to say, the backgrounds are great and do their jobs perfectly) and you've got everything very solid.
Positives
+Simple controls
+Easy learning curve
+Replayability
+Simple Graphics
+Smooth Gameplay
+Up to 4 players
+Hilarious Gameplay
Negatives
-Boxes appear randomly and give random rewards
-Online mode causes slowdowns, especially in bigger maps (or with lots of stuff)
-No single player
Is this a game worth buying? Sure, but I recomend keeping it as local as possible with friends and family as the online isn't too stable yet (but it works), however it's still in beta so who knows, maybe it'll fix itself slowly and over time.

First off. Huge warhammer fan. Both fantasy and 40k. Have played table top and most of the video games for years.
This game is great because it combines two of my favorite games, Warhammer and D&D. You go to a dungeon and explore, killing mosters and getting loot/gold. Its kinda like a dumbed down version of Balder's gate but with Warhammer character stats. Its a fun way to kill some time.
you don't get to walk from place to place but you do get random encounters while 'fast travelling'. Could be you found bandits, get attacked, had to find shelter in a storm, rock slides you have ot avoid, or any number of other events. Event will also happen when you go to towns. Has that good ol' D&D feel for event setups.
However it does have some bugs and major draw backs in a few areas.
It tends to be repetitive in the sense that all you do is fast travel around and only control the heroes while in a dungeon. I sometimes enjoy this when I don't feel like doing the old Balder's gate exploring games.
There are some minor glitchs in the game i noticed. Like sometimes your Mages spells/actions will reset his movement points.
The random monster encounters while in a dungeon seems to random. A few times I have been engaged by new enemies 2 or 3 turns in a row. Ending up with 20+ monsters in the area. At that point you just die and restart in town losing all xp you earned in that dungeon, But you retain any loot you found. The last few dungeons I entered were suppose to be Orc/goblins but end up fighting zombies and vampires. End up getting jumped by 2-3 vampire dread knights(which are the most powerful monster I have come across) at one time.
In the end the game can be alot of fun but can also be very aggrivating and requires ALOT of patients. I got it on sale for $2 and think its worth that but no more. Needs some major balance tweaks with the RNG for monster encounters.

That's a game I really wanted to have. Orly did a giveaway for it and I got a key like that. However, while I was interested a lot in it, I got disappointed for now.
Stop Online is a game where you're trying to find nouns beginning by a given letter for five defined themes. The good part of it is that you can set the language you want to use, though after that, you need to find people speaking it to play. When you completed all, you can stop the game and then...
Here is probably the main problem of Stop Online. Indeed, the validation of all the answers are done by players. And if you're playing with people that don't give a damn about real words but care only for their own scores/rank/achievements, you'll see stuff that shouldn't be validated but is anyway, and your own answers being refused despite being correct.
Thus, the game is prompting you to play only with friends and with a room denying access to those not having a password... and again, even there, you may have a problem. I've played with Samurai Vader as I've asked him to be my partner in order to write a review (and he wrote one too). Suddenly, my watermelon wasn't validated as a fruit, despite myself and himself validating it. Even video games weren't validated when Final Fantasy and Far Cry were. Italy wasn't a country. I mean, I know that the themes are defined by the creator of the room. But we were both validating the answer and yet, we got 0 points. Sometimes, however, all were fine.
So, yeah, Stop Online, even if improving apparently with the language and the chat room during the game, which is better for communication, isn't really to recommend in this state. The concept is great but there should be at least something preventing players that aren't fair to others to validate stuff that isn't right. And perhaps correct that problem of validating. Seeing my answer being denied points when we both validated the answer - as Samurai explained in the thread he opened in the discussion.
With these non-enjoyable discoveries, I suppose that if I tell you that the game is lacking people online, you'll tell me that the game is buidling its community and I accept that. However, I've opened a French room and I got joined by something that didn't know anything about my language. How do you want to play fairly in that case? So yeah, the advise of the devs to play with friends only is making sense.
In this state and because my denied watermelon and our denied names for videogames that I don't accept at all when I know we were both validating and that it's something in the game that is doing that, nope, I can't recommend it in this state. When this problem will be solved, I'll change my review and thumb it up.

Stop Online - Battle of Words is a game that you have probably already played at primary school on paper. You have to think as fast as you can of word of given themes and with specified starting letter that's chosen randomly. Depending on originality and corectness of your answers, you get points - and after few turns, the winner is the one with highest amount of points.
What have I told you right now, is something the game itself doesn't tell you. I know it's mentioned in the Steam description, but as many people currently got this game for free (developers are giving away this game a lot to make at least a small active playerbase), many people doesn't know what to do and you'll have to explain it. There isn't any tutorial which is a big con considering there isn't anything complex to explain. Why the developers didn't make a minute long video explaining the gameplay and put it in the game? That would help many newbies for sure.
Anyway, there's one bigger problem - not newbies but the lack of players. From many times I've started the game, there were only one time I got to really play the game with random people who, in the end, weren't even playing seriously. There was a guy who answered "velociraptor" to everything and thought how funny he is. On the other hand, since the correctness of the answers is decided by players themselves, you may get rejected your answers even when they are correct - just because your opponents are salty or just want to win in any way possible.
That leads to me to thinking about the fact this game is worthy only to play within a group of friends who trust each other - but if you get such group of friends (who meet in real life), why don't you just go somewhere and play it on the paper, the good old way? Why would you have to use computers to play this? If this was a free browser game, it might definitely get more attention, but I don't think it's worth paying for Stop Online, with exception of people who can't meet each other in person.
: I've tried it again with Vic=HKC= and we found that the word validation works weirdly in some cases. Even if both players validate some answers as correct, they can be marked as nonvalid somehow, not adding any points to player.
My copy of Stop Online was obtained for free - I won the game in a giveaway that might have been sponsored by the developer. This fact hasn't changed my opinion about the game (and the review) in any way.

Well... First off, don't take my "not recommended" as if i don't like the game, because i do.
Several features in this game are great, especially all the different modes of play. Sandbox can be quite boring after a while, so it's good there is something else to do as well (dogfights, races etc.) which pushes your designs comfortzone.
However, as i have played tons of hours in Kerbal space program, which also features plane construction from modules, I find the construction in simpleplanes very tedious.
KSP manages to comfort me in construction, in simpleplanes I'm afraid to click somewere in case a part goes away from where I want it and it's an♥♥♥♥♥♥getting it back.
KSP makes symmetry easy (one button toggels symmetry and it shows the symmetric part while constructing), where as in simpleplanes it's a menu option to symmetry (or mirror in this case). Usually one would do one side of the plane and finish off by mirroring, however if corrections are made to a part, a new mirroring is needed and that just feels inorganic for my construction habits.
Flying is where the game is strongest, planes fly realisticly and feels like actual planes. They stall, spin, tumble and crash if the centre of lift is in the wrong place.
Pleny of flexibility in locations, airports, airstrips, approaches and carriers, which is great.
And of course a healthy modding scene adds up for a lot.
In the end, I just find Kerbal Space Program more fun to play around in. Constructing is intuative and fast.
In simpleplanes it's just fiddely and the black backdrop in construction is just boring.
Simpleplanes however, allows more flexibillity within aircraft design (helicopters yay!)

Pix the Cat is a beautiful arcade game with terrible controls.
The presentation is certainly top-notch. The art style is quite similar to Chu Chu Rocket even if the gameplay itself is quite different and much closer to Snake.
Unfortunately the controls are the weak link here. Getting a high score is highly reliant on keeping your multiplier up and this requires memorizing the maps and minimal mistakes. Unfortunately the controls are nowhere near precise enough for this. Both keyboard and gamepad controls felt quite loose and unresponsive.
Without the control issues Pix the Cat would be a decent arcade game with nice artwork. With those issues there's no way I'd recommend it.
The good:
- Great presentation
- Decent variety of content
The bad:
- Terrible controls
- Relies too much on memorizing the maps

I enjoyed this game, but I wouldn't recommend it unless you love puzzle platformers and can overlook the issues.
The puzzle design is clever. Each room is "completed" in isolation, but sometimes the way rooms are connected, and the ordered in which they're solved, matters.
There are definite frustrations. It's extremely difficult to work out how to get from A to B on the world map, even with the help of the (mostly useless) minimap. This gets worse as you progress through the game.
The art style is nice and clean, though with the exception of one late-game forest area it's not particularly charming. The black-and-white style can also be wearing on the eyes - rooms constantly fade in and out as you move between them, sometimes very rapidly.
One of the bigger letdowns was the technical implementation. Being locked by 640x480 made for an uncomfortable playing experience, and I couldn't try the bundled Flash version (which I understand is plagued by its own technical challenges) because the save games are incompatible.
So... Just imagine for a second Flappy Bird with levels and a difficulty curve. Here you have it. Crazy, hardcore and highly enjoyable if you're ok with dying ~5-10 times per minute.

This is the worst game I played in all of 2015.  It's nothing more than an extremely boring walking simulator.  The premise of the game is that you have returned home from university and your entire family is missing from the house.  You spend the entire game walking around trying to find clues as to their whereabouts, especially your younger sister.  The main problem I had with this game is that it initially leads you to believe that it is some kind of psychological thriller, when in fact nothing could be further from the truth.  Where has your younger sister gone?!!  Was it ghosts?!  Was it kidnappers?!  No,
Not only is this the lamest, most anti-climactic plot ever, but the game never gives you any reason at all to care about any of the characters.  It was actually a relief that this game only took three hours to beat because I don't think I could have stood the drudgery of the game any longer than that.  If you are thinking about buying this game, let me just say, don't do it.  In fact, even if you are offered this game for free, it's not worth letting this genital sore equivalent blemish your Steam library.

****THIS IS NOT A HORROR/JUMPSCARE/SURVIVAL GAME*****
Now that we have made that clear (which seems to be the biggest reason for a lot of the bad ratings of Gone Home) I just want to say that I loved this experience! I'm not sure it technically counts as a *game* as I did not find any inherent failure state and I don't think that it is possible for you to die, I think it's more like a walking/exploring-sim-point-and-click.
I played Tacoma before I played this game, so I went into it expecting a similar experience and was not dissapointed at all. It's a short, sweet sort of coming of age story told through journal entries/narative found throughout the house. It has a nice creepy suspenceful aesthetic. There's plenty of hidden nooks and crannies to explore (and cats)! The 90s-ness of it is pure pog-slammed, surge-soaked, acid-washed nostalgia, so be prepared for some feels there (If you were alive then... otherwise it will probably seem antequated and garish..which it is now I suppose hah!) and the story is raw, heart-felt and warm; evocative of the sort of hormone fueled passion and ache that only teenagers are really capable of feeling. I was crying like a child at the end. Strongly recomend. 9/10
