I personally don't recommend this game but, rather than simply say it's trash, I'm gonna go in detail about the pros and cons. This isn't so much to disuade people from buying it so much as a fair warning before dropping $40 on it. Keep in mind I've played this game using mouse & keyboard just as easily as I have on Dark Souls 1. So let's start with the pros.
-The graphics are much more beautiful in comparison to Dark Souls 1.
-The camera isn't on a grid and is a lot smoother and finer to use than in Dark Souls 1.
-The player message system has quite a few more options now.
-It's a bit easier to co-op with a friend using rings that work with covenants.
-I'd DEFINITELY say the game is a bit more challenging than Dark Souls 1.
I'm really hard pressed to find things to say that I like about this game, so here are the cons in my opinion.
-Unlike Dark Souls 1 and, from what I've read, 3 you CAN AND WILL be invaded while hollow.
-NPC invasions are a LOT tougher and behave almost like fighting real players.
-Poise and defences DO NOT MATTER. Welcome to fashion souls. Have fun being stun locked to death.
-NPCs have poise, sometimes even carrying through hitting your shield. And magic is inneffective against NPC invaders.
-Parrying even the slowest attacking enemies seems nearly impossible versus Dark Souls 1 where you just wait for them to start swinging forward. The pattern remains the same in Dark Souls 1, attack speeds just increase depending on who you're fighting. This, to me, is indecipherable. I'm sure there are parry-gods on Dark Souls 2 though. You're better off just hiding behind a 100% Physical shield.
-This game thinks it's as cool as Demons' Souls, taking away your maximum health with each death. Which would be fine, in my opinion, if you couldn't be invaded while hollow. Regular NPCs are easy enough.
-It's just Troll Mario levels of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, in my opinion. The few enemies that set themselves up for a plunging attack are easily capable of being over shot and then proceed to just stun lock you do death as their friends you didn't get to see charge in to help murder you.
-The bosses are probably the easiest thing about this game. To be quite honest. Like any Dark Souls game, you get your summons and it's cake.
-Enemies can be farmed to extinction in a zone and won't respawn, hampering farming.

favorite in the Souls series and I haven't even played Dark Souls 3. By all means, don't let me stop you from buying it but this is just the real facts from a filthy casul. Cook, Serve, Delicious is a great filler/palate cleanser with surprising depth.
You run a restaurant inside of a business tower in which you are the sole proprietor of all things that happen. While the game is mostly casual feeling and reminiscent of classics like Diner Dash, you additionally have to run the actual cooking as well as manage the flow of customers. It may seem like a lot at first but it ramps up the difficulty fairly nicely. Additionally, you are in full control of what is on the menu itself. So if something just has too many options you can dial it down regardless. However, you can ramp it up as well giving you added buffs should you be able to maintain good customer service.
The actual cooking is incredibly satisfying, each food item has a specific way to prepare it and has its own recipes. Meaning it can only be ordered in certain ways making it an important thing to note regarding strategy in menu selection. Some types have more recipes than others. While in control of the menu you'll find some decent depth in choosing plates that require cooking and prep while other things that are instant and can be done in between the cooking stages and are a good way to increase revenue.
There are stat buffs and debuffs that occur, such as menu rot or foods that have bad aromas early in the morning that effect you every day. Your performance can also affect your buzz which will effect the amount of customers coming in, especially during non-Rush hour times.
There is equipment upgrades that help in the increasing of the waiting time for customers regarding their patience for you as well as equipment to help with chores that you'll need to do throughout each day. New equipment for cooking different types of food are also available.
You'll have extra tasks to complete everyday should you choose to take them on such as bets with other chefs. There are e-mails that you'll receive after each day that are actually quite enjoyable to read. As well as warn you of upcoming events such as health inspections.
There are also iron chef challenges that occur weekly and compete with other online challengers.
Additionally, there is a ton of control options. Options between Keyboard, 360, X1 and DS4 pads make choosing what you're most comfortable with a non-issue.

1000 Amps is a greyscale indie puzzle platformer in which you play as Plug, a little dude who lights up whatever he touches. Your goal is to restore power to the Amp-Tree-System, a now-darkened labyrinth of over 150 compartments, and defeat the intruder who caused the outage.
Every room contains light nodes and activating them all will illuminate that room permanently. A battery meter, which fills based on the percentage of nodes activated, is also present for each room and determines how high you can jump there. As with a Metroidvania, you will have to work your way to the special power-up and story rooms to progress. Power-ups include click-to-warp, increased touch radius, light node radar, double jump, and the ability to destroy creatures that eat light.
The game lacks a proper soundtrack, is Flash-based with slowdowns at high resolutions and, due to the open-world design, can be frustrating if you haven't found the right power-ups yet. Despite these flaws, it's still enjoyable.

Finished Warhammer Quest. Completely played on Linux via Steam.
Warhammer Quest is the PC version of the famous Warhammer Quest Tabletop game. You have a party of up to four warriors including a warrior, a dwarf, an elf and a mage. You delve into dungeons of various sort to either kill a special mean boss enemy or grab a precious item from the very depth of the labyrinth. All these “quests” are embedded into cleansing three rural regions of the Warhammer universe realm of Goblins, Orcs and Skaven. On some quests you come along some Vampires and Undead which provide a some more challenging task since Vampire Lords are very powerful and while wielding some magic spells they can also deal a very serious amount of damage in melee. Between the dungeons you travel from village to village where you can sell your loot, buy new equipment and visit the training grounds to achieve new levels and therefore skills for your character. As such Warhammer Quest presents itself as a typical Hack & Slay Dungeon crawler viewed from atop when navigating your party through the dungeons.
It is fun. It is entertaining.
But huge epic quests are not found in this game. The dungeon runner part of the game is good looking and plays well. Tactics is seldom an obstacle: leave your mage and the archer (elf) behind and rush in with a berserk and the dwarf. Usually this is solves any problem. On higher levels micromanagement of potions and spell points (healing) of your staff is a bit demanding but this game is not a real hard problem to get around. Graphics and sound are nice done and appropriate.
In a village the menu dealing with inventory and merchants goods could be solved a bit better. Buying and equip you fighters could have been done less awkward, though the way it is done may be better suitable for Tablets and/or XBox or Playstation. Not a real nuisance, but leaves you easily with an idea that it could be done slightly better than it has been done.
The real fun stops, when you characters reached the level limit. And that’s quite too early in the game. After this the game gets highly repetitive. You get the best equipment fast, learned all spells and even the toughest opponent does not bear and really real threat to your party. So about 1/3 of the game you simply do the same over and over again.
But as stated above: it still provides you with fun sweeping through a dungeon.
I never played the original tabletop but I assume that this game strictly obeys to the rules found there and serves as a nice game for up to 4 players each one controlling his own character. This is different to a single PC player game. Here you lack the (unknown) decisions of your co-players but have full control. E.g. swapping one heal potion from one character to the next is not a matter of discussion and arguing among the players but rather a sole act within one, two mouse-clicks. Attacking the mean boss behind with the archer or the nearly dead minion in front of the archer so that the heavy berserk can right walk up to the dangerous mage nearby is not a group act, it’s one single player choice. So this is different environment and targeted audience to entertain. This is fun on a tabletop where social group interaction of the players contribute to the fun. On a single player PC game this is inherently lost.
So, Warhammer Quest succeeds in bringing the original tabletop game to the PC and creates fun. Could it have been done better? Yes, of course. But only if you bend the core rules of the original and this would then render another game, not entitled to “Warhammer Quest”.
Despite some claims I read elsewhere I never had a crash or some technical difficulties encountered. The game runs smoothly.
Fun. With obvious missed potential.
Final verdict: 6/10

This game is like some bizarro version of Pac Man Championship Edition DX+, requiring many of the same skills. It’s also much harder.
The goal of each board is to grab all the eggs, then walk over every circle. A chick will hatch out of every egg you touch and start following you, forcing you to play Snake until you can drop them onto the circles and get rid of them. For maximum points, you need to pick up every egg on the board before stepping on a single circle, turning most boards into a tough pathfinding puzzle. The most creative idea at work here is the way you can take portals back to previous levels at any time, which is sometimes required for playing optimally.
The biggest difference from Pac-Man, and the reason why this game is so hard, is because of all the sharp turns. There were no sharp turns in Pac-Man: every single turn was made at an intersection, giving you at least one extra moment to plan your turns ahead. Pix the Cat forces you to constantly make sharp turns while running at high speeds and painting huge swaths of the level with intricate space-filling paths if you don’t want to break your combo. As with all puzzle games which attempt to slide you smoothly across a fixed grid (like Chuck’s Challenge, some versions of Boulder Dash, and so on) it can be very difficult to tell when you’re properly “inside” a square and how long you have to make a turn, which is very much an issue here. Furthermore, each board is presented at a different zoom level and Pix is constantly speeding up, making it nearly impossible to judge turns by intuition alone. Your instincts will fail you unless you focus intensely on your every move. It’s very difficult and requires a lot of skill and practice, but fortunately the game was (at least for me) addictive enough that I was inspired to keep trying until I succeeded.
The boards are mostly the same every time, except for some small randomized details to mix things up, and you’re given 5 minutes (with no way to earn additional time) to clear as many boards as possible and earn a high score. It’s possible to memorize some basic routes that will work every time, but you’ll have to slightly adapt them depending on how the levels change, and you’ll have to earn speed if you want to progress further before time runs out. While it might seem like a dubious design choice at first to have all of the levels be the same every time, you’ll be thanking the heavens for the consistency if you’re serious about earning high scores and getting those tough achievements. And if you want variety, the game comes with two more level sets of varying difficulties.
Aside from the main game, there are also two puzzle modes which honestly could’ve been games by themselves. My favorite is the Nostalgia mode, a series of 70 action-puzzle levels which adorably try to pass off the main character as a Felix the Cat / Mickey Mouse ripoff from the 1930s, complete with a sepia tone filter and authentic old-timey music. The other puzzle mode has you playing through 100 thinking levels, trying to find the optimum solution to each room in the least number of moves. It’s a bit slow compared to the other game modes, but the puzzles are respectable brainteasers with clever solutions. There’s also a multiplayer mode that I haven’t gotten to try, but it looks hilarious.
Overall, it’s a worthy, addictive Pac-Man variant with tight (but punishing) gameplay, and it was given far more coats of polish than I honestly would have expected from a game like this. I’d recommend it to any gamer who has the type of determination and OCD that would inspire one to perfect a BIT.TRIP level, but probably not for the casual achievement hunter. I’d give it 20-30 hours of gameplay to 100% depending on how good your reflexes are.

Sundered is an attempt to combine the exploration and discovery of a Metroidvania with the constant death and procedural generation of a roguelike. It does so by making the basic layout of the map the same between runs but the rooms within that layout will change. For instance, a boss or an ability will always be in the same place but the rooms in between will be different. Much of it feels like Rogue Legacy in structure, along with the dying and returning to a sort of hub place to use the currency that you gain from enemies and containers in the environment to upgrade your character to make subsequent run easier and more managable. For the most part, its suceeds in doing so, making for a very fun and engaging game that constantly gives the feeling of progress, be that discovering more of the map, an ability, or upgrading your character. However, there are some decisions in the Sunder's design that are frustrating.
One of first thing I noticed was how utterly great the movement and combat feels in this game. Jotun's controls felt slow and clunky to me in a way that really turned me off but Sundered does not suffer from that problem in the slightest. Your character runs fast and she feels intuitive and easy to move around. I never struggled with the controls and I always feel like my character is moving exactly how I want her to. Combat similarly feels great with a ton of flexibility in how you fight enemies. You have a basic attack and a roll that goes through enemies and their attacks but there are lots of smart choices made with that simple moveset. You can attack in all directions to perform different attacks and can do so in the air as well. When you get the double jump, if you attack an enemy in the air, that allows you to double jump again, so you can keep yourself in the air while attacking. It all just feels right. You have a stamina bar so you can't dodge with reckless abandon as well as a recharching shield that compliments your health. The shield can take quite a bit of damage but your health is fagile and can drop extremely quickly if you don't give time for your shield to recharge. Overall, moving and fighting is a joy.
You'll find new abilites as you explore and in true Metroidvania style, you often backtrack and use those abilities to reach previously inaccessible areas. Most abilites help you in both traversal and combat, giving you even more options to move about. There is a rather intersting decision presented in the game regarding these. Defeating minibosses and the main bosses gives you elder shards. You either destroy these or you can corrupt your abilites, altering them in some way. I won't spoil what they are as finding out is one of the biggest joys I found in the game, but some are defintely more useful than others.
Now for my biggest gripe with the game. Since the game is mostly procedurally generated, that presents a challenge in enemy placement. Sundered will randomly throw enemies at you that, for all intents a purposes, come out of no where. Some might pop up here and there to give you something to fight for a bit but there are moments when a gong rings signaling a large horde of enemies will be coming. When I say large hordes, I mean it, they can often times be overwhelming. There are a range of opinions on these hordes and I'm in the camp of finding them frustrating. There can be nearly 15 enemies of varying size on screen all doing their attacks and it can be extremely hard to parse out all the visual noise that is happening, so much so that I often lose sight of my character. This has the combat devolve into me mashing the attack button and dodging what I can. It turns the graceful looking act of fighting enemies and timing the dodge to get around them into a absolute mess of effects and enemies all moving about. And these enemies will chase you to hell and back if you try to run. Dying to these hordes never felt like a lack of skill on my part but losing sight of my character and being unable to dodge a large barrage of neverending attacks and I come away from it feeling frustrated and cheated. You can make the argument that dying is a large part of the game, and it is, but the death shouldn't feel so cheap. It's artificial difficulty. Granted, as you upgrade your character, the hordes become a lot more manageable as the upgrades do feel meaningful but then they just become an annoyance. I'm harping on the hordes so much because it is the single biggest blemish in the game for me.
The hordes aside, I am having a ton of fun with Sundered. The movement and combat feel as good as they can be, the abilites are fun to use and are useful in traversal and fighting enemies, and the upgrades you gain in between deaths feel meaningful, serving as a constant source of progression. I highly recommend it, just be prepared to be frustrated from time to time.

"Gone Home" is a walking simulator with not so much little gameplay and a simple but kind of touching story.
You are Katie, an American young woman/older teenager from Oregon, returning from a long trip across Europe. But as you enter the big family mansion, there is no family member welcoming you, as the place seems to be empty.
So your job is to find out what might have happened that led to this. Maybe some family drama? ...
As mentioned, you do not much in this game. It's mainly about exploring lots of rooms and hallways, finding secrets that will unfold themselves once you progress. You won't work or communicate with other people, it's really about objects and places.
When it comes to the story, I don't wanna tell you more about it even though it's not that spectacular or awesome but as I said it can be touching and since the story takes place in the mid-1990s you can understand some of the issues between characters.
What bugs me though are mainly two things:
- A story issue. It's hard to explain without spoiling but let's say this: I had some questions unanswered in the end and I don't think these unanswered questions make "Gone Home" better. Like some ghost story is suggested to be going on and then just dropped or proved to be not leading anywhere in the end. And next to that other few questions remained.
- I feel like wasting a good bunch of time after looking at too many useless objects standing around (because you never now if one of them might have something mysterious underneath or on them!). Like mugs. Or 3-ring folders. Or kitchen food. Ugh.
The gameplay is simple and fast to learn, you use the keyboard to go in any directions, look at the house map and get into the game menue while the mouse is used for leading Katie's view and click at the objects you want to look at, take, open or close.
The graphics are not really fantastic but some details support the game's atmosphere well like the weather effects (rain on windows, lightning) or even smaller details like typical 1990's style on objects so I would even call "Gone Home" a little tribute to 1990's teen culture.
I did enjoy the sound. The sound effects themselves were rather minimalistic but the music and the voice overs were really nice to listen to. If you dig (girl) punk music you will definitely have some joy while playing and discovering some songs.
Do I recommend the game? If you enjoy walking simulators (especially with some romance/social drama), then I surely recommend to try this one out. If you hope for some thrilling horror game, better don't disappoint yourself right away.

There’s plenty to love about this game: the house is creatively designed and the attention to detail's fantastic; the “riotgrrrl” soundtrack's fun and conveys the 90s vibe well; the voice acting's brilliant and the delivery's on point. However, at its core, this is a story-driven game, so I feel obliged to grade it based on that, and, unfortunately, this is where things begin to unravel. The plot so overtly attempts to evoke pathos that it loses all sense of subtlety. "Get invested!" it screams, but only offers up trite character development and an empty atmosphere in return. A well-executed story should draw out emotion naturally, with its intent at least partially obscured, but this just comes across forced and schmaltzy. It has moments of promise, though, so I remained relatively optimistic throughout, seeing it through to the end in the hope that my apathy would eventually subside...but it didn’t. There's definitely potential here, and I think that given time this studio will produce something of real worth (I'm certainly open to trying Tacoma at some point). They just need to work on cleverer, more layered storytelling in the future.
Also, as a side note, I was left feeling extremely nauseous because of the awful FOV and “head bob” effect (which I later discovered I could turn off), so to the more sensitive among you, beware.

This is a game I've been fairly interested in ever since I saw the advertisements back in 2015 (to my knowledge) and I finaly bought it about a week ago although I've only played about 6-7 hours as of writing this.
Verdun in terms of a game is a fairly barebones experience of a game because of onlt having 4 game modes avalible to the players but what this game may lack in production quality compared to Battlefield 1 this game makes up for in regards to fairly unique and interesting gameplay.
The whole concept of Verdun is supposed to be a multiplayer only FPS game which is set within the Trenches along the Western Front from 1914-1918 despite being named after the Battle of Verdun which lasted from 1916-1917 if I have got my dates correct. This means you can play on the various battlefields of the Western Fronts and can play as the Entente Powers consisting of the French Army, not faction but Army please get it right. The British Army, the American Army when they joined the fight in 1917 and the German Empire yet if I'm not mistaken I do belive Austro-Hungary sent units to this front as well as Portugal in 1917 so to see them not present is a shame.
The developers have gone for a more Historical re-encactment of the war on this front which means most, if not all of the maps are based on trench warfare and all the game modes are based around trench warfare. Frontlines is the embodyment of this mentality as it sees teams of up to 16 players a side fighting over the other team's trenches constantly trying to repell enemy attacks and then trying to go on the attack themselves. Rifle deathmatch is a FFA only using bolt action rifles with the matches being set in trenches and no man's land on the maps, the same goes for the other deathmatch mode but thats just TDM on the same maps and fianaly there's a horde mode which I've yet to play where you hold a trench against waves of bots/AI enemies until your squad of 4 players is over run.

This game started out fantastic.  It plays virtually identical to Magic The Gathering, as others have pointed out, simple and easy to learn mechanics.  When you start out you will get rewarded quite handsomely, gold, packs, even some decks.  The AI will be fair and your matches won't be overly difficult or frustrating due to RNG mechanics, like opening hand/card draw.
After you have bested the campaign you will have new options available to you for play.  The Forge and Gauntlet. The Gauntlet is a constructed format where you take your best deck and face off against AI opponents for rewards, which increase the more you win, up until you beat the final opponent, which is the 7th battle.
The Forge is an Arena/Draft type format where you pick 1 of 3 cards for your deck that you are building at a cost of 2500 gold per run.  The decks are smaller than the standard 75 cards and there is much more RNG involved, but overall the format is the most fun.  The rewards are also greater, with more packs, cards and gold up for grabs if you can win.
Eventually though, these rewards will be almost unobtainable.  For what I can only specualte is the need to make tons of money, the games AI changes after you have played some amount of time.  Where earlier I was winning and going flawless in Forge and Gauntlet, gaining great rewards and bulding up a card pool, now I can't win but maybe 3 games in either format.  The game will give you the WORST draws and top decks, while giving a massive buff to the draws and hands of the AI opponents.  This now happens so much so that many times I just concede during the first game.  I speculate this is done to get the player to feel frustrated and purchase gems to buy packs, hoping those packs will bless the player with cards they can use to win (at least in the Gauntlet mode or PvP modes).
So for me this review is a negative.  The game starts out fantastic, doesn't feel Pay To Win at all, it actually feels Free To Play, but as I said, this doesn't take long to disappear.  It's a real shame as the game otherwise is so enjoyable.  I hope the devs will make adjustments to the AI - specifically to the card draw aspect - soon.  Make this game great again, fix the horrible card draw failures which occur far far too frequently to be anything other than intentional.
EDIT: After Scarlatch, the developer informed me (see comments) of how the AI works in this game I am changing my review to reflect it.  I now endorse the game and recommend it.  You will still get hosed with the Sigil's on occasion but hopefully this gets adjusted in the future.  Overall just that happening on occasion isn't enough to warn anyone to stay away from the game.  Knowing the decks and opponents increase in difficulty as you get better explains a lot of the frustration I was facing, again thanks to Scarlatch for explaining this. Check the game out, you can play for free so all it's costing you is some of your free time.

When I first started playing this game on Android, there were some weird design decisions that stood out pretty far to me. 25 starting health, 75 card deck, things like this. After my first few real games my skepticism only increased. The downsides of these mechanics are really obvious, and when you lose to flood and screw, it does sting.
I've played a lot over the past week and I have to say, as unintuitive as it is, all of the mechanics that I thought would be bad have somehow come together to make an insanely good CCG.  For the examples I used earlier, the larger deck sizes means mirror matches, or repeated matches against the same deck can play wildly differently. The larger health pool means getting stuck or flooded for a turn or two isn't as bad as it is in other games. This also allows low cost cards to be very aggressively statted, to the point where they can be more relevant late game, without making aggro too powerful.
There are other ways to achieve these things, but the more I play, the more I realized the designers of this game made all these decisions very deliberately. At least 2 sets in, this has resulted in one of the most interesting and diverse card games I've ever played.
F2P mechanics are generous, even in PvE. Game runs very well, even on phones. Streamer community is helpful and friendly. It's a game that's really worth getting into.

Dark Souls II provides more of the (now classic) Dark Souls challenging gameplay, with small and extra mechanical improvements, beautiful graphics, a greater variety of weapons and magics, and even ambidexterity/dual-wielding (which is awesome).
However, I feel that Dark Souls II misses out on some of the progress gained by Dark Souls I. Some changes reduce the quality of the overall experience. Begin_rant
Humanity and Hollowing is a mess, pumping up artificial difficulty (as opposed to the good, intelligent, use-your-wits kind of difficulty).
Exploration is comparatively unrewarding, and sometimes feels obligatory due to lack of direction (in Dark Souls I plenty of direction was given, often delivered to the subconscious).
Fast travel is available immediately, which cuts much of the need to learn the world and acts as a distraction to the direction (while playing I often had to explore the entire world so far over again just to find the next area).
There are too many NPC invaders (they become a nuisance and forgettable).
The bosses are easy (I often defeated them first time), making them forgettable and pointless;
whereas, some common enemies are nonsensically difficult (again, artificial difficulty, like ways that can only be countered by grinding).
Text (such as item descriptions) is often poorly translated.
There is a distinct lack of tail drops (no drop for Sinh!?! WHAT!).
Animations and sound effects are unsatisfying. They miss the chunkiness of Dark Souls I.
The main storyline is meaningless and in the end turns out to be (SPOILER)
.
The majority of the NPCs are forgettable, leaving you to not care about them (whereas in Dark Souls you felt like part of a community and cared what happened to them).
Finally, the lore sucks.
What happened?!
Well, it may appear that my experience of Dark Souls II should leave me to feel that it is not worth playing. I struggle on that point a lot, thinking of how much more I got out of the first 120 hours I put into Dark Souls I, where I completed the enthralling game (leaving me exhilerated), having seen everything it had to offer (areas, covenants, secrets, everything) in NG and NG+ (and kept me playing for another 200 hours), whereas in Dark Souls II I only just got through NG, including all DLC, most of it feeling like a grind, and done without seeing every secret - I have missed a few entire areas, and I don't intend to go back to find them, in fact, I don't think I'll ever install Dark Souls II again.
As much as I am frustrated at how much has been lost moving to Dark Souls II, there are still some epic moments that really hit that SUCCESS! feeling that is one of the greatest draws to the difficult gameplay of Dark Souls (espcially on the final DLC boss), and so I will go with 'recommended'. You had better play Dark Souls I first though.

As an ex mtg player and card game lover, I really do love the concept of this game. The game is set similair like that of magic where there are 5 colors which each do their own things to various extents. The game has a nice deck building feature which you can make decks or varying colors and see what little combos you can make. Which was the selling point for me for awhile. Such as the g/w legendary temple speaker and the w legendary acedant you can basically draw almost all of your deck out by simply shooting all your destiny lands out and drawing a card to replace the destiny land AND a card for ascendants empower.
However the severe issue i have with this game is the lack of deck shuffling interactions there are, mainly because the biggest issue in this game is sigil screw (drawing all sigil or none for 4+ turns). Now some say that shuffling the deck wont matter as you can't see what's inside your deck or the order. Well that is true however magic players would know that shuffling is also a form of rearraging the deck to simply just change the odds in the deck as it stands, ie* When i go to draw a forest out i dont search the first forest but see clumps of lands and grab one from those. Except in this game when i play the 1 mana seek power, I get a sigil of my choice RANDOMLY from my deck, meaning it could be a mana from a clump of 5 or a land from my next draw. Which brings me back to the lack of deck interactions in the game, there is no way to shuffle your deck so once the game starts you are stuck with the order that the game shuffled it which tends to always have land clumps by the dozen of 2-4 lands meaning you could get 12 lands in 12 turns with no way of stopping it.
Another thing is the fact of seeing what cards are in the deck through some spells does incur an imbalance of card knowledge, in g/r you can see the top card of your deck if you have buffed it, ie* warcry. Meaning if i play the 4 mana search a unit or weapon from my deck, I can see all my units and weapons. From there I can see which ever weapon or unit is buffed then that would be my next card to draw. So thus I would avoid picking that one and choose another, thereof affecting the entire game through an unfair advantage of knowing what is in your next draw. It is knowledge any other player wont have and due to the non-shuffling implement they get that card.
So as much as i love the mechanics and deck design and card interactions, I can not get past this lack of deck shuffling mechanics. As it stands the most frustrating aspect of the game is the least worked on with no hopes in the future of ever being fixed. Perhaps if they change the deck shuffling feature the game could hold up hope but as of now is just another chernobly waiting to happen.

Although the visuals and atmosphere of this game are great (I especially love the night vision camera effect), I didn't enjoy it very much.
I find the 'adaptive sound' stuff kind of annoying rather than evocative; for example: the suspenseful strings and heavy breathing when enemies draw close often alerted me to an enemies I hadn't even seen yet (even through walls!), breaking all sense of immersion. Similarly, more than once I was trying to listen for footsteps, but couldn't hear them over the incessant orchestra following me around the building.
Also, I understand the whole 'helplessness' thing and how it adds to the tension, but it feels really forced to me. Apparently I'm playing a man so feeble that he can't even try to shove someone out of his way, let alone pick up a chair leg and swing it. Despite this, he's athletic enough that he can vault over desks without trouble and climb along ledges by his fingertips. I guess he's just philosophically opposed to violence, because he's certainly not incapable of defending himself.
If you don't mind playing along with the strange horror tropes and glossing over the inconsistencies, I'm sure the visuals and atmosphere alone make this worth playing; I didn't get far enough to evaluate the story, but it seemed fairly interesting so that's a strong point as well. For me the gameplay just feels too fake and forced to really appreciate the more artistic aspects of the game. I'm not trying to say it's a bad game (it seems very well made in fact) but it seems likely that other people might find it annoying for the same reasons and I want them to have some warning.

Many of the many negative reviews have at least half a dozen hours under their belts. Perhaps because, despite its many, many flaws, it's quite pleasant to play.
Just like in the other adaptations of old Games Workshop games, randomness permeates the gameplay to its very core: the FTL-like text events have saving throws instead of multiple choice problems, seemingly every turn there's a chance for enemies to suddenly appear right next to you (or far away, if they're ranged), all your attacks have a goodly chance of missing, the amount of mana your wizard gets each turn is random, and so on and so forth. However, the (randomness-soaked) events of a single turn are very unlikely to screw you over on their own. It's a very cautious game about threat mitigation where standing still for too long is guaranteed to make you lose eventually.
Now, to complain about a thing other reviewers missed: the animations are stupid. Characters all walk with their legs splayed out in an awkward and uncomfortable fashion, and the attack animations should really have less build-up and cool-down time (it looks really awkward when this guy goes in for a big swing, steps back to his own square, does it again several times, then puts down his weapon, pulls out a bow, shoots someone once, puts back the bow, and picks up his weapon again).

Even though the past few years have brought along a number of horror titles that haven't really been up to par, Outlast is a survival-horror experience that shines through.
It's been stated previously that Outlast isn't the most innovative or creative work available, and although that statement rings true on a cetain number of levels, it's definitely a title to consider and invest in, especially if you're a horror-junkie who's looking for some more nightmare fuel.
Outlast contains the same atmosphere-type horror as the most-all-around praised Amnesia: The Dark Descent, although it also features several other elements that keep the game flowing smoothly and keep the player on the edge of their seat. The game does contain a good amount of jumpscares along with the overall tense feel of the environment, and even if you're not a fan of cheap spooks, Outlast does a wonderful job of placing them in areas you probably wouldn't expect them to be, getting the best reactions out of the people playing it.
Outlast also has fantastic aesthetic value, as the graphics are some of the most realistic I've seen in a long while. That being said, if you want to enjoy the full visual factor of this game, you might want to make sure your computer is up to speed.
The game does have its flaws, of course. The story is well placed together, but in order to fully understand it, you'll have to make sure to collect all of the documents and notes you come across, making the experience a bit confusing and monotonous at certain times. I personally also had my dislikes with how the entire thing came to a close at the end, as it wasn't the best wrap-up I've seen.

Sometime in the 90s, Harvey Danger said:
"I want to publish zines /
And rage against machines"
The irony of the jaded subject of the band's hit, 'Flagpole Sitta,' was lost on the developer of this game, who took every lyric of the song as gospel, and would go on to make a game as gratingly pretentious as 'Gone Home.'
The game's story hits every cliche of the American liberal: wealthy but distant parents, rebellion, a semester of creative writing at Reed, a backpacking trip around Europe, environmentalism, queer issues, and Portland OR. The amalgamation of the stereotype comes at the end of the game where the developers have appended the names of their cats to the credits. If 'Gone Home' had come out a few years later I'm sure few nods to white privilege and digitized "I'm With Her" stickers would have been plastered around the map.
Alas, it is surprising that a story as immature as this one would be paired with such competent, well designed, gameplay.
Although 'Gone Home' is the equivalent of a 3D first-person hidden object game, the atmosphere is exquisite.
It left me genuinely spooked, and intrigued enough to keep poking through the Greenbriar manor. Unfortunately, the experience is far too brief to ever cash in on the ghoulish overtones. Gone Home, in the end, feels like a demo; caveat emptor unless heavily discounted.

This will be an extensive review that will try to cover all my thoughts about this game. It will contain spoilers about the abilities and key details of Sundered. Ill section this review into 3 parts that will go over my experience, what the game could improve, and a message to the developers.
TLDR: If you like hard games with a hack and slash feel and tough boss fights – its amazing.
-----------------------------------------------------------
1. My Experience
After reading other reviews and hearing about the difficulty, I took the game on as a challenge and did my first playthrough on hard. The first hour is like the honeymoon phase where the game is just letting you learn basic mechanics and what to expect. I liked the combat and how quick you could jump from mob to mob and just tear them apart. But very quickly the game starts to ramp up the difficulty when it introduces new monsters and gives you access to new abilities. I realized I could always handle the first horde that appeared, but after the first I would have to consider running. This wasn't necessarily a bad thing but slows down progression because I would have to return to the sanctuary before I got a chance to continue from the furthest point I got to in the previous life. I didn't mind this very much because traveling across the map is pretty fast especially once you unlock later abilities.
Playing on hard was frustrating but rewarding. Anytime I beat a boss, miniboss, or horde, I felt that I had overcome a big disadvantage.
In terms of pacing, the game spaces out unlocking abilities to avoid letting you get to content that is too hard. This is good because you don't get stuck going the same route that you can't beat. For example, unlocking the energy cannon helps you kill large packs of mobs and unlocks new areas. Therefore, delaying the acquisition of the energy cannon makes sense. But unlocking the double jump just felt like an ability that should have been a standard feature (although this is justified thematically because Eshe is only human, although unlocking it alongside the shield would make sense). The air dash also felt like it comes in too late in the game, this doesn't ruin any part of the game it’s just a slight annoyance. But, the grappling hook being the last ability unlocked is disappointing, because having more to play around with it would be great.

It makes you decide on focusing on either damage (kill boss faster and rely on dodging) or survivability (allow room for mistakes but boss fights can last a long time). Any path you take is viable and this makes the game feel great, as you’re unlocking new talents because you can’t really mess up your talents. On hard, there are times when you're going to have to slow down and grind for new upgrades and this can be kind of tedious, but I think on normal you can make consistent progress without slowing down and grinding.
So, after about 35 hours I finished my playthrough and started a normal playthrough to see the difference between normal and hard. I could play much more carelessly and rush through the first area very quickly. Most of that can be attributed to already knowing most of the locations of objectives and where to go, but after 2 hours of my second playthrough I had already killed the first boss (took me about 8 hours on hard) and started on the second area. I believe hard mode makes you get less points for upgrading, and makes the damage upgrade give +2 (+3 on normal). Personally, I think it should not reduce the effectiveness of the damage upgrade and take longer to get upgrades.
I loved the variety between zones, the first area is a good and has both open and tight rooms that force you to consider ways of dealing with enemies in different situations. The second area is more claustrophobic and easy to get lost in, you must watch your map closely or else you won’t know where to go. The third area is my favorite because of how open it is and the how much the grappling hook is utilized. The other areas tend to make you travel horizontally and downwards, but the 3rd area makes you travel upward. Using the grappling hook makes travel so fast and makes combat even more fast paced, there’s also no downtime getting back to where you were because the elevator can get you close to where you want to go.
-----------------------------------------------------------
2. What the game can improve
(I’m omitting things that have been pointed out in other reviews to avoid redundancy)
Limit flying mobs to stay out of walls. It really kills the momentum when you can’t reach a mob 	because it’s inside a wall or its shooting you from another room.
Movement abilities could’ve been introduced earlier.
Have a bigger incentive for killing hordes, they’re a big struggle for not much pay off.
Shift power from perks into talents, the difficulty of playthroughs can be determined by which perks 	randomly drop.
The ending. With how many crystal rooms there were that build up the lore, I was expecting the story to 	be tied up nicely but no it feels like an abrupt cliffhanger (I got the “no escape” and the resist 	ending).
After killing the final boss, give hints on what you need to get 100% clear. I spent 3 hours after killing the 	final boss looking around for the hidden shards, perks, finding one miniboss in 3rd area that did 	not show up on map for some reason. I had to look through the steam discussion forums 	because there are no real hints (or even knowledge that they exist) as to where these things are. 	I suggest a feature on the map that shows %clear for each region that way you know which area 	you need to fully explore.
When picking hard difficulty tell what disadvantages that entails. (I thought it would only be mobs have 	more health/damage)
The bullet hell boss fights where the whole arena is being bombarded is good as a concept, but for me 	it devolved into just running around wildly and focusing on upgrading damage to avoid having 	to deal with too many of these segments. My suggestion is to not cover the entire map, 	but 	focus where the player currently is and where they try to run to. This way there is more	strategy during these parts rather than just praying you survive and healing any damage you   	took in 	that phase.
Introduce a way to upgrade perks with upgrade points, I had to use a rank 1 shield converter and a rank 	2 assassin perk for the last boss fight.  ;_ ;
Mark where lith enemies spawn after you get the scavenger perk.
-----------------------------------------------------------
3. Message to the developers
Thank you for making this game, it feels thematically perfect. The music, the difficulty, the mysteriousness of the setting as you progress really captures the theme of being alone vs. the world in an alien environment. Having to choose resist vs embrace (especially when embrace is presented with so much promise) is a tough choice that feels rewarding and different. Feeling Eshe get stronger and stronger as new abilities are unlocked is great.

This game is absolutely incredible.  I have to say it took a little bit for me to get completely into it.  It started ok, and was immediately atmoshperic and beautiful.  After playing another, similar, recent game though, I wasn't totally sure of how I felt about the mechanics of the game.
Last night I pressed forward for a few more hours, and everything just clicked, the game took off, and now I think it may be one of my absolute favorites of this style.  The key was to think about the combat differently than the other game.  Instead of trying to be pixel precise, this game has more of a delicate and graceful flow to its combat.  I described this elsewhere as a flying ballet of death.  :)  Like playing Crouching Tiger.  Instead of rigid combat, one can flow and float from one enemy to the next by rolling, floating, flipping, and basically fly across entire screens smoothly chaining from one enemy to the next.  It's absolutely beautiful and savage.  As more skills and drops become unlocked things just get better and better.
The game makes you feel like a total badass without getting too easy.
At first I thought this game may need some tweaking, but now I can't put it down, was up WAY to late playing it, and I really don't think the devs should change a single thing.
As you already know if you're looking at the videos and shots above, this game is absolutely gorgeous.  The sound is every bit as good as the visuals, the controls, while different than other similar games are very precise (if you grant the inertia effects).
I really couldn't be happier, and now I'm going to buy a couple more copies and gift them to a few friends.
Excellent work devs!
Edit:  I thought I'd add a quick comment after doubling my play time.  It just keeps getting better the more one plays.  I see a lot of people complaining about things, and it's their right to do so, however, I think much of it stems from the way they are approaching this game.  The depth in combat comes from acrobatics, chaining attacks, and creating a flow to each battle.  If one just runs in and mashes the attack button, A) it's not going to be too fun, and B) it's not going to work very well.  I think the key to the early game is learning the tricks of better mobility, and getting a certain mobility upgrade.  Once one grasps the movement well, this game is perfection.

Recommended not because I liked it or think it's value for money, but because it is a well made example of its genre.

As far as I'm aware, about 45% of the community from what I can see arn't that excited about having DLC so early on in development. I can understand their concern for that, especially from those that have never used a flight simulator before coming from other platforms and the way they do their DLC is different to the way flight sims do DLC.
Flight sim DLC is almost 100% of the time made by 3rd parties, with the actual sim developers working on the sim, so 95% of the actual content for flight sims, is sold seperatly.
This may sound like a crap deal. But, due to the vastness and variety of flight simulation this is the best way. It would simply be impossible for DTG to make the required content that each and every one of us seeks to a high standard. For example, study level airliners, large scenery areas, the never ending number of GA aircraft and helicopters. The 3rd parties make this content and sell it, whether through Steam or their own vendors. That gives us, the simmers, the choice of only buying the content we wish to use.
For example, I primarily fly in Australia, there is no sense in me buying DLC scenery for other parts of the globe since I would hardly use it! Same goes for aircraft.
The current DLC that IS available for FSW on Steam are from developers that have been allowed early access to the SDK, this is so DTG can finish the SDK and make a public release, and by then, I suspect the floodgates will most likely open and DLC will flood this page.
I am sorry but that is just how flight sims work!
Do I recommend this sim? Yes, yes I do, get it now, commit to it, and in a few years it will have paid off! I only use it about once every 2 weeks, to test out a new update, maybe submit a bug report or two, then wait till the next one since right now, the content I desire is not available. But the base sim is still worth it.

What to say about this game? You spawn in with high aspirations of being the next big thing, only to get gunned down before you even know what your uniform looks like.
It's the dark souls of FPS games, a game that doesn't want or need your love, just your time and sanity.  Spend too long playing it and you will quickly find that you grow to hate dirt.  But there is a beautiful gulf where you suddenly learn where not to tread, where to aim your rifle, and where to throw grenades or drop mortar rounds on your enemies and suddenly you feel amazing.
And thats when you find yourself under arrest for shooting people in a public place.
I swear that if mainstream shooters ever decided this was the type of game that they wanted to produce the CoD kiddies would just scream for DLC that would let them suddenly have triple health and rapid fire machine guns.
As for mechanics, it's essentually a massive game of push.  You fight over a trench, if you win, they get to counter attack. If you hold, you shove them back a bit further.
Odds are you won't win repeatedly unless you severely outlevel their team... at which point it's more or less like the real WW1 was, veteran troops survived while noobs just choked to death on their own teeth.
Classes are pretty balanced, the majority of them using bolt action rifles or pistols, a fair group of them having a 'nade or two, and occasionally you'll see someone rocking an MG. Either they will be very good at placement and hold off waves of attackers... or they will think this game is Rambo/CoD/Battlefield and will just get wrecked over and over and over again.
Your officer (or yourself if you play the leader of your 4 man squad) will have the ability to slap down objectives and call in support (mortars, smoke screens, poison gas, or spy planes... depending on squad type). The rest of you get the job done, anyway you can.  Death is pretty much garunteed unless you are a useless sniper, sitting back 2-3 trenches and trying to kind of influence small skirmishes... which I've annoyingly seen far too many times.  It's a 3x scope, and lets face it... it's trench warfare. Snipers are damn near useless (I've only seen 1-2 decent ones in this game), so take that scope off and join the rest of us bleeding on the trench floor.
Some things I'm surprised to see missing is rain/mud.  Both were severely dangerous in WW1... albeit the engine obvious doesn't allow for terrain damage effects.  Your squad levels up based on how often you play with specific players... an interesting mechanic that basically says 'make a good group of friends and♥♥♥♥♥♥the enemy over and over again and we will reward you!'
So in closing, if you feel like the traditional shooters were a bit too pedestrian and you wanted to explore a far more brutal shooter that just wants you to cry in the corner like your soldier does when his arm/leg is blown off by a rifle... then Verdun is it.
Just don't assume you are going to be good at it for at least a few hours.  Because odds are you'll die like the rest of us.

My life with video games started back in the mid-80s with a BBC Acorn Electron. My favourite game at the age of 6 or 7 was called Boxer, a pixelated annoyance, but I loved it. VVVVVV calls back to those blocky Commodore 64 days with amazing chiptune music that you will have in your head for months after playing the game.
You control Captain Viridian, lost in an alternative universe where instead of jumping, you can control gravity. He must search for his (largely inept) crew who is scattered around the open world. While it is technically a platformer, it really is more of a puzzle and memory game more than anything else. Some of the puzzles will annoy the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you and take a few (hundred) tries to get past, but the game rewards you with more puzzles, more fun, and more great music.
The game lasts maybe 2 hours if you play in one sitting, but for me, this 2 hour playthrough was one of the most compelling and influential 2 hours of my life. Before I played this game (which I got in the Humble Indie Bundle #3 in 2011,) I was an AAA-title-only kind of man and a console gamer. Now, I largely stay away from the top games and stick to the indie titles that give me new and interesting ways to escape reality.
I have lost count of how many times I have played this game. I have had times where people walking past my "office" (My comfy chair in the living room) when I have been playing this game on my laptop, where people would stand and watch me play the game in a daze. If you are someone who is all about modern graphics, you have probably already made up your mind regarding these types of game, but for anyone with an open mind or a love for something different, this game is worth any value of money you throw at it. I love it.

The voice acting is surprisingly good. But that's the only offering of this short, dry, uninteresting walking simulator. Don't get me wrong, I really like the genre ("Firewatch" and "Beginner's Guide" being the best I've yet played), but this is a great example of how not to do it. The house is ominous and atmospheric; the "puzzles" are unremarkable; and the story...  well, "what story" is the right question to ask.
This got a ton of attention because it's about a girl who's gay. It's not a big reveal. It's not under adversity or oppression. It's just... "I'm a teenage girl and I like a girl." That's it. That's the story. There's no spoiler warning, because there's no story to spoil. The characters talk at you quite a bit, but there's no arc, growth, geniunity. Just extremely banal "I think I like this person, but I don't know if I should."
So it's a walking simulator with good voice actors whose talents are wasted on something that isn't a story. It's not provocative; it's not deep; it's not even interesting. There's nothing to be interested by. It's a house that seems like there's going to be a horror scare at any minute, but it's just nighttime and empty. It's a story that's populated by flat characters. And then it ends abruptly. There's no narrative structure; there's no central theme. It ends. Unsatisfyingly and right at the moment the story could have possibly turned into something interesting. But no. Not in Gone Home.
I wanted to like it. I heard good things about it. I didn't go in with a bad attitude. I'm the kind of person this game is intended for: open-minded, patient, lover of stories, walking simulator fan. And this manages to miss the mark completely.
The simpering, fawning worship of this game is due to overhype and people who are too eager to rubber stamp something simply because the protagonist is LGBTQ. That doesn't make a good story; that doesn't make a good game. It's dishonest to treat characters as automatically interesting because their single defining quality is "not straight."

I tried to keep this short but then couldn't because there is so much that is thoroughly enjoyable about this game.
Very similar in its aesthetic to games like Hyper Light Drifter. This game is an audiovisual feast that exerts an excellent atmosphere over you. The plot is mysterious and foreboding - it's delivered in short and impactful snippets and is very effective in doing so. The game's world as a whole is quite confusing at first and requires you to think as you would if you were existing in this plane of existence. While I haven't finished the game, I am eager to learn the fate that befell this broken world. It seems to be the intricate tale of an ancient kingdom, once strong and powerful, now fallen due to betrayal at the hands of one of its greatest leaders. Knowing that there are multiple endings makes the story even more deep.
The combat is near-constant. This is where this game could do a little better at times. Throughout your exploration, enemy hordes will spawn at random. This can at times, be overwhelming, whilst also hampering your exploration. However, it is entirely possible to come up with far more effective ways to deal with enemies. This is entirely necessary as the game will throw enemies at you in spades at times. The game has a simplistic and satisfying combat system. You will be rewarded with success in battle through the use of aerial attacks and directional hit combos. In a sense, the fighting is almost like a beat-em-up because you can chain long strings of attacks together to defeat your foes. My main gripe is that sometimes you may need to resort to button mashing to deal with weaker mobs of enemies that are more easily slain.
An interesting feat of this game is that while you have main objectives that are visibly marked out on your map, the areas between your spawn and these objectives are procedurally generated. This means your route is never the same and at times, results in a satisfying sense of tension as you quickly try to get to your objective before the inevitable mobs of enemies start spawning. The procedurally generated areas can however cause some problems with navigation if you are not acquainted with how to use your map.
While combat is a large component of this game, exploration is also nearly as important. The game rewards you handily for your exploration. The protagonist of Sundered is able to upgrade her abilities through an expansive set of upgrade trees. You collect "shards" in game, which are your currency for purchasing these upgrades. Sundered also has a perks system. Perks are discovered as you explore or defeat enemies in the game. Interestingly, the perks you equip will always offer a distinct advantage and conversely, a disadvantage. The perks let you shape the kind of build the protagonist has and give you some satisfying creative control over how you will face your enemies.
You will gain ever more shards if you choose to explore every area available to you. There are many hidden pockets of secrets and other rewards you can gain. Sundered will also reward you for your skill in combat - some areas will lock you in, preventing your escape, forcing you to deal with the brutal enemy hordes that spawn mercilessly. Upon succeeding these hordes, you will receive satisfaction through the unlocking of new perks and a large sum of shards.
Even when you lose battles in Sundered, the game is forgiving - death is not penalised. Instead, you respawn at the nexus of the game, where you have access to your upgrade trees and unlike Souls-esque games, you do not lose any of your currency upon death. This means you always get stronger and this allows near-constant progression. Furthermore, you unlock the access to new abilities as the game progresses. These new abilities unlock previously inaccessible areas and further aid your exploration of this bizarre and misshapen world.
I have been playing this game on the Hard difficulty from the beginning of my first playthrough. I will admit that it is indeed quite challenging but also fair if you are careful with the fights you choose to take and explore areas within which you know you can handle the enemies.
I personally, highly recommend this game. While it is not perfect and is at times frustrating, it will reward you for your persistence and hard work. If you can accept its difficulty and are ready to immerse yourself with a confusing albeit deeply intriguing world, then you should play this game.

Sundered is gorgeous. Drop dead beautiful, with painterly backgrounds and lush animations. It's quick and responsive, with movement a joy once you unlock all the different ways to get around; combat feels great too, with quick combo attacks, a dodge roll and additional options opening up as you explore some mysterious ruins at the behest of a tentacle-moustache-twirling "benefactor".
It seems that humans had some sort of violent falling out with things with lots of tentacles, and now the whole facility is in a bit of disrepair; it's up to you to... well, kill everything in your path, and open some doors. But it's mostly killing everything in your path: the human's leftover machines, gone haywire, and their betentacled erstwhile enemies. Which seem to have gone feral. Fun!

The gameplay very much falls in the Metroidvania mold, with more than a few quirks. Sundered randomizes much of the level layout - the main outline of the game world is boxed out, but there are variably-sized "tiles" within those areas are swapped around whenever you die. The enemies, too, are randomized from a pretty rich (and nasty-looking) selection.
One difference with other games of this style is that you're rarely threatened by lone or small groups of monsters; the true threat is that periodically hordes of them converge upon you mercilessly. Combat tends to be more about trying to manage attacks from all quarters, trying to keep away to let your shields to regenerate, and cause damage without sustaining too much yourself. It took me a while to get used to it, and it caused some severe difficulty spikes that seemed down more to bad luck than me doing anything wrong, what with dozens of weak enemies piling the damage on (something the developers have stated they're aware of and are trying to fix).
The bosses I've encountered so far were great fun and pretty fair. And their activation/death sequences are stunning.
Character advancement is driven by a node-based skill tree in which you choose stats to improve (bought with shards dropped by enemies), and abilities and equippable perks that can be found during exploration. There's another layer on top which I won't spoil, but discovering it was a treat.
There is no penalty for death other than being teleported back to the beginning; this is mitigated by a huge number of shortcuts opened during exploration, and by a really great touch: as soon as you respawn, you can use all of the shards that you accumulated to improve your stats. You don't really need to die to do this (just go back to the starting screen), but it effectively removes part of death's sting. It feels like a reward, and if it was designed to work this way- well, hats off to the developers.
Exploring the sprawling levels is very enjoyable. There's not a huge amount of visual variety within each individual area, but as mentioned before, they're exceptionally well rendered. And the game does a good job of sprinkling special rooms to find with minibosses, vistas, lore, perks and other rewards small and large.
There's a bit of lore to find (some of it related, Souls-style, in ability descriptions) and there's a good sense of history, but there isn't much of a plot - the script mostly focuses on building ambiance, staying on the sidelines while you weave through the map as you will.
It's not without its flaws, but I'm enjoying the game thoroughly. I'll cop to be swayed a fair bit by the amazing visuals (the Aberration's unholy churning animation will stick with me for a long time after I finish this game, I suspect) - but there's a seriously good game in here if you're willing to stick with it through the rough patches; Good enough that I've barely played anything else since I picked it up. Can't wait to see what the studio does next.

It may look like a Hearthstone copy, but the looks are basically the only thing they copied. The Gameplay is more like M:tG, including cards that are playable in the Opponent's turn and using a classic 5-Color-Wheel, with some abuse of the game being digital, allowing rather creative Abilities like Warcry (give the top Card in your deck +1/+1), Revenge (Shuffle back into your deck on death, and play for no cost when drawn afterwards) or Echo (Draw another copy of this card when drawn). Unlike both Hearthstone and M:tG, you don't actually have to put in loads of money to get your hands on competetive decks.
Many of the negative Reviews here talk about this game being reliant on RNG, however this is not entirely true, since just as in Magic, you can get screwed or flooded on Mana and it does feel rather bad, when it happens, just as it feels sort of bad, when it happens to your opponent. However both of these usually don't happen very often unless your deck is badly built (like being 50% Mana generation).
About deck variety, I think it's rather healthy, as even if many people complain about popular netdecks like Chalice (TJP Control) or Stonescar Aggro (Burn/Rally/Jito/Jitoless or whatever is currently popular Queen) (Hint: these two are the cheaper of the good (net-)decks), you can still basically play anything you want as long as you understand how to build and how to play it. Additionally, Meta's shifting every week, even without patches, because decks are kind of rotating in "Flavor of the Week"-Style.

I have been playing FSX since its initial release back in October of 2008, and I find FSW to be a huge upgrade to an outdated game. Please remember it is currently Early Acces, what is with currently available I am satsified, as long as they stay on this path and continue on with the Free Flight mode it will be great.
Pros:
- Multiplayer has been streamlined to a much simpler system
- Graphics overhauled, and the planes look beautiful
- Flight physics seem much better then FSX by a long shot
- The new flight planner is wonderful compared to FSX, simple for beginners
- The UI is streamlined and looks great
- Setting up my flight stick and throttle combo was easy, everything was automatically configured to perfection. The only thing I want to do is change buttons to the controls I would like for my own convenience.
- The checklist they added in for Engine start up is a wonderful and new feature
- The things you can do within the aircraft now is absolutely amazing
- The controls are about the same so it is easy to use for all the FSX vets out there
Cons:
- Optimization is not the best currently, I am not running this on no old potato I have had sitting around
- I have had a few times now mid flight I crash out badly
- This ties in with my initial con, but the Weather system seems to run heavily in game causing FPS drop
- I find the flight planner as simple as it is, complicated to setup ILS flights and to locate the VOR/LOC frequencies
- I wish there were more checklist i.e. Take off, Landing, Cruise, and so on
- I have a concern that the amount of heavy aircraft included will be extremely limited and most will have to be bought seperate in DLC. I have no basis for that truthfully, just a feeling.
- The major airports still have lack of buildings, and remind me greatly of FSX
Overall I find FSW to be a wonderful experience, it definitely has the potential to set the tone to take over as the go to Flight Simulator on the market. The simplicity of the whole Simulator as a whole is something I found to be amazing, this keeps the door open for newer folks looking to get into the Flight Simulator world. I truly hope they leave the game as open as FSX in terms of Freeware and Payware aircraft, along with textures and airports. If they keep that going then they can easily win the hearts of those out there not wanting to leave the legacy of FSX completely behind. I am assuming since it was a lot of UI and graphical updates it will be easy for developers to upgrade their payware into FSW. I hope you all found this review to be helpful, but I definitely recommend this game. I was hestitant when I first bought because everything it was missing, but it is shaping into a great Flight Simulator. Fly safe!

It's probably just not doing it for me gameplaywise... Lemme explain a bit.
Having played hollowknight and dead cell like crazy the past few months i tend to be biased by them i know, but the gameplay isn't "tight". The dodge for example is utterly useless with the enemies spawning everywhere you'll mostly end up in a spiked plant or in another enemy. The biome that spawns platforms on the first and second part of the game (I presume the 3rd as well) is also frustrating, Most of the time, they are a millimeter too high for the normal jump forcing you to use walls or doublejump. Wall jumps are not really nice either, you'll have to walljump 5 or 6 time to get up a tiny ledge because the walls are too spaced out to get high enough. double jump is also annoying you can only use it once per landing, based on how often you have to use it, it's just breaking the flow of platforming a lot.
The horde system is quite unique and interesting, but it's not rewarding enough so you'll probably end up just running not because you fear them, but because they get boring. Getting swarmed every minutes or less by mobs could've been fun if it wasn't the only core mechanic related to ennemies. The most frustrating "feature" is the lack of feedback when you are getting hit, you get wrecked in no time in this game, so don't blink. Most game gives you immunity when you're hurt giving you time to get back into the fight with the "pseudo-immunity" patch i haven't notice any changes still got swarmed and wrecked in seconds by boucing back and forth between foes.
On the Combat side it's alright there's no big deal here, it's quite standard button mashing with a bit of combo possible when you jump and get used to it. I've read there's more to it though unlock, but i doubt i'll be playing more to uncover this part.
The devs are really nice and trying to overcome a lot of their issues related to the game difficulty, i'm sure given time they'll manage to fix most of the games flaws. But based on what i disliked being at the core mechanics of the games it's highly unlikely they'll dive into the core gameplay i flagged as annoying to me. It's the kind of design decision you take in the prototyping phase not while patching.
Fun game, but not a lot of long-term playability. At a certain point it's not worth continuing a game. We'll see what it evolves to.

I personally don't recommend this game but, rather than simply say it's trash, I'm gonna go in detail about the pros and cons. This isn't so much to disuade people from buying it so much as a fair warning before dropping $40 on it. Keep in mind I've played this game using mouse & keyboard just as easily as I have on Dark Souls 1. So let's start with the pros.
-The graphics are much more beautiful in comparison to Dark Souls 1.
-The camera isn't on a grid and is a lot smoother and finer to use than in Dark Souls 1.
-The player message system has quite a few more options now.
-It's a bit easier to co-op with a friend using rings that work with covenants.

-NPCs have poise, sometimes even carrying through hitting your shield. And magic is inneffective against NPC invaders.

-The bosses are probably the easiest thing about this game. To be quite honest. Like any Dark Souls game, you get your summons and it's cake.
-Enemies can be farmed to extinction in a zone and won't respawn, hampering farming.

If the Need for Speed franchise is tyring to get back to their roots (and I have completed the newest game) they really need to look to these guys for inspiration as this game does a much better job of mixing a good motive to get you started as well as keeping to many of the gameplay elements that made older need for speed games legendary. Having domination and customization at its core. As well, This game is ambitious to say the least, mapping the entire U.S.A to a scale that offers a surprizing veriety of locations to visit and scout. After a year they looked to reinvigorate the game by releasing a sort of overhauling DLC, adding new mechanics, game modes, and vehicle types, Even updating the graphics with new textures and weather effects. the DLC costs $30 but the base game has been reduced putting the whole game with the new overhaul somewhere around 40 - $50, which is well worth the entry for a great example of how to handle an aging brand without pumping out another game within an unrealistic deadline. The mechanics and physics are not on par with the best of the old Need for Speed arcade type open world racer, they feel very loose and a bit unpredictable at times, but for the overall experience the handling gets a pass by me. the open world and storyline feel overarcing and important, something we sorely lack in AAA titles these days, A sense of importance. One problem that holds this game back is the fact that it is set up as an MMO, which means microtransactions, which means spiked economy costs for things that a singleplayer would allow within much more reasonable values, if it were a singleplayer game it would probably have a much longer story and a much bigger payoff to upgrading cars and progressing, but instead we have every car roughly as fast as eachother and performance upgrades unlocking in a random loot counter sort of setup wich makes buying upgrades almost pointless. Just one example of how MMO is most often not the way to go with your game. I think the game would have greatly benefited on being singleplayer focused while having the same online components it already does, the MMO features in the core game are like any other AAA game that tries to go MMO, theyre pointless, its immerssion breaking, its economy stifling, it simply doesnt work.
So I give this game a 7/10 (Buy instead of that new NFS)

I'm not really going to offer a constructive review here tbh, I simply want to gush for a little while.
Final Fantasy X was one of the defining games of my childhood. For a solid 6 months, I lived and breathed this game.
Me not being a reader as such, this game offered the first great story that I ever experienced. I was completely absorbed and sucked into the world of Spira.

If you’re someone who enjoys a racing game with beautiful, customisable cars, but gets bored of the usual race-to-the-finish-line gameplay, The Crew is what you’re looking for.
At first glance, the game seems to lack in its graphics quality, but as you speed through the streets of the United States in over forty main missions, prove yourself in eight different skill types, and swap from all-terrain trucks to exotic sports cars to suit the occasion, you’ll quickly forget about that. And while the game is designed for multiplayer, most of it is just as suitable for single player.
Underlying the beautiful gameplay of The Crew is a deep story following Alex Taylor as he joins the FBI to take vengeance on the leader of a nation-wide underground motor club named the 5-10s. As he travels from state to state, he recruits friends to help him rise through the ranks of the criminal organisation.
The multiplayer game features five distinct car specifications; you’ll find yourself teaming up with friends and other online players to weave through the streets of New York in your Street car, drifting on dirt roads in your Dirt spec, racing down Route 66 in your Performance supercar, taking down rivals in your Raid truck, and hugging the racing line of designated tracks in your exotic Circuit spec.
However, you’ll find that the game has its fair share of drawbacks. The first few missions, which are completed in your Street car, are quite short and hence less rewarding. Once you move onto Performance, the races will become much lengthier, allowing the pace to ramp up to frantic speeds as you narrowly dodge traffic on windy highways.
The rubber-banding is also definitely lacking; if your car is too levelled up in late-game, the other AI racers will fall behind in the first stretch, and the distance will grow as the race progresses. This isn’t an issue during multiplayer, when you can focus on beating your friend – but when you’re playing alone, it often feels like more of a cruise than a race.
On top of that, don’t expect the police chases to be too challenging. While this isn’t the game’s main feature, this is one aspect that could have been implemented much better. I’ve found myself too easily losing track of the cops because they can’t keep up, and this takes away from the enjoyment of having the police hot on your heels while drifting around the block.
While the game can definitely be enjoyed in single player, I would recommend grabbing a few friends and hitting the roads. If none of your friends are crazy for a racing game (or, alternatively, if you have no friends…), you can join up with whoever’s online around the world to give yourself a better challenge. Either way, The Crew is a truly enjoyable game for the story-driven gamers looking for varied gameplay.
