I Played quite a bit of it and I would have to say that it's a great game. It's better than KSP when it comes to building planes.
Pros:
-Good customization, your planes don't have to be made out of voxels.
-Challenges to keep you occupied so it isn't just a sandbox game.
-Includes weapons.
-Decent physics, I don't know if they're realistic but the physics are alright.
-Smooth framerate
-Good mobile port, compared to other mobile ports.
Nitpicks:
- Difficult to fly with a keyboard, much like all piloting games. Joystick is a must if you're planning on doing some of the challenges.
- Difficult build mode controls, but you can get used to them after about 30 minutes of building.
- Not enough warbird parts/weapons.
- Not enough air intake parts for Jets.
- Pulsating glowing rings in race matches are annoying, they mess with your depth perception.
-Weapons are too powerful, 1 bullet will make your aircraft explode no matter where it hits.
-Some bugs when it comes to part collisions, specifically the landing gear.
-Lack of texture for planes, though this can be atributed to the art style or the fact that it's a mobile port.
Cons:
-Some challenges are too difficult for the average player.
-The Lack of flares / missile countermeasures make fights with missiles repetitive.

The game is great in theory, but has little in execution. The building system is comprehensive enough that it would take a good couple hours to get a proper plane built, but there's frankly just not enough to do once you have something airworthy. There are a handful of races and events available. Yeah you'd need to build a couple different aircraft to complete them all but once that'd be done you would have nothing to do.
On top of that the game did not detect the rudder axis of my Logitech Extreme 3D Pro flightstick; no amount of configuration would get it to work, and it works fine in other games. When I attempted to use an Xbox 360 controller instead, I found that no matter what buttons or sticks were mapped to increase/decrease throttle it would still reset the power to 0% the moment I decreased throttle. Anything other than keyboard bindings wouldn't work as intended for throttle.
Uninterested in taking the time to meticulously craft an airworthy vehicle I downloaded some custom aircraft, beat a few of the events, tried a couple AI dogfights (which helped me notice that many of these planes control like absolute garbage), then turned it off and requested my refund. If you are willing to spend time making aircraft and have little concern with content beyond that then give this game a shot, but if you just want to fly a bunch of different planes get FSX or X-Plane.

A GREAT INTRODUCTION TO ADVENTURE GAMES
This game is well done, but easy.  The concept is very simple.  You've come home from your trip to Europe and nobody seems to be there.  There's clues all over the house about what might have happened.  Most of the game is just wandering around the house looking at ordinary household objects trying to find clues.  One thing I like about it is that you can interact with most household objects, down to your little sister's empty pizza boxes.  So, you have to actually think about what objects are important and what ones aren't.  Some games will only let you click on important objects, so this is a refreshing change.
The game has a good story and I enjoyed playing it.  However, it's fairly short and I found it fairly easy.  I think this would be a great introduction to adventure games for anyone who wants to pick them up or just see what all the fuss is about.  It's much easier even than Myst I, which some people found relatively easy, so it's definitely beginner level.  I think it will give people new to the genre a great sense of how the game play typically works, though this particular game has relatively simple game play compared to some I've played.
One thing I did like quite well is that the problem solving is logical.  There are some adventure games I've played where the solutions to the problems were simply not logical.  I'd tear my hair out trying to figure out the answer only to find out that the game designers had just put together a stupid problem with a non-sensical solution.  This game had very logical solutions, however, which is real good.
One thing I like about it, as I do with many adventure games, is that it's non-violence based.  If you'd rather avoid violence in your games and particularly dislike the "you have to kill them just cos... well... they're 'bad guys'..." type violence, this is definitely for you.  The problem solving is just cerebral.  There's no manual dexterity involved.  The story, which you interact with through finding objects around the house, is mostly relationship and character driven rather than just "good guys" fighting "bad guys" for no particularly good reason.
My advice is that if you can get this game at a significant discount (like I did), you'll probably have a great time with it while it lasts.  But I wouldn't pay full price, just because it's much shorter than most adventure games (think maybe one age of one of the Myst games).
Overall, though, I think it's quite enjoyable and, since I got it at a really huge discount here on Steam, I didn't mind how short it was.

English:
When I heard about Outlast it thrilled me. The idea of being alone in a dark asylum, unable to fight against its crazed denizens, tantalized me and I was eager to buy the game and explore its surroundings. In the end, I was disappointed.
The game's environment is interesting, but you're never encouraged to explore it. Instead, you're given extremely repetitive tasks you must repeat over and over to advance the story along. Most of the game can be described as turning on valves/switches, as you're chased by random enemies over and over again. These enemy encounters eventually went from tense and apprehensive to aggravating, similar events (eventually I could predict where and when an enemy would appear). Not to say Outlast doesn't have its scares, but they lessen as the game goes on, due to the games increasing predictability. Any feelings of fear are eventually replaced with feelings of annoyance and anger as the game's plot is painfully dragged out.
The gameplay itself is unrealistic. At one point the main character, Miles, was beaten violently and fell at least thirty feet and then got up without a scratch. Earlier his fingers were cut off, but he somehow ignored the pain and kept going despite massive bleeding and trauma.
Miles himself does not seem to act like a normal human being. Throughout the game you are forced to make stupid decisions that a rational human would not. At one point I had to retrieve my camera from a dark foreboding place and although the game insisted I needed the camera to see, I could see fine without it. A note system also exists in the game that supposedly contains the Miles's thoughts, but these seem to be jokes and are not the thoughts of a normal person.
In the end Outlast is only worth it if on sale. Its repetitiveness, predictability, and overwhelming lack of realism doom it in the end, and there are much better horror games on steam, worth full price.
* This is a review of the main game of Outlast, and not the DLC.
Español:
Cuando me enteré de Outlast que me emocionó . La idea de estar solo en un asilo oscuro, incapaz de luchar contra sus habitantes enloquecidos , me tentaba y yo estaba ansioso por comprar el juego y explorar su entorno. Al final , me ha decepcionado .
Entorno del juego es interesante , pero nunca se le anima a explorar. En cambio, te dan tareas muy repetitivas se debe repetir una y otra vez para avanzar a lo largo de la historia . La mayor parte del juego se puede describir como encender las válvulas / switches, y cuando usted está perseguido por enemigos aleatorios una y otra vez . Estos encuentros enemigos finalmente fueron de tensión y aprensión a eventos similares agravantes ( el tiempo que podía predecir dónde y cuándo aparecería un enemigo ) . No quiere decir Outlast no tiene sus sustos , pero disminuirá a medida que el juego avanza , debido a los juegos cada vez mayor previsibilidad. Cualquier sentimiento de miedo puedan ser sustituidas por sentimientos de disgusto y enfado como la trama del juego es dolorosamente arrastrado .
El juego en sí no es realista. En un momento el personaje principal , Miles , fue golpeado violentamente y cayó al menos diez metros y luego se puso de pie y sin un rasguño. A principios de los dedos fueron cortados , pero de alguna manera ignoraron el dolor y siguió su camino a pesar de la hemorragia masiva y el trauma.
Propio Miles no parece actuar como un ser humano normal. A través del juego se ven obligados a tomar decisiones estúpidas que un ser humano racional no lo haría. En un momento tuve que recuperar mi cámara desde un lugar oscuro presagio y aunque el juego insistió en que necesitaba la cámara para ver , pude ver bien sin él . Un sistema de notas también existe en el juego que supuestamente contiene los pensamientos de los kilómetros , pero éstas parecen ser las bromas y no son los pensamientos de una persona normal.
Al final Outlast es sólo vale la pena si la venta. Su repetitivos, predecibles , y abrumadora falta de realismo condenan a la pena al final , y hay mucho mejores juegos de terror de vapor, vale la pena el precio completo.
*Esta es una revisión del juego principal de Outlast, y no el DLC.

Personally, I enjoy being scared.  Whether it's cause by an emotionally provoking moment, intense suspense, or just a simple pop and go "boo" moment. At first you think to yourself "something else is going to try and kill me any moment now." and still nothing.  Then comes the sense of security.  And right when that sense of security starts to sink in, pop goes a psycho patient and the intense suspense starts again.
The gameplay is fairly common.  Your enter an area with the intention of getting out but something prevents you from doing so.  So naturally you have to go into the darkest placed packed with people fond of the shadows to get the thing(s) that enable your progress to continue.  What I like is that you aren't some closet Rambo that suddenly finds the power within to be the hero the world needs against this specific threat.  No, you're just some guy with a camera surrounded by nut-jobs and killers and guess what the reaction is of a mild mannered video journalist.  Run and hide.  And that's exactly what you have to do.

I want to like it, but I dont.
Pros
- Stunning visuals and art.
- Controls feel good, movement and jumping.
Cons
- Confusing saving and continuing. I never figured out what would get saved and what wouldn't at what time. It's not like clear save points. If you exit the game it doesn't give you a prompt, but you reappear at a hub and half the stuff is gone. So it's hostile to just pickup and play.
- Uninspired maps. It may as well just have been procedural. The textures are beautiful. But the layout is haphazard and boring. I had no incentive to explore, no feeling of discovery. Just hallways of the same blocks and platforms.
- Bad maps. Shows doors and boxes but nothing of what's in the rooms. And not super accurate. But then just marks explicitly "this is a come back later when you get an item spot". The parts of these exporation platformers that feel good are discovery and learning. Explicitly saying there's a roadblock takes the fun out of it.
- Enemies are a drag to fight. They clip through textures so you can't engage them with the spaces in the level. Though that barely matters because the spaces are random and uninteresting. They can attack you from off screen and fly through obstacles. They pour in in droves, but not in a rewarding way. Just keep appearing and piling on. Same enemies, same patterns, same mashing attack and hoping.
I feel bad leaving a harsh review. Because a ton of good work went into this project, and it's beautiful. But ultimately it's not fun, it's not well put together, and it doesn't feel good.
It's like a Michael Bay movie, except it's good and fun.

Thank God that somebody finally stopped copying Dark Souls by making you drop your money when you die. Dark Souls built their whole game with that design in mind and most other games I've seen it in don't put that level of thought into it. They just design old school levels with a new school mechanic with out any effort to make the two harmonious. Good games like Nioh and maybe not so good games like The Surge come to mind. This game just lets you go back to base when you die, and I did not realize how refreshing that could be. That alone gets my vote.
So far everything seems good. Controls feel a lot like Strider, very responsive. The upgrade tree always had something interesting I wanted to get and what I did buy felt meaningful. It has nice touches, like having your health, shield and energy bars grow visually as you upgrade. They look great and I must admit, I'm a scamp for some good looking gauges.
I feel like there's a good bit of adaptability as well, with out adding a verbose amount of stats. For instance, I noticed that I was mostly dying when I was slowly chipped down by the infamous big hordes of hard mode, so I equiped a perk that regenerated some shield for each individual kill and found myself in much better shape. And it felt great to finally survive some of the long waves and get a kill on the first boss. The adds felt just right, to my taste. Not too hard to pick off most as you fought, but rarely so easy that I felt I could take them all out.
Very interesting game so far and I'll be very impressed if it keeps up this level of quality to the end. I'll edit my review if my opinion drastically changes by then.

You step into the shoes of freelance journalist Miles Upshur as he investigates rumors of corporate misdeeds at Mount Massive Asylum in Colorado. Your red Jeep leisurely glides up the dark path to the front gate recalling Half Life's tram ride into Black Mesa. Upon exiting his vehicle and locating an way into the monolithic nut house it doesn't take long to corroborate the information that led Miles to Mount Massive. The build up to first contact with the horrors within the asylum is classic. Strange noises assault your ear drums, your character's breath becomes shallow and ragged, human figures dart across long halls and lock themselves in rooms and pools of blood stain hallway carpets... Your trusty camera documents your findings and allows Miles to take notes. These notes act as an internal monologue relaying your character's thoughts and feelings. Documents can be collected a la classic Resident Evil and flesh out the motivations of the dastardly Murkoff Corporation. It's a tale that swirls science and religion together in a mostly compelling package.
Unfortunately, Miles didn't get his concealed carry license so that he could tote a rocket launcher around under a trench coat like a proper video game hero. Instead he is armed with only a camera that has night vision. It's this feeling of helplessness that is the crux of the game's scares. Upon encountering Mount Massive's monstrosities you are left with two options: run or hide. Most of the lights in Mount Massive don't seem to work anymore giving you plenty of cover to sneak past the mangled psychos that stalk Miles provided you move slowly. If you choose to sprint past the opposition you have keys that allow you to look back and survey your lead. Not every Asylum patient is a threat and this helps keep tension high since figures in the distance can be benign or send you to an early grave. Unfortunately, the pace of Outlast is hampered by a lack of puzzles and a reliance on key collecting or switch flipping for progression. These sections are predictable in addition to being uninspired since flipping switches alerts your psycho stalkers and generally prompts a mad dash for a hiding spot. Proper puzzles might have provided better opportunities for frights as well as encouraging exploration. Outlast is also very linear with few places worth poking your camera lens. Dark corners and dead end rooms often yield extra batteries for your camera or documents that flesh the proceedings out but fail adequately reward players who poke their noses around. Consequently the strict adherence to the critical path means that completing Outlast takes a mere four to six hours.
The halls and rooms of Mount Massive are soaked in blood and covered in viscera, sinks are littered with severed limbs and diabolical looking medical instruments are scattered around. It doesn't seem as though the Murkoff Corporation spent much on renovations as the interior of the facility is crumbling and decaying. All of these foreboding details are rendered with a liberal amount of grain and noise giving everything a course texture. Lighting is dynamic and moody and the limited field of vision when viewing the game world through the night vision on your camera is intense. Miles animates well, his hands grasp corners as you peer around them and that way the camera bobs to emulate the motion of his head while running creates a very immersive game experience. The excessive motion blur isn't exactly welcome however and may make players with sensitive stomachs nauseous. Enemies look like they belong in Leatherface's family photo album with their mangled and stitched up visages. It's unfortunate that there are so little variation among them. Also the animations of your foes are not as commendable as those of Miles. They look more clumsy than menacing and watching them slide across the floor as you hide under a bed dimishes their stage presence.

UPDATED REVIEW:
TL;DR = Long-haired metal-head turned doctor changes his mind on disliking Sundered to having a blast playing Sundered with a different expectation.
Previously, I did not recommend this game and you can read the reasons why below. I have since changed my mind about it because of the following. I am a huge metroidvania geek, love difficult combat-oriented games and adore Lovecraftian horror. Needless to explain, I have been looking forward to this game for the better part of a year and was extremely bummed the first two days after launch. My error, which led to the negative review, was expecting the game to be in a similar vein to Hollow Knight, Dead Cells and the Soulsborne series. While it is a metroid-esque game, the only other thing it has in common with these games is the opaque lore and Lovecraftian horror (with Bloodborne). The devs reached out to me because of my review and I'm glad they did, because now I am really enjoying this game.
With their advice, I realized that the combat system is not about tactical combat, fighting enemies with complex moves requiring adaptation to their unique combat style such as Souls-like games, Hollow Knight, Dead Cells, etc. (i.e. learning patterns). Rather, the combat system in this game is about learning how to MANAGE the hordes of enemies with simple attack patterns. I started having more fun with a sense of accomplishment when I gave up on trying to kill all the enemies and instead, managed the hordes until they disappeared. This is a very different game compared to what I'm used to, but I'm glad I gave it another chance because I can't wait to see what the next powerup is going to be.
Oh, and the bosses are EPIC and you can't beat TL's visual style.
Initial Review Below:
I really, really, really want to recommend this game but at this time I cannot. I love the aesthetic and visual style. I love the enemy types, the audio, the mystery of the world and Lovecraftian horror. I also am a giant metroidvania and dark souls geek. All of these things should spell a favorable review from me. The fact is, I am not really having fun playing it. I don't care for the horde mechanic because it doesn't respect the player's skill level. Difficulty and death are not due to player mistakes but rather to overwhelming numbers of enemies. Smart combat is not present in this game. I have encountered more than a few hordes that are unending until you die. You cannot run away from them nor does the cannon work as well as the loading screen suggests. Which brings me to my biggest gripe. I have had load screens that have lasted literal minutes until I had to force quit the game in frustration.
I loved Hollow Knight and Dead Cells. Combat was smart, not cheap. I understand the level of randomization in this game is to create a sense of dread and novelty for each playthrough, but what it does instead is create frustration and boredom. When I kill a horde, I don't feel a sense of accomplishment like I did when defeating a tough enemy in Hollow Knight, Dark Souls or Bloodborne. Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game at this time.

Decent Tower Defense game set in space, with four quadrants to defend instead of a single path.
In every town, there's at least one local diner that puts its own unique spin on very basic dishes; 'Edna's Eatery' might serve bacon-and-onion studded ground beef with a brown sugar and tomato glaze, along with multigrain-noodles served under a three-cheese spread.  Somehow, this all sounds much more appealing than Meatloaf with a side of Mac'n'Cheese.... even if it's basically the same ol' recipe you make at home.
Well, if Infinium Strike was food, it would be an appropriate dish for any of these hometown diners - satisfyingly filling, with a unique spin to glamour it up... but not exciting enough to truly titillate your tastebuds.
Infinium Strike is a Tower Defense game that follows the basic TD formula reasonably well (towers, upgrades, abilities, multiple difficulties in the campaign), although the game doesn't do much to improve on that.  The major change Infinium Strike brings to the genre is four different screens to defend instead of a map with set routes, and this comes with both pros and cons.
Defending attacks from four directions adds a fun frantic element to the gameplay, since you can only see 1/4 of your defenses at a time.  However, with a significant portion of the fighting occuring offscreen it is difficult to get a good sense of the action, and it feels like you have less control of the battle than in a traditional tower defense.  Moreover, since each of the four defensive areas is simply a line of towers that cover the entire quadrant,  it seems like the game is merely swapping the usual strategic tower placement (along a set route) with four separate lines of defense.

In general, everything about Infinium Strike - graphics, audio, storyline, and gameplay - seems to be satisfactory, just not extraordinary enough to brag about.  Infinium Strike is a decent game, and will likely appease players looking for a new tower-defense game to play through.  However, it also also didn't seem that exciting, and may not entertain folks who are not fans of the TD genre.
Just like a serving of 'gourmet' meatloaf at Edna's Eatery, there's absolutely nothing wrong with this reasonably tasty dish, and it will certainly fill you up well enough... but you probably won't remember the meal in a month or two.

LOG2 is the 2nd game in the series and continues being an action role-playing video game developed and published by Almost Human. It is the sequel to the 2012 title Legend of Grimrock, and was released for Microsoft Windows for PC on October 2014. Like LOG, it is a first-person action role-playing game with realtime game mechanics. The Player again manages a party of up to 4 NPCs which they move through a grid-based dungeon.
Like LOG, the player in the game is again a prisoner. The games starts out where you and three- (3) other prisoners are located in the hull of a prison transport ship, in a cage... Yea! How Joyous!
As a result of a strong storm and unknown magic (hehehe) the party of prisoners gets stranded on the mysterious Island of Nex. The prisoners need to explore the island and discover its secrets if they are to survive. Unlike LOG, this game is played outside and inside. You will travel through forests, rivers and swamps, as well as, ancient ruins and crypts below the island.
There is another Big Bad Guy, too, the elusive Island Master who alternates between providing hints to the prisoners and taunting them of upcoming challenges.
The party of prisoners will need to gather a elemental gems scattered around the island, and use them to enter the Castle that towers in the middle of the island. On top of the castle, they encounter the Island Master! Defeating him is possibly their only escape... or is it?
Gameplay consists of using a Keyboard/Mouse to navigate through the the Island, Underground Dungeons, solving a combination of puzzles and combat. Characters within the party gain experience for slaying creatures and beasts within, allowing them to increase in level and progress skills which enhance combat abilities and allow the casting of new spells, and equipment is obtained through exploration and solving of puzzles throughout the dungeon.
I had a blast with this game, too. It met my expectations of an Action Role-Playing, Dungeon Crawler set in an atmosphere of constant dread and mortal danger.

I haven't played many games of this type in recent years. We have to go back to the Megaman era to find my last love for a platform side-scroller.
Diving into this game, the first impressions are mediocre, as they game is lacking in introduction, but eventually this also becomes its charm.
The game is frustratingly awesome. Prepare to die a lot, and as I write that, I'm all too aware of the understatement embracing it. Besides a few hints, there isn't any real tutorial, but this eventually triggered my passion for exploration in games. As I knew very little going into the game, trial and error was the only way.
The map function (including the Minimap) gives you minimal information, and you have no clue whether the area is suited for you at this point in the game or not… Just go and find out.
So you die a lot, get resurrected at the beginning and either try something new, or after doing some upgrades, you try again… But each time you must travel to the location you died. While it can be frustrating to go through the same content, repeatedly, the procedural generated areas contribute to the variations which ensures you can’t cognitively remember every step. Also, at least in the beginning, it is good practice to learn to combat the common foe.
I find the game very beautiful in its own sense, challenging, very fun, and rewarding after you finally defeat a foe… somehow, I feel like I’ve improved because it took learning and effort to move forward in the game.
This game is very recommendable, it is worth every penny 😊

Banished is a good city building simulator that I would recommend to anyone who likes city building simulators. Some concerns I have with the game are a decided lack of replayability. Upon building every building and expanding my city outwards I found myself wondering why I was continuing to do so. Having more people wasn't particularly beneficial and there was no real 'end game' to work towards. Unlike games like Anno 2070 or Civilization, your purpose in banished is simply to survive, which for me wasn't particularly challenging (might just have been luck). Even when a tornado leveled a portion of my town, I found it relatively easy to recover.
All in all a good game for 10-15 hours of gameplay.

The Tower Defence genre is one much maligned, and perhaps rightly so. It is a relatively straight forward concept, and outside of setting and a few tweaks, it hasn’t evolved a huge amount since the days of WarCraft III. There are more reasons for this than I care to discuss here, but one reason is that in such a stagnant genre, innovation is key – yet rarely are attempts at innovation successful.
Infinium Strike is such a game. In seeking to innovate on Tower Defence, it has dulled down what is, in my opinion, and already rather dull genre. Overly simplistic, and drawn out, Infinium Strike is all looks, and little substance, featuring a derivative plot and mind-numbing gameplay. Oh, and then there is the ludo-narrative dissonance of a giant starship that doesn’t move at all during battle, because it has towers on it…

First, you have the 4 sides of your ship (front, back, left and right) as areas with lanes for enemies. Then you have to have the right guns for the enemies' range. This creates quite the frantic tension as you can't just build up and sit back. You have to really stay on top of things and manage quite a lot of moving parts. The UI takes a little getting use. Making the pause button an X is a strange decision, for example. The game has a nice tutorial that lets you learn the ropes and then gives progressively harder missions. Graphics are nice. Summed up, this game is essentially the result of throwing Test Drive Unlimited 2, Driver: San Fransisco and Need For Speed: Undercover intro a breeding pen together. Being a massive fan of TDU and the Driver series, i'd say that sounds pretty damn good.
It has the exploration and collectibles of TDU2, the "undercover ex-street racer who was jailed up but picked by the FBI to catch bad guys" plotline, which i suppose is a mix of D:SF and NFSU, and then the attention to detail around the maps and customization of TDU2.
The plotline is pretty short. Like i mentioned earlier, i completed the storyline within 23 hours, and that's with quite some extra time added into exploration. You could probably sprint trough the game in 17/18 hours. Though, the exploration is what makes this game so enjoyable. Like, for ♥♥♥♥'s sake, there's a unicorn and a bigfoot walking around for you to almost run over in your Paris-Dakar specced muscle cars and circuit spec classic cruisemobiles.
The map is large. Very, very large. It's basically the entire US, and even though it's downscaled, you'll still spend over an hour getting from one end of the map to the other. It's also surprisingly well detailed, with a ton of stuff to discover, like a giant ski jump to launch your car off, or 5 different race tracks, or wrecked cars, which is another thing very similar to TDU2.
It's a good time if you enjoy cars and exploring♥♥♥♥♥♥

This was probably the most famous PlayStation 2 exclusive game ever. Also one of the top favorites by fans. Now 10 years after, it's back on newer generation consoles and PC (and yes, it is a good port!).
Final Fantasy, as one of the very first JRPG besides Dragon Quests, is well famous for interesting detailed world and character designs, authentic JRPG gameplay with new different mechanics, great storyline. top notch graphics, and the soundtracks. All of which FFX has everything included. Something that might need to be noted: Although the stories are connected, X and X-2 are quite different in many ways. E.g. FFX has Conditional Turn-Based Battle (CTB) system which means characters with higher speed will be able to take more turns than slower characters, thus making speed more important. On the other hand, FFX-2 has the traditional simpler ATB system but with quicker speed than the classic ATB games.
For this version basically has the same contents as the PS2 International version (aka complete version) but with HD Visual Upgrade (resolutions and also textures), rearranged soundtracks with options, Keyboards and Mouse support, Autosaving, and boosters that make the game more flexible/customisable.
Note: 1. Text language can be changed at the game launcher > settings > then change 日本語 to you preferable language (assuming your game is in Japanese by default).
2. For the first playthrough, It is recommended to use default settings for authentic experience.
3. The battle speed and ATB for FFX-2 can be adjusted. It is recommended to use Wait Mode for the first playthrough.
4. For FFX, the standard sphere grid is more linear and has more of hp bonus, while expert grid allows you to level up more freely.
5. While FFX has a fixed class for each character, FFX-2 has switchable class system called Dressphere.
6. The world in the game, Spira, was inspired by South Pacific, Thailand, and Japan.
And no, you don't have to play FFI to IX to play this since the story and world are independent each installment.

At the time of writing this review, it seems that the microtransactions are on the verge of being removed from the game follower user feedback.  I didn't find it at all necessary to buy gold in the game (and didn't), so I won't mention it in this review.  Note also  that I've only levelled my party up to level 3, so this is perhaps an 'incomplete' review, but I'm not certain that I'm going to make the effort to finish the game any time soon.  Anyway....
They made a Warhammer Quest game.  Yay!  Due to Steam's binary recommendation system, I am recommending this game.  You can be reasured that this is not shovelware, however this game is not all it could be.  It is, of course, a port of a tablet game, and it does show, in that this is quite a bare-bones adaption of the original board game, and lacks much of the original's depth.
THE GOOD
* The art style is very similar to the original board game, and using 3D models on 2D backgrounds enhances this.  The writing also reminds me of the original board game.  This is a good adaption of the original in terms of look and feel.
* The Game of Thrones-esque popup book intro scenes for the towns are quite delightful.
* Giant Spiders are just as cute as the old plastic models were and make a squeaky-toy noise when attacking.  A
* Since it was designed as a tablet game, the game is very easy to dip in and out of on a casual basis.  It's a nice change of pace from some of the more heavyweight RPG titles.
THE NOT-SO-GOOD
* The game is very bare-bones, in some places it almost feels unfinished (for example Orcs make no sound when killed).
* The selection of monster at low level is limited and becomes quite repetetive.  However my Level 3 party were occasionally encountering Vampires, which seems OP (in the original game, a minotaur was the usual 'big bad').
* There are some odd design choices.  For example it is impossible to select your party composition to be anything other than the default until after the first mission.  Also I can name the party, but not the party members.
* The characters feel unbalanced, with some seeming much more effective than others.  This was something of an issue in the original game, but shouldn't have been copied.#
* When you are under a temporary status effect from a consumable or ability (like +1 strength) there is no on-screen information on what the effect does, just its name.
* The shop in the settlements seems to stock items at random, and only one of each item.  This makes it difficult to stock up on healing provisions, for example.
* The original game had a whole deck of distinct treasure items, most of which could by used by most characters.  However in this game the treasure is often specific to just one character.  I've even seen character starting items come up as treasure, which seems redundant.
None of these things are game-breaking, but they give the impression of limited development and a lack of polish.  This has all the makings of a good game, and I'd love the developers to make a properly fleshed-out, fully-developed version of this game.  Failing that, there are a number of immediate ways the game could be optimised for PC use which would make gameplay smoother and less click-heavy, for example a permanently present "end turn" button and auto-scrolling when your mouse hits the screen edge.   Ultimately, this was designed as a casual game and you should keep that in mind when deciding whether or not to purchase.

Dark Souls II (SOTFS) is considered the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the series; some might call it a mistake, and generally a♥♥♥♥♥♥game. It had a troubling development cycle, Miyazaki acted as a supervisor rather than director, dubbing two men co-directors; Shibuya and Tanimura. The former is why the base game of Dark Souls II sucks in comparison to its other siblings (BloodBorne included); halfway through development, Shibuya was booted for the undesired path that Dark Souls II was leading, and too many assets etc where already made to accomodate his work.
Tanimura assumes his role and has to try to clean up Shibuya's mess with limited time and cut budget. He did a pretty good job, not exactly 'saving' Dark Souls II but making it a better product than what we would've seen, had Shibuya continued directing until its release.
The DLCs released for Dark Souls II (under Tanimura's full control) are leagues above what we saw in the base game, and Miyazaki has complimented Tanimura's work in an interview, which for the A-Team lovers should acknowledge. Fortunately for you, they are included with SOTS, which happens to be Tanimura, once again, attempting to polish Dark Souls II, which he did. Thank you for that.
Is this a huge improvement over the original 2014 Dark Souls II? No, there are obvious differences, and this (being the newer release) is much more active than the former. The only reason why I'd consider getting the 2014 release over SOTFS is modding support. Albeit, Souls games have very limited modding compared to The Elder Scrolls titles, but with the original you get ENB support, and a variety of different injectors, texture modding, etc. With SOTFS, it appears that you can get soft-banned for these enhancements, which is an absolute damn shame.

An excellent mix of dungeon traversal, monster battling and puzzling.
Unlike the original Grimrock, which was set entirely in one large dungeon, this game is set on an island where there's a single connected overworld and many medium-sized dungeons scattered around the island.
As a result, this game is a bit less linear compared to the original game.
It still steers the player into a relative order by putting stronger enemies in certain areas, but after the second area the player has a higher degree of freedom.
In a way it's easier than the original, but that's not a bad thing because part of the difficulty from the original was due to the difficulty of satisfying hunger and keeping torches lit.
This game has more opportunity to stock up on food by revisting old areas where some of the enemies respawn.
It's also a lot easier to revisit old areas because you're not restricted to travelling up and down between floors - the areas are spread across the 2D overworld.
The original Grimrock set a precedent with its excellent dungeon designer that allowed people to create masterpieces on the workshop.
Grimrock 2 has taken the original designer and turned it up to 11, meaning that even when the main game is over, there's still a glorious trove of adventures to be had.

This is my first review, so take what i say with a pinch of salt as some will agree and some will disagree.
After beating the story i find myself feeling disappointed, the game had potential and like so many others it didn't utillize it, i feel myself wanting more, like i haven't actually finished the story and there is more to it, even though there isn't.
Going back to the first homefront, i loved it, most games around the release of the first homefront had you playing a hero/soldier fighting in other countrys trying to save the day, so it was refreshing being on the backfoot as the good guys, having the enemy in your backyard invading your home, it was a welcome change of pace and an interesting idea, at least to me.
However both games had this arcadey feel to them which just made them feel like most of the generic shooters out at the time, i wanted to see more grit, give the games a darker feel, its an occupation, your home is being invaded, yet it feels like its taking place in a random country that has no meaning to you, the first homefront set it's self apart from other games at the time using the idea of revolutions and the enemy being the occupying force.
It was nice to see something different, a different perspective to a war, yet in homefront the revolution they havent used that as a driving force to set themselves apart, the game, for me needed a darker back tone to it, war is hell and so are occupations and revolutions, yet throughout the whole story i felt like the game was holding my hand, nothing was challenging, the streets are littered with soldiers, drones and APCs and i just run down the street and jump in a dumpster, it comes aross as lazy, which shows after 2-3 hours of gameplay as in all the different sections, you end up doing the same thing as you did in the first 30 mins of gameplay. I not going to go into bugs as i didnt encounter anything that was problematic, just silly AI.
If the devs ever read this, which i doubt, and you are making another homefront, make it dark, make it actually feel like im someone fighting for their home, someone who is living under a brutal occupation.  Ask a soldier what lengths they would go to if their country was being invaded, if their countrymen and women were being pulled from their homes and executed, the emotions they would feel, the things they would do and then convey those emotions into the game, if you managed that you would have something most generic shooters seem to lack.
(SPOLIER ALERT FOR SOME)
Take for example TWD:EP1 at the end where clem has to choose to let lee turn or shoot him or The Last of us where his daughter dies in like the first five minutes of playing, god damn im a grown♥♥♥♥♥man yet that was tuggin on the ole heartstrings, i was invested in those characters playing as them through their own story. in homefront i found the characters annoying, the only person i liked was the Doc and that was only because he seemed normal, rational.
The game fulfilled its purpose for why i bought it, to pass time, would i recommend it, no not really, it offers nothing you can't get from most other similar shooters, if you intend to buy it, do it on sale because it's not worth it otherwise. personally i had more fun with ME:A even though it was a complete mess on release.
That's my 2 cents, i know it was long but i really wanted to like HF: The revolution and always hoped it would capatlize on what sets it apart but it didn't and that disapointed me.
And the DLC, i played them all, they didnt really add much to the game tbh, especially beyond the walls, talks alot about a nato invasion fleet of the coast, but you dont actually get to see any nato other than a couple of jets at an end scene, if you are gona mention a massive nato fleet that is massing of the coast, show it, show the boats landing, and the tanks and troops unloading, show cruise missiles( or their equivalent ) heading inland to target KPA infastructure, that would have been a much better ending scene that what we have.

I'm undecided on this one. I'd probably rate it 2.5---3/5 stars.  I've wanted to play it since it came out and I'm not sure it lived up to the hype. It had an interesting concept, that's for sure. As it isn't hard to figure out, it's set in an old mansion (old even for the time period) in 1995.  The atmosphere was spooky from the get go, but don't expect any real spooks, it's all atmospheric. The game doesn't have any real plot movement, as in there aren't scenes in this game. You walk around the house, look at objects and start to unravel a mystery though the objects you pick up and journal entries that will be read aloud by the character you control's sister. It's very unique in that it was able to tell a story with absolutely no characters being seen, except in pictures in the house. I give them props for that, but I also kind of miss real characters. The graphics and sound effects were nice, but the voice actress for the journal entires was in no way 17 like the character.
Also, it does have a bit of a nostalgia factor. As someone born in 1991, it was fun to see some of the things I remember from my early childhood, and some of the things I didn't. There are more rooms than my brain thinks are possible in this house, and lots of items to check out.

I don't like to go to deep into research on games because I don't like spoilers so the fact that it's more romance than anything was a bummer, eve with the surprise. I had an inkling of what this game was before going in, but when I started it up, I was extremely unsettled. The atmosphere made it feel like something was deeply wrong with the house. As I walked around and explored the area, I felt less and less afraid of the storm, or of anything paranormal popping up. The environment was very well developed, it felt like a real home. Finding and playing those punk rock tracks really helped calm me, but it also put me in the world - lightning freaks me out, so some noise in the background is soothing. That, plus turning on all the lights, was a nice touch.
I would have liked to know more about the other characters in the house - it's mostly about one central character. There's a few notes that show the other character's stories as you explore, but it's left as really short b-stories. There were clues for the main characters in other character's rooms, and that kind of annoying.
The puzzles were neat and extremely believable. Discovering a new space was pretty exiting, even it it meant just getting a small piece of simple exposition.
I think the buildup to the finale was great. It's not supposed to be grandiose, it's supposed to be real. It wasn't really a revelation, but it was a good finale. I did not truly realise which character I actually was playing as until that final ending. This is a great game to share with people who don't understand how gaming can create and manipulate emotion just like any other piece of entertainment.

Legend of Grimrock 2 is a sequel to 2012 released game Legend of Grimrock. The game sets you on the mystical island where your ship just crashed. Your party is the only one left alive in a cage. What I was longing for the game was more story. The story was revealed to the player similarly like in the dark souls series. There are notes and writing that can be found in the game but no NPCs to talk to.
All in all, I would humbly recommend this game. Probably the best Finnish game set in a fantasy world.

Let's just get this out of the way:
You. Will. Die.
The majority of game time is spent exploring while being swarmed by monsters. These swarms will range from about 6 to easily over 20. Many other negative reviewers express their exasperation with the monster swarms, and I am inclined to agree with them. The monsters are not placed around the map with tact or purpose, but rather summon up whenever an alarm decides to blare at random. They are able to ignore geometry and obstacles in order to get to the player. Luckily, any experience gained will not be lost upon death, and every respawn restocks the player's health potions and ammo to the maximum the player has unlocked. Loading times are a bit of a factor as well. Continuing a game at a later date, the player can expect to load into the home base, and then immediately greet another load screen as they exit the home base. Thankfully, this will only happen once per session.
The game does have it's bright spots. Animations for the player character are crisp and look great as do the other visuals. 60 FPS is no problem to maintain. Destroying entier hordes of enimies feels great after sufficent leveling and ability unlocks.
This game definetly has its flaws, but if the random horde spawns and load times can be overlooked, then it is worth anyone's time.
TL;DR
I would never twist anyone's arm to get Sundered, but I would still recommend the game, especially during a sale.

Infinium Strike is a space tower defense game. It’s not your typical tower defense game as it’s based in space and you have this huge ship which you must defend against the Wrogs. You can setup turrets on your ship and have several other things like drone ships which help you defend against the Wrogs.
The graphics are pretty average, it’s a space based strategy/tower defense game so you should expect boring dark visuals. While the backgrounds and effects look nice the ship itself looks horrible. The graphics menu has many options so you can lower the graphics if you don’t have a powerful GPU. There’s not a problem in performance of the game as I played on extreme detailed options without any problems with over 100 FPS all the time.
The music in this game is great though. From the moment you launch the game and you hear that epic battle almost Star Wars like music, you get hooked. The narration is also pretty nice though it seemed sometimes that the narrator was bored.
You have this huge ship called the Freedom Strike. You can place turrets on it and send out drones to attack the incoming enemy. The enemy will attack from all 4 sides and you have the ability to add turrets on all 4 quadrants of your ship. You also have a strategic view which shows a top down blurpeint of your ship and where the enemies are. This is super useful as a lot of enemies can be attacking you at a time and this helps you figure out which quadrant you should focus on. The main currency of the game which you use to purchase towers and upgrade them is called Infinium. When you kill enemies they will drop Infinium which your ship automatically collects.
The enemies and turrets are sort of like rock paper scissors. One turret kills one range of enemy ship but cannot kill others. Certain turrets can destroy projectiles while special types of turrets are required to kill the bigger ships in range 3. So you have to figure out which turret is best for which enemy range. You can upgrade turrets as well and as expected every level of upgrade costs more than previous. New turrets get unlocked when you upgrade Freedom Strike. Turrets like rail gun, super pulse rifle etc.  Upgrading the Freedom Strike gives armor/shield bonuses as well as new turrets are unlocked for purchasing.
You can also deploy drone machines called TSF fleet. These come in different varieties too, one of these turrets kills the furthest and biggest enemy ships, while the other kills normal enemies which are closer. The last of these targets enemy projectiles only. These TSF fleets can be upgraded which costs points. To spawn new drones, you also need these points. These points charge overtime.
There are also the TSF supertech bonuses. These give you extra help with your missions and include things like the super salvage which doubles the rate at which infinium is collected, or the super shield which insta-charges your shields. These have a cool down and cannot be used unless the cool down period has expired. There are other things as well like the Sentry Sattelite which deploys a stationary satellite which shoots at the enemies in a certain range.
A short gameplay video of a round can be found below:
It’s a tower defense with a little bit of strategy games elements. I wasn’t impressed with the gameplay mechanics. The point that the turrets only kill enemies in a certain range is not that good. Enemies could be in range one and your super awesome pulse rifle cannot do anything about it and will only shoot at range 3 enemies. The game can also be pretty hectic in managing all 4 quadrants where you have to focus on stopping enemy projectiles, keeping a watch on your shield and armor, deploy the correct turrets for what the wave of enemies is, upgrading turrets, spawning the correct TSF Fleet drones etc. It seems more like a chore than gameplay. So buy it only if you really love space strategy games or the game is on sale.

However, Flight Sim World chugs along below 30FPS near big cities and in less populated areas, while the frame rate is higher, there are still lots of micro stutters.  I requested a refund.
With today’s cutting-edge hardware this kind of performance is just unacceptable.  Based on the graphics quality, which is just OK, I should be getting over 100FPS.  This is critical for a flight sim.  If Dovetail can't get the rendering to run smoothly why bother at all.  It just amazes me how poorly this runs.  By way of comparison I have XPlane 11 and while that is also a bit of a FPS hog it is far better than FSW.
There are good aspects to this sim like the maps and flight planning (much better then XPlane) but who cares if the flight experience is full if micro stutters and FPS problems.
In fairness, since this is early access, I may give it another try once it is released but can not recomend it now.

This game felt distant and not very tactile to play. By that I mean the game is too static and you don't feel or see exploisons of the enemy or damage to your ship in a way that was immediately apparent to me. Enemy ships fire tiny shots at you (for the most part) and your only indication of being hit is seeing your shield or armor meter at the top of the screen decrease. There is no obvious impact sound or jarring of the screen or klaxons to indicate "Wham! We've been hit!" That really broke immersion for me.
It all feels very impersonal, like you are controlling something far away. Furthermore, the game feels incredibly artificial and gimmicky in that enemy fighters are only effectively harmed by one type of gun, cruisers by another, and battleships by another. It is quite chivalric for the enemy ships to remain in specific quadrants dependent on their ship class and dutifully do predictable damage over time while you crunch the numbers to determine the most efficient deployment of turrets and fighers to defeat them within a given time frame.
The numbers and mechanics behind the game are far too transparent and it feels very gamey and like a pretty spreadsheet more than actually being a weapons officer on a super advanced human warship fighting against all odds to prevent the genocide of the human race.
The ship doesn't feel like a ship full of people, it is a stationary blob that magically cranks out turrets and drones. It just all felt very flat and prosaic.
This is the future of flight sim. It is not for those without patience, it will take time to become a Gold but the foundations and people are there and I am sticking with it.

Infinium Strike is a neat tower defense concept in that you mount weapons and manufacture drone fighters onboard a static capital starship, by quadrant. The main drawback to the game is the arbitray limitations of each weapon systems` firing ranges - there are four engagement ranges, and each weapon engages only at one specific range. No matter the nature of the projectile or beam, get too close or too far and your weapon will not shoot at the enemy. Maximum ranges in space games are reasonable, but such mechanics here seem regrettable. Wrapping one`s design head around more conventional treatments of engagement ranges would have made/would make Infinium Strike much better. Also, often you are without play recourse in the face of incoming attacks - that is, you feel removed from play against whatever is coming at you. You set up your turrets, upgrade them, launch fighters, and yet still feel as though you`re missing something as each enemy attack blasts your hull. Infinium Strike is still fun for what it is, and its a nice exploration of a customized (static!) capital ship action game. Full points to the developer for a playable demo.

Ahh... The Crew. I must say, this is probably the best racing game I have ever played. Yes, I do have experience with racing games, as I have played NFS:UG, NFS:HP, Forza 4, Forza Horizon 2, GT, and GT5. However, I have never had more fun on a racing game than I have had playing The Crew. The Crew features a HUGE open world MMO (and by huge, I mean that it's literally a condensed version of the United States). The map has 5 major regions: the Midwest, the East Coast, the South, the Mountain States, and the West Coast. Each region has it's own main city, except for the Midwest, which has two. The Midwest has Detroit and Chicago, the East Coast has NYC, the South has Miami, the Mountain States has Las Vegas, and the West Coast has Los Angelas. Each region  has it's own smaller states too, such as Salt Lake City from the Mountain States, and Sacremento from the West Coast. The map is so big I probably haven't even explored 75% of it yet.
There is a pretty large selection of cars to choose from, from a Ford GT to a Nissan Skyline R34, and each have at least one out of five specs (the starter cars have all specs, and so do some other cars). The specs are: Street, Dirt, Performance, Raid (which is basically almost monster level), and Circuit. Street is the middle child when it comes to speed, but it handles great and can take corners easily. The best car for Street is probably the Nissan Skyline R34. Dirt is for slight off-roading, as it is very fast on dirt and road, but can still go offroad faster than Street, but not much faster. The best car for Dirt is porbably the Ford Focus RS. Performance is the second fastest, and is the one you'll probably race with the most during the story. It take corners well, but not as well as Street, but it's speed makes up for it. The best Perf car is probably the Koenigsegg Agera R, Ferrari LaFerrari, or Lamborghini Aventador. Raid is for straight-up offroad and taking people out. It's the slowest, but it doesn't need a road to get to one's destination. It is the fastest offroad. The best Raid car is probably either the Chevrolet Silverado or the Ford Raptor. Now for Circuit. Circuit destroys on roads, hands down, but when it comes to offroad, you're better off just fast-traveling to the nearest street. The best Circuit is probably the Ford GT or Saleen S7.
The story is great. I had a lot of fun playing it. Play as Alex Taylor, who was put in prison for being framed for the murder of his own beloved brother, Dayton, by a V2 from the 5-10s named Shiv, and a corrupt police officer named Coburn. Travel across the U.S.A. to climb to the top of the 5-10s to get revenge on Shiv.
All in all, this is a great game. I don't think I can stress how much I loved it.

I've tried this game 3 or 4 times, each time coming to the same inescapable conclusion. DS2 is a game designed to be as un-fun as possible. I'm not even refering to the difficulty of the combat system, which is not a problem. I've played numerous monster hunter titles...the combat isn't too hard.
The problem is three-fold.
-1.) The save system, a core part of the game's structure, is archaic and needlessly punishing. now I don't need Skyrim levels of freedom, but fixed save points need to be plentiful and available whenever they're needed. The bonfires are neither.
-2.) The respawn system. Everything respawns. Every. Time. You. Do. Anything.
Die? Respawn.
Want to go to town? Respawn.
Want health back -while at a save point?!- RESPAWN.
This system reminds me of early mmo dungeons that took an hour to clear trash which had a hour long respawn timer. meaning you screw up a boss fight. you've got to kill everything all over again. Now, to be fair, this system has some merit as it alows you to "farm" souls in case you get stuck. But there are Waaaayyyy better ways to do that than forcing you to waste your time murdering the same Sh-t. It's not hard, the mobs weren't hard the first half dozen times I killed them.
Doesn't mean I should have to spend half an hour killing them all over again cause I miss-timed a damned jump.
-3.) The big one- Invasions. In a nutshell, are forced pvp encounters/pve boss fights. the only way to avoid them is to use an item that-like most items in the game- is extremely rare/expensive. In DS1 simply remaining hollowed effectively opted you out of this bull---- on top of this, the invasions them themselves are terrible. Out of the half dozen I've trudged through/worked my way around, maybe one was against a player/boss of my gear level. Other the others just 1-2 shot me. Maybe that's due to the age of the game? I don't know, and frankly, don't care. It's terrible and makes the previous two problems worse by effectivly killing you at random, forcing you to go back to whereever the hell the last bonfire was, and kill everything again.
If that sounds like fun to you, you'll love this game. As many people do, I keep coming back trying to figure out why, but no more. This game isn't for me. I like hard, but this is hard for all the wrong reasons.
TLDR; If you like hard games, by yourself something that'll play a monster hunter game. DS2 is just a chore/punishment masquerading as a game.

You ever wanted to Captain a Battlestar? This is basically it, and it feels good, though you are stationary.
Simple concept: Aliens want to kill you. Build towers and send out drones to stop them from doing that.
Advanced concepts: Four quadrants of attack, three ranges (close, medium, far) for each. Plenty of differences between the enemies that show up. Defense against projectiles thrown at you, vice just preventing enemies from getting to you. Basically, killing things before they get to their optimal zones to engage your ship.
There are some things that are rehashed from other types of the typical Tower Defense game: Fast but low damage turret, Slow but High Damage turret, and Deuce Medium turret. However, along with the speed and damage of each turret, you also need to worry about the ranges in which they can defend your ship. A lot of the rapid turrets do you no good if the enemy battleships are sniping you from afar.
Also, the ways in which the aliens engage can change in the middle of missions, which forces you to be quick about how you set up defenses. Combine that with the fact that you're defending four different quadrants of combat, and you have a concept that makes you multi-task well, keeping up with projectiles coming in, switching between different zones, upgrading turrets, sending out drones, and activating the special ship abilities in a timely manner.
It's pretty awesome, but there are a few nitpicks about it, such as the inability to skip the AI's briefing before each mission. You could skip the Captain's Logs, but they sound pretty decent, especially in later ones. The game has enough of a story to justify its setting and its mechanics, which is something I haven't really seen in the Tower Defense genre. It's like they actually cared about it, and put a bit of effort into it. Not too shabby.
There's at least one issue: sometimes when trying to exit the game, there's a weird UI overlap issue that makes me also click on a mission, when I'm clicking to, well, "Exit Game". Shouldn't do that, but, I'm willing to overlook it.
I'm not sure if I missed anything in the Tutorial, but I would appreciate a way to activate ship abilities and send out drones from the Strategic View (where you can see all four quadrants at once). It would make things a little simpler, and allow for the more accurate timing of those necessary Super Salvages and Shield Boosts. Having to click out of Strategic View, and then click on the Ship Abilities or the Drones individually is a little bit of a pain, but nothing that supremely affects gameplay. Again, not sure if I'm unobservant, or the ability isn't there on this one.
All in all, I like it. Space-themed, Well-Twisted Tower Defense with an active and passive management of waves, good resource management, and a bit more complexity than your standard of this genre.
TL;DR
Battlestar Freedom Strike. More complex than initial concept. Fun.

FNaF, the 'Best Horror Game of 2014' was given an early-released sequel, Five Nights at Freddy's 2. It is, indeed, the 2nd location, but set in 1987, meaning that FNaF 1 was the last Pizzeria Location in Fazbear Entertainment's Franchise (I know, not a real company).
The jumpscares in this game were a little improved on the first game's jumpscares, however still getting stale after a while of getting them. However, 11 Animatronic Characters in this game is absolutely fantastic! it really adds a massive challenge to the game, featuring everyone's favourites: Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, Foxy and Golden Freddy, but it also introduced new fan favourites, Toy Freddy, Toy Bonnie, Toy Chica, The Mangle, everyone's least favourite: Balloon Boy, and my favourite from this game: The Puppet (Or Marionette). It also gave us mind-breaking easter eggs that fit nowhere into the story for what is said to be a laugh: that is another 3 animatronics that are rarely seen. Theres Shadow Freddy, Endo Skeleton and (He has a confusing name) RWQFSFASXC. (Or more simply Shadow Bonnie).

I love the souls series, they are some of my favorite games of all time. But if you're wondering if you should get this game you should reconsider unless you have already played and beaten the other games in the series. This game is good but it is easily the worst in the series, from the bosses and the horribly designed areas (Black Gulch, Huntsman's Copse, etc.). There are so many bosses that are badly designed and were just downright lazy.
1. The Bosses:
For example, the Belfry Gargoyles, they are a reskin of one of the first bosses in dark souls 1. The boss itself has nothing new to offer except for there are about 5 of them rather than 2. They have no new attacks or mechanics, which says a lot about how lazy this game is. That's one of the problems in this game, it seems like the developers wanted to have quantity over quality in this game. And the Belfry Gargoyles are a prime example of that. And there aren't just only reskins from previous bosses in the series, there are reskin bosses from Dark Souls 2 itself! There are many examples of this, The Smelter Demon -> Blue Smelter Demon, The Last Giant -> The Giant Lord, Aava, The Kings Pet -> Lud and Zallen, The Kings Pets. In this game there are 41 bosses (including the DLC bosses), that might seem good at first, but I would consider most of the bosses to be less fun and feel more like an obstacle that isn't fun to fight at all. In the other games in the series there are about 17-21 bosses in the whole game, and some of them are the best bosses in all of gaming. One of the biggest draws of the Souls series is its grueling difficulty and the sense of accomplishment when overcoming those challenges, but the difficulty should be fair and come from the gameplay and not stupid mechanics.
2. The Areas:
I can confidently say that the worst areas in the series lie in Dark Souls 2. Many of the areas feel lazy in there design and make them ganky to simulate difficulty. A prime example of this is the Huntsman's Copse. If you want to go to fight the Executioners Chariot, you have to kill or run through what seems to be an entire army of enemies just to get to the boss and once you reach the fog wall there is an npc waiting there for you just as another annoying obstacle. And who could forget the Black Gulch, in this game poison does ridiculous amounts of damage and if you want to move in the Black Gulch you will most likely be poisoned in the process. it is also dark ganky and an annoyance to go through unless you use a Fragrant Branch of Yore to open the second bonfire in the area. And what waits at the end to reward you for going through this terribly annoying area? One of the worst bosses in the whole series, The Rotten. But don't worry the area that is before the Black Gulch is JUST AS BAD (The Gutter).
3. Design (summary):
Some things that I would consider design flaws in Dark Souls 2 is the statement I mentioned earlier, quantity over quality. It seems like the developers threw some things together, gave it a larger health bar and a name and called it a day (Prowling Magus and Congregation and the Covetous Demon are great examples). Another thing that bothers me in this game is the down-right horrible hitboxes. I just wonder if the developers even tested them. And last but not least the areas feel lazy and ganky to simulate difficulty. There are also some designs that bother me personally like the hollowing. I personally think it is actually stupid how if you die you lose a chunk of your max hp every time you die. And you don't get it back until you use one of your human effigies. Also I don't like how little piviting there is in this game it personally bothers me. And lastly I HATE how long it takes to use your estus flasks and how long it takes for them to actually heal you.
4. Things the game does right!:
The game itself is not bad, it just falls short of the other games (by a lot) in my opinion. The pvp in Dark Souls 2 is amazing, this is definitely the best pvp in a Souls game. And there are still some good bosses and rewarding things to do in Dark Souls 2 like the Sir Alonne fight as well as The Fume Knight.
All in all Dark Souls 2 isn't a bad game but I think there are some things that the developers could've and should've done differently. And I would still buy this game if you have already played and beaten the first and the third.

At some point during my experience with "Gone Home", I realized I was turning all the lights off and closing all the doors after I was done with a room.  It is not usually something I bother with in video games.  You open, you explore, you leave, but closing things when you are done never even crosses the mind normally.  I had decided that I was doing it because if it were my own house and I found a drawer left open, naturally, I would close it.
At some point, I stopped turning lights off, only because I had to backtrack a little bit, but, this was where I found myself in "Gone Home": completely immersed and far deep into a story that had me hooked to the very end.  I have never played a video game in all my life that had touched me like this.  It was funny when it was necessary, somber when the mood struck, and always consistent with its depth and emotion.  Explorers such as myself will love examining every floor, every room, every drawer, and every item, anything and everything to get more information about why Katie Greenbriar's family is not there to meet her and what had happened during her year away from home.
The attention to detail around the house was what struck me the most.  Labels on food nearly exact to how I see them in real life, cobwebs in the corners, the sound of the rain and thunder, and the creaking of the old mansion.  You feel slightly on edge, as though some monster will jump out, until you realize, you can turn on a light or turn them off as well, then it becomes almost tranquil.
As I went around the house, eventually, I began to feel like I was not just playing as Katie, but I was next to Katie, helping her figure things out.  How could so much change in a year?  I would have hugged her if I could, told her things would be okay.  I picked up a letter and started to read, but when it got too personal, she put it down and refused to read it, no matter how much I clicked it.  The name of her sister, Sam's stuffed dinosaur, Katie couldn't recall, until I picked it up and looked at it, which made her remember.  Listening to Sam's audio journals throughout the game made me miss her, even though I had never met her before.
The love story within had pulled on my heartstrings.  Two people falling in love, and feeling like the world is against them and the whole story being told through reading letters, scraps of paper, journals, hidden notes...  We go through the house and we piece everything together, like a jigsaw puzzle, from the past to the present.
I loved "Gone Home".  I loved how I connected with it so much.  I was looking for a beautiful experience and I found it.

I'm overjoyed to say that this felt NOTHING like one of those burn outs.
Now, admittedly, I am a pansy when it comes to horror games. So, usually it doesn't take all that much to scare me, but Outlast had me more terrified than I have ever been while playing a video game. It's like a mix of Snake and Pac-Man CEDX. Collect a chain of ducklings and deposit them on designated spots on the field, and then in a weird aesthetic twist, go to the next level by entering a portal in the walls that shrinks you down ever smaller. Collect all the ducks before depositing them for a bonus, but don't run into walls or the chain following you. Starts with just one field to play, and lets you unlock progressive fields once you've pretty much mastered the current one.
You can also unlock a couple extra modes: a puzzle mode where you try to get a perfect run on a single field while only moving in full rows or columns, and a "nostalgia" mode that's basically straight up classic Snake, with some twists in the level design.
It's not quite the insane, perfectly designed adrenaline rush that Pac-Man CEDX is but it's a very interesting take on Snake and well worth a few bucks, i.e. as part of the Weekly Humble Bundle.

I feel like this game is getting mixed reviews because 2 things. The first is the combat system, more specifically the horde system, and the second is the repetitiveness.
The horde system is essentially when a group of enemies spawn and try to kill you. Some people seem to think it's a cheap way to inflate difficulty because there are a ton of monsters and it can be hard to not get hit. I personally like it, although I didn't in the beginning. I would get hit from all angles, but once I started to use the environment, force enemies into certain positions and even run (you will have to run sometimes), the game became more fun. You also need to learn how each horde works since different types of enemies make up hordes in different areas. I think it could be tweaked a bit though, since it seems impossible to not take health damage sometimes. You also have a shield and managing it is super important. The game can be punishing, but whenever you die, you get to use the shards you've collected fom enemies. loot, etc and invest them into your skill tree.
The combat is perfectly executed for the amount of enemies you'll be facing. If I could compare it to anything, it's almost like a bullet hell game. You're almost always attacking, but you watch for certain attack ques and then dodge and make your way around the enemies. Hitting an enemy stuns them and while the enemy is stunned you can air juggle, which then resets your double jump and allows you to move through the horde while dodging attacks and focusing others. It's super fun and intuitive when you get it down.
Now, the repetitiveness is something that affects almost all metroidvania games. The procedurally generated levels in this game spawn different layouts whenever you die, however the main layout is still the same. This also ties into the lore about the world constantly shifting. The map itself is essentially a collection of boxes within a bigger box. The little boxes within the big box is what changes. Even though the world changes, I felt like backtracking in this game was actually easier than other metroidvanias since the map shows you exactly where to go.
If you enjoy this genre, you will most likely enjoy this game. The combat is the meat and bones, but there is still exploring, finding abilities, and a huge♥♥♥♥♥skill tree for you to dive into. Give it a shot!

One of the best titles I played this year. This is a slasher/rouge-lite/metroidvania style game with a bit increased difficulty. I find a lot of similarities to Dead Cells and  Rogue Legacy but it also feels somewhat different than those two. Sundered is much faster than Rouge Legacy and have slasher elements with the hordes of enemies attacking from all directions. In other ways it is very similar: you collect money, buy upgrades and die often. It also has a lot from metroidvania - you find new abilities that allow you to access levels previously inaccessible. You also need to be ready to do some grinding - but in this game it is really fun and pleasing to grind.
Sundered has quite interesting level structure when the level has predefined major structure, but the lesser structure is generated randomly. I was quite sceptical towards this, I usually don't like randomly generated levels, but after playing this game I think they managed to make it very good. In fact, it is the first time I like randomly generated levels since probably Diablo 1.
