I love the souls series, they are some of my favorite games of all time. But if you're wondering if you should get this game you should reconsider unless you have already played and beaten the other games in the series. This game is good but it is easily the worst in the series, from the bosses and the horribly designed areas (Black Gulch, Huntsman's Copse, etc.). There are so many bosses that are badly designed and were just downright lazy.
1. The Bosses:
For example, the Belfry Gargoyles, they are a reskin of one of the first bosses in dark souls 1. The boss itself has nothing new to offer except for there are about 5 of them rather than 2. They have no new attacks or mechanics, which says a lot about how lazy this game is. That's one of the problems in this game, it seems like the developers wanted to have quantity over quality in this game. And the Belfry Gargoyles are a prime example of that. And there aren't just only reskins from previous bosses in the series, there are reskin bosses from Dark Souls 2 itself! There are many examples of this, The Smelter Demon -> Blue Smelter Demon, The Last Giant -> The Giant Lord, Aava, The Kings Pet -> Lud and Zallen, The Kings Pets. In this game there are 41 bosses (including the DLC bosses), that might seem good at first, but I would consider most of the bosses to be less fun and feel more like an obstacle that isn't fun to fight at all. In the other games in the series there are about 17-21 bosses in the whole game, and some of them are the best bosses in all of gaming. One of the biggest draws of the Souls series is its grueling difficulty and the sense of accomplishment when overcoming those challenges, but the difficulty should be fair and come from the gameplay and not stupid mechanics.
2. The Areas:
I can confidently say that the worst areas in the series lie in Dark Souls 2. Many of the areas feel lazy in there design and make them ganky to simulate difficulty. A prime example of this is the Huntsman's Copse. If you want to go to fight the Executioners Chariot, you have to kill or run through what seems to be an entire army of enemies just to get to the boss and once you reach the fog wall there is an npc waiting there for you just as another annoying obstacle. And who could forget the Black Gulch, in this game poison does ridiculous amounts of damage and if you want to move in the Black Gulch you will most likely be poisoned in the process. it is also dark ganky and an annoyance to go through unless you use a Fragrant Branch of Yore to open the second bonfire in the area. And what waits at the end to reward you for going through this terribly annoying area? One of the worst bosses in the whole series, The Rotten. But don't worry the area that is before the Black Gulch is JUST AS BAD (The Gutter).
3. Design (summary):
Some things that I would consider design flaws in Dark Souls 2 is the statement I mentioned earlier, quantity over quality. It seems like the developers threw some things together, gave it a larger health bar and a name and called it a day (Prowling Magus and Congregation and the Covetous Demon are great examples). Another thing that bothers me in this game is the down-right horrible hitboxes. I just wonder if the developers even tested them. And last but not least the areas feel lazy and ganky to simulate difficulty. There are also some designs that bother me personally like the hollowing. I personally think it is actually stupid how if you die you lose a chunk of your max hp every time you die. And you don't get it back until you use one of your human effigies. Also I don't like how little piviting there is in this game it personally bothers me. And lastly I HATE how long it takes to use your estus flasks and how long it takes for them to actually heal you.
4. Things the game does right!:
The game itself is not bad, it just falls short of the other games (by a lot) in my opinion. The pvp in Dark Souls 2 is amazing, this is definitely the best pvp in a Souls game. And there are still some good bosses and rewarding things to do in Dark Souls 2 like the Sir Alonne fight as well as The Fume Knight.
All in all Dark Souls 2 isn't a bad game but I think there are some things that the developers could've and should've done differently. And I would still buy this game if you have already played and beaten the first and the third.

This is how flight simulators should be made! With actual goals. I hate pointless flying with no goals, and always wanted a flight sim with a point to it besides just flying for the sake of flying. In this one you have to work towards getting your licenses, and do lessons and stuff, plus you need a certain amount of flight hours in free flight to unlock certain lessons, which I love. The only downside to this sim so far is that it uses basically the exact same scenery and terrain elevations as flight simulator x, and the performance is awful. I'm getting about 20 fps in some places with a GTX 1070. It is playable, and 20 fps is the worst it gets, so not too bad, but I expect much better performance from a graphics card like this. I'm sure it will get fixed though, because it's still in early access. Another strange bug I noticed was when I did the take-off lesson, there was a random red plane spazzing out and glitching all over the place on the runway. It did not affect the lesson in any way, it was simply entertaining, although immersion breaking to see that happen. There is an issue with keyboard controls when using the rudder and the throttle. The buttons don't always respond, and controlling the plane on the runway using the keyboard to rudder is nearly impossible. The flying with the mouse is the same as in FSX, which is good, but since you can't rudder and throttle with the mouse, you have to use the keyboard for that if you have no joystick. The graphics of the planes themselves and the shadows and lighting looks good, but the terrain is basic 2006 FSX copy and paste as of right now. I would like to see them use real world height maps to make the mountains look like they should, and also update some cities to make them like they are today. Airports also have outdated names. I get this is early access and this game was made by using FSX as a foundation, but just some suggestions for improving it in the future. Oh yeah, one more thing, community made add-ons and scenery should be uploaded to steam workshop, because at the moment you can only download missions from there. Would be nice if I could download stuff there that would make my home town look like it does in real life. One more suggestion I have is to add a career mode, and make it function similar to Euro Truck Simulator 2, but instead of trucks, it's planes. Also, planes can do more types of missions than just delivering cargo, so there is potential to be even better than euro truck sim in that regard.
TL:DR: This is a great sim with real potential. Loving that there are actual goals to work towards in this instead of pointless flying, and I can see a great future for this sim!

I have used Flight Simulator since version 5.0 in year 1993. At that time we had to use a lot of imagination to think that we were flying, and even then, "fly".
Today with the launch of the Flight Sim World some leave to fight developers criticizing that lack this or that, that's not good, etc. ..
To me, that still use the FSX, with a lot of add ons, I see the beginning of this platform is already very good. Of course it's not perfect, far from it, but if the DTG staff continue to develop the product, your future can be great. I can point out how good start: the landcape architecture is very beautiful. The color of the sea is well closer to real than in FSX, the coast of Brazil, where I live. The textures of cities and generally are more defined, as well as the autogen. As I fly in real life, I see the visual of the mountains on the horizon, look closer to what I see in my actual flights. The outer glow of aircraft and the internal shadows are also pretty cool. IE: the flight environment is much more realistic.
Now the criticism: we need aircraft with instruments that work. Aircraft interiors far more developed, including panels. General lighting, especially airports, need to improve a lot. Are large and diffuse lights, quite different from the real one.
Suggestions: elect people from various parts of the world that can edit minor problems, such as a radar and a building at the airstrip of Recife (SBRF), city close to where I live. A problem coming from the FSX and that persists in FSW is the landscape in the Northeast region of Brazil. In the dry season (summer/autumn) the soil textures are acceptable, but in rainy station (winter/spring) here everything is green and not as it appears in the Simulator. Long before I got the guts to migrate entirely to the FSW, but I think it's a good start, and how do I know that the development of a new platform is quite slow, I believe we may have in the future, a good platform to enjoy our flights.

Being a long-term X-Plane user I was sceptical about this, and first impressions didn't do too much to dissuade me.
However after the latest lighting update, and having spent more time with each plane exploring more of the different regions, I'm really starting to like this sim.
The flight model seems more alive than X-Plane; the planes react to the weather more naturally and the sounds they make as they're buffeted by the wind are great.
Regional / seasonal textures and autogen make the environment an engaging place to explore, much more than the generic, two regions and one season approach of X-Plane.
There's a lot that still needs to be done, and judging the product before 3rd party involvement has been realised is a bit send-defeating, but this is turning into a pretty good flight-sim and shows potential to be the rightful heir to the MSFS franchise.

The game mechanics may look simplistic but under the hood there is details galore to be had revealing itself as the player journeys onward for treasure and fame leveling their characters to powerful epic proportions. Graphics have a lively old school feel to them with plenty of color and enjoyable detail in the world and the player characters. Music is a mix of bombastic and 1980s-70s b-movie action ala Conan and a Ralph Bakshi Lord Of The Rings soundtrack with a rich undertone flavor of 1990s pc rpgs such as Dragon Wars and Drakkhen. Sound effects get the point across and feel very satisfying during battle as combatants lay down the medieval smack down of swords and arrows singing upon the winds of fatal destinations. This game is as simple as the title suggests. Cook the food, serve it to the customer, and rake in that delicious cash!  However, something so simple very quickly gets complex. Each food has buffs and defuffs to your "Buzz". the higher the buzz the more people show up, but too much buzz may be a bit hard for you to handle. Menu rot occurs if you serve the same dishes 3 days in a row. This does not apply to foods listed as staples. which you can serve whenever. Simpler food to make does not give a good pay, and some can't even be tipped on (if it wasn't so broken with it's payout lasagna could go die in a hole) . Rush hours show up during lunch and dinner time, in which no snacks will be ordered (ice cream, pretzels, etc.) and the game almost doubles in speed. You can upgrade food to make it more appealing to the customer, at the cost of adding new recipies. Oh, that's right, food isn't always made the same way. you have to learn different recipies for every item, which speedy players will learn the names of (Kids delight is ranch and cheese salad, Dry twister is pretzel with nothing on it, etc.), but this is not neccecary as a tooltip tells you the recipie.
Those are just the basics about the FOOD. there are a whole lot more mechanics that i'll let you discover for yourself. This game comes bundled with a silly multiplayer mode, weekly challenges, ingame challenges, emails, and a whole lot more to make one of the best indie games i've played in a while.
PROS:
Fun, chaotic action
Lots of depth
Many gamemodes
Quite a bit of strategy required

Wacky artstyle
Weekly challenges (that i suck at)
CONS:
Kevin McLeod music, but they are obscure tracks. Not sure all of it is Kevin either. (not a big deal, just saying)
Can get repetitive
Quite a bit of luck involved, game is random event heavy.
Very random side note but why the heck do i start in an office building? just a bizare start, not really a con.
Overall, this game gets an 8.6/10 from me. Great, but not perfect.

Whilst I've only played a relatively short way into this one, I think I can safely say that it's by far one of the best "turn-based fantasy roleplay quest" games you could hope to buy.  It's incredibly newbie-friendly - the minimalism of the tutorials not really mattering, provided you've played one or two similar games before, be they in the digital and/or paper and/or board-game realms - and while I can't comment on the controversy regarding the pay-for-gold scheme and its alleged "necessity", thus far I can't really see that I'm going to NEED to expend such extra funds, as long as I resist the urge to jump straight to the more challenging dungeons and just stick to the easy-peasy ones for now.

In all honestly, I mostly lost interest in this kind of "high fantasy" stuff a long, long time ago (I'm in my early forties, and played the original Warhammer ROLEPLAYING game  - the one with dice 'n' paper - back in my late teens/early twenties!), but this brings back fond memories of murdering snotlings and orcs and what-not like it was only yesterday.  Ah, to be young and nerdy again...and sure, it might lack the STRATEGY of the otherwise quite similar Space Hulk (the first video game adaptation, not the unnecessarily convoluted Ascension, which I'm yet to make my peace with), but if it's a more casual, jump-in/jump-out turn-based game you're looking for, you can't go far wrong here.  Hell, I played for six hours straight the first night, and I don't do that with ANY games, ever.  Simple, fast-paced, addictive, and sure to give you a severe case of "just-one-more-dungeon-before-bedtime", even when it's already past five o'clock in the morning.

Verdict: 9/10.
(Oh, and PS...make sure you get the Deluxe edition, unless you really can't afford it...'cause I can only imagine that the variety inherent within the gameplay - hardly the game's strong point as it is - would be even more limited without it.)

I liked the story but the gameplay leaves something to be desired.
Youll get a mission or two in a zone and then told to win over the hearts and mind of the people by destroying outposts, helping to free prisoners, turning on radios, or sabatoging generators. After you win over the people its another two missions then your off to the next zone. Rinse and repeat. Thats not to bad until you consider that most of the missions are done in a few minutes, hardly worth the time. The ones that are not over in a few minutes usally have some sort of on the rails type "action" like walking at a reduced speed or waiting for enemies to spawn.
You can do jobs to earn extra cash to unlock gear faster. I did most of the jobs up until the 3rd zone. It seems like most jobs are unlocked after their objective becomes rare or impossible to spot. Several of them requir you to wait for strike points to randomly spawn to complete. While the money is decent, you can only carry 3 side missions at max. Occasionally some missions cant be picked up when you already have two other activate missions. It seems like a bug that should have been fixed.
Enemies have popup targeting in that once they swivel around they will shoot you without a second thought. I noticed this a few times when doing takedowns. The takedown skill to auto loot also did not go off several times.
My play time shows about 21 hours but its more like 12 or 15. I left the game running for several hours while doing something else.

Since the time of launch to now, December 31st, 2017, the game has received many patches and you can tell that the developers are really trying hard to make the game playable. Their efforts, at the time of writing, seem to be for nought though as many players, including myself, are experiencing a huge number of bugs, freezes, crashes and lockups. It's a real shame too.
The gameplay is very similar to that of the Far Cry series and it isn't necessarily a bad thing. I enjoyed those games, especially 4 since it had co-op play. From what I was able to experience in my short time with the game, it seems very apparent that if any good comes from this game, it's that hopefully a sequel will use the same ideas but execute them better, and that a future Far Cry game NEEDS to take place in a dense city.
Pros:
The game is GORGEOUS! The lighting is top notch while not being a giant resource hog thanks to Cryengine, which to this day continues to look absolutely brilliant.
The weapon modding system from the first 2 Crysis games (Never played 3) is here. It's one of the few things that this game has taken from other games and 100% done better. Each gun has multiple attachment slots that you can place various types of attachments to. However the biggest feature is that each weapon has 3 variants of the same frame. You can purchase these variants from weapon vendors and then be treated to a very well done animation of stripping the weapon from the frame and then attaching a new frame. The only example I was able to experience in my time with the game was changing a normal pistol into an SMG by ripping the receiver off the frame and attaching a new one. It was very well done and honestly fun to watch.
The city. I left this one for last because it's my favorite part of the game and 100% of the reason I spent so much time trying to get it to work. Oh my god is the city nice to look at. The world designers did an amazing job of placing objects to make the world feel lived in and cluttered. The city is dirty, covered with trash and has KPA soldiers beating citizens on every street corner. After starting the game I wandered into the city for the first time to see the KPA raid a house just next door. The animations for the citizens are usually very well done and there's so many of them to watch. The city really feels alive because of all these events you can come across. Absolutely one of my favorite worlds in any game ever, and that's saying a lot since I only played 2 hours.
I won't make a cons list because I really didn't experience enough of the game to accurately have opinions of it.
If you can get this game to run, I highly recommend picking it up while it's on sale. Under all of the performance issues and bugs, there is a halfway decent game buried deep down somewhere, and it really shows when you just walk around the city and take in the sights.

It just feels like Surgeon Simulator's rejected brother, it fails just miserably at trying to be one of these simulation games. Where should I start? These are some of the worst controls I've ever experienced in a game. I'm not even kidding when I say I've spent about 15 minutes trying to grab a cup to even start the tea making process. Yeah, I know for sure that this is the humorous nature of the game, but it shouldn't be this difficult, and hell, it just becomes annoying and not even slightly challenging. I couldn't feel anything else but disappointment while playing this, it's just not what I was expecting. Graphically, it does look bad too, even on the highest settings. Also, all the meme references shoved in your face feel downright unfunny. Thank god I bought this on sales, and as much as I hate to compare things, you should go for Surgeon Sim if you're looking for a better game overall. Ampu-Tea is a 2/10 for me.

I really wish there was a mixed option - personally I'm content with my purchase, the atmosphere and style of the game is right up my alley, but it needs work in its current state as it sometimes comes off as blindingly frustrating rather than hard.
I'll start with the positives.  It looks and sounds ♥♥♥♥ing astounding.  The controls are tight and responsive.  The combat, while barebones, is complex enough to require skill, and mastering the various aerial attacks in order to position yourself to target a weak spot or perform a drop attack to obliterate a mass of weak enemies is incredibly satisfying.  Dodging feels safe - I see a threat, I push the button, I don't get hit; when it comes down to attacks I saw coming, I have very, very rarely felt as if I have been hit when I should not have.  I like the way the map is laid out - it's not completely randomized so you always know where you're going, and it's usually pretty clear where you need to go, as things like upgrades, bosses, locked doors, shortcuts, and lore rooms are marked, and the map will often give you a 'hint' as to how to get to the next thing by causing the door you need to go through to blink.  I'm really, really happy with a lot of how this game works.
My problem lies with the fact that it wants to be hardcore, but it doesn't quite seem to know how to do that properly.  There are two aspects to that.
The first: crisp controls and a useful dodge are all well and good, but during hordes, there is so much happening, so many enemies cluttering the screen, that there is literally no way to avoid taking damage - even if you do your best to remain airborne, avoiding the fog of weak terrestrial enemies swarming over every surface, there are a number of enemies that make that particularly difficult, /especially/ when you factor in the way that there is no method of dodging while airborne.  The normal dodge only works on the ground, and while there is a 'pound' attack that rapidly drops you to the floor, you float in place for a split second before deploying it, and that's enough to get you hit.  I legitimately do not understand how the game wants me to tackle hordes.  Stay on ground and dodge?  Too many enemies, can't dodge 'em all, take damage or die.  Get airborne, pound terrestrial groups, use air attacks against airbornes?  Can't dodge, get hit by hunter cannons, panzers, meteors, or something else, take damage or die.  Use the valkyrie cannon when it's unlocked to try to wipe groups of enemies?  Takes a long time to charge, too many enemies, cannon gets interrupted by an attack, take damage or die.  The only times I have escaped a horde unscathed have been the product of luck, or by being overlevelled for the starting area, and the presence of a shield does not mitigate nearly enough damage, given the punishment I'm recieving on normal difficulty.
The second: the main boss I've faced so far (Dominion) is overkill unless you have tremendous patience and superhuman reaction time.  He absorbs a frankly insane amount of damage, and starts hard, gets rapidly more difficult, throwing in a quickly-growing horde of minions that you need to keep culled to survive, while dodging his two-hit KO main attacks, and also chipping away at his vast health bar.
This game wants to be dark souls 'tough but fair' but rather than giving you all the tools to succeed against steep but realistic odds, it gives you a basic toolkit then throws threats at you faster than you can destroy them until you get completely overwhelmed and die.  The horde problem could be mitigated by the implementation of some sort of aerial dodge, but the fact remains that enemy tells become next to useless during hordes, which is a deeper problem in and of itself.  As for Dominion, his health bar is definitely too big, and he would be hard enough without the constantly-expanding mob of minions chasing me around the map, new spawning portals opening up as fast as I can destroy them.  This game needs to take a deep breath, calm down, and decide if it wants to be a game where you chew through hordes of enemies that come at you by the thousands, or a game where tells mean the difference between life and death.

Nothing beats the bond between a video game cat and their army of rescued ducklings in this trippy descent into the never ending layers of a television screens circuits - the pixelated blue mascot running, sliding, and kicking its way through each exceedingly flashy and bright stage of navigational chaos.
The game starts you out being greeted by our adorably rotund cat hero and his or her admirable bedroom of awesomely geeky references to the likes of
,
,
, and
. This nostalgia inducing bedroom acts your base of operations and where you'll be choosing from the four very different modes, starting with the very important main Arcade mode where you'll ease into your new digital life of aviary rescue.
The rules seem simple enough; navigate a seemingly never ending series of Pacman-like mazes while collecting the carefully placed eggs within its labyrinthine halls of neon twists and turns. For each egg collected an awestruck duckling trails behind in a line, eventually adding up into one long chaotic conga-line. Hitting the tail of trailing ducks ends your combo and loses you the line you've collected which severely reduces your score (this is about where I ragequit every time), so planning your route quickly and on the fly is especially important as you gain momentum with each success.
Once ducks are collected they need to be returned to their rightful targets on the current floor, which with the time limit taken into consideration becomes a mad dash against against the clock forcing you to pinpoint the quickest route to collect each one while avoiding running into your trail or walls. There are plenty of small tricks to toss into your routine once you've got movement down including wall slides and quick dashes around corners when your turns are timed to perfection. In the end what you have is one of the most hyperactive combinations of classic
maneuvering combined with the flashy, fast and addictive pathfinding of
with even more split-second precision required.
Aside from the immense feeling of satisfaction, reaching different landmark scores in each of the three wildly different Arcade levels (from Beginner to the appropriately named Dessert stage) will net you some pretty sweet rewards in the form of new music jams to jam, new announcer voices ranging from rad to hilarious, tons of adorable concept art, and of course the different obtainable modes.  Though score is your main driving force in perfecting your zig-zag routes throughout each stage, this vast amount of awesome and usable unlockable content is sure to keep you going even deeper.
Pix as a character is just way too damn cute and suave in a creatively simple way, a way that the most iconic and memorable of gaming characters are portrayed. He's one of those video game personalities you don't easily forget, and stands out as a classic and memorable character just as much as the gameplay itself. Even cuter, possibly, than our retro mascot are the lines of saved ducklings and their attitudes matched only by the badass-ness of their savior cat, and in a game with such an overwhelmingly sharp and cool style they're just the icing on the cake.
The varied visual themes of each stage provide some serious eye candy for something of such a simple nature. Subtle changes from complex motherboard patterns to cold steel monochrome textures breathe life into the twisting mazes around you, as the eggs and ducklings you collect change with it. Crazy multicolored squares light up in rhythmic sequence like some kind of insane Disco Dancefloor set to hyperspeed, all the while the heavy and bass-y beats of Xavier Thiry's soundtrack pulsate in your eardrums. Despite its retro nature,
is a real assault on the senses.
Every dumb little mistake you make is for the better in
, because this is all about practice, endurance, and getting better all the time. With each new invigorated and admittedly rage-inducing restart of a level you come back with a clear vision in your head of what caused your downfall the last time and your new found perseverance will carry you to even higher scores, and in turn even crazier and harder modes. With the addition of a Ghost mode to play against your own past runs or runs of the developer, there's a whole plethora of ways to practice and continue bettering your score for what is the most endlessly replayable game around.
tldr;
If
were an actual arcade cabinet at a pizza parlor I'd be flat broke by now and already exchanging my life savings for fistfuls of quarters. When it comes to modern arcade score-chasing obsessions, Pix is as good as it gets

TL;DR version:
Music 8/10
Art 10/10
Gameplay 2/10
Overall 5.5/10
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Pros:
+ this game's main strong asset is its beautiful art: the bosses, ability animations, locations, enemies, etc - the art is what kept me playing when I was about to give up on the game
+ once you have invested quite a bit of time into the game and have unlocked better platforming capabilities and decide to corrupt them - moving around the map becomes easier and decently satisfying. The animations for the corrupted abilities are really neat and a pleasure to watch but this once again ties in with my first point about the game's art
The Cons:
- early platforming and traversing around the map is a chore and is quite frustrating even for a platformer veteran like myself
- this game forces you to grind in order to progress. If you aren't strong enough and haven't invested enough points into the skill tree then you have a low chance to endure the next boss fight or sometimes even the next area with regular enemies. The game's skill tree IS basically the game. Each time you upgrade an ability the next one will cost more shards so in the late game scenario you will have to grind a while to get rewarded with only a few skill points in the said tree.
- the hordes that chase you around the map discourage exploration and eventually you will simply start ignoring them
because fighting them gets boring and consumes time even if the enemies don't present any danger to you at that moment. This forces you to adopt a playstyle going strictly from objective to objective and fighting only when you actually can't leave the room until the enemies die, as a result you can't really leisurely explore the map and enjoy the surroundings much.
If you are stronger than enemies in the area - you will ignore them because why waste time one-shotting them for the little shards that they drop. If you are weaker than the enemies in the area (but you've cleared other areas entirely already)  - then you will definitely ignore them and run away to your next objective (unlocking a new ability or a shortcut so when you die you don't have to backtrack THAT much).
- To expand on the previous point, the game ends up being difficult in the wrong way. You are overwhelmed with enemy hordes while attempting to make your way through the environment that also has traps and ways to hurt you. In games that are generally considered to be challenging (let's say Dark Souls) you eventually truly get better at the game and adapt to the level. You become better at predicting enemy movements, avoiding damage etc. And then because of that you progress. In this game though, you can be good at platforming and combat - but still die just because of how many enemies the game throws at you on top of environmental hazards. Can you keep up with 10+ enemies trying to attack you at the same time in a confined space on top of avoiding traps? You may very well can. Or at least you think you can and then you end up in an area with endless hordes (they spawn without breaks) and then you die even while trying to traverse it avoiding all fights and focusing solely on platforming (even if you have absolutely all abilities already unlocked).
- enemy design feels lazy (and I am not even talking about having 10 laser Hunters that can attack you multiple screens away). What I mean is in each area you will have a certain few types of enemies that are mostly unique to that location, I'd say about 5 different enemy types per area. The way they are made stronger is by simply changing their colors from their default color to a different one and making them more tanky (maybe throw in a minor ability upgrade as well). So now instead of fighting grey Hunters you will fight red Hunters that have quite a bit more health than their weaker counterparts. I feel like I would be more satisfied if there were simply more enemy types in the game instead of repainting the existing ones and making them more beefy.
- there is practically no story in the game, the lore is given to you in such tiny bits - the amount I've received in my 11 hours into the game so far could probably be told in less  than a minute.
- the load times sometimes are insane, in fact I am adding this point into my review as my game is still in the load screen. Your first load of the game after you launch it every new time will take about 2-3 minutes even if you have an SSD.
- I am getting pretty close to the end of the game and only had 2 major boss fights, which are actually quite fun and epic, but I feel like the game will only have 2 more at most. The minibosses differ little from minions sometimes - just a beefier version of them.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion:
If you can tolerate the early game platforming until you unlock better abilities and if you can tolerate adopting a playstyle that forces you to ignore fights most of the time OR grinding and grinding and grinding until you are strong enough to deal with enemies in a reasonable time frame - then you might like this game if you are a fan of platformers like Hollow Knight. You will eventually get annoyed of the hordes though and then it will just be a pain forcing yourself to progress.
What will keep you going (if anything) is the game's art, which is well made and satisfying to look at. So buy the game when its on a decent sale just to appreciate the very well made designs.

My progress: defeated 3 bosses, unlocked three main abilities and explored a second area that is locked at the beginning of the game. Here's my take on it:
For every paragraph, I post a CRITIQUE, marked as "CR"
> The lore is slowly revealed by visiting certain rooms and activating. So it's there, just not presented right at the beginning for you.
CR: No one likes to do stuff without reasoning, much less when it comes as a demand. They could at least tell you a bit of the place, or give you just a bit more to work with. You're not given any motivation to continue, as the first thing you hear in the game is your weapon's spirit talking to you and giving you orders.
> It's not for everyone. It has Dark Souls levels of difficulty mixed with precise platforming, and fast-paced combat, all requiring quick reflexes.
CR: There needs to be a difficulty slider for 'Easy' mode. The way progression is made in the first hours feels like a chore and I feel many people will refund it or drop the game right away out of frustration.

> The three abilities I've unlocked are not game changing and you keep using the same combo over and over.
CR: The gameplay feels stale as there is no variation on your main combat style. The game constantly relies on you positioning yourself and dishing out as much damage as you can before having to dodge or suck up the damage.

> Whenever you idle on a room, expect a horde of enemies to come and assault you. This just makes you adopt a playstyle where you try to go as fast as possible to marked places on your map. Their numbers get extremely overwhelming, as everything around you seems to run faster than you, fly towards you as fast as a bullet, or lasers that will traverse many screens. All of this is happening as you try to navigate the scenario with moving platforms, laserbeams and jumps that require good timing.
CR: The amount of enemies could be reduced by 50% and it would feel much better already. Then you could compensate by having them have more attacks or do different things instead of trying to constantly headbutt you.

> After playing for this long, I could already tell some of the room patterns. The fact that they keep changing doesn't add to the gameplay.
CR: I think the game would be way better if they gave up the random factor and just built a beautiful and crafted world like they did in Jotun.
> The general idea and overall feel I got from the gameplay is that you're supposed to go as fast as possible to the areas marked on your map, using a trial and error approach - if that doesn't work, go to another area OR rinse and repeat until you got enough shards to get to a big upgrade.
CR: Slowing the pace of the game would make it more enjoyable and interesting. Having more meaningful rooms, or different things you could do besides 'running and gunning'.
> My biggest complaint is that you're forced into a defensive playstyle right away. The skill tree makes you go health, shield, and armor, as damage upgrades are minimal along the path.
CR: The game would be more interesting if it gave you more options when building your character. I would raise attack early on to be able to get rid of the small enemies with 1 hit instead of having to use 2-3 attacks on the smaller ones.

DSII supposedly wasn't that great on release. So after playing the original, I picked this up a while ago on sale and was not disappointed by the purchase.
Super positives:
++Near god level character customisation. Things such as power-stancing and a variety of different weapon styles, not to mention a non-linear method of imbuing/deimbuing elemental weapons and the ability to reassign your stat points gives the game massive longevity.
++Fantastic PVP (when the community isn't undergoing a lull). Plenty of locations and arenas to conduct said PVP. There are drawbacks (See 'super negatives' )
Positives:
+Just as hard as any other 'Souls' entry, so there's plenty of time to digest the game
+The 'Illium Loyce' DLC is one of the coolest DLCs I've ever had the pleasure of playing in any game.
+ Bonfire aesthetics are an awesome way of tooling players to fight bosses or areas again without progressing to New Game +.
Neutral point:
The bosses are a bit on the 'dudes in armour' side of things. Some rehashes at times from earlier bosses. You'll either like this as a player or you'll hate it; it's a very subjective thing
Negatives:
- World is VERY mishmash in its overall visual design and there are some jarring transitions. There's also no consistent theme like DS1, nor the interconnectedness of the first one or the ability to shortcut through certain areas. The world IS non-linear at the very least but there's not a lot of technical non-linerarity that the first game was praised for by the community.
- Quality of story immersion is pretty poor, partially due to the above and due to some very obviously chopped and changed plot details mid to late in the game.
Super negatives:
-- SOUL MEMORY!
An awful mechanic which I will rip to shreds.
The Souls series is bolstered by its semi-online functionality. The idea that you can call for help by summoning people or have people invade you to kill you for experience is pretty much a given. There's also conditional multiplayer areas as well.
In DS1, match-making with players was based on Soul Level (for newbies to the series, it's basically your RPG level). If you're within a range of levels (say 1 - 10 as an inaccurate example), you can play with players in the same bracket (whether it's co-op or versus)
This meant that experienced players could delibrately circumnavigate the problem of over-levelling, or getting to a level bracket that was bereft of players. Buying items and upgrading equipment also did not count towards your 'soul level'; items were often used in a lot of PVP strategies and were key to the game's meta. You could always guess what range you were roughly at and which ranges in which areas yielded higher player populations for play.
You could also, using the original's interconnectedness, skip or run through areas that were tougher in exchange for items or equipment that might provide an unexpected fight to your opponents at lower levels. It rewarded players for taking risks and exploring the game and figuring out optimal strategies.
DS2 has soul memory.
Every enemy you kill gives you souls. Which counts towards your soul memory bracket. Meaning you can't kill enemies for fear of getting pushed out of a level bracket if you want to build PVP characters. Even if you wanted to play the dedicated co-operation player and help people at tough bosses, eventually you lose the ability to because you're auto-levelling.
The only way of circumnavigating this is equipping a ring, bought from a merchant in an obscure location in the game. The quickest route gurantees that you will kill at least three bosses before getting to said merchant. This absorbs any souls you pick up and your soul memory will stay the same so long as you have the ring on as you kill enemies.
Soul memory is unhealthy to the game's meta for many reasons that I can claim:
- It punishes players who lose souls WITHOUT spending them by inflating their Soul Memory and putting them at risk of being invaded by players who statistically are better
- It discourages PVP and Co-op PVE by elevating a player's soul memory beyond a bracket they might want to stay at (a bracket, for example, that might have more players therefore more opportunities to match with people)
- It doesn't even allow you to circumnavigate soul memory by buying items or consumables for use in fights or upgrading equipment. Because soul memory IS affected by gaining souls no matter what method you use.
It's a huge blow to the game's otherwise decent offerings.
Despite this, it's very recommended to play.

Outlast ist ein First Person Survival Horrorgame, das mir persönlich sehr viel Spaß gemacht hat.
Das Design der Welt und der NPCs ist ziemlich morbide und die ein- oder andere Szene sowie einige Areale sind definitiv nichts für schwache Nerven oder einen schwachen Magen.
Das Gameplay in diesem Spiel ist exzellent. Von dem Fakt, dass der Protagonist einen Körper besitzt (man sieht beim Runtergucken den Körper, die Beine, die Füße...), einmal abgesehen, ist es möglich, anch Waten durch Blutlachen Fußspuren zu hinterlassen, während des Rennens nach hinten zu schauen und mit seinem Camcorder alles aufzunehmen, um Notizen des Protagnoisten zu erlangen. Die Kletteraufgaben, vor die einen das Spiel stellt, werden durch den Körper und die Kameraführung umso besser und neben einigen Jumpscares herrscht generell sehr viel Spannung in der Luft, da man nie weiß, was als nächstes passiert, oder ob einen der Suchtrupp versehentlich doch noch findet und in Stücke reißt.
Die Story, um die es sich dreht ist interessant und wirft einen Blick in die Abgründe menschlichen Daseins, wobei die "Testsubjekte" einem doch irgendwie Leid tun. Auch, wenn sie einem Leid antun wollen.
Spieler, die sich bereits bei Amnesia in die Hose gepisst haben, kommen bei Outlast voll auf ihre Kosten. Das liegt am Gampeplay, an der Spannung und am Gorefaktor. Wehren kann sich der Protagonist auch nicht, rennen und verstecken sind das Ziel zu einem verlängerten Leben.
Als Horrorspiel definititv zu empfehlen.
Ich selbst allerdings habe mich nicht wirklich gegruselt, aber ich kenne genügend, die alle halbe Stunde ihre Hose wechseln müssten. Vertraut mir.

As usual, I’m late to the party. But I have to say that in spite of all the negative stuff I’ve heard about this game, I came away rather liking it. Gameplay-wise it’s your typical walking simulator with no real gameplay going on. It tries to be clever at first by making the player assume that the creepy atmosphere hides a horror game somewhere in there, but before long, you’ll figure out that there’s nothing there. Literally, it’s another case of a game where the devs got away with not modeling, rigging and animating living things.
The interactivity here is certainly higher than in something like Dear Esther, but that’s not saying much, because most of the things you can interact with are just not worth it. You can pick up tons of objects in the house but it won’t matter. Only a handful of items actually reveal audio logs or other items hidden beneath them and there’s only a marginal puzzle aspect in the sense that you need to find lock combinations and keys for certain parts of the house. But technically, you can also sequence break the entire house (which I almost did, because I’m used to clicking on absolutely everything) by heading straight towards the place that nets you the attic key and you could “beat” the game in less than a minute.
What I really like about the game however is the narrative. It’s really sweet and endearing in a way that made me care more than usual about stuff like this, which at the very least means that the writing of both the audio logs as well as the letters you find in the house is pretty good, as well as the voice acting of the audio logs. If you look at more than just the central narrative, the inner workings of the mother and father of the protagonist are also fairly detailed and tell another interesting story.
It’s not monumentally deep stuff or even a story that hasn’t been told before in some capacity, but I still left the game with a smile on my face. At 2 hours, it’s pretty much the right length, although I’d not recommend it at the $20 they’re asking for it. It’s good, but not that good.

Put Pacman DX+, Snake, ChuChu Rocket into a blender. Mix for 10 mins, and you end up with Pix The Cat.
The game is basically snake (old mobile game), with Chu Chu rocket style graphics and Pacman DX+ mechanics.  Good for a quick 10/15 minute blast, the concept is simple, as Pix the cat you have to collect eggs which spawn chicks that follow you. Walk over the targets to deposit the chicks and score... Seems simple enough.. Except..
The only way to get a decent score is to collect ALL the chicks first BEFORE you deposit them. Deposit them too early, and the remaining shells crack and your combo multiplier drops. Run into your own tail of chicks and all the remaining eggs crack your combo multiplier drops. Run into various enemies and all the eggs crack, and your combo multiplier drops.  The longer you can go without dropping your combo multiplier the higher score you can achieve, but also, the game gets quicker (hello pacman DX+). The game is played against the clock (arcade mode) so you have to choose the quickest path without trapping yourself. Get enough perfects in a row and it goes into fever mode, even higher scores can be obtained! (ps. scoring tip, in fever mode you can EAT the enemy monsters for even MORE SCORE).
Each level is inside the current level, a warp gate opens when you complete a level (successfully or not) to the next level. This allows two way acesss, which in some levels is needed to complete the next level.
Oh about controls, you only turn when Pix is directly on the center of a square. You can pre-turn before that for a slight speed boost (sparks appear). Keyboard or D-Pad is a must, analogue stick really isn't going to cut it.
The game have a lot of unlocks, to get you to come back and have one more go. You are contanstly chasing the high score, with high score tables for local, friends and worldwide to conquer.
There are other modes, I haven't got around to playing them yet. Including a local multiplayer arena mode, which appears to be a bit like bomberman.

The wurms are minor, you can easily just walk away and not play their game of wait till they land and stop hurting to attack them, but the next enemies are flying orbs that charge you. You can always hit them but since they fly 99% of the time they're out of your reach waiting to chage in, and you can just take it.
Then come laser guys, laser guys spawn in the furthest parts of the room you're in and shoot you through walls, the game has a big tell to let you know a lasers coming and its theoretically easy to dodge, but their intro level is also filled with natural unkillable wall lasers and if you get stuck between the two your only recourse is deciding who's taking half your HP crappy level designers or crappy enemy ones.
Now in sane games♥♥♥♥♥♥enemies are an acceptable thing. The archers outside anor londo are war criminals who should have been at the nuremberg trials but you know they're there after the first time. Sundered doesn't like that idea though, it prefers random hordes of enemies. Since no two maps are that alike there's no preset enemies, they arrive every so often, sometimes a couple times in a room, sometimes a couple rooms, since they travel to you it's hard to tell the exact formula, and usually its a small fair group, but far too often its a utter horde of them. If the devs see this review, (they won't what do they care I only paid for the games inital existance my parts done) of all the things, fix this. Add something. Pix the Cat is very fun. If you like arcade style games you will like this.
Arcade mode is impressive. Level design is good and tricky. The ramp up in difficulty is nice though. There are different stages. The beginner stage does well in introducing you to the controls. The Main stage is where it starts to get very tricky.
The main stage introduces you to some tougher gameplay. Planning out the fastest route without breaking your combo gets tougher. The unique nesting of the levels inside the stage provides for some shortcuts, if you can find them.
Laboratory mode is a nice change of pace from arcade mode. It is more focused on puzzles and you have to complete a stage in as few moves as possible.
Arena mode is alright. There are a good amount of stages to choose from. There is standard ammunition to throw at your friends as well as missiles and mines to plant. Rounds are over pretty quickly and this mode could use a little more variety.
There are challenges with unlocks. The unlocks are actually prizes worth doing the challenges for. Different announcers are up for grabs, as well as art, new stages and more.
Overall this game is worth the money. A good mix of puzzle and twitch reflexes.

Counter Strike is a simple yet addicting concept of the Terrorists fighting against the Counter Terrorists in various maps and settings. There's various versions of this game, like 1.6, Condition Zero, Source and Global Offensive. I own almost all of the Counter Strike games but somehow I only like the Source version. Sort of like. In this review I will explain why I enjoy it more than the rest and some pros and cons about the game. This is all from my personal experience, so don't get wound up if you favor a different version of Counter Strike.
.
I like games that are easy to pick up but hard to master, and Counter Strike definitely fits that bill.
It's very simple: at the start of the round you get a bit of time to purchase your gear (or simply make binds to do it for you) and you're off to kill the opposing team or fulfill the objective, like planting the bomb or rescueing the hostages.
The number one problem with this game is that, believe it or not, this is largely is a "pay to win" game. Not noobs, not grievers, not hackers, but pay-to-winners. Many servers have a so-called premium option. Especially Saigns.de servers are notorious for this. Even the admins are guilty of it. For a small fee per month, you gain access to a set of plain ridiculous and unfair advantages over fair and honest players, included but not limited to:
- more starting health
- health generation
- faster walking speed
- ability to respawn
- infinite money
- start with m4a1/ak-47 and vesthelm
- grenades replenishment
- availability to purchase all weapons
That's fun huh, when you die and read:
Any gamer will know that you start off with 100 health. And yes, this actually happens. More than once. But why should they care? They already fed the tumour that is pay 2 win servers all over this game and got the putrid rewards for it.
There seems to be something going on with this, like nobody really cares that noobs with cash to waste join and cause imbalance in the teams. Yeah I said it, noobs. Not all of them, but having spectated some leads to the conclusion some use it solely as a crutch for their unskill, kind of like exo-skeleton soldiers versus regular recruits.
They always wave it away or say something inflammatory when you address them on it, further fueling the abhorrent reputation every Counter Strike community has, even though they're caught red-handed. I also like how it says "Premium player" and "Donator" next to their name on some servers, but really, just read it as "Pay to winner".
I can give you one positive side of this however that it's not a bad practice opportunity to play against them and actually owning them is satisfying as fùck.
About the last thing I mentioned in the list above, that is another problem: weapon imbalance.
Don't get me wrong, weapons like the m4a1, ak-47, Deagle, etc. are all balanced perfectly well. The two real suckers here are the AWM Magnum Sniper rifle (or simply the AWP), and the Autosniper. These two are so damn overpowered that almost every server has restricted these to premium players, and even within pay to win players there's usually a restriction to 1-2 per team. They are
overpowered, but really, what can you expect when the AWP can instakill a fully armored player from full health from a single shot anywhere on the body with exception of the legs, where nobody aims at anyway.
If you're not prepared to cash in your honest and fair play for a pay to win stamp with its associated features, you're not going to play with these a lot unless you find an unrestricted server, which is like a needle in a haystack.
Another thing with all these premium and custom servers, is that I've never found a regular game. You know, like in CS:GO you have a thing called the pistol round, eco, anti-eco, all that stuff. Well, forget about it in CSS. Even though it's the standard for bot matches, good luck finding any such thing. It's all custom-set to having enough cash to get a nearly full gear every single round into eternity.
If you have any conscience at all, favorite a bunch of servers that do not have any unfair advantage options players can access with money.
Furthermore, there's not much to say. If you enjoy an abundance of overpowered players and largely the same kind of rounds (it's kind of relaxing still), CSS is for you. If you prefer a fair challenge and actually want to play normal games, stick with CS:GO. Or you know, play a decent game instead.
And yet, despite all my frustration with this game in the franchise, I still think it's the best of them all, even with all the problems included. Maybe it's the short, laid-back nature of the many quick games, the Source engine or the weapons and sounds themselves, that somehow make me enjoy the game. Sometimes.
CSS, a love-hate relationship that I keep coming back to... If there was a neutral rating, I'd give it that instead.

If you *really* liked Grimrock 1, you'll probably like this too. (And for people new to Grimrock, I'd suggest trying 1 first anyways.) You may or may not like this game, but I got sick of it pretty fast.
Mechanics are comparable to LOG1. In terms of the combat: Enemies have smarter attacks this time around compared to 1, so they can turn and hit you even when you're trying to flank from the side, which is a neat change to me. It seems like more enemies have ranged moves and/or charge attacks (i.e. running towards you) which is cool too. But even in easy mode, they seem way tougher than in LOG1. Lots more health and evasion in some cases; as a specific example, I had trouble fighting just a single rat rogue with a full party, full HP/energy since most of my attacks missed and it had well over 100hp (this was the 2nd dungeon area of the game I think). And some places force you to fight a handful of these enemies, in tight spaces, where you can't move around and do flanking tricks. From what I've seen, it looks like magic is still 100% accurate, but I had lots of trouble getting throwing weapons to hit even when my rogue threw them with high Dex. Enemies still react as soon as you press the movement keys, so they can start turning and attacking you as soon as you begin moving to their side, which is pretty jarring.
Speaking of stat changes (compared to LOG1): Dex is what is used for missile weapon damage (as it should be). There are several more classes now, although I personally felt some were distinctly better than others (e.g. Fighter > Barbarian and Wizard > Battle Mage IMO) and others just seemed not worth picking unless you're on a fun run (e.g. Farmer, which is comparable to the Deprived class in the Souls series). The skill system has been revised so everyone gets access to the same set of skills and 2 points to spend at the start (and 1 per level), and I believe skills max at 5. In particular, accuracy also has a skill associated with it, so every skill point gives you +10 accuracy. Which is kind of neat, since you can just spend 1 point and one of your Minotaur fighter's biggest problems (accuracy) is resolved (he has -4 dex). Oh, there's also a new Ratling race, which is kinda neat too. Your characters can have their body parts injured (e.g. you have a chance of damaging legs/feet when falling down a pit), and you need to heal those with potions, otherwise they have negative effects e.g. no energy recovery or unable to move at all. I'm mostly indifferent about this change, except it forces you to use health potions more often, which might make fights even harder than they should be.
IIRC, your 4 main attributes (Str/Dex/Vit/Will) never increase by leveling up skills. You can only raise them by using permanent stat boost potions. So planning out your characters' builds when you start the game is pretty important. To sum up my thoughts on this part: the stat system changes are good overall. It feels more intuitive but might screw you if you don't spec your characters well. It's not a bad idea to check out a guide or spend time planning your characters out before starting your campaign.
The few puzzles I encountered were roughly the same level of difficulty I found in LOG1. I've seen other reviews mention that they thought the puzzles got worse as they progressed in this game, but I haven't played enough (only 4 hours right now) to determine if they're right. I will say that I thought LOG1's puzzles weren't intuitive enough, so I dislike that they've stayed the same here.
Overall: I mostly like the stat changes, and dislike the combat and puzzles. However, the latter 2 comprise most of the core gameplay so I guess it's natural that I don't really like this game much. Quite a few people might still like it though. Just be ready for some hard combat (I *really* recommend Easy mode) and don't be ashamed to look up puzzle solutions (they're hard too...).

This game does a lot of things right. It's pretty easy to see what they were going for, but in my opinion, it falls short in some aspects.
This game is an fps about WWI, complete with trench warfare and basic rifles. It captures the tension of its battles fairly well, and rewards you for taking good aim and hitting your shots. Its definitely not an easy shooter game to learn. Immediately when I launched the game, it told me how the game plays, how the progression flows, and how the combat works. I played a couple matches and I can say the gunplay can be very rewarding.
But sometimes the game just isn't fun. Most of the time, servers aren't full of players, and more often than not, they're terribly unbalanced. The game uses a balance system that asks you very kindly to switch teams. People are resistent to switching because the mindset is generally, "screw switching, i just want to win". To get full enjoyment from a match you'll want to find a squad of vocal players to play with. I honestly didn't really bother looking for one, so I can't really be sure how hard the hunt for one is.
I just can't recommend this game to people because its such a large departure from a traditional fps game, and unless they specifically want a mildly hardcore wwi shooter, there's other games for them. It captures the tone of trench warfare extremely well, but is flawed with team imbalance and a small playerbase

Sundered is a great game with amazing visuals and some quirks to set it apart from other games in its genre. My favorite thing by far about this game is its beatiful art and incredibly smooth animations. It creates a great atmosphere throughout the game combining the visuals with the sound design. In essence it is a metroidvania with some light RPG elements in the form of an FFX-esque skill tree and three unlockable perk slots.
I was quite impressed with how robust this system was, but as I've played more it has become clear that it really wasnt the focus of the design and has suffered for it in parts. The skill tree is good allround, but some of the perks are just poorly designed. These perks are designed around having an advantage and a disadvantage to them (they're literally listed as such). One specific perk that comes to mind was a lifesteal perk. Now, the disadvantage on this perk was that your health was reduced by 30%. That makes perfect sense as the fear with lifesteal in a game like this would be that it allows you to facetank whatever comes your way and trivialises the content. So you would think the lifesteal was pretty good right? No. It is 0.5%. Putting that into perspective; I've invested a lot into damage, because that's how I like my characters and at what seems like roughly the halfway point of the game I hit for 100-150 when I dont crit. That means per hit on a single enemy I maybe get 1 hp if they round up. Like I said, there are good things about the RPG elements and I'm really quite impressed that there is any in the first place, but some things clearly didn't get the attention they deserved.
The thing that truly sets this game apart from other metroidvanias is the fact that you are mostly being chased around the game world. Usually in these games you have set enemy placements and you fight your way through as necessary. In this game however you find yourself walking through the game world exploring when you suddenly hear this foreboding sound. It fills you with the feeling that something bad is about to happen, and indeed it is. The horde is coming for you. It's quite unlike any other metroidvania I've ever played and lends to the overall mood this game tries to cultivate.
The combat is, as with most metroidvanias, pretty bare bones until you get a few powerups under your belt, but it does the job. You face a good amount of minibosses that are often a hyped up version a normal enemy, but not always. The real imaginative enemy design comes in with the bosses though. They are HUGE and excellently designed both in art and mechanics.
My biggest issue with the game is quite frankly how stiff the controls feel. This gets much better the more mobility powers you collect, but it doesnt change that the base movement is fairly clunky and doesnt feel that great. I feel like part of why it's so jarring is how fantastically smooth the animations are. That disconnect bothered me throughout the starting parts of the game.
Another part of the game that seemed great on paper but fell a bit flat in action was the procedural nature of the levels. It's a popular concept in games these days, and when done right it can be great for replayability, but I feel that for this genre it needs a lot of polish to really work that well. Not that it's bad in this game... It just doesn't really contribute anything either.
Writing this review I feel like I've suddenly focused a lot of the flaws I found in the game rather than how great I actually think it is. I guess that's just because it is a flawed game in a lot of ways, but I feel the positives far outweigh the negatives. If you like metroidvanias and lovecraftian stuff you should give this game a chance. It's easily worth the price

I have noticed that occasionally the game can be unstable but crashes are rare and dealing with them is worth it for the intense gameplay. The main game mode is a fun juggling act of attack and defend and one quickly learns to reserve ammo and remain in cover should thy want to survive. The squad system  is certainly a welcome addition in my opinion as it encourages squad and tactical gameplay. If you are a fan of tactical shooters or just feel as if the fps genre is getting stale then I definitely recommend this, just don't expect any crazy special abilities or fast paced firefights

This might have been a great 2001 game, and if you're getting this for the nostalgia, go ahead.
This is not a good 2017 game. For most people playing this for the first time expecting something worthy of the 'Overwhelmingly Positive' rating on steam, it will be painfully bad. There is almost no actual gameplay in the 7 hours I've played - the vast majority of your time is spent in cutscenes. The voice acting, dialogue and animation unfortunately make most cutscenes extremely difficult to watch - this part of the game did not age well at all.
The combat is okay, but almost nonexistent. The sphere grid is just annoying. Using an XBox controller, for some reason 'B' is the button that confirms dialogue/selection and so on, and 'A' is the button that cancels. This will be a huge mind♥♥♥♥ for a few hours unless you change it in the controller settings for this game on steam (but be aware that there are also prompts during certain attacks to press specific buttons).
The story is beyond boring, and is not told efficiently - far too many unnecessary cutscenes which just make you want the whole thing to end as soon as possible. I enjoyed the way it started, but the time-traveling thing was just wholly unnecessary - you get this weird effect where the story started with a huge amount of momentum and then just completely grinds to a halt as you introduce yourself to new people and then (god knows why) help them prepare for a blitzball tournament. So far the entire game has revolved around some weird underwater version of soccer, and the fantasy monsters seem to almost be an afterthought.
Bottom line, if you were going to buy this because you've played it before, go ahead. If you're new to the series, absolutely do not start here. And if you've already played some other final fantasy games, I seriously recommend you watch a video on youtube of the first hour or so of gameplay (including cutscenes) before buying.

I am hopeful that this is the next great addition to the FSX-like collection.  FS-XI (eleven) as it were!
Downs:  The earliest release of anything will have bugs.  That is to be expected.  I am not terriblly worried about that.  How well 3rd party developers decide they want to gleen onto this, versus run with X-Plane 11 & P3Dv.4, might have some great bearing on future success, but if we have ORBX in our corner, I think that's a major player right there.  We shall see.
Ups:  If Dovetail intends to stand behind their word and their product, I do believe they will listen to their users and make proper improvments over time.  The fact that it's 64-bit, I think gives the sim potential and great room to grow, utilizing multi-core and putting an end to OOM errors once and for all.... (I think)?  If it's structure is designed to utilize more of the heavy-lifting on the part of the GPU, instead of putting all that responsibility on the CPU, that may serve as a major asset as well.
I think the most important thing to remember is that at any one point, the simulator is only a snap shot in time, and whatever you find unappealing now, you may see has been addressed 3 months from now.  Be patient and check back often is what I plan on doing, me personally.

I originally bought SimplePlanes as a fun little mobile game about 1, 1/2 years ago. Little did I realize how enjoyable the game actually was. At the time, the game had few features, but was fun nonetheless. After the death of my Ipad (the device it ran on) I switched to android and lost the game. So when I found it for online, I was more than happy to spend a few dollars. And now its on Steam, and has many more features than before.
So why do I recomend the game?
Pros-
*Easy to run (will virtually run on anything).
*Extensive library of player made planes to choose from.
*Cross platform capability (planes on Ios will work on PC or Android).
*Simple to use, but fully capable of creating good looking planes.
*Excelent playerbase.
*Plane physics. ie: wings tearing off, falls apart on crash.
*Simple and fun.
Cons-
*Graphics are minimal (definitely not a bad thing, I personally love it).
*No workshop (but is extremely easy to download planes).
*No multiplayer (not that I'm complaining).
Overall a good game, simple and fun.

The Crew features an open and persistent world for racing and free-roaming across a scaled-down recreation of the contiguous United States. The map is split into five regions: The Midwest, East Coast, Mountain States, West Coast, and The South. Each region has its own unique geographical features. Six main cities (one in each region, two in The Midwest) are featured in the game: Detroit and Chicago in the Midwest, New York City on the East Coast, Miami in The South, Las Vegas in the Mountain States, and Los Angeles on the West Coast. Various other cities, such as San Francisco, Seattle, Salt Lake City, Dallas, New Orleans, Washington D.C., and St. Louis, are also featured in the game. Over thirty smaller cities and towns line the countryside like Nashville, Norfolk and others. It takes approximately 45 minutes in real time to drive from coast to coast in-game. The single-player campaign is 20 hours long, and entails infiltrating criminal groups with protagonist Alex Taylor (Troy Baker). Players can also participate in mini-games called skills challenges that are peppered across the world. They are triggered when a player drives through them and it involves completing challenges such as weaving through gates and staying as close to a racing line as possible for a period of time. Players' scores are automatically saved so friends can try and beat their scores, in similar fashion to how Autolog works in games of the Need for Speed franchise. Missions can be played alone, with friends, or with online co-op matchmaking. The multiplayer mode lets a maximum of eight players to compete in races and other gametypes. There are no in-game loading screens or pauses.

Following in the wake of the rising trend of 'walking simulators'
attempts to create an intriguing atmosphere with its setting but ends up disappointing with its lack of depth.
Gone Home sets up a quite interesting premise. You return from your trip to Europe back home, in the middle of a storm, only to find it empty. Your family is not there and it's up to you to discover what has happened to them. The story is unfolded in written form with some audio cues when some events are triggered and that formula works well up to a certain point in the overall plotline.
It does sound fascinating right? Especially if you add the creepy undertones in the various notes and letters you'll find and combine that with visual and audio effects the game lays out for you, you have a tantalizing plot for you discover. However Gone Home will not push beyond what it has in the surface. Whatever you might or might not expect, disappointment is always around the corner and with an incredibly short duration, there's not really room to further explore the characters or some hints to subplots which might compensate for a very predictable main arc.
The magic of the walking simulator genre lies in creating a vibrant world and characters who will excite the imagination of the player. Pure expositional dialogue is the genre's own worst enemy and Gone Home has that in spades. The plot is revealed very early in the game and after that you're left with a very predictable outcome which you will see coming a mile away. All the air of mystery and perhaps hints for supernatural elements are quickly dissolved away within the first 20 minutes. After that the experience becomes more of a chore and less of a unique perspective into the world of the characters and the story itself.
Without spoiling too much of the
story, some of the dialogue and voice acting are decent enough but the game never dares to go someplace different than where you expect it to go. It doesn't experiment, it doesn't challenge, it will not evoke a strong emotional response, it will leave you there half-interested and feeling like you need to get this over with. For me that's a mark of a poorly designed game.
Regardless of that, I can understand why some people might relate to the story, and if you do then more power to you. My problem with Gone Home is not the story itself but how it is presented to the player. It is very uninspired and sophomoric to say the least and that's the game's greatest downfall. I'll admit that there were times where the spirit of the game merges well with the otherwise quirky soundtrack but all of that crumbles down when you listen to the next part of the expositional monologue.
I did enjoy some parts of Gone Home but overall it felt like a very disappointing experience. Partly because of expectations I had about it but mostly because of the sub-par execution. I got the game as part of a bundle and perhaps I could recommend it then for hardcore fans of the walking simulator genre, but at full price I'd advise consumers to look someplace else.

Edit: After a bit more playtime, I've come to enjoy fighting the hordes. As you get more tools to deal with them, they become more enjoyable and less frustrating. I'm not saying the game is perfect, but having a broader toolset alleviates most of the frustration. There's something satisfying about a cannon shot that kills a screen full of enemies.
Let's talk about these hordes for a moment.
At points in the game (including boss battles), masses of enemies will spawn near you and proceed to end your run. I don't know if you can escape them; they spawn from off screen and it seems like the quickest way to deal with them is to kill them. You have to think about your positioning, what tools you have available, the terrain, what enemy types take priority... it's exciting and initially fun. The combat might not amaze you, but it gets the job done. Find a wall, put your back to it, and murder hordes of enemies so you can loot those sweet, sweet crystals from their corpses. Unfortunately, the horde doesn't seem to realize when it's no longer wanted. Well after when you've exhausted most of your options they keep coming. The developers state that they'll end after a minute or 20 kills, but it seems like neither is true. They just keep coming, which means eventually you're going to be overwhelmed and die. Not so big a deal most of the time, but if you die on a boss fight because part of the boss battle - and the boss is lethal in its own right - is a horde, you're probably not going to be very happy.
You know what would make the hordes much easier to deal with? Invincibility frames after you've taken damage, like in pretty much every other game ever. I have no idea why someone actively decided to not include these, but there's a stickied post in the discussion forums saying they are testing and plan to implement them. Probably should have shipped the game with them. I'm not saying it's as bad as Tekken 7, but I was exercising my right to aerial combat and somehow got juggled to death in the middle of a horde of flying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Not fun.
Aside from the hordes being frustrating, obnoxious, and in my opinion bad game design, this is a very good game. Mild spoiler, you'll get an ability a few hours in that made hordes much, much easier to deal with. Unfortunately, it seems hordes can be composed of any enemy, including one that can attack you from off screen (one or two screens away, in my experience). When you're dealing with four or five of these enemies, it is an exercise in frustration. Maybe I'm incorrect about horde composition and these are just extremely annoying enemies. Anyway, you'll see that sentiment, frustration, echoed in a lot of these reviews. Yes, it is frustrating to arbitrarily lose your exploration progress, but you can generally get back to where you were with a minute or two's travel. No, that doesn't make it feel any less cheap, and the vast majority of my deaths are because of hordes, but the rest of the game is more than good enough for me to recommend it. There are rogue-lite and RPG elements that help differentiate it from similar games, the art is extremely good, the Metroidvania ability gates are in full force, and the story is... well, I have no idea what's going on, but at least it's interesting. There's some background music, and maybe some combat and boss music, but I'm generally too busy fighting for my life to pay attention to it. The boss battles have been familiar concepts executed well, and the environments I've been through were interesting, though there is quite a bit of familiar corridor traversal in the early game. The platforming took me a few minutes to get used to, but it is executed well. There is a double jump, which always helps.
Overally I think this is a solid 7.5, 8 game. It'd easily get a point back if the hordes weren't so dumb.

Review changed from negative to positive. Originally, the functionality of online play was so ridiculously awful that I and plenty of others found it impossible to play a full game without at least 50 random failures first, but a lot of work has been done since then. I still have trouble connecting to servers sometimes, and I occasionally can't move after an online game starts, but it's nothing too major anymore, and the developers are continuing to work on it.
The actual game itself? It's absolutely wonderful. Half platformer, half stab-your-friend-in-the-back-with-cheap-tricks simulator, and fully hilarious, it's easy for anyone to really get into the game and have lots of fun with it. It's the first multiplayer game I've found where I don't even care in the slightest who wins at the end, because every round, every increasingly impossible setup of objects, and every trap placed by a player in a mean spot all works together to give me a good laugh, so much so that I'm too busy cracking up to even pay attention to the scoreboard most times. How someone can make a platforming game all about competing for the finish line without the overall 'feel' of the game being competitive, I'll never know, but it's truly refreshing to find a game that's so simple and easy to get behind, and always so entertaining.
It's also pretty fun to build deathtraps out of conveyor belts, honey, and sawmill blades.
