Counter Strike is a simple yet addicting concept of the Terrorists fighting against the Counter Terrorists in various maps and settings. There's various versions of this game, like 1.6, Condition Zero, Source and Global Offensive. I own almost all of the Counter Strike games but somehow I only like the Source version. Sort of like. In this review I will explain why I enjoy it more than the rest and some pros and cons about the game. This is all from my personal experience, so don't get wound up if you favor a different version of Counter Strike.
.
I like games that are easy to pick up but hard to master, and Counter Strike definitely fits that bill.
It's very simple: at the start of the round you get a bit of time to purchase your gear (or simply make binds to do it for you) and you're off to kill the opposing team or fulfill the objective, like planting the bomb or rescueing the hostages.
The number one problem with this game is that, believe it or not, this is largely is a "pay to win" game. Not noobs, not grievers, not hackers, but pay-to-winners. Many servers have a so-called premium option. Especially Saigns.de servers are notorious for this. Even the admins are guilty of it. For a small fee per month, you gain access to a set of plain ridiculous and unfair advantages over fair and honest players, included but not limited to:
- more starting health
- health generation
- faster walking speed
- ability to respawn
- infinite money
- start with m4a1/ak-47 and vesthelm
- grenades replenishment
- availability to purchase all weapons
That's fun huh, when you die and read:
Any gamer will know that you start off with 100 health. And yes, this actually happens. More than once. But why should they care? They already fed the tumour that is pay 2 win servers all over this game and got the putrid rewards for it.
There seems to be something going on with this, like nobody really cares that noobs with cash to waste join and cause imbalance in the teams. Yeah I said it, noobs. Not all of them, but having spectated some leads to the conclusion some use it solely as a crutch for their unskill, kind of like exo-skeleton soldiers versus regular recruits.
They always wave it away or say something inflammatory when you address them on it, further fueling the abhorrent reputation every Counter Strike community has, even though they're caught red-handed. I also like how it says "Premium player" and "Donator" next to their name on some servers, but really, just read it as "Pay to winner".
I can give you one positive side of this however that it's not a bad practice opportunity to play against them and actually owning them is satisfying as fùck.
About the last thing I mentioned in the list above, that is another problem: weapon imbalance.
Don't get me wrong, weapons like the m4a1, ak-47, Deagle, etc. are all balanced perfectly well. The two real suckers here are the AWM Magnum Sniper rifle (or simply the AWP), and the Autosniper. These two are so damn overpowered that almost every server has restricted these to premium players, and even within pay to win players there's usually a restriction to 1-2 per team. They are
overpowered, but really, what can you expect when the AWP can instakill a fully armored player from full health from a single shot anywhere on the body with exception of the legs, where nobody aims at anyway.
If you're not prepared to cash in your honest and fair play for a pay to win stamp with its associated features, you're not going to play with these a lot unless you find an unrestricted server, which is like a needle in a haystack.
Another thing with all these premium and custom servers, is that I've never found a regular game. You know, like in CS:GO you have a thing called the pistol round, eco, anti-eco, all that stuff. Well, forget about it in CSS. Even though it's the standard for bot matches, good luck finding any such thing. It's all custom-set to having enough cash to get a nearly full gear every single round into eternity.
If you have any conscience at all, favorite a bunch of servers that do not have any unfair advantage options players can access with money.
Furthermore, there's not much to say. If you enjoy an abundance of overpowered players and largely the same kind of rounds (it's kind of relaxing still), CSS is for you. If you prefer a fair challenge and actually want to play normal games, stick with CS:GO. Or you know, play a decent game instead.
And yet, despite all my frustration with this game in the franchise, I still think it's the best of them all, even with all the problems included. Maybe it's the short, laid-back nature of the many quick games, the Source engine or the weapons and sounds themselves, that somehow make me enjoy the game. Sometimes.
CSS, a love-hate relationship that I keep coming back to... If there was a neutral rating, I'd give it that instead.

I'm still unsure how I feel about Walking Simulators as a genre; but of the ones I've played, this is my favourite.  A lot of that is the fact that there's actually quite a lot to do as you explore the house.  There are plenty of little secrets hidden away to find as you explore.  Exploration itself requires action, with locked doors and hidden passages to unlock and find.  And there's plenty of environmental details that hint at elements of character and back-story that reward the simple act of looking around.
This ties in to the well-told nature of the story.  The main plot is gradually revealed through journal entries.  The need to unlock and open areas gradually ensures that these come in order and as a benefit of reaching somewhere new.  Perhaps more interesting are the side stories, told indirectly through the items you find, and needing some reflection to piece together.  But the most appealing elements to me were the characters and the resolution.  All the family are nicely fleshed out. In particular I found it easy to emphasise with Sam's story and challenges, despite the familiar elements of teenage drama.  The climax of the story has disappointed some, but I found it satisfying emotionally and narratively.
The biggest weakness is that this is a short game, at only 2 hours.  Other than that, it's hard for me to criticise it beyond the inherent limitations of its genre.

I very much enjoyed the beta (maybe 1/3rd of the map in total?) and I am thus far enjoying the full release more. Combat has a steep curve to start with, but as you learn the dodging mechanics and attack types, it becomes intuitive and fun.
The non-linearity is particularly enjoyable, with many areas being locked not by mechanics, but your own skill/upgrades. If you're good enough you can go to the harder content much faster.
Whenever you die, you return to the Sanctuary location, where you can upgrade your gear with the currency you earned, so death never feels like failure, as much as 'how much further can I get?'. If you're having trouble you can always go elsewhere and farm some currency for quick upgrades, or else get lost on side-challenges, miniboss rooms, or arifact hunting.
The bosses are intentionally huge and intimidating, but never unfairly punishing. They may take a couple of attempts to figure out, I enjoyed every minute of it.

Eternal is an incredible card game all around.
Similar to Magc: the Gathering in many ways, Eternal streamlines the formula and adds its own twists to make a game that plays faster, more balanced, and with deep strategic interplay both over the course of individual games and in deckbuilding.
Eternal rewards skill and strategy, and thanks to its generous free-to-play system skill really does matter (easily the most generous of any card game on the market - this game is actually free to play, even at competitive levels).
For existing card game fans, this is a masterfully designed game that takes existing concepts and improves them while adding its own spin. For those looking to get into card games for the first time, Eternal is also a great place to start, as its generous card structure and deck building methods reward experimentation and clever play, while also allowing you to learn as you go.

Sundered is a massive unknown world for you to fight, run, and die. The game rewards you for exploration and even death. It's extremely difficult and very unforgiving even for the most seasoned gamers. The visuals are beyond words really, the creativity in visual design is of the best work you'll see among video games. Overall Sundered delivers exactly what it says. A horror metroid survival with a cool progression system. The game visuals are out of the park but the combat leaves a little to be desired. I don't think it's one you should miss if you're into the genre. Just be warned hard difficulty actually means hard. I've had to give this game a thumbs up, but I think it would be better if we were able to give a mixed rating.
I do like the game. I think the dungeons are reasonably interesting and the enemies are reasonably varied. But it's only really good to play for, say, half an hour to an hour before you feel like playing something else. It's a time filler, but that's as far as it goes.
Permit me to go off on a tangent for a moment: To me, it's a bit like trying to play Dungeons and Dragons solo. It's like you setup your characters, have a random roll d20 table to determine each of the rooms, and what's in them, and away you go. Now, if anyone has ever tried to play D&D in that manner, you'll know that it's fun... For about 15 minutes. Any longer than that and the constant move, random room, monster, move, random room, monster, move, random room, empty, move, random room, monster gets a bit dull. Playing D&D this way is fine with friends, or if occasionally the game is designed to do something to surprise the player, but nothing ever really happens.
And, coming back to the main topic, that's what I find with Warhammer Quest. It's pretty much D&D-ish with a solo player and a random roll table to determine the contents of each room. Okay, they tried to spice it up by tying everything together with quests. But, for the most part, it really is just one random dungeon crawl after another. So. I do like it? Sort of, but only in small doses. It'll probably be one of those games that I play for a few days and then forget about.
I do "recommend" it, but only because I can't choose any other option. To say "no" is a little unfair in my opinion,  but "yes" I think is a little too generous. If there were some way to choose a rating that's inbetween, I would.
If I was going to give it a star rating out of 5, it'd be 2.5.

You want to buy the deluxe edition and it's this edition I'm reviewing.
The game is very simple - same basic principles as space hulk - but imo with a little more diversity in unit type; so there is melee, range, caster, but then a whole plethora of special abilities for each of the 11 classes you can choose for your party. Special abiltiies unlock as you level up.
Also, scrolls and potions add to this diversity.
I went for the dwarf ironbreaker, marauder, wood-elf waywatcher and witch hunter. Witch hunter is ace for demolishing undead so he is a good choice when you do undead dungeons.
Graphics are simple but cool, and overall a decent top-down representation of  a boardgame. Character animations could have been much better, but it's ok.
The Music is great, very warhammer dark fantasy: orchestra style fantasy from haunted melodies and charging trumpets. It fits very well.
Now a major criticism of this game is gold micro-transactions. However,I don't see ever having to buy gold btw, as i get enough gold from questing and selling drops for my needs. So yeah there is the buying gold mirco-transaction malarky and this is not cool, but so long as it is unecessary to actually buy gold then criticism of this feature remains moot for me. If that situation were to change then I would reassess this.
My only real critcism is the lack of voice-acting. One of the coolest features of the warhammer universe is the over-the-top regional UK accents: Orcs being cockney hooligans; elves upper class English; dwarves Scottish working class; human warriors usually English northerners etc. So I really would have liked voice actors and thus the lack therein makes it a little less immersive.
I would recommend this as a neat little game that you can dip into for 15-30 min sessions. For me it's reasonable value for money, but that is all relative to what one's budget is and what one considers a reasonable cost vs hours-of-enjoyment ratio. So, If the price seems steep for you then you know that at some point in the next year it will be on sale for 40%, 60% or 80% off, so just pick it up in a sale.
I would like to see some meaty dlcs in the future and  voice acting added if that were feasible. That would keep me hooked.

I love the original Warhammer Quest board game (and several of the additional characters etc.). This review is largely a comparison with that.
I have been wanting a WQ PC game for over a decade now, and now it's finally here! Let's see how it stacks up with my hopes/expectations.
The positives:
* It looks and feels a lot like the original (board) game (which I love).
* It has a good selection of characters, if you buy the deluxe version...
* The random dungeons/events mean that you get the same "I can't believe we survived" feeling I used to get from the original game.
The negatives:
* You can only buy one of each item for each visit to a town (in the original you could buy at least D6 bandages, for example). Who stocks a single bandage?
* Almost all the events seem to be negative, rather than the mix in the original, and non-combat events are few and far between. Travel events are almost non-existent.
* You don't seem to get so much "objective room" (awesome) treasure at the end of a dungeon.
* The special settlement locations are missing. As a result, the wizard can't change his spells or charge his staff, the dwarf can't get runes for his axe, and the elf can't buy arrows of sure flight.
In summary:
If you liked the original board game, you will probably like the feel of this, but long for some of the old mechanics.
If you haven't played the orginal board game, you might find it irritating at times, but it's a decent enough game.

This is a hesitant recommendation. I liked the game a lot at first, but as I play more it feels like bundle fodder more than a solid game. It's short and focused on replaying for completion, but the game doesn't seem to change much in replaying. The only real reason to replay is to seek out all the achievements, but that will be an agonizing process of precision and deaths.
I like how it focuses on one mechanic, flipping gravity, and plays with it in many good ways. However, that makes platforming a bit rough. Since "jumps" are based on left/right motion and timing of flips, I think the devs intentionally made left/right motion INCREDIBLY slipppery. See, you slide on every surface like you are a dog♥♥♥♥♥♥icicle, accelerating like a madman and never able to take a small step. Platforming becomes very unforgiving with smaller windows of mistakes. A lot of the negative reviews on this game basically say "lol micro transactions", which I think are pretty unfair to this great game.
Firstly, do you know what Warhammer Quest is?  If you don't know the Games Workshop board game, then stop reading this review now and go elsewhere.  This game isn't for you.
Second, BUY THE DELUXE VERSION.  The standard version is terrible, it's missing practically half the game.  No one likes in-game purchases, and I think it was a stupid idea to include them here.
Gold purchasing; like in the early days of Diablo 3, you are given the option to spend real money to purchase in-game gold.  This is a terrible idea, and is both unwanted and unneeded, you get plenty of gold just playing the game normally.
The game itself is excellent.  Turn-based dungeon crawling set in the Warhammer world with a huge range of heroes, skills, abilities and items to choose from.  Undead, Orcs & Goblins, Skaven and critters (bats, spiders, rats etc) inhabit the dungeons, all with an impressive range of monsters and their own skills and magic items.  The game becomes very challenging early on, which is great as you don't every dungeon to be a walk in the park.  One minor gripe is that the skaven claw leaders use the same model as the normal clanrats, which can make it difficult to differentiate between them when both types are in play.
Protips: go for quests which have high-value items as rewards, the gold you get from selling them (as long as you don't need them for your own warriors) will help progress your characters.  Always play on hardcore mode, it's much more exciting than the other modes.
TL;DR - if you liked Games Workshop's Warhammer Quest board game, then buy the deluxe version.  Otherwise, don't bother with this game and get something else.

This is my first serious review, sorry if it looks unprofessional.
I haven't experienced this game on release so I can't comment on that, but we live in an age when patches can actually change the game for the better (or worse). And in its current state Homefront: The Revolution seems highly underrated for what it is and what it accomplishes.
Gameplaywise it can be compared to the later FarCry games: do some story missions, capture territory, do side missions, buy weapons and upgrades, etc. but there are certainly differences, especially in the "Yellow Zone" territories where stealth is more inportant. There is also a pretty interesting weapon customisation system where you can change your weapon to an alternative weapon at any time (for example the crossbow can be changed to a flamethrower or a big shotgun). The territory capture mechanic is also more interesting than in other games. Yes, there are some outposts that can be captured by killing all the enemies in the area, but many of them will have you figuring out a puzzle, doing some platforming on rooftops or finding and collecting items.
While the "America gets conquered by a foreign power" is not an unique concept, it is executed pretty well in this game. The areas you visit are varied and atmospheric, ranging from abandoned toxic ruins to well maintained districts where collaborators live or a prison district where the undesirables are kept. The atmosphere is pretty similar to Half-Life 2 and Freedom Fighters and even Metro 2033 in some cases. The areas are also varied gameplaywise. The "Red Zones" are locked off to civilians and are under constant surveillance from Zeppelins. In these areas the fighting is constant and resistance fighters actively help the player. But in the "Yellow Zones" the player needs to take a different approach, being stealthy is more important, like planting a bomb in front of a patrolling jeep unnoticed or knifing a "peacekeeper" bullying civilians and slipping away before his buddies notice. Doing things like this will slowly get the population on your side and the district will visually change as they rise up and start rioting against the occupying forces.
Lastly the bad things. The gameplay can get monotonous after a while, and the side objectives can be boring and tedious. Some side objectives can also be impossible because enemies stop spawning in areas that you completely conquered. The character animations (both player and NPC) and both friendly and enemy AI can be wonky and stupid sometimes, but there's nothing that we haven't seen in other open world games. The most annoying thing is the weird spawn/despawn system for enemy group/patrols. A few times enemies spawned right next to me, while other times I tried go around a building to get behind a parked jeep and it despawned when I got there. Also sometimes objects like tables and boxes don't appear and that makes some items appear floating mid-air, but again that's not an uncommon thing in most open-world games.
In conclusion, this game could have been so much more if it had a higher budget and a bit of polish, but all-in-all despite the wonkiness and ocassional bugs I've found it an enjoyable and memorable experience, with a nice and atmospheric setting.

Before I begin my review, I want to preface it by saying I'm not what I would consider this game's target audience to be, in that I am male and was alive as an adult during the period this game takes place. I say this, because I think it probably colors my perceptions in the way the game is presented, so I want anyone who reads this to bear this in mind.
In short, this is a fairly short linear adventure-type game where the gameplay involves you, the protagonist, searching a rather enormous house for clues as to why there is no one home to greet you after an extended period away. These clues come in the form of objects you discover that trigger story snippets to be revealed to you. Typically, this kind of presentation requires a fairly tight, compelling story and immersive elements that make up for the lack of gameplay.
I'm sorry to say that, "Gone Home," doesn't quite make it on either story or immersion, but I'm recommending it anyway, under a very specific set of criteria, which I will give at the end of the review.
First and foremost, this game is almost certainly not what you think it is from reading the copy or watching the trailers. This is not a haunted house exploration, there is nothing that's going to jump out at you. Even playing the first five minutes of the game, that's what it feels like it's going to be, but that's a false feeling. Oh sure, there's a loud thunderstorm and creaking boards and - was that  someone whispering? - but it's all a red herring. This game loses the spooky factor within the first 5-10 minutes. I'm really not even sure why it's there.
The immersion here, what there is, comes from the way the game presents the house to you. The decor and the flavor elements have a decidedly mid-to-late 1980s feel to them (the game takes place in 1994), including the soundtrack, which is presented to you through cassette tapes you find in many rooms throughout the house (if you see a cassette player in a room, there's a tape in there somewhere, guaranteed). There is also a very strong, "high school teenaged girl," vibe throughout the decor and found objects, which you may find nostalgic, endearing, or cringeworthy, depending on your perspective. Personally, I was in the cringeworthy category, but in my defense - as per my preface - I don't think I represent the target audience this game was meant for. This is a game I believe female players will get a lot more out of.
A word about the music. It's punk. Now, personally, I don't remember a whole lot of punk music being played in the 1990s, but I guess it had to be getting played somewhere, because the game creators chose it specifically. And there is most definitely an anti-establishment punk vibe in a lot of the flavor objects you find. But I'm telling you this because the music is one of the stronger points to the game, that they really went all out to put together a set list that is one of the key selling points to the game...if you happen to like punk. Which I don't. (Remember the preface?) But as I gamer, I can still appreciate the effort that went into it.
Visually, the game is...okay. Nothing horrid. Nothing superlative. It gets the job done. Other than the layout and sheer size of this house, I found nothing unusual, but you are going to get the standard, "same background objects again and again," phenomenon you see in adventure games attempting to depict familiar surroundings.
Controls were simple enough. You will use crouch, which was a pleasant surprise. I had to turn my mouse sensitivity waaaaay down; I've never had to do that with any game before, but on the lowest setting, it was tolerable.
Let's talk about the story. Without giving too much away, there is a main story you are attempting to uncover, and three side stories. The side stories are really just about giving you something else to chew on while you work your way through the main story; they have no bearing on moving you along in the game. I tell you this because in the beginning you're writing names down and trying to keep everything straight...relax...just enjoy the ride. They are there for flavor. And for those three side stories, you never really do get a resolution to any of them, you just get some hints about how it might have ended or is still proceeding. A little good...a little depressing...and a little WTF was that all about?
Now the main story is driver in the game. And again without giving away details, it's pretty strongly telegraphed in the beginning what the story is about. In fact, I will go so far as to say that the main story is a pretty heavy cliche for teenage angst, rebellion, and personal discovery and experimentation. The story will torque some people off, I'm afraid. So I will say right now that if you are strongly traditional when it comes to relationships, just take a pass on this one. I can see by reading the reviews that did not recommend the game, the ones who did so pretty much solely because they reject non-traditional relationships. Well, that's on them; I don't have a problem with such relationships.
What I do have a problem with is that this, "love story," referencing the New York Times review claiming this to be the, "greatest video game love story ever told," is not very good. And with respect to the NYT, if this was - to you - the greatest love story ever told in a video game, then you have *got* to start playing more video games.
What this story consisted of is a cliched telling of experiencing the first blossom of love, followed by acting like a pair of impulse-control-challenged teenagers. This is the standard, "Brenda & Eddie" scenario, from Billy Joel's "Scenes from an Italian Restaurant," where you'd like to be happy for them, but you can't help but roll your eyes at it. I note that the story was courtesy of a writer from BioWare, to which I can only say, the trials that Shepard and Tali'Zorah needed to overcome in Mass Effect 2 & 3 are light years ahead of the story told here. (The line, "But I *have* a home," breaks my heart to this day.)
But again....preface...I'm not who this story is intended for. I'm sure some people out there will find this story immensely charming and romantic, much in the same way, "Romeo and Juliet," could be seen as romantic, except for - you know - all the other stuff that happens.
BUT...did the game do it's job? Did it tell a story that kept me interested until the end? Did I play it in one sitting? Did I give a crap enough about it to write an overly wordy and opinionated review for it? Yes, yes, yes, and apparently yes.
Summary:
So having said all of that, I think you *should* play, "Gone Home," if you meet the following criteria:
1. You can get it on sale. I'm afraid the value really just isn't there for the full $19.99 on Steam. There's just not enough meat on the bone for me to say it's a good value at $20. Especially when I've seen it offered for both free and less than $5 on Steam sales. Wait for a sale for this one.
2. You aren't philosophically opposed to non-traditional relationships; because if you are, you're just going to find the game irritating and preachy, and probably not get anything positive out of it. Don't be that guy who buys a game he knows he's going to have a problem with and then ♥♥♥♥♥es about it later.
3. You have an interest in the late 80s/early 90s and or the punk scene and will enjoy the immersion from the music and setting, either through nostalgia or visiting an era from before you were born.

Homefront: The Revolution is a decent game at best. I really tried to enjoy it, believe me, but I just couldn't. Here's why:
I got this game on a free weekend, when it was on a sale. I played about 2 hours and thought that the game is quite good and that it may be worth a buy. And was I wrong. It feels like after 2 hours of playtime, you experience about everything it has to offer.
The story feels just like any other game about overthrowing an opressive regime. You are a new member of the resistance after the US has been invaded by koreans. The icon of the revolution, Walker, gets captured and you spend the whole game trying to free him and start a riot. It features a silent protagonist where I think there was really no need for one.
The graphics are one of the only strong points of the game, since it runs on Cryengine and that just makes the game beautiful from the start. Philadelphia looks the best it has ever did in the gaming scene.
The gameplay is repetitive and boring. It has you taking key points/buildings for the resistance and that's about it. Yeah, that's everything you do for the duration of the game, but at least the game isn't absurdly long (we're looking at about 10 hours of gameplay here).  The map is divided in red zones and yellow zones. The red zones are completely destroyed areas of the city where the korean military roams freely. For red zones, you can either cross the map on foot or on a motorcycle. The yellow zones are civilized places where americans and koreans coexist and where you have to blend it to not draw the attention of the military upon you. Yellow zones are smaller so you can only travel on foot. The game features light parkour elements, but don't let this statement fool you, this isn't Dying Light. Regardless, be it red or yellow zone, the sole thing you continue to do is take outposts.
The mechanics are pretty basic, with alright shooting. You have quite a limited weapon range at first, but as you progress you can convert weapons (for example turn an assault rifle into a light machine gun) and buy new ones. There are 6 weapons in the game, each having 2 options for conversion. You also have some equipment such as molotov cocktails, pipe bombs, etc. No real innovation here.
TL;DR: The thing that stood out the most for me in this game is the fact that it is just a big repetitive mess. The side missions have abolutely no value since they are the same missions as in the first sequence of the map, just over and over again up to the point where it just becomes frustrating, plus the main missions don't bring anything new to the table. Literally everything you do in this game is take outposts, basically. The story doesn't shine either, it's just another generic game where you have to start a revolution against some kind of opressing regime. The shooting mechanics are almost fine, but it still feels like the game lacks polish. Got it on a sale but I still can't really reccomend it. It's just not worth your time.

When you're an early-80s-born queer yourself, and you were an awkwardly closeted gay teenager in the 90s, this game hits like one brick-laden truck after another right in the chest.  I may be Swedish rather than American, but with the personal knowledge of how hard it was just coming out to your own self in those times, when the story of this game really starts unfurling itself from those voice-lined journal entries, it's an endless chain reaction of sucker punches to the gut.  Even as someone who never really could get into that egregiously atonal punk rock genre, the various songs that crop up on those cassette tapes (ah, nostalgia for a level of technology I'm really not all that sad to have seen replaced) give that realness to the setting that only amps the experience up even further.
This is the kind of story that needs to be told, if only so that future generations of LGBT+ youth can see themselves mirrored in the hardships of a still not distant enough (never distant enough) past.

You should buy this game if you like old school megaman games (Talking megaman X, though this plays closer to Megaman Zero), Early Metroid, Early Castlevania, and Strider. It's playstyle is clearly aimed towards a retro style combat first approach.
The game gets funner as you go, a lot like metroid, and megaman, as you get more abilities and become stronger.
The fun of the game is in it's combat. If you don't like megaman zero, or Strider style combat, this game probably isn't for you. If you do like those things like I do, then you will love this game because it does those things better in my opinion. It does that combat better than megaman zero, however. Every direction has a basic attack, both in the air and on the ground. The comboes go together fluidly and it feels very responsive.
It is a rogue-like. This means procedural generation. The purpose the procedural generation plays is it keeps your brain from falling asleep when you're forced to walk from the spawn back to where you were headed. It also softens death because the only way to get spend your shards (the souls equivalent in this game) is to go back to spawn. This means goodies await you at each death. The skill tree is large, and you'll always have something to hunt for.
It has exploration, but not the type you might expect. You aren't really supposed to take your time and explore in this game. All secrets can be heard, so there's no reason to stop yourself from just rolling through because you'll hear a little jingle when there's treasure to be searched for. There's also a mechanic where hordes will come after a certain amount of time, which is essentially a massive rush of mobs. Talking about 30 or more. To be honest, this needs some balancing on hard mode, but the devs already have a beta out to start tackling it.
So far about 10 hours in on writing this review and have cleared out the first area, and have yet to really make a dent in the second area. For an $18 game this is some of the most value you're going to get.
There is also replayability, as the game has an "Embrace or Resist" mechanic. There are special shards called elder shards. On getting one, you have a choice. Corrupt an ability you gained from the remnants of past explorers (And as a consequence corrupt yourself as well), or destroy the elder shard and gain an improvement to your base abilities available in the skill tree, as well some shards to spend. So far I've went with the resist option, because I like to pick the pure option first, and I'm very satisfied with the upgrades I've got, so I'm really looking forward to the corrupting option on my second play through.
This game is good for the money. It will take your time, and you will be able to come back to it in the same way you're able to go back to a megaman or metroid game once you've forgotten the levels, except with this game you don't have to forget what with the procedural generation.

Time played: 13 hours
The criticisms of Sundered are valid. It's a massive scale Metroidvania Rogue-like that will feel boring at first when you don't have your powers and you're just slogging through swarms of enemies. The game massively improves once you acquire all your powers, then you're zipping around dodging and striking swarms of enemies. The game falls into the trap that some Rogue-likes do; in that it throws swarms of enemies at you with the belief that you'll be able to overcome it through stats.  The massive scale of the boss fights are incredibly fun and made the grinding worth the trouble.
The visuals and music are good, but will get samey fast unfortunately.
It is an above average game that could have been great.
Sundered could be better as a tighter game or with more variety. I enjoyed it, so in the end I recommend it. But if you don't have the patience to grind, you might find yourself regretting buying this game.

Legends of Grimrock 2 is a Dungeon Crawler with real-time combat, lots of riddles and secrets, magic and potions, all wrapped up in gorgeous graphics. I’ve just replayed it after a couple of years and it is still fantastic, the best dungeon crawler out there.
+ 77 secrets, 11 buried treasures, 17 “epic items” to find in 34 different areas
+ Lots of different enemies with various attack types and weaknesses
+ The game looks fantastic, the enemies and the different areas are very unique and memorable
+ Absolutely worth its money length-wise, easily 35 hours or more if you don’t play with a guide
+ An (optional) auto-map that allows you to make notes and mark places
+ Very fitting soundtrack, creepy sounds
+ You can build your own dungeon with the dungeon creator or play lots of fan-made dungeons!
o Some people might not like the real-time combat (It can get hectic but it is definitely doable. I’m a middle-aged woman who usually plays strategy or point-and-click adventure games and I just beat the game on hard; if I can do it you can, too)
- The weapons and magic system could have used some more balancing (for details see below)
You are stranded with a band of four on an island that is teeming with monsters and other hostile creatures. You hack and slash (and use spells, and shoot, bash, and throw things) your way through several dungeons and the extensive surface levels while gearing up because it is clear: If you want to get off of this blasted island, you will have to eventually confront the mysterious Island Master, who leaves you taunting messages and really seems to have it out for you.
There are two different endings and you can find a bit of lore in item descriptions and elsewhere but this is not a game you play for its elaborate story line.
You move in a grid-like fashion with WASD, move items around and push buttons etc with left mouse button, and use attacks or apply items with the right mouse button. Combat is real-time which can get hectic but weapons and spells have a cool-down period, so there is a limit to how fast you can attack and often it is more your movement rather than button spamming which decides a fight.
The game starts with assembling your group. There are several species (Human, minotaur, insectoid etc) and character classes (Barbarian, Knight, Wizard, Rogue, Alchemist etc) to choose from and to combine. The species have specific unique traits you can choose and different stats, the character classes determine some additional perks and which stats are increased when you level up. You also get a skill point each level-up that you can use to increase various things like accuracy, proficiency with different weapons or magic types etc.
Having a good group is extremely important and you can make the game very difficult for yourself if you don’t pay attention to the descriptions while assembling your group. My tip is to just play with the default group for an hour or two to get a feel for the game and then start a new game with your own group.
There are three different difficulty levels (“hard” is really hard, let me tell you) and a few different play modes that restrict how often you can save, for example, and an old school mode which has auto-mapping disabled because there are apparently enough people who like to punish themselves.
In one word: Fantastic. There are 77 secrets in this game, 11 buried treasures, 17 “epic items” to find. You’ll likely spend more time solving puzzles and looking for hidden buttons than fighting enemies.
There is an (optional) auto-map feature in the game that lets you mark puzzles you haven’t figured out, yet, so that you can return to them later. The game is not linear for the most part, almost all areas are open for you from the start. You’ll get murdered in an instance if you happen to enter an area that you’re supposed to leave for later in the game but there are always a few actually accessible areas you can go to while you think about a puzzle and maybe even find additional clues to solving it.
As I’ve said in my summary on top, there are a few balancing issues surrounding the weapons and spell system. Good heavy weapons are more frequent than strength- and dextery-based light weapons. There are only a handful different missile weapons in the game; one of the better ones is in a place where you have to choose between this very good bow (while not knowing its stats or how rare these are) and three other loot boxes containing also potentially very useful equipment.
Firearms are completely useless since their damage doesn’t scale with skillpoints and/or your stats. The most powerful firearm in the game requires a special ammunition of which you find less than 50 in the whole game. The most powerful spell in the game is fire magic. If you specialise on any other type you won’t get anything even remotely comparable.
The game is also extremely unforgiving if you put a skillpoint towards the “wrong” skill; especially for first-time players there is no way to know how many skillpoints you can expect to get or what you might need them for and it can happen that in the end you might have to choose between getting heavy armour proficiency and being able to use a really powerful spell (which you also didn’t know the requirements for) because way back at the start you put one point in athletics since extra health can’t be that bad, right?
A couple more available skillpoints really wouldn’t have hurt.
All of these are problems mainly for first-time players who don’t know these details but it is also bad for replayability since it leaves you with less choices in creating your group and picking their specialities, at least if you want to play optimally.

To be honest, this game could be the best Free2Play FPS out there, if the company, Crytek Kiev, knew how to actually run it.
I saw a lot of promise when I started this in May 2015, and what I heard about it before then, there were some decent changes and fixes.  As of now, Jan 2017, most every major issue is being ignored, the North American server is dying, only filled with majority Argentine players, or players that are not skilled enough to do any of the CoOp modes. If you don't care for any of that, then give it a try, just never, EVER, put any money into this game. It's easy enough to use most weapons, and if you live on the East Coast of the U.S. or Canada, or are a lagger from a South American country, you'll do fine.  The people who live on the West Coast and only get 1 or 2 bars of ping in-game got screwed when they moved the server (yeah, that's right, single server for the entire Continent) from Texas to Virginia, so we get the worst of it, because we do not benefit from the broken lag compensation at all.
I only still play this because I'm a masochist, and have so much time in it already, that I'm willing to watch it go down in flames (which feels pretty soon to me, if I'm being honest).  Like I said, if you live in or around Virginia, or live on the opposite side of the world from it, you'll have a good time.  PVE is a joke now, and PVP is only fun for the two groups I mentioned before.  If you hate yourself and live on the West Coast, this game is for you to beat yourself up even further.
Not gonna mention bugs, too many to count, some can be game-breaking, and it varies with every person.  Look at any forum page on their site to see what people complain about the most.
In conclusion, avoid until they fix their sh*t, which looks like may be never, so just avoid.

Final Fantasy 10 is one of the cringiest games I’ve ever played. The writing and dialogue is bad and the voiceacting is horrible, especially from the protagonist. There are a lot of laughs to be had playing this game in the so bad its good kind of way. It’s a very awkward game overall like the way characters react to certain situations and each other, those weird gaps of silence between lines of dialogue and the awful lip syncing, it all adds to the hilarity. The way they show expression is hilarious, it’s usually them saying AAH or OHH in a very over the top manner to what’s going on or replying to what somebody has said. There is a lot of grunting and someone saying ‘huh?’ a lot too… The dialogue can also be very annoying because almost every minute somebody says something that makes you go ‘Wtf?’ or ‘Why would you say that?’ or most of all ‘No sh*t Sherlock’. The characters love to point out the obvious, keep a counter of how many times they say ‘We have to defeat Sin’. The characters themselves are a mixed bag, Tidus is to me by far the worst protagonist in the series, worse than Squall, unbelievably unlikable, obnoxious and annoying. Other characters on the hand like Lulu and Auron I didn’t mind. The story has some good ideas but its ruined by the dialogue and voiceacting, just wasn’t able to get invested into any of it. The game has the best battle system in the series in my opinion, I thought the removal of the active time based system was a good move and switching between characters mid fight feels seemless as well as leveling up in the sphere grid. However I don’t have the patience to finish this game, the combat even though it’s the best in the series doesn’t not make up for how slow paced and boring everything else is. I was able to beat 4,6,7,8 and 9 but for some reason this game just drains me. It might be franchise fatigue or it might be the linearity of the game and how it’s 80% awful cutscenes and 20% gameplay (judging from the first 20 hours). I just can’t bring myself to invest more hours in a game that I dislike playing this much. The game relies on you to be invested in the story and characters and if you don't, what's the point of playing?...

I like Dark Souls 2 better compared to the first game in some aspects. I still think Dark Souls 1 is the better game.
Anyway Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the first Sin is an optional version of Dark Souls 2. It sports graphical improvements, all content dlc and some changes in enemy placement. Prepare to be surprised once more if you played the original version.
Buy this if you don't own Dark Souls 2 at all, this is where the pricing makes the most sense and it's a solid recommendation of mine.
If you miss the dlc for the original game buy this only on a discounted price, as you rebuy the original game. Otherwise just buy the season pass.
OR buy this if your friends play this version, as both versions work seperatly in multiplayer.
(EDIT:) as I can't review the DLCs on their respective page, I'll do it here from the view of a pve player:
Crown of the Sunken King
My least favorite of the three in terms of bossdesign. You'll encounter two Bosses at the end and one optional bossfight.
The two mainbosses are worth fighting though, they both reward you with two of my favorite weapons, as well as the namesake of the DLC.
You can argue about level and enemy design, I find it decent, even if it is annoying at times.
Keep your eyes open for secrets!
Crown of the Iron King
Has my overall favorite bosses in the entire game, the one and only main boss and two optional bosses.
Both of the later are annoying to find, but at least one is well worth it in my opinion.
The level and enemy design is ok...not my cup of tea.
You are rewarded with some great bossweapons. One is an all time favorite of mine.
Crown of the Ivory King
My favorite DLC of the bunch.
Everything you find affects your boss fighting experiences in some way. You have to go through the entire area (which is huge) twice, once where much of it is blocked and a second time when everything is free to explore.
The bosses are fun and the final boss is epic in my opinion, he reminds me a lot of the first game's endboss.
There's also an optional area, which in my opinion is too much of a pain to get through for a double boss fight with a recycled boss you have encountered in the same dlc. Once you fought the first one look up the rewards and decide for yourself if it's worth it.
All DLC hold many new items I always look forward to, some of them require long farming sessions in CotIK...
Overall good additional content, not the best, but better than other games had

You will read alot of negative reviews about microtransactions in this game.  Bullcrap.  Pure bullcrap.
Perhaps if you only get the 'basic' version you run into this problem:  I can see extra characters and tiles/monsters are available for money in game, but I was a fan of the boardgame and invested in the 'deluxe' version.  I've not been bothered for microtransactions, nor have I run into any paywalls.  I could BUY extra gold if I wanted...but there's absolutely zero need to.  Your characters are perfectly competitive without the extra help.
Now the game:  Turn based, based on a boardgame.  You control four characters and run them through a dungeon.  As you level up you pick up special abilities to help, and there are plenty of magic or special items, but this loot and kill scheme is pretty much it.
The four characters that come with the basic game are a marauder (barbarian/fighter type), dwarf ironguard (heavy fighter), elven...waywatcher? (bowman), and grey wizard.   This is a pretty good standard party composition.  All the deluxe pack adds here is more variety:  Ogre Irongut (massive damage fighter) or Archmage (another spellcaster) for example.
The game play is somewhat linear:  You go through a quest to find and get to new cities, and each city has a quest or two to go through.  Off the top of my head each adventure/quest takes around 30 minutes, so this is a good game when you need to kill a little time.  You earn experience for killing monsters, and get gold to buy supplies at market.  Hint:  Anything to do with healing is vital.
There are three levels of play:  Casual with easier combat - I suppose that's okay if you're new tot his genre or just experimenting.  Adventurer (I think...medium), and Hardcore.  In Hardcore you can permanently lose characters, whereas the others they're just knocked out for the adventure.  I prefer Hardcore for the sense of 'danger' it adds:   Just now, my party was TPKed.  In any other difficulty level, and most other games, I'd simply shrug and go back to my last save.  Now I have to keep going with new characters.  It changed my tactics towards the end as I realized I was going to lose, as now the objective became keeping one of my higher level characters alive long enough to escape.  (Damn zombies.)
If you're looking for a rich RPG with sandbox gameplay and side quests...no, that's not this game.   If you're in the mood for a throwback to when adventurers plundered dungeons, risked life and limb, and came out only to do it again next adventure?   This game and you can do business.  Don't worry about all this crap about microtransactions:  They're not there unless you WANT them to be there.

An absolutely delicious game! It's so engaging and complex for a cooking game! I would definitely recommend it if you're into cooking games and enjoy a challenge. The graphics are mouthwatering, and the recipes get more and more complicated as you upgrade them. You can set your own menu for your restaurant, you have to give 100 percent of hard work every second of the in-game day, to create positive buzz (popularity) from customers, and you have to invest in your restaurant in other ways except buying new equipment. It's quite realistic to a point. I won't spoil it further. The only annoying thing I've encountered is the "menu rot" thing, having to change the dishes in your menu every couple of days, I've seen other fans commenting on it. But come to think of it, it's great to get a fresh change in menu every other day, it keeps the game interesting and creative.
I also dislike how some of the negative buzz created by some menu items doesn't seem to be very realistic. Why would anyone mind for having alcohol on the menu? I'd say, in an office building, it's a plus.
I really love the music, it's so playful and it really keeps you engaged during rush hour, when you need to focus a lot in order to do a good job!
The customer animations and sounds are priceless. I like how they get more upper class too once you gain more stars for your restaurant.
I also love how there are a lot of in-game games, like the Iron Cook Challenge (think MasterChef).
This game is such a delight, it always demands more of you, it's a game you can truly try your best to play to perfection. Kudos to the creators for creating such fun, interesting and original content. And for making it truly challenging. I've been playing cooking games for a long time but this is by far my favorite.
For such a reasonably small price, considering the amount of game content (some of it, high-end dishes, recently added) this game is definitely worth trying out! It's a bargain, and a must-have for any foodie with a gaming passion! :)

Outlast is an indie first-person survival horror game where you play the role of Miles Upshur, a freelance journalist tipped-off by an anonyomus source to investigate Mount Massive Asylum, where a lot of really messed-up things are going on.
This is a stealth-based game and you are /completely/ defenseless -- the only options you have are to run and/or hide from the mental patients known as The Variants. The only item you have on your person is a camcorder which has night-vision capability, which you will need to utilize quite a lot to maneuver throughout the poorly-lit asylum. Of course, this requires battery power, those of which can be found scattered around in various places in the game -- use them wisely.
As terrifying as all hell as this game is, it's rather cliche as far as horror goes, and it's repetitive and very predicatble with the Variant encounters; you can usually always tell when an encounter is about to happen, sometimes just by simply surveying the area. Regardless, I still get scared because you have to move around through the darkness stealthily, having poor judgement on where the gore-lusting nutjob is lurking. This game also has its share of pop-out scares, which I hate and give me a heart attack every time.
The atmosphere is absolutely amazing. The game was inspired by mental asylums and real cases of mental illnesses, so the level design feels very genuine and authentic. The unnerving dark ambient soundtrack is excellent and really helps compliment the atmosphere of the game, There is heavy detail and lots of corpses, blood and guts lying around everywhere -- I often find myself staring at them because of how detailed they are.
Outlast has truly impressive graphics, very detailed sound effects, and is overall very dark and immersive. If you're looking for a scare, this game is pretty brutal.

The DLC is short - think Metro Last Light short.  Each story DLC is a couple of hours at best but your character actually gets a voice for the last 2 which just adds so much to him.
In short - buy it in a sale for a bit of fun - it won't blow your mind but its not as bad as it may appear based on reviews from when it was published.

Today marks one year since I founded Imperial Reviews and it seems quite fitting that I go back to my review writing roots so to speak and publish an article on the genre that I used to focus at the very start. A gorgeous 2D indie platformer once again. Sundered is the brainchild of Thunder Lotus Games, known until now as the developers of Jotun: Valhalla Edition. Well, their second Steam (& console) project shares its visual DNA with Jotun but other than that, it is an entirely different genre and experience. I was surprised to read that Sundered’s successful Kickstarter campaign, had amassed nearly ten times as much as its initial goal. If that doesn’t speak by itself about this developer and the expectations from their already established fanbase, then I don’t know what it might be.
From its very first minutes, Sundered introduces players into a fascinating and mystical post-apocalyptic world in which survival of the fittest seems to leave room for interpretation. The game’s protagonist isn’t exactly silent, but I’ll just consider her taciturn. Despite the sprite and the character clothing which may reflect ambiguity, the consensus is that Sundered has a heroine. Her name is Eshe and she seems like a cross between the Prince(ss) of Persia and Dirk the Daring (Sundered’s animation style did remind me of Dragon’s Lair afterall).
Please forgive the gender discrepancies. You may regard her as heroic as Shantae or Samus Aran instead. Following her odyssey through an unforgiving desert, Eshe gets captured by the mysterious Shining Trapezohedron (obvious H.P. Lovecraft influence) which tasks her with reactivating certain shrines within the ruins of former civilization. The reasons for this endeavour are as elusive as the entity whose now controlling Eshe’s destiny. A trapezohedron is a complex geometric figure by the way. I really appreciate the abstract elements to the storyline and how the lines between good and evil are blurred within Sundered.
I had to dig deep within the game files in order to have the confirmation that Sundered is indeed another Unity Engine project. Or I could have simply assumed this fact since Jotun shares the graphics and the hand-drawn, classic 2D animation. I grew up in the ‘90s so I may be biased towards “simpler times” when 3D animations were a far cry, but video games which emulate memories from my childhood are indeed a pleasure for me to play and look at. I couldn’t find a single flaw to the visual style no matter how hard I tried searching for one. Sundered is both a sight to behold and a stable gaming experience. The fonts & sprites are upscaling nicely to my native resolution of 3840x2160 and the frame rate never dropped below 60, no matter how many foes Eshe was fighting simultaneously.
The soundtrack is top notch and the sound effects are on par, but I was really pleased by the voice acting, particularly that of the Shining Trapezohedron. Its voice resembled the Semitic language group but I think it was fictional in the end. Constructed languages count among my many interests, so the dev team’s efforts have been duly noted by yours truly. Few platformers contain noteworthy sound assets and the ones on Steam suffer from this even more so. Indie devs simply can reach the Nintendo level of quality (budgetary constraints and all) but I think Thunder Lotus Games are an exception which proves the rule.
Since I already mentioned Nintendo, it seems that Sundered is another fine example of “Metroidvania”: a subgenre of the action-adventure which draws gameplay inspiration from the eponymous Metroid or Konami’s Castlevania series. It goes without saying that difficulty plays center stage in the aforementioned classics as it does in Sundered’s case as well. Trial & error are deeply imbedded in both the story and gameplay. As one of the messages from the loading screens boldly states: “Even death won’t save you from this place”. It is in fact, just another phase through which you must travel and at the end of that proverbial tunnel, the heroine only emerges stronger and more determined.
In-game fatalities result in a return to the Shining Trapezohedron Sanctuary and its eloquently named Trapezohedron (Skill) Tree where Eshe can spend shards (consider it currency, if you will) on upgrades which she will surely need if she wishes to advance and eventually defeat the hordes of abstract enemies standing between her and the coveted shrines. These crucial shards shall be obtained through combat, once defeated foes reveal them or by breaking certain objects such as glass cyclinders. What, you thought that only Link has to smash pots in order to better himself? Aptly named as hordes since the enemies will constantly try to swarm the protagonist whose magical shield, shatters almost as fast as her health bar.
Eshe’s journey is both perilous and tedious at times. Sad indeed, since the game’s superb looks have to mired by repetitiveness. Combat, enemy variety, locations, you name it. And backtracking is just another nail in the coffin at this point. Pun is intended since death shall return you to the Sanctuary and after you spend shards on new upgrades, guess what? Here comes the long road towards the last place you died and hopefully THIS time, you’ll fare better. You have a lot of time to reflect on that as you backtrack in a useless manner which could have been entirely averted if only Sundered would have implemented even the most basic form of automated progress saving. Checkpoints, naturaly. A gameplay mechanic that has been around for almost two decades. Why is it not present here?
I did mark the difficulty as a weak point, even if I am aware that Eshe has to perish and “respawn” in order to improve himself. I can understand gaming difficulty just for the sake of it. Of course I’m a fan of the Dark Souls series and that sort of digital punishment isn’t without its merit. And there are platformers on Steam, far more difficult than Sundered. Super Meat Boy and Shio come to mind. But I have to acknowledge sadly, that even its lowest tier called “Normal” seems like an insurmountable achievement  at times. Why is “Easy” used so rarely today, is it some sort of fake validation intent, as if playing the easy mode was not worthy of some gamers?
I really don’t want to lower Sundered’s rating any further than this, since the game is highly entertaining, beautiful and the potential to right some of its wrongs is there. Checkpoints could be added in a subsequent update I hope? They are crucial in the long run and players will appreciate them even more, if they are implemented soon. As for the price tag, it certainly doesn’t feel overpriced and it includes Steam auxiliaries from day one. Say what you will about Sundered, but it’s an obvious step forward for 2D indie platformers. Quality and beauty mixed with difficulty which in turn simply masks the true sense of progression. The game’s motto mirrors this. Resist or Embrace.
+ Gorgeous art style and soundtrack.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.
+ In-game death as a means of progression.
- Unbalanced difficulty even on its lowest tier.
- Too much backtracking.
- No save checkpoints.

Sundered is a metroidvania, action-platformer that features hand-drawn animation and lovecraftian impossible-to-pronounce dialect, made by those who worked on Jotun.  This review aims to inform users of what the game is and debate a controversial topic, hordes.
In sundered, Eshe's (the main character you play as) main form of attack and one you can use infinitely is her melee with which she has a basic 5-hit combo, an air combo which can maintain your elevation indefinitely if hitting an enemy (also refreshes double jump), a downwards thrust that deals a fair amount of damage while sending Eshe to the ground and an uppercut which she can also use as a platforming element to gain a bit of height to reach a platform if you narrowly miss it.  Her attack's wide sweep double as a means of dishing out damage and by stun-locking multiple opponents momentarily.  The combat is easy enough for even most beginners to grasp and allows you to pay attention to the surrounding area to identify the enemies that don't run straight at you and those that cannot be stun-locked so easily (mostly flying enemies that fire projectiles/ charge at you).  There's plenty of dodging and important tactical decision the player needs to make to successfully survive many of the encounters.  Most of it boils down to knowing if you fight off the horde given your current prediciment, whether your health's too low, location is getting badly swarmed, flying enemies are off-screen, or if you start getting some lilith versions of enemies (theses are essentially mini-boss esque dudes that don't tons of damage)  After dying a lot through trial and error you should be able to have a firm enough grasp of the game to understand how to work about these scenarios.  It should be noted that there are a plethora of additional abilities and perks to equip that increases the combat depth and allows for some truly stellar combos to be displayed, several of which are suited towards the massive hordes you fight throughout the journey.
The game is pretty damn huge, boasting a 23 hour long campaign first playthrough and a 46 hour long 100% achievement run-through (I played on hard initially and insane afterwards) with randomly generating levels in-between objectives to keep each playthrough of the game unique and exciting as you weave through treasure chests and the suspense of staying alive as the game slowly tries to engulf you in an overwhelming force.  Areas are unique in both visuals and level layouts, the bottom path opts for cubical level layout, the left path has almost a maze-like pattern where each cardinal direction is used within each contained "box" to offer additional challenge and the right path which has the most breadth and distance between each location housing near double the size of the former two paths.  The stark contrast between each of the areas also allows for the hand-drawn aspect to really shine.  Backtracking is required for every death but the areas are relatively close enough to make your ascent/descent shorter than the last (mostly due to you knowing exactly where you need to go after you respawn) I gauruntee you'll make progress with each subsequent death.  You know what's also pretty damn huge?  The bosses.  There's plenty of them and they're all rewarding-to-kill and massive in scale, they really show the beauty of the hand-drawn visuals as they dwarf your character by comparison, simultaneously showing the strong force that Eshe carries with her throughout her journey.
The biggest positive with the bosses is definitely the music associated with each. The game dynamically changes the music to suit the mood and really gets your adrenaline pumping in the finale.  It also makes your but clench as you narrowly dodge a monolithic beast slamming down towards you in the 2nd boss. The progressive chanting of Dominion, the thunderous slam + footsteps of Hysteria and the final moments of Splice really resonated with me.﻿
The game throws hordes and hordes of enemies at you when you least expect it, most of these hordes range from easy to difficult but managable to even near-impossible.  Most people will argue that it's unfair and bad  game design to have the later but i'm here to argue that it's sufficient to use here for a variety of reasons in the below bullet points.
(Hordes)
- Now why did I say earlier in the review that the occasional near-difficult enemy waves suit this game?   One of the biggest reasons I assume why they did this was to enforce the idea of showing you what the ruined world of Sundered is all about, overwhelming forces of enemies that want you to leave their home, but the game refuses you leave, you're better than this, you'll laugh in the face of danger, heck you laugh at the face of certain death!  You'll get more powerful, more apt in dealing with these issues and truly prevail to experience what this massive game has to offer at any damned cost! ... *Ahem* got a bit carried away.
- The game is of course very tough as i've detailed, while the player may choose at any time to return to the main hub it's very important that the player is spending their cash into the appropriate upgrades since the game is designed around your progression (I'm sure the game could be completed with none of them if you're a true masochist but that's aside the point).  By refusing to upgrade, you limit your ability greatly and are obviously making the game way more difficult and frustrating than intended.  Some may argue that the game feeds money and improved stats to the player, I honestly believe that the player must earn the money on their own by finding treasure chests and destroying enemies to acquire said gold while also getting better at the game as time goes on.
- Dying teaches you what you did wrong, I admit this is somewhat of a cliche/general argument that can apply to a multitude of games but it also applies to Sundered, I can't count the number of times I was too trigger-happy to use dashes to only get away (when I could've also been using them to dodge enemies) Plus, times I should've ran from the horde instead of fighting it throughout, the game is generally very clear in telling the player when you need to run, whether it be your health or how much the enemies are hitting you.
I will admit that the horde-style is NOT perfect and is often beyond the capability of the player to escape some situations, however it's clear that the devs are working hard to remedy this issue.  I played the game in hard and replayed the game in insane but recommend you play through normal if you want the most enjoyable version of the game.  I look forward towards the promise of new DLC, really enjoyed my experience with this one.
Will you RESIST or EMBRACE Sundered?
The choice is yours.

If you liked the first Grimrock but thought it was a bit easy or you just love dungeon crawlers you'll probably really enjoy this game. Combat requires good awareness of environment and individual enemy behaviours, movement, and weaknesses vs. simple side stepping that, at times, made the first game's combat boring or too easy. End game boss actually feels like an end game boss and provides a challenge that requires a nice level of strategy and planning. The downside maybe being that the jump in difficulty curve was definitely high, but, personally, prefer that over the sudden drop in difficulty the boss of the first game had. Only complaint is that it would be nice if there was a simpler way to have quick access to potions and other consumbable items than the hotkeys for character menus or taking up the alternative gear spaces, as they are rather essential for times when your party is weaker or during bosses, and seconds can matter in battle.
Some puzzles can be rather difficult, it felt like a nice upgrade from the puzzles of the first game and there is good variety. There is something to be said about making it more clear if you have or should have run across the appropriate scrolls/hints needed to solve certain ones yet though. This can mean a lot of back tracking, which may not be everyone's cup, but also provides ways to help build levels that will be needed to progress to areas with more difficult enemies, as some enemies respawn and some locations provide new sets of them after certain events (and gives more opportunities to look at the rather lovely environments). There is often secret secondary routes that take a lot of the pain out of any back tracking. Making notes on the map for hints you can't take with you can save a lot of time and make finding certain secrets much easier, it would be nice if this was automatic though as memorization and note taking feel like rather arbitrary ways to add difficulty to a modern game. Appropriately, the hardest puzzles are typically reserved for secret areas and bonus gear not needed to complete the game. Overall they were very good and stepping away and coming back to them later was often enough to make things click for the harder ones.
Side note, light spoilers:
You may run into a bug with one of the puzzles in the pyramid if you are very unlucky. There is a puzzle where you must place the correct items on the correct sarcophagi, but after verifying in multiple guides and videos that it had been done correctly, found out that the puzzle simply just wasn't opening a door it was supposed to. Unfortunately, found little word from anyone else (either here or the official forums) having the exact issue and, having no earlier saves, had to use a console command to bypass the door. Considering the amount of bugs in most games and that the pyramid is technically optional just this one wasn't that offputting, but feel it deserves a fair warning.

Awesome, TRULY F2P TCG for steam or android. Eternal's game play is very similar to Magic the Gathering.
Decks are composed of a variety of different cards with unique powers and divided into several factions represented by a color (black, blue, yellow, green and red). Decks can range in size from 75 to 150, but at least 33% of the deck must consist of 'sigils' which are played for free and become the main resource pool from which one plays cards (ie lands or mana).
Gameplay procedes with each player turn having 3 phases: pre-attack, attack and post attack. Sigils, spells and new units can be played in either of the pre- or post- attack phases. When you do decide to attack, the defender chooses how their units will block. There are also a variety of 'fast spells' which can be played instantaneously, even if it isn't the caster's turn.

The cards themselves are interesting, seemingly cost effective and balanced. The feel and theme of each color faction feels on point and the variety of cards allows for several different strategies.
As we move into the 3rd major expansion and 3 Campaigns, card balance still seems fairly even overall. Additionally, DWD has made several changes to existing cards, making them more competative and powerful, rather than relying on using the nerfbat (ie... reducing the effectiveness of trendsetting cards).

Eternal is constantly adding more free content all the time, currently it now offers 8 game modes, instead of 5.
I've only been playing for a few months and I already have most of the cards that are currently available, which makes ranked matches very even - relying on strategy and tactial prowess rather than card rarity. The fact that the game can be played on PC or on mobile is fantastic and the gameplay is just fun, interactive and seems pretty balanced overall.
Really looking forward to future expansions! Keep up the good work!

Worthwhile if you're interested in Early Access to a work in progress flight simulator and want to help DTG improve their product. Flight Sim World is playable as-is and no doubt will be improving and adding functionality over time. The default aircraft have payware quality modeling and texturing and with good flight dynamics for the most part. Personally I think he PA28 Cherokee purchased standalone as an FSX addon would cost you more than this entire simulator. I found the program is quite stable even with Ultra graphics settings (compared to FSX which tends to freeze or crash on high graphics settings).
Visual effects such as cockpit shadows and windshield rain effects are very immersive and I think the best I've seen in any simulator.
There are some bugs but nothing that I found prevented me from having lots of fun and successful flights. Content-wise there's a good selection of missions to try out plus flying lessons if you are an aviation novice (in which case I also recommend looking at YouTube for some introductory videos just to get your bearings). If you like to tinker a little, this product also includes Pro Mission Editor which is an excellent program worth the purchase price on its own and makes it easy to create your own flying scenarios and challenges. The mission editor is based on FSXME in case you are interested and looking for documentation and tutorials, just Google search for FSXME or FSX Mission Editor.
Despite all the positives I'll also point out some attributes that we're left hoping that DTG will get to either with upcoming updates or followup release versions:
- The terrain engine itself plus scenery elements such as landclass is the same as FSX. Apparently airports and some Nav Data has been updated, and also landclass textures and autogen are from Orbx. Airport textures for things like buildings and runways do not appear to have been updated. In addition I feel that the lighting has changed from FSX but the Orbx textures were not tuned accordingly, so overall the scenery is needing some attention. If you are more concerned with scenery eye candy than with flying, you might want to wait until DTG does more work in that area. For this first release they appear to be much more focused on aircraft modeling, physics and weather.
- ATC so far is VFR only. There are some IFR capable aircraft but if you want to fly in bad weather you are on your own
- Weather themes plus only very basic weather settings only so far. No real-world weather or detailed weather configuration yet but this seems to be high on DTG's list
- Performance in terms of FPS is not great, particularly in very dense scenery areas. This is another thing DTG expects to be improving on in the near term.
- In-flight changes to weather or date/time not possible yet.
- My understanding is that night lighting is poor, though I haven't done any night flying yet. Dusk and dawn look good.
- The flight planner has potential to be far better than FSX, but for now it's still very basic. Contrary to what some people say it IS possible to see a map in-flight, just hit P for pause and click on the Flight Planning tab and then on the map, you can see your flight plan and the aircraft position, but it's still not possible to click on an airport to get info on runways or radio frequencies. You can look up this information in the GPS however (at least with the G1000 I've been able to).
- AI seems rather poor. So much so I just turned it off, I'm not much of an AI fan anyway. Maybe if they upgrade the ATC system then AI will be worthwhile
- No cold and dark startup states or beginning a flight from a parking space, unless you slew the plane yourself to  parking and shut it down.
- Other than the Mission Editor, no SDK is available unless you're partnering with DTG. DTG has not revealed what they will be offering in the way of a public SDK or what access freeware developers (of which I am one) will have.
Despite the above limitations I'm enjoying FSW and look forward to seeing it mature into a fun flight simming platform.

I like Dark Souls 2 better compared to the first game in some aspects. I still think Dark Souls 1 is the better game.
Anyway Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the first Sin is an optional version of Dark Souls 2. It sports graphical improvements, all content dlc and some changes in enemy placement. Prepare to be surprised once more if you played the original version.
Buy this if you don't own Dark Souls 2 at all, this is where the pricing makes the most sense and it's a solid recommendation of mine.
If you miss the dlc for the original game buy this only on a discounted price, as you rebuy the original game. Otherwise just buy the season pass.
OR buy this if your friends play this version, as both versions work seperatly in multiplayer.
(EDIT:) as I can't review the DLCs on their respective page, I'll do it here from the view of a pve player:
Crown of the Sunken King
My least favorite of the three in terms of bossdesign. You'll encounter two Bosses at the end and one optional bossfight.
The two mainbosses are worth fighting though, they both reward you with two of my favorite weapons, as well as the namesake of the DLC.
You can argue about level and enemy design, I find it decent, even if it is annoying at times.
Keep your eyes open for secrets!
Crown of the Iron King
Has my overall favorite bosses in the entire game, the one and only main boss and two optional bosses.
Both of the later are annoying to find, but at least one is well worth it in my opinion.
The level and enemy design is ok...not my cup of tea.
You are rewarded with some great bossweapons. One is an all time favorite of mine.
Crown of the Ivory King
My favorite DLC of the bunch.
Everything you find affects your boss fighting experiences in some way. You have to go through the entire area (which is huge) twice, once where much of it is blocked and a second time when everything is free to explore.
The bosses are fun and the final boss is epic in my opinion, he reminds me a lot of the first game's endboss.
There's also an optional area, which in my opinion is too much of a pain to get through for a double boss fight with a recycled boss you have encountered in the same dlc. Once you fought the first one look up the rewards and decide for yourself if it's worth it.
All DLC hold many new items I always look forward to, some of them require long farming sessions in CotIK...
Overall good additional content, not the best, but better than other games had
