The survival horror genre has been getting flooded with mediocrity after Amnesia the Dark Descent raised the bar and received critically acclaimed awards.   The developers at Red Barrels have taken notes and broke the trend by creating a worthy experience in Outlast.
The story, setting, atmospheric lighting, and ambient sounds in Outlast will keep you in constant tension.  While the jump scares and adrenaline pumping chase segments will get  you reaching for the esc key to take a break.
The game play in Outlast can become a little repetitious as most levels boil down to doing the same thing, which is find 3 keys / switches / fuses and unlock door to next area.  Although it's very formulaic, the variations in the areas you explore keep it interesting, exciting, and most importantly creepy.  While I enjoyed the key hunting and ensuing chases, I would have loved to see more depth in the puzzles by additional inventory management and clues found in notes.
The story of Outlast may be considered cliche, but I really loved the way the story is told.  You play a reporter sent in to investigate strange going ons, and by recording specific imagery with your camcorder you document the horrors.  Along the way you'll also find case files scattered about revealing backstory details.  It fits perfectly into the situation and doesn't seem as oddly out of place as voxaphone recordings laying around Bioshock.
So, in the year that brought us another Amnesia game Outlast outshines the competition.  In my opinion it was outstanding and worthy of any survival horror fan's time.  Looking forward to the prequel  Whistleblower DLC, which tells the story of an employee who contacts your character to start the events of Outlast.

In Sundered you play as female protagonist Eshe in a mysterious and desolate dimension which you are dragged to by an even more mysterious entity.
The game is made up of three worlds.
All worlds is huge and vast with their own unique environment, flora and monsters.
A world is made up of huge sectors which then contains a vast amount of different sized rooms.
You explore these rooms and unlock new paths and short-cuts as you venture forth.
It is also here you will find treasures, perks, abilities and of course the hordes of monsters.
You will wander about only to be ambushed by small groups of monsters while evading traps and other hazardous elements. Treasures is gently spread across the rooms and will grant you lots of shards which is used for upgrades and perks which is key to survival.
Then you will hear the sound of the Gong ring and this means a Horde has gotten the scent of you. Prepare for a fight or try to flee if you feel overwhelmed. Do not underestimate their initial numbers as soon you will have your whole monitor filled to the edges with monsters, while Eshe is desperately slashing and dashing in order to survive. If you are really (un)lucky a 'Lith' version of a monster will appear. While being super tough, they might drop things that you will fancy.
Progression is a maze and farming is obligatory. Perks are 'emblems' that you can find, upgrade and use to aid you in your quest. A perk might give you more Shield, HP, more Shard drop rate and so on. However every Perk has a positive effect as well as a negative effect. Don't panic as the positive effect always outweights the negative. While the story progress you will be able to equip up to 3 Perks and combine their strengths.
Then you will find Ability Shrine rooms that contains an altar which grants you 1 new ability. These abilities grants key powers that not only makes you stronger and faster, but opens up new pathways that you could not cross before.
In order to reach the Main Bosses of each worlds you have to destroy their mini-bosses who roams the sectors in certain rooms. These mini-bosses are strong enemies that needs to be taken down. The Main Bosses are even stronger, but epic and awesome.
Decide to resist, or embrace, as you move on and fight hordes of enemies to reach your mysterious goal. The game only gets more tough and the monsters more vile, but with some good preparation, necessary back-tracking and shard farming you will find yourself strong and agile and Eshe will slash through the hordes with amazing powers. Do not let your guard down however, because despite even the greatest of powers, this odd dimension will show no mercy and will suddenly lash out and kill you.
-Great game.
-Great graphics, design of monsters and environment.
-Good controls
-Difficult, but farming can make you so strong it becomes easy. You can always get stronger.
-Nice ability and skill system. Very entertaining to unlock skills in the huge skill tree.
-Farming is actually fun!
-Great story with 3 endings.
-All in all a really well made game
People complain about difficulty is too hard. I do not agree, but then again some people might find it hard and some do not. I just think that most of those who find it hard has not understood (I say this friendly) that you have to farm and unlock more skills in order to get stronger. The farming and unlocking skills is a big part of this game. Honestly if you have to correct Perks and some skills unlocked (skills can be more HP, Strength, Shield and so on) the game is not THAT hard and even quite easy at times. Of course it will be harder the further you go, but about that time you should be good to fight and evade.
Recommended!

I really wish I could recommend this game.  Unfortunately, the game falls flat both as a metroidvania and as a rogue-like platformer.  The biggest problem I had with the game was the enemies.  Instead of having enemies placed smartly around the level and placed as an obstacle, the game decides to randomly throw 10-15 enemies at you randomly while you're exploring that swarm you.  It's very difficult to get away from them because some may charge you while others shoot lasers at you that can go through walls.  Some might say this is a challenge, but in my opinion, it's just lazy.  In action-platformers like this, one of the most important things is enemy placement.  Good enemy placement can make or break a game, and in the case of Sundered, it absolutely ruins it.  Getting swarmed by hordes of enemies randomly is not fun.  It's extremely frustrating since they can drain your health extremely fast since there is little to no invincibily after getting hit.  Exploring is also extremely boring as a result of their decision to throw enemies at you randomly instead of having them placed througout the level.  You'll go for a while during your time exploring without encountering any enemies.  It's just running with extremely basic platforming and having to dodge the occassional environmental hazard.  There is nothing interesting going on and the game quite literally goes from 0 to 100 in a matter of seconds from running around to getting swarmed by enemies.
This game is so close to being amazing.  The visuals and sound design are great.  The one boss I fought was a lot of fun due to the combat being fun mechanically, it's just fighting 10-15 enemies at a time is not fun.  Due to the insane decision to have enemy encounters be seemingly random, the game just becomes frustrating to play.  If you are looking for a game that merges rogue-likes and Metroidvanias, Dead Cells is your better option.  While that game is still in Early Access, it's a thousand times more fun than Sundered.

I make this comparison as I notice that the horde mechanic fuctions very simarly to Risk Of Rain. Enemies randomly spawn to try to take you down while you explore randomized environments, basically the more enemies you kill and the longer you stay alive the worse the horde of enemies gets.
-The game is gorgeous, it's more beautiful than Hollow Knight and Ori and The Blind Forest.
-The combat and abilities are fun
-The skill tree/upgrade system is great and permanent
-The controls are responsive
-It has a unique lovecraftian setting
-Great soundtrack
-Great hand-drawn animation
-Awesome bosses
-Long load times after death (even with ssd)
-Game doesn't do a great job of explaining how to progress/objectives not clear
-The hordes can get annoying when you want to explore, forcing you to run from an area
-Protagonist is silent with no background, explanation to involvement or reason of being involved
All in all, this is a good game but has it's share of issues (just as any Metroidvania game really). I find that the game does an excellent job of explaining some things and a horrible job of explaining others and I fear that it's with the excuse of "Non-linear progression" or "No hand-holding". I've played plenty of non-hand holding games but I feel like something is missing with this game. I think this is my only REAL issue with the game, I wish things were clearer so that I can progress faster and not question what the hell I am doing and for what reason.
So what keeps me playing? Well I realize that this game (like Risk Of Rain), is a time-sinker, I know I'm going to have to spend hours and hours before any real progression occurs - especially the 1st playthrough... regardless of it being a 15 hour game with multiple endings. The lovecraftian theme, the fear of the unknown and the insanely cool abilities. If it wasn't for those three things then to be honest, I'd probably refund this game but I do find myself wanting to move forward and progress the character even though very little is known about the character causing me not to care much about their well-being in general compared to other games.
I will say that Sundered is a huge step-up from Jotun though, and for that I congratulate the developers on. I see the mixed reviews but this is really a good game that should be up there with Hollow Knight and Dead Cells - at least it is for me as far as Metroidvania genre goes.

Awesome, TRULY F2P TCG for steam or android. Eternal's game play is very similar to Magic the Gathering.
Decks are composed of a variety of different cards with unique powers and divided into several factions represented by a color (black, blue, yellow, green and red). Decks can range in size from 75 to 150, but at least 33% of the deck must consist of 'sigils' which are played for free and become the main resource pool from which one plays cards (ie lands or mana).
Gameplay procedes with each player turn having 3 phases: pre-attack, attack and post attack. Sigils, spells and new units can be played in either of the pre- or post- attack phases. When you do decide to attack, the defender chooses how their units will block. There are also a variety of 'fast spells' which can be played instantaneously, even if it isn't the caster's turn.

The cards themselves are interesting, seemingly cost effective and balanced. The feel and theme of each color faction feels on point and the variety of cards allows for several different strategies.
As we move into the 3rd major expansion and 3 Campaigns, card balance still seems fairly even overall. Additionally, DWD has made several changes to existing cards, making them more competative and powerful, rather than relying on using the nerfbat (ie... reducing the effectiveness of trendsetting cards).
I can only imagine that this trend will continue, with new mechanics, factions and deck strategies emerging as time goes on.


I usually play Hearthstone, so when I started playing Eternal I was downright SHOCKED by the generosity of their reward structures!
In addition to the daily quests and random chest upgrades, DWD has instituted a 'Win of the Day' reward... awarding the player with a pack of the latest expansion on their first win of the day.

Eternal is constantly adding more free content all the time, currently it now offers 8 game modes, instead of 5.
I've only been playing for a few months and I already have most of the cards that are currently available, which makes ranked matches very even - relying on strategy and tactial prowess rather than card rarity. The fact that the game can be played on PC or on mobile is fantastic and the gameplay is just fun, interactive and seems pretty balanced overall.
Really looking forward to future expansions! Keep up the good work!

Just Cause 2 is, indeed, an open world sandbox action-adventure game in which you play a slick Latino hombre named Rico Mother♥♥♥♥ing Rodriguez (I'm pretty sure that's his real name), who, in the words of Ben "Yahtzee" Croshaw, possesses two superpowers: one, to shoot steel cables from a scorpion-shaped apparatus on his left arm like some kind of gritty Spider-Man, and two, to pull an infinite number of parachutes out of his♥♥♥♥♥

If you played and enjoyed the first game, you should enjoy this one. It expands on all of the concepts of the first, and improves on many of the mechanics in my opinion.
Exploring dungeons is as fun as it's ever been, and now there is an overworld of sorts to keep you interested in the overarching goal and plot of the game: which is to find the 4 elemental orbs to unlock the castle in the middle of the island.
The essential gameplay hasn't really changed dramatically, and in my opinion the combat tends to be pretty boring, as was the case in the first game. It's a lot of positioning yourself to avoid attacks, and while there are some enemy weaknesses to exploit, but they are few and far between. For the most part, you will be side-stepping enemies in a little dance as you chip away at their health until they die. There are a *few* instances of interesting combat scenarios, but most of them boil down to this. Not very much strategy to the combat.
If you don't mind the tedium of the fighting, the exploration and puzzle-solving is as fun as always, and the addition of the map has made recovering treasure and solving puzzles a much more rewarding process. And there are a handful of very fun and clever puzzles in here. Most of them are very obvious in their solution, however.
I feel this game would have been nearly perfect if they refined the combat and made the scenarios a little more interesting, and given more focus to difficult puzzles. As it stands, it is an enjoyable adventure, and the graphics are beautiful. It does ultimately get a bit tedious, though.

{{{FULL DISCLOSURE: I have strong ties with a member of the Dev Team, I was given a copy and my voice is featured in the game. I'm one of the Brit soldiers, if you must know which}}}
I have played very little of the game, given that my voice is in it, it would feel weird to hear my own voice yelling at me for being insignificant and weak, but the very little time I have spent in it, I found a fairly well made game, with realistically modelled weapons.
The weapon models have had a lot of attention to detail lavished on them, and given that I've had a behind the scenes look at some of it (I can't say much as I'm under an NDA), I've seen the almost autistic level of attention to detail the team puts into their work in this regard, though having said...
...Where the maps are concerned, I feel there could be more detail put into the ground itself, more debris, pebbles, heck even partially buried helmets etc, the trench entrances themselves for instance could do with looking more dug out than smoothed off.
Another area I think could be improved is in the sound department, I feel the gunfire should be somewhat louder, and a the audio a lot punchier, from what I played there didn't seem to be many echoes, and given you're in the trenches, and open fields of Verdun, Flanders and The Somme, you'd expect to hear more echoes than you do.
All in all, I do have to recommend this game if you're looking for something a bit more grounded in realism, but take my fairly meager review with a pinch of salt, as I said, I'm likely to be highly biased, given my ties to this game and the devs that made it.

***THE TRUTH ABOUT MICROTRANSACTIONS AND THIS GAME:***
A lot of discussion about the "pay to play" microtransactions. Developers say they are "completely optional." This is halfway a lie.
The truth is that around level 4-5 you get to a point where you must buy additional gold for this game or else you will be stuck in a grind where you are raiding dungeons WITHOUT gaining experience. "How is this possible?" you say. Well, you must pay gold to level your heroes. If you don't pay to level them up, any XP they gain is *lost* until you do(!).
In my game, I did not buy a single item, but saved all gold so that I would not have to be stuck in the rut. But I was still stuck by a long shot (looking at 15-20 dungions to grind through without gaining XP if I don't break out the credit card and pay to play).
***FAQ***
-Q: Is what you say also true of the deluxe edition?
-A: Yes. Even at 25€ the game is still rigged to get you to use the credit card if you don't want to waste all XP on ~30% of the levels you play (after reaching level 4-5).
-Q: Why do I need to pay to level up? Don't heroes in fantasy games level up once you have *earned* the experience?
-A: Yes, it is deliberately desinged this way as a way to get the player to fork over more money.
-Q: Is it true that even the deluxe edition, has no PC-support?
-A: Yes, it's a blind mobile port. Keyboard doesn't work at all. Forget about WASD and arrow keys, let alone hotkeys.

I was excited to see Warhammer Quest coming to the PC, having enjoyed the original board game many times. Unfortunately I'm sorry to say I don't have much that is positive to say about this version.
On the gameplay side:
Short version: it does not do the original game justice, it's not quite the same, as other reviews say "a simplification", and some mechanics have been rename which is a bit alienating to existing Warhammer Quest fans.
-The combat mechanics are OK (they have the deathblow mechanics in there), but for some reason your characters don't have an initiative order. Since it's a PC version of the board game it would also be nice to be able to see the dice (maybe even throw them by moving the mouse)!
-The treasure, spells and equipment are not implemented in the same way as the board game, they are simplified a bit. Equipment is weird, you can only equip a certain number of items of a particular rarity that will be available during combat on each. I'm guessing they saw this as a balance thing... so they can kill you off more easily, or something.
-Also where is character generation? You pick your party of four, from the four basic characters and any DLC characters you have bought, with random names you can rename (Feels a bit more like recruiting). I don't know if some of the DLC charactor are more intesting to "recruit" but things are missing like the Wizard getting to choose some random spells, at the moment you always get the same starting spells.
-Levelling is also a bit different, feels slower to get gold than the original game, like they want you to use real money to buy their DLC gold...
-Hot-seat or multi-play is missing complelty! At the moment I don't think the game is interesting enough to play with multiple people (without the lite character generation that the board game had it would be hard for a group of people to have much attachment to their characters).
Comments on the user interface/engine:
Short version: a lazy PC port.
-No-vertical sync!!!  The game is running at over 1000FPS on my computer.... I really don't need to burn out my GPU playing a board game on my PC.
-The interface is odd. So the game was first released for a touch screen interface, it seems like they have made zero effort to make it suitable for a PC. It took me ages to work out how to open my inventory. It's an RPG, whycan't I press 'I' for inventory.
-The artwork is very mixed. Some parts are nice, the world map, and backgrounds, and there are a few nice animations, but there are lots of things that feel like they should be animated on the UI that are not. The 3D models in the dungeons are adequate (who managed to paint all their miniatures for the original board game anyway?).  I found the board sections are a bit poor (resolution wise) especially given some of the other bits of art in the GUI, and town.
-The biggest disappointment for me in the artwork was the lack of art from the original game, I would have liked to see the classic treasure cards, and spell cards, and some of the classic boards sections.
Summary:
Not a re-make of the original board game (it's simplified), there is also an aspect that it feels a bit like they want to milk you for money on DLC or gold. It's a mobile phone game ported to a PC. If you have not played the original Warhammer Quest you might want this game on your phone.

Dark Souls 2 is one of the most captivating games I've ever played in my life. It really is one of those games that takes hold of you until you finally finish it. It's one hell of a challenge, and while sometimes seemingly unfair, it’s completely worth pushing through for an unparalleled feeling of accomplishment and the fascinating and beautiful environments. Almost every location in the game is breathtaking, with some of my favorites being Heide’s Tower of Flame, Iron Keep and Shrine of Amana. Chances are you'll want to keep going regardless because of how much fun the combat is. Think along the lines of a more developed version of the combat you’d find in a 3D Zelda game.
There’s tons of optional content in the game for those who want more during/after the main story. It’s worth mentioning the included DLC from the original game in the Scholar of the First Sin edition. It’s definitely a nice touch and makes for excellent post-campaign content. After you finish everything else the game has to offer, new game plus is always there for you to venture through, or alternatively you can always start a new game with another character and play through the game with a completely different playstyle. Perhaps you want to dual wield greatswords this time, or even play a ranged character that deals devastating amounts of magic damage. The vast amount of playstyle possibilities keeps the game fresh and interesting on repeated playthroughs and acts as an even greater incentive for the player to return to the world of Drangleic once again. Not to mention the game is enjoyable on a different level once you are familiar with all the levels, and makes for a much quicker round two.
If you can't tell already I love Dark Souls 2. It really did check all of my boxes and enthralled me into its massive world. This game is not for everyone though; those with low tolerance for high difficulty games will likely find this one too frustrating to enjoy. That said, if you are up for the challenge, Dark Souls 2 is an incredible game that you have to experience the whole way through. Just remember: don’t give up until the end. You’ll see why I love it so much. With all of that said, I can't recommend this one enough.

The survival horror genre has been getting flooded with mediocrity after Amnesia the Dark Descent raised the bar and received critically acclaimed awards.   The developers at Red Barrels have taken notes and broke the trend by creating a worthy experience in Outlast.
The story, setting, atmospheric lighting, and ambient sounds in Outlast will keep you in constant tension.  While the jump scares and adrenaline pumping chase segments will get  you reaching for the esc key to take a break.
The game play in Outlast can become a little repetitious as most levels boil down to doing the same thing, which is find 3 keys / switches / fuses and unlock door to next area.  Although it's very formulaic, the variations in the areas you explore keep it interesting, exciting, and most importantly creepy.  While I enjoyed the key hunting and ensuing chases, I would have loved to see more depth in the puzzles by additional inventory management and clues found in notes.
The story of Outlast may be considered cliche, but I really loved the way the story is told.  You play a reporter sent in to investigate strange going ons, and by recording specific imagery with your camcorder you document the horrors.  Along the way you'll also find case files scattered about revealing backstory details.  It fits perfectly into the situation and doesn't seem as oddly out of place as voxaphone recordings laying around Bioshock.
So, in the year that brought us another Amnesia game Outlast outshines the competition.  In my opinion it was outstanding and worthy of any survival horror fan's time.  Looking forward to the prequel  Whistleblower DLC, which tells the story of an employee who contacts your character to start the events of Outlast.

Sundered is a metroidvania that could have been good, but has too many major flaws that bring it down.
First off, the art-style and animation is beautiful. It's reminiscent of oldschool hand-drawn animations, of such high quality that you rarely see nowadays. The character and enemy designs are quite cool. Within the different areas you visit, you'll find a decent variety in design themes.
Unfortunately, that's where the game starts to go downhill. After you've started the game, enjoyed the scenery and atmosphere for a bit, you'll start to see how the game can be a little bit shallow.
There are a few important areas in the game that contain objectives or upgrades that will stay static. Meaning the layout and art within them will never change. However, the rest of the level design in between those static areas will change every single time you die. Not drastically, but they will be enough so that you can't memorize your way back.
In theory, this sounds good as it would cut down on repetitiveness after dying, and add to replayability, however it doesn't impact the game as much since all of these procedurally generated rooms are pretty much the same. You'll most likely not notice the differences, as they all have the same art, assets, enemies, and copy pasted platforms. So that means not only might you have to retrace your steps through a place after dying, but it won't be the same so you can't just memorize it and go through as fast as possible to catch up. There are no checkpoints in the game, so whenever you die, you will respawn in the same centre-place of the map, the sanctuary.
Along the way you'll unlock shortcuts through having new abilities that allow you to access places faster, or perhaps opening doors from the other side, but sometimes these shortcuts are too scarce, or you might miss them.
Ontop of that, even if you didn't die, and don't have to replay sections of the game, entire areas can have very little variety when it comes to environments, so it will get stale anyway.
It's a shame, because the few times you reach the "static" rooms that are actually hand-crafted, it really shows, and it's quite enjoyable. Sometimes they'll contain obviously thought-out platforming sections that require you to think of how to progress, or time your jumps well. Other times, they'll contain a bit of backstory, or some beautiful art in the background. Unfortunately, most of the game is not like this.
The platforming is quite simplistic, and while it doesn't feel exceptionally interesting, it's not boring. You can double-jump, wall jump, grapple, etc. It's all quit fluent and tight.
The combat is also simple, but fun. For a while. You will mainly just be mashing one button to kill enemies. This button has you go through 4 hits of a combo. You can also point upwards and then press it to stab upwards, or do a few aerial attacks. There aren't really any combos or heavy/light/charged attacks. You can also use a secondary giant cannon if you want to, although the ammo is finite, but it is very strong, and really satisfying to use. The recoil from the weapon will send you flying backwards, and just rip through enemies, it's a joy to watch.
That's pretty much the extent of fighting. The interesting stuff comes from the huge amount of enemies you will be encountering. Whenever you fight enemies, it will be a horde. On average, I'd say 20 enemies at a time. So the strategy with fighting comes from grouping enemies up dealing as much damage as possible, and then fleeing to let your shield recharge if you took a bit of damage.
Your health system works similarly to games like Halo. Your shield takes damage, and recharges if you don't take anymore hits for a while. If your shield is broken, you will start to take permanent health damage, which can be restored with Health Elixirs if you find any. There isn't really a huge punishment to dying. You don't seem to lose shards (which you use to upgrade your character), or anything like that. The only punishment is having to go through the tedious level design again.
When you kill enemies or break open "treasures", you gain shards that can be spent in the sanctuary to upgrade yourself. The upgrade tree is really big, and allows for a pretty personalized character build, which is nice. You can choose exactly what upgrades.
You'll also be able to equip perks. Perks give you benefits, while at the same time disadvantages. For example: "You gain 1% health from every enemy killed, however health elixirs heal you less". It's a good way of making you really think about if you want the perk or not.
Bosses are one of the highlights of the game. Although there aren't that many, they're quite a spectacle.
Beautifully animated, and absolutely huge, bosses will give you quite a challenge. Some of the attacks can be quite "bullethell-y". And while the fights are ridiculously hard, most of the difficulty comes from the amount of time you need to spend fighting. Your attacks barely chip away at their health, and so it's a trial of endurance if you want to defeat these guys. Perhaps if I spent a bit more time grinding and leveling up my character, it would be easier, but I didn't feel too motivated to do that due to the repetitive nature of the game.
Overall, I was quite disappointed. The game seemed to have potential, as it looks great, the atmosphere is nice, and the enemies are interesting. However, the lack of level design makes running through empty corridors feel really lifeless, and I just couldn't have fun, not matter how hard I tried. Perhaps picking it up on a steep sale would be alright, but that would only be if you really think you'd enjoy the game. I would instead redirect you to better games of the genre, like Dust an Elysian Tail, Ori and the Blind forest or Dead Cells.
I hope the devs take these criticism into account for their next game.

Most people would describe games like this with pros and cons. However, I'm not most people. This game is the sequel to the first Five Nights at Freddy's(although in the storyline it comes before the first game, confusing I know) and improves everything about the original. Now, there are 10 main animatronics, a mask, your cameras, vents, but no doors. The only way to keep your character away from death is to put on the mask, that or shine your flashlight down the hallway in front of you as some are not tricked by the mask. Instead of Pirate Cove, you have Foxy standing in your hallway, which you have to flash the light at him every fifteen seconds or else. There is also a music box that replaces Pirate Cove and its mechanics with a semi-new idea.
Although not my favorite in the series, this one revealed the story(well, more in-depth in comparison to the original as that one gave you only the slightest bit of info on the backstory of the place), added a higher challenge(probably why I personally didn't like as much as the first as at times I found the second one too difficult), and added extra scares! I recommend this to people ONLY if:
1. They are an experienced gamer
2. They have tried the first one, since a few of the mechanics carry over to this one
3. They can function under stress
4. They can handle jumpscares, as this game has a lot of 'em.
I hope that someone found this review helpful and that they will consider what I have said about this game.

Please, do yourself a favor and buy this game. It's already a masterpiece, and I am eager to see what plans they have for DLC in the future, more of this game could never be a bad thing. I've already played to 100% completion on both Resist and Embrace during the SuperSecretBeta, and I can't wait to do it again now that it's on full release and seen some new content already!
I cannot praise this game, or the Developers, enough. I backed the game on Kickstarter and have had the pleasure of being involved in the Beta and SuperSecretBeta testing phases, and in communication with the Devs to give direct feedback. For those unaware, about two dozen testers were directly emailed by the CEO of Thunder Lotus Games and invited to participate in a secret phase of testing, called the SuperSecretBeta, with access to the full game, for the purpose of direct final feedback for final game balance and adjustments in a Discord channel with the entire Thunder Lotus dev team. Special shout out to Med and Ian who always seemed to be around to talk to the testers!
The entire experience has been amazing, the game itself has been solid all the way back to the Alpha, and has only become better and better as patches have come in to add content and rebalance portions of the game, on some days of the SuperSecretBeta we would have 4-5 patches within a few hours. The Devs are very receptive to feedback and are a fun, friendly group to be involved with. They value our opinions and took what we said to heart in their rebalancing all the way to the end of the Beta period.
As for the game itself, it is a riveting, haunting tale of humanity, courage, desparation, temptation, corruption, and salvation. Your choices affect the way the game plays out, and there's really no bad choice to make. All the outcomes are well implemented and thought out, and provide a compelling story. The art is gorgeous, screenshots I've taken during my testing have become my new desktop backgrounds and lock screens. The music is hauntingly beautiful, I've found myself just sitting and listening to the haunting strings so many times. The minibosses are fun and challenging, while the region bosses are EPIC confrontations requiring skill and thinking outside the box, I don't think I've had more fun on boss fights in a very long time.

I've played way more time management & simulation games and put more hours into them than I'm willing to admit. This one really falls short. I'm actually surprised to learn that this isn't an early access game.
- UI needs a lot of polishing. There's literally a part of the interface where if you have nothing selected, a screen just reads "NO."
- Parts of the game occasionally freeze/lock up. There's about a 50% chance that when I see one of the "clean up for the health inspector" minigames that it'll freeze in some way or not count down the game tmer.
- The parts of the game that should be fun, like making orders, are more tedious than anything and it's very difficult to measure if you're improving on your pizza making skills at all or if it's just a total crapshoot on whether or not you get a perfect order. It just generally results in you having characters perform all tasks for you and you just click/drag icons to people's faces.
- It just feels very clunky and unfinished. Hard to describe, but it has that very general "this game is not done" feeling.
- Delivery part is the most fun, but the navigation is weird, the map doesn't show your destination, and as you buy car upgrades the cars seem to actually get worse in terms of handling and helping with perfect orders. Who would've thought that hitting the breaks on your car would flip it frontwards, implying that the pure stopping force of your breaks is stronger than the pull of the earth's gravity on your car/it's weight. aka upgrading your car turns it into tissue paper.

I'm going to try to keep this short and sweet
-Getting the best cards and the cards you want in this game is really easy. Within 30-50 hours you can have a top tier deck (depending on how many legendaries are in that deck) without paying a dime. The beginner decks also are very balanced and can somewhat compete with top tier decks.
-The draft in this game is incredible. It's not like MtG or hearthstone where you either draft merfolk or rogue otherwise you lose. In this draft environment there is an incredible amount of possibilities in what deck you want to draft, all of them being very well balanced. And after your draft, you get to keep the cards you drafted, as well as get free chests/gold/packs depending on how many games you won. If you are a fan of drafting, this game is for you, and even if you don't like drafts, you may still like the draft here
-Animations and actor lines are good and clear. In fact some of the lines that play after you play a specific card are pretty catchy and they get stuck in your head
-Ladder has the same issues other tcgs have. Certain cards are broken and the meta usually forms around those cards, then when they get nerfed, the meta shifts to the next best card. This is normal and what you should always expect from tcg. However the problem arises when a deck revolves around a card that makes games 2-3 times longer than they should be. The card's name is "Crystalline Chalice", regular players know that name well. Card is not broken, it's just the fun police. It encites making games really long, grindy, boring and frustrating. Usually games take 2-10 minutes, games against chalice are usually 10-30 minutes. This card/deck is my only problem with the ladder right now.
-Gauntlet is fun and a great way for new players to test decks, get some gold, shiftstone and cards while playing relatively easy AI.
-Campaign is fun. Right now, since this game is kinda new, the campaign is short. They add a new campaign and cards every so often. The extra campaign story lines outside of the tutorial one you go through when you load up the game cost a bit of gold to play. You can usually just pay $10 for each campaign story, which each gives you a whole bunch of cards, all being of the uncomon rarity to the legendary rarity. For me, paying $10 for these campaigns was ok since this game is free to play. You can grind for the gold though and not have to buy the campaign story lines
-Forge is like draft, except you face AI and you don't pick from packs, you pick from a selection of 3 cards that are randomly shown to you. All 3 of those cards will be in the colors you drafted for. Forge is good for new players but adds nothing to the veteran players
I do recommend this anyone who likes MtG or Hearthstone. It's fun, addicting and IMO, going to be a force to be reckoned with when it comes to who's the top TCG.

Are you looking for a Magic The Gathering alternative that won't break the bank? You've tried Hearthstone, Shadowverse, Gwent etc. and although all of these cards have great aspects to them, there are also aspects that just makes you hesitant to go all in.
Well Eternal is what you have been looking for this whole time.
Eternal is a card game that takes the best part about the granddaddy of all card games and adds its own twist. Many themes in the game will feel similar if you have played Magic The Gathering in the past. But do not be mistaken, Eternal is its own game by improving on some ideas, simplifying others and implementing their own.
Eternal offers a lot to its players. You can play Ranked with your own deck and you can participate in arguably the best Draft mode of any digital card game available. If on the other hand you want to take things easy, there is Gauntlet and the Forge, two games method which mimics Ranked and Draft except that you play against a computer. All of this is in addition to the campaign which provides everyone a good set of starting cards.
Not only does Eternal offer a lot in terms of pure gameplay, this game has been the most rewarding experience for any F2P game I've ever seen. Both the Gauntlet and the Forge are easily accessible to new players while giving the said players the time to get used to all the different mechanics / rules while generating significant monies to get the cards you want. Ranked on the other hand also provides rewards for each match won. There is no limit to the amount of these rewards you can win per day.
All this to say that I really want Eternal to succeed. This game is one of the few that doesn't insult its players base by falsly slapping the "F2P" tag on their game or by dumbing down the content to make it as casual as possible. Instead Direwolf (the developpers) provide a fun, interactive and rewarding experience and hopes for the best. The fact that this game isn't more popular is ludicrous to me. That is the only reason why I am writting a review. If I can get even 1 more person to experience this game, I did my job.
I hope you try this game with an open mind and go through all the different modes at least once. The game may seem to be too complex at first, but over time I promise you'll get the hand of it and enjoy it.
Tl;DR: This game rocks! Try it and you won't regret it.

Bought this game in the bundle with part 1 and am currently playing it.
I think I'm about halfway through and so far enjoy it incredibly!
It has all the positive aspects of the first game, in that is is a fun, true-to-the-genre kind of grid-based Dungeon Crawler with a solid automap, amazing puzzles and interesting level design, but boy, does it have more!
After the success of the simple-yet-fun first game, this one has a lot more production value to it. There are more tilesets in the first hour or two than in the entire first game. There are way more monsters, way more options for your characters, and so on. They also improved (in my opinion) the already-solid class, leveling, magic and alchemy systems of the previous game.
I feel that the difficulty is sometimes quite a bit higher than before. There's a bunch of fights that just seem broken, but once you figure them out, and finally decide to use some of those consumables you've been hoarding "in case you ever need them", become doable. But you need to think and play well. An actual challenge, who'd have thought!?
The one thing I disliked at first was the new injury system. One bad roll of the dice against the wrong enemy, and your hero can't use one of his hands anymore, walks super slow, or the likes. But then that makes you actually use (and not just hoard) all those healing potions, which turns out is kind of a good thing.
I highly recommend the first game to anyone interested in this genre and I absolutely recommend playing the first one first, because having played it definitely improved my experience of the second one. But man, the second one is even better! :D

"Do you recommend this game?" Yes and No. (But mostly yes.)
First some pros. (From a veteran card player stand point.)
- If you like M:TG but wish it were a little simpler, Eternal fits that bill.
- If you dislike variance that means you get hand screwed by CCGs, well Eternal at least does SOMETHING about it. (more on this below.)
- 5 factions (Yellow - Time /Green - Justice/Purple - Shadow/Red - Fire/Blue- Primal)  that meld in interesting ways and don't force you to choose between them the way Sol Forge or HS do is nice. Keep in mind that 5 color strategies often strain the same way they do in M:TG.
- Quests happen daily like HS and Pox Nora and they vary quite a bit. You get one reroll per day so if a quest is hard to do and you want to try your luck, you can.
- Campaign Mode (and also the P2p campaign mode) is full of ways to get more cards and also teaches the game. You can pay for the P2p campaign with ingame gold (though the price is steep at 4x the cost of a draft.)
- Achievements award varying amounts of ingame gold (varying in degree of significance from 10 to 2500) which is used for buying packs and or drafts. (I recommend never buying packs that way and instead open packs in draft.)
- You earn Gold in every mode via opening chests. Chests range from Bronze (~50 gold and a common, or a chance to rank up to a better chest), to Silver (~250 gold and an uncommon, or a chance to rank up), to Gold (~500 gold and a Booster Pack, or a chance to rank up) to Diamond (~2000 + a pack).
- You earn chests in Gauntlet mode (the more games you complete the better the chest rewards up to 3x Silver). And as you rank up from Bronze to Master in that mode you get a rank up chest.
- You earn 2 bronze chests and a silver chest every 3 games you win in Ranked. (So after the first win you get a bronze, your next win gets you another bronze and another yields a silver, and so on.)
-Draft starts out awarding you a minimum of 2 chests (and you get to keep the stone for opening the packs and also any cards you drafted.) You can win up to 7 games in any one draft and losing 3 times eliminates you. When you win a game your end prize increases in quality. If you win 7 games you will end up with 3 Diamond Chests. Draft tends to be the best way to collect the rares, as they tend to be over powered compared to the uncommons and commons (though of course not always appropriate for your color choices).
- The crafting system is primitive but allows you to make almost every card in the game. I say primitive because you need to either destroy other cards to get the requiste "shard stone" or open packs (do this in draft). You will enventually have more than 4 of each common and uncommon and crushing those is fine. This is NOT a  trading card game.

The Belgian field I'm peering over is quite picturesque, actually. Treeline off ahead of me, quaint wooden fence and a little country road off to my right. Looks even nicer when you're not in a trench.
I'm up on the ground just forward of the trench, to be clear, laying prone at the base of a tree. I'm peering down the sights of a beautifully rendered Lee-Enfield Mk IV rifle (all ninety or so rifles in this game satisfy my long held bolt action rifle fetish), scanning the treeline, where the German trenches are. Ostensibly, I should be charging, as the objective right now is to capture that bit of territory. But no. Our advance has halted, and it's quiet. No one sees an enemy. We're all peering out, waiting for a silhouette to pop up into our sights.
Some unseen Austrian prick fires a shot from a spot I can't see. At some impossible angle, I'm killed. It's my tenth death in four minutes. I have no kills.
Welcome, friends, to Verdun.

Ignore the micro-transaction / IOS-port haters. This game is great for those who love turn-based combat (think XCom), especially great for those who love the Warhammer universe, and extra-specially great for anyone with fond memories of the excellent boardgame, of which this is a fairly faithful implementation. Anyone who does a little research will find that buying the Deluxe edition is the way to go, as this represents the best value for money - this is a lot cheaper than buying the same package on IOS (where micro-transactions are the only way forward).
The graphics can be pumped up from the main menu though it appears many people would prefer to ♥♥♥♥♥ that it's a lazy port with crappy IOS graphics than actually go in and look for that option. Mouse-based control works perfectly, so again any complaint about that is equally petty. True there are no PC key mappings, but the game doesn't need them. At all.
Just bear in mind it is a port of a dice-based boardgame, with all the pitfalls that come with RNG, and the slow pace of a boardgame, and you'll be fine.
So then, a fun game whose depth slowly reveals itself as your party levels up and acquires new items and skills and items that give new skills. Frustrating at times, as you will wipe due to bad rolls, but there's a great sense of progression as you move from town to town tackling increasingly difficult dungeons with an increasingly potent party. I am really enjopying this.
ADDENDUM: After playing considerably further after writing the above review, I am changing me review score. As your party becomes more potent and yourselves and the enemies get a lot more abilities to play with, the game really starts to shine. ESPECIALLY as a single player experience where interaction between heroes becomes more interesting and thought-provoking. This allows the game to show some tactical depth as you start to worry about carefully positioning your party and ordering your attacks to maximise very large Death Blows from your heavy-hitters that sweep away a LOT of enemies at once. In the end this offers more tactical depth than, say, late-game XCom, which was a pleasant surprise. Raising my score to 8.5 (from 7.5) accordingly.

This is one of the hardest games I've ever had to review because I genuinely liked the game right up until the ending.  Even then, I've recommended games before with feeling an ending was less bad.  So what makes this one different?  What makes me say I enjoyed the game itself but that changed after I finished it?  To me, it's all in how the game is advertised. Bottom line, the game is very well done it's ashame that the developers resorted to bait and switch tactics to sell the game. This game came out earlier than expected, almost rushed, but still pretty great. The second best game in the franchise.
FNAF 2 improved on its predecessor by allowing only a mask and no doors, which really shocked the FNAF community during the hype stage.

Wanted to practice with the old animatronics? Set the AI numbers of the "new" animatronics to 0.
Wanted to find easter eggs? Set everybody to 0 (not that Foxy and Puppet are still active somewhat).
This helped with its legacy and place with the community, and set itself as a "successful sequel" despite the fact that it seemed rushed.
Overall, a great sequel, recommend with FNAF 1.

It's a $20 walking simulator.
Okay... It seems that several people are already disagreeing with my review. I was hoping to keep this review short (just like this game), but I guess not. And it appears that Steam hasn't updated my review on the store page with each edit I made, so if I'm gonna be downvoted I might as well make sure everyone can see my full review first.
Okay, I’ll actually explain myself... This game, by definition, is a walking simulator since it lacks all of the traditional elements of a video game, such as a scoring system, goal, win/loss conditions, etc. This game is mostly narrative driven, and the one action you are allowed to do is walk around and observe everything. I normally have have no problem with walking simulators, but my biggest issue with this game is the ridiculous default price. 20 f*****g U.S. Dollars?! The length of this game hardly justifies this unreasonable price tag. The game be completed under an hour if you don't end up wasting your time inspecting every plastic duck you see.
In fact, the fastest speedrun for this game was 47 f*****g seconds. SECONDS. Are you seeing the problem here? Everything between you and the story is pure filler. Some of you may make the argument that the game is intended to be played blind, and you shouldn't cheat your way through with Wikis or video walkthroughs, but I'm gonna have to disagree there. That's just artificially stretching out the play time longer than it should be. There's no fun to be had wasting 13 damn minutes of your life trying to find the next event trigger, only to waste another 13 minutes looking for yet another event trigger. It's just frustrating and headache inducing.
I cannot recommend this game for this ludicrous price, so you might as well wait for a sale or Bundle. 5 dollars may be a tad bit of a stretch, but it's far more reasonable than $20. In fact, this should've been the price, day one.

Overall, this improved on grimrock 1 in basically every way.  More varied dungeons: check (albeit they're each smaller), more characters: check, non-linear: check.  The move to an outside environment really improved things for me, going through a dungeon and escaping into the light was IMHO a welcome improvement to just descending more.
I do agree that leveling is basically scripted, you're rogue will do accuracy + light + some ranged attack, you're tank will do light + armor, and so on.  Essentially, the most important choice is in creating the character, and sadly there weren't any surprises in the leveling unlike the first game where level 50 gave a massive buff.  This doesn't IMHO make it bad, but it does mean that if you're looking for distinguishing you're insect fighter from other insect fighters then you're in the wrong place.
The puzzles are both improved and worse.  They are more natural, and varied than in the first.  The biggest downside is needing certain equipment to complete some.  This means if you left some item you had no idea you'd need then you'd have to search for it.  I had left the serpent staff unknowing it would be important, and had to search for a long time to find where I left it.  Leaving a mess in the hub area is you're best bet, it's generally relatively accessible.  On that same note there's way more stuff, the weight limits seem too low, I basically never could even carry the cannon just because it weighted too much.  Ditto, for the spells; this meant I only stuck to a handful of spells I could remember, and the rest were just untouched, which is disappointing.
Finally, the last downside, some puzzles have timing components, and these can be a drag.  There was one late in the game it probably took a dozen tries to get through, there was just not much room for error (I was turning instead of walking backwards, and this just ate too much time).  The controls aren't bad, but the low margin on some of the timing puzzles was a bit annoying.
Combat is very much like the first.  This is good, though it does mean you'll spend the game circle-strafing, or finding a hole while attacking the enemies one at a time.  It does feel like some enemies have too much health, most notably the crabs.  They're a trash mob, but have such high armor and HP, it takes too long to finish them off that it makes the fight a bit of a bore.  This is the exception though, most enemies are well-balanced.  They've also introduced a bunch of new attacks to prevent circle-strafing from being the ultimate move...the downside of this is that it means you'll be waiting a good bit more during the combat.
Overall, despite the gripes (which are minor over the course of the game) this is a fantastic game, and is a vast improvement over the original.

"Do you recommend this game?" Yes and No. (But mostly yes.)
First some pros. (From a veteran card player stand point.)
- If you like M:TG but wish it were a little simpler, Eternal fits that bill.
- If you dislike variance that means you get hand screwed by CCGs, well Eternal at least does SOMETHING about it. (more on this below.)
- 5 factions (Yellow - Time /Green - Justice/Purple - Shadow/Red - Fire/Blue- Primal)  that meld in interesting ways and don't force you to choose between them the way Sol Forge or HS do is nice. Keep in mind that 5 color strategies often strain the same way they do in M:TG.
- Quests happen daily like HS and Pox Nora and they vary quite a bit. You get one reroll per day so if a quest is hard to do and you want to try your luck, you can.
- Campaign Mode (and also the P2p campaign mode) is full of ways to get more cards and also teaches the game. You can pay for the P2p campaign with ingame gold (though the price is steep at 4x the cost of a draft.)
- Achievements award varying amounts of ingame gold (varying in degree of significance from 10 to 2500) which is used for buying packs and or drafts. (I recommend never buying packs that way and instead open packs in draft.)
- You earn Gold in every mode via opening chests. Chests range from Bronze (~50 gold and a common, or a chance to rank up to a better chest), to Silver (~250 gold and an uncommon, or a chance to rank up), to Gold (~500 gold and a Booster Pack, or a chance to rank up) to Diamond (~2000 + a pack).
- You earn chests in Gauntlet mode (the more games you complete the better the chest rewards up to 3x Silver). And as you rank up from Bronze to Master in that mode you get a rank up chest.
- You earn 2 bronze chests and a silver chest every 3 games you win in Ranked. (So after the first win you get a bronze, your next win gets you another bronze and another yields a silver, and so on.)
-Draft starts out awarding you a minimum of 2 chests (and you get to keep the stone for opening the packs and also any cards you drafted.) You can win up to 7 games in any one draft and losing 3 times eliminates you. When you win a game your end prize increases in quality. If you win 7 games you will end up with 3 Diamond Chests. Draft tends to be the best way to collect the rares, as they tend to be over powered compared to the uncommons and commons (though of course not always appropriate for your color choices).
- The crafting system is primitive but allows you to make almost every card in the game. I say primitive because you need to either destroy other cards to get the requiste "shard stone" or open packs (do this in draft). You will enventually have more than 4 of each common and uncommon and crushing those is fine. This is NOT a  trading card game.

I did enjoy this game, but ultimately I have more problems with it than things I like about it. I'm not trying to get down on the developer mind you, this is an astonishing feat for a single person. This game is very visually appealing, it has a kind of Diorama like charm to it that is present in most city building games but with an extra air of peacefulness and quaintness.
There are no Zombies or Bandits or other goons out for your blood, which is a plus because in similar games things like that aren't implemented in a way that really adds anything. Your biggest enemy is the environment, in both a game and on an unfortunate meta level. The starting environment is restricted to a choice between 'Mountains' or 'Plains' and then you decide how harsh the weather is and then you begin.
The world generator is however; not all that great, I find even the Plains setting to be prohibitively mountainous to allow for sufficient growth and the nature is just visually boring. This means that often the game will screw you over by starting you in a tiny area that can barely fit one good size farm. Expanding is way too difficult, the buildings cost far too much to make expanding really worth it. Additionally things take an
amount of time to build, even with 15 workers it takes in game
to construct a single house simply because half of the time they aren't doing anything, even if all of the materials are availible they often just won't build.
I've heard stories of people whose villages had over 200 people in them, but I can rarely exceed 20, maybe I'm just bad at the game but I can never get sufficient space to do anything. The Villager A.I. for the most is surprisingly good, but all of the jobs necessary for greater growth such as Stonecutter and Miner are not coded very well and half of the time they don't do their jobs.
Lastly; the game just doesn't have enough content to justify it's price of 20 dollars, this game would go better for 15 or 12 but currently it just doesn't have enough to have good replay value.

I've contemplated whether or not I should recommend this game. There's quite a bit wrong with it, and yet, there's a lot more right with it. In the end, I think the positive aspects of this game outweigh the negatives.
To begin with, LOGII isn't your typical RPG. In place of the towns, gold pieces, dungeons and dragons you may be used to, LOGII only has one kind of locale: The Dungeons.
The game world is comprised entirely of labyrinthine dungeons which take the forms of beaches, forests, mines, castles, catacombs and more. There are no towns, no gold for you to earn from killing monsters, and no NPCs to babble your ears off.
This is a killer idea! As much as I like traditional RPGs, the only reason I ever play them is for the thrill of exploring the dark depths of the dungeons, and in LOGII, that's all you really do.
LOGII plays in First-Person perspective. You have four characters at your disposal which you can make yourself or have the game generate for you. From there on, you march your way through labyrinths full of monsters and items. The thrills don't come from finding treasures or beating the dungeon boss, but rather from finding better, more useful stuff to help you survive.
The gameplay is very similar to the old Dungeon Master games on DOS. You march about, kill monsters, pick up items, and check your map every so often. I personally loved Dungeon Master, but LOGII doesn't have the same amount of challenge. It feels like it was designed for the newcomer types.
The two things that REALLY sold me with this game are the Custom Portraits feature, and the Dungeon Editor. The characters you make in LOGII are invisible. Instead of animated models, they are represented by 2D portraits. If you have the artistic know-how, you can use your own portraits, just in case you want to fulfill your fantasy of a buxom elf chick, a dragonborn, an anime guy and Rainbow Dash rummaging through a dungeon.
The dungeon editor is a mixed bag for me. On one hand, it's very easy to make a basic map with monsters, items, keys and switches. But if you want some of the more advanced stuff, you'll need to know LUA scripting and how to use certain entities and all that stuff. Whatever you do, don't touch the floor and ceiling adjusters at the top of the editor, especially if you're using any other tileset beside "dungeon."
All in all, Legend of Grimrock II is a little rough around the edges, but it's still a lot of fun. The main campaign is enjoyable, but the Dungeon Editor could be a little easier. Or at the very least, have a comprehensive tutorial with it.

I can't say that I've played a lot of puzzle and/or dungeon crawlers in my time, but I don't doubt that the legend of grimrock series might be one of the finest modern iterations on the genre. I was surpriced at how fresh and different they made every puzzle considering how seemingly simple the game mechanics were. The puzzles were challenging, but I seldom found myself truly stuck and there were more than one "Lightbulb" moment. In other words the puzzles gave a sense of achievement. The combat definitely is an aquired taste, but I can imagine that some grizzled players might feel right at home with it. The combat can instill dread and extreme stress at times and there is often quite a bit of planning involved as well. Personally I liked the combat a lot and I think it compliments the rest of the game very well. With other games it can be very jarring when a story driven game jumps from "story section" to "puzzle section" to "combat section", but this line becomes somewhat blurred with this kind of combat system.
The game can be quite hard at times. The first game is much more linear than this one and you can have puzzles that stretch over the whole map so you might yourself having to put a lot more effort and walking a lot more than the first game. I consider this to be a negative thing and it would be nice to have something to indicate your progress in a area or something similar. This is why in part the game can be a bit exhausting. You are always doing puzzles or in combat (or finding secret buttons) and both require you to focus and think, meaning that you seldom get to rest. You could say that grimrock is a bit intense in that way, it's not a relaxing game. Combine this with a game that you can't really pick up whenever you want because then you might have forgotten your plans, planned builds and parts of puzzles. I think this might puts pressure on the player to solve the game faster and further exhausting the player. Another thing that might exhaust players is the mood of the game. While the game is more colourful and varied than the first game, the mood will mostly be creepy, somber and maybe something else depending on how you roleplay. One could make a comparison to old corridor shooters which didn't often didn't have much variety in mood and/or visuals. I will say however that the map design isn't bad. The world does interconnect in interesting ways even though game have a hub design, but it makes perfect sense in combination with the story.
One thing that irks me with this series is the secret buttons. There are A LOT of secret buttons to find and IT IS fun to find these buttons, however it isn't fun looking for them. You don't have to find these buttons, but you can miss a lot of secret areas and loot without it which I found to be important. I did play on hard though, so for a normal playthrough it might not be as important. Completionists beware.
The story is barely there, but it does leave a lot of room for a little roleplaying which is nice. The snoopiest of you will find a lot of interesting tidbits about the settings/world which I found to be surpricingly intriguing. Other than that it's a lot of fun to building your team. It has a great menu theme. With how the combat system works you can have fights that lasts for a day or two (in game time) which looks really badass. In on of the final battles I found myself fighting from when sun dawned until the next morning. That was badass.

Eternal is a card game with a playstyle that's modeled after Magic: the Gathering, and a card collection style modeled after Hearthstone (but better!). It is completely free to play, with the helpful but unnecessary option of spending money on drafts or packs to help buoy your early game card collection.  You get to keep all the cards you draft, and you also get a decent amount of shiftstone (the card-crafting currency) for each pack you open.  The game is so free to play that I was compelled to basically donate to them so I could have an uninhibited play experience.
This game is for all the people who enjoy playing Magic, but have issues with the Magic Online program for any of the possible reasons.  All I wanted to do with Magic was just jam games for free and against quality opponents.  Third party software did not quite scratch that itch, so when I saw Eternal was released I jumped on board and have really taken to it.  This is perhaps Eternal's greatest strength - the bingeability of the game - yet it can also be its greatest weakness.  Because people can just queue up indiscriminately, they play a LOT more games than normal, and the dreaded "variance sucks" argument comes to a head more often, because you literally are more likely to be screwed by variance when you're increasing your number of games played.  If you like to complain about variance, honestly, stop playing all card games, because variance is literally what makes card games fun. That or learn to accept your lord and savior Variance McGee into your life and keep a lingering smile on your face as the game engine hands you an unwinnable hand.
The game design has done a phenomenal job with the first set, with an unbelievable number of playable archetypes in constructed mode.  It won't all be tier one, but with as wildly as the meta shifts in this game, it can be fun to find that one random deck you played 2 months ago which you just realized has a strong matchup against the current meta.  Some decks will seemingly never die, but Dire Wolf Digital has shown a willingness to step in and nerf cards it sees as problems, while also buffing a few underutilized cards a bit more rarely.  Gone for me are the days of learning the combat tricks in each color, which was a very fun process to learn much like a new Magic draft format, but a new player will certainly delight in learning how to play around the opponent's tricks.  Until a new Eternal set comes out, the intellectual enjoyment on my end predominantly comes from attacking the meta in a favorable manner.
I've really enjoyed the product that Dire Wolf Digital has put out, and I think it has a lot of portability over from any other popular card game a new player might be more familiar with.  If you're new to card games, there will obviously be a bit more of a learning curve, but hey, this is completely free - might as well try it out!

First above and beyond I will say what this game should have promoted to begin with: BEWARE, HERE BE MICROTRANSACTIONS, also THIS IS A PORT OF AN IOS GAME. That said for those not fleeing in terror aready here is a more accurate review:
At it's core Warhammer Quest is not a bad little game, it captures the spirit of the old board game pretty well, it looks pretty good for the atmosphere it's going for, and runs well without any signifigant bugs. For about $5 to $10 it would come with a strong recommendation for those looking for a simple Strategy-RPG fix.
The problem is that the game is a money leech portal. Every character you buy will set you back additional real money in addition to the purchuse price. This is less of an issue for those who purchused the deluxe edition (like I did) which included all extra microtransaction content to date, but the game's greed doesn't stop there. This game also sells gold, gold is used in game for everything from training to buying gear for your party. The dungeons give gold out, but in very small amounts. What's more random events vampire your gold. One of the reasons I wrote this review so quickly was that I was sitting there after being irritated by the microtransactions thinking "well maybe this isn't so bad" and then while flipping through town menus I hit a random event telling me my character just got rooked by a con artist, and BAM there went a big pile of gold right down the tube, nothing I could do about it. "lukily" Chilled Mouse has included the option to buy more gold right next to the area where the gold is listed... all I need to do is pay them real money.
Now in theory I suppose with the patience of a saint you could play this game and not have to buy gold from the devs, but from the way it seems the entire gimmick here is  the game being designed in such a way that it is a serious pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥without buying gold for money. The game even stealing your gold (seriously, this happened) when you earn it in game with nothing you can do about it.
What's more it should be noted your paying $13 to $23 for a game on IOS with a single digit price tag that has simply been ported to PC. This inflated price being you paying for the right to pay them more money to play what is admittedly a pretty goot lite RPG/Strategy title.
To be frank I wouldn't even begrudge them selling the characters or tile sets like they are as DLC assuming they were honest about it and listed it that way (DLC section in store page) but the gold system needs to go for this to get any recommendation from me.
To be honest I'll probably play it a bit more to see how it develops and perhaps update this, but right now all I can say is that if you are remotely considering this stay far, far, away.
Also I wanted to say that STEAM itself needs to be more attentitive to this kind of thing. It's one thing for MMOs with overheard to make money this way, as much as I dislike that (and begrudingly accept it) but with single player games this is ridiculous. One of the reasons why I stick to PC titles and "real" portable games (Vita, DS) is to get away from this garbage and I find it annoying to see these business practices sneaking onto steam. Charging for DLC is one thing (even if it's abused) but in game micro-transactions for a non-MMO? That's something STEAM shouldn't be supporting especially at this level.

To be honest, I can't remember the last time I have read so much controversy surrounding a computer game and it is getting quite ludicrous. I have no illusions whatsoever that my humble writing skills will change anyone's mind so I want to write a fair review of this so that folks who are willing to hear both sides can make an informed decision. So, once more unto the breach!!
In 1995, UK games monolith Games Workshop answered Milton Bradley's Heroquest with a dark, quirky, face kicking boardgame called Warhammer Quest. Set in the rich fantasy world of Warhammer, a party of four intrepid adventurers raided dungeons that were randomly created and more often than not, died horribly and rather creatively. Expansion packs were released and in those early days of the most holy internet, people even created homebrew dungeon tiles, monsters, and treasure packs that were as good looking and perfectly playable in the game. But alas, the joy was short lived as Games Workshop decided to pull the plug. The boardgame faded into the madness of the aftermarket and is commanding rather exorobitant prices. Sad.
Fast forward to January 7th and WQ is back! The game faithfully recreates the experience of playing the original murderous and funny experience of the boardgame in all of its gory glory. As you know, it's a port from iOS but does that detract from the core game experience? In my opinion, no. It's clear that developer Chilled Mouse put a lot of love into this little gem and given the fact that GW is very VERY protective of its intellectual property, Chilled Mouse has done a splendid job.
But every review must be fair so I'll point out a few negatives first. The omission of multiplayer was a very bad decision. WQ and games like it are BEST played with others. That said, it IS a fun singleplayer game and you can of course, play it hot seat! Imagine that; people actually getting together to play a game like the old days! The RNG is again faithful to the game but there should be an option to see a chart of the result of dice rolls as in the original boardgame.
Now to the good stuff! First off, let's get this out of the way: there are NO mandatory microtranactions in this game. It is NOT "P2W." The option is there to buy in game gold for those who would rather rush through the game but all you gain is getting a higher powered party sooner, and, as this IS a single player game, no one is hurt if a person decides TO avail her/himself of the MT.
The game's dungeons ar randomly generated and faithfully retain the look of the original. If there is one thing you need to know to survive this game is to expect the unexpected and that the unexpected is usually quite nasty.  But the game has a sense of humor in all of the darkness too. There is one bit early in the game where a person hanging upside down is making a speech and that speech is cut short by a well thrown piece of cauliflower to his face.
This is a turn based game so don't expect to running like a mad person like the equally excellent Runers. This game's weapon is to make you THINK; to make you wonder what lurks in that next room or corridor. It's about positioning your characters for maximum face punchage to the great unwashed nasties that stand between you and glorious loot. The UI is simple: everything can be done with the mouse and unlike some other iOS ports, the game responds very well to mouse dragigng and other iOS strangeness.
I only have three hours into this game and yet my party is leveling up very nicely and I haven't spent a single real coin of the realm beyondthe purchase price. If you are a WQ fan, this game is a no-brainer must buy; you will not be disappointed. If you are a gamer that wants to get out of her/his comfort zone and test the waters of something different; something that isn't the 900th iteration of CoD, and you enjoy tactical thinking, this game has it in spades.
I strongly recommend this game and if you buy it, go all the way and get the Deluxe version. Contrary to what you may have read, this game is much less expensive than the iOS version when you figure in the additional DLC. And resist the temptation to OPTIONALLY buy gold or else you will rob yourself of a classic gaming experience!
UPDATE: 9.2 hours in game and it just keeps getting better. But the main reason I wanted to update is for those who may not know, namely, that the optional MTs are gone. So, buy the Deluxe version and have a blast and not  pay another penny - unless of course later DLC becomes available and I for one hope it does!!

Flight Sim World is what might be regarded as the spiritual successor to the MS Flight sim series, finally dragging it into the 64 bit realm and utilising the GPU more, two things which FS has sorely needed since the time that MS were still the custodians of the franchise, but never got around to because it was such a large task. So credit is due to developers Dovetail Games for having taken that on. Clearly there is still a long way to go, and if you are not wanting to participate in an early access 'test', you would still be better off with the Steam Edition of FSX, but as time progresses and DTG get on the case, I'm sure we will eventually see FSW take over the role of 'go to flight sim for home users'. As it stands it's nice to see a preview of things, and there is fun to be had with it, but don't expect everything to be perfect in it right from day one. As long as one approaches it knowing what one is getting, it is definitely worth a look, because there is a good chance it will be the future of PC-based flight simming.

I am having fun with this game so far. yes, there are a lot of issues even with the patches, but that doesnt mean thegame can't be enjoyed still. I would reccomend buying this on sale. I am about 9 hours in with some side tasks completed and im not finding it too repetitive, buggy or as bad as some reviews say.
Pros:
Enviromet: The idea of this world is really cool, with you being hunted down in red districts by huge air ships, and when you get into the yellow districts ( where citizens live and are watched by the KPA) the world and ideas can be really good.
Combat: guns are all solid for the most part, and im enjoying switching modifacations between fights. Such as using a sniper to take out guards on a tower before switching it back to a DMR to put down a group of heavy units. the interface can be a little slow, but nothing too bad. equipment is also cool as you can hack patrolling drones to kill soliders and place detonating teddies.
Cons:
AI pop in:Now i havent had any crashes or major bugs so far, however the one gripe i do have with the game is that AI can often pop in and out at random. if you walk any more than 20 yards or so from a enermy they may just vanish, which can kill the experience if you were planning to kill them in some way. ive only had one situation which this has got me killed in when a entire heavy armoured truck spawned on me and some fighters as we ran past and just killed us all. but as i say, only the once.
slugish menu: the map, messages and objectives are all on a phone, which sounds cool, but it runs like an old Iphone after Apple releases a new model and decides to slow down the software.
Ai can be dumb and funny sometimes, but not game breaking, their dumb vision is made up by their damage. you will die a lot if yiu dont plan with equipment and ammo as you can run out fast and be down to your pistol.
what you get here is a game with a cool idea for a story, but not executed well. semi openworld areas to kill, liberate and explore with hints of farcry tasks such as bases to capture and radios to activate. good and sometimes hard combat. could be a good game to blast through over a weekend and experience the ambition.
