I think that, in comparison to the other Fromsoft Souls-esque titles (DS1, DS3, Bloodborne, Demons Souls) that DS2 is easily the weakest of the bunch. The lore isn't quite as deep or connected, and there's some elements of gameplay that frustrate me about this game.
This does not make Dark Souls 2 a bad game, but rather inferior in comparison to the others. It certainly feels like the black sheep of the franchise.
For starters, what did it get right? Well the game both runs and looks very well. I suffered almost no lag the entire game, so its very well optimized. The soundtrack and environments are very good, and I think Dark Souls 2's level design is in some ways better than Dark Souls 1 by giving you a better idea of where to go. PVP is also undeniably at its best in this game.
What does it do wrong? Well, for starters, the Effigy system. I am aware it is a holdover from Demon's Souls, where as you die and lose your health. However the fact that the item for turning human is finite is a bit dumb. You can circumvent this by completing Vendrick's quest or using the Shrine of Amana altar. However this is so late in the game it hardly matters at that point.
Difficulty seems more artificial and cheap. Dark Souls 2 is the only game in the franchise not directed by Miyazaki, and it shows. Bosses, instead of being more difficult, simply add mobs (like Royal Rat Authority, or Elana, the Squalid Queen) as a cheap means to win fights, or in some cases just rehash older boss fights in the series (Belfry Gargoyles, Old Dragonslayer). The Smelter Demon in Iron Passage is just a blue version of the Red Smelter Demon earlier in Iron Keep, except with Magic Damage instead of Fire Damage. There are also too many bosses where you have to fight multiple people at a time, because otherwise the fight would be too easy (Lud and Zallen, Throne Watcher and Defender, Twin Dragonriders, etc). Combat also is very biased to dodging over tanking. The patient and tactical gameplay styles for most of Dark Souls 1 bosses simply don't work here. For about 3/4 of the bosses you have to learn to dodge and play very aggressively because your armor won't mean jack. In Dark Souls 1, the only bosses to my recollection that you couldn't be patient with and didn't have a unique gameplay mechanic to prevent said patience (Like Gwyndolin or Bed of Chaos) were Stray Demon and Four Kings. At the same time however in Dark Souls 1 you could go aggressive at any time for almost all bosses. However I'll admit this is more a fault of my playstyle and others may enjoy this. Other moments in the game feel cheap because you die due to an ambush you couldn't prepare for. The worst offender happened during Memory of Vammar when a Giant burst down a wall killing me instantly, and gave me no warning to react to it. Lots of tough enemies are placed together to make fights more difficult, where as in Dark Souls 1 weaker enemies came in big mobs and you fought tough enemies one at a time for the most part.
The Hitboxes in this game are pretty bad, and there's around a second long input delay on mouse and keyboard. It takes about a half second for the game to register you raised your shield, and then another half second to play the animation of raising said shield. Coupled with many hitboxes being absolutely horrid (Mimic's in my opinion being the worst offender, where they can grab you from the front whilst you are standing behind them, with a close contender being Aava's grab attack) this simply adds unnecessary frustration. Drinking Estus takes longer, and buffering attacks feels odd. I'll try and explain. In Dark Souls 1, you're attacking, so you mash your buttons. When you finish the attack animation the game checks to see if you're still clicking the button and then readies another attack. In 2, it simply depends on how many times you pressed the button, which is an odd change to get used to.
As said before, I think that the more linear level design and obvious methods of where to go helped, but some areas felt badly made or balanced. The worst offenders are the Bonus Areas in the three DLC, of which are honestly simply too frustrating for me to complete. Dark Chasm of Old stands out for me because of its reliance of Human Effigies to enter, giving you a finite number of tries. Other bad examples include Iron Keep and its overloaded amounts of mobs, The Gutter due to simply being a combination of Blighttown and Tomb of the Giants from the last game, and Shrine of Amana for reasons that will take too long to describe but are well known to anyone who played through it. There are simply too many areas as well. Dark Souls 1 had about 30 areas, where as Dark Souls 2 has about 45. By the time I was doing the DLC I just wanted the game to end as it felt more of a chore at that point (Though I will give the Burnt Ivory King credit for being genuinely fun). Souls are also finite in this game to a point. After killing an enemy too many times it goes away for good. This makes runups to bosses easier, but also means its harder to farm for items and gear. One can use a Bonfire Ascetic to reset the area, but that only makes the area harder as well, making the job of farming more difficult.
I wouldn't recommend this to someone who liked Dark Souls 1. I think Dark Souls 3 did a better job of what Dark Souls 2 tried to do by allowing for both patient and aggressive gameplay to work depending on style as well as having overall better lore and designed areas. Still, this doesn't make the game bad, I just didn't enjoy it much compared to the others. I feel someone who played Demon's Souls prior to Dark Souls 2 will be more experienced with the dying penalties (Cling Ring and Ring of Binding, Human Effigies and Stones of Epehemeral Eyes etc) but this just wasn't my cup of tea.

If you came here to expect a better Hearthstone alternative, go look elsewhere (I'd recommend Elder Scrolls Legends in that department). Eternal is a great adaption of a Magic the Gathering style cardgame. I played various different card games over the past 20 years and can explain the reasons for my perspective (even with the current small amount of playtime in eternal)
Eternal Card Game is remodelled version Magic the Gathering. it only differentiates in a few aspects. This isn't entirely negative as Eternal focuses on online gameplay while most people know that the MTG online client is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for most parts.
Let me go into detail about the things Eternal has in common with Hearthstone and Magic (I'll only use these two as examples, since they are the most known).
Hearthstone similarities:
- Presentation (UI, Voiceover, Design, Boardinteraction, etc...)
- Business model (prices for packs/arena/story/etc...)
Magic the Gathering similarities:
- Core game mechanics
--> Blocking attackers
--> Using counterspells
--> Building up mana using cards (without tapping)
--> Keyword mechanics (such as flying, trample/overwhelm, etc...)
--> Mixed decks (using cards from more than one faction/hero/color)
Even though the looks and the online play model are very similar to Hearthstone (which I believe is a great feature (Hearthstone UI is beautiful)), the core mechanics of the entire game are vastly different, a lot more like magic the gathering: building up mana requires "manacards" (sigils/lands), attackphases have room for interaction (i.e. blocking/counterspelling), damage distribution of minions is altered (not easy to explain in short), "arena" (draft) has a slightly different model than hearthstone and you get to keep all drafted cards, other minor differences.
I see quite a potential in Eternal as a card game, especially as it delivers a very good online mode for a mtg style game, while adding unique features to not make it look and feel like a carbon copy. It's also quite easy to pick up, but unlike Hearthstone, where netdecking (copying playermade decks) alone can get you to high ranks without much effort, eternal requires some good mechanic and card understanding to rise from amateur to novice and even more to master.
Presentation: 8.5/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Accessibility: 7/10
Overall Rating: 7.8/10 (for now).
I recommend Eternal to any/all card game fans.

A summary of a review from me would be "Not bad". Or "A good start". Or "It's gonna be super great someday".  For an early-access it's pretty good.  As you'd expect, there are some good things and some things that need polish.  I won't beat on Dovetail too hard as I got the game gratis as a previous owner of Dovetail Flight School.  That was a very nice and much appreciated gesture.
What I like:
The planes are really good looking.  Beautiful in fact.
The new menus are a huge improvement. Very modern, up-to-date.  Well done.
What is so-so:
The default scenery is certainly better than FSX.  But it isn't anything much to write home about.  Put it this way; the default scenery isn't as good as FSX after-market scenery.  I'm OK with that.  The after-market exists for a reason.  Most of the scenery I use is after-market anyway. So that fact that the default FSW scenery isn't all that great isn't really much of a bother for me.
Not many planes yet....  I'm guessing that's a temporary thing.  So no grudges from me (at least not now....).
What needs fixing:
Frame rate.  Biggest thing keeping me away at the moment.  Surprising actually.  FSW is optimized for DirectX11 where as the aged FSX is not.  I thought that alone would give better graphics performance.  I'm running an AMD RX480 with 8Gig GDDR5 on-board, an Intel i7 6700k proc @ 4Ghz, 64Gig of DDR4 RAM, and a 480Gig PCIe M.2 SSD.  I'm getting about ~15FPS with default scenery (3 monitors, 5940x1080 total res).  The older FSX with upgraded scenery gives ~45 to ~60.  Surprised to see this much of a difference between FSX and FSW to be honest.
Panel support isn't there yet.  The yokes, trim wheel, pedals, throttles, and IR tracker work fine.  The Saitek flight panels don't.  No drivers yet.
No VR support.  I would really like to see VR support integrated into the base product.  Or at the very least, I hope FlyInside creates a plug-in for FSW.
Net-net:  There's a lot of potential here.  The things that are broken are certainly fixable.  Or at least I would hope so.  I'm hoping that this becomes my go-to simulator.  Like most of us, I'll keep watching with great anticipation and hopes that this becomes the game-changer that it certainly can be!

SimplePlanes is an arcade, build and fly, flight ‘simulator’ developed by Jundroo. In SimplePlanes you design your own aircraft and then take to the sky with them! From high-speed jets to slow and steady sea planes if you can think it, you can probably make it. As you can guess from the name, the game’s selling point is that it’s pretty simple and easy to get the hang of, and it is indeed pretty simple and easy to get to grips with.
Consider this an ‘on the fence’ review rather than a straight up positive one. It took me a hell of a long time to decide whether or not I should choose positive or negative but in the end I decided to go positive since, as you’ll read towards the end of the review, it is pretty fun for a few hours but because of its issues which I’ll talk about in my review it just isn’t worth buying at full price.
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
The appearance of the aircraft themselves in SimplePlanes is reasonably good, as you’d expect it’s pretty simple, nothing flashy, but they get the job done while looking reasonably good. The map on the other hand, not so great. By no means are the textures awful, painful to look at or anything else along those lines but the map has a completely different graphic style to the aircraft parts, I just thought that was a little odd. The building menus were reasonably easy to use and the UI when flying was good too, basically just the visual displays you need to be able to fly the plane.
As I mentioned, SimplePlanes is mainly a ‘build and fly’ game where you build whatever you want to with the available parts and then take it for a flight around the map. There’s not really much to say about just flying around but I will talk about the build mode itself. The build mode is effectively a more simplified version of what you’d find in Kerbal Space Program, if you’ve played that before you’ll know what you’re doing. You select a part from the list of available parts and just drag it to wherever you want to place it. Some parts will change slightly to fit with everything around them but most are just static. Once an object is placed you can edit its properties (depending on whether the part has properties to change), for example you can change how much fuel is held by a fuel tank or the size of a wing. You also have some other options like the ability to mirror your aircraft so that whatever goes on one side, goes on the other.
The game doesn’t have a huge amount of parts available for you to use but if you’re creative enough there are a lot of possibilities with the game as can be seen from some of the awesome mods that have been made. The other issue with lack of content comes from the fact that the game only has one map and that map is very small. If the game’s pricing was closer to that of the mobile version then perhaps this would be acceptable but even with the launch discount, one map just isn’t good enough, this is a real problem for the game. It is possible to make your own maps and share them (see comment section) but I'm a firm believer that just because you can get extra content elsewhere doesn't make the base game's lack of content acceptable.
As well as the build and fly mode, SimplePlanes does have a few scenarios for you to try out, such as scenarios where you need to make a plane to use in a machine gun only dogfight or something similar. These are pretty good, and will no doubt be enjoyed by those good enough at building planes in the game to make planes for these scenarios, but there aren’t a huge amount of them and there’s no way to make your own, again limiting how much content the game has.
With a name like SimplePlanes you’d be silly to think this is going to be an ultra-realistic flight sim but since it’s been labelled by the devs as a simulator and described as having "realistic physcis" it’s fair to expect a reasonable amount of realism. Sadly what we’ve got is a bit of a mixed bag. There’s the basic physics in place for weight distribution, thrust, lift etc. and it’s reasonably good for a game edging towards the arcade side of flight sims but there are some inaccuracies dotted in there. For instance if you do a full ninety degree bank turn you would expect to lose velocity, how much depends on how far you pull back, but when I performed such turns in SP my velocity remained constant. I also had a couple of experiences where pitching and rolling simply didn’t work despite the fact that the control surfaces were visibly moving.
SimplePlanes, for what it is, is pretty fun but a lack of content and its high price tag make it a game I simply cannot recommend at full price. If you really want to try it out I’d suggest getting it on mobile until it gets a good discount on Steam.

I picked up Cooking Mama 2: Dinner with Friends back in 2008 or so for DS, which was an enjoyable little romp in cooking games that I could play on the go, with an added plus that I could share this with my less game-focused friends and family. The cutesy appeal and the cooking mini games combined into a game that I enjoyably shared with my younger girl cousins from out of town, and cemented in me an interest in the genre. So when I saw Cook, Serve, Delicious!, I saw the good reviews, figured I'd try it. I was very pleased with the results.
Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a unique cooking game that has enjoyable RPG elements intelligently spliced into a restaurant owning sim. You start out with a simple menu selling corn dogs and beer, and through an enjoyable menu customization system, you slowly build up to a fast-paced five-star restaurant. Controls let you use either a controller or keyboard (2 player co-op as well), with you needing to manage a real-time restaurant and prepare dishes quickly by pressing keys/buttons to add ingredients to different dishes. The same dish (like Pizza) could be simple or complicated depending on if they want a cheese pizza or a supreme, since you need to press a button to add every ingredient.
The menu customization in particular is very well done, since in a manner reminiscient of Diablo 3's difficulty tuning, you can modify your game's difficulty in how you build your menu of dishes; an easy menu will be comfortable and relaxing to cook, while a more complicated menu of dishes might earn more cash while keeping you on the edge of your seat, frantically trying to multitask cooking multiple dishes at once before you lose a customer. By being able to cater (no pun intended) my menu toward a difficulty I desired, I was able to challenge myself mechanically with my dishes as well as not get overly frustrated or overwhelmed from too many difficult dishes.
By the end game, you will start to upgrade your favorite dishes to their highest level, making them worth more but also making them more complicated by adding new ingredients, requiring more work to prepare. This actually results in the game staying enjoyable for much longer than I expected, as steady increase in complexity meant the game was always mechanically challenging, and more importantly, not overly repetitive. In the end, I was quite enjoying whizzing through 8 dishes at a time, feeling as mechanically pleased with my ability to cook complicated dishes as I would by doing a particularly difficult combination of abilities in a MOBA or MMORPG. It really was that fun.
This is not a game with a ton of action, or a deep story, or super impressive graphics. That said, Cook, Serve, Delicious! does provide a mechanically enjoyable, great-for-all-audiences game that kept me playing for 30 hours plus. Give it a chance, and it will impress you.

There seem to be a great many negative reviews of this Sim, despite it being only a couple of days old and with very limited functionality compared to what I would expect the final product to have. Essentially, this is a paid Beta test and, while I've seen cheaper Beta tests out there, you stll have to make allowances for where it is in its lifecycle - particularly if you're going to compare it to FSX or P3D, both of which share the same DNA. The question is: does it have the potential to replace FSX and compete with P3D? Well, it's too eary to answer that, yet!
There's no doubt Dovetail have cleaned up the interface and made the game more accessible to the new simmer. The (very limited number of) bundled aircraft are impressively realised, though to me their flight characteristics aren't where they should be yet. Graphically, FSW is better than vanilla FSX or P3D - it appears to use a simplified Orbx texture set - but it's nowhere near as good as XP11. However, the sim community has already discovered that many FSX aftermarket products can be installed into the game - though that's against the EULA, I believe, and hardly in the spirit of testing the game as produced so that Dovetail can get valid feedback to improve their product.
There are some graphics issues out of the box; the draw radius is pretty poor and FSW displays the annoying FSX behaviour of showing airfield structures at a far greater distance than any of the autogen scenery. The framerate on Ultra settings worked fine for me at around 30-50fps on my test system (i5 4690, 4Gb R9-380, 8Gb RAM), but some people have reported problems. Shadows have some odd behavious (the aliasing on in-cockpit shadows is dire!), and the overall visuals seem to be heavily HDR-influenced, which rarely improves their believability in my experience.
However, the sim works, it recognised all my hardware, and it's very accessible. It already appears that some FSX aftermarket software will work (though it won't take advantage of the 64-bit framework), and no doubt the community will quickly find ways to make more and more third-party stuff work. is it better than FSX? Not yet, but it probably will be. Is it better than P3D? No, but it's a lot cheaper! And you can use it legally for entertainment... Is it better than XP11? No, not by a long way - yet. But, if you're a long-time FSX/P3D simmer, you're far more likely to get on with it and be able to use your DLCs with this.
So, it's a tentative thumbs-up. And a strong 'well done - but don't stop there' to Dovetail. I hope this will mark the start of a new age in the MSFS timeline.

Before I go forward, I need to start off with this:
I didn't like Amnesia much at all.
The story was interesting but the gameplay itself as well as the scare factor was, to me, very overhyped. The gameplay seemed very much minimal and out of body. The entire time I felt I was looking in, and was not much immersed at all. Add to that the scare factor was greatly exaggerated and well... I was left disappointed.
And then I bought Outlast.
While there are many things I love about this game, I do need to put out a few warnings:
This game is really gory. Not much for the squeamish at all.
This game becomes very intense. I had to break at points because I just got too freaked out, something that hasn't happened to me since being hounded down by Nemesis in RE3.
I'll start off with the immersion.
Even though you -know- you're another character, his background is left vague and the only true objective you have is "survive”. In this sense, it really becomes easy for the player to integrate his or herself with the character. That YOU are being chased, that YOU are cramming yourself in a locker, breaths stuttering and heart pounding as the door to the room is broken in. It makes it a very real sensation. I suppose it also helps to see hands reaching out to interact with objects rather than them floating in midair as well.
The second thing is the environment.
Very eerie, creepy setting… and just about every little thing gets you. Floorboards creaking will leave you on-edge trying to determine if that was you, an enemy, or just those old floorboards. The lighting is also pretty dynamic and fantastic in this game, striking scattered chairs and disfigured faces leaving you with a feeling of uneasiness.
But I would have to say the piece du resistance is the music. What a fantastic arrangement this game has. As enemies find you, a shrill shriek of horns and strings alert you that your presence has been noticed. As enemies wander around, low, lingering tones with the occasional, random rise reach your ears, lulling you into a calmed state as you adjust only to be jarred from it over and over. And when wandering around with a new objective, subtle notes run across your ears, masked by footsteps and creaking doors.
If you're a horror nut, this is the game for you. If Amnesia just wasn't doing it for you, this will. And for $20, I couldn't ask for more.

Still playing through the game, but I feel like I'm so close to the end that I can't feel like my opinion would change at all from here until I finish the game.
Legend of Grimrock 2 is mechanically the exact same as #1, albeit with more spells this time around and special moves that items have.
The graphics are slightly upgraded from LoG1 as well, but a lot of enemy assets have been re-used (mushroom people, twigroot enemies, spiders, cudgels etc). There's so many new things added and their fidelity is quality enough that I don't care, and it doesn't detract from that game at all especially if you haven't played #1 yet (lots of these enemies have new tricks up their sleeves too).
Enemy AI has been upgraded in LoG2, where enemies are harder to kite because most of them have been equipped with side-swipe attacks and the rest of them will hesitate to move in front of you if they know you're camping a square trying to get a free side hit on them. The latter is bad because it drags out gameplay in what is an otherwise core mechanic of playing Grimrock.
I feel that the gameplay is too slow; at the point I'm at, enemy encounters are a slog because each common enemy I fight can take upwards of 3-4 cycles from my party members. Stuff like frogs stealing weapons out of your party members hands, but then subsequently only dealing 3 damage per attack is annoying when it means that 1/4 of your DPS is taken away for a while; considering that these frogs respawn, it gets old really quick. The same goes for the blue lightning lizards that deal AoE damage to your party while you're walking around the hub world, and the blue gremlins who lurk in the water who block underwater paths until you kill them in the hub.
Boss battles are new to Legend of Grimrock 2, but are a bit underwhelming. The majority of them come down to rushing the boss down while tanking his minions (if they summon them constantly), or just crawling into a corner and fighting all the enemies one at a time (if the minions are non-respawning). Like I said, when each common minion takes 3-4 cycles of your entire party, then you'll understand how boss fights get annoying really quick.
Stat boosts through crystals, potions, and spells feel useless. There are only maybe two enemies in the game who deal shock damage that I've encountered so far, and armor that gives only +4 protection and maybe some points into vitality negates their damage so much that I don't understand why I'd brew potions or cast spells to negate their baby damage any more. By the time I walk to wherever I want to go, I'll heal it back anyways.
The overworld is a really nice addition to LoG2, and I really enjoyed it... at first. By the time you complete two of the main areas, you'll be so tired of walking back and forth from untracked dungeon #698 to untracked dungeon #699 that you'll wish it was streamlined like LoG1 was. Beyond that, it's hard to tell which dungeons are required to progress and which ones aren't. You'll end up in a dungeon that takes you thirty minutes to complete just to get some power crystals (which are used to progress the game), but your inventory is probably full of them by now so there's no reason to grab more.
Like I said above, armor is kind of bungus in this game. You're better off just getting health on your characters who you want to tank. Lots of skill trees feel useless to me, especially when my party is only specializing in very specific characteristics. My light weapons character had light weapons maxed out at level 5, and is now throwing points into skills like accuracy (because literally every other attack in this game misses for some reason, I don't know). The problem with accuracy is that the "milestones" for this skill tree give me perks like "can attack from the back row" which is useless because my melee attacker is already specced to be in the front row. I'd have to be hella early in the game for that to be useful, back before my mage got spells and my alchemist got good guns. And early in the game, there's no point in attacking from the back row because you won't have enough weapons OR have enough skill points to use said weapons.
Every character runs into this problem where late-game speccing is just everywhere and there's no skill point reset at all. So if you put one single point into the wrong ability and want to change it later, you're SOL. My Heavy-Weapons character ran into it, my Alchemist ran into it, and my Mage is running into it too I don't have any desire to teach my fire-mage any air magic, but after you max the fire damage tree the only other good option for Mage to be able to sling spells better is just adding +20 mana to your pool per level. Spell at my rank cost like 40 mana per cast, so you can see how this is sub-useless at the point I'm at.
It's really easy to get lost and have nothing to do in Grimrock 2. After you complete a dungeon, you're left scouring the hub world map for little spots you haven't covered, or maybe some puzzles you might have accidently not seen. I had to look up a guide just because one mandatory area had a puzzle in the entrance. The clue, which is the only way you could solve the puzzle, was hidden in a dungeon that I had already completed apparently. It was a piece of paper that I had overlooked on the ground after a tough fight, and I just totally walked past. I was walking around the island for two hours trying to find out what to do until I came across it because I resorted to using a guide for help.
Save-scumming is basically a necessity in Grimrock 2 unless you want to be repeating hours of gameplay after every single unexpected ambush death. Get ready to press F5 + F9 a lot.
This might just be me, but I feel like a lot of the puzzles this time around make less sense. Not all of them, but some of them have such niche solutions that you'll know the answer that the designers want you to think of, but you won't know how to express it in-game (without spoiling anything, a good example of this is in the cemetary).
I mentioned special attacks, but here's my issue with them : In Grimrock 2, to perform any kind of attack you need to right-click on the characters weapon (or drag your mouse over a set of runes in order to cast a spell). To use a special attack, you need to hold down the mouse on a single weapon for around 1.5-2 seconds. In the time it takes to charge up a single special attack, I could have probably used my entire team's regular attacks including my Mage. If my Minotaur guy winds up an attack to deal 210 damage instead of his regular 120, but it takes so long that I have to miss an entire team rotation (60 damage from my light attacker, 40 damage from my alchemist, and another 140+ from my Mage), then there's no point in wasting that time; especially because if I miss the attack (which special attacks can and very often will miss) you basically cut out a quarter of your damage if not more. Special attacks should be able to be queued up, like how spells can be queue'd up before you cast them. That way, if I want to just blow up a small enemy with a barrage of special attacks I won't have to waste time with kiting a single petty mob.
Enemy health values are a bit ridiculous in Grimrock 2. One particular enemy you have to fight in a mandatory dungeon has such a high protection rating that neither of my hard-hitters hit above 1-damage on the enemy for the entire fight; I had to use my mage, who completely ignores armor, and spent five whole minutes just walking circles around this particular enemy just waiting for my spells to recharge. There's all kinds of cheesy enemies which I won't go into detail about how ridiculously time consuming it is to deal with them.

This game is the ultimate sandbox.  Infact, the campaign FORCES you to play with the sandbox.  You have two forms of currency in the game.  One is actual currency, money, and the other is "Chaos."  You earn Chaos by destroying buildings and killing Panauan military forces, as well as completing side-missions.
The game's voice acting is AWFUL, the story is pretty much garbage (You're an 'undercover' US agent whose mission is to dethrone the dictator of the island.  You do this by causing as much chaos as possible) but I cannot stop coming back to this game.
You can use any mode of transportation you want: run on the ground, fly a plane, drive a car, fly a helicopter, use a boat, a motorcycle, pretty much all forms of transportation are covered.  Oh, did I mention that there is a ♥♥♥♥ing GRAPPLING HOOK AND PARACHUTE?  Because there is.  You use the grappling hook to give yourself speed, and the parachute to control everything else.  Not only is this one of the fastest modes of transportation (only fast travel and planes are faster) but it's always fun to find new routes to move.  You will hardly ever use anything else, because this mode is so efficient and just plain fun.
Technically, the game will run excellently on any computer that has a graphics card in it.  It's built on a proprietary engine, and runs excellently and beautifully.  A few of the screenshots in the store page are touched up (blur here and there) but for the most part those are actual in-game screenshots.  There's no FoV slider, but I never had a problem seeing.
If you ever played Grand Theft Auto, or any open world game, and instead of going for the main missions you just roam around enjoying the sandbox goodness, you will love this game.

The PC version is the best remake you can get for this amazing game.
Even after completing FFX multiple times in the past, it is still a game that I can play through completely again now. The gameplay is nostalgic and the combat system is unique and enjoyable. The game allows a lot of customisation as you progress through the game, and with the ability to easily switch between different characters in battles, you can decide which characters you want to focus on, or whether you want to balance between all of them.
The gameplay has some gridy elements that will feel dated and possibly frustrating to some players now, but the remake adds some added "boosters" to the game that reduce the grind slightly.
The music of the original release was top notch, with this version featuring remastered versions of many tracks. You can switch between the original or the remastered music in the settings to bring back the nostalgia of playing it on PS2 or just to listen to the differences between the original and the remaster.
The story is interesting and emotive, and the characters have different backstories and personalities.
Although many people skip FFX-2, it is an interesting game to play at least some of. The combat system and gameplay may well put many players off, but I would suggest giving it a chance beyond the first hour or so of play. It does explore some more deep elements than just Yuna, Rikku, and Paine dressing up. For players who really enjoyed FFX, you will get some extra story by playing FFX-2 that you will find interesting too.
For anyone who hasn't played a FINAL FANTASY game before and is put off by the older titles that don't have high-definition 3D graphics, I would recommend trying this one out. Some gameplay elements will feel a bit dated by modern game standards but it is definitely worth playing through.

A very decent port of a classic JRPG.
The story is a little cheesy, the voice acting is infamous. Still the game is beautiful. The music is redone for the HD version to be live all the way. Cinematics are great. The Other World theme is true. The whole game has a unique art style, kinda sorta fantasy Maori culture. Characters are OK. The combat is fun, often puzzle-like. Interesting gameplay twist is this game uses a system now common in RPGs: there's a clear distinction between the main tutorial-like game and challenging post-game. It's not that there are no challenging battles in the main game; it's just they don't require much preparation. Side activities like monster Arena give you stronger enemies to fight and provide better equipment to fight those enemies. All the grind and optimization are for post-game; base game requires relatively small effort. This creates a very fine difficulty curve and allows you to stop whenever you want - just go for the final dungeon when optional bosses seem ridiculous.
PSA: when asked about Sphere Grid use the simple, basic option. It basically means that for most of the game character development is almost linear. This may save you from going on the wrong track and missing important abilities or getting duplicated characters. Advanced version gives you much more freedom in selecting abilities but it's very easy to end up with, say, same stats and abilities for Rikku and Kimari.

I think that, in comparison to the other Fromsoft Souls-esque titles (DS1, DS3, Bloodborne, Demons Souls) that DS2 is easily the weakest of the bunch. The lore isn't quite as deep or connected, and there's some elements of gameplay that frustrate me about this game.
This does not make Dark Souls 2 a bad game, but rather inferior in comparison to the others. It certainly feels like the black sheep of the franchise.
For starters, what did it get right? Well the game both runs and looks very well. I suffered almost no lag the entire game, so its very well optimized. The soundtrack and environments are very good, and I think Dark Souls 2's level design is in some ways better than Dark Souls 1 by giving you a better idea of where to go. PVP is also undeniably at its best in this game.
What does it do wrong? Well, for starters, the Effigy system. I am aware it is a holdover from Demon's Souls, where as you die and lose your health. However the fact that the item for turning human is finite is a bit dumb. You can circumvent this by completing Vendrick's quest or using the Shrine of Amana altar. However this is so late in the game it hardly matters at that point.
Difficulty seems more artificial and cheap. Dark Souls 2 is the only game in the franchise not directed by Miyazaki, and it shows. Bosses, instead of being more difficult, simply add mobs (like Royal Rat Authority, or Elana, the Squalid Queen) as a cheap means to win fights, or in some cases just rehash older boss fights in the series (Belfry Gargoyles, Old Dragonslayer). The Smelter Demon in Iron Passage is just a blue version of the Red Smelter Demon earlier in Iron Keep, except with Magic Damage instead of Fire Damage. There are also too many bosses where you have to fight multiple people at a time, because otherwise the fight would be too easy (Lud and Zallen, Throne Watcher and Defender, Twin Dragonriders, etc). Combat also is very biased to dodging over tanking. The patient and tactical gameplay styles for most of Dark Souls 1 bosses simply don't work here. For about 3/4 of the bosses you have to learn to dodge and play very aggressively because your armor won't mean jack. In Dark Souls 1, the only bosses to my recollection that you couldn't be patient with and didn't have a unique gameplay mechanic to prevent said patience (Like Gwyndolin or Bed of Chaos) were Stray Demon and Four Kings. At the same time however in Dark Souls 1 you could go aggressive at any time for almost all bosses. However I'll admit this is more a fault of my playstyle and others may enjoy this. Other moments in the game feel cheap because you die due to an ambush you couldn't prepare for. The worst offender happened during Memory of Vammar when a Giant burst down a wall killing me instantly, and gave me no warning to react to it. Lots of tough enemies are placed together to make fights more difficult, where as in Dark Souls 1 weaker enemies came in big mobs and you fought tough enemies one at a time for the most part.
The Hitboxes in this game are pretty bad, and there's around a second long input delay on mouse and keyboard. It takes about a half second for the game to register you raised your shield, and then another half second to play the animation of raising said shield. Coupled with many hitboxes being absolutely horrid (Mimic's in my opinion being the worst offender, where they can grab you from the front whilst you are standing behind them, with a close contender being Aava's grab attack) this simply adds unnecessary frustration. Drinking Estus takes longer, and buffering attacks feels odd. I'll try and explain. In Dark Souls 1, you're attacking, so you mash your buttons. When you finish the attack animation the game checks to see if you're still clicking the button and then readies another attack. In 2, it simply depends on how many times you pressed the button, which is an odd change to get used to.
As said before, I think that the more linear level design and obvious methods of where to go helped, but some areas felt badly made or balanced. The worst offenders are the Bonus Areas in the three DLC, of which are honestly simply too frustrating for me to complete. Dark Chasm of Old stands out for me because of its reliance of Human Effigies to enter, giving you a finite number of tries. Other bad examples include Iron Keep and its overloaded amounts of mobs, The Gutter due to simply being a combination of Blighttown and Tomb of the Giants from the last game, and Shrine of Amana for reasons that will take too long to describe but are well known to anyone who played through it. There are simply too many areas as well. Dark Souls 1 had about 30 areas, where as Dark Souls 2 has about 45. By the time I was doing the DLC I just wanted the game to end as it felt more of a chore at that point (Though I will give the Burnt Ivory King credit for being genuinely fun). Souls are also finite in this game to a point. After killing an enemy too many times it goes away for good. This makes runups to bosses easier, but also means its harder to farm for items and gear. One can use a Bonfire Ascetic to reset the area, but that only makes the area harder as well, making the job of farming more difficult.
I wouldn't recommend this to someone who liked Dark Souls 1. I think Dark Souls 3 did a better job of what Dark Souls 2 tried to do by allowing for both patient and aggressive gameplay to work depending on style as well as having overall better lore and designed areas. Still, this doesn't make the game bad, I just didn't enjoy it much compared to the others. I feel someone who played Demon's Souls prior to Dark Souls 2 will be more experienced with the dying penalties (Cling Ring and Ring of Binding, Human Effigies and Stones of Epehemeral Eyes etc) but this just wasn't my cup of tea.

This is a great, fast paced game that will challenge your memory and your time management skills. It is also on occasion hilarious. You must juggle many tasks all at once and finish within a certain time frame. The game is fun, and the developers are not money grubbing jerks who take your money and run. This is money well spent either way you look at it.

Video Review -
Before we get into the mechanics of the game I want to express my annoyance at the pricing of the game. As is common these days with mobile ports the game is more expensive on Steam than it is on mobile devices. Warhammer Quest is $5 on mobile but $15 on steam, that is a crazy price jump for the same game. Not only this but they have carried the in game purchases over from the mobile version, which I personally think they should have included all content in the full price considering your charging an extra $10 just for the ability to play it on steam. But you can buy the game with all the optional content in the deluxe edition for $30 but seriously I don't need to be the one to tell you that this game is not worth $30 do I?
Oh and did I mention you can buy gold in the game for ridiculous prices, oh yes that's in there. Now I have yet to encounter a point where I could not progress in the game without purchasing gold however, the gold that drops organically seems low, not to mention the various reviews of the mobile version that claimed that purchasing gold at some point was required.
The pricing annoys me further when no real effort has been put in to optimize for the PC market. You control everything with the mouse which renders the keyboard useless which becomes particularly annoying when you want to scroll the map with WASD but can't and have to click and drag everywhere. The developers haven't even bothered with placing in higher resolution textures for any part of the game nor even upgraded the movie resolutions which makes the small CGI movies when entering a town look worse than awful.
The premise of the game is simple, take your group of adventurers through the dungeons of the Warhammer World in the search for wealth and glory. The standard edition of the game comes with four playable characters of a roster of eleven. The other characters are available to purchase, because of course they are.
This all being said the actual game mechanics are faithfully representative of the source material. Each dungeon you visit works from a grid system, by selecting your characters one by one you can see the available movement options. You will only be able to see the rooms you are either in or have been in, everything else will be shrouded in darkness until you step foot in it. This fog of war play means that you'll never know what enemies are waiting in the next room, it could be rats or it could be a giant blood hungry beast. While moving in the hallways room to room, you'll occasionally get attack by enemies that will spawn around you, which is fun towards the start but when your running low on health and out of potions, it becomes both frustrating and worrying.
Combat revolves around basic attacks, inventory items, spells and abilities. Attacking a target requires a simple click as does using items and spells once you've selected them from the bottom HUD menus. Everything has a hit chance or some kind of roll involved and example would be a healing spell for which a roll occurs to determine how much or how little the spell heals. One of the most famous combat mechanics from the original board game was 'deathblow' in which should a character kill an enemy with one hit then they could continue to carry that attack to any other enemies in range. In game this mechanic means that should your marauder be surrounded by enemies you essentially have a chance to kill them all from one attack, potentially. This mechanic has saved me many times from tight spaces.
While the combat mechanics in essence are fairly solid. The hit chance can cause you to have a run of bad luck and inconvenient times. It can make combat feel unfair, punishing and outright brutal when you need the hits to swing your way in an important fight. Once a character dies in battle you can use that character again once you complete the dungeon which on one hand is ok but in my opinion a permadeath state for characters would have been much for fun and meaningful. Mages and units that require things like mana or willpower for abilities will regenerate an amount at the start of each turn.
When your not in a dungeon, there's the world map and town screens. World map travel consists of travelling from town to town eventually visiting all three regions. To travel to a unvisited town you must first complete the dungeon on the way, after doing this you can move from that town to a previous town freely.
Once in a town you have a few options available to you. First if any of your warriors have gained enough experience to level up then you can go to the training ground to level them up which requires gold to do so, clearly a mechanic for draining your gold to get you to buy some more. Each town also has a market where you can buy equipment and potions as well as sell your unwanted items. Usually markets will have a few unique items that are specific to that town or relate to that towns quest in name only.  The adventurers guild is where you can see all the characters that are available to use included ones that are DLC. In the towns temple you can pay gold to have one of your warriors pray for a chance to receive a unique buff that can be activated only once during the next dungeon.
Random events involving your warriors will also take place in towns that can end up having buffs and debuffs for the next dungeon. My witch hunter decided to get very drunk and ended up having a debuff for the entirety of the next dungeon. Finally Towns each have their own unique quests that have a short story attached to it. These quests are optional and incur some difficult dungeons but there's also the chance for some great loot too. These quests are presented in text form and are relatively well written with some interesting characters and humour stuffed in.
An big element that I feel is missing from the game is multiplayer. Having multiplayer in the game would have done wonders for re-playability. Its the perfect genre for multiplayer, I mean come on the source material is a board game for goodness sake. Multiplayer should have been a given for Warhammer Quest and yet sadly we have none.
The game overall is pretty solid yet I personally cannot recommend it. There is no reason why you would buy a mobile game from 2013 at an inflated price just to have it on steam. The fact that the game is riddled with micro-transactions plus no real effort has been made in both controls and aesthetics for the transition to PC leaves me thinking that it was an easy cash grab. Even if your a big Warhammer fan or a fan of turn based games and your dead set on playing this, there is no reason not to play it on your mobile device especially considering the price difference.

This game is the ultimate sandbox.  Infact, the campaign FORCES you to play with the sandbox.  You have two forms of currency in the game.  One is actual currency, money, and the other is "Chaos."  You earn Chaos by destroying buildings and killing Panauan military forces, as well as completing side-missions.
The game's voice acting is AWFUL, the story is pretty much garbage (You're an 'undercover' US agent whose mission is to dethrone the dictator of the island.  You do this by causing as much chaos as possible) but I cannot stop coming back to this game.
You can use any mode of transportation you want: run on the ground, fly a plane, drive a car, fly a helicopter, use a boat, a motorcycle, pretty much all forms of transportation are covered.  Oh, did I mention that there is a ♥♥♥♥ing GRAPPLING HOOK AND PARACHUTE?  Because there is.  You use the grappling hook to give yourself speed, and the parachute to control everything else.  Not only is this one of the fastest modes of transportation (only fast travel and planes are faster) but it's always fun to find new routes to move.  You will hardly ever use anything else, because this mode is so efficient and just plain fun.
Technically, the game will run excellently on any computer that has a graphics card in it.  It's built on a proprietary engine, and runs excellently and beautifully.  A few of the screenshots in the store page are touched up (blur here and there) but for the most part those are actual in-game screenshots.  There's no FoV slider, but I never had a problem seeing.
If you ever played Grand Theft Auto, or any open world game, and instead of going for the main missions you just roam around enjoying the sandbox goodness, you will love this game.

This game is a straightforward fantastic example of its genre. Anyone who has encountered rpg's of this kind will find that it is exemplary, and those who have not encountered them will find themselves a rare gem and newfound appreciation for what this playstyle has to offer.
As for specific clarification for newcomers, the game is grid-based, and people's ablity to act is on a cooldown, making it essentially turn based in a certain sense. So think a strategy and jrpg mix, with the best of both genres mixed together. IE you can dodge and manuever in 3d space but actions are predicated in an orderly predictable fashion. And all your men occupy one space so you don't spend a half hour manuevering people around like in Shining Force.
Outside of the combat the exploration is puzzle based, and no puzzle is so obtuse you can't figure it out on your own. The game is tempered to the extent that any non-fooligan can complete everything by themselves, but still contains enough secrets locked away for the more conscientious player. At the same time nothing is strange or nonsensicle; no puzzle will have you looking at a guide and asking how anyone would decide to do something so strange. And the game shines because of this fact.
Outside of this, the games' outdoor setting is a straight upgrade to its predecessor in the sense that,"it isn't dark and unhappy all the time", and it uses it's new environment to add puzzles, complications, and scenery that wouldn't be afforded to a strict cobblestone backdrop.
All in all I find it difficult to find any fault with this game, and the mod support means there is even some community campaigns worth trying. It's worth a buy for anyone even vaguely interested in this type of game, or even rpgs in the broader sense.

My review of Verdun
Pros: Incredibly immersive.  Very realistic.  Historically accurate maps.  Gives you info about the real war during loading screens and such.  Squad types are varied and interesting.  Great voice overs for the languages of all the squads.  Easy to learn hard to master.  Frontlines mode is amazing.  Very tense and at times quite frightning.  Good amount of options and the abuilty to turn off gore
Cons: Occasional frame drops. Multiplayer only (Not really a big deal but it should be noted).
Rating: 10/10-Masterful: Verdun is a staggeringly immersive and wounderfully realistic multiplayer FPS set in WW1, it features multiple gamemodes but the best by far is Frontlines which is hands down the most immersive and atmospheric multiplayer/FPS experiance I've ever had, from the moment you enter a game you'll be surrounded by sounds of gunfire, mortors shelling your trenches, soldiers yelling orders and the haunting screams of the wounded, this is a fairly slow paced game when compared to other Multiplayer FPS games but it never seems dull or boring, you'll spend a lot of time crawling around trying not to get shot, but no matter how hard you try you are going to get shot, a lot, this game as a realisticly short TTK so most of the time if you get shot once you're dead, the challenge of this game makes doing well incredibly fulfilling and you feel a sense of accomplishment for every gunfight you win
In closing let me say that this has quickly become one of my favorite games in the FPS genre and I highly recommend it to fans of first person shooters and also to anyone with an interest in World War 1

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I've been flight simulating since the late 90's--beginning with FS98 (that's three versions before FSX). I enjoy this hobby because  I have a passion for aviation, I can't afford a pilot's licence, and I'd rather do this than sit on my couch and stare at a TV show. I've tried P3D and X-plane, and found them unsuitable compared with the accessibility of the Microsoft franchise. Aerofly2 is, in my opinion, a bit of a joke as its default "scenery" looks worse than MFS2004. For the past 10 years, FSX has been my game of choice, but over that past three years, as I have loaded it with third party scenery and aircraft to keep it looking current, it has become very slow to load, and generally unstable.
After Flight School came out last year, I found myself playing it much more often than FSX because it was far more stable, easier to use, and better looking. Now, after playing FSW through the weekend, I've removed FSX from my harddrive. The default aircraft in FSW would cost you over $100 dollars to get into any of the other sims. The default scenery is made by ORBX. Sure it's a bit buggy and pale, but it's early access; the developer is committed to responding to the community. Also, as some of the biggest players in the third party world--ORBX, Carenado, and A2A--have their software built right into FSW, it's a pretty solid bet that this game will be around for a long while. The fact that FSW is based on FSX is really a big "So what?"--so is P3D, and X-plane itself is built on 20 year old code. Don't be misled by the negative reviews; I think the segment of the sim community that is most negative about this game does not represent the market Dovetail is pursuing. Dovetail is looking for gamers who enjoy flight simulation because it's fun. This Early Access FSW is fun.

For Early Access, this is really promising. Like many other reviewers I've been through a ton of flight sims from MS flight sim 95 to various Xplanes, P3d, FSX and many more inbetween (remember Fly? and the flight unlimited series?). I've got so many add ons for FSX for weather/scenery/aircraft/mechanics that I really can't remember what the vanilla version is like but I'm quite certain that it's nothing near as good as FSW.
The scenery is crisp and fluid with a mix of photorealistic elements and autogen trees, buildings etc. The included aircraft are typically excellent with a nice range of GA aircraft (and they are finished which is something Lamina Research couldn't manage with the recent release of Xplane 11). They fly pretty well and the blurb on Steam mentions integration of Accu-Feel which is A2As' very nice flight realism package. So Dovetail are clearly incorporating some very decent code into FSW. I suspect they've built up some good business partnerships with A2A, Carenado etc through their work on FSX:SE and they are working this into FSW.
At the moment (a few days after release) it's quite a way from the finished, polished v1.0 and I've had many crashes on my machine although promisingly, not during flight (mainly going through the menus and starting a flight). Dovetail do seem genuinely interested in engaging with the community to develop the sim which bodes well and if you're bored enough to sit through their developer diary videos they do talk lots about FSW being for the long term. They've got some form so fingers crossed. If they get it right, this could certainly be the best flight sim on the market for years to come. And for £20? Just Cause 2 is like an exciting trip to a foreign country. You never know what to expect from the locales , or if the stuff you are currently eating includes 1 or more domestic animals inside it.
Story:
The Game has you starring as Rico, formerly known as "Scorpio", an buff, stereotypical white latino.Your job is being a♥♥♥♥♥♥to the self aclaimed new president "Panay", which is trying to distance panau, the island you play on, from the western world. He's doing that by the obvious way. Establishing his own dominance via painting every single combustable/explosive in his signature colours. Red and white. Why that is important ? You wont ask me again when you have already read this review further. Your Job is trying to "Liberate" Panau for 'murica'.Doing that is quite easy. Blowning up gas containers, facilities, military bases, all nice stuff.
Gameplay:
As you can guess, the game doesnt take itself too serious, however, this might not be as much of an flaw, as you might imagine in the first place. Did I mention that Rico has a Grappling hook ? No ? Well, in the context of the "serious" plot, Scorpio has this weird♥♥♥♥♥thingy, that allows him to do ridiculous stuff, like attaching two enemies onto each other , and giggle at their frustration, as they get smashed against each other, trying to get the hook loose, that is piercing through their flesh. Sounds like fun, now doesnt it, you jerk ? Well, to be honest, it is. It's a blast. Using the grapling hook to pull yourself onto vehicles, get around, or just do the before mentioned with cars, planes, boats..you get the Idea. On top of it all, you get  the most reliable parachute in the world. Using it in combination with your personal zipping device, you can fly through the air to get to new places, extent your life by a few more seconds, or dodge great threats all together.
As for the goal of the game, your job is to cause chaos. You do that via the before mentioned blowing up of important infrastructures, that are all conveniently marked by Panays Signature colours. By doing that, you will unlock more Items for the so called Black market. A mysterious delivery service, that is run by the " Sloth demon", and delivers everything you could ask for in a game like this, like cars, weapons,planes  aswell as extracting you too any previously discovered location. With the right amount of chaos, you will constantly unlock new stuff to buy there, and  if you're lucky enough to dfin new vehicle/ weapon parts on your journey, you can even go as far as upgrading the Items you buy from him. Havent I told you, how much this abscense of a real story brightens up the game ? See ? Awesome.I sincerely wish that there were more games like this.
Graphics and PC performance, mods, and tweaking:
Just cause 2 is an relatively old game, as you might have guessed already.That however doesnt keep it from having a solid technical build quality. The environment look nice, especially in places with a lot of fauna, Ricos clothing is very detailed, and nothing clips through him (*Cough* Assassins Creed*Cough*) , and the draw distance is very nice.Surprisingly enough, the water is looking awesome, if you have an corresponding Nvidia Card. I sugest atleast having an GTX 280, because it´s rendered via cuda cores, but it runs just as well on AMd cards of the same quality. For a DirectX 10 Game, the lighting is very beatiful, and eyecandy such as Godrays enhances the overall experience.Panau is very detailed, and optic fidelity can be found everywhere. from the harsh mountain tops, that are covered in snow, to the green jungle,small villages, and deserts, the game looks absolutely gorgeous.It´s colourful, cramped with detail, and fun to play in.
As for the mod side of things, you can find a lot of interesting stuff besides all the cheats, vehicle, and weapon mods.
Guessing that your PC is fast enough, I would sugest to Use Sweet FX, if I were you. Sweet Fx is a mod, which allows modern Anti Aliasing technologies, such as FXAA, and SGSSAA, to be forced into a game, which doesnt natively support said options. It also can be tweaked to your liking , and there are many user created presets for it, which enhance saturation, contrast, and overall optical Fidelity a lot.
Speaking of optical enhancers, how well does the game actually run ? To be honest, it runs like a charm. my GTX470 always can keep up smooth 60 Frames per second, while having sweet FX, and the ingame MSAA to work with.there is no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t frame cap, no forced Vsync, a nice Field of view, and advanced graphical options, to tweak the game to your liking.
Conclusion:
Just Cause 2 delivers what it promises. Action without any compromises. It isnt held back by its serious plot, social commentary, or anything similar to those dfancy♥♥♥♥♥triple A Titles you always hear about. It´s just pure fun with an Story construct build beneath it. Did I even mention the multiplayer mod ? So far, all i can say is that I am really enjoying this game.
It was definitely worth every cent I spend on it, and I can only give my recommendation for it to you. If you enjoy mindless action, hilarious situations, and all out rampages, then this game is for you. buy it.

I'll start with 2 Discaimers.
1: I bought this game knowing exactly what I was getting into
2: There will be spoilers
To be honest WAAAAYYYYYYYY back when I bought it, I already knew pretty much everything about the story. This however in no way swayed me from not buying it. Why? Because although I knew what I was getting into knowing it and experiancing it are two different things. Which is something most people who keep away from spoilers don't fully grasp(no offense meant here). It took me some time to actually play though cause at the time the computer I had would not have been able to run it. So, it took a backburner for a long time.
Now that I have finally played it. I'm not disapointed. If anything, I'm even more happy that I purchased it in the first place. The ending almost had me left in tears & I had stayed up to 2am to finish it in one go. Will I play this again? Much like a certian movie with a similar though somewhat comedic story, the answer is yes.
Regarding the characters, the person I least liked the more and more info that was presented would have to be the mother. She came accross as unfaithful & I'm glad at least she decided to move back towards the father.
The father of all people I felt the most for. It pained me to see all the extra copies of his failed book series he had as I explored the house. Not to mention the.......other not so good thing. There was a nice silver lining as I got closer to the end though.
Sam, oh boy Sam. I feel happy for her bittersweet ending but at the same time..........I wish she had waited just a bit so she could see her sister(us) return. But than if that had been the case, this would be a very different story. And I can totally understand why she left. Her thinking it impossible to speak with us directly makes sense. Because if she waited only to be rejected for her being a Lesbian by her own sister who she cares so much for. I think, it would have left the ultimate scar for her. And unlike with her just leaving and there being a chance of returning some day. I don't think she would have returned. As is the case of most gay people who get rejected by their families.
All in all, I really loved this story and most of all I love that although we learn the journal entries as we go. Ultimately, it's actually all being read after we get to into the attic.
Just remember, if you don't like just walking around picking things up & reading things. This game will probably not be for you.

Legend of Grimrock 2 is a good looking, fun to play and hard to master game.
It starts of like any other RPG too - you strand on an island and have to free yourself from a cage. However, the game is slightly different than all the other RPG's: You play a party of 4, while in first person. You can arrange the position of your party members to have meele characters stand in front, ranges in the back [...]  It's a nice, at least for me new and fun concept. However it also has its flaws - but i will come back to that later.
The gameplay is basicly you and your party moving around on square tiles, killing monsters, finding treasures, solving puzzles and overall exploring the newly found area. I'ts not a bad thing to do and i enjoyed it! THe monsters are generic, yes, but look great nontheless. The puzzles were okay to solve but still not bad enough to be instantly revealed.
Look-wise the game is fantastic. The details are awesome and it ran very smooth on my - for todays standards - okay-ish pc.
However, what makes me 'Not recommend' the game is the following: After 1-2 hours of gameplay you meet your first boss. And here is where things start to get bad. Fighting the boss on tiles, with your party arranged to your needs, cooldowns on your attacks, and very limited movability is just horrible. I tried it over and over and over again to be able to beat him, but i just couldnt do it. I was never even close to finishing him off.
The slow, limited combat possibilities against a Tentacle boss who can spawn, despawn and attack from anywhere is just not working out! Having such a boss as first 'hard' encounter was demoralizing and frustrating.
Unless you like huge challenges like that even on normal difficulty and are a fan of the movement / combat system itself, you might want to think about skipping on this game.
Please keep in mind that this is just how i experienced it and how i think about the game. It's really not bad, but i cannot recommend it to the broad majority of user out there.

I've finally completed it after playing 2 years off and on. My expectation was that it would be like the first Grimrock, but pushed too far for the engine to support the larger ambitions. My skepticism was wrong and it turned out to be better in every way. The world, combat, items, skills, puzzles, and everything else have all been reworked to perfection. The switch from linear to more open world turned out great and fits perfectly with the adventure style.
My favorite thing about the game is the puzzles. Some are self-contained and about observation or logic. But others are long-form riddles where you might find a hint in a secret area and then come across the thing it was hinting at hours later. Some you might never solve, but optional puzzles often just give access to better loot.
Combat is still a dance on the grid, but this game has more enemies that use the grid in interesting ways. For example there's a frog that hand hops into the air and then lands on a random space nearby. The non-dungeon environments feel strange at first, but eventually add some nice variety. There's a dozen distinct areas (forest, swamp, desert, graveyard, beach, etc.) and most have some unique enemies.
The story is extremely thin and comes in the form of notes you find scattered around the island. There's no NPCs or dialog. It becomes an epic quest, but it's really about exploring every inch and finding all the gems to unlock the final temple. Along the way you might even find the best pants. Great game!

Even bigger RNG fest than Curvestone because you have 75 cards in decks (with up to 4 copies of the same card), so your draws are VERY inconsistent.
More often than not you are left with either excess sigils (i.e. lands from MtG) or creatures/weapons/spells you can't play because you didn't draw sigils to do that.
Because of the two reasons above most of the people play aggro decks where many of the cards cost 3 or less. Imagine a game where everyone is playing small creatures and hits face... pretty sad.
Another bad thing about this game is that there are no comebacks at all: if one of the players is winning, he's winning by a lot.
Granted, the developers are trying to fix this by changing the redraw mechanics (didn't help because you can't redraw a single card, you either keep your whole hand or discard all of the cards) and by introducing weekly quests when you have to win with a predefined deck that is not aggro. But again, the outcome of the matches is so dependent on what you draw, it's not fun even to win as you know your skill has little to do with that. And losing to ideal top decks made by your opponent is even more frustrating than in Curvestone.
There were games I couldn't play anything by turn 6 because i got a bad hand, and after redrawing still got only 6+ cost cards and sigils. And playing against aggro decks that means you are dead.
On a good side, there's also a mode (similar to HS's arena) where you make a deck from random cards. And this mode is actually much better than ranking because you have only 30 cards in the deck so your draws are much more consistent. And you get to keep all the cards you get in the draft! Alas, this leads to another problem: most of the cards in the draft are common, so you can't possibly explore all the mechanics the game has to offer.
***
Everything else in the game (art and visuals, sound, single player campaign, card design) is really well done, but inconsistent draws and aggro decks ruin all the fun.
P.S. On top of RNG draws, this game has some really counter intuitive interactions. For instance, when you attack and the opponent blocks your creatures with his creatures, you can cast fast spells. So, when you kill one of the blockers with a fast spell (so your blocked creature can attack face), your creature simply doesn't attack at all but becomes exhausted (meaning it also can't block enemy creatures this turn)!
Another weird interaction is when the opponent blocks your non-flying creature with his non-flying creature and you give your creature "fly this turn" via fast spell, his creature is still able to block your creature even though non-flying creatures can't block flying ones.
What's the point of fast spells if you can't surprise your opponent or bait him into blocking/attacking and then ruin his strategy with a spell?

I'm sure everything I'm about to say about this game has probably been said before, but I'mma put my two cents in anyway.
Cook, Serve, Delicious is ostensibly a restaurant management game. In reality, it's something more like a rhythm game, especially when you get to the harder stages. You're put in charge of preparing and serving every dish and doing every chore and all of this is done by hotkeys (or controller buttons) - but watch out, 'cuz new tasks are constantly coming in and it's up to you to juggle them before the customers get impatient and leave. The better you do, the more popular your restaurant becomes and the more people come to eat there, which of course means more for you to do.
The one thing this game does well - very well, possibly better than any other game I've played - is inducing a flow state, which is to say once you get into the rhythm of handling tasks you'll be tapping away at keys like a madman and become completely oblivious to the world around you. There's no time to think, so don't: just learn the recipes off by heart and then let your instincts take over. I mean, just look at me: I play on Extreme Difficulty just because the normal difficulty is too damn slow and boring. I NEED THE RUSH. GIVE IT TO ME.
If you haven't already bought this game, please do: they're bringing out a CSD2 soon and I want it to be as fabulously spectacular as possible. Besides, don't *you* want to become so good at this game that your hands fly across the keyboard like a pair of tap-dancing spiders? Of course you do.
